en: The *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Volume One. Chapter One: The Introduction.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
Homage to all Buddhas.
If for a hundred billion kalpas, through inconceivable time,
one goes to the place of exhaustion for the sake of all sentient beings,
solely for the sake of the world— homage to Great Compassion!
Because the Dharma is difficult to understand,
I bow my head in prostration to the profound and subtle Dharma that, through successive births,
brings forth the world; it tears asunder, destroys, and utterly exhausts the net of ignorance and afflictions.
If one possesses the practice of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation,
and diligently cultivates meritorious virtues— such a Sangha is a field of merit for all;
I now take refuge with a single mind, prostrating with my head at their feet.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem and expounded the meaning of the Vinaya,
so that the True Dharma may long abide and benefit and enrich all sentient beings—
by virtue of this merit, may all evils and afflictions be eliminated.
If one delights in upholding the precepts, by upholding the precepts one leaves behind all suffering.
It is said:

"In the beginning of the Vinaya Piṭaka, at that time, the Buddha was staying at Pārileyyaka; with Upāli as the foremost among those who recited it, he then assembled a great community of five hundred bhikṣus."

Why is this? When the Tathāgata first attained the Way, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park; finally, he preached the Dharma to deliver Subhadra. Having completed all that was to be done, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month, between the twin śāla trees in the Śāla Grove of King Malla at Kuśinagara, he entered parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Seven days later, Kāśyapa arrived from the kingdom of Śrāvastī with five hundred bhikṣus and proceeded toward Kuśinagara to pay his respects to the World-Honored One.
On the road, he encountered a Daoist practitioner, and Kāśyapa asked him:
"Have you seen my teacher?"
The practitioner replied:
"Your teacher, the śramaṇa Gautama, passed away seven days ago.
Since Gautama entered nirvāṇa, all humans and devas have made offerings to him; it is from them that I obtained these celestial māndārava flowers."
When Kāśyapa and the great bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa, they rolled on the ground, weeping and wailing until they fainted and collapsed.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Subhadra, an elder, who said:
"Stop, stop! Do not grieve."
"Why should you weep?
When the Great Śramaṇa was present, there were things pure and impure, and things that should be done and those that should not be done.
Now, according to our own wishes, we shall do what we wish to do and desist from what we do not wish to do."
At that time, Kāśyapa remained silent and recalled these words; he then reflected to himself:
"Before evil dharmas have arisen, it is fitting to compile the Dharma-treasury.
If the True Dharma remains in the world, it will benefit sentient beings."
Kāśyapa thought again:
"When the Buddha was in the world, he said to Ānanda:
'After my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma and Vinaya I have taught shall be your Great Teacher.'"
"Therefore, I shall now expound this Dharma.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"When the Tathāgata was in the world, he bestowed upon me his own kashaya robe and inner garment."
He further reflected:
"In the past, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
'When I enter the first dhyāna, Kāśyapa also enters dhyāna.'"
"The Tathāgata has praised me in this way; my noble benefit is complete and no different from that of a Buddha. This is the majestic power of the Tathāgata bestowing his grace upon me.

Just as a great king removes the armor from his own body and gives it to his son to protect his lineage, so too, O Tathāgata, you should know that after my parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa shall protect the True Dharma; for this reason, the Tathāgata has bestowed this robe upon me."
Kāśyapa immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"At one time, I heard the words of the mahallaka Subhadra:
'When the Great Śramaṇa was alive, he declared what was pure and what was impure, what should be done and what should not be done.'"
"Now this accords with our own wishes; we shall do what we intend to do, and cease from doing what we do not.
"Venerable Elders!
It is fitting that we bring forth the Dharma-piṭaka and the Vinaya-piṭaka."
The bhikṣus said to the Venerable Kāśyapa:
"Venerable One!
You should select the bhikṣus, O Venerable Kāśyapa!"

In the Buddha-dharma, one penetrates all nine gates; among all those in training—Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Bhikṣus whose craving is exhausted—there are not merely a hundred nor a thousand who, having mastered the Three Piṭakas, attain the four analytical knowledges, possess great supernormal powers, and have attained the three types of transcendent knowledge, as praised by the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had exhausted craving, minus one—namely, the venerable Mahākāśyapa!
The reason he selected five hundred and was short of one was for the sake of the Elder Ānanda.
"If there were no Ānanda, there would be no one to bring forth the Dharma;
the reason Ānanda was not permitted to enter [the assembly] was precisely because he was still on the stage of training.
"Venerable Kāśyapa, it was for the sake of severing all slander that Ānanda was not included."
The bhikṣus said:

"Although Ānanda is still at the stage of a learner, he has personally received the Sūtras and Geyas from the presence of the Buddha; he has rendered service to the Dharma, and moreover, he is an elder. He is of the Śākya clan, the son of the Tathāgata’s own paternal uncle, and he is free from the partiality of the three poisons."
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
You should include Ānanda to complete the number of five hundred; this is the intention of the noble assembly.
Then the venerable bhikṣus reflected thus:
"In what place shall the Dharma-piṭaka be compiled?

Only Rājagṛha is fully endowed with all necessary provisions; we should go to Rājagṛha to observe the three-month rains retreat and compile the Vinaya-piṭaka. Let no other bhikṣus dwell here during this retreat."
"Why is this? It is because I fear that other bhikṣus might not comply; therefore, he has been expelled.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation), as explained in detail in the *Saṃghabhedavastu*.

"Then, seven days after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there was a great assembly; for another seven days, they made offerings to the śarīra. After these two weeks had passed, with one month and a half of the summer retreat remaining, Kāśyapa knew that the period of *varṣā* was drawing near."
Kāśyapa said to the elders, "The time for our departure has come; let us go to Rājagṛha.
Then the Venerable Kāśyapa, leading two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, set out along one path.
The Venerable Ānanda, taking the Tathāgata’s saṃghāṭī robe, was followed by two hundred and fifty bhikṣus;

surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, he proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī to reach the former dwelling place of the Tathāgata. The Venerable Ānanda, taking the Tathāgata’s saṃghāṭī robe, was surrounded by the bhikṣu-saṃgha as they went to the city of Śrāvastī, arriving at the former residence of the Tathāgata.
When the people of Śrāvastī saw Ānanda, they were filled with anguish and wept bitterly, asking him:
"Where is the Tathāgata now that you have come alone?"
The people wailed and wept, as if at the time of the Tathāgata’s initial parinirvāṇa.

The Venerable Ānanda taught the people with the Dharma of impermanence; having finished teaching them, he entered the Jeta Grove, opened the Buddha’s chamber, took out the Buddha’s bed and seat, wiped them clean outside, and then went back inside to sweep and sprinkle the room.

Having swept and sprinkled the area, he took the old flowers used for offerings from within the room and cast them outside; then, taking the beds and seats, he restored them to their original positions.
The Venerable Ānanda made various kinds of offerings, no different from when the Buddha was still present.

Thereupon, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda sat leaning for a long time until his four elements became heavy and weary. Desiring to treat himself, he consumed milk for three days; having taken it for the sake of relief, he remained seated in the monastery.
At that time, a Śvapāka Brahmin came to invite Ānanda, to whom Ānanda replied:
"Today I have taken medicine and cannot comply with your request; I shall attend tomorrow."
On the appointed day, he took an elder bhikṣu and went to the house of Śūbhana.
Śūbhana then questioned him on the meaning of the sūtras; for this reason, it is called the *Śūbhana-sūtra* within the tenth chapter of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Thereupon, Ānanda, having performed various acts of maintenance and protection within the Jeta Grove, desired to enter the rains retreat and head toward Rājagṛha.
"Venerable Kāśyapa, together with Anuruddha and the entire assembly of bhikṣus, has arrived at Rājagṛha."

At that time, he saw the eighteen great monasteries all collapsing at once; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the various bhikṣus had abandoned their clothes, bamboo racks, and other belongings, leaving them scattered and strewn about, which is why they lay in such disorder.
These five hundred virtuous bhikṣus, in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, shall maintain and protect the dwellings.
If they do not maintain them, the non-Buddhists will say:
"While the Śramaṇa Gautama was in the world, he repaired and maintained the dwellings; now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, they have been abandoned and left behind."
"In order to quell this reproach and suspicion, it is appropriate that we attend to these matters.
Kāśyapa said, "When the Buddha was in the world, he praised the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat); first, one should attend to the repair and protection of the dwellings."
Having made this plan, he went to King Ajātaśatru and requested what he needed.
When the king saw the bhikṣu, he prostrated with his head at the bhikṣu’s feet and asked:
"Venerable sir, what is it that you require?"
Kāśyapa replied, “The eighteen great monasteries have fallen into ruin and decay; we now wish to repair and protect them, so may Your Majesty take note of this.
The King replied:
"Excellent! he replied, and immediately provided laborers.
During the first month of summer, Kāśyapa and his companions renovated the monastery; having finished the repairs within the temple, they went again to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"The temples we have repaired and protected are now all complete; we shall now set forth the Dharma-piṭaka and the Vinaya-piṭaka.
The King replied, "Excellent!"
"May your wishes be fulfilled.
The King spoke again, saying:
"I shall now turn the Wheel of Royal Authority; you, Great Virtuous Ones, should expound the Unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
The king addressed the assembly of monks, saying:
"I now place myself entirely at the disposal of the Venerable Ones.
The monks replied:
"First, establish the lecture hall.
The King asked,
"Where shall it be built?"
He replied, "It may be constructed by the door of the meditation hall on the slopes of Mount Pāṇḍava; this place is secluded and tranquil.
The King answered:
"Excellent!

Then, by the sovereign power of King Ajātaśatru, which was like that of Viśvakarman in the second heaven of the Trāyastriṃśa, the structure was established in an instant; the beams, rafters, pillars, walls, and stairways were all completed, adorned with various exquisite carvings and engravings.

Within the lecture hall, they adorned it with rare and exquisite jewels; various flowers were suspended and arranged in profusion, and the ground below was likewise decorated. It was of such diverse and wondrous beauty that it was no different from the palaces of the Brahma heavens. Five hundred woolen rugs, cushions, and mats were spread upon the beds, and all sat facing north.
Furthermore, the high seat was adorned with various jewels; from among these, the most exquisite one was selected and prepared for the Dharma-preaching seat, facing east.
The assembly of monks said to Ānanda, "Tomorrow the assembly shall gather to recite the Vinaya Piṭaka. Since you have not yet attained the path of a Srotāpanna, how can you enter?"
"Do not be indolent.
Thereupon Ānanda reflected to himself:
"Tomorrow the assembly of noble ones will gather to compile the Dharma; how shall I, being at the stage of a beginner, enter into their midst?"
Ānanda, having observed the body from the first watch of the night until the middle watch had passed, had not yet attained anything.
Ānanda reflected:
"In the past, the World-Honored One spoke these words:"
"You have already cultivated merit; if you enter meditative concentration, you will quickly attain Arhatship.
The Buddha’s words are not false, yet they must be due to my own mind being overly diligent; I shall now weigh this and adopt a moderate course.

Thereupon, Ānanda descended from his place of walking meditation to the place for washing his feet; having washed his feet, he entered his room and sat back upon his bed. Desiring a brief rest, he leaned his body down intending to lie down; while his feet had already left the ground but before his head had reached the pillow, in that very interval, he attained arhatship.
"If anyone asks who it was that attained the Way within the Buddha-dharma while apart from walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, it was Ānanda.

Then, on the second day of the middle month—the seventeenth day of the sixth month—after the midday meal had concluded, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa prepared his robes and bowl and entered the Dharma Hall.
The venerable Ānanda, wishing to personally realize what he had attained so that the great assembly might know it, did not enter with the community of monks.
After the community of monks had entered and sat down in order, they left a seat vacant for Ānanda.
The junior monks prostrated themselves toward the seniors, and then, turning to an empty space, they asked:
"For whom was this place reserved?
They replied:
"Imitating Ānanda," he asked again,
"Where is Ānanda now?"
Because Ānanda knew the minds of the assembly and manifested his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he vanished from this place and reappeared seated where he had been.
Once the monks were all seated, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the elders:
"Shall we first recite the Dharma-piṭaka?"
"The Vinaya Piṭaka?
The bhikṣus replied,
"Venerable sir!"
The Vinaya Piṭaka is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, the Buddha-dharma also remains. Therefore, we shall first bring forth the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Who shall serve as the Dharma-preacher?
The Elder Upāli asked the assembly:
"Is it not permissible for Ānanda to serve as a Dharma-preacher?
He replied:
"You must not act as a Dharma teacher. Why is this?
During the Buddha's lifetime, he constantly praised me, saying: 'Among my śrāvaka disciples, Upāli is the foremost in upholding the Vinaya.'"
The assembly said,
"Now it is precisely appropriate to question Upāli regarding the production of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa performed the formal motion (jñapti-karman) and questioned Upāli:
"Venerable Sangha, listen. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent.
I shall question Upāli regarding the Vinaya-dharma.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
Upāli performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
I shall now answer the Venerable Kāśyapa regarding the Vinaya rules."
"Thus it is declared.
Having thus performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), Upāli adjusted his robes, prostrated with his head at the feet of the venerable bhikṣu, and paid him homage.
Having paid homage, he ascended the high seat and sat down, taking up a fan adorned with ivory.
Once Kāśyapa had resumed his seat, he asked the Elder Upāli:
"Where was the first *pārājika* taught?"
"By whom was it originated?
He replied:
"The schism at Vaiśālī was originated by Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka."
He asked, "What offense has been committed?
He replied:
"An offense of impurity has been committed.

Kāśyapa questioned Upāli regarding the offense, its causes and conditions, the person involved, the formal enactment of the precept, and whether it was an offense according to that enacted precept; he questioned him both concerning what was an offense and what was not.

Just as with the first *pārājika*, so too for the second, third, and fourth; Mahākāśyapa asked about the origins of these causes and conditions, and Upāli answered each question exhaustively. Therefore, this is called the Chapter on the Four *Pārājikas*.

Furthermore, having asked concerning the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, then asked concerning the two *aniyata* rules, next asked concerning the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, next asked concerning the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, next asked concerning the four *prātideśanīya* rules, next asked concerning the seventy-five *śaikṣa* rules, and finally asked concerning the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas—in this manner, the Great Prātimokṣa was completed.
"Next, the eight *pārājika* rules for bhikṣuṇīs are questioned; this is called the *Pārājika-varga*.

Furthermore, the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are questioned; next, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are questioned; next, the sixty-six *pāyattika* rules are questioned; next, the eight *pratideśanīya* rules are questioned; next, the seventy-five *śaikṣa* rules are questioned; and finally, the seven methods for settling disputes are questioned. In this manner, the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa has been completed."

"Next, he asked about the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Sanskrit), which in the Han language means 'Miscellaneous Matters'; next, he asked about the *Pārivāsika* (Sanskrit), which in the Han language refers to the 'Three Expulsions and Four Karmas. In this manner, the Vinaya Piṭaka was completed."
"Venerable Kāśyapa questioned Upāli on all matters, and Upāli having answered them, it is therefore said that the five hundred arhats have completed the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka."
Thereupon, the Elder Upāli set down his fan, descended from the high seat, paid homage to the venerable bhikṣus, and having paid homage, returned once more to his original seat.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"The compilation of the Vinaya is finished.
Now we shall inquire concerning the Dharma-piṭaka."
"Who shall be the Dharma Master to bring forth the treasury of the Dharma?
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Elder Ānanda."
Thereupon, the Venerable Kāśyapa performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Sangha, listen. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent.
I shall question the Elder Ānanda regarding the Dharma-piṭaka."
"Thus it is announced.
Ānanda then performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
"I now answer the Venerable Kāśyapa regarding the Dharma-treasury;
thus I speak.

Thereupon Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, paid homage to the Sangha of Venerable Elders, and immediately ascended the high throne. Having ascended the high throne, he took in his hand a fan adorned with ivory.
The Venerable Kāśyapa asked Ānanda:
"In which part of the Dharma-piṭaka is the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* taught?
Ānanda replied:
"It was spoken in the house of King Āmrapālī, between the two kingdoms of Rājagṛha and Nālandā.
"On account of whom did it arise?
"It arose on account of the brahmin Ganda, who was practicing the night-vow (rātriparyāya) of compassion; it arose because of these two persons."
The Venerable Kāśyapa asked Ānanda about the causal origins and introductory narrative of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.
He then asked:
"In which location is the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* taught?"
Ānanda replied, "It was spoken in the Jīva’s Grove at Rājagṛha.
[The Buddha asked: "To whom was it spoken?"
"For King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, and others.
Such was the introductory narrative (*nidāna*) of the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*; by means of this expedient, he questioned [the Buddha] regarding the five classes of sūtras.
"What are the five divisions? He replied:
"The *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Kṣudraka Āgama*, and the *Khuddakapāṭha*."
Question: "What is meant by the *Kṣudraka Āgama*? Answer:
"Except for the four Āgamas, all other teachings of the Buddha are collectively called the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Within the four Āgamas, all miscellaneous sūtras were produced by Ānanda, with the sole exception of the Vinaya Piṭaka."

The Buddha’s teaching is of a single flavor, yet its application is distinguished as twofold; in its initial, middle, and final expositions, its flavor is said to be threefold. The Three Piṭakas are likewise so: the Piṭaka of Precepts, the Piṭaka of Concentration, and the Piṭaka of Wisdom. If categorized by their divisions, they comprise the five classes of Sūtras.
"If one were to distinguish them individually, there would be nine divisions of sūtras; when thus gathered together, they constitute the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma.
He asked: "Why is it called 'one flavor'?"

“World-Honored One, from the time you attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* until the time of your parinirvāṇa, during that intervening period of forty-five years, you have acted as one flavor for the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; and this single nature of liberation is likewise one flavor.”
“What are these two? “The Dharma-piṭaka and the Vinaya-piṭaka.
“Why are they taught in terms of the beginning, middle, and end?”
“The Buddha’s teaching is presented in three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Thus it is said in verse:
‘The cycle of rebirth does not consist of a single life; One runs through it without ever finding satisfaction.’”
Constantly seeking a dwelling to live in, one undergoes suffering life after life;
now that I have seen your house, I shall no longer build another.
All the ribs of my spine are broken and shall not grow again.
"The mind has already departed from afflictions; with craving exhausted, one reaches Nirvana.

Furthermore, there was a Dharma Master who explained this Udāna verse: "This was the first teaching spoken by the Tathāgata; on the third day after the moon’s appearance, he attained all-encompassing wisdom and joyfully contemplated the causes and conditions."
He spoke this verse:
"The accomplishment of the arising of dharmas at their proper time is taught in the Khaṇḍaka.
When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he instructed the bhikṣus:
“‘Be careful not to be indolent within my Dharma’—this is the final teaching;
that which lies between these two is called the intermediate teaching. He asked:
"What are the three baskets? He replied:
"The Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sūtra Piṭaka, and the Abhidharma Piṭaka—these are called the three baskets."
He asked: "What is called the Vinaya Piṭaka? [The Buddha replied:
"The two Prātimokṣas, the twenty-three Khandhakas, and the Parivāra—this is named the Vinaya Piṭaka."
Question: "What is meant by the Sūtra-piṭaka? Answer:
"Beginning with the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, forty-four sūtras are all included in the *Dīrgha Āgama*;
beginning with the *Mūlapariyāya*, two hundred and fifty-two sūtras are all included in the *Madhyama Āgama*;
and beginning with the *Udāna-avadāna*, seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two sūtras are all included in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*."

Beginning with the *Cchandogarbha-sūtra*, nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven sūtras are all included within the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*, as well as the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Khuddaka-pāṭha*, the *Itivuttaka*, the *Nipāta*, the *Vimāna-vatthu*, the *Petavatthu*, the *Theragāthā* and *Therīgāthā*, the *Jātaka*, the *Apadāna*, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, and the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
"If one uses the Piṭaka, it is divided into fourteen sections, all of which are included within the *Kṣudraka*; this is what is called the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.
He asked: "What is meant by the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*?"
He replied:
“The Dharma-saṃgha, the Vibhaṅga, the Dhātukathā, the Yamaka, and the Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa—these constitute the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.”
Question: "What is the meaning of *vinaya*?
He answered with a verse:
"The methods for subduing are not of a single kind;
one who knows the meaning of the Vinaya and tames the karma of body and speech—such a person is said to know the meaning of the Vinaya. He asked:
"What is meant by the various five categories of the Prātimokṣa?

"With the *pārājika* as the first, there are the offenses of the five categories and seven groups; these are called the various 'mothers of the precepts. They serve to establish firm conduct and broad skillful means, following the formulations based on unwholesome actions of body and speech. Since these involve the karma of body and speech, they are therefore called *vinaya*."
Question: "What is meant by Sūtra?
He replied with a verse:
"Elucidating manifold meanings, well-spoken like a towering peak,
woven like warp and woof, gushing like a spring, threaded like a line through a mark—
this is called Sūtra, the most profound and subtle meaning."
Question: "What is meant by 'initiating the meaning'? Answer:
"The meaning that arises from oneself can bring forth the meaning for others.
He asked: "What is meant by 'well-spoken words'?"
He replied:
"First observe the person's mind, and only then speak well. He asked:
"What is meant by 'standing out'?
The answer is:
It is like rice and grain standing out and forming ears."
Question: "What are meant by 'longitudinal' and 'latitudinal'? Answer:
"It is woven with silk thread.
He asked: "What is meant by 'gushing spring'?"
He replied:
"It is like a spring from which many draw water, yet it is never exhausted. He asked:
"What is meant by 'the plumb line'?
He replied:
"It is like a straight line that can remove crooked wood."
He asked, "What is meant by 'thread'?
He replied:
"Just as scattered flowers, when strung together with a thread, cannot be blown apart by the wind;
so too is the sūtra: it strings together the characteristics of all dharmas so that they do not disperse."
Question: "What is meant by Abhidharma?
He answered in verse:
"One who understands the phenomena of mind and consciousness, praises the teaching of cutting off [defilements], and speaks of the extension of the Dharma—for this reason it is called Abhidhamma.
This is the verse of the Abhidhamma; "mind," "consciousness," "praise," "cutting off," and "extension"—these constitute the meaning of Abhidhamma.
Question: "What is meant by 'mind'? Answer:
The Sūtra passage states: "Some say, 'What is the most intense state of mind?
This is the meaning of Abhidharma.
"What is meant by consciousness?"
He replied:
"The sūtra passage 'abhi' day and night—this is the meaning of the term *abhi-vidyā*.
What is meant by 'praise' (*praśaṃsā*)?"
He replied:
“King Abhiya; ‘Abhi’ is the meaning of praise. [The other asked:
“What is meant by ‘cutting off’?”
He replied:
"Pāda-pāda-avī; this 'avī' has the meaning of cutting off.
[The other asked: "What is meant by 'long'?"
He replied:
“Abhiyukta means ‘long’ in the Han language; this is the meaning of *abhi* as ‘long.
Furthermore, it is said:”
"Born in the Form Realm, one pervasively contemplates one direction with a mind of loving-kindness; this is the meaning of *vihāra*.
As for 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*), it refers to consciousness of forms, sounds, and so forth, up to tactile objects; this is the meaning of consciousness."
"Praising" refers to the qualities of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the unsurpassed worldly qualities; this is the meaning of "praising.
"Cutting off" refers to the attainment of training through contact with the Dharma; this is the meaning of "cutting off."
"Elder, the Great Dharma is immeasurable; the Dharma that is *anuttara* (unsurpassed) is the meaning of 'great' (*āyuṣmat*).
This meaning should be understood.
Furthermore, it is said:"
"‘Dharma’ means the Dharma.
"What is meant by ‘pitaka’ (storehouse)?
He answered in verse:
“The meaning and flavor of the Piṭaka, for those who are vessels of learning through its meaning—I shall now speak of them as one. You yourself shall know the meaning of the Piṭaka;
this is the meaning of the Piṭaka.”
Question: "What is meant by 'storehouse'? Answer:
“‘Treasury’ (garbha) refers to study; this is the treasury of the Dharma.
Furthermore, a sūtra passage says: ‘It is as if a person were to come carrying a hoe and an axe.
This conveys the meaning of a vessel.”
Now that the three piṭakas have been explained in general, one should understand these two meanings.
The Vinaya Piṭaka has already been briefly explained;
the Abhidharma Piṭaka is also called a "vessel of meaning," and the Sūtra Piṭaka is likewise so described.
It is further said:
"The Abhidharma is the Piṭaka.
This has thus been understood.

Furthermore, within the Tripitaka, various causes and conditions are used to point toward the Buddha-dharma; through linguistic analysis, one follows what is clung to lightly, learning to eliminate profound characteristics and learning to break down and then reunite that which is separated. Thus, as the sequential phrases reach their conclusion, the meaning emerges of itself.
Now, these three baskets (tripiṭaka) are manifested in succession.
The Abhidharma states:

"Abhi" has the meanings of meaning (*artha*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), cutting off (*chedana*), extensive transcendence (*vyutkrānta-vistara*), greatness (*mahat*), and unsurpassedness (*anuttara*)."
What is meant by "mind" (manas)?
It is that which recollects and maintains.
What is meant by "consciousness" (vijñāna)? It is that which discriminates.
"Praised" means that one is constantly praised by the sages.
"Cutting off" refers to the analysis of verses.
"Transcending" means surpassing other dharmas.
"Vast" means it is the most vast among all phenomena.
"Great" means it is the greatest among all phenomena.
"Unsurpassed" means that among all phenomena, nothing can surpass it.
*Tan* signifies the meaning of uplifting (*uddharaṇa*), the meaning of supporting (*dhāraṇa*), and the meaning of protecting (*rakṣaṇa*).
What is meant by "uplifting"?
To "uplift" means to raise sentient beings and establish them upon the wholesome paths.
"Upholding" means to sustain sentient beings so that they do not enter the three evil realms.
"Protecting" means to shield sentient beings so that they may attain various forms of happiness.
"Treasury" (garbha) means a vessel.
What is meant by a vessel?
A vessel is that which is capable of gathering together manifold meanings.
Question: "Are the Piṭaka and the Abhidharma the same or different? Answer:
"Exactly so.
He asked again:
"If they are the same, then it would suffice simply to say 'Abhidharma'; why is it necessary to further call it a 'Piṭaka'?"
He replied:

"The Sage established the teachings so that the words and phrases would be complete; thus, he further established the 'Treasury' (piṭaka) characters, and the meaning of the Three Treasuries (Tripiṭaka) is likewise."
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of indication, for instruction, for analysis, for binding, for relinquishment, for the characteristic of profundity, and for separation and conjunction.

If a bhikṣu, wherever he goes, manifests all such meanings as these, this constitutes the Tripiṭaka; thus, in this sequence, the true meaning is manifested through its majestic power, according to transgressions, according to analogies, according to the teachings, and according to the distinctions of name-and-form within the entanglements of concealed views.

If a person practices in reliance upon the Vinaya, they will attain meditative concentration; having attained concentration, they will possess the three types of supernormal knowledge. This shows that the precepts are the foundation of practice; because of samādhi, one then possesses the six supernormal powers.
If a person studies the Abhidharma, they can generate true wisdom; once true wisdom has been generated, they will possess the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
If a person conforms to the discourse of the Vinaya, they will attain worldly happiness.
What is meant by worldly pleasure?

It is when a person of pure precepts is praised as virtuous by humans and devas, and constantly receives the four kinds of worldly offerings; this is worldly pleasure, excluding the pleasure of sensual desire.

As stated in the sūtras and as taught by the Buddha, I have already understood that it is not appropriate to remain at home; rather, one should leave the household life to study the Way and thereby attain the fruits of the Way.
The attainment of these fruits of the Way consists of the powers of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Those who follow after evil do so entirely due to a lack of wisdom; because they lack wisdom, they misunderstand the Buddha’s teachings; because they misunderstand them, they slander the Tathāgata; by committing various evil deeds, they destroy their own bodies, and from these causes and conditions, they extensively give rise to false views.

Those who study the Abhidharma with biased views grasp the mind too tightly; consequently, the mind gives rise to distractions regarding what should not be contemplated. As stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four things that should not be contemplated, yet if one contemplates them, the mind will become deranged."
The Dharma Master said:
"Having thus explained in sequence the breaking of the precepts, distorted views, the distracted mind, and what is wholesome and unwholesome,
he spoke these verses:"
"Whether one is endowed with them or not, they are obtained according to one's practice;
a bhikṣu who delights in learning should cherish and revere this Dharma.
Thus, one should know that the meaning of this treasury encompasses all the words of the Buddha.
"What is meant by 'Āgama'?
The Dharma Master replied:
"There are five Āgamas."
What are the five? First, the *Dīrgha Āgama*; second, the *Madhyama Āgama*; third, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; fourth, the *Aṅguttara Āgama*; and fifth, the *Kṣudraka Āgama*.
Question: "What is meant by the *Dīrgha Āgama*? Answer:
"Among the three sections, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the first; forty-four sūtras are all contained within these three sections, and this is called the *Dīrgha Āgama*."
The Dharma Master asked:
"Why is it called 'long'? [He replied:
"Because it involves the greatest number of people in the legal assembly, it is called 'long'."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'Āgama'?
He replied:
The meaning of "receptacle" and "accumulation" is called *āgama*.
As stated in the *Sūtra*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Within the three realms, I do not see a single *āgama* that is like the *āgama* of animals—a place where sentient beings are purely gathered together."
For this reason, it should also be understood that the *Madhyama Āgama* is so named because it is neither long nor short.
Among its fifteen sections (*varga*), beginning with the *Mūla-śikṣā-sūtra*, there are one hundred and fifty-two sūtras; these are called the *Madhyama Āgama*.

“When the Dharma of the Sunrise in the Seventh Month was completed, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had successfully accomplished the Dharma of the Ten Powers, the great earth rejoiced like a person and exclaimed:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”

Thereupon, the earth reached down to the Yellow Springs and shook in six ways, and various other wondrous and marvelous signs appeared; this was the name of the first assembly of the five hundred great Arhats.
And he spoke these verses:
"Five hundred Arhats in this world have emerged from this Dharma;
therefore it is named 'The Emergence of the Five Hundred,' as all the worthy ones know together."
At that time, the great assembly spoke, and the Venerable Kāśyapa asked Upāli:
"Where was the *pārājika* offense established?
He also asked about the place of its transgression, the causal conditions, and the person involved."
"Does the Venerable One know the answer to this question? He replied:
"The precepts were established based on specific persons at specific times; therefore, I shall now explain the sequence of all these established precepts."
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Pileyyaka.
A question was asked:
"When did he speak [this]?"
Answer: "It was spoken after assembling a great assembly of five hundred people, and such various meanings had thus emerged. He asked:
"Why did Upāli speak thus?
He replied:
"Because the Venerable Kāśyapa had already asked about this core of the precepts."
Who currently upholds it?
Where does the upholder dwell?
I shall now explain the root.
Now the meaning of the chapters and verses is explained.
At that time, the Buddha was dwelling at Pāṭaliputra; thus it is said at the beginning of this fundamental Vinaya Piṭaka.

The Elder Upāli held [the teaching] before the Buddha. While the Buddha had not yet entered parinirvāṇa, countless tens of millions of arhats possessing the six supernormal powers received it from Upāli.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, with the Venerable Mahākāśyapa at their head, the assembly of those of great compassion gathered on Jambudvīpa.
Who was able to uphold [the teachings]? With Upāli at their head, the Vinaya masters upheld them in succession, continuing down to the third great assembly where the Venerables upheld them.
Now, the names of these teachers are set forth in order: Upāli, Hastaka, Sunakṣatra, Śāṇavāsa, and Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya.

Five men attained victory over the afflictions (*kleśa*), and in succession they maintained the Vinaya within Jambudvīpa without interruption; even down to the third generation of all the Vinaya masters, they all descended from Upāli—this constitutes the continuous lineage of Upāli.
Why is this? Upāli heard it from the Golden Mouth [the Buddha], gathered it within his heart, and then opened it up to bestow upon others.
Once people came to know it, there were countless persons in training—Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Anāgāmins—and one thousand bhikṣus whose craving was exhausted.

The great elephant Kuśī was a disciple of Upāli; he heard everything from Upāli’s own mouth and personally realized the most profound and ultimate principles. Among those who first received his teachings, they were beyond counting, including one thousand bhikṣus whose craving had been exhausted.

Sunāka was a disciple of the great elephant Kūṭadanta. Having received the Vinaya from his teacher’s own mouth, Sunāka mastered its recitation and came to know the Vinaya by nature; there were countless students who first received it from him, including one thousand bhikṣus whose craving had been extinguished.

Siggava was a disciple of Sona Kuṭikaṇṇa; having received the Vinaya from his teacher’s own mouth, he possessed the most excellent nature among a thousand arhats in his self-knowledge of the Vinaya. The number of trainees who first received instruction under him is incalculable, and the bhikṣus whose craving was exhausted cannot be measured by hundreds or thousands.

At that time, countless bhikṣus gathered on Jambudvīpa. By the supernormal power of Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya, this third assembly intended to manifest such a Vinaya-piṭaka; it should be understood that the various Dharma masters throughout Jambudvīpa, in succession, up to the third assembly, upheld it.
Question: "What is meant by the third great assembly? Answer:
"This is the sequence of time when [the teaching] has already emerged; it is for the purpose of employing wisdom regarding the radiant and sublime Dharma.
Then he spoke this praise:
"His lifespan shall abide in the world For five hundred years of luminous wisdom."
Among the five hundred great virtuous ones, Kāśyapa was the foremost;
like a lamp when its oil is exhausted, they entered nirvāṇa without attachment.
Chapter Two: The Vatsiputriyas. Regarding the Compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka: "Thereupon, these noble sages departed one after another, day and night."
One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One, ten unrighteous practices arose among the Vajjiputtaka bhikkhus in Vaiśālī.
What are these ten?

First, purification by salt; second, purification by two fingers; third, purification regarding the interval between villages; fourth, purification regarding the dwelling place; fifth, purification according to one's will; sixth, purification through long residence; seventh, purification through the arising of harmony; eighth, purification by water; ninth, purification regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) that does not require additional thread; tenth, purification regarding gold and silver.
These are the ten illegal acts.
These ten illegal acts were manifested at Vaiśālī; among the Vṛjiputrakas, there was one named Aśoka, son of Sunāga, who at that time was king and sided with the Vṛjiputrakas and others.

At that time, the Elder Yasujuka, son of the Kātyāyanas, was wandering through Vaiśālī. Having heard that the Vaiśālī monks, the sons of the Vṛjis, were manifesting ten unrighteous practices within Vaiśālī, he thought:
"I ought not to remain in hiding while the Dharma of the One of Ten Powers is being destroyed; by what means might I extinguish these evil practices?"
He then went to Vaiśālī.
Upon his arrival, at that time the Elder Yaśas Kauṇḍinya was residing in the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāraśālā forest in Vaiśālī.
At that time, when the bhikṣu Vatsīputra was reciting the precepts, he took a bowl filled with water and placed it among the community of bhikṣus.
Then, various upāsakas from Vaiśālī arrived, and the bhikṣu Vatsīputra spoke thus to the upāsakas:
"You should give money to the Saṃgha; give half a coin or one coin as you please, so that the Saṃgha may obtain robes."
"All should be spoken; this is the meaning of the compilation of the Vinaya.
That the seven hundred bhikṣus were neither fewer nor more is called 'the compilation of the Vinaya by the seven hundred bhikṣus.'"
Within that assembled multitude, twenty thousand bhikṣus gathered.
The Elder Yaśas, the bhikṣu, initiated this matter. Among the Vajjiputta bhikṣu community, the Elder Revata questioned Sabbakāmī, and the bhikṣu Sabbakāmī replied:
"In the Vinaya Piṭaka, ten unrighteous acts are to be eliminated, as well as the methods for extinguishing disputes."
"Venerable Sir!

We should now produce the Dharma and the Vinaya by selecting those who have mastered the Tripiṭaka. Once the Bhikṣus possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) have completed their selection, let the assembly gather at the Vāluka-ārāma in Vaiśālī, just as there was no difference from the first compilation of the Dharma-treasury by Kāśyapa."

Once all defilements within the Buddha-dharma have been washed away, there arise questions based on the Piṭaka, questions based on the Āgamas, questions based on the branches and leaves, and questions based on the collection of all dharmas; from these, all dharmas and the Vinaya-piṭaka emerge in their entirety.
This was the great assembly, which had gathered by the eighth day of the month; they spoke this verse in praise:
"Seven hundred among the world, This constitutes the seven hundred;
Just as previously explained, You yourselves should know it."

At that time, Sarvakāmin, Svāgata, Revata, Kṣemaka, Upasena, and Vanaśrava—these were disciples of the Venerable Ānanda; and Sumaṅgala and Vāsagāmin—these two were disciples of Anuruddha. Having already seen the Buddha, they spoke these verses:
“The second auspicious assembly has gathered; The Great Dharma has emerged in its entirety.
Having reached the place where the Dharma is honored, What was to be done has been fully accomplished.”
“The monk whose craving is exhausted—this is called the second assembly.
Chapter 3: King Aśoka. Third Assembly of the Dharma-Treasury. “Venerable sirs, you should reflect thus:
‘In future ages, will such defilements arise regarding our Teacher’s Dharma?’”

The Venerable One then foresaw that in a future age, the defilements of non-Dharma would arise; from this point forward, within one hundred and eighteen years, King Aśoka would be born in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Once born, he would bring the entire land of Jambudvīpa under his sway, and he would possess profound faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, making most magnificent offerings.

Thereupon, when the various non-Buddhist brahmins saw that King Aśoka had such faith in the Buddha-dharma, they entered the Buddha-dharma and became śramaṇas for the sake of seeking offerings; yet they continued to serve the non-Buddhists as before, using the teachings of the non-Buddhists to instruct and convert people.
Thus, the Dharma of the Buddha is extremely defiled by turbid impurities, and these impurities are about to come into being.
Thereupon, the great virtuous ones had this thought:
"Will we, along with those of future generations, behold these impurities?"
Each observed that their own lifespans were insufficient, and they further thought:
"Who will propagate [this teaching] in the future?
The venerable ones surveyed all the people and throughout the desire realm, yet not a single person was found.
Furthermore, they observed that among the Brahmā devas there was one being of short lifespan who had previously contemplated the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The great virtuous ones thought to themselves:

"We should go and request this Brahmā deva to descend to the world and take conception in the womb of the Brahmin Maudgalyāyana. Thereafter, we shall instruct him so that he leaves the household life; once he has left the household life and attained unimpeded mastery over all Buddha-dharmas and the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), he will defeat the non-Buddhists, resolve all points of dispute, and uphold the Buddha-dharma."
"Then those Great Virtuous Ones went to the Brahma Heaven. The name of the Brahma there was Śikhin.
When the Great Virtuous Ones arrived, they said to Śikhin:

'One hundred years from now, during eighteen years, great defilements will arise within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. We have surveyed all the worlds and the realm of desire, and we see not a single person capable of protecting the Buddha-Dharma, even down to the Brahma Heaven, where we see only you alone.'"
“Excellent, O virtuous one!
Since you have been born into this world, you should uphold and maintain the Dharma of the Ten Powers.

When the Great Virtuous Ones had spoken these words, Mahābrahmā Śikhin heard that defilements had arisen within the Buddha’s Dharma and that he should wash them away; having heard this, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, replying:
"Excellent! Having replied thus, you have made a vow with the Great Virtuous Ones; having completed what was to be done in the Brahma Heaven, descend from the Brahma realm.

At that time, there were two Great Virtuous Ones, Sāṇavāsi and Caṇḍavajji, who among the youth had mastered the Tripitaka, attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), and were Arhats whose taints were exhausted; yet these two were unable to settle the dispute.
The Venerable Ones said to the two elders:
"You two were unable to settle this dispute; therefore, the Saṃgha now inflicts a formal penalty upon you.

In the future, there will be a Brahmā named Tiṣya who shall take birth in the family of the Brahmin Maudgalyāyana. One of you two should go to welcome him and bring him forth to ordain him as a monk, while the other shall teach him the Buddha-dharma."
Thereupon, those great virtuous Arhats, each according to the length of their lifespan, entered parinirvāṇa and spoke these verses:
“The second assembly of seven hundred, In harmony, extinguished what was not the Dharma;
For the sake of future causes and conditions of the Dharma, They have ensured that it shall endure for a long time.”

Having exhausted craving, one attains mastery; Skillfully penetrating the three types of supernormal knowledge, One gains mastery through spiritual powers— Yet even such a one cannot escape impermanence.
I now speak these names, To be transmitted and circulated for the sake of the future.
"Thus, birth is impermanent; knowing that birth is difficult to obtain, if one wishes to attain the permanent, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor.
This was the second proclamation by the Saṃgha.
"Mahābrahmā Devendra has descended from the Brahma Heaven and taken birth in the womb of the Brahmin Maudgalyāyana.
Thereupon, Upagupta perceived that Devendra had already entered the Brahmin's household to receive conception.
Knowing that he had entered the womb, Upagupta went daily to his house to beg for alms for seven years. Why was this?
It was for the sake of fulfilling the conditions of dependent origination; thus, during those seven years, he could not obtain even a meal of rice, nor could he obtain water.
After seven years had passed, he went again to beg for food, and the members of that family replied:
"The meal is finished, Venerable Sir!
Please go to another house."
Vāgīśa thought to himself,
"Now that I have spoken with him, I shall return.
Thereupon, the brahmin returned from another place and saw Vāgīśa on the road.
"Hey, you renunciant!
Have you come from my house?
Did you receive anything?"
He replied, "I have.
The brahmin returned home and asked his family members:
"Does the bhikṣu go for alms? Is anything given to him?
The family members replied, "Nothing at all is given to him."
The brāhmaṇa said, "The bhikṣu speaks falsely; if he comes tomorrow, I shall interrogate him.
The next day, as he sat outside the gate, the Venerable Upagupta arrived. The brāhmaṇa asked:
"Venerable Sir!
Yesterday you said that you had obtained something through begging;
yet you certainly obtained nothing. Why do you speak falsely?"
"Is it not the law for a bhikṣu to obtain false speech?
The Venerable Upagupta replied:

"I went to your house for seven years and obtained nothing at all; only yesterday did I finally receive some words from a family member, and I said I had 'obtained' them because I was going to other houses."
The brahmin thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu speaks correctly, yet says that he has something attained.
How excellent!"
"This man is one who knows contentment; if he obtains food and drink, he should be greatly rejoiced.
The brāhmaṇa immediately set aside his own portion of food and drink to give to Upagupta, saying:
"From this day forward, take your meals here every day."
Thereupon, Upagupta went daily to fetch his food.
When the brahmin saw that Upagupta’s deportment was perfect, he felt great joy; having felt this joy, he invited him again, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"From this day forward, do not beg from other houses; come here regularly to eat.
Upagupta accepted the invitation in silence.
After eating every day, [the householder] gradually taught him the Buddha-dharma, and having taught it, he departed.
"At that time, the son of the brahmin was sixteen years of age and had already studied the three Vedas of the brahminical dharma.
Since his initial descent from the Brahma Heaven, the brahmin’s son had always cherished purity and cleanliness; his bedding and *pātrī* bowls were never shared with others."
If he wished to go to his teacher’s place, he would take his bed and mat, wrap them in clean white cloth, suspend them in the space between the rafters, and depart.
After he had gone, the Venerable Sāṇavāsī arrived and thought to himself:
"The time has now come!"
"He has been coming and going for many years, yet this son of a brahmin has never spoken with us.
By what skillful means can he be converted?
He then used his supernatural power to cause the beds and seats in the house to vanish from sight, so that only the śibikā carried by the son of the brahmin remained visible.

At that time, the brahmin saw Upagupta approaching; though he searched everywhere for a seat, he could find none, until he saw the *śibikā* (palanquin) his son had previously raised, which he then took and gave to Upagupta to sit upon.

When the Brahmin’s son returned, he saw Upagupta sitting upon his father’s couch; having seen this, anger arose in his heart, and he immediately asked his family members, "Who brought my father’s couch for the śramaṇa to sit upon?"
When the Venerable Gavāmpati had finished eating, the Brahmin’s son had his anger subsided.
The Venerable Gavāmpati said to the Brahmin’s son: "What do you know?"
The Brahmin’s son said: "Ho, Śramaṇa!
I know nothing; who else should know?"
The son of the brahmin asked Upagupta,
"Does the śramaṇa know the Vedic teachings?
Having asked this, he was certain that this śramaṇa would know them.

The Venerable Upagupta was thoroughly proficient in the three Vedas, as well as in Gandharva (which in the Han language means "names of all things"), Kṣapaṇa, Itihāsa, and grammar; he understood all their distinctions.
The Brahmin’s son was unable to penetrate the teachings that he doubted.
This was because his teacher did not understand them.
When the Brahmin’s son questioned Upagupta, he asked about all the difficult points, and Upagupta answered every question.
Upagupta said to the son of the brahmin, "You have already asked many questions;
I shall now ask you one thing in turn, and you should answer.
The son of the brahmin replied:
"Excellent, śramaṇa!
Shall I answer you by distinguishing between the two?
Thus, within his dual mind, Upagupta questioned the son of the brahmin.

"If the mind of a person arises and does not cease; if the mind of a person ceases and does not arise; if the mind of a person ceases and then ceases; or if the mind of a person arises and then arises?"
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son looked up toward the void and down upon the earth; not knowing what to do, he instead questioned the śramaṇa: "Ho, śramaṇa!"
"What does this mean? Upagupta replied,
"This is the Buddha-veda."
The son of the brahmin said,
"Venerable sir, may you grant it to me?
He replied:
"It is attained.
He asked again:
"How can it be attained?"
He replied, "If you renounce the household life, then you may attain it.
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son was filled with great joy; he went to his parents and said to them:
"This śramaṇa knows the Buddhist Vedas; I wish to study under him, yet he will not give me these white robes. Only after I have left the household life shall I obtain them."
After his parents had formed this thought, they said: "Excellent!
If you go forth and complete your study of the Vedas, you must return home quickly."
The Brahmin’s son thought to himself:
"Once I have finished learning the Buddhist Vedas from this śramaṇa, I shall return.
As he was about to depart, his parents gave him these instructions:
"If you can study diligently, I shall allow you to go.
He replied, "I have no leisure for further instructions."
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son went to where Upagupta was.

Having arrived, Upagupta immediately took the Brahmin’s son as a novice (śrāmaṇera) and instructed him in the contemplation of the thirty-two dharmas of dhyāna; in a mere moment, the Brahmin’s son attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Upagava thought to himself:
"This son of a brahmin has already attained the path; he does not wish to return home.
Just as parched grain does not sprout again, so it is with this śrāmaṇera."
Upagupta spoke again:
"If I were to grant them the profound dharma of meditative concentration, those who attain arhatship would abide in tranquil stillness and would no longer train further within the Buddha-dharma."
"I shall now send him to Cāṇḍadeva to study the Buddha-dharma and to convey my message.
Upagupta said, "Welcome, Śrāmaṇera!"
"You may go to that venerable Cāṇḍavajja to study the Buddha-dharma!
Once you have arrived there, you should speak these words:
'Venerable sir!'"
"My teacher has sent me here to study the Buddha-dharma. Candavaja replied,
"Excellent, śrāmaṇera!"
"Tomorrow I shall teach you, Diśu, all the Buddha-dharma and its meanings, with the sole exception of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Having completed his instruction, he received full ordination; before even a year had passed, he had mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka and possessed complete knowledge of all three piṭakas.
Once the Upādhyāya and Ācārya had entrusted all the Buddha-dharmas to Tiṣya, they entered nirvāṇa according to the length of their respective lifespans.
At that time, Tiṣya practiced meditative concentration (dhyāna) deeply and immediately attained arhatship; he then instructed all the people with the Buddha-dharma.
"At that time, King Bindusāra fathered one hundred sons.
When King Bindusāra passed away, within four years, King Aśoka killed all his brothers, leaving behind only one brother born of the same mother."
After four years had passed, King Aśoka was then formally installed as king; this was one hundred and eighteen years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Subsequently, King Aśoka governed the land of Jambudvīpa, and there were no kings who did not submit to him. By the majesty and spiritual power of the king, he exercised dominion over one yojana of space above and one yojana beneath the earth. The spirits of Lake Anavatapta daily offered sixteen vessels of water—eight jars in total—to provide for the king’s use.

"At that time, King Aśoka, having already placed faith in the Buddha-dharma, offered eight vessels of water to the community of bhikṣus; he gave two vessels to those who were masters of the Tripiṭaka, two vessels to the king’s queens, and the remaining four vessels for his own use."
Furthermore, the spirits of the Snowy Mountains daily offer *lābujā* wood—soft, fragrant, and beautiful.

The king, his queen, and sixteen thousand court ladies, together with sixty thousand bhikṣus in the monastery, constantly provide these tooth-sticks every day as offerings to the community of monks; they ensure that both the king, the queen, and the court ladies are fully supplied with them.

Furthermore, there were mountain spirits from the Snowy Mountains who offered medicinal fruits called *āmalaka* and *harītakī*; these fruits were the color of gold, with rare and exquisite fragrance and flavor.
Furthermore, there were spirits who offered ripe mangoes.

There were also spirits who daily offered five kinds of garments, all of golden hue, as well as hand-towels; they also daily offered honey-syrup for the worthy and holy ones, as well as fragrant ointments and *jāti* flowers.
The Dragon King of the Sea further presented him with a famous eye medicine.

On the shores of Lake Anavatapta, there was naturally growing fragrant fine rice; mice stripped away the husks and selected only the perfect grains, which a parrot carried ninety loads every day to present to the king.
Furthermore, they skillfully constructed a hall where honeybees built their cells to produce honey for the king's use.
The kalaviṅka birds came to the king’s presence and entertained him with various exquisite songs.
The King possessed such supernatural power.
Furthermore, on one day, the King had a golden chain made and sent it to summon the Naga King Sāgara.
This Naga King has a lifespan of one kalpa and has previously seen four Buddhas of the past.
When the Dragon King arrived, he was invited to sit upon a lion throne and covered with a white parasol; various fragrant flowers were offered as worship.
King Aśoka removed the necklaces he himself was wearing and adorned the body of the Dragon King Sāgara with them, while sixteen thousand dancing girls surrounded him in worship.
King Aśoka said to the Dragon King Sāgara, "I have heard that the Tathāgata’s marks and signs are exceptionally sublime; I wish to see him, so you should manifest him."

Thereupon, the Sāgara Dragon King received these instructions and immediately manifested his supernatural power, transforming his own body into the form of the Tathāgata. Adorned with various merits, it was subtle and wondrous, possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics. Like a lotus or an *utpala* flower blooming and adorning the surface of the water, or like the constellations adorning the void, it was adorned with various light-colored rays—blue, yellow, red, and white—extending one fathom from the body. It was like a green rainbow, or like a flash of lightning encircling it as it departed; it was like a mountain of gold surrounded by the radiance of myriad jewels. All sentient beings gazed upon it without weariness, and the Brahmās, dragons, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others looked up at it for seven days, their eyes never turning away for a moment.
When King Aśoka saw this, he was filled with joy.
From the time he ascended the throne until the third year, he had served only non-Buddhist paths; it was in the fourth year that he developed faith in the Buddha-dharma.

As for why the King had previously served non-Buddhists: at that time, King Aśoka’s father, King Bindusāra, had himself served non-Buddhists and daily provided offerings to sixty thousand Brahmins; the King and his consort within the palace all served non-Buddhists as well, and thus they had followed this tradition.

On one day, King Aśoka provided offerings for various brahmins; as the king sat upon his throne, he observed that the brahmins looked about to the left and right, entirely lacking in dignified deportment.
Seeing this, the king thought to himself:
"I shall test them further; whoever possesses the true method, I shall provide for.
Having had this thought, he spoke to his ministers:
"O ministers!
If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas whom you serve, you may invite them to my palace, and I shall provide for them with offerings.
The ministers replied:
"Very well," they replied, and each departed.

Thereupon, the ministers attended to the Nirgranthas and other non-Buddhist practitioners according to their respective duties; they each led them to the royal palace, and having arrived, addressed the king, saying:
"These are our Arhats.
At that time, King Aśoka immediately prepared and offered seats, each differing in height, quality, and coarseness.
The King said to the various non-Buddhist practitioners, "Each of you should sit according to your own capacity.
Upon hearing these words from the King, the non-Buddhist practitioners each sat down after assessing their own strength; some sat upon the *śiṃśapā* tree, while others sat upon wooden blocks.
The king, having observed this, thought to himself:
"These various non-Buddhists certainly possess no mastery of the Dharma.
Having realized this, the king spoke these words:
"Heretics such as these are unworthy of receiving offerings.
Having finished his meal, he immediately ordered him to leave.

On another day, while the King was in the palace hall looking out from a window, he saw a śrāmaṇera named Niquta passing before the palace; his gait was steady and upright, and his deportment was perfect.
The king asked,
"Whose novice monk is this?
His attendants replied:
“Nigrodha the śrāmaṇera was the eldest son of the former king and the son of Sumana.
The Dharma Master said:
“I shall now explain the causal conditions in their proper sequence.”

At that time, King Bindusāra was gravely ill. King Aśoka returned from his fiefdom of Ujjayinī to his father’s kingdom, where he immediately executed Prince Susīmā and took charge of the affairs of state himself.
After King Aśoka had executed Prince Sumana, he conducted a search within the palace.

Sumana’s consort, who was already ten months pregnant, fled in disguise; not far from the city, she reached a village of caṇḍālas. Beside the village stood a tree named Nyagrodha, which was inhabited by a deva who served as its guardian spirit.
The tree deity saw Queen Sumana and said to her,
"Welcome! Hearing the tree deity's call, the queen immediately went to the place where the tree stood.
The tree deity, through her supernatural power, manifested a house and said to the queen, "You may dwell in this house.
Having heard these words, the queen immediately entered the house; that very night she gave birth to a son, whom her mother named Nigrodha.
Thereupon, the Cāṇḍāla chief served her with a respectful heart, no different from a servant attending to his master.
Thus the princess, the queen, resided within the tree-spirit’s dwelling for seven years, until Niṅguda had reached the age of seven.

At that time, there was an arhat bhikṣu named Vāriṇa who, observing Niṣṭhita with his supernormal powers, perceived that he was ready to be delivered through the appropriate causes and conditions, and thought to himself:
"The time has now come."
Desiring to be ordained as a śrāmaṇera,
he immediately went to where the consort was and requested ordination as a śrāmaṇera.
The consort then granted him permission to be ordained.
Varuṇa was immediately ordained as a śrāmaṇera; before his hair had even fallen to the ground, he attained arhatship.

One day, after the śrāmaṇera had finished preparing his requisites, he went to his teacher’s place to pay his respects. Taking his bowl and kashaya robe, he went to his mother’s residence, entered the city from the south, passed in front of the palace, and exited through the eastern gate.

At that time, King Aśoka was walking back and forth on the palace terrace facing east. He saw the śrāmaṇera Niṅgūḍha passing before the palace, his deportment fully perfected, looking at the ground seven feet ahead as he walked with a pure mind.
The causes and conditions for this have been explained previously; now they shall be explained in detail.
Thereupon, King Aśoka thought to himself:
"That śrāmaṇera bows his body with such dignified and orderly deportment; he must surely possess the noble and beneficial Dharma."
When the king saw the śrāmaṇera, his faith was filled with joy, and he immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion. Why was this?
In a past life, this śrāmaṇera was King Aśoka’s elder brother, and they had once together cultivated merit.
And he spoke in verse:
"Due to causes and conditions from the past, I am now filled with joy once more;
Just like an *utpala* flower, Which blooms vibrantly upon receiving water."
Thereupon, King Aśoka, having given rise to compassion that he could not restrain, immediately dispatched three ministers to go and summon the śrāmaṇera.
When those ministers had not returned for a very long time, he dispatched another three ministers.
When the three ministers arrived, they said to the śrāmaṇera,
"Śrāmaṇera, go quickly! Thereupon,
the śrāmaṇera proceeded with composed dignity and steady deportment.
Having arrived, the King said to the śrāmaṇera, "Observe for yourself and sit as you please.

Thereupon, the śrāmaṇera looked throughout the assembly and saw that there was no bhikṣu present. Knowing this, he intended to approach the high White Parasol Throne and employed a skillful means to cause the King to receive his bowl.
When the king saw that the śrāmaṇera had employed such skillful means, he thought to himself,
"This śrāmaṇera will surely become the master of this house.
Having presented his bowl to the king, the śrāmaṇera then took his place upon the royal throne.
The king gave the food he himself was eating to the śrāmaṇera, who accepted it, taking only as much as he required for his own needs.
When the śrāmaṇera had finished eating, the king asked him:
"Does the śrāmaṇera know all that his teacher has taught?"
He replied,
"I know a small portion.
The king said:
"Excellent! Speak it for me. "Excellent, Great King!"
"I shall explain it for you.
The śrāmaṇera then thought to himself, gauging what the king was capable of receiving, and immediately preached the Dharma and offered a prayer of blessing, reciting half a verse:
"One who is not indolent attains nirvāṇa; One who is indolent remains in saṃsāra."
Having heard this, the king said to the śrāmaṇera:
"I understand; speak on until you have finished.
After the śrāmaṇera had completed his benediction, the king said to him:
“I shall provide offerings eight times a day.
The śrāmaṇera replied,
“Excellent!”
"I shall instead give it to my teacher.
The king asked,
"Who is this novice's teacher?"
He replied:
"One who points out my faults when I am without fault and reproaches me for them—this is called my teacher.
The king said:
"Give him another eight portions," the śrāmaṇera replied,
"Very well!"
"I shall give it to the ācārya.
The king asked again,
"Who is the ācārya?"
He replied,
"The one who, together with me, taught and instructed me in wholesome dharmas so that I might understand them is my preceptor.
The king replied again:
"Excellent! I shall give you eight more portions," the śrāmaṇera replied.
"Give these eight portions to the community of bhikṣus.
The king asked again,
"Who is the community of bhikṣus?"
He replied:
"My teacher, my preceptor, and my one upon whom I rely have granted me full ordination.
Upon hearing this, the king’s joy redoubled, and he said to the śrāmaṇera:
"If that is so, I shall give you eight more portions.
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"Excellent!"
[The King] accepted [the invitation]. Having accepted it, he departed.
On the following day, thirty-two śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus came to the royal palace; having arrived, they finished their midday meal.
The king asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Are there any other bhikṣus?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"There are. "If there are, bring thirty-two more people.
In this manner, the number gradually increased until it reached sixty thousand.
At that time, sixty thousand followers of the non-Buddhist sects lost their share of offerings.
The Venerable Niṅgūda then conferred the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts upon the king, the palace ladies, and all the ministers, who all received them.
At that time, the king and all the people experienced a doubling of their faith, never turning back from it.
For the sake of the assembly of monks, the king erected a great monastery to provide them with a dwelling, and he provided daily offerings to as many as sixty thousand of them.

The king commanded the eighty-four thousand kings under his rule to construct eighty-four thousand great monasteries and eighty-four thousand stupas. At the king’s command, the various kingdoms established these stupas and monasteries, each receiving the royal decree with joy and carrying it out.
"On another day, he held a great almsgiving at the Aśoka Monastery. Having completed the distribution, the king sat amidst an assembly of sixty thousand bhikṣus and spoke these words:
'I possess four kinds of provisions—medicines, food and drink, clothing, and bedding—which I shall freely bestow upon the Saṃgha.'"
Having spoken thus, he asked this question:
"Venerable sirs!
How many kinds of teachings are there that the Buddha governs?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"There are nine branches of the Dharma and eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dharma.
Having heard this, the king took to heart the Dharma with sincere devotion.
The king thought to himself:
"I shall establish eighty-four thousand monasteries in order to make offerings to the eighty-four thousand collections of Dharma.
On that very day, he issued ninety-six billion silver coins and summoned his great ministers.
When the minister arrived, the king said to him:
"Of the eighty-four thousand kingdoms under my rule, I have dispatched messengers to issue a proclamation that each kingdom shall establish one monastery.
King Aśoka himself then built the Aśoka Monastery.
When the Sangha saw that King Aśoka intended to build a great monastery, there was a bhikṣu named Indagutta who was an arhat with great supernormal powers and whose outflows were exhausted.
The community of monks immediately appointed Indragupta to oversee the affairs of the monastery.

At that time, Indragupta observed that there were deficiencies and shortcomings within the temple; using his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he repaired and completed them. The king contributed silver coins, and through the power of the Arhat, the work was finished in three years.

The various kingdoms had begun constructing temples and sent reports to inform the King; on a single day, they all arrived together and said to the Chief Minister, "The construction of the stupas and temples is complete.
The Chief Minister entered and informed the King:
"Eighty-four thousand kingdoms have been built with eighty-four thousand temples and stupas, all of which are now complete.
The King replied,
"Excellent!"
The King said to a high minister:

"Have the drum beaten to proclaim that the temple and stupa are now completed; seven days hence, there shall be a great offering and distribution of alms. All people within and without the kingdom shall receive the eight precepts and purify their bodies and minds."

After seven days had passed, he adorned himself in preparation to respond to the king’s summons; just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is surrounded by the celestial hosts, so too was King Aśoka’s kingdom. When the preparations were complete, the people gazed upon the sights without ever feeling satiated, and they all entered the monasteries.
"At that time, the assembly gathered, consisting of eight hundred million bhikṣus and nine hundred and sixty thousand bhikṣuṇīs; among those assembled, there were ten thousand arhats."
The community of bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"We shall, by means of our supernormal powers, cause the king to see the merit he has created; once he has seen this, the Buddha-dharma will thereafter flourish greatly."

The bhikṣus, by means of their supernormal powers, caused the king to behold all at once the stūpas and monasteries that had been erected throughout the land of Jambudvīpa under his rule—extending forty thousand leagues from coast to coast—and all the various merits arising from offerings and acts of charity therein.
Having seen this, the king was filled with joy in his heart and addressed the assembly of monks, saying:
"As I am now, making great offerings to the Tathāgata and performing such vast acts of charity, is there anyone whose heart rejoices as mine does?"
Thereupon, the assembly of monks selected Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya to respond to the king.
Tiṣya replied to the king, saying:
"When the Buddha was in the world, the offerings made by all people did not equal those of the king; indeed, you alone, O King, are beyond compare."
When the king heard these words from Tiṣya, joy arose incessantly within his heart, and he thought to himself:
"In the Buddha-dharma, there is no one who performs such great giving as I; I shall uphold the Buddha-dharma as a son loves his father, and thus I shall have no doubts."
Thereupon, the Great King asked the community of bhikṣus:
"May I receive and uphold the Buddha’s Dharma?
At that time, having heard the King's words and seeing that the Prince by his side named Mahinda possessed the complete causal conditions, Tiṣya then formed this thought:
"If this prince were to leave the household life, the Buddha-dharma would flourish most greatly.
Having thought this, he addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!..."

Such merit as this has not yet entered the Buddha-dharma; it is like a person who piles the seven treasures from the earth up to the Brahma Heaven and uses them for giving—such a one has still not gained entry into the Buddha-dharma, let alone a king who hopes to gain entry through his own giving!
The king asked again:
"How does one enter the division of the Dharma? Diśu replied:
"Whether poor or rich, may my own children be born to me, and may I cause them to leave the household life and enter the Buddha-dharma.
Having spoken these words, the king thought to himself:
"Though I have practiced such giving, I have still not entered the Buddha-dharma; I must now seek the causes and conditions for entry."
As the king looked around and saw Mahinda, he thought to himself:
"My younger brother Tissa has already gone forth as a monk.
He then appointed Mahinda as the crown prince, yet the king further deliberated: "Is it appropriate to appoint him as the crown prince?"
"Would it be good for you to go forth?
He then said to Mahinda,
"Do you wish to go forth?"

When Mahinda saw that Cūḷa-Tissa had gone forth as a monk, he wished to go forth himself; hearing these words from the king, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately replied, "I truly delight in going forth."
"If I leave the household life, the King shall attain entry into the Dharma through the division of the Dharma.
At that time, the king's daughter named Saṃghamitrā stood near her brother; her husband had already left the household life together with Tiṣya.
The King asked Saṃghamittā,
“Do you wish to go forth?
She replied:
"Truly happy.
The King replied,
"If you were to leave the household life, it would be most excellent."
The king, knowing his thoughts, felt joy in his heart and said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!
These two sons of mine have been ordained by the Saṃgha, enabling me to enter the Buddha-dharma."
The *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle One.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
"The Sangha has already accepted [him]; they have immediately appointed Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya as his upādhyāya and Mahādeva as his ācārya to confer the ten precepts;
and the Venerable Māitrāyaṇīputra acts as his ācārya to bestow the full ordination."

At that time, when Mahinda had reached the age of twenty, he received full ordination; within the ordination platform, he attained the three types of supernormal knowledge and became an Arhat with the six superpowers whose outflows were exhausted.
The Ācārya was named Ayupala and the Upādhyāya was named Dharmapala.

At that time, Saṃghamitrā was eighteen years old; he ordained her and allowed her to leave the household life, and upon the boundary of the precepts (sīmā), he immediately conferred the six rules (ṣaḍ-dharma) upon her.
Six years had passed since the king ascended the throne when his two sons entered the religious life.

Thereupon, Mahinda received the Sūtras and the Vinaya Piṭaka from his teacher; within the Tripiṭaka, Mahinda mastered all the Buddha-dharma through total retention (*dhāraṇī*). Among his one thousand fellow students, Mahinda was the most eminent.

"At that time, nine years after King Aśoka had ascended the throne, there was a bhikṣu named Tiṣya, the son of Kūṭa. He was gravely ill and, holding his alms bowl, begged for medicine and obtained a pinch of ghee. As his illness worsened and his life was about to end, he said to the bhikṣus:
'Be careful not to be indolent within the three realms.'"
Having spoken thus, he soared into the void and sat within it; he then manifested as fire and consumed his own body, entering into *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, King Aśoka heard of this from those who were proclaiming it and made offerings on his behalf. The king thought to himself:
"The bhikṣus in my kingdom sought medicine but were unable to obtain it."
The king established medicinal treasuries at the four city gates and filled them with medicines.
