At that time, there were four thousand guest halls at the four city gates of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; each hall received five thousand coins daily to provide for the king’s needs.

At that time, the king provided one thousand coins for the Venerable Niquta; one thousand as the value of flowers and incense for offerings to the stūpa and its images; one thousand to support the Dharma Hall; one thousand for the various Vinaya masters; and one thousand for the community of monks.
At the four city gates, there were medicinal treasuries, from which ten thousand coins were spent daily for the purchase of medicine.

At that time, the Buddha-dharma flourished, while the various non-Buddhists declined and lost their offerings and profits. Forced by hunger and thirst, they went everywhere begging for alms but obtained nothing at all; consequently, they entered the Buddha-dharma as śramaṇas in disguise, yet continued to uphold their own original doctrines to teach the people, saying, "This is the Vinaya; this is the Dharma."

Since they do not employ the Buddha’s Dharma, Vinaya, or proper decorum in their conduct and movements, they obtain nothing of the Dharma; yet they come to reside in the monastery and enter the midst of the Saṃgha on the day of the Poṣadha, whereupon the virtuous bhikṣus do not associate with them.
At that time, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya thought to himself:
"Now that the dharma of dispute has arisen, it will soon flourish; if I remain among the Saṃgha, this dharma of dispute will not be extinguished."
Having thus entrusted his disciples to Mahinda, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya entered the Aḳkhuda mountain range to dwell in solitary seclusion.
"The bhikṣus of the non-Buddhist sects, wishing to intermingle their own scriptures with the Buddha-dharma, have thereby caused it to become defiled and turbid."

The non-Buddhists still practice their own methods: some serve fire, some scorch their bodies with the five heats, some enter the water during great cold, and some destroy the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, virtuous bhikṣus do not join them in the uposatha, the pravāraṇā, or any other monastic affairs.
In this manner, it was passed on from one to another until seven years had elapsed without the *poṣadha* being recited.

King Aśoka, having learned of this, dispatched a high minister to enter the Aśoka Monastery and inform the Saṃgha, instructing them to extinguish their strife and dispute and to recite the *poṣadha* in harmony.
Having received the king’s command, the minister entered the monastery and announced the royal decree to the assembly of monks, but there was no one at all who responded.
The minister then returned and further consulted his fellow ministers:
"The King has issued a command that the assembly of monks should extinguish their disputes, yet they do not comply."
"What do you think?

The ministers replied, "We have seen Your Majesty go forth to subdue various kingdoms; when there were those who did not submit, Your Majesty would immediately execute them. This law should likewise be applied here."
After the attendant official had finished speaking, the messenger went to the monastery and said to the Elder:
"The King has issued a decree that the assembly of monks should recite the precepts in harmony, yet you do not comply."
The Elder replied, "Virtuous bhikṣus do not perform the poṣadha together with bhikṣus who are followers of external paths; this is not a failure to comply.
Thereupon, the minister followed the order of the Elder and executed them one by one, until he reached the King’s younger brother, Tiṣya, at which point he stopped.
When Emperor Śiśunāga saw that the bhikṣus had been killed, he thought to himself:
"This minister received the king's command and has therefore killed the assembly of monks. He asked:
"Who is Tiṣya? He replied,
"He is the king's uterine younger brother."

At that time, King Aśoka ascended the throne and established his younger brother as the crown prince. One day, while the prince was wandering for amusement in a forest, he saw a herd of deer engaged in sexual union.
The Prince thought to himself:

"If even these deer, who eat grass and drink water, behave in such a manner, how much more so must this be the case for a bhikṣu living in temple quarters, with soft and fine bedding and food that suits the palate—there surely could be no such thing!"
The Prince returned from his excursion to the King’s presence and addressed him, saying:

"Just now, while out on my tour, I saw herds of deer mating; even among these beasts that merely graze on grass and drink water, such things still occur. How could it be that among the community of bhikṣus, who reside in temple quarters with every necessity provided, such things do not occur?"
Having heard these words, the king thought to himself:
"I have given rise to doubt where there was no cause for doubt.
One day, Prince Diśu offended the king's mind; the king, filled with anger, spoke to Prince Diśu:
"I now relinquish the royal throne to you; once seven days have passed as king, I shall put you to death.

At that time, although Prince Dīrghāyu had received the throne, throughout those seven days—amidst the various offerings of music, dance, food, and drink day and night—his mind remained unstained by attachment. His physical form grew emaciated, and his grief and distress intensified.
The reason for this was that he still feared death.
When the seven days had passed, the king summoned Tiṣya and asked:
"For what reason have you become so emaciated? Are food, drink, and music not to your liking?"
Dixu replied, "The law of death oppresses me; my heart finds no joy in it.
Having heard these words, the king spoke to Dixu:

"You already know that you shall die in seven days and yet you still feel dread and fear; how much more so for the bhikṣus, who, with every inhalation and exhalation, constantly fear impermanence—how could their minds have any defiled attachment?"
After the king had spoken thus, Diśāṃpati immediately conceived faith in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, on another day, Prince Diśāṃpati went out to hunt; traveling gradually forward, he reached a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
He saw a bhikṣu sitting there named Dharmagupta; an elephant approached, broke off a branch from a tree, and brushed the bhikṣu with it from a distance.
Upon seeing this, the prince’s heart was filled with joy, and he made this vow:
"When shall I become like that bhikṣu?"

The Bhikṣu Dharmagupta, knowing in advance the mental aspiration of Diśāsu, immediately used his supernormal powers to fly up into the air and sit there so that Diśāsu could see him. From the sky, he flew to a large pond within the Aśoka Saṃghārāma and sat or stood upon the water. He then took off his saṃghāṭī and uttarāsaṅga robes and placed them in mid-air, before entering the pool to bathe.
At that time, Prince Tiṣya, seeing that the Great Virtuous One possessed such supernatural powers, was filled with great joy and said:
"Today I shall leave the household life!"
He immediately returned to the palace and said to the king:
"I wish to leave the household life; Your Majesty must look upon me with compassion and grant me permission to go forth!
When the king heard that Diśu sought to leave the household life, he was greatly astonished and replied:
"The palace maidens, with their hundred flavors of delicacies and the pleasures of entertainment—why do you wish to leave the home life?
The King employed various skillful means to cause her mind to desist.
With firm resolve and never wishing to remain, he answered the king, saying:
"The pleasures of the palace maidens are but temporary; sooner or later, we must inevitably part."
The Great King sighed in admiration,
saying, "Excellent!
He immediately dispatched his ministers to level and repair the roads, sweep and sprinkle them until they were pure and clean, and to erect banners and streamers with various kinds of adornments.
Once the preparations were complete, the minister addressed the king, saying, "The regalia are ready.

The king took the prince’s official robes, celestial crown, and jeweled necklaces to adorn him; then, surrounded by a retinue of thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen, they escorted him to the temple.

When the community of monks saw that Prince Tiṣya had gone forth, their hearts were filled with great joy. Some prepared saṃghāṭī robes, some uttarāsaṅga robes, some antaravāsaka robes, and some alms bowls, intending them for the Prince as soon as he had gone forth.
At that time, the Prince went to the meditation hall and approached the bhikṣu Dharmagupta, seeking to leave the household life.
One thousand youths, sons of the wealthy and noble elders of the kingdom, followed the Prince in leaving the household life.
When the people of the kingdom saw that the Crown Prince had left the household life, they each thought to themselves:
"Even though the Crown Prince is so noble and honorable, he has still renounced the royal throne to leave the household life and practice the Way."
"We are poor; what is there for us to cherish?
Having thought thus, countless people followed him and left the household life.
Four years after King Aśoka ascended the throne, the crown prince renounced the world.

Furthermore, there was a Brahmin named Āśī, who was the king’s maternal nephew. When Saṃghamitrā learned of this, she had a son also named Āśī; upon hearing that the prince had renounced the world, he was filled with joy and wonder. He went to where the king was and addressed him, saying:
"I now wish to follow the prince and renounce the world; I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission."
The king replied, “Excellent!
and immediately went forth from home together with the crown prince.
"In this way, within the Buddha-dharma, there will be many kṣatriyas who leave the household life, and the Buddha-dharma will flourish.
At that time, Diśu said:
"You should know that this minister has perversely taken it upon himself to follow the king's will and has killed the bhikṣus."
Before the ministers had finished killing them, the bhikṣu Diśāmpati stepped forward to shield them.
Unable to kill him, the ministers laid down their blades and went to inform the king, saying:
"We received Your Majesty’s command to have the bhikṣus recite the precepts in harmony; yet they did not comply. We have already executed them one by one according to their offenses."
"While they were not yet all killed, the bhikṣu Diśāmpati immediately shielded them, so that they could not be slain.
The minister said to the king,
"Did the bhikṣu Diśāmpati act as their protector against being killed?"

Upon hearing the minister’s words that he had killed the bhikṣus, the king was immediately struck with great alarm; his heart was filled with anguish, and he fell to the ground in a faint. Cold water was sprinkled on his face, and after a long while he regained consciousness. He then spoke to the minister, saying:
"Alas! Alas!"
"I sent you to the monastery with the intention of having the assembly of monks harmoniously recite the precepts; why did you act on your own authority and kill the monks?
The king went to the monastery and addressed the assembly of monks:
"Previously, I dispatched a minister to instruct you in harmony and the recitation of the precepts; I did not command you to kill the bhikṣus."
"This minister acted on his own authority and unjustly killed many monks.
I do not know who will incur the sin for this matter.
A bhikṣu replied:
"Because of the king, the killing occurred; this is the king's fault.
Or some bhikṣus might say:
"Both parties incur the offense."
A certain bhikṣu then asked the king:
"What was your state of mind? Did you have the intent to kill?
The king replied:
"I originally dispatched him with a mind of merit; I had no intention to kill.
"If it is as the King says, the King himself is without fault, while the one who killed is guilty of the crime."
Having heard these words, the king felt doubt arise in his mind and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is there anyone capable of severing my doubt?
If there is one who can sever the doubting mind within me, I shall once again establish the Buddha-dharma."
The bhikṣus replied,
“There is Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya, who can sever doubts and establish the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, four Dharma masters were dispatched, each with a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus, and they departed.
Again, he dispatched four ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand followers, to go and welcome the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya; having received him, they returned.
"At that time, the two assemblies went to Mount Axiu River and went to welcome Maudgalyāyana-putra Tiṣya; having arrived, they said:
'The King summons Tiṣya!'"
Emperor Śuddhodana did not leave.
The king again dispatched eight Dharma masters, each with a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus;
he also sent eight high ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand attendants.
Having arrived, he spoke again:
"The King summons Tiṣya!
But Tiṣya did not go.
The king waited for the two messengers for a long time, but as they did not return, his mind became filled with doubt.
The king again asked the venerable ones:
"Venerable ones!..."
"I have already dispatched two messengers to go and welcome Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya; it has been some time since they were sent, yet he has not arrived?
The assembly of monks replied, "We fear that the messengers may have misrepresented the King's intent and told Tiṣya that he was being summoned!"
"Therefore, he does not come.
The king asked again:
"How might one phrase the invitation so that he would come?"
The assembly of monks should answer the king with these words:
"The Buddha-dharma has already vanished; we pray that you, Great Virtue, will deign to come and together re-establish it.
Only then may he come.
Upon hearing these words, the king dispatched sixteen more Dharma masters, each with a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus;
he also sent sixteen ministers, each leading one thousand men.
The king asked again:
"Is that Dharma master old or young?
The assembly of monks replied:
"Old. [The Buddha said:
"If he is old, you should welcome him with a palanquin.
The assembly of monks replied:
"One must not ride in a carriage.
The King asked again:
"Where does that Great Virtuous One reside?"
He replied, "On Mount Ākhyu River. [The king said,] "If that is so,
you shall dispatch a boat to go and welcome him."
He commanded the messenger, saying:
"Once you have arrived, you must invite the Venerable One to stay upon the great vessel and ensure that it is guarded on all sides by those bearing weapons."
At that time, the great assembly and the messengers set out and, upon reaching the mountains by the Ākṣu River, they addressed the Mahāsattva with the King’s command, saying:
“The Buddha-Dharma has now vanished; we humbly entreat you, Great Virtue, to come and together establish it once more.”
Thereupon, having heard the messenger’s words, the Venerable One said:
"I have gone forth specifically for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; now the time has come!
He immediately took up his sitting mat and rose.
Emperor Aśoka thought to himself, "Tomorrow I shall arrive at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
At that time, King Aśoka saw such a vision in a dream during the night: a white elephant came and rubbed the king's head with its trunk, then took hold of the king's right hand.
At dawn the next day, the king summoned a physiognomist and said, "Last night I had a dream with such a vision; is it auspicious or ominous?
A certain physiognomist immediately replied to the king:
"He who grasps the King's hand is the likeness of a śramaṇa.
Having heard the words of the physiognomist, the Great King immediately received a message from the messenger, who reported:
"The Venerable Tiṣya has arrived today."
When the king heard that [the Venerable] had arrived, he immediately went out to meet him.

The king entered the water until it reached his knees; as the Venerable Tiṣya wished to step onto the shore, the king received him with his right hand, and the Venerable Tiṣya then grasped the king’s hand.
The attendants drew their swords, intending to strike the Venerable Tiṣya.
Why was this? According to King Aśoka’s law, if anyone should seize the king’s head or his hand, they were to be executed immediately; therefore, they drew their swords with the intent to strike him.
At that time, the king saw the reflection of his drawn sword in the water;
turning back, he said: "Alas! Alas!

In the past, I commanded my ministers to go to the monastery to cause the assembly of monks to harmonize and recite the precepts, yet they perversely took it upon themselves to kill the bhikṣus. Do you now wish to kill them once again?"
"Stop, stop!
Do not commit this sin against me.
The Dharma Master asked:
"A bhikṣu must not grasp the hand of a layperson; how then could he do so?
He replied, "The King, wishing to hear the Dharma, went to invite him [to come]."
The king was indeed a disciple of the Great Virtuous One; therefore, he was permitted to take hold of his hand.
Thereupon, the king took the Great Virtuous One to dwell within a grove, where it was guarded by three layers of protection.
The king personally washed the Venerable One’s feet, rubbed them with oil, and once he had finished, sat down to one side.
The king thought to himself:
"Will this Venerable One be able to sever my doubts?"
"If one can sever my doubts, they will also be able to sever the factors of contention; only then will the Buddha-dharma be firmly established.
The King thought:
"I shall first test this Great Virtuous One."
"I wish to see the great virtue's supernormal powers; I pray that you will manifest them for me.
Tiṣya replied, "What kind of supernormal power do you wish to see now?"
The king said,
"I wish to see the great earth tremble. Diśu asked:
"Do you wish for one side to move,
or for all of it to move?
The King asked again.
"Of these two kinds, which is more difficult?
Diśu replied, "Suppose there is a copper basin filled to the brim with water; if someone were to shake the basin, would it be difficult for all the water to move?"
"Is it difficult for something to be half-moving and half-still?
The King replied,
"To be half-moving and half-still is indeed very difficult."
Dīrgha replied, "So it is,
Great King! The king said:
"I wish to see that which is half-moving and half-immobile.
Diśu said to the King:

"Draw a boundary line for four *yojanas* in each of the four directions. Place a chariot in the east, a horse in the south, a man in the west, and a copper basin of water in the north. Have each of them stand upon the boundary with one foot inside and one foot outside. The copper basin of water should be placed upon the boundary so that it is half inside the boundary and half outside."
The king immediately followed these instructions and performed them.
Thereupon, Diśāmpati entered the fourth dhyāna; emerging from that meditative concentration, he spoke to the king:
"O Great King, Sudarśana!"
The Venerable Tiṣya immediately employed his supernormal powers such that everything beyond four *yojanas* in the four directions was shaken violently, while within the boundary it remained unmoved;
the wheels, horses, and people moved their feet on the outside but not their feet on the inside;
and the water was half-moved and half-unmoved.
Then, Great King, seeing such great spiritual power as this, he was filled with immense joy and said:
"The doubts I previously held have now been severed, and within the Buddha-dharma, unwholesome dharmas have been extinguished."
The king then asked the Venerable Tiṣya:
"I previously dispatched a minister to the monastery to have the monks assemble for the recitation of the precepts;
however, that minister acted on his own authority and killed the bhikṣus."
"Who would incur this sin?
Diśu replied, "Great King!"
“Did you have the intent to kill?
The king immediately replied,
“I had no intent to kill.”
"If there was no intent to kill, the King is without fault.
He then recounted for the King the *Jātaka-sūtra*:
"The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:..."
"First one deliberates with the mind and then performs an action; all actions arise from the mind.
Then, Diśa wished to expound the *Jātaka*:
"Great King!..."
In the past, there was a partridge that had been captured by a person and confined in a cage upon the ground; overcome with grief and fear, it cried out loudly.
Its kind gathered like clouds, only to be slaughtered by the person.
The partridge asked the Daoist,
"Do I have any transgressions?
The Daoist replied:
"When you cry out, do you have the intention to kill?
The partridge replied, "I cry out so that my companion may come; I have no intention to kill."
The Daoist immediately replied,
"If you had no intent to kill, you are without fault," and spoke this verse:
"Contact does not arise without karma; it necessarily arises because of the mind.
When a virtuous person dwells with a restrained mind, no calamity shall befall them."

"In this way, the Venerable Tiṣya, having used skillful means to make the king understand, remained in the park for seven days and instructed the king on what is discipline and what is not discipline, what is Dharma and what is not Dharma, and what was spoken by the Buddha and what was not spoken by the Buddha."
When the seven days had ended, the king issued an edict:
"Use portable screens to create partitions; those who saw the same thing shall gather within one partition, while those who saw different things shall each gather in separate partitions."
From within each of these partitions, a bhikṣu emerged, and the king himself asked him:
"Venerable sir!
What is the Buddha-dharma?"
Some bhikṣus answered, "It is eternal," or "it is annihilated," or "it is non-perception," or "it is neither perception nor non-perception," or "it is the world and nirvāṇa."
Having heard the words of the bhikṣus, the king thought, "These are not bhikṣus; they are merely non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas).
Once the king realized this, he gave white garments to the non-Buddhist practitioners and drove them away, compelling them to abandon their monastic lives.
Regarding the sixty thousand bhikṣus in the remaining sections, the king asked again:
"Venerable Sirs!
What is the Dharma of the Buddha?"
He replied,
"The Buddha has explained it through analysis.
After the bhikṣus had spoken thus, the king again questioned the Venerable Tiṣya:
“Did the Buddha explain this in detail?
He replied, “It is so, Great King!”
Having understood that the Buddha-dharma is pure, the king said:
"Venerable sirs! May the Venerable ones perform the poṣadha and recite the precepts."
The king dispatched guards to protect the assembly of monks and returned to the city.
After the king had departed, the assembly of monks immediately gathered sixty thousand bhikṣus.
Within that assembly, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya served as the presiding elder (*sthavira*), capable of refuting the followers of heterodox views.

From among the multitude, one thousand bhikṣus who were experts in the Tripiṭaka and possessed the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) were selected. Just as the Great Virtuous Kāśyapa had previously convened the assembly, and just as the second [council] convened by Sunakṣatra, they compiled the Vinaya Piṭaka without deviation; it is pure and stainless within all the Buddha-dharma.

The third council for the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka was completed on the ninth day of the ninth month; at that time, the great earth shook in six ways. Because one thousand bhikṣus participated in this recitation, it is called the Third Council.
The Dharma Master asked:
"In the three assemblies, who shall serve as the Vinaya Master?
[He replied: "I shall now recite their names in succession for the land of Jambudvīpa:"
First, Upāli; second, Dāsaka; third, Sunākṣa; fourth, Siggava; fifth, Moggaliputtatissa.
These five Dharma masters, within Jambudvīpa, transmitted the Vinaya-piṭaka in succession so that it would not be interrupted, continuing until the third compilation of the Vinaya-piṭaka.

After the third [patriarch], Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya, on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, entrusted [the lineage] to his disciple Mahinda; Mahinda was the son of King Aśoka, and he took the Vinaya Piṭaka to the Lion Island (Siṃhala).
When Mahinda was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted [the teaching] to his disciple Ariṭṭha.
From that time until today, it has been transmitted from one to another; this you should know.
I shall now declare the names of the masters of old: five men who brought the Vinaya Piṭaka from Jambudvīpa to Siṃhala Island.
The first was named Mahinda; the second, Itthiya; the third, Uttiya; the fourth, Sambala; and the fifth, Bhaddasāla.
These five Dharma masters possessed incomparable wisdom; their supernatural powers were unimpeded, and they had attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
In the kingdom of Siṃhala, each of them instructed his own disciples. When Mahinda was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he entrusted [the lineage] to his disciple Arittha;
Arittha entrusted it to his disciple Tissadatta; Tissadatta entrusted it to his disciple Kālasumana. Kāla...
Rāśīmaṇa transmitted it to his disciple Dīghanakha; Dīghanakha transmitted it to Rāśīmaṇa;
Rāśīmaṇa transmitted it to Karāśīmaṇa; Karāśīmaṇa transmitted it to Dharmagupta;
Dharmagupta transmitted it to Tiṣya; Tiṣya transmitted it to Deva; Deva transmitted it to Rāśīmaṇa; Rāśī...
Manas gave it to Cānaka; Cānaka gave it to Dharmavīra; Dharmavīra gave it to Kṣema;
Kṣema gave it to Upendrasūri; Upendrasūri gave it to Dharma-pāla;
Dharma-pāla gave it to Apaya; Apaya gave it to Deva; and Deva gave it to Śiva.

Such Vinaya masters as these were foremost in wisdom, possessed unimpeded supernatural powers, attained the three types of supernormal knowledge, and were Arhats whose craving was extinguished; such teachers have passed the lineage down to one another until the present day without interruption.
The Dharma Master said:
“I shall now further explain the fundamental causal conditions.
At that time, in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the compilation of the third Piṭaka, the Vinaya-piṭaka, was completed.”
In the past, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya had this thought:
"Where will the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time in the future?
He then used his supernormal powers to survey Jambudvīpa and perceived that it would flourish in the borderlands.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya assembled the community of monks and addressed the elders:
"Each of you shall uphold the Buddha-dharma and establish it in the borderlands."
The bhikṣus replied,
"Excellent! and immediately dispatched the Venerable One.
“Mācchanda! You shall go to the kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra. Mahādeva!”
He arrived at the country of Mahāpuruṣa. Lekhita!
He arrived at the country of Vaṇavāsī.
Dharmagupta! You have reached the country of Aparāntaka.
Mahā-Dharmagupta!
He arrived at the kingdom of Mahārāṣṭra. Mahārāṣṭra!
He then reached the country of Yona, which is the land of Han.
Māṭhara! Go to the country on the borders of the Snowy Mountains.
Sunakṣatra and Uttara!
They arrived at the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi.
Mahinda, Uttiya, Sambala, and Bhaddasāla then arrived at the Lion Kingdom (Siṃhaladvīpa).
"Each of you shall establish the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, each of the great virtuous ones, together with their respective retinues of five people, went to various kingdoms to establish the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, there was a dragon king in the kingdom of Kaśmīra named Aravāḷa. When the rice and grain planted in the country were just beginning to form ears, the dragon king sent down a great torrential rain, causing the rice and grain to be submerged and destroyed as they flowed out into the sea.

At that time, the five bhikṣus, including the Venerable Māluṅkyāputra, flew through the air from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra and descended into Lake Āravāla at the edge of the Snowy Mountains; there they walked, stood, sat, and lay upon the water.
The youth, a member of the dragon king’s retinue, entered and addressed the dragon king, saying:
"We do not know who this person is, but wearing red robes, he dwells upon the water and has violated us."

Upon hearing this, the Dragon King immediately became greatly incensed and emerged from his palace. Seeing the Venerable Māṭhara, the Dragon King’s wrath increased even further; he manifested various supernatural powers in the sky, not just one kind, to terrify the Bhikṣu Māṭhara. He further unleashed violent winds and torrential rains, thunder and lightning bolts, causing mountain crags to collapse and trees to be shattered, as if the very void were crumbling away.

The youth who was the retinue of the Dragon King further gathered all the dragon youths; their bodies emitted smoke until they produced a great, fierce fire and rained down large stones, wishing to terrify the Venerable Māṭhara.
Feeling no fear, he instead reviled him, saying:
"Shaven-headed man! Who are you that wears red robes?
Though he was thus insulted, the Venerable One’s countenance remained unchanged; the Dragon King then reviled him once more, saying:
"Seize him and kill him!
Having said this, he summoned his troops and manifested various supernatural transformations, yet still could not subdue him.
"The Venerable Māṭhara, using his supernormal powers, eclipsed the power of the Dragon King and addressed the Dragon King, saying:"
"If you could cause all the devas and people of the world to come in terror, not even a single hair of mine would move;
even if you were now to take Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all the smaller hills and cast them upon me, they still could not reach me."
After the Venerable One had spoken these words, the Dragon King thought to himself:
"I have exhausted my supernatural powers, yet they lead nowhere.
With a heart filled with resentment and anger, he then came to a halt.
At that time, the Great Virtuous One, knowing the mind of the Dragon King, taught and showed him the flavor of the Dharma of ambrosia, causing him to rejoice and submit with devotion.

Having received the Dharma of ambrosia, the Dragon King immediately took the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; together with his retinue of eighty-four thousand, they all received the Five Precepts.

Furthermore, there were snow-mountain ghosts, yakṣas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍa ghosts, and others who, having heard the Venerable Mahācandraprabha preach the Dharma, immediately received the three refuges and the five precepts.
Furthermore, there were five yakṣas who came together with their retinues; the yakṣī Hārītī had five hundred sons, all of whom had attained the stage of srotāpanna.

"Then, the Venerable Māraṇtī summoned all the yakṣas and nāga kings, saying: 'From this day forward, do not give rise to anger; do not harm the people or their crops; cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all living beings, and cause them to attain peace and happiness.'"
All the nāgas, ghosts, and others replied: "Excellent!
We shall comply exactly as the Venerable One instructs."

On that very day, the Dragon King made a great offering. The Dragon King sent for his own bed of the seven treasures and gave it to Mucilinda; Mucilinda sat upon the bed, while the Dragon King stood near him and fanned him with a fan.
At that time, the people of the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra-Lañkā were accustomed to gathering on festival days to go to the shrine and worship the Dragon King.
Having arrived there, they saw the Venerable Māṭhara and said to one another,
"The supernatural power of this bhikṣu surpasses even that of the Dragon King."
Thereupon, the people all paid homage to Māndhātṛ; having paid their respects, they sat down.

Māndhātṛ then preached and recited the *Avadāna-sūtra* for the multitude. When he had finished speaking, eighty thousand sentient beings immediately attained the fruits of the Path, and one thousand people left the household life to become monks.
The Dharma Master said:
"From antiquity until now, those in the kingdom of Kaśmīra have all worn the kāṣāya, thereby adorning their realm with its radiance.
And he spoke this verse:
"In the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, at that time, the Mahānagna dragon king,
who was full of hatred, was taught and led to receive the Dharma.
Furthermore, there were other great multitudes who were liberated from their bonds."
Eighty thousand attained the divine eye, and a thousand joined the community of renunciants.
"Venerable Mahādeva, go to the kingdom of Mahiṣamandala."
Having arrived, he preached the *Devadūta-sūtra* for them; when he had finished speaking, forty thousand people attained the fruits of the Path and all followed him into the homeless life.
He then spoke these verses:
“Mahādeva possesses great supernormal power and has attained the three types of transcendent knowledge.”
Arriving at Mahesha,
he preached the *Devadūta Sūtra* for them; he delivered all sentient beings,
and forty thousand attained the divine eye, all of whom followed him into the homeless life.
"The Mahādeva-ṛkṣita went to the country of Pāṇāvasika and sat in mid-air.
Having sat there, he preached the *Anādibhūta-sūtra* for them."
Having spoken thus, sixty thousand people attained the divine eye, seven thousand went forth into homelessness, and five hundred monasteries were immediately established.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Great Dharakīrti possesses great supernormal powers."
Arriving at Pāṇa-bha-si, he sat in mid-air.
For them he preached the *Anādikāla-sūtra*, whereby sentient beings attained the divine eye.
Seven thousand people left the household life, and five hundred monasteries were established.
“The Venerable Dharmagupta went to the country of Aparāntaka.
Having arrived, he preached the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra* for the sake of the people. Having finished preaching, he caused them to rejoice;

thirty thousand people attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and were made to partake of the nectar-like Dharma (*amṛtadharma*). From the Kṣatriya caste, one thousand men and one thousand women each left the household life. In this way, the Buddha-Dharma spread.”
And he spoke in verse:
“The Venerable Dharmagupta, Possessing great supernormal powers,
Went to Aparāntaka To preach the Dharma of the *Agniskandha-sūtra*.”
Causing them to partake of the Dharma of nectar, sentient beings attained the divine eye;
one thousand bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs were likewise [transformed].
"Venerable Mahāsaṃghadeva, go to the kingdom of Mahāraṭṭha."
Having arrived, he preached for them the *Mahānāradakassapa-jātaka*.
When he had finished speaking, eighty-four thousand people attained the Path, and three thousand went forth as monastics; thus the Buddha-dharma spread.
And he spoke in verse:
“The Venerable Mahādaṇḍin, possessing great supernormal powers,
went to Mahāraṭṭha and preached the *Kāśyapa-pūrvayoga-sūtra*.”
Sentient beings attained the fruits of the Path; three thousand people left the household life.
"The Venerable Mahālekhita went to the land of the world-system of Yona."
Having arrived, he preached the *Kālakārāma Sūtra* for them.

When he had finished speaking, seventy-three thousand people in the kingdom of the Yona world attained the fruits of the Path, one thousand people left the household life, and the Buddha-dharma spread throughout the Yona world.
And he spoke in verse:
"Mahākauṣṭhila, possessing great supernormal powers,
has gone to the world of Yona."
When he preached the *Makāla-sūtra*, sentient beings attained the fruits of the Path, and one thousand people left the household life.
The Venerable Maśīma, the Venerable Kāśyapa, the Venerable Devapūrṇa, and furthermore the Venerable Deva went to the vicinity of the Snow Mountains.
Having arrived, he preached the *Sūtra on the First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma*.
After the teaching was concluded, eight hundred million people attained the Way.

The five virtuous elders each went to a separate country to teach and transform others; five thousand people left the household life, and thus the Buddha-dharma spread throughout the regions bordering the Snowy Mountains.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Venerable Madhuvāsa possessed great supernormal powers;
having gone to the borders of the Snowy Mountains, he preached the *Ādi-dharmacakra-sūtra*."
Sentient beings attained the fruits of the Path; five thousand people left the household life.
"Venerable Sunakṣatra-Uttara, go to the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi."
Having arrived, there was a yakṣiṇī in the Golden Land who emerged from the ocean and went to the royal palace; whenever a lady gave birth to a child, the yakṣa would seize and devour it.
At that time, the king’s consort gave birth to a son. Upon seeing the venerable Sunakṣatra approaching, she was seized with great terror and thought to herself, "This is an associate of the yakṣiṇī."
He immediately took up his weapons and went to kill Sunakṣatra.
Sunakṣatra asked him,
"Why have you come bearing these weapons?"
The people replied,
"A son was born in the royal palace, but a yakṣiṇī companion snatched him away and ate him.
Could you not be that very companion?"
Suṇāga replied: "I am not a companion of a yakṣiṇī;
we are called śramaṇas. We have abandoned the taking of life, we protect and uphold the ten wholesome paths of action with courageous diligence, and I possess wholesome dharmas."
At that time, when the yakṣiṇīs heard that a son had been born in the royal palace, they gathered together, surrounded [the city], and emerged from the ocean, saying:
"Now that the king has fathered a son, we shall go and seize him for food."
When the people within the royal palace saw the host of yakṣas approaching, they were all greatly terrified and went to inform the Venerable One.
At that time, Sunakṣatra immediately manifested himself as a great multitude of yakṣas, twice the number of the original host, and surrounded them.
When the yakṣiṇīs and others saw the transformed yakṣa, they thought to themselves:
"That yakṣa must have already obtained the kingdom; he is now about to come and harm and devour us."
Having formed this thought, they immediately fled in all directions, unable to look back.
Thereupon, the transformed yakṣas pursued them from behind, ceasing their pursuit once they could no longer see them.

The Venerable Sunakṣatra then recited mantras to protect the kingdom, ensuring that the yakṣas could no longer enter. He then preached the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* for the people of the country; once it was finished, sixty thousand people attained the fruits of the Path. Furthermore, there were those who received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, while three thousand five hundred became bhikṣus and one thousand five hundred became bhikṣuṇīs, whereby the Buddha-dharma spread throughout the land.
The Dharma Master said:
"From ancient times until now, whenever a king has borne a son, they have all been given the name Suyodhana.
Then he spoke this verse:
"The Venerable Sunakṣatra and the bhikṣu Uttara, possessing great supernormal powers,
went to the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi and preached the Brahmajāla Sūtra;
through this, sentient beings attained the fruits of the Path."
"There are three thousand five hundred monks and one thousand five hundred nuns.
"Venerable Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya, together with the community of monks, dispatches Mahinda to the island of Siṃhala."
Mahinda then thought to himself,
"Is it now the right time to depart?
Mahinda then entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and observed.

"The King of the country of Siṃhānuvata is named Dharmasiva; he is already advanced in years and decrepit, incapable of receiving transformation. If one were to go there to transform him, the Buddha-dharma would not remain for long."
I shall wait for now; the time has not yet come.
When the King passes away and the Crown Prince succeeds him to the throne, I shall go with you to establish the Buddha-dharma.
For now, I will first go to my maternal family to pay my respects to my mother.
He further reflected to himself:
"Once I have reached my mother's country, shall I return here,
or shall I instead go to the Lion Island (Siṃhaladvīpa)?"

Mahinda went to his teacher’s residence, prostrated at the feet of the teacher and the community of bhikṣus, and departed from the Saṃghārāma of King Aśoka. With Mahinda as the elder, accompanied by the śrāmaṇera Saṃghamittā’s son Sumana and five others—making six in total—and a lay devotee named Paṇḍuka, they set out together. They passed through Rājagṛha and reached the village of Dakkhiṇagiri; from there, they proceeded in succession until they arrived in his mother’s kingdom.
The Dharma Master said:
"For what reason?

Formerly, King Aśoka conferred the kingdom of Ujjayinī upon him. When he first arrived in that country, he proceeded by stages until he reached the Southern Mountains. At the foot of the mountain was a village named Bhṛtikā."
The great wealthy householder gave his daughter to King Aśoka as a wife. Upon arriving in the kingdom, she gave birth to a son named Mahinda.
When Mahinda was fourteen years old, King Aśoka ascended the throne; he left his wife behind in the kingdom of Ujjayinī, where she resided in the village of Vedisa.
Therefore, the commentary on the sūtra states:
"Mahinda arrived at his mother's place after six months.

At that time, having reached his mother’s country in due course, Mahinda’s mother came forth and prostrated herself in greeting; once the salutation was completed, she provided him with a midday meal and immediately established a great monastery named Vidiśā.
At that time, Mahinda had resided in the monastery for a short while and thought to himself:
"The work to be done here is finished; is it now time to depart?
Mahinda then reflected further within himself:
"I shall now wait until King Aśoka dispatches an envoy to the island of Siṃhala to install Prince Priyadarśin as king; only after that shall I go."
If that prince should ascend the throne, he will receive his investiture as king from King Aśoka; furthermore, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s merits, he will surely be filled with great joy.
"I shall wait for him when he goes out to travel to Mount Miśaka; at that time, we shall meet.
After one month has passed, I shall go there.
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, when the community of monks had assembled for the *poṣadha*, they deliberated together, and each member of the community replied:
"It is time to depart.
The Dharma Master said:
"In the past, a verse was spoken in praise: [text follows]"
"The Elder Mahinda, the Venerable Uttiya, the Venerable Bhaddasāla,
the Venerable Sambala, and the novice Sumanas."
"All have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge;
Vāsavadatta has already attained the vision of the path—such are these great beings.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that King Muṇḍa had already passed away, descended and said to Mahinda:
"The King of Siṃhapura, Aṇurādha, has passed away at the end of his natural lifespan; now the Crown Prince Devānampiya Tissa has ascended to the throne as king.
I recall that in the past, when the Buddha was in the world, he prophesied that the bhikṣu Mahinda would cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish within the land of Siṃhala."
"Therefore, Venerable One!
You should depart now; I shall also serve as your attendant, and we shall go there together.
Thus spoke Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
"At that time, the Buddha was beneath the Bodhi tree; surveying the world with his divine eye, he saw that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in Siṃhala Island. He then commanded me, saying:
'You should go together with the Venerable Mahinda to Siṃhala Island to establish the Buddha-dharma.'"
"Therefore, I now speak these words.

Having received the words of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Venerable Mahinda immediately took flight from Mount Vipula together with the great assembly, soaring through the air to the kingdom of Siṃhapura in Aṇurādhapura. He went to the foot of Mount Missaka in the east; for this reason, it has been known as Mount Vipula from ancient times until the present.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now I shall recite a verse from the past:
'Dwelling in the village of Xiadi for thirty days already.'"
The time has come; you should now depart, And travel to the Lion Island (Siṃhala).
From the land of Jambudvīpa, You shall fly upward in succession, Like geese in the sky, Arranged in an orderly sequence.
Thus these great virtuous ones, arising from their fundamental causal conditions,
[appeared] on Mount Miśa to the east of the kingdom; dark and billowing like black clouds,
they reached the mountain summit and then descended, circling about as they came down.
"At that time, when the various venerable ones had arrived in the island of Siṃhala, Mahinda served as their presiding elder (sthavira).
It should be known that at that time, two hundred and thirty-six years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma had spread and reached the island of Siṃhala."
At that time, eight years after King Ajātaśatru had ascended the throne and after the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the youth Siṃha was first established as king on that continent.
There was also a youth named Vijaya who went to the island of Siṃhala and completed the establishment of the people’s dwellings.

At that time, the king of Jambudvīpa, named Udayabhadda, had been on the throne for fourteen years; meanwhile, Vijaya passed away in Siṃhala, and when it had been fifteen years since Udayabhadda’s accession, Paṇḍuvāsudeva ascended the throne in Siṃhala.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, Yaśodharman had been on the throne for twenty years when King Puṣpabhūti died; thereupon, Apahāra succeeded him as king.

In Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Śūrabhānu who reigned for seventeen years; King Apaya reigned for twenty years. Then, Bhañjaka Bhāgya raised an army and defeated King Apaya, subsequently establishing himself as the successor to the throne.
The king of Jambudvīpa was named Kālāśoka; he had already been on the throne for sixteen years, while Pukkusakavāya had been [ruling] for eighteen years.
The king of Jambudvīpa was named Candragupta; fourteen years had passed since his accession, and Pukkusakavāya had passed away, with Vindusāra succeeding him.
The king of Jambudvīpa, named Aśoka, having already been on the throne for seventeen years, heard that Tiṣya had passed away and that Priyadarśin had succeeded him.

At that time, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Anuruddha and King Munda each reigned for eight years; Nāgadāsaka reigned as king for fourteen years; Kākavarṇī reigned as king for eighteen years; and his son, named Aśoka, succeeded him and reigned for twenty-eight years.
King Aśoka had ten sons, all of whom reigned as kings for twenty-two years.
Next, Puṣyadharma succeeded him and reigned for twenty-two years.
There was also Candragupta, who reigned for twenty-four years.

During the reign of King Piṇḍasāra, he occupied the throne for twenty-eight years; by the time Aśoka had already been on the throne for eighteen years, Mahinda arrived in Siṃhala-dvīpa. This is the succession of the royal lineage, which should be understood accordingly.
At that time, King Devānampiya Tissa had been warned by an unfavorable astrological omen. He ordered his ministers to beat the drums and proclaim that the king must go out.

The ministers beat the drums and proclaimed that the king must go out to avoid the omen; surrounded by a retinue of forty thousand men, he departed from the city and reached Mount Missaka, where the king intended to go hunting.

At that time, there was a tree spirit in the mountains who wished for the king to see the Venerable Mahinda; the spirit transformed himself into a deer and, not far from the king, appeared to be grazing on grass while walking slowly.
When the king saw the transformed deer, he immediately drew his bow, took up an arrow, and pulled it back, intending to shoot.
The king thought again:
"I must shoot this deer with precision."
The deer continued to turn toward the road to Śrāvastī and ran away.
The king immediately pursued it and reached Śrāvastī.
Knowing that he was not far from Mahinda, the transformed deer vanished.
Then, seeing that the king had drawn near, Mahinda thought to himself:
"Now, by means of my supernormal power, I shall cause the king to see only me alone, and not anyone else."
The Venerable Mahinda then called out:
"Tiṣya! Tiṣya!"
"Welcome, you!
Having heard this call, the king thought to himself:
"Who in this kingdom dares to address me by name?"
"Who is this person, wearing robes made of cut-up red cloth, calling out my name?
He gave rise to a mind of doubt,
wondering, "What kind of being is this?"
"Is this a human being?
Or is it a spirit or ghost?
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahinda replied:
"We śramaṇas are sons of the Dharma King of the Śākya clan; out of compassion for the Great King, we have come here from Jambudvīpa.
At that time, King Devānampiya Piyadasi and King Aśoka had already established a correspondence, maintaining a long-distance friendship through letters.

At that time, King Devānāmpriya Priyadarśin possessed auspicious signs of merit. There was a mountain named Cetaka; by the side of this mountain grew a bamboo grove, within which were three bamboos as large as carriage poles: the first was named Vaṃśadaṇḍa, the second Puṣpadaṇḍa, and the third Śakunadaṇḍa.
As for the cane-staffs, their color was white like silver, encircled by golden vines.
As for the flower-staffs, they were adorned with various kinds of flowers—yellow, green, crimson, black, and white—as well as diverse mixed flowers and floral garlands.
As for the winged creatures, there were hawks, falcons, *śyena* birds, *kapiñjala* birds, and various other such birds.
Furthermore, there were four-footed beings that were no different from living persons.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now I shall recite a verse from the past:
'Beside Mount Cakravāḍa, Suddenly a grove of bamboo sprang up.'"
Within the grove there are three bamboos, their color white like silver;
yellow, white, crimson, azure, and black, entwined and encircled by golden creepers;
various birds and four-footed creatures, and diverse flowers of every kind illuminate them.
“Furthermore, from within the ocean there emerge various miscellaneous treasures such as coral, pearls, maṇi-jewels, gold, and silver; moreover, there are eight kinds of pearls:
horse-pearls, elephant-pearls, chariot-pearls, bharaka-pearls, bhāraya-pearls, finger-wrapping pearls, kāyūtabhara-pearls, and worldly pearls.”
Thus, King Tiṣya, beloved of the gods, dispatched a messenger bearing three superior bamboo poles, various precious objects, and eight pearls to present them to King Aśoka.

Upon arrival, King Aśoka saw them and was greatly delighted; he immediately sent in return five kinds of garments, a parasol, a fly-whisk, a sword, a celestial crown, sandals adorned with the seven jewels, and countless other precious objects.
What are the various objects? They are:

the *tandaka* caterpillar, the ever-full river water, the *taṃsakā* flower, a pair of garments dyed the color of a *piṅgala* partridge, a hand-towel, blue sandalwood, earth with the color of early dawn, *āmalaka* fruit, *āmalaka* fruit, and the princess.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now I shall recite a verse from the past:
'Celestial crown, fly-whisk, parasol, and sword, Leather sandals adorned with the seven jewels.'"
A *kiṃnara* and a *tāṇḍava* cicada, a pair of robes the color of hair,
a set of golden alms-bowls, water from Lake Anavatapta,
a fresh white and precious hand-towel, and priceless blue sandalwood.
At dawn, the ground was white with earth; the dragon king named Yan-yao [Eye-Medicine] offered amala and haritaki fruits—
supreme nectar-like medicines— and parrots presented five hundred loads of rice.
"These various exquisite objects are the merit of King Aśoka.
"Such exquisite objects as these are the gifts for the world.
Furthermore, there are gifts for the Triple Gem," King Aśoka said.

"I have taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Saṃgha; I am now an upāsaka. This is the dharma of the Śākya lineage: within the Three Jewels, you should with a sincere heart believe in and accept the Buddha's teachings."
King Aśoka dispatched a messenger to reply to King Priyadarśin’s gift and to confer upon him the royal throne.
On the fifteenth day of the third month, King Priyadarśin received his investiture to the throne.
After one month had passed, Mahinda and his companions arrived.
Furthermore, Mahinda spoke, saying:
"I am a son of the Śākya clan."

King Devānampiya Tissa, while in the hunting grounds, immediately recalled the letter from King Aśoka which spoke of a son of the Śākya clan; he then cast aside his bow and loosed his arrows, withdrew to sit on one side, and they exchanged greetings with one another.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now I shall recite the verses from the past in praise:
'He cast aside his bow and released his arrow, then sat down to one side.'"
Once the Great King was seated, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable One; the words followed one another in meaningful sequence.
At that time, forty thousand people went to the place where the King was and each surrounded him individually.
When the army had arrived, the Venerable Mahinda then manifested as six persons.
Upon seeing this, the king asked:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"When did these six people arrive?
He replied, "They came with me."
The king asked again:
"In Jambudvīpa, are there any other such śramaṇas?
He replied:

"In that land, śramaṇas are numerous; the saffron robes shine resplendent throughout the realm. They all possess the three types of supernormal knowledge and unimpeded spiritual powers, knowing the minds of others by intuition. They are arhats whose outflows are exhausted, and the disciples of the Buddha, the śrāvakas, are many."
The king asked again,
"By what means did you great virtuous ones come here?
They replied:
"We did not come by way of water or land.
The king thought to himself,
"They must have come through the void."
Majjhantika then thought to himself:
"Does the king possess wisdom,
or does he lack it?"
"I shall test him.
There was a mango tree nearby where the king was seated;
Māṇavaka questioned him by means of that tree:
"Great King!
Is this an amra tree?
The king immediately replied:
"This is a mango tree.
"Setting aside this mango tree, are there any other trees?
He replied:
"There are more.
"Setting aside this tree for a moment, are there any other trees?
He replied:
“There are more.
“Setting aside this tree for a moment, are there any other trees besides it?
He replied immediately:
"There is. He asked again:
"Setting aside other trees, is there yet another tree?"
He replied,
"Is this an *āmra* tree? Mahinda answered:
"Excellent, Great King!
You possess great wisdom.
Thus spoke Mahinda.
"Does the King have any kinsmen?
He replied,
"Very many."
"Venerable sir!
Setting aside the king's own kinsmen, are there others who have kinsmen?
He replied:
"Very many.
"Setting aside the king's own kinsmen and setting aside the kinsmen of others, are there yet more people besides?
The king then replied:
"It is I," Maṇḍiya replied. "Excellent, excellent! he said.
"O Great King, you are wise!
You have realized for yourself that this body belongs neither to oneself nor to others.
Then the Venerable Mahinda said:
"This king possesses the wisdom to establish the Buddha-dharma.
He then preached for him the *Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant Tamer*.
Having finished speaking, the king and a great assembly of forty thousand people simultaneously received the Three Refuges.
At that time, having listened to the Dharma, the king dispatched a messenger back to his kingdom to fetch food and drink.
The king thought to himself again:
"Now is not the proper time; this is not the meal for a śramaṇa."
When the food and drink had arrived, the king wished to eat alone; his mind being again filled with doubt, he asked:
"Venerable sirs! Will you, Venerable sirs, eat?"
He replied,
"This is not the time for us śramaṇas to eat.
The king asked:
"When will it become pure?
He replied, "From dawn until midday, it attains the state of being 'pure by agreement' (yathāsamstuta)."
The king said,
"Venerable sirs!
May we now return to the kingdom together?"
He replied, "We do not follow; we shall remain here.
[The others said,] "If you Great Virtuous Ones remain here, please let the youth go with us?"
He replied, "This youth has already attained the fruits of the Path and possesses thorough knowledge of the Buddha-dharma; he now wishes to leave the household life.
The King said:
"If that is so, I shall send a carriage tomorrow to welcome you.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself with his head at [the elder's] feet and departed.
Not long after the king had left, Mahinda called the novice Sumana:
"Now you should preach the Dharma; it is time for you to proclaim the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Sumana addressed his teacher, saying:
"If I were to proclaim it now, to what extent would the sound reach?"
He replied,
"Let the sound fill the entire kingdom of Siṃhala. Sumana answered:
"Excellent, Great Virtue!

Having thus entered the fourth dhyāna and arisen from that meditative absorption, he instructed his own mind so that all the people of Siṃhala Island might hear his voice; he then proclaimed it three times, and having finished the third proclamation—
Upon hearing these sounds, the king immediately dispatched messengers to the place where the great virtuous ones were, asking:
"What transgression have you committed against the great virtuous ones that has caused such a great and startling clamor as this?"
The Venerable One replied, "There is no cause for alarm;
this is merely a proclamation intended to expound the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, the Earth Deity heard the voice of the śrāmaṇera and immediately cried out with great joy, the sound piercing through the void. The deities of the void passed the sound on to one another until it reached the Brahma Heaven. Having heard it, all the deities of the Brahma Heaven assembled.
At that time, Mahinda preached the *Samacitta Sūtra*.
Having finished preaching it, countless devas all attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
the mahoragas, garuḍas, and others all received the Three Refuges.
Just as in the past when the Venerable Śāriputra preached the *Samatā-sūtra* and countless people attained the Path, so too is it now with what Maṅgīraṭa (Majjhima) preaches.
After spending the night until dawn, the king sent a carriage to welcome them.
Upon arrival, the messenger addressed the venerable ones:
"The carriage has now arrived; we pray that you will deign to depart."
He replied to the messenger, saying:
"We do not travel by carriage.
You may return first; we shall follow shortly after."

Having given this reply, he immediately soared into the void and went to the east of the city of Aṇurādhapura, where he alighted; for this was the dwelling place of former Buddhas. Because Maḥinda and his companions first descended at this spot, it was named the "First Dwelling Place."
"The King dispatched messengers to welcome the Great Virtuous Ones, and immediately summoned his ministers to prepare the dwellings together.
Upon hearing the King's words, the ministers were filled with joy."
The king thought again:
"In the Dharma taught yesterday, it is said that for one following the śramaṇa-dharma, high and broad couches are not permitted.
Before the king had finished his deliberation, the messenger who had been sent out returned and arrived at the city gate.
When the messenger saw that the great virtuous ones had already arrived at the eastern part of the city, their robes solemn and dignified, he was filled with great wonder and joy.
He entered and addressed the king, saying:
"The great virtuous ones have already arrived."
The king asked the messenger,
"Did those Great Virtuous Ones travel by carriage?
The messenger replied:
"He refused to ride in the carriage.
The messenger spoke again:
"I returned first, while the various Venerable Ones arrived later; I have already reached the city gate ahead of them and am staying there."
Having heard the messenger’s words, the king commanded, saying:
"There is no need for a high and wide bed.
The king instructed his ministers to spread mats upon the ground and place cushions and rugs thereon.
Having given these instructions, the king immediately went out to welcome the Great Virtuous Ones. The ministers then took a woolen rug and spread it as a thick mat upon the ground.
A diviner in the kingdom, seeing the king spreading mats upon the earth, thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas shall cause this ground never to shift again."
When the King had welcomed the Great Virtuous Ones and they had arrived, he prostrated with his head at their feet and, having honored them with various offerings, escorted them into the kingdom.
Thereupon, the Great Virtuous Mahinda and the others, seeing mats spread upon the ground, each thought to themselves:
"According to our tradition, we shall not move from this spot; let us each take our seats."

The king, with various delicacies, foods, and diverse sweet flavors, personally served and provided them in abundance. The king then sent a messenger to summon the chief consort of the palace, named Anurā, along with five hundred ladies-in-waiting, commanding each of them to bring flowers and incense as offerings for the king; they then withdrew and sat to one side.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahinda bestowed the great rain of Dharma upon the assembly, preaching the *Peta-vatthu* Jātaka and the *Vimāna-vatthu*, and expounding the Four Noble Truths.
Having spoken thus, the five hundred ladies all attained the fruits of the Path.

The people of the kingdom who had previously accompanied the King to Mount Miśaka each proclaimed to one another, extolling the sublime and majestic merits of the Great Virtuous Ones (Mahāsthaviras). From both far and near throughout the entire kingdom, they all came; the multitude at the capital was so dense that they could not see the Great Virtuous Ones, and they raised a great cry.
The king asked, "What is this sound of crying?
They replied,
"The people of the kingdom have not been able to see the great virtuous bhikṣus, and for that reason they are crying out loudly."
The king thought to himself:
"This place is too narrow for them all to enter.
The king then spoke to his ministers:

"You should further prepare the elephant stable, covering the floor with white sand and scattering five-colored flowers upon it; hang up curtains and canopies, so that the Venerable Ones may sit in the presence of the Elephant King."
When the ministers had finished preparing the seats, they entered and informed the King.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went to the elephant stable.
Having arrived, they each sat down and preached the *Devadūta-sūtra* for them; when they had finished preaching, one thousand people attained the Path.

"As the crowd of people increased further within the elephant stables, they moved again outside the southern gate of the city to a garden named Nanda. There, mats and seats were spread out; the venerable bhikṣus went there and preached the *Āḍakajātaka-sūtra* for the assembly, and one thousand people attained the Path."
From the first day until the third day, he preached the Dharma, and two thousand five hundred people all attained the fruit of the Path.
"Venerable ones, while you were staying at the Nandana Garden, the wives of the elders from the country came there."
Having arrived, they paid their respects and exchanged greetings from dawn until dusk.
The bhikṣus then rose from their seats, whereupon the ministers were struck with wonder and asked:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Where do you intend to go now?
They replied,
"We wish to return to our own abodes."
The minister then addressed the Great King, saying:
"The various Dharma masters wish to depart; does Your Majesty grant them permission?
The King then replied:
"Venerable Sir!
It is already dark today; how can you go?
Please stay here for now."
Then the bhikṣus replied,
“We do not dwell [there].
The king invited them again, saying:
"My father, the King, has a garden named Migāramātu-pāsāda, which is neither too far nor too near from here; you may dwell therein, as it is convenient for coming and going.
Thereupon, the Great Virtuous Ones accepted the King's invitation and resided there.
At dawn the next morning, the Great King went again to inquire after his well-being.
Upon arrival, he prostrated himself and addressed him, saying:
"Did you sleep peacefully last night?"
"How is your health?
Is it possible to stay in this garden?
The Venerable Ones replied:
"You may stay.
He then recited a sūtra verse, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to dwell within groves."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy. He immediately took a golden pitcher and poured water into the hands of Mahinda;
as the water fell upon his hands, the earth and land shook violently. At that moment, the king was struck with terror and said to the Venerable One:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Why is it that this earth is shaking so violently?
Makhādeva replied: "Great King!"
"Do not be afraid; this land is where the Dharma of the Ten Powers shall flourish. We wish to construct a great monastery on this site, and therefore the earth has manifested these omens beforehand."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s joy redoubled.
Thereupon, on the following day, Mahinda went with the assembly to the royal palace for a meal; having finished eating, they returned to stay at the Nandana Garden.
The *Sāriputrābhidharma-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Two. [Fascicle Three].
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
"For the sake of the people, he preached the *Anādikālika-dhātu-sūtra*; on another day, he preached the *Agniskandha-sūtra* for the assembly.
In this manner, continuing for seven days, eight thousand five hundred people all attained the fruits of the Path."
The light of the Buddha-dharma was spread throughout this grove; for this reason, it was named the Grove of Radiance (Prabhāsvatī).
After seven days had passed, the Great Virtuous Ones went to the royal palace, and having preached the *Anālasya-sūtra*, they proceeded to Mount Cetiya.
At that time, the Great King discussed with his ministers:
"These bhikṣus have instructed us, making our resolve exceedingly firm.
Have these venerable ones already departed or not?"
The ministers replied to the king, "The assembly of monks came and departed of their own accord; they likewise did not inform Your Majesty.

Thereupon, the king, together with his two queens, mounted a precious chariot and was surrounded by thousands of carriages and tens of thousands of cavalry as they galloped in pursuit of the monks until they reached Mount Cetiya.
Having arrived, he left his retinue behind and went in person to where the Great Virtuous Ones were; the King was greatly fatigued and his breath was labored.
Maṇḍiya asked the Great King, "Why do you breathe so heavily?"
The king then replied:
"The Great Virtuous Ones have already instructed us, causing us all to become firm; I wish to know when the time will come for the Great Virtuous Ones to depart?"
They replied,
"We shall not go, for we wish to observe the three-month summer retreat.
The king asked:
"What is this three-month summer retreat?
He replied,
"It is the dharma of the śramaṇas that one should observe the three-month retreat."
"Your Majesty should know for yourself that we have no place to stay, and moreover, the appointed day is drawing near.
At that time, there was a great minister named Ariṣṭa, with fifty-five brothers standing by the king's side, who addressed the Great King:
"We wish to follow these Great Virtuous Ones and leave the household life."
The King replied:
"Excellent! I grant you permission to leave the household life."
Having heard this, he went to where Mahinda was and was immediately ordained as a śramaṇa; before his hair had even fallen to the ground, he attained arhatship.
The king said:
"In front of the Kānaka courtyard, construct sixty-eight cells."
Having spoken thus, the king immediately returned to his kingdom.
Mahinda further converted ten brothers of the king, causing them to establish a firm and steadfast faith in the Buddha and the Dharma.
The bhikṣus observed the three-month summer retreat in the Kāñcana chamber on Mount Cetiya.
At that time, sixty-six individuals attained arhatship.
Then, after the three months of the summer retreat had passed and on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the bhikṣus informed the king of their *pravāraṇā*:

"The summer retreat is concluded; we have resided here for a long time, and it has been too long since we were separated from our Teacher. We now wish to return to Jambudvīpa to pay our respects to our Teacher."
The king then replied:
"I provide for the Dharma Master with the four requisites; furthermore, there are other people who, by relying on the Dharma Master, have attained the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts."
"Now, Venerable Sirs, for what reason are you sorrowful?
The Venerable Ones replied,
"Previously we resided under the direct supervision of our teachers, providing them with morning and evening offerings and paying them homage."
"Now there is no teacher here; for this reason, we are filled with sorrow.
The King said, "Venerable sirs!..."
"Previously it was said that the Buddha had already entered nirvana; why do you now say that he still has a teacher?
The Venerable Ones replied, "Although the Buddha has entered nirvana, his relics still remain."
The King said:
"I already know that you, the Great Virtuous Ones, desire to have me erect a stūpa. If this is so, I pray that you, the Great Virtuous Ones, will measure out a suitable location."
The King thought again:
"While the location for the site can be obtained, how shall the śarīra be obtained?
Makhādeva replied:
"The King himself shall deliberate upon this together with the śrāmaṇera Sumana.
The King replied,
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, the Great King went to where the śrāmaṇera Śūmāna was and asked him:
"Virtuous One!
How may I now obtain the relics of the Tathāgata?"
Sumana replied: "Excellent, Great King!

You should simply purify and sweep the roads until they are clean, erect various banners and pennants, scatter flowers and burn incense, and adorn them in every way. Let the King and his retinue together observe the eight precepts. Adorn the elephant upon which the King rides with necklaces and ornaments, and place a white parasol over it. When the elephant proceeds directly toward Mount Mahānāga Garden, you shall obtain the relics of the Tathāgata."
The King immediately replied,
"Excellent, excellent!
and at once accepted the instruction.
"The Venerable Ones then proceeded to Mount Cetiya.
Having arrived there, Mahinda said to the novice:
'Sumana, welcome! Sumana, you must now go to Jambudvīpa and convey my message in full to your grandfather, King Aśoka, speaking thus:'"

“Great King, your acquaintance, Devānampiya Tissa, the King of Siṃhala, has already placed faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and now wishes to erect a stūpa; if Your Majesty possesses any relics, we pray that you will grant them to him at this time.”
"Once you have obtained the Great King's relics, you may go once more to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and say to Śakra:
'Śakra, you possess two relics: one is your right canine tooth, which you shall keep for your own worship; the other is your right clavicle bone, which you must entrust to me to bring back.'"
He asked Śakra again:
"Previously you said that you would go to Siṃhala with your attendants;
why then do you remain here so calmly and not come? Sumana replied:
"Excellent!

Having received these instructions, he immediately took up his *kāṣāya* robe and held his alms-bowl, soaring into the air. In a brief moment, he arrived at the city gate of Pāṭaliputra in Jambudvīpa and descended. He went to the king’s location and addressed him, saying:
"Mahinda has sent me here for that purpose."

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately took the śrāmaṇera’s bowl, anointed it with fragrant ointments, opened a casket of the seven precious gems, and personally took the śarīra relics—white as pearls—to fill the bowl, which he then presented to the śrāmaṇera.
“After the śrāmaṇera had taken it, he went again to the palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
When Śakra saw the śrāmaṇera, he addressed him, saying:
‘Venerable Śramaṇa!’”
"For what reason have you come here?
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"Your Majesty previously dispatched various virtuous ones to the Kingdom of Siṃhala, yet Your Majesty has not yet departed."
Śakra replied, "What would I do by going?
The śrāmaṇera asked Śakra:
"Śakra has two relics: one is his right canine tooth, which he leaves here;
the other is his right clavicle bone, which he gives to me for worship.
Śakra replied:
"Excellent! Excellent!

he exclaimed, and immediately taking hold of the door-leaf, he opened the stupa made of the seven treasures. The stupa was one yojana in length and breadth; he then took the śarīra and bestowed them upon Sumana.
Having accepted [the invitation], Sumana went down to Mount Cetiya, where there were Mahinda, Uttiya, Sambala, and Bhaddasāla.
He immediately took the relics of King Aśoka and placed them on Mount Cetiya; as for the remaining fragments of the skull-bone, he carried them at the hour of *pradoṣa* (dusk) to the Mahāvana Grove.
All matters previously commanded by the śrāmaṇera, such as the leveling of the roads and other preparations, had already been fully completed.
The king immediately mounted the elephant, holding a white parasol in his hand to cover the śarīra, and proceeded to Mount Cetiya.
The king thought to himself:
"This is the śarīra of the Tathāgata; let the elephant prostrate itself on the ground and the white parasol descend of its own accord, so that the śarīra of the Tathāgata may rest upon my head."

Before the King had finished his thought, the elephant prostrated itself on the ground of its own accord, and the white parasol descended by itself; at that moment, the reliquary casket ascended onto the top of [the elephant’s] head.
As the King spoke these words, his entire body was filled with joy, as if he had tasted the flavor of nectar (amṛta), and he immediately asked the Mahāsthavira:
"Mahāsthavira!..."
"The śarīra is upon my head; what should I do now?
The Great Virtuous One replied, "Place it upon the head of the elephant."
Thereupon, the Great King placed the reliquary casket upon the head of the elephant.
Having received the relics, the elephant gave rise to a heart of joy and made an offering to the relics with its voice.

At that time, clouds arose in the void and rain poured down according to the needs of sentient beings; the great earth shook as far as the edge of the waters. When the devas, nāgas, and spirits saw that the Buddha’s relics had reached the borderlands, their hearts were filled with joy, and they spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s true relics Descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Like the full, radiant moon, Coming to transform the borderlands.”
"Standing atop the head of the elephant, he made offerings with music.
At that time, various musical performances were produced, surrounding the great elephant in a most sublime offering that cannot be fully described.
The elephant faced west and walked backward toward the east; upon reaching the city gate, it entered the city, where the people within made offerings and paid him homage.
Exiting through the southern gate, it went around the western side of the stūpa garden; having reached Pāṭali, it turned back toward the stūpa garden and remained within it.
"In the past, the relics of the three Buddhas were all located within the stupa gardens.
In ancient times, the country of Siṃhala was called Oṃja Island; its kingdom was named Abhaya, and its king was also named Abhaya."
Mount Cetiya was named Devakūṭa;
at that time, the park for the stupa was named Pāriyātra Park.

Then, the Buddha K Krakucchanda appeared in the world. A disciple of the Buddha K Krakucchanda named Mahādeva, together with a thousand bhikṣus, arrived at Devakūṭa and resided there, just as Mahinda had resided on Mount Cetiya.
At that time, the sentient beings on the continent of Aṅga were afflicted by defilements and suffering.

The Buddha Kruśānu, observing these sentient beings in such distress with his divine eye, immediately set out for the continent of Aṅga accompanied by seventy thousand bhikṣus and extinguished all their diseases.

Once the disease had been extinguished, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for the people of the country, and eighty-four thousand people all attained the fruits of the Path. The Tathāgata then placed his water-straining bottle within the kingdom.

At that time, the Tathāgata returned to his native land. The people erected a stūpa and placed the water-straining vessel inside it, naming it the Mahādeva of Pāriyātra Garden; they scattered flowers as an offering, and the people thereafter resided within the kingdom.
“During the time of the Buddha Kanakamuni, the continent of Siṃhala was called Brahmaloka; the kingdom was named Vatsa; the king was named Śāntideva; and Mount Cetiya was called Suvarṇaśṛṅga.”
At that time, the land of Vārāṇasī was suffering from a great famine; all were destitute and endured immense suffering.

The Buddha Kanakamuni, surveying the world with his divine eye, beheld the island of Vārāṇasī. The Tathāgata then went to the island accompanied by one thousand bhikṣus. By means of his supernatural powers, he caused the heavens to send down rain, so that the five grains ripened in abundance according to the seasons. The Buddha preached the Dharma for the people of the country, and eighty-four thousand beings all attained the fruits of the Path.
The Buddha left behind a bhikṣu named Sumana, who remained surrounded by a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus, and he also left behind his waistband.
At that time, the Tathāgata returned to his kingdom together with the great assembly.
The people erected a stūpa and placed a cord inside it as an offering.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Lion Island (Siṃhaladvīpa) was named Mandara; the kingdom was named Viśāla; the king was named Jita; Mount Cakravāḍa was named Śubhakūṭa.
At that time, great strife arose in the continent of Mandā, and many sentient beings were afflicted by suffering and distress.

The Tathāgata, surveying the world with his divine eye, saw the great suffering in Mandā; he then arrived at this continent together with twenty thousand bhikṣus. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he extinguished the strife, and for all the people of the land, the Buddha preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, whereby eighty-four thousand people all attained the fruits of the Path.
The Buddha appointed a bhikṣu named Sarvananda, together with a thousand bhikṣus, and the Buddha left behind his bathing robe.
The king and the people immediately erected a great stūpa and placed the Buddha’s bathing robe inside it for veneration; thus, the name of that stūpa park became known by successive tradition.
In the past, the three Buddhas all left behind their personal effects to have stūpas erected for them in this manner.
The three realms are impermanent, leaving only empty ground; thus, devas and humans planted thorns upon the sites of these ancient stūpa foundations.
Why is this? Because they have severed all defilement and evil.
