At that time, the great elephant carrying the *śarīra* naturally proceeded to the site of the old stupa’s foundations in the garden; the king and the people then cut down the thorns and leveled the ground until it was as smooth as the palm of a hand.
The elephant went to the north of the old stupa site and stood facing the stupa at the location of the Bodhi tree.
When the king wished to deposit the relics, the elephant would not allow it.
The king questioned Mahinda again:
"Venerable Sir!
How can one attain the lower [realms]? Mahinda replied:
"It cannot be lowered.
Your Majesty must first establish a foundation as high as the elephant's head, and only then can it be brought down.
Thereupon, the great assembly hurriedly worked together to haul earth and build a wall; within three or four days, the elephant still stood there bearing the śarīra upon its head.
Once the king had laid the foundation, he again addressed the Venerable One,
saying, "What shall be the shape of the stupa? Mahinda replied:
"It is like a heap of gathered rice.
The King replied,
"Excellent!"

Upon the foundation of the stupa, he erected a small stupa; the King made various kinds of offerings, and as he was about to deposit the relics, the people of the entire kingdom came with flowers, incense, music, and dance to behold the relics.

"At that time, when the great assembly had gathered, the relics immediately rose from the top of the elephant into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees. They manifested various supernatural transformations, appearing in five colors—dark blue and yellow—and at times emitting water, at times emitting fire, or at times emitting both together. This was no different from the supernatural power of the World-Honored One while he was in the world at the *Khaṇḍa-āmra* tree; it was not the supernatural power of Mahinda or the devas."
Why is this? In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the world, he left behind an instruction regarding his relics:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when you go to the Lion Kingdom and arrive at the Cetiya Garden, manifest various supernatural powers."
"The Tathāgata has already given the command; it is for this reason that he now manifests.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now recite the verses from the past:"
“The Buddha is inconceivable, and the Dharma is also inconceivable;
for those who possess faith, their merit is likewise inconceivable.
On this Lion Island, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni has already arrived three times.
First, after having converted the yakṣas, he immediately commanded them, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, my śarīra relics shall remain here."
Regarding the second visit, he converted his maternal nephew, the Dragon King Jyotiska.
During these first two visits, the Tathāgata went alone.

On the third visit, surrounded by a hundred bhikṣus, he arrived at the Mahācaitya, the site of the Stūpa Garden, the site of Bodhi, and the site of the Eastern Gaṇadīpaka Vihāra, where the Tathāgata entered into samādhi.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during his final fourth journey with the relics, he manifested supernatural power to produce water; all the people within the land were sprinkled with this water, which removed their hunger and thirst.
"At that time, the śarīra descended from the midst of the sky; the great assembly immediately saw it descend onto the king's crown and come to rest there.
Having received the descent of the śarīra, the king thought to himself:
'That I have now obtained this human body is due to my sincerity.'"
He immediately made great offerings and took the *śarīra* relics to enshrine them within a stūpa; at that moment, the great earth shook in six ways.

At that time, the king’s younger brother, named Abhaya, went forth into homelessness together with a thousand people. Furthermore, five hundred youths from the kingdom went forth together, and another five hundred and five youths from the country likewise went forth. In this manner, the number increased until thirty thousand people had gone forth.

At that time, when the construction of the stupa was completed, the Great King’s consort, along with the King’s sister, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, each made their respective offerings.
When the offerings were completed, Mahinda returned to the Magadha Garden.
Upon his arrival, Anurādha, desiring to renounce the world, addressed the king, saying: [Please allow me to go forth.]
Having heard this, the king felt despondent in his heart and said to the Venerable One:
"The lady Āṇumā is now wishing to leave the household life; I pray that the Venerable One will ordain her."
Majjhantika replied, "We śramaṇas are not permitted to ordain women.
I have a sister named Saṃghamittā who is currently in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; you may go there to welcome her."
"In the past, the Bodhi trees of the three Buddhas all came to be planted in this kingdom; now, our Teacher’s Bodhi tree should likewise be planted here.
Therefore, Great King, you should dispatch a messenger to King Aśoka to request the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃghamitrā and seek his Bodhi tree to bring back and plant here."
The King replied, "Excellent!
Having received the command, he immediately summoned his ministers to deliberate together.
The king called his nephew and said:
"Can you go to the land of Jambudvīpa, to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, to invite Saṃghamitra and to bring back a branch of the Bodhi tree?"
He immediately replied,
"I can. Thereupon,
the nephew made a prior agreement with the king:
"If Your Majesty permits my renunciation of the household life, I shall depart now;
otherwise, I will not go.
The king replied:
"Excellent!
If you can bring the bhikṣuṇī Saṃghamitrā and the Bodhi tree here, I shall grant you permission to go forth.
Thereupon, the nephew first received the instructions of Mahinda and then the royal command.
Having accepted [the invitation], Mahinda used his supernormal powers to cause the king’s nephew, Abhaya, to reach the island of Jambukola in a single day.
Upon arrival, he immediately boarded a ship and crossed the sea, reaching the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.

At that time, Lady Anulā, together with five hundred young maidens and five hundred women of the royal palace, all received the ten precepts. Donning the saṃghāṭī robes, they went outside the city and erected separate dwellings by the city wall to reside there.
When Ambaṣṭha had arrived, he addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, your son named Mahinda has commanded me to come here and speak these words:
'The Great King’s acquaintance, Queen Ānula, the consort of King Tissa Devānampiya, desires to go forth into homelessness, yet there is no one to ordain her.'"
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me the nun Saṃghamittā and the Bodhi tree.
Thereupon, the messenger, having delivered Mahinda’s command, went to where the nun was and said to her:
"Venerable One!"
The Venerable Elder Mahinda has sent me here with these instructions:

"The Queen Anulā of King Devānampiya Tissa of Siṃhala, together with five hundred young maidens and five hundred female attendants from the royal palace, all desire to go forth into the religious life. They now request the Venerable One to be their preceptor; we pray that the Venerable One will come at once."
Upon hearing her brother’s letter, the bhikṣuṇī rose in haste and went to the king’s presence, where she addressed him, saying:

"Great King, my brother’s letter has arrived. Queen Devī and the other women wish to leave the household life to practice the Way; they have requested me to be their preceptor and are now waiting for me."
"I now wish to depart and inform the King so that he may know.
The King immediately replied:

"Since my son Mahinda and my grandson Sumana departed, I have always felt no different from a man whose hands and feet have been severed. Not having seen these two for a long time, I have been consumed by grief day and night, never leaving their faces from my mind. Seeing your face has brought comfort to my heart; if you now depart again, I shall surely die. Stay, do not go!"
Saṃghamittā replied:

"Great King, my brother’s faith is most profound and cannot be disregarded; furthermore, the Kṣatriya lady Anulā wishes to renounce the world and is now waiting precisely for me. Therefore, I must go there."
The King immediately replied,
"If your elder brother believes this to be so, you may go together with the Bodhi tree.
Saṃghamitrā addressed the King:
"Where is the Bodhi tree?
The Great King replied,
"It is in the araṇya."
"The King previously had the intention to take the Bodhi tree, but it cannot be cut down with knives or axes; how, then, can it be taken?
The King was bewildered and without a plan, so he questioned his minister, Deva."
Deva replied,
"Venerable Bhikṣus, you should know.
The King answered:
"Excellent! Please partake of the midday meal.
When the assembly of monks had finished eating, the king addressed the bhikṣus:
"May we go to the Lion Kingdom (Siṃhala) to visit the Bodhi tree of the Tathāgata?
The community of monks then recommended Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya, as he was knowledgeable in this matter.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya replied:
"The Bodhi tree may be taken to the Lion Country (Siṃhala). Why is this?"
At that time, while the Tathāgata was still in the world, there were already five decrees.
What are these five?
When the Buddha was lying on his bed, on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, he spoke these words:

"In the future, King Aśoka shall take a branch of the Bodhi tree to the Kingdom of Siṃhala; let a branch from the southern side of the Bodhi tree break off spontaneously without the use of knives or axes, and once broken, it shall fall into a golden basin—this is the first command."
If my Bodhi tree, at that time, should immediately rise from within the basin into the void and dwell amidst the clouds—this is the second command.

Once it has entered the clouds and remained there for seven days, it shall descend naturally; having entered the golden basin, it will immediately flourish, spreading its leaves and bearing fruit. The colors of its leaves, appearing in various shades of dark and yellow, are beyond full description.
"This is the third injunction.
If you go to the Kingdom of Siṃhala, you may plant it; at the time of first planting, perform various supernatural transformations—this is the fourth injunction."

"If one *dou* of my relics reaches the Kingdom of Siṃhala, they shall immediately manifest there with the same appearance and form as when I was in the world—possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics, with a brilliance more intense than that of the sun and moon;
this is the fifth injunction."

"Upon hearing that there were five royal edicts, the Great King was filled with great joy; departing from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, he proceeded on foot to the site of the Bodhi tree, bringing with him a great quantity of purple-gold."

At that time, Viśvakarman, the skillful artisan of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having known the king’s intention, assumed the form of a smith and stood by the king’s side. The king then called out to him, saying:
"Smith, take this gold and forge it into a basin."
The smith addressed the king:
"What is meant by 'vast'?
The king then replied:
"This is your karma; you yourself must know it.
The smith replied, "Excellent!"
"I shall now do so.

He then took the gold and, using his supernatural powers, moved it back and forth with both hands until it formed a golden basin nine cubits in circumference, five cubits in height, and about eight inches in thickness; the mouth of the basin was perfectly round like the trunk of an elephant king.

Thereupon, King Aśoka’s retinue and great assembly—consisting of thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of cavalrymen—raised various banners and streamers, adorned with all manner of rare jewels, flowers, incense, necklaces, and musical performances. The procession was three *yojanas* wide and seven *yojanas* long;
they departed from the city, surrounding it as they went, and further led the community of bhikṣus to the site of the Bodhi tree, where they remained encircling it.
The Great King Aśoka, together with a thousand minor kings, went forth to welcome the Bodhi tree.
King Aśoka took his place in the center, while the minor kings surrounded him on the outside; thereupon, King Aśoka and the others gazed upward at the great tree and its southern branch.
At that time, by means of its supernatural power, the tree caused itself to become hidden and invisible, leaving only a single branch four cubits in length.

When the Great King saw that the tree had vanished through its supernatural power, he immediately conceived a heart of joy. He then offered all the lands of Jambudvīpa, as well as royal attire, necklaces, perfumes, flowers, and various other offerings; circumambulating the tree in the eight directions, he prostrated himself with his head at the base of the tree and installed it as king over the sovereignty of Jambudvīpa.
Having prostrated, he addressed the assembly of monks and made this vow:
"If you grant me permission to take the tree for the Kingdom of Siṃhala, let the entire tree appear along with its southern branch."

The King immediately fashioned a lion throne out of the seven treasures and placed a golden basin upon the high seat. King Aśoka then ascended the high seat, took up his painting brush, and ground realgar on a stone. The King further made this vow:
"If the Bodhi tree truly permits me to go to the Lion Country (Siṃhala), and if I possess a sincere heart of faith, may a portion of the Mahābodhi tree spontaneously fall into the golden basin."
"When the king had finished making his vow, the tree immediately returned to its original state.

At that time, he used scented ointment as mud, filling a golden basin with it. Using a brush, he drew ten lines on the curved parts of the tree branches; nine lines produced roots while one line remained severed. The roots grew four inches long and further produced fine rootlets, which crisscrossed and interlaced like a net, while the main branches reached a length of ten cubits."
Furthermore, there were five branches, each four cubits long; from each of these five branches grew a single fruit, and there were also a thousand small twigs.

When the Great King saw such miraculous transformations of the Bodhi tree deity, his heart was filled with great joy. He joined his palms toward the tree, let out a great cry, and the assembly of monks chanted "Svāhā."

Thereupon, all the minor kings, their attendants, and the entire great assembly raised a great cry. At that time, the Earth Deity was struck with wonder and likewise let out a great shout; this sound pierced the void, and as it was passed on from one to another, its resonance reached the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, the branches of the tree spontaneously broke off from their bases and fell into the golden basin; there were immediately one hundred roots that extended straight down to the bottom of the basin.
Furthermore, ten roots pierced through beneath the basin, while ninety fine roots grew encircling them. In this manner, they grew and increased day and night in succession.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways; in the void of space, the various devas performed manifold music; all the mountains and trees trembled greatly, like the gestures of a person dancing; gods and humans clapped their hands; yakṣas and spirits laughed with great joy; the asura kings sang hymns and offered praises; Brahmā rejoiced; amidst the void, there was thunder and lightning; four-footed creatures ran about and cried out; birds flew about, emitting various sounds; King Aśoka and the various minor kings together performed music. These manifold sounds reached upward as far as the Brahma-heaven.
At that time, the Bodhi tree seedling emitted light of six colors, its radiance shining everywhere throughout the Sahā world and reaching up to the Brahma Heaven.

The Bodhi tree then ascended into the void and remained suspended there for seven days. When the seven days had passed, the great assembly saw only light; they could see neither the golden basin nor the tree. The King then descended from his lion throne made of the seven treasures and performed offerings to the Bodhi tree for seven days.

When the seven days had ended, the tree again emitted radiance that illuminated the Sahā world, reaching upward as far as the Brahma Heaven; the light then withdrew and returned. In the void, the clouds all became clear and bright. Leaves sprouted and fruit formed upon the Bodhi tree, and the trunk of the *māndārava* tree descended from the sky and entered the golden basin.

When the Great King saw the tree enter the golden basin, he was filled with great joy; he further offered the land of Jambudvīpa as an offering to the small Bodhi tree, providing sustenance for the land of Jambudvīpa for seven days.

"On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the day of the *pravāraṇā*, at the hour of *pradoṣa*, the Bodhi tree entered a golden basin; it remained in the golden basin for seven days, then ascended into the void and stayed suspended there for seven days, before descending from the void and entering the golden basin once more. The King then made the Bodhi tree the sovereign of Jambudvīpa for seven days."

On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, the day of the *poṣadha* for the community of monks, the Bodhi tree came forth from its place of origin and arrived at the eastern side of the city of Pāṭaliputra in a single day; it was placed beneath a *śāla* tree, whereupon the Bodhi tree immediately grew lush and verdant.
Having seen this, the king was filled with great joy; he further appointed him as king over the land of Jambudvīpa.
After making these offerings, he said to Saṃghamitra, "It is time for you to depart."
He replied, "Excellent, Great King!

He then assigned the eight classes of spirits and deities to protect the Bodhi tree. There were eight kinds of ministers, eight kinds of brahmins, eight kinds of householders, eight groups of Pūga people, eight groups of Lāḍha people, and eight groups of Kaliṅga people. The king had eight golden jars and eight silver jars carried on a palanquin, and they poured water over the Bodhi tree.
Having received the King’s instructions, they acted accordingly.
The King, together with the great assembly, surrounded the Bodhi tree and escorted it along the road in succession; gods, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras made offerings day and night.
Upon reaching the shore of Tāmaliptī, the king personally carried the Bodhi tree into the water until it reached his neck, then placed it upon the ship alongside Saṃghamitrā.
The king called out to Abhaya: "Abhaya!..."
"The Bodhi tree is in my kingdom; I have ruled over Jambudvīpa by prostrating three times. I myself carried the Bodhi tree into the water until it reached my neck, and then placed it upon the ship."
He then commanded Ābhyaṣika:

"If the Bodhi tree goes to that country, you must tell your king to personally descend into the water up to his neck to welcome the Bodhi tree, carrying it upon his head as if wearing a crown, just as I have performed various offerings here without distinction."
Having issued this command, the ship immediately set sail.
At that time, in the midst of the sea where the ship was stationed, there was an area one yojana in length and breadth that was entirely free of waves. The king thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s Bodhi tree is now departing from my kingdom."
As he was thinking this, he shed tears and choked with grief.
After the ship had departed, the king looked out from afar and saw various kinds of miscellaneous flowers emerging from the seawater, following behind the ship as an offering to it.
Furthermore, various flowers were scattered in the air and offered with music and dance; the water deities also made offerings to the Bodhi tree with various flowers and incense.
In this manner, the successive offerings continued until they reached the palace of the Dragon King.
The Dragon King immediately emerged, intending to seize the Bodhi tree; thereupon, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃghamitrā transformed herself into a Golden-Winged Bird King (Garuḍa).
When the Dragon King saw that the bhikṣuṇī’s supernatural powers were such as these, he immediately prostrated with his head at her feet and said:
"I now wish to invite the Bodhi tree and the Venerable One to return to my palace to receive my offerings for seven days."
Thereupon, the Bodhi tree and the great assembly all entered the palace of the Dragon King.

The Dragon King invested the Bodhi tree as king with his own throne and made offerings for seven days. After the seven days had passed, on the first day of the tenth month, the Dragon King personally escorted the Bodhi tree for one day to the island of Jambukhanda.
King Aśoka gazed into the distance but could no longer see the Bodhi tree; he returned weeping.

At that time, King Devānāmpriya, following the prior instructions of the śrāmaṇera Sumana, leveled the roads, swept them clean, and erected banners and streamers as various offerings. From the northern city gate to Kuṇāladvīpa, the ground was made as level as the palm of a hand, awaiting the arrival of the Bodhi tree.
By means of his supernatural powers, Saṃghamitra enabled the king to see the Bodhi tree from within the city as it approached.

The king immediately departed from the city, scattering five-colored flowers everywhere until he reached the island of Jambukhāṇḍa; he arrived there in a single day. Performing various kinds of music, he entered the water up to his neck and thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s Bodhi tree has now come to my kingdom."
Before his thought had even concluded, the Bodhi tree emitted light of six colors; upon seeing this, the king was filled with great joy and immediately placed it upon the crown of his head.

The kingdom had sixteen great clans of elders who, together with the king, went to welcome the Bodhi tree; having reached the shore, they remained for three days, making offerings to the Bodhi tree from Sīhaladvīpa.

The sixteen great clans who administered the affairs of the kingdom, having completed three days and reaching the fourth day, carried the Bodhi tree in succession until they arrived at the country of Anurādhapura. Upon their arrival, the people of the entire nation rejoiced, prostrating and making offerings.

"On the fourteenth day of the tenth month, after midday, the Bodhi tree entered through the northern city gate, proceeded to the center of the city, and then exited again through the southern city gate. Five hundred *dhanus* from the southern city gate is the place where the Tathāgata once entered *samādhi*; it was not only Śākyamuni Buddha, but all Buddhas of the past have likewise entered *samādhi* therein."
The Bodhi tree of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Mahāśālipa;
the Bodhi tree of Kanakamuni Buddha was named Udumbara;
and the Bodhi tree of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Nyagrodha.

In the Migāra’s Park, the novice Sumana was commanded to oversee the construction of the foundations, the measurement and layout of the surrounding perimeter, and the placement of the gatehouses and the site for the Bodhi tree; he was to ensure that all were properly arranged, with the royal gatehouse being established at its designated location.
At that time, the men of the sixteen great clans, all dressed in the robes of kings and nobles, surrounded the Bodhi tree and planted it upon the ground of the royal gatehouse.

As soon as they released the tree, it immediately ascended into the void to a height of eighty cubits, emitting light of six colors that illuminated the entire Kingdom of Siṃhala, reaching as far upward as the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, when the multitude saw the various transformations of the tree, their hearts were filled with great joy; ten thousand people among them simultaneously resolved their minds to recollect the Buddha, successively attained arhatship, and immediately went forth together into the homeless life.

While the sun had not yet set, the tree remained suspended in the void; after the sun had set, it descended from the void like the comet Lou-xi (Aldebaran) among the lunar mansions, and the earth shook violently everywhere.
At that time, Mahinda, together with King Saṃghamitta and the people of the kingdom, gathered at the Bodhi tree.
Then, seeing a single fruit on a northern branch that had ripened and fallen from the branch, the multitude presented it to Mahinda.

Mahinda gave the seeds to the king and instructed him to plant them. The king immediately received them in a golden basin, covered them with rich soil, and further spread fragrant ointments over them. In a mere moment, eight saplings sprouted, each four cubits tall. Seeing this, the king was filled with wonder and amazement; he covered them with white parasols and consecrated the young trees as kings.

The King took one branch and planted it on the island of Jambukhāṇḍa; he took one branch and planted it in the village of Bakula-Brahma; he took one branch and planted it in the village of Śigru; one branch he planted in the monastery garden of the Stūpa; one branch he planted in the temple of Maheśvara; one branch he planted in the center of Mount Cakravāḍa; one branch he planted in the village of Lauhitya; one branch he planted in the village of Vaira; and four remaining branches remained upon the tree. These ripened and fell in succession, resulting in a total of thirty-two trees. He took them all and planted them in the Yojana Garden, where they multiplied and spread until they filled the land of Siṃhala. Because of these Bodhi trees, the kingdom became peaceful and secure, free from all calamities.
Thereupon, Lady Anulā, accompanied by a thousand women, went to Saṃghamittā; Saṃghamittā then ordained them as bhikṣuṇīs.
After they had crossed over [to liberation], they attained the state of Arhat one after another.
The king’s nephew, Abhaya, together with five hundred people, went forth into homelessness; after going forth, they also attained the state of Arhat one after another.

On another day, the King and Mahinda went together to pay homage at the Bodhi Tree. Upon arriving at the location of the Iron Palace (Lohapāsāda), the people offered flowers to the King; the King presented these flowers to the Dharma Master Mahinda. After the Dharma Master had accepted them, he used them as an offering for the Iron Palace. As the flowers fell to the ground, the earth immediately shook.
When the king saw the earth tremble, he immediately asked:
"Venerable Sir!
Why does this earth suddenly shake?"
He replied: "Great King!
The assembly of monks shall come to this hall to recite the precepts; for this reason, the earth has manifested this auspicious sign."

Proceeding in order, he arrived at the place where the mango trees were. Someone presented a mango fruit, perfect in both fragrance and flavor, to the king; the king offered it to Mahinda. Mahinda ate it, took the seed, and said to the king:
"You may plant this seed."
The king immediately planted them and sprinkled water upon the ground; the earth shook all over.
The king asked, "For what reason does the earth tremble?"
The Venerable One said, "In a future age, this will be the place where the Saṃgha assembles; therefore, these auspicious signs have appeared.
The King then scattered flowers eight times, prostrated himself, and departed.

Upon arriving at the site of Cetiya, someone offered a *campaka* flower to the King; he then paid homage at the place where Mahinda had made his offering, and as soon as he finished prostrating, the earth shook.
The King asked, "Why has the earth shaken?"
The Venerable One replied:
"A great stūpa for the Tathāgata shall be erected at this site in the future; therefore, this auspicious omen has appeared.
The King said:
"I shall now establish a stūpa," [the king said]. Mahinda replied, "There is no need for the King to establish one;
the King has many projects to attend to. In a future age, there will be a descendant of the King named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, who shall erect a great stūpa."
The king asked the Venerable One,
"Will I obtain the merit from the deed of my grandson building this stūpa?
The Venerable One replied:
"It shall not be obtained.
The King again devised a skillful means to cause [the merit] to enter his store of merit; he immediately took a stone pillar twelve *zhang* high and inscribed upon it:
"My grandson, named Mukhacūḍāmaṇy-abhaya, shall come hereafter to erect a great stūpa within this place."
The King asked the Venerable One again:
"Venerable One!
Has the root and trunk of the Buddha-dharma now taken hold in the Kingdom of Siṃhala?"
Maha Māyāntika replied, "No.
The king asked:
"When was it established?
The Venerable replied:
"If one goes forth among the people of Siṃhala, both his father and mother must be Siṃhalese and not of mixed descent with people of other nations."
"Once he has gone forth, he will take up the Dharma-piṭaka and the Vinaya-piṭaka; it is only then that the root and trunk of the Buddha-dharma will take hold in the Land of Lions.
The King questioned the Mahāsthavira again, and the Mahāsthavira replied, "The King's nephew Abhaya is this bhikṣu; he is exceedingly courageous and resolute regarding the Buddha-dharma."
The king asked again:
"What, then, shall I do now?
The Venerable One replied:
"Let the assembly of monks gather in the hall," the King replied,
"Very well."
"At that time, the great king had a minister named Meghabhāṇḍa.
In the residence of Meghabhāṇḍa, he constructed an assembly hall that was no different from the palace of King Ajātaśatru."
Having performed this through the majestic power of the king, all manner of musical instruments were each spontaneously distributed throughout their respective locations.
The king thought to himself:
"I shall now go to behold the root of the Buddha-Dharma."
"Several hundred thousand people surrounded the Great King and proceeded to the monastery garden.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Three;
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra from the foreign lands during the Xiao Qi period:
"At that time, within the monastery grounds, Mahinda was together with one thousand bhikṣus.

He spread out his sitting mat and sat facing south; he also spread out a mat for the Venerable Abhaya to sit facing north. The Venerable Mahinda requested the Venerable Abhaya to serve as the Dharma-preacher. Abhaya, following the precedent of the former Venerable Upāli without deviation, took his place. Mahinda was surrounded by sixty-eight members of the Great Sangha as they encircled the Dharma-seat."

The King’s younger brother, the bhikṣu named Madhuvāsiṣṭha, together with five hundred bhikṣus, desired to study the Vinaya Piṭaka; they all surrounded the high seat of Ābhyaśoka, while the other bhikṣus and the king sat down in their respective order.
Then the Venerable Ābhāsvara immediately spoke for him, saying:
"At that time, the Buddha was dwelling at Pīlanjana-aliṇḍa-vana on the island of Mandāra trees, preaching the Vinaya."
Having finished this narration, a great cry arose from the heavens in the void:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
At that time, there was thunder and lightning out of season, and the earth shook violently amidst various miraculous manifestations.

Then, the Venerable Arittha and Mahinda, together with sixty monks who had attained the destruction of craving, surrounded by sixty thousand bhikṣus, proclaimed the virtues of the Tathāgata within the Thūpārāma monastery.

Out of compassion for the unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind of sentient beings, the Tathāgata taught the Vinaya Piṭaka to subdue the actions of body, speech, and mind. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he had finished teaching the Vinaya Piṭaka to his śrāvaka disciples, and only thereafter did he enter parinirvāṇa without remainder.
At that time, from within the assembly, a verse was spoken:
"All dwelling apart from the community, The sixty-eight of great virtue who together know the matters of the Vinaya-piṭaka— These are the Śrāvaka followers of the Dharma King."
Having attained mastery through the exhaustion of craving, possessing supernormal powers and the three types of penetrating knowledge,
he used supreme wisdom to teach and transform the Lion King.
His light illuminated the Land of Lions, pervading everywhere so that nothing remained unseen.
"Just as a great mass of fire, when its fuel is exhausted, enters nirvana.

"After the Great Virtuous One entered nirvana, his disciples and followers—namely Tiṣya Datta, Kālasumana, and Vigasumana—were the disciples of the Great Virtuous Ābhaya. In this manner, the lineage was passed down from teacher to teacher until the present day. Therefore, at the third council, it was asked within the assembly:
'Who brought the Vinaya Piṭaka to the Lion Island (Sīhaladvīpa)?'"
He replied:
"This was Maṅgala; after Maṅgala came Abbaya, and Abbaya’s disciple—thus it was received and maintained in succession."

For example, it is like a vessel of white lapis lazuli filled with water, which is transparent both inside and out so that no water leaks away; so too it is with the venerable ones who uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Thus it continues down to the present day: if there are those who possess faith, constantly maintain a sense of shame and remorse, and take pleasure in studying the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time.
Therefore, if a person wishes for the Buddha-dharma to endure long, they must first study the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Why is this? Because there are those who practice for the benefit of others.
What is meant by "benefit"?
If a son of good family leaves the household life with a sincere heart, the Vinaya-piṭaka is his father and mother.

Why is this? It is because it grants him the going-forth and enables him to attain full ordination; it teaches him the rules of deportment; by relying on the Vinaya-piṭaka, he maintains the precepts himself and can sever the doubts of others; when entering the Saṃgha, he is free from fear; and if a transgression occurs, he can adjudicate according to the Vinaya, ensuring that the Dharma endures for a long time.
The Dharma masters said:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'If you receive and uphold this Vinaya, there are five benefits.'"

What are these five? First, being able to maintain the precepts oneself; second, being able to sever the doubts of others; third, entering the Saṃgha without fear; fourth, establishing the Buddha-dharma; and fifth, causing the Dharma to endure for a long time.
The Buddha said that one who upholds the Vinaya is the very root of merit; because of this root, one gathers and masters all dharmas.
The Dharma Master said:
"The Buddha taught the precepts for the purpose of ceasing evil causes. Because evil is ceased, a mind free from regret arises. Because of this mind free from regret, joy is born."
Because of joy, one attains the birth of peace and happiness.
Because of peace and happiness, one attains the birth of samādhi.
Because of samādhi, one attains the birth of the eye of wisdom.
Because the eye of wisdom arises, one develops revulsion toward defilements.
Because of this revulsion, one attains freedom from desire.
Because of freedom from desire, one gives rise to liberation.
Because of liberation, one attains the knowledge of liberation.
Because of the knowledge of liberation, one sequentially enters nirvana.

For the sake of speaking, for the sake of explaining, for the sake of reliance, and for the sake of hearing—in this sequence, the mind attains the knowledge of liberation. Therefore, one should diligently study the Vinaya.
"This is the fundamental teaching spoken in the Vinaya.
The Dharma Master said:
"And he spoke in verse:"
"If a person at such a time, for what reason should they uphold [this], and where will that person go or abide?
Having thus spoken, it is now explained in sequence.
"This is the meaning of the verse; now I shall explain the introductory section outside the Vinaya.

'At that time' marks the beginning, though its meanings are not of one kind. I shall now expound the meaning of the Vinaya; therefore, it is said in the Vinaya: 'At that time, the Buddha was staying at Pāvā.'"
Regarding the first meaning: at that time, the Venerable Śāriputra arose from samādhi and requested the Buddha to establish the precepts.
At that time, the Buddha was residing at Pīlava.
"At that time" carries the sense of an occasion or an initiation.
"At that time" refers to the specific event being described.

Why is this so? As stated in the Vinaya, at that time Sūdena committed an impure act with his former wife; it was on account of Sūdena that the Buddha established the precepts for the śrāvakas. This is the first meaning.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ḍanika stole royal timber; at that time, the Buddha established a precept in Rājagṛha in a similar manner.
"At that time" (tadā) carries both the sense of an introductory narrative and the sense of a causal condition.
"Buddha Bhagavān" will be explained later.
"Dwelling" refers to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
"Verañjā" is the name of a country.
Nāḷīra is a name for a yakṣa; it is so called because the yakṣa-demon dwells in this tree.
Piñjūla-mandāra is the name for the *lián* (練) wood tree.
"Under a tree" refers to a place covered by the shadow when the sun is at its zenith.
It is also said:
"It is the place where leaves fall to the ground when there is no wind."
Question: "Why does the Tathāgata dwell beneath this tree? Answer:
"This tree is lush and flourishing, the foremost within the grove; it is not far from the city, making it convenient for coming and going.
He asked, "The Tathāgata dwells in the Pārileyyaka forest, yet you say he dwells under a tree; the Tathāgata should not dwell in two places at once."
He replied:
"Do not raise this objection.
A *vilanja* is a place for coming and going; the space beneath the tree is the actual dwelling place."
Question: "Why did Upāli speak of Vairaṇyā? Answer:
“Out of compassion for those in white robes. He asked,
“Why do you dwell under trees?”
He replied:
"It is for the sake of the disciples, so that they may follow the dharma of renunciation and eliminate craving. He asked:
"Why does it rely upon and stay near the country?
He replied,
"It is for the sake of the four great elements."
Question: "The former phrase is for the purpose of preaching the Dharma; the latter phrase is because the Tathāgata wishes to enter stillness.
The former phrase is drawn forth by compassion; the latter phrase is because one enters from suffering into bliss."
The former phrase is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings; the latter phrase is for the sake of one’s own peace and happiness.
The former phrase is for the sake of bestowing the Dharma upon sentient beings; the latter phrase is for the sake of personally fulfilling one's own noble benefit.
The former phrase is for the sake of acting as a bridge for sentient beings; the latter phrase is for the sake of all devas and humans.
Regarding the former phrase, it refers to being identical with sentient beings; regarding the latter phrase, it refers to not being identical with sentient beings.

As for the former phrase, the Buddha alone is uniquely honored throughout the three realms, and because sentient beings rely upon the Buddha, they attain great peace and happiness—this is called "one.
As for the latter phrase, it refers to the Buddha’s birth occurring within a forest, where he delighted beneath the trees.
The Dharma Master said:
"This meaning is very extensive; I shall now explain it briefly.

Regarding 'together with a great community of bhikṣus': it is called 'great' because greatness arises from smallness; thus, the merit of the community of bhikṣus is so immense that it is termed 'great.'"
Furthermore, there is a great significance: even those of the lowest capacity attain the path of *srotāpanna*.
Furthermore, there is a great significance: because a great assembly of five hundred has gathered.
As for the Sangha, they are equal in precepts, equal in views, equal in wisdom, and equal in the community; this is what constitutes the Sangha.
"Together" means being in one place at the same time.
"Five hundred bhikṣus" refers to the number five hundred.
"The Brahmin Vairaṇyā" was born in the country of Vairaṇya; he was named after that country.
"Brahmaṇa" means pure conduct.
Furthermore, "brahma" refers to knowing the Vedic scriptures of the non-Buddhists, while "maṇa" means hearing.
According to the Buddhist sūtras, a "brahmaṇa" is one who can eliminate afflictions; "maṇa" means listening. When sound reaches the ears, one comes to know the Dharma through the words of others.
The śramaṇa Gautama is one who has extinguished unwholesome dharmas.
"Gautama" is how the brāhmaṇas address him by his clan name.
"Sakyan seed" and "of the Sakya clan" point to his illustrious lineage.
"Leaving the Śākya clan to go forth into homelessness—this refers to going forth out of a mind of inspired faith and joy.

There are those who go forth because they owe debts, those who go forth because they have lost their kingdoms, those who go forth because of poverty, or those who go forth to avoid royal conscription; the Tathāgata did not go forth in such a manner."
"Thus, one who has a good reputation"—this is the phrase "thus," which serves as a concluding particle.
"Good" means being endowed with all virtues and further signifies being supreme.
"Reputation" means receiving renown through praise, and furthermore implies making it known to others.
"Bhagavān" is the first of the ten titles of the Tathāgata; it causes sentient beings to place faith in the Buddha, and for this reason, the Dharma Master proclaims the merits of the Tathāgata.

“*A-ra* refers to the spokes of the chariot of the three realms; *han* means to strike and destroy. Because the Tathāgata strikes and destroys the spokes of the chariot of the three realms, he is called an Arhat.”
Furthermore, it is said:
"A-ra means 'slayer of thieves. Because the Tathāgata has slain the thieves of the afflictions (kleśa), he is therefore called an Arhat.
It is also said:
"Ā" refers to all evil karma;
"han" refers to dwelling far away.

The three realms constitute the chariot; ignorance and craving as conditions for volitional formations are the spokes; old age and death are the rim; birth is the hub; and the various afflictions are the axle.

In the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, which flows on without ceasing, the Buddha, beneath the Bodhi tree, took the precepts as his level ground, diligence as his feet, a sincere mind as his hands, and wisdom as his axe, thereby hewing off the spokes of the chariot of the triple world.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The world without beginning is the chariot; ignorance is the hub, old age and death are the rim, and the ten unwholesome actions are the spokes. Why is this so?"
Not knowing the nature of suffering,
if one is born in the desire realm, one performs the three types of karma due to ignorance;
if one is born in the form realm, one performs karma of the form realm.
If one is born in the formless realm, one performs karma of the formless realm.
Within the desire realm, consciousness arises conditioned by ignorance; it is the same within the form realm; and within the formless realm, it is also conditioned by ignorance.
Furthermore, regarding name-and-form within the desire realm: name-and-form in the desire realm has as its condition the six sense bases conditioned by ignorance;
name-and-form in the desire realm and three sense bases in the form realm have as their condition ignorance within the formless realm.
Within the form realm, one base conditions the six bases of the desire realm; within the desire realm, the six contacts condition three bases of the form realm.
Within the form realm, three contacts condition one base of the formless realm;
within the formless realm, one feeling conditions the six contacts of the desire realm.
The six pleasures of the desire realm take the three contacts within the form realm as their object;

the three pleasures within the form realm take the one contact within the formless realm as their object; and the one pleasure within the formless realm takes the six pleasures of the desire realm as its object.

The six pleasures of the desire realm give rise to six types of craving; the three pleasures within the form realm serve as the objects for three types of craving in the form realm; the single pleasure within the formless realm serves as the object for one type of craving in the formless realm; and [the pleasures] serve as the objects for craving directed toward all locations.

Born within birth, if a person among the five desires possesses unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind because they desire to engage in sensual pleasure and experience it for themselves, they will immediately enter hell.
Within the hells, due to karma, one undergoes birth after birth; this is birth by way of karma (*karmaja*).

From karma the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise, and subsequently the five aggregates age. That which ages becomes decayed, and the disintegration of the five aggregates is what is called death.

Within the three realms, I desire sensual pleasures; I practice desire within the heavens, performing wholesome deeds or practicing patience. Because of these wholesome deeds, I am born in the heavens; this is because of the cause of wholesome karma that I am born again.
There was a person who, desiring to experience the bliss of Brahmā, recollected four dharmas because of that desire for the experience of bliss.
What are these four? They are loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
When one’s mental recollection is fully perfected, one attains birth in the Brahma Heaven.
Within the Brahma Heaven, because one is born due to karma, this is "birth by karma.

Furthermore, there is another person who thinks, "I wish to be born in the formless realm; I shall next be born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception," and constantly enters meditative concentration and reflection; they are then born in that place—this is birth attained through karma.
"The remaining sequence you should know for yourself.

"In both the past and future worlds, everything proceeds from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations; I have now explained this briefly, and you should explain the rest in detail for yourself."
Ignorance conditions volitional formations; this constitutes one category.
The six consciousnesses, name-and-form, the six sense bases, the six contacts, and the six feelings; these constitute another category.
Craving, clinging, and birth constitute one category;
existence and old age and death constitute another category.
The former category refers to the past life; the middle two categories refer to the present life; and the latter category, old age and death, refers to the future life.
When grasping (upādāna) is conditioned by ignorance (avidyā), it is invariably accompanied by craving (tṛṣṇā) and feeling (vedanā); these five factors belong to the past life.

With the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) as the first [of the middle group], this is the fruit of retribution; if grasping is accompanied by craving and feeling, these five factors constitute the present birth of karma.

Regarding birth and death, there are all five aggregates (*pañca-dharma*) and the remaining six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), which enter from beginning to end; this constitutes birth in a future life.
"If explained through detailed classification, there are twenty-four kinds."

Conditioned by the formations, there are the six consciousnesses; between these two is one category. Between sensation and craving is one category. Regarding birth and existence, between these two is one category. Altogether, there are three categories and four segments; because of these categories, twenty kinds of fundamental causes and conditions arise.
The Tathāgata has already seen, observed, and delivered [beings]; because he knows them with reality, he is called "one who knows truly" by virtue of his knowledge of reality.
As for "seeing," what is meant by seeing?
Because the seer penetrates [reality], it is called "seeing.
As for "contemplation" (vipaśyanā), what is meant by contemplation?
Because one universally knows all things, it is called "contemplation."

Having attained deliverance through the vision of knowledge, and having known the reality of the Tathāgata, one conceives a sense of weary detachment and gives rise to the mind of renunciation, desiring liberation. Because one first destroys the spokes of the chariot of the three realms, one is called an Arhat.
Furthermore, the name "Arhat" means "one who is worthy of offerings.
He asked: "What is meant by being 'worthy of offerings'?"
"Because he receives the offerings of devas and humans, he is called 'Worthy of Offerings' (Arhat).
In the past, there was a Brahmā King who offered to the Tathāgata jewels as large as Mount Sumeru; for this reason, he is called 'Worthy of Offerings.'"
At that time, the great kings of the world, such as King Bimbisāra and King Kośala, again made various kinds of offerings; thus he was named "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the great king of Jambudvīpa named Aśoka again used nine hundred and sixty billion gold coins to erect eighty-four thousand jeweled stūpas and further practiced great and manifold acts of giving; thus he was named "Worthy of Offerings."
The rest of the great assembly who made offerings were beyond measure and calculation.
Furthermore, it was said:
"Regarding 'Arhat,' 'rahan' has the meaning of concealment; 'a' means non-existence, thus it is named 'without concealment.'"
What is meant by "being without concealment"?

For example, when worldly people commit a transgression, they constantly conceal it from themselves; because the Tathāgata is forever free from such [transgressions], he is said to be "without concealment."
“Regarding ‘Samyaksaṃbuddha’: because he thoroughly knows all phenomena (dharmas), he is called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
As for ‘Buddha’: he knows the phenomena that should be known; he abandons the phenomena that should be abandoned; and he emerges from those that should be emerged from—this is called a Buddha.”
Furthermore, it is said that "Buddha" has another meaning.

What is it? If one perceives the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of Origination, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path with the eye of wisdom, seeing them clearly and in their proper sequence, such a person is a Buddha.
Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness;
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact;
and the mental noting of the eye, the mental noting of the ear, the mental noting of the nose, and the mental noting of the tongue.

The mental noting of the body and the mental noting of the mind; mindfulness of the eye, mindfulness of the ear, mindfulness of the nose, mindfulness of the tongue, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of the mind;
craving for the eye, craving for the ear, craving for the nose, craving for the tongue, craving for the body, and craving for the mind;
and volition regarding the eye, volition regarding the ear, volition regarding the nose, volition regarding the tongue, volition regarding the body, and volition regarding the mind.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) consist of ten contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), ten reflections (*cintā*), and ten recollections (*anusmṛti*). Beginning with the bloated corpse (*vyādhmātaka*), there are ten such [contemplations].
Beginning with the [corpse] cut into pieces (*vikhādita*), there are thirty-two. There are the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Beginning with the desire for birth, there are the nine and four dhyānas, beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Furthermore, there are the four formless meditations (*ārūpyadhyāna*), the four formless samādhis, and the forty-two links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One contemplates them in reverse order from old age, death, sorrow, and lamentation back to ignorance, and then contemplates them in successive order up to the suffering and affliction of old age, sickness, and death.
Old age and sickness are the truth of suffering;
existence is the truth of the origin;
that which emerges from these two is called the truth of cessation.
Knowing the cessation through skillful means is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows all things one by one; this is why he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This "knowing" consists of three kinds of knowledge and also eight kinds of knowledge; that there are eight kinds of knowledge is taught in the *Tridhātuka-sūtra*, which you should know for yourself.
Furthermore, according to the *Āmrapālī-sūtra*, the knowledge of samādhi, the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the six higher knowledges together constitute eight knowledges.

"The perfection of conduct" refers to either the concealment of the six consciousnesses, moderation in food and drink, moderation in sleep, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the four dhyānas; these are the fifteen dharmas that one should know for oneself.
The Tathāgata practices by means of the Dharma; therefore, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct.
The Tathāgata proceeds to Nirvāṇa by means of this practice of the Dharma; therefore, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct.
It is not only the Tathāgata who is so; the Śrāvakas are likewise.
The Tathāgata is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (vidyācaraṇasampanna) because he is fulfilled through the knowledge of practice.
Because of his knowledge of characteristics, the Tathāgata attains all-knowledge (sarvajñatā); because of his practice, he is named Great Compassion (mahāmaitrīkaruṇā).

All sentient beings are nothing but a collection of suffering and affliction; the Tathāgata knows this all. Because of his great compassion, he understands the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings and is able to skillfully teach them so that they may abandon suffering and attain happiness; for this reason, he is called the Sugata.
Therefore, the Śrāvaka is a Sugata who proceeds as a Sugata, not as a non-Sugata.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who proceeds to the supreme destination is called a Sugata."
Furthermore, because his gait is level and upright and his majestic deportment is complete and without deficiency, he is also called Sugata.
Moreover, because he has gone to abide eternally and will never return again, he is named Sugata.
Because the path of the Arhat does not reach [the ultimate], he is named Sugata.

From the time he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he has compassionately sought to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; even until his time at the foot of the Bodhi tree, his virtuous conduct was such as this, and thus he is named Sugata.

Not following the view of annihilationism, nor following the view of eternalism; with the body free from weariness and suffering, not falling into annihilationism or eternalism—he is called the Sugata.
He preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings without failing to meet the proper time—he is called the Sugata.
He does not speak of what sentient beings do not delight in, but speaks of what they do delight in; thus he is called the Sugata.
All that he speaks is of true meaning and not of false meaning; furthermore, when all sentient beings hear it, they are all made to rejoice; thus he is called the Sugata.
Furthermore, he does not speak words that are meaningless; whatever he speaks is always meaningful and beneficial, and for this reason he is called the Sugata.
As for "Knower of the World," because he knows all worldly dharmas, he is named the Knower of the World.
Because of the truth of origination, because of the truth of cessation, because of the means to cessation, and because of the understanding of the world, this is called "understanding of the world.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Neither born, nor aged, nor dead, neither falling away nor abiding—without having to travel, I have reached the further shore of the world; this is called 'understanding of the world.'"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"I have not yet reached the ultimate limit of the world; I do not say that suffering has been exhausted.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"This body, measuring one fathom, is called a śramaṇa; yet it is impossible that by practicing the worldly truth of origination, the worldly truth of cessation, and the worldly truth of suffering, one could reach what has not yet been reached and emerge from suffering. Such a thing cannot be."
Furthermore, there are three kinds of "worlds.
What are these three?
First, the world of formations; second, the world of sentient beings; and third, the world of locations.
Question: "What is meant by 'practicing in the world'? Answer:
"All sentient beings are born from food and drink; this is what constitutes the world of conditioned existence (*saṃsāra*).
“What is meant by the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*)?
He replied:
"The eternal world and the impermanent world—these constitute the world of sentient beings.
"What is meant by the 'dwelling world'?
He answered in verse:
"The sun and moon soar aloft, illuminating the world; their radiance is peerless, without any obstruction.
This is how they abide in the world."
Furthermore, it is said:
"One world, two worlds, three worlds, four worlds, five worlds, six worlds, seven worlds, eight worlds, nine worlds, ten worlds, and so on, up to eighteen worlds."
Question: "What is meant by 'one world'? Answer:
"All sentient beings obtain life through food and drink; this is called the first world.
"What is meant by the second world? Answer:
"Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) constitutes the two worlds.
"What is meant by the three worlds?
He replied:
"Suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—these are the three worlds.
"What are the four worlds? He replied:
"The four nutriments constitute the four worlds.
What are the five worlds? He replied:
"The five aggregates.
"What are called the six worldly realms?
He replied:
“The six sense bases.
“What are called the seven worldly states? He replied:
"Seven consciousnesses.
"What are the eight worldly dharmas?
He replied:
"The eight worldly dharmas.
"What are the nine worldly [dharmas]?
He replied:
"The nine abodes of sentient beings.
"What are the ten worldly realms?
He replied:
“There are ten bases (āyatana).
“What are the twelve worldly [bases]? He replied:
“The twelve bases (āyatana).
“What are called the eighteen worldly dharmas?
He replied:
“The eighteen elements—these constitute the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-loka*).
The Tathāgata knows each and every one of them; therefore, he is called the Knower of the World (*loka-vidū*).”

The Tathāgata understands the afflictions of sentient beings; he understands their conduct, he understands their intentions, and he understands both minor and major afflictions. He understands sharp faculties and dull faculties, he understands wholesome conditions and unwholesome conditions, he understands those who should be made to know and those who should not be made to know, and he understands both birth and non-birth. This is called knowing all that exists within the world of sentient beings; this is what constitutes being a Knower of the World.
"One who dwells in the world.
He asked: "What is meant by 'dwelling in the world'?"
He replied:

"The Cakravāḍa Mountains are twenty-three thousand four hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and three million seven hundred and three hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference. The earth is forty-two thousand yojanas thick, resting upon the water; the water is eighty-four thousand yojanas thick, resting upon the wind; and the wind is six hundred and ninety thousand yojanas thick. This is the extent of the world-system."

Furthermore, the base of Mount Sumeru enters the ocean for eighty-four thousand yojanas; the height of the King of Mountains, Sumeru, is likewise. It is encircled by seven precious jewels and surrounded by seven mountain ranges.
And he spoke these verses:
“By Gandhāra, Iṣadhāra, Kālapika, Sutasoma, Nimindhara, Vinataka.”
The seven great mountains, Aśvakarṇa and the rest, surround Sumeru;
there dwell the Four Great Kings and the celestial yakṣas, rising one hundred yojanas high.
A great mountain of piled snow, a thousand yojanas in extent, equal in its length and breadth,
with eighty-four thousand peaks adorning its summit.
There is a Jambū tree, two thousand li in height and two hundred li in circumference;
its branches spread out in all directions, covering an area of one hundred yojanas.
Because of this tree, the land is called Jambudvīpa.
Its depth extends eighty thousand yojanas below, and its height is likewise;
eternally abiding and indestructible, it completely encircles the world.
It is forty-nine *yojanas* in circumference; the disk of the Sun King is fifty *yojanas* in circumference.
Furthermore, the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, is ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; the palaces of the asuras are likewise so, as are the Avīci hell and the land of Jambudvīpa.
Aparagoyānī is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; Pūrvavideha is likewise; and Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Each continent is surrounded by five hundred minor continents; this is within the Cakravāḍa Mountains.

Between the Cakravāḍas, all is hell. The Cakravāḍas are immeasurable, and the worlds are likewise immeasurable. Therefore, because the Buddha perceives everything with his immeasurable eye of wisdom, he is called the Knower of the World (*Lokavid*).
"As for the 'Unsurpassed One' (Anuttara): because his own merit surpasses that of humans and devas, he is named the Unsurpassed One;

because he is fully endowed with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he is named the Unsurpassed One. Therefore, the unsurpassed and the one who is unsurpassed are identical."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"I do not see anyone in the world—whether among Brahmā, Māra, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—who can equal me in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, or liberation; furthermore, I have no teacher. Therefore, I am called 'Unsurpassed'."
“Regarding the ‘Tamer of Men’ (Puruṣadamyasārathi): whenever there is one who ought to be tamed, he immediately tames them.
Why is this? It is like an elephant or a horse that is headstrong; only after being struck with a staff or a whip is it subsequently subdued.”
The Tathāgata is likewise thus; because he is able to tame all sentient beings, he is called the "Tamer" (Vināyaka).
In the past, the Buddha subdued various animals, nāga kings, and male beings, such as Apalāla;

among male beings, there were also Cūḍapanthaka, Makhādeva, Ajita, Tiṣya, Tissadatta, and others. The Buddha tamed these male beings through wholesome dharmas, causing them to enter the True Dharma and receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
There were also men such as the son of the Nirgrantha, Śarabha, as well as the Brahmin Tiṣyaka, Aṅgulimāla, and others, numbering in the tens of millions.

Furthermore, there were yakṣa males named Āravaka, Śūcimukha, Pāpamāna, and Khara; these and countless other celestial beings, such as the yakṣa males and Śakra Devendra, were disciplined by means of the True Dharma.
In the Sūtras it is said that the Buddha’s words were entrusted to Śuka—whose name in the Han language means "elephant trainer"—who declared:
"I am the Tamer of Men; I teach all sentient beings by means of gentle methods."
If they do not accept [the teaching], one should instruct them by means of forceful methods;
if they still do not accept it, one should further instruct them with both firmness and gentleness;
if they still do not accept it, then one does not enter into harmony with them.
The Dharma Master said:
"This sutra should be explained extensively according to the Dharma; therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men.
He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans. 'Teacher' is like a caravan leader who is well-acquainted with the dangers and difficulties."
He asked, "What are these hardships? [The other replied:
"First, the hardship of bandits; second, the hardship of tigers, wolves, and lions; third, the hardship of famine; and fourth, the hardship of lack of water."
The Lord, amidst all hardships, enables all to cross over and reach the place of peace and bliss; therefore, he is called the Teacher.
The Tathāgata is likewise. Why is this so?
“The Tathāgata is able to deliver sentient beings, enabling them to pass beyond perils and difficulties.
“What are these perils and difficulties?
“The first is the peril of birth; the second is the peril of illness; the third is the peril of old age; and the fourth is the peril of death.”
"Such various perils as these, the Tathāgata is able to deliver one from and lead them to a place of peace and happiness;
therefore, he is called the Teacher. He asked:
"Why does the Buddha alone serve as the Teacher of gods and humans, and not as the Teacher of animals?"
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the world, he also preached the Dharma for animals;
why then is he called solely the Teacher of Gods and Humans? The Sūtra says:
"At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Campā, by the side of the Kālaka pond, preaching the Dharma to the people of Campā."
At that time, there was a frog in the pond who, hearing the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma, rejoiced and immediately emerged from the pond to go beneath the roots of a grass.

At that moment, a cowherd, seeing the great assembly surrounding the Buddha to listen to his teaching of the Dharma, went to where the Buddha was; desiring to hear the Dharma, he prodded the ground with his staff and, by mistake, struck the frog on its head.
The oyster immediately passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Gods.

By virtue of his karmic reward, his palace measured exactly twelve yojanas in length and breadth. Thereupon, the celestial being formerly an oyster suddenly attained awakening; seeing the various female musicians and the sounds of their entertainment, he reflected as soon as he had awakened:
"I was previously an animal; by what causes and conditions have I been born in this celestial palace?"
He then observed with his divine eye that [the frog] had previously listened to the Buddha preach the Dharma by the side of the pond; by virtue of this merit, he obtained this karmic reward.
The frog-deva immediately mounted a celestial palace and went to where the Buddha was, prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked:
"Who are you that suddenly prostrates at my feet?
Your supernormal powers, radiance, and marks of excellence are peerless, illuminating this entire place."
The Śaṅkha devaputra replied with a verse:
“In former times I had the body of a clam; Seeking food within the water, I heard the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma, And emerged to take refuge beneath the roots of a grass.”
"There was a cowherd who came to listen to the Dharma carrying a staff;
the staff pricked my head, and upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the heavens.
Then the Buddha, using the verse spoken by the frog and the celestial being, preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people within the assembly all attained the fruit of the Path, while the frog-deva attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Having thus attained the fruit of the Path, the frog-deva departed with a joyful smile upon his face.
Therefore, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Regarding "Buddha Bhagavān": "Buddha" means self-awakened, and being able to awaken others as well, he is named Buddha.
It is further said that he "knows.
What is meant by "knowing"?
Because he knows the Truths, he is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that one who awakens the world is called a Buddha.
This should be understood from the *Tri-vidyā-jñāna Sūtra* itself:
"The term Bhagavān has four meanings: first, benefit; second, unsurpassed; third, reverence; and fourth, honor."
Why is it called "reverence and respect"?
Because one is worthy of reverence and respect by the world.
There are four names for the world:
"First is following, second is recording, third is cause, and fourth is designation.
He asked: "What is meant by the name 'following'?"
He replied:
"Just as people in the world call a small ox a 'calf,' then a 'young bull' when it is older, and a 'bull' when it is large, these names are not fixed; they are called according to the time."
Question: "What is meant by 'the name of the mark'? Answer:
"Just as when a person holds an umbrella or a staff, they are called 'the one with an umbrella' or 'the one with a staff,' this is what constitutes a designation based on a mark.
He asked: "What is meant by a cause?"
He replied:
"For example, it is like a poor man who obtains a treasure because of his servant; therefore, he names the servant 'Much Treasure' (Prabhūtaratna).
This is naming based on a cause. 'Bhagavān' is a title."
Why is this? It was not King Śuddhodana who gave him this name; nor did his eighty thousand kinsmen give it; nor did Śakra, the Lord of Devas, nor those such as the Tuṣita devas, Brahmā, or Māra.
Why is this? The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"My name was not made by my parents, nor by the eighty thousand attendants, nor by Śakra, nor by the Tuṣita gods, Brahmā, or Māra. It was explained in sequence; beneath the Bodhi tree, having attained equal omniscience and perceived it with true insight, only the Bhagavān himself [bestowed] it. Therefore, the Buddha made the name for himself."
"No one dared to establish a name for the Buddha.
Why was this? Because the Buddha himself, observing the majesty, virtue, and wisdom of his own body, manifested them so that sentient beings might know him and thus establish a name."
Regarding "Bhagavān": *bhaga* means "to transcend";
*vān* means "existence. Because he has transcended existence, he is called Bhagavān.
Furthermore, it is said:

Greed, hatred, delusion, and the perverted mind; lack of shame and lack of dread; *upanāha* (in the Chinese language, "fury" or "intense anger"); lack of joy; malice toward others; jealousy; a hollow mind, a crooked mind, and a clouded mind; arrogance and extreme arrogance; intoxication; indolence; craving, ignorance, and the unwholesome roots; impurities and defilements; unevenly directed thoughts and the four perversions; the floods, bonds, attachments, and the five aggregates of grasping—of which contact is the first; the five hindrances; the sixfold strife of mindfulness; disputes; the root of craving and the afflictions of sentient beings; the eight wrong views, the nine roots of craving, the ten paths of unwholesome action, the sixty-two views, and the one hundred and eight afflictions; the exhaustion of thirst and the myriad afflictions—in brief, these are the five clusters of affliction.
"Devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—such multitudes as these cannot destroy the Tathāgata; therefore, he is called Bhagavat.
It is further said:
"The Tathāgata can destroy and eliminate desire, hatred, all forms of delusion, the afflictions, the outflows, and evil dharmas; therefore, he is called Bhagavat."
Furthermore, he said:

"The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics; his marks and characteristics are peerless, and being free from all afflictions, gods, humans, and those of the world constantly desire to be reborn there."
"Having arrived, the Buddha observes sentient beings and, according to what their minds delight in, he immediately teaches them; for this reason, he is called Bhagavān.

There are six kinds of *bhaga* in the world: first, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); second, dharma (*dharma*); third, fame (*yaśas*); fourth, excellence (*śrī*); fifth, desire (*kāma*); and sixth, wisdom (*jñāna*)."
Question: "What is meant by 'receiving'? Answer:
"Because one governs one's own mind.
"What is meant by 'Dharma'?
He replied:
"Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is fully endowed with all [qualities].
"What is meant by 'name'? Answer:
“The name of the Buddha is ‘Pure,’ because there is nowhere he does not pervade.
“What is meant by ‘sublime’?
He replied:
“The Buddha’s body is endowed with all subtle refinements, for one never tires of beholding it.
[The questioner asks: “What is meant by ‘desire’? He replied:
"When the Buddha wishes to go somewhere, he arrives there as soon as he thinks of it, because he desires to act for his own sake and for the sake of others.
"What is meant by 'mindfulness' (smṛti)? He replied:
"Because all sentient beings make offerings with a mindful heart, he is called Bhagavān.
Furthermore, it is said:
'Bhagavān means "the one who discerns. "
Question: "What is meant by 'discrimination'? Answer:

"Beginning with merit, one discriminates all dharmas—the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), the eighteen elements (dhātus), the four truths (satyas), the six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)—discerning and understanding each one individually."
The oppression of suffering and its instability is the Truth of Suffering;
attachment and the failure to relinquish the aggregates is the Truth of Origination;
the cessation of the sensation of suffering is the Truth of Cessation.
To emerge through causes and conditions is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Because he distinguishes [the teachings] in this way, he is named Bhagavat.
Furthermore, regarding "Bhagavat": *bhaga* refers to the three realms, and *vat* means to vomit forth; [thus, he is so named because he has vomited forth the three realms].
Because he has vomited out the afflictions of the three realms, he is named Bhagavān.
As for the world, it consists of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; this is called the world.

"Devas and humans" refers to the devas of the six heavens of desire; "Māra" refers to the [devas of] the six heavens; "Brahmā" refers to the *Pūrvavideha* heaven; and "śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas" refers to those who are enemies of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, as for "devas and humans," the various kings of the world are also included among devas and humans.
Moreover, "devas and humans" encompasses the devas and humans of the desire realm;
"Māra" encompasses the realm of the celestial Māras.
"Brahmā" refers to the formless Brahmā heavens;
"śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas" includes the fourfold assembly of the world.

This is because [the Tathāgata] encompasses both the higher and lower realms, fully entering into the merits of the Tathāgata, and is able to penetrate all such places. One who "knows by oneself" is so called because they know for themselves how to preach the Dharma, knowing it through their own skillful means.
To know by means of the eye of wisdom is what is called "knowing.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Knowing is called knowing because it is unobstructed."
"To speak" means to awaken others so that they may know; this is what is meant by "speaking.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Because it opens up all phenomena, it is called speaking."
Question: "For what reason does the Buddha teach for the sake of sentient beings? Answer:

"Because one gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, one delivers them to unsurpassed peace and happiness; to preach the Dharma for sentient beings—whether it be a single phrase, a single verse, or more or less than that—is what is called 'preaching.'"
It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is subtle and exquisite, pure and unadulterated, complete in all respects, and entirely of one flavor.
Furthermore, it says:
"The first chapter is good in the beginning, the middle chapter is good in the middle, and the final chapter is good in the end."
He further said:
"The precepts are good in the beginning; attaining the Way through samādhi is good in the middle; and nirvāṇa is good in the end.
He also said:
"Precepts are the excellence of the beginning of samādhi; meditative concentration and the Path are the excellence of the middle; and the fruit and nirvāṇa are the excellence of the end.

The Buddha is 'awakening well,' which is called the excellence of the beginning; the Dharma is 'good Dharma,' which is called the excellence of the middle; and the Sangha is 'following well,' which is called the excellence of the end."
Question: "For what reason is the Sangha called 'good in the end'? Answer:
"If, having heard it, one is unmoved and unshaken because of attaining the benefit of the noble ones, this is called 'good in the end.
The Bodhi of the Buddha is called 'good in the beginning'; the Bodhi of the Pratyekabuddha is called 'good in the middle'; and the Bodhi of the Śrāvaka is called 'good in the end.'"
Regarding "good in the beginning": having heard it, one immediately abandons the five hindrances regarding all wholesome qualities; this is called good in the beginning.
Having heard it, one follows it; this is called good in the middle.
Having followed it, one gradually attains the Path; this is called good in the end.

In this way, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to them, whether in brief or in detail; within both the brief and the detailed, there is goodness in the beginning, the middle, and the end, with excellent meaning and excellent phrasing.

Why is this? When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma—the Dharma of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and the path of the holy life—he reveals and makes it known through various skillful means; this teaching possesses meaning, and thus it is called "excellence of meaning" (*arthasampad*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"The term 'good meaning' (sārtha) refers to that which reveals, that which analyzes, that which does not conceal, and that which is a continuous succession of connected phrases; this is called 'good meaning.'"
As for "excellent words" (*su-akṣara*): they are able to uphold profound meanings and point toward profound meanings; thus they are called excellent words.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)—only those who are intelligent can know these principles; they cannot be understood by the foolish. Their meaning is so profound that only the wise can discern it; thus they are called excellent words.

Regarding "perfectly complete": since the meaning is already perfectly complete, it does not require anything further to fulfill it; thus it is called "complete," revealing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Question: "What is meant by 'the holy life' (brahmacarya)? Answer:
"This dharma is practiced by the Brahmā-devas and humans; therefore, it is called the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*). Why is this?
