It reveals the Brahma-faring as good in the beginning because it is introduced with causes and conditions; it is good in the middle because its meaning is not inverted; and it is good in the end because those who hear it rejoice and follow it. This is called revealing the Brahma-faring."
Question: "Why is it called 'beautiful and complete'? Answer:
“Precepts constitute the first of the five aggregates of dharma; this is called ‘perfection.
That their meaning is not intermingled is called ‘purity.
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, he does not crave offerings; this is called ‘purity.’”
"Brahmacarya is that which is practiced by Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; this is called brahmacarya.
Excellent is such a mode of practice; you may go to inquire after his well-being."
Question: "What is meant by 'well said'? Answer:
"Because it brings forth all manner of myriad virtues, it is called 'Excellent' (sādhu).
It is also said:
'Because it brings about peace and happiness, it is called "Excellent. "
"Thus" refers to the words of the feet;
"the characteristics of practice" refers to that which is practiced by the practitioner;
"the marks surpassing those of humans" refers to the perfection of physical features.
"You may go to inquire after his health; you may go to behold the Buddha.
He asked: "What is meant by 'beholding'?"
"To look with both eyes is called 'contemplation' (vyavalokana).
Having reflected thus, the Brahmin Vairaṇyā proceeded to where the Buddha was and exchanged greetings with him."
The brahmin asked the Buddha:
"Are the four great elements enduring?
Are your śrāvaka disciples free from much illness and affliction, and are their four great elements light and functional?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
This is called an inquiry of courtesy.
When one engages in dialogue with a brahmin, the sequence of its meaning and flavor brings joy to the heart, which one then remembers and does not forget.
Having exchanged greetings, he withdrew and sat to one side.
"Withdrew" means as the sun turns;
"sat" means his body was spread upon the ground.
Regarding "one side": it means being at one side.
When a person of wisdom approaches a place where those of long-standing virtue reside, they should sit while avoiding six things; only then may they sit.
What are these six things?
First, being extremely far away; second, being extremely close; third, being upwind; fourth, being at a high elevation; fifth, being directly in front of one's eyes; sixth, being behind one.
He asked, "What is the fault in sitting at a distance?
He replied:
"If I wish to converse with you, my voice cannot reach you.
[The other asks: "What fault is there in being so very close? He replied:
"You have offended those of long-standing virtue.
[The other asked,] "What fault was there from being upwind? He replied:
"Because the bodily odor would be foul.
"What is the fault in [sitting] on high places?
"Because it shows a lack of respect."
“What fault is there in sitting directly in front?
“Because it is difficult to look at [the teacher].
“What fault is there in sitting behind?”
He replied:
"Because it is difficult for those of long-standing virtue to converse while looking back and forth.
The brahmin sat apart from these six practices; therefore, it is said in the Vinaya that he sat to one side."
A śramaṇa is one who subdues the afflictions, or as it is said, one who repels the afflictions, or one who has stilled the mind.
A brāhmaṇa is a true brāhmaṇa of the world whose lineage is not mixed with that of parents of other castes.
A "senior elder" (gṛhapati) is one whose body is large and whose years are advanced.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who possesses majestic virtue is called a senior elder."
One who possesses wealth is also called an elder (*śreṣṭhin*).
As for being "greatly aged," it refers to the falling out of hair; furthermore, it is said that one is born, and sons and grandsons are successively born from one another—this is called old age.
One who is decrepit has skin that is withered and wrinkled, and speech that is confused and erroneous; this is called being decrepit.
One who has exceeded [the normal span] is one who has already lived through two or three reigns of kings and yet still remains alive; this is called having exceeded [the normal span].
"Extending one's life" means that when one has lived past the age of a hundred years, this is called "extending one's life.
"Reaching the end of one's years" refers to the final year of one's life; this is called "reaching the end of one's years. "Alas!"
“Why does the śramaṇa Gautama act in this way?
These were the words of the brāhmaṇa.
Having approached the Buddha’s dwelling, he saw that the Buddha did not rise, did not receive his salutation, and did not offer him a seat; therefore, he spoke these words.
"According to what I have heard, I now see that the Tathāgata wishes to exalt himself and disparage others.
The Buddha, with a heart of compassion, replied to the brāhmaṇa:

'I do not recall when I was born in the forest and took seven steps toward the north, looking upon hundreds of billions of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, seeing that none were capable of receiving my prostration.'"
Having observed this, he proclaimed by himself:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored.
When Brahmā heard the Bodhisattva’s proclamation, he immediately joined his palms and said:
"The Bodhisattva is uniquely honored throughout the three realms; there is none who surpasses him.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva let out a lion's roar:
"I alone am uniquely honored."
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

"At that time, even before I had attained the Way, I was already uniquely honored within the three realms; how much more so now, when all manner of wholesome merits have designated me as a Buddha? Why then should I pay homage to you?"
"If anyone receives my prostration, their head shall immediately fall to the ground; therefore, do not hope to pay homage to the Buddha.
Thus did that Brahmin, blind and ignorant, speak these words to the Buddha.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"If this is so, then form is without flavor. Why is that?
"It has form only; it truly has no flavor.
Because the Buddha wished to subdue the brāhmaṇa, he replied:
"As for what you say regarding its lack of flavor, it truly has no flavor."

Why is this? Just as worldly people take form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch to be their "taste," the Tathāgata has severed these; it is like cutting down a tāla tree, from which nothing can ever grow again.
The brahmin said, "If it were so,
that would constitute arrogance.
The Buddha replied:
"Because of your words, I have become arrogant. Why do you say I am arrogant?
The Buddhas of the three periods of time in the past did not prostrate themselves before worldly people; my lineage is such as this, and for that reason I am arrogant."
The Brahmin said, "If that is so, then there is nothing to be done.
The Buddha replied:
"As you have said, I truly do not perform them.
What is meant by 'not performing'?
I do not commit theft, false speech, deception, sexual misconduct, or any other evil deeds of body, speech, or mind; because I do none of these at all, it is called 'not performing.'"
The brahmin asked,
"Does this person then cut off his own lineage?
The Buddha replied:
"It is indeed so. Why is this?
Because within the three realms, I have severed all various kinds of afflictions; therefore, I am called 'One Who Has Severed the Roots.'"
The brahmin was bewildered and did not know how to answer, so he changed his words and asked:
"Is this person base and impure?
The Buddha replied:
"In my opinion, there truly exists impurity; when there are those who let their minds and mouths commit evil, this is a base form of impurity.
The brāhmaṇa then spoke in anger:
"This man has also heard my words, yet he suppresses them according to the circumstances."
The Buddha replied again:
"Among all the afflictions within the three realms, I have indeed extinguished them.
The brahmin spoke once more:
"This person is worthy of pity, yet he is not fit for conversation.
The Buddha replied, "It is indeed so;
I too think that these foolish people are most pitiable, for they constantly engage in evil deeds and do not think to cultivate goodness."
The brahmin then became enraged and reviled him, saying:
"This man must have been awake day and night, seeking out literary compositions until he has exhausted all the people in the world."
The Buddha replied:
"It is indeed so. Why is this?"
"Because I do not enter the womb to sleep, nor do I enter the heavens to sleep, I am therefore called 'Sleepless'.

Thus, after the brahmin had reviled the Buddha with these eight points, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, out of a heart of compassion, gazed upon the brahmin with his eyes, desiring to cause him to partake of the flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, and thereupon preached the Dharma for him.
At that time, the Brahmin’s mind was pure, like the void free from all clouds and obscurations, or like the sun and moon illuminating all darkness.
Through various skillful means, the Tathāgata taught him until he understood; the Tathāgata declared of himself:
"I have attained unsurpassed wisdom and abide eternally in nirvāṇa."
He said to the brahmin:
"Old age and death have approached you closely; that you have come to me, you have indeed gained something of great value. Why is this?"
"It is, for example, like chicken eggs—whether eight, ten, or twelve.
He asked: "Why are they distinguished by these three numbers?"
He replied, "This is a complete phrase; it also makes the wording elegant and perfect. [The Buddha said:
"'Just as a hen broods over her eggs, turning them at the proper times.'"
As for "lying prostrate," it means covering itself with its two wings.
When the time comes for birth, seeing light with its eyes, it pecks at the shell with its beak.
Having emerged, it beats its wings and calls out as it moves forward, asking, "Shall I be large or small?"
The brahmin replied,
"The former is greater.
The Buddha said:
"I am also like this. Why is that?

The shell of ignorance covers and obstructs the three realms; I have used the beak of wisdom to peck through the shell of ignorance and emerged from the three realms. Between these two, who is great and who is small?"
He replied,
"Gautama is indeed great.
The meaning of the subsequent phrases is self-evident.
"In the world, 'one' means there is no second.
Samyak-saṃbodhi is unsurpassed enlightenment. He asked:
"What is meant by 'unsurpassed enlightenment'?
He replied:

"If a person is on the path of a *srotāpanna* and asks about the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, I explain it to them; likewise, up to one on the path of an *arhat* who asks about the fruit of an *arhat*, I explain it to them. Just as with the paths of the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and Buddhas, I answer according to whatever is asked; therefore, it is called unsurpassed enlightenment, and for this reason, I am the greatest."
Just as a hen brooding her eggs turns them at the proper times,
so too did the Buddha, beneath the Bodhi tree, contemplate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths— suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
The Buddha then spoke to the Brahmin:

"I have attained the unsurpassed, supreme state through right exertion and diligence, not through a mind of indolence or negligence. By means of courageous and right exertion and diligence, I [attained it] beneath the Bodhi tree through four kinds of diligence. What are these four?"
First, correctness; second, lack of haste; third, lack of laxity; fourth, non-abandonment—by means of these dharmas, one attains the unsurpassed path.
That which is not supple does not abide.
That which gives rise to the mind proceeds toward the object of observation.
That which does not regress is without weariness.
"The mind of samādhi is a single-mindedness.
It further states:
"To place the mind skillfully for the sake of samādhi is to achieve one-pointedness; being neither excessive nor lax—this is the first wholesome dharma."
"By means of this Dharma, one attains the first dhyāna; from the first dhyāna, one proceeds in succession until reaching the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) as the ultimate goal.
Because the Buddha wished to bring forth the unsurpassed Dharma, it is stated in the Vinaya that the Buddha said:
"O Brahmin, I am pure amidst desires, and I am likewise pure of evil."
Question: "What is meant by 'desire'? Answer:
"Greed is desire, the desire for greed is desire, and the thought of desire is desire; these are the names for 'desire.
What are called 'all unwholesome dharmas'?
He replied:
“Desire and doubt—these are called unwholesome dharmas.
The Tathāgata has attained tranquility regarding these two points.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'purity within desire'?
He replied: "Detachment from desire is also called the relinquishing of desire."

Why is this? For one who first enters the first dhyāna, ignorance is the harbinger of desire, and desire is the enemy of dhyāna; because one has already abandoned desire, one attains dhyāna—therefore, desire is called the enemy.
Those who wish to be free from desire and evil come through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); once desire and evil have been extinguished, meditative concentration arises.
The meaning of these two statements should be understood by oneself.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of tranquility: tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, and tranquility of concealment; these constitute the three kinds of tranquility.
These three kinds of tranquility are also included within the tranquility of the preceding two phrases.
Question: "What is meant by 'desire'? Answer:
“There are two kinds of desire:
first, the desire for objects; second, the desire consisting of afflictions. He asked:
"What is meant by 'abiding in desire,' and what is meant by 'affliction-desire'?
He replied:
"One who dwells in desire has a mind attached to the sphere of form.
One who possesses afflictive desire leads people to the objects of desire.

Regarding these latter two phrases, they correctly explain what is to be abandoned; the former phrase is for the sake of discarding the desire for pleasure, while the latter phrase is for emerging from affliction.
Thus, regarding the desire for sense objects and the desire for afflictions, the mind becomes utterly pure in both respects.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The former phrase eliminates the desire for sense objects; the latter phrase eliminates the desire for afflictions."
The former phrase excludes agitation caused by causal conditions; the latter phrase excludes the signs of delusion.
The former phrase involves attachment to purity; the latter phrase brings desire to rest.
One should understand this sequence for oneself.
Question: "Regarding 'desire' (rāga), is the craving itself the desire?
Or are craving and desire distinct?"
He replied: "They return to One. Why is this?"
All evils, in terms of their underlying principle, converge into one, yet they are differentiated as distinct.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Vinaya: "Greed" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), while "desire" refers to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Likewise, concentration is the enemy of sensual desire;
joy is the enemy of ill-will;
and reflection is the enemy of drowsiness.
Peace and bliss are the enemy of wavering doubt;
measurement is the enemy of skepticism, just as the first dhyāna has sensual desire as its enemy.
"Those who possess greed are included within the five hindrances; those who possess various unwholesome dharmas take up the hindrances.
"What are called the hindrances? He replied:
"The three roots of poison; the five desires and five sensory objects as perverse greed;
and the subsequent phrase, which distinguishes the various objects of attachment as the outflows of hatred and delusion.
As for the preceding phrase, it refers to the outflow of desire, attachment to desire, the spring of desire, the acceptance of desire, the murderous intent, the fetters, and the craving for desire."
Regarding the latter phrase, it refers to the attachment to various streams and springs;
regarding the former phrase, it refers to various cravings and so forth;
regarding the latter phrase, it refers to ignorance and so forth.
The former phrase refers to the eight types of mental states associated with craving and so forth;
the latter phrase refers to the arising of the four unwholesome mental states.
Thus, within the realm of desire, both the pure and the defiled are purified.
"Regarding 'mindfulness' (smṛti):
what is meant by mindfulness?
He replied:
"It moves and turns.
Why does it move and turn?
Because one first places the mind upon the object of observation; this is called mindfulness."
Question: "What is meant by volition? Answer:
"The practitioners of dhyāna place the mind within the object of contemplation, and the mind lingers upon that object.
Furthermore, it is said:

'Vitarka (initial application) is the investigation, fixation, and continuity of the mind; it is like the sound of a bell, which is loud at first and faint thereafter. The initial loudness is like vitarka, while the subsequent faintness is like vicāra (sustained application).'"
It is like a bird soaring: its initial movement is like *vitarka* (applied thought), and its subsequent stabilization is like *vicāra* (sustained thought).
It is like a bee gathering nectar from flowers: its first arrival is like *vitarka*, and its subsequent selection [of the nectar] is like *vicāra*.
The first dhyāna has five factors. What are these five factors?
First, mindfulness; second, volition; third, rapture; fourth, bliss; fifth, concentration—these are the five factors.
It is like a great tree that has both flowers and fruit, or as the first dhyāna has both mindfulness and volition, arising from stillness.
He asked: “What is meant by ‘stillness’?”
He replied:
"To be free from the five hindrances is tranquility.
As for joy and happiness: 'joy' refers to being full of joy."
What is meant by "fulfillment"?
It is the fulfillment and joyful satisfaction of body and mind; this is the flavor of the limit of joy (*prīti*).
As for bliss (*sukha*), it is the abandonment of the two types of suffering.
"Bodily suffering and mental suffering—these are called pleasure; one who experiences pleasure becomes attached to the flavor of that perception.
He asked again:
"What is meant by joy?"
He replied:
"When the mind is robust and its perceptions are rarefied and excellent, this is called joy (*prīti*); that which is pleasant is what one attains and experiences.
Furthermore, it is said:"
"These two dharmas cannot be separated from one another: where there is joy (*prīti*), there is pleasure (*sukha*); where there is pleasure, there is joy.
Joy is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); pleasure is subsumed within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*)."

It is like a person traveling on a road who, parched with thirst and lacking water, feels joy upon hearing that there is water; this is called *prīti*. Having arrived and drinking the water and bathing, this is called *sukha*.
"Regarding 'the first dhyāna-samādhi': 'first' refers to the primary dhyāna; 'samādhi' means skillful incineration, and it also refers to the dharmas contemplated by the dhyāna master.
What is meant by 'skillful incineration'?"
He replied:
"It is extremely capable of burning away the coverings.
He further said:
"Severing the afflictions is also called 'seeing. What is meant by 'seeing'?
He replied:
"Contemplating and perceiving the characteristics of dharmas, one receives the eight samādhis of deportment. Why is this?
*Kāśyana-arvāmāna*—translated into Chinese as the 'characteristics of the thirty-eight dhyānas'—is called 'dhyāna-samādhi' because one contemplates *kāśyana-arvāmāna*."
This is the fruit of the path of vision.
Why? Because it is for the purpose of observing characteristics.
What is meant by the characteristic of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-lakṣaṇa*)?

It is because one contemplates impermanence; through such contemplation, the Path is realized, and through the fruit, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is contemplated. For this reason, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is called the characteristic of contemplation.
As explained in the Vinaya. He asked:
“What is meant by the first dhyāna?”
He replied: "There is applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and concentration; this is called the first dhyāna. [The interlocutor asked:
"Suppose a person possesses property and a person possesses a retinue. Once the property has been set aside and the retinue has been set aside, would there be anything remaining?"
He replied: "There is no other name.
Dhyāna is likewise: when mindfulness, volition, joy, bliss, and concentration are established, there is no further name; it is simply dhyāna."

For example, when there are men, soldiers, elephants, horses, and weapons in an array, it is called an "army"; once the men, soldiers, elephants, horses, and weapons have dispersed, the name "army" no longer exists.
Dhyāna is likewise: if one sets aside the five factors mentioned above, the name "meditative concentration" (dhyāna) no longer exists.
"Entering" means arriving; it is also said to mean accomplishment.
"Abiding" refers to dwelling beneath the Bodhi tree through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
When the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree, what did he contemplate?
"Observe the out-breath and the in-breath.
He asked: "Is there [this practice] in the other dhyānas as well?"
He replied, "There are also.
The Dharma Master said:

"Regarding the dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), if I were to explain it extensively within this *Śāntipatha-sūtra*, its profound meaning would become overly complex; you should learn of it yourself from the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*."
What is now being explained is the *Viniyavibhāṣā* of the correct treatise; other matters will be explained somewhat briefly.
This is the first chapter on meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Regarding "the cessation of mindfulness and volition": when these two factors, mindfulness and volition, have passed away, one enters the second dhyāna-concentration.
Upon arising from the second dhyāna, these two factors cease. Why is this?
Because it transcends two major factors, it is called the second dhyāna-samādhi.
Furthermore, it is said:
"In the second dhyāna-samādhi, the factors of the first dhyāna-samādhi are absent, though other factors remain.
In the first dhyāna-samādhi, the factor of contact (*sparśa*) is primary; here, having transcended those two major branches, one attains the factors of the second dhyāna-samādhi."
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya: "With the cessation of applied and sustained thought, one enters the second dhyāna;
the internal phenomena are now manifest. He asked:
"What is meant by 'manifestation'?
He replied:
"'Manifestation' arises from the body; 'clarity' means being free from defilement."
Dhyāna is also called "purity.
Why is this? It is like a person in blue clothing; because they possess the color blue, they are called "one in blue clothing."
"Meditation is also like this: because there are pure dharmas, it is called 'pure meditation.
He asked: "Why is it named 'concentration-purity'?"
He replied:
"Mindfulness and volition are the roots of movement; when mindfulness and volition have ceased, that is what is called purity.
'One characteristic' means the arising of a single dharma."
Question: "What is meant by 'the arising of a single dharma'? Answer:
"Because it is free from recollection and reflection, this is called the characteristic of the one dharma, and it is also said to be unsurpassed.
Furthermore, it is said:
'The one characteristic is that which is already detached from recollection and reflection;'"
It is also said that there is no second; this is called the "single characteristic. Question:
Why is the characteristic of a single dharma called the "characteristic of a single dharma"?
He replied, "It is samādhi. He asked:
"What is meant by 'samādhi'?
He replied:
"It is a single mind without duality."
It is called "concentration" and it is also called "immovability"; therefore, the second dhyāna has a single characteristic. Why is this?
It is for the sake of its name.
He asked: "What is meant by 'name'? [The Buddha replied:
"Neither the self nor the vital breath—this is what is called 'name'."
Question: "Is there no purity in the first dhyāna? Answer:
“There is. “If that is so, the first dhyāna is also called ‘one characteristic’; why then is only the second dhyāna designated as ‘one characteristic’?
He replied:

"Just as when there is mindfulness and volition, the water moves and waves arise so that the reflection of the face cannot be seen—likewise, in the first dhyāna, because there is mindfulness and volition and the mind is not pure, this is called 'not having a single characteristic.'"
Why is this? Because the samādhi is not clear. He asked:
Question: "Why is it that only the second dhyāna and samādhi are clearly elucidated? Answer:
"Because the mind is pure. As for 'joy and bliss arising from samādhi,' this refers to the joy and bliss arising from the samādhi of the first dhyāna concentration."
This is the second dhyāna.
"Second" refers to its numerical order.
Just as the first dhyāna has five factors (aṅga), the second dhyāna has four factors.
What are these four?
First, purity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
If explained extensively, there are four; if explained concisely, there are three, as stated in the sūtra.
"When will the three factors give rise to joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind?
The Dharma Master replied, "I shall now realize a single phrase; the rest you shall know for yourselves."
This concludes the second chapter on the Dhyānas,
concerning "the one who is free from joy.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"What is meant by 'separation from joy'?
He replied:
"When even slight joy is called excessive joy or the cessation of joy, and at that time mindfulness and volition have ceased, yet joy arises once more."
Question: "In the second dhyāna, mindfulness (smṛti) is discussed; once mindfulness and volition (cetanā) have ceased, there is joy (prīti). Why is it stated again with such emphasis? Answer:
"It is for the purpose of praising the third dhyāna that this is spoken. Why?

For example, just as wrong views are not extinguished by the third path but were already extinguished at the first stage of *srotāpanna*, they are now mentioned again within the context of the third path."
What is meant by "praise"?
Because it pertains to the third path, it is likewise so here.
As for "dwelling in relinquishment":
“What is meant by equanimity?
He replied:
“Equanimity is the vision of equality, the absence of partiality, and the absence of factionalism; it is constant, great, and courageous equanimity—this is the third dhyāna.”
It is further said:
"There are ten kinds of relinquishment. He asked:

“What are the ten? First, the seeking of relinquishment through *śramaṇa*; second, the seeking of relinquishment through *brahman* and *māra*; third, the seeking of relinquishment through *bodhi*; fourth, the seeking of relinquishment through *vīrya*; fifth, the seeking of relinquishment through practice; sixth, the seeking of relinquishment through contact; seventh, the seeking of relinquishment through contemplation; eighth, the seeking of relinquishment through *mañju*; ninth, the seeking of relinquishment through wisdom; and tenth, the seeking of relinquishment through purity.”
These ten kinds of relinquishment are of one characteristic when viewed by those in every stage of the human path; this is because they have been explained in brief.
They have already been explained in detail in three places: within the *Śāliya*, the *Dharmasaṃgrahaṇī*, and the *Viśuddhimārga*; you should know them from those sources yourselves.
If I were to explain them in detail here in this *Vinaya*, it would result in excessive prolixity.
Question: "Regarding the 'ten relinquishments,' which relinquishment is being taken up? Answer:
"Take Mañjuśrī and seek his renunciation.
He asked, "What is meant by 'Mañjuśrī and seeking his renunciation'?"
He replied, "I do not know;
it arose from joy regarding another matter. He asked:
"Are there no *masa-jūsha* (equanimity of relinquishment) in these two stages—the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna?
Is it only in the third dhyāna that it exists? He replied:
"It exists in the first and second dhyānas as well, yet it remains subtle and unmanifest.

Why is this? Because it is obscured by applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), and joy (prīti). In the third dhyāna, however, one has already become detached from applied thought, sustained thought, and joy; therefore, it becomes manifest."
"One who knows through right reflection.
He asked: "What is meant by 'reflection'?"
He replied:
"Because the mind gives rise to many perceptions, it is called 'volition' (saṃskāra).
As for 'knowing' (jñāna):"
Question: "What is meant by 'knowing'? Answer:
"It is thorough understanding.
He asked: "What is meant by right reflection?"
He replied:
"Right mindfulness means not forgetting;
it is also called consciousness."
Furthermore, it says:
"One who knows through arising. He asked:
"What is meant by 'knowing'?
He replied: "It is discernment; it is also called gathering."
Furthermore, as for what was said regarding "extensive," this is a brief explanation; one shall come to know it for oneself within the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*. He asked:
"In the first dhyāna-concentration, is there no cognition through reflection?"
He replied: "There is. Why is this so?"
"If there were no one who knows through volition, from where would the first dharma proceed?
He asked: "Why is it that volitional knowing does not manifest within the first dhyāna?"
He replied:
"It is because it is still very dull. For example, when sharpening a blade, it is blunt at first but becomes sharp later;
the same is true for the knowledge gained through reflection: at the initial stage of observing within dhyāna, it is still very dull, and for this reason it does not manifest."
It is also like a person suckling milk; though the calf is driven away, it returns from time to time.
It is also like the bliss of the third dhyāna, which is not far from joy (*prīti*); if there is no mindfulness, awareness, and guarding, one immediately joins with joy.
When one maintains mindfulness, awareness, and guarding, and these qualities are strong, one then becomes free from it.
Bliss is the unsurpassed bliss, the bliss of ultimate happiness (Sukhāvatī).
Why is this? Because it is known through reflection and maintained through mindfulness.
The meaning of the text is as stated above; one should understand it for oneself.
Regarding "experiencing pleasure with the body," [the interlocutor] asked:
"What is meant by 'body'?
He replied:
"It is the body of name-and-form (nāmarūpa); it is through the body of name-and-form that one knows pleasure."

Why is this? Because pleasure joins with name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and the union of these two principles is an exquisite flavor; because one knows it and becomes attached to this exquisite flavor, one becomes aware of its arising. Therefore, it is through the body that one knows pleasure.
The virtuous person says, "Having abandoned conditioned existence, one dwells in bliss. He asked,
"What is meant by 'the words of the virtuous person'?"
He replied:
"The Buddha, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas explain the causes and conditions of the third dhyāna for those practicing the third dhyāna; this is called the speech of virtuous persons."
“What is meant by ‘speech’? He replied:
“To open up and show is called ‘speaking’; it is also called ‘discriminating,’ and furthermore, it is called ‘praising.’”
Question: "What is meant by 'dwelling in bliss through the abandonment of volition'? Answer:
"It is for the sake of entering the third dhyāna.
How does one enter it?
For the sake of supreme bliss."
Because of the perfection of the bliss of Sukhāvatī, one relinquishes the third dhyāna so that joy (*prīti*) ceases to arise; this is called "possessing volition" (*sa-cetanā*). Why is this?
One is mindful of by virtuous persons and enters into joy; this joy is pure and unmixed, and is thus praised by virtuous persons.
This meaning fundamentally explains that one dwells in joy through the relinquishment of volition; such is the praise of virtuous persons.
Regarding the entry into the third dhyāna: as with the entry into the first and second dhyānas, so it is with the third.
The difference is that the first has five factors, the second has four factors, and the third has two factors, as explained in the original sūtra.
Question: "At what time do the two factors emerge from within the third dhyāna? Answer:
“Delight in one-pointedness of mind.
This concludes the third dhyāna category.
*Śariputrābhidharma-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Four.”
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Western Regions during the Qi Dynasty.
"Abandoning pleasure and abandoning pain. Question: "What is meant by 'abandoning pleasure and abandoning pain'? Answer:
"In the fourth dhyāna, one abandons both the mind of pleasure and the mind of suffering.
Furthermore, it says:
"What is termed 'pleasure' and what is termed 'suffering' are both abandoned."
Question: "Regarding the statement that 'the mind of pleasure and the mind of suffering [are abandoned] in the fourth dhyāna,' when are they actually discarded? Answer:
"It is abandoned within the gateway of the fourth dhyāna.
He asked: "Where does bodily suffering cease and come to an end?"
He replied: "As it is stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
'Having become pure through the departure from desire, one enters the first dhyāna; herein suffering is extinguished.'"
Question: "Where do the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure cease without remainder? Answer:
Regarding the fulfillment of cultivation, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“In the fourth dhyāna-samādhi, [all things] are extinguished without remainder; suffering, pleasure, and joy are all extinguished without remainder within the gateway of this dhyāna.”

Why is this? Because in the first dhyāna-samādhi, since mindfulness (smṛti) and volition (cetanā) have not yet been abandoned, there is mental suffering; when mindfulness and volition cease, suffering also ceases. This is likewise for the second, third, and fourth dhyāna-samādhis, where mindfulness is the first [to be abandoned] and they cease in successive order.

As for joy (*prīti*), it ceases completely at the gateway of the fourth dhyāna; one attains bliss (*sukha*) in the fourth dhyāna, enters into and abides in that bliss with equanimity (*upekṣā*), and there is no arising of anything beyond that bliss. Therefore, suffering (*duḥkha*) is extinguished without remainder within the fourth dhyāna; this is called "neither-suffering-nor-bliss" (*aduḥkhāsukha*).
This Dharma is extremely subtle and cannot be grasped by the mind.

Why is this? It is like a wild ox that a herdsman cannot catch; he therefore builds a pen, drives the herd into it, and leads them out one by one in succession until he reaches the wild ox. Once he has reached it, he knows, "This is the one," and only then can he seize it.

The Buddha is also like this: first, for the sake of attaining bliss, he enters into all phenomena; having entered, he emerges from them in succession. This is neither-pain-nor-pleasure; it is a mind that is neither pained nor pleased; this is the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
He asked, "Can this neither-painful-nor-pleasant state be grasped?
He replied:
"It cannot be grasped.
He asked again:
"Why did the first line say it can be grasped?"
He replied:
"Because one knows its characteristics by means of its name, it is as if one has grasped it; when the description of the characteristics is thus given, one will naturally understand them.
As stated in the sūtra:..."
“There are four conditions, Venerable One, by which one attains liberation through neither-pain-nor-pleasure; because of samādhi, one abandons both pain and pleasure and enters the fourth dhyāna.”

Venerable sir, these four conditions are neither painful nor pleasant; they are called liberation because of samādhi. Just as wrong view is the first to cease among all phenomena, so it is in the third path.
"This praises the third path; herein it is likewise.
He asked: "What are called 'all phenomena' (dharmas)?"
He replied: "Anger and delusion are primary; one should understand this for oneself.

It is also like the fourth dhyāna, where the mind of suffering and pleasure is primary: because of pleasure, desire arises; because of suffering, anger arises; and because anger arises, the mind of pleasure is extinguished. Therefore, it is extremely remote from the fourth dhyāna; this is called 'neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.'"
Question: "What are the characteristics of that which is neither painful nor pleasant? Answer:
“Abandoning pleasure and abandoning displeasure.
He asked: “What is its flavor?”
He replied:
"Having abandoned the taste of suffering and the taste of pleasure, one also speaks of not recompensing for that taste.
This is the purification of consciousness through relinquishment."
Question: "What is meant by 'the consciousness of relinquishment is pure'? Answer:
“Equanimity causes consciousness to attain purity; this is the purity of consciousness in the fourth dhyāna.
Once consciousness is pure, three types of consciousness arise, all of which are produced by equanimity and not by any other factor.”

Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: "The abandonment of consciousness is pure and clean, like the light of the moon; when clouds cover it, its radiance is not bright, but once the clouds are removed, the moon immediately becomes luminous, pure, and clean."
In this regard, volition and pleasure are also like this; when one is free from volition and pleasure, consciousness is pure and clean.
He asked: “Do the first three dhyānas exist [therein] or not?”
He replied, “There is. He asked:
"Why does consciousness not emerge?
He replied:
"Because it is obscured by initial volition (vitarka), it does not emerge."

Furthermore, the equanimity (*upekṣā*) of the fourth dhyāna is like the night consciousness, which is like the full moon; it is only when the principles are in accord that the moon’s radiance becomes manifest.

Just as the first dhyāna has five factors, so too the fourth dhyāna has three factors: equanimity, consciousness, and one-pointedness of mind. As explained in detail, there are three, but in brief, there are two, as stated in the sūtras.
"At what time do the two factors arise?
They arise within the fourth dhyāna-concentration.
This concludes the fourth stage of dhyāna-concentration."
"This is the fourth dhyāna.

Some desire to cultivate the stage of insight (vipaśyanā), some desire one-pointedness of mind, some desire to cultivate the stage of supernormal powers (abhijñā), and some desire the stage of the cessation of truths (nirodha-satya). Those who have exhausted craving for rebirth seek one-pointedness of mind."
How does one enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to attain single-mindedness?

Having dwelt in bliss for a day and completed the *kāṣīna* practice, I arose from the eight samādhis and trained; when ordinary people arise from samādhi with a single-minded and attentive mind, I observe this, which is called the "contemplation of the earth" (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*).

Furthermore, there are those who, having accomplished the eight samādhis and entered the stage of supernormal dhyāna, arise from samādhi and manifest supernatural powers—such as transforming a single body into ten million bodies—and so forth, as one should naturally understand in sequence; for this reason, dhyāna is designated as the ground of supernormal powers.

Furthermore, having practiced the eight samādhis and entered the samādhi of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), he entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for seven days; this is the nirvāṇa of this world.
He thought, "I shall enjoy the bliss of these seven days," for this is the ground of the Truth of Cessation.
There are those who enter the eight samādhis; from within meditative concentration, they do not find delight and think, "I wish to be born in the Brahma Heaven"—this is entering the stage of birth.

When the Buddha entered the fourth dhyāna-samādhi and arose from that samādhi beneath the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata contemplated the stages of the earth and meditation, speaking of them as both penetrating the stages and entering the stage of the cessation of suffering (nirodha-satya). These two entries encompass all dharmas:
mundane dharmas and the dharmas of noble benefit.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now, this brief explanation of how to attain it is thus; one should naturally understand the sequence of the fourth dhyāna-concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) for oneself.

By means of this method, one enters the fourth dhyāna-concentration with the single-mindedness of samādhi; therefore, it is called 'pure,' as stated in the Vinaya-mūla: 'having already abandoned consciousness, it is pure.'"
Question: "What is meant by 'purity'? Answer:
"It is white, not black;
it is also called luminous.
Because of joy, one becomes free from desire; having become free from all afflictions, once freedom is achieved, the mind is pure and white, capable of functioning according to its purpose."
Why is this? Because they have already been instructed and made supple, reaching the ultimate state.

As stated in the sūtra: "If the mind has become supple and is capable of being employed as required—just as refined gold, having been gradually forged until it is supple, becomes capable of being employed as required; if one wishes to fashion various ornaments from it, it will not break when struck—the mind is likewise, following whatever it is directed to do."
As stated in the sūtra, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"I do not see a single dharma like the mind that, when tamed, becomes more than once supple and humble, capable of being applied, and abiding in extreme purity. Because it abides, it is called 'immovable'; because it is diligent, it is not indolent; its single-mindedness cannot be shaken.

When gathered, it is not a restless mind; it can move with wisdom. When gathered, it is not obscured by ignorance; it is embraced by consciousness, not humiliated by delusion. It is embraced by light, not obstructed by the darkness of afflictions. Embraced by these six dharmas, it cannot be moved or turned aside. Thus, once the mind has entered the eight branches, it discriminates all dharmas according to its capacity."
By means of the samādhi of the fourth dhyāna, one attains single-mindedness (*ekacitta*). Because of this single-mindedness, all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are removed;

the mind is free from defilement and turbidity, and thoughts and reflections have passed away. Having attained purity of mind and wisdom, no hindrances can obscure it. Because of the absence of discursive thought (*amanasikāra*), one immediately reaches the immovable state; having departed from afflictions (*kleśa*), one is likewise called "immovable."
This phrase is spoken within the Sūtras; you should know it for yourself.
"Knowledge of past lives" arises from the stage of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-bhūmi*).
"Past" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) of previous existences.

As for abiding, one is born into this family and born into that family; one dies in this family and dies in that family; one further falls into that family and this family; and departing from this family, one is reborn in that family. Using one's own wisdom, one discerns and knows each of these things individually, thus personally recollecting one's past lives.

As stated in the Vinaya-mūla, regarding the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*): by means of this recollection, one knows the dwelling places and births of previous existences; whether it be one birth, two births, or proceeding further in succession, one knows and recollects them with the mind.
As when a Buddha reaches the perfections (pāramitā), there is no longer any need for further discipline; his mind and mind-objects are tranquil, and he is aware [of this].
A beginner, however, becomes aware [of it] only after having performed the practice.
I have now spoken briefly; one should come to know this in detail from the *Viśuddhimārga-vibhāṣā*.
Herein, it is explained according to the *Vinaya-mūla*.
Regarding "one birth":
Question: "What is meant by 'one birth'? Answer:
“From one single entry into the womb until death, this is called ‘one birth.
Following this sequence up to countless births—‘three *vibha* kalpas’; in the Han language, *kalpa* means ‘destruction.’”
Question: "What is meant by 'countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas'? Answer:
"The sequential extinction [of the world] is called the *vibhavā-kalpa*; the *vibhavā-kalpa*, in the language of Han, means 'the kalpa of formation' (*vivartakalpa*).
He asked: "What is meant by the *vibhavā-kalpa*?"
He replied:
"They arise in succession; this is called the *vibhaṭa* kalpa.
As for taking the *tribha* kalpa, it is included within the *tribhaṭa-kalpa*, which is the root of the *bhaṭa*."
If one takes up the *vibhakta* kalpa, one immediately enters the *vibhakta-cāyika*; this kalpa is known by the mind’s subduing of consciousness.
As stated in the sūtra, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"There are four asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
What are the four? They are: Trapuṣa, Trapuṣaka, Bhallika, and Bhallikaka.
What is meant by Trapuṣa?
There are three *tribhāṭas*. What are these three?
They are the fire *tribhāṭa*, the water *tribhāṭa*, and the wind *tribhāṭa*.
There are three *tribhava* realms:
the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and the Bṛhatphala devas.
When the fire of the *tribhava* arises, it descends from the Ābhāsvara heaven and burns everything to ashes.
When the water *tribhava* arises, it descends from Mount Sumeru and submerges everything;
when the wind *tribhava* arises, it blows away everything from Mount Vipula, extending across the breadth of a single Buddha-field.
The Dharma Master asked:
"What is the Buddha’s realm? He replied:
"The realm of arising, the realm of cessation, and the realm of knowledge.
He asked: "What is meant by the realm of arising?"
He replied:
"If a Buddha were to be born in ten thousand worlds, those ten thousand worlds would all tremble.

The Buddha’s majestic virtue pervades a hundred billion worlds; if there are those who hear the Buddha preach the Jewel Mantra, the Accumulation Mantra, the Heṭha Mantra, the Aṭa Mantra, or the Nila Mantra, yet do not follow them, a wind will immediately arise and blow them away beyond a hundred billion worlds."
The knower of the spheres is immeasurable.

Regarding the three spheres of the Buddha—the sphere of cessation and the sphere of arising—both are utterly destroyed; yet that which flourishes is likewise established. I have now explained this briefly; one should know it in detail from the *Vibhāṣā* on the Pure Path (*Viśuddhimārga-vibhāṣā*).
In this way, the Buddha attained all-knowledge beneath the Bodhi tree; it was not in one or two kalpas, but he fully realized it throughout three *vibhata* kalpas.
"Regarding 'one born in a certain place. He asked:
"What is meant by 'one born in a certain place'?"

"If one were to dwell during the period of world-destruction (saṃvarta-kalpa), whether born in the heavens or entering the human realm, whether by transformation-birth, womb-birth, or moisture-birth—one would know all such sequences: 'This is my clan; these are the names of my parents; my name is either Kāśyapa or [another], my clan is either Brāhmaṇa or [another], my caste is either Kṣatriya or [another];
my experience of suffering and pleasure, and my physical form, are thus—whether white or black.'"

Their food and drink are likewise: fine rice, wheat, millet, and the sweet fruits and exquisite fragrant flavors of trees. Their actions of body, speech, and mind are performed in such a manner, and their lifespans are of such duration. From the world above up to the first heaven and even as far as the Brahma Heaven, they take birth; thus proceeding through successive stages, they are later born in Tuṣita Heaven as those who dwell there for one final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*). In Tuṣita, they share the same clan name as the devas, being named Sātakaṭa (in the Han language, "White Banner"). Their bodies are golden-yellow in color, they consume ambrosia (*amṛta*) as food and drink, and they enjoy celestial bliss for a lifespan of five billion seven hundred and sixty million worldly years.

Descending from the celestial palace, he took birth in the house of King Śuddhodana; he entered the womb of Queen Māyā and, regarding all his previous places of birth—including his lineage, the quality of his physical form whether handsome or ugly, his wealth or poverty, his nobility or low status, and his features—he knew them all completely.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Does only the Buddha know this?
Or do others know it as well?"
He replied: "Others also know this;
the pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and non-Buddhist brahmins each distinguish it for themselves.
The non-Buddhist brahmins know forty kalpas, but they know nothing beyond that."

Because their wisdom is narrow and inferior, they cannot know things at a distance; they merely possess correct knowledge regarding their own rebirth, while being unable to know anything else. Why is this?
Because their capacity is narrow and inferior,
there are eighty great arhats who know ten thousand kalpas;
there are two superior arhats who know one asaṃkhyeya kalpa plus ten thousand kalpas.
Pratyekabuddhas also know one asaṃkhyeya kalpa and ten thousand plus some additional kalpas; this is known according to their respective practice.
What the Buddha knows is inexhaustible.
The non-Buddhist brahmins can understand this sequentially; if they wish to grasp it in brief or skip over it, they are unable to discern it for themselves.
It is like a blind person walking: they must proceed step by step, for it is impossible to do otherwise.

The Śrāvakas attain knowledge by joining both ends; the Pratyekabuddhas do likewise. As for the Buddhas, they attain knowledge according to their will, knowing all things throughout the cycles of ascending and descending over countless kalpas; this is what I know, O Brāhmaṇa.
The Buddha said to the brāhmaṇa:

"Beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained unsurpassed wisdom and immediately knew of the countless kalpas of the past; now that the darkness of my ignorance has been extinguished, I have attained the light of wisdom."
"From what is it obtained?
It is all obtained through diligent effort, not sparing even one's body or life, just as a chick breaks its shell with its beak.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

"My knowledge of past lives serves as my beak; the ignorance that shrouded my previous existence served as the shell. Now, with my beak, I have broken the shell and emerged from it; therefore, I am named the One of Unsurpassed Wisdom."

In the Chapter on Knowledge of Past Lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), one knows the births of others. Through wisdom, one knows the beings who have fallen into birth; therefore, it is called "knowledge of falling into birth.

With the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one observes sentient beings. Because the Tathāgata has already fulfilled the *pāramitās*, he knows them from the very moment of observation; other people must all know them through cultivation. Now I shall speak briefly; the *Viśuddhimārga-vibhāṣā* (Commentary on the Path of Purification) should naturally explain this in detail.
"Noble One," he asked,
"What makes one noble?"
He replied:

"Because the physical eye is no different from the noble eye; it is through the various virtues practiced by devas and humans that this eye is accomplished. Being free from all physical eyes and free from all defilements, it is able to illuminate afar."

Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, that which is observed with the noble eye by means of the wisdom-eye is attained through diligent effort; it is no different from the noble eye itself. Why is this so?
Having already abided in the noble state, one subsequently attains it; therefore, the wisdom-eye is called the "noble eye. Why is this?

Because by relying upon the noble through the body, one attains noble radiance; and because the mind gathers this light, one attains far-reaching vision that penetrates stone walls as if they were transparent, no different from true illumination. Thus, with the pure wisdom-eye, one observes sentient beings falling and taking birth.

Therefore, the non-Buddhist brahmins see falling but do not see arising, and thus give rise to the view of annihilationism; furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who see arising but do not see falling, and thus give rise to the view of eternalism.
Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings, the Buddha both observes them through the view of permanence and observes them through the view of annihilation.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, he perceives with the eye of wisdom that sentient beings fall into birth.
"Regarding 'extremely pure':
the Tathāgata is free from eleven afflictions; therefore, he is called extremely pure.
As stated in the sūtra, the Buddha said to Anuruddha:
“Doubt is a mental affliction; once wisdom has arisen, one abandons it.
That which does not restrain the mind is an affliction; a drowsy mind and a sleepy mind are also afflictions;

a mind of startled joy, a mind of great [arrogance], a mind of excessive diligence, an excessively soft mind, an excessively talkative mind, a non-discriminating mind, and an excessively contemplative mind regarding forms—such are the various afflicted minds.

Ānanda, because the Tathāgata has practiced with supreme diligence, he is free from these eleven afflictions. Whether he perceives a form but does not perceive its light, or perceives the light but does not perceive the form—beginning with such instances—the Tathāgata has transcended these eleven afflictions and has likewise surpassed the human eye.

Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla: one who observes with the pure noble eye that transcends the worldly fleshly eye sees sentient beings exactly as they are, no differently than with the fleshly eye; one also sees sentient beings falling away from their current state and being reborn.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Does the Buddha see sentient beings when they are first born and fall [into the world]?
He replied:
"One sees [the object] at the moment of its initial arising and falling away, but not in between.
Therefore, what is stated in the Vinaya-mūla is likewise.
O base one."
Question: "What is meant by 'lowly'? Answer:
"To practice unwholesome dharmas through the conduct of delusion is called base.
Furthermore, being born into poverty is also base; it is that which people detest and despise. As for the noble: [they are those who... "
Question: "What is meant by 'noble'? Answer:
"Taking birth through the mind of wisdom is therefore called noble.
Those of beautiful appearance arise from non-anger; those of ugly appearance arise from anger; and those of the good paths are born into the good paths."
Some say:
"Abundance of gold, silver, and precious treasures is also called a good path.
As for the evil paths, being born into poverty and lowliness due to stinginess and greed is also called an evil path."
"As for those of low station, food and drink are difficult to obtain, and they are not provided even morning and evening.
The Tathāgata knows all that beings do according to their karma.
Furthermore, he observes sentient beings undergoing various agonies and torments within the hells.
Having seen this, the Tathāgata thought:
"By what roots of evil have these sentient beings sown that they undergo such suffering day and night without ceasing?
Upon observation, the Tathāgata realized: "Because these sentient beings committed evil deeds, they now receive this retribution."
Furthermore, he observes the heavens and sees the devas in the Caitraratha grove, the Miśraka grove, and the Pāruṣyaka grove, where the devas look upon one another and sport.
Having seen this, the Tathāgata thought to himself:
"What meritorious deeds have these sentient beings planted that they have been born here to receive the status of celestial bliss?
It is by planting various roots of goodness that they obtain such retribution.
This is what is known through the activity of karma; that which will be known in the future is likewise so. The Tathāgata, with his noble eye, knows this and has attained great supernormal powers.
This concerns those who have committed evil deeds with their bodies.
Question: "What is meant by 'committing evil with the body'? Answer:
"Evil is defiled and impure; such is the commission of evil karma by means of the body.

The Tathāgata fully knows the commission of evil karma by means of speech and the commission of evil karma by means of the mind, all of which are explained without difference from the preceding passages."
"One who slanders virtuous people.
He asked: "What is meant by 'virtuous people'?"
He replied:
"The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, as well as even laypeople who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna, are also called 'good people'. He asked:
"What is meant by 'slander'?
He replied:
"To revile and disparage all wholesome dharmas—this is the speech of slander."
Furthermore, there are others who say:

"The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas all practice evil dharmas rather than the true Dharma; they possess no dharma of meditative concentration, no dharma of nirvāṇa, and no dharma of the fruits of the path."
Thus they slander, slandering in such a manner;
whether knowing [the truth] they slander, or not knowing they likewise slander—both enter into the category of those who slander the virtuous.
"Such people as these commit grave karma; because of this grave karma, the gates of heaven are closed and the gates of hell are opened.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now provide proof for this."
In a certain village there were two bhikṣus, one old and one young. The two entered the village together.
Upon first arriving at a house, they received a bowl of thin, warm gruel. Having received the gruel, the old bhikṣu thought to himself:
"There is wind in my belly, and this gruel is warm; if I consume this gruel, it will dispel the wind within my abdomen."
At that time, there was a man who, wishing to make a door-sill from a piece of wood, threw it aside; the old bhikṣu then sat upon the wood and drank his gruel.
When the young bhikṣu saw the old bhikṣu drinking the gruel, he thought, "Bhāradvāja has brought me shame.
After the old bhikṣu had finished drinking the gruel and returned to the monastery, he asked the young bhikṣu, "Elder!..."
"Is there anything to be attained within the Buddha-dharma?
He replied, "There is;
one attains the stage of Srotāpanna."
The elder bhikṣu said:
"If it is so, there is no need to further seek other paths. Why is this?"
"You have slandered me, a bhikṣu whose craving is exhausted.
Upon hearing this, the young bhikṣu immediately repented, saying:
"Venerable Sir! [I am sorry]."
"I have committed unwholesome deeds against you, Venerable Sir; I pray that you will accept my repentance.
Having said this, he departed with joy.
The Dharma Master said:
"If someone reviles a noble one or a great bhikṣu, saying these words:
'Venerable One! I now repent before you; I pray that you will accept my confession.'"
If there are fewer [monks], they should prostrate with their heads at his feet, join their palms, and speak thus:
"Virtuous One! This was my transgression; I now repent before you, Virtuous One, and pray that you accept my confession."
If they do not accept [the invitation], they shall go to another region or to another monastery.
Upon arriving at the place of the bhikṣus, if they are elders, they shall prostrate with their heads at the feet of the bhikṣus, join their palms, and say:
"Venerable Sir!"
"This was my fault; may the Venerable One accept it.
If [the other] is junior, he should say:
"Elder, this was my fault; I now repent, and pray that the Elder will accept it."

If one who has entered nirvana performs repentance at the place of nirvana, and having performed that repentance, the gates to the heavenly realms and the path to nirvana shall not be closed; it will be exactly as before, no different.
"Regarding those with wrong views. He asked:
"What is meant by 'wrong views'?"
He replied:
"Perverted views—this is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Having already assumed the form of wrong view, one further teaches others; because of the evil of speech, one slanders the noble ones (*ārya*), and the same applies to the evil karma of the mind. Having already adopted wrong view, all various evil karmas are subsumed within it."
Holding wrong views is a grave karmic offense and constitutes a heinous crime.
As stated in the sūtra, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"A bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the precepts, fully endowed with samādhi and wisdom, and possesses right view himself, should likewise teach others."

Śāriputra! Wrong view is likewise; it does not depart from body, speech, and mind. Just as when a person throws a clod of earth, it does not depart from the earth, so too the evil karma of wrong view does not depart from hell.
"Why is this? Because it constitutes a grave offense.
As stated in the sutra, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I observe that among evil deeds, none surpasses wrong view as the greatest of sins.
[He said: "If one dies with such a body... Question:
"What is meant by death?
He replied, "Death means falling into hell due to one's transgressions, from which there is no time of escape."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The four great elements disintegrate and scatter, yet it is also said that one undergoes rebirth.
The Dharma Master said:
"If one takes up the hells, one immediately blocks the gateway to the heavenly realms and liberation.
Furthermore, it is said:
'If one takes up the evil destinies, the hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras are all included therein.'"
He further said:
"As for the hells, Avīci is the first; whether one is white or black, one knows it oneself.
He further said:
"Regarding 'the good paths,' the human realm is also a good path.
He asked: "What is the meaning of 'heaven'?"
He replied:
"Form, sound, fragrance, and flavor are most excellent; these are called 'heaven.
That which knows them is known by the eye; as for the rest, you should know it yourself. I have now briefly finished explaining the Chapter on the Noble Eye."
Just as ignorance covers past lives, and because the beak of past lives pecks through it, ignorance covers the shell; likewise, one falls away from present knowledge.

Regarding the "knowledge of the destruction of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñāna*): it is the knowledge of the cessation and exhaustion of outflows within the path of the Arhat; this is called the knowledge of the destruction of outflows.
To place the mind below the [upper] limit is the contemplation of the mind;

through this contemplation of the mind, one is able to know suffering. Regarding this cessation, one thoroughly penetrates and understands all the characteristics, flavors, and aspects of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Furthermore, one contemplates from what the Truth of Suffering arises: it arises from accumulation (*samudaya*), which is precisely the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
Furthermore, one contemplates the cessation of suffering; this is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya). That which leads to the Truth of Cessation is the Path (mārga).
Having contemplated the Four Truths, their characteristics are thus: they are truly real and without difference, and one penetrates and fully knows them all.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "I know the Four Truths; thus have I seen them, thus have I known them.

Regarding the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*): it flows forth from desire; this is an indication of the fruit. Within the context of that fruit, he says, "I am now liberated," and furthermore, possessing the knowledge of realization, having contemplated, he knows: "I shall not be born again."
"Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha said to the brahmin:
'I shall not be born again.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Is it that which was not produced in the past, is not being produced in the present, or will not be produced in the future?
If you say it was produced in the past, that which was produced in the past has already ceased;
if you say it is being produced in the present, that which is being produced in the present has already arisen."
If one asks, "Regarding future birth, since future birth has not yet arrived, what further birth could there be?
the answer is:
"Because the causes have been severed, this is called non-arising."
"To dwell" means to dwell in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
As for "the holy life," it refers to dwelling together with virtuous persons and the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*); this is what the Buddha pointed out as the life of one who has gone forth.
"Having done what was to be done" means that regarding the Four Truths and the Four Paths, what was to be accomplished has been completed.
For this reason, the Buddha said to the brahmin:
"What I had to do is finished; I shall not return."
Question: "What is meant by 'non-returner' (anāgāmin)? Answer:
"The outflows of all afflictions no longer return to me; therefore, I am one who does not return, and there is no further need for diligent exertion.
The Tathāgata has already perceived and known this; this is called the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows."
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata wishes to reveal [the truth] to the brāhmaṇa; the Buddha has already attained the threefold knowledge—the knowledge of the past, present, and future.
The Dharma Master said:
"One who speaks thus should not praise themselves; for what reason, then, does the Tathāgata praise himself?
He replied:
"The Buddha spoke these words because he desires to have compassion for the world, including the brahmins and others."
“I am a holy man; I am the eldest, the unsurpassed honored one, and all-knowing. I do not prostrate myself before others.
When the Brahmin heard these various teachings of the Buddha, his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately repented before the Buddha, saying:
“Śramaṇa Gautama possesses such noble benefits and fulfillment. I truly did not know this; Śramaṇa Gautama is indeed one who has fully perfected the merits of his previous lives.”
The brahmin then reproached himself; having reproached himself and heard the teaching of the Dharma, he immediately praised it, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Śramaṇa Gautama, please point out for us the flavor of the Dharma.
The Dharma Master asked:
“For what reason did he twice praise him, saying ‘Excellent’?”
He further spoke in verse:
"When anger is extinguished, one should quickly offer praise; With earnestness, one should respond with great surprise and laughter.
With a mind of faith, sorrow, contentment, and beauty, Each line should be repeated with gravity."
"This is praise herein. Why is that?
Because when the brahmin heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, his heart was filled with joy; having no other way to offer thanks, he sang this song for himself."
The Dharma Master said:
"The Brahmin’s mind should have this reflection:
'The Dharma taught by the Buddha is profound in meaning and exquisite in expression; it skillfully enters the human heart, giving rise to great compassion, and is truly a source of joy.'"
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I was like an overturned bowl; now that the Buddha has preached the Dharma so that I may hear it, I am like a bowl turned upright, able to receive the nectar of immortality."

It is as if a person were to conceal a precious treasure beneath grass and wood, and another person points it out so that it may be known; or as if a person had lost their way, and another takes them by the hand and points out the correct path; or as if one were in great darkness, and another provides a lamp or candle so that they may see the road—I am just like this.
The Dharma Master said:
"As for why the Brahmin spoke these words, I shall now further expound this meaning.
The mind of the Brahmin was like an inverted bowl, unable to receive the flavor of the nectar of immortality; the Buddha has now opened it up for him to show him how to receive that nectar."

Why is this? Just as grass and trees provide concealment, since the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, false views have acted as grass and trees to conceal the True Dharma; with no one to point it out, the present Buddha now points it out so that it may be known.

The "lost" refers to those for whom the paths of externalists and false views serve as their way; they are deluded within the wondrous path and fail to see the good path. The Buddha takes the Dharma as his hand, pointing out the way so that they may attain liberation.
Just as those who are ignorant and shrouded in darkness cannot see the three realms, the Buddha takes the Dharma as a lamp and bestows it upon them so that they may attain illumination.
Having offered this praise, the Brahmin Vairaṇya’s mind became exceedingly pure, and he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Śramaṇa Gautama."

"To take refuge" means to follow, and it also means to rely upon. One knows that the Buddha has destroyed the afflictions; next, one takes refuge in the Dharma and takes refuge in the Sangha. Regarding taking refuge in the Dharma:

the Tathāgata accumulated practices to attain this Dharma and shall no longer fall [into lower realms]. If a person follows the Dharma, they will receive the Dharma and shall not fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.
"Dharma" means that which is rightly received; it is also said to refer to the Noble Path and Nirvana, for the Path is Dharma.
As stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Dharma is not something created; there is the Eightfold Path, the supreme among all dharmas."
The Dharma Master said:
"I have now given a brief account.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin named Cāturmānava who praised the Buddha with songs and composed this verse:”
"Free from desire, unshakable by desire, not creating the conditions for sorrow,
not flowing against the current of sensual flavors— one who possesses such supreme discernment is truly wise."
Among all dharmas, it is supreme; one should receive refuge in it.
To those who have entered the four stages of fruition, there are eight types when distinguished.
Among the Sangha, it is supreme, and one obtains a great karmic fruit.
"By taking refuge in this, one is called a true upāsaka.
Thus the brāhmaṇa said:
"May the Buddha know that I have received the three refuges."
The Dharma Master said:
"If one were to explain the Three Refuges here, it would result in excessive prolixity.
If you wish to know them, you should learn of them from the Abhidharma-vibhāṣā itself."
"May the Śramaṇa Gautama know that I have become an upāsaka; may the Buddha declare me to be an upāsaka of the Buddha.
He asked: "What is meant by an upāsaka?"
Who is an upāsaka? Who is not an upāsaka?
In what way does one become an upāsaka by virtue of possessing precepts?
Is there one who possesses the mind of an upāsaka?
What is called an upāsaka? And what is not called an upāsaka?
The Dharma Master said:
"The meanings here are very numerous; they cannot be fully explained within this [text].
One should come to know them from the *Śrāvakabhūmi-vibhāṣā* itself."
"From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall not accept any other teacher; may the Buddha know this.

Even if someone were to cut off my head with a sword and force me to say that it is not the Buddha, not the Dharma, and not the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, my head might rather fall to the ground than for me to utter such words."
The brahmin, entrusting his body and life to the Tathāgata and desiring to make offerings himself, spoke these words:
"May the World-Honored One accept my invitation to stay for the three months of the early summer retreat at the kingdom of Vairaṇyā together with the community of bhikṣus."
The brahmin said:
"I have now become an upāsaka; I pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me and accept my invitation to the kingdom of Vairaṇyā."
The Tathāgata accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Why did the Buddha not answer the Brahmin's request?"
He replied: "I have answered.
While people of the world answer with body and speech, the World-Honored One answers with a mind of forbearance."
"Out of compassion for the brahmin,
he knew that the Buddha had accepted his invitation. He asked:
"What is meant by 'accepting an invitation'?
He replied:
"If one does not accept an invitation, one should respond with both speech and body."
The World-Honored One remained silent, his countenance serene and joyful; thus, the brahmin knew that the Buddha had accepted his invitation.

He immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and paid homage in the four directions before departing. Joining his ten fingers and palms together at the crown of his head, he walked backward until he could no longer see the Tathāgata, whereupon he again prostrated and turned back to leave.
At that time, the kingdom of Vairaṇyā was suffering from a severe famine.
"At that time" refers to when the Buddha accepted the invitation of the Brahmin of Vairaṇyā for the three months of the early summer retreat.

Regarding the "famine": food and drink were difficult to obtain; even if a person possessed food and drink, if they did not give it because their mind was not pure or sincere, this too is called a famine.
"In the kingdom of Virañjā it is not so, because the five grains do not produce fruit.
This is the second doubt. He asked:
"What is meant by 'the two kinds of doubt'?
He replied:
"The two refer to the doubt concerning two types of mind."
"What are the two kinds of mental doubt?
He replied:

"Mental doubt regarding these three months of the summer retreat consists of doubting whether one will obtain alms-food or not, or doubting whether one will be able to sustain life or not; these are the two kinds of mental doubt."

"White bones" refers to the skeletal remains of poor and lowly people who, unable to obtain alms, die of hunger and are cast away in wild deserts in a state of disarray; these are called "white bones."
It is also said:
"When the five grains do not produce ears and their whiteness is like bone, this is also called 'white bones' (pāṇḍuka).

As for 'like counting-sticks' (śalākāvasthā), it refers to when the grain has just begun to form ears but encounters a great drought; the stalks stand upright like counting-sticks, and this is called 'like counting-sticks'."
Furthermore, it is said:
"It is not so; during times of famine, tally-sticks were used for the marketplace, and this is what is meant by 'like tally-sticks. Why is that?"

When it was time for the market, those who were strong were able to enter while the weak were not; the latter cried out from outside. Seeing the weak people, the rice-seller felt compassion and gave rise to a mind of equanimity; he opened the door and let them in, seating them in order. He first received their payment and then gave them the rice, using tally-sticks to calculate the amounts according to how much each had purchased.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"In this region there is famine and scarcity; everything is calculated by tallying sticks. When the bhikṣus enter seven or eight villages, they sometimes obtain a small amount and sometimes obtain nothing at all."

At that time, a merchant from the north drove five hundred horses southward to trade goods; having gained two or three times his profit, and for the sake of seeking further gain, he traveled through various kingdoms in succession until he reached the kingdom of Vairaṇyā, where he stayed for the four months of the summer retreat.
Question: "For what reason did the horse dealer not depart but remain for four months? Answer:
"Because of the heavy rains, the roads were impassable for horses; consequently, they established stables outside the city and built houses, fences, and enclosures for themselves.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went to the merchants' quarters to beg for alms, receiving five *śīrṣa* of horse-rye each."
He asked: "Was it out of faith or out of lack of faith that you gave the barley to the bhikṣus?
He replied:
“Faith. A horse-dealer entered a village and saw, day after day, various bhikṣus begging for alms and returning with empty bowls.
Having seen this, the merchant returned and told his companions of what he had witnessed, and they each thought to themselves:”

"The bhikṣus are extremely weary from begging for alms and have obtained nothing at all. We should deliberate together: if we provide [food] every day, it may not suffice for the duration of the morning. We should therefore reduce our own horse-ration shares and give five *liǎng* each to the bhikṣus."
"The bhikṣus will receive this horse-barley and will not become exhausted; it will not cause much harm to our horses.
Having deliberated thus, the merchants went to where the bhikṣus were, paid their respects, and said:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"You may accept from us five *śīrṣa* of barley per person each day, as well as various foods and whatever meals you wish to prepare.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, one gives barley to the bhikṣus daily; having put on their robes, they go out for alms in the morning.
Question: "What is meant by 'morning'? Answer:
“From dawn until midday is called ‘morning.
As for ‘putting on robes,’ it means wrapping the body in the *kāṣāya*.
As for ‘begging for alms,’ he could not obtain any food by begging in the village of Pirañña; he traversed the entire village, yet not a single person came out to respond to him.”
Regarding "returning to the monastery with barley": having obtained barley by begging at various places, one returns.

Regarding "taking the barley, pounding and winnowing it for food": when an elderly bhikṣu has no *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) and no one else to do the work, he prepares the gruel and rice himself. Whether eight or ten people work together until the task is finished, they shall divide it and eat.

The venerable Ānanda took the Tathāgata’s hand and ground it himself; Ānanda, being fully endowed with wisdom, prepared the food so that it was of supreme flavor. The devas further infused it with nectar (*amṛta*), and when he had finished, the Buddha accepted and ate it, immediately entering into *samādhi*. From that time forth, he no longer went out to beg for alms.
Question: “At that time, was the Venerable Ānanda attending upon the Buddha?
Answer: [He was.]

“Attendant, since the Tathāgata arose from beneath the Bodhi tree, those who have served the Buddha for twenty years have not been constant.
