At times it was the Venerable Nāga, or the Venerable Nāgita, or the Venerable Miṇḍika, or the Venerable Upavāna, or the Venerable Sākata, or the Venerable Sunakṣatra; such great virtuous ones would come to serve as they pleased and depart when they were displeased, or all would leave at once. It was then that the Venerable Ānanda came to serve.”
He asked: "The country is suffering from famine; why is there not a single person who performs meritorious deeds by portioning out a small amount of rice to offer to the assembly of monks?
Furthermore, a Brahmin invited the World-Honored One for the preceding three months of the summer retreat, yet you did not provide for him. For what reason?"
“The Māra Pāpīyān shrouds an area of one yojana, causing all the people within it to lose their resolve so that none offer any worship; having done so, he departs.”
He asked, “Does the Tathāgata not know [this]? [The other replied,] “Excellent!”
Because he wished to establish the precepts and preach the Dharma, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You virtuous people are already superior; future bhikṣus shall seek out rice, grain, and meat."
The Dharma Master said:
"I do not yet understand this meaning; the Tathāgata should have spoken thus: 'Ānanda!'"
"You virtuous ones, because alms-food is difficult to obtain during times of famine and scarcity, you have maintained the True Dharma through contentment; for this reason, you are superior.
Because you are able to subdue the mind of greed during times of famine and scarcity, for this reason, you are superior."

In other villages, rice and grain were abundant, and there was an abundance of sweet fruits and exotic flavors; yet no one went there. Among the multitude, not a single person thought of it, nor felt resentment, nor uttered a complaint, saying:
"Why do we stay here?"
“World-Honored One!
Why do you not go to that abundant village where food and drink are easily obtained?
He did not say such a thing, nor did he harbor any resentment.
"Why has the Brahmin of Vairaṇyā invited us here for the summer retreat yet failed to provide us with offerings?
Furthermore, they had no other thoughts of seeking gain or profit, nor did they praise one another,
saying, "This person has attained the Way."

To cause others to understand this and to hope that they may make offerings to such words, each person should seal their lips in silence and rely single-mindedly upon the Tathāgata; for this reason, it is superior.
Question: "Do you know the obscuration of Māra?
Answer: "I do."
“I know. He asked again:
“Why did the Tathāgata not go to Śrāvastī, Rājagṛha, or other countries to observe the rains retreat, but instead come to this country?”
He replied:

"Even if one were to leave the kingdoms of Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha and go as far as Uttarakuru, or ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Māra would still come to obscure them; there would be no way to hide or escape."

Why is this? This year the King of Māras is greatly incensed; the Tathāgata has already observed everywhere and sees that there is only the horse-dealer in the kingdom of Vairaṇyā upon whom one may rely for the rains retreat.
A question was asked:
"If the Māra-king is capable of obscuring other people, for what reason did he not obscure the horse-seller, so that the Buddha and the assembly of monks could not obtain food?"
He replied:
"It was indeed able to conceal him. Why is this?
After the Māra-king had departed, the horse-seller arrived later; therefore, he could not be concealed."
Question: "Why did the Māra not further obstruct the horse-seller? Answer:
"One must not cover it entirely.
The Dharma Master said:
"There are four kinds [of cases] where Māra cannot cover it."
What are the four?
First, making offerings within the palace; second, ensuring that medicinal decoctions are never lacking; third, the lifespan of the Tathāgata; and fourth, the radiance of the Tathāgata.

"The light of the sun, moon, Brahmā kings, and others, upon reaching the presence of the Tathāgata, was eclipsed and did not appear; therefore, the Māra King could not obscure it by any various means.
"At one time, the Buddha heard the sound of mortars and pestles."
The bhikṣus had obtained horse-barley and were returning when they began to pound it; this is why there was a sound.

As for knowing yet asking, knowing yet not asking, or knowing and therefore asking: the Buddha asks because he knows that there is a causal condition through which he may benefit sentient beings. Thus he asks.
One who knows but does not inquire does so because there is no benefit; therefore, one does not inquire.
One who inquires at the proper time does so by inquiring when it is the right moment; therefore, one inquires at the proper time.
Regarding "not asking": the Tathāgata knows it is not the proper time and thus does not ask.
He asks when there is meaning; he does not ask when there is no meaning.
There are two causes and conditions for asking:

First, it was because he wished to preach the Dharma; second, it was because he intended to establish the causes and conditions for the precepts for his śrāvaka disciples, whether they be light or heavy.
For this reason, he asked Ānanda: "What sound is this?"
Ānanda replied,
“This is the sound of the bhikṣus pounding barley.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
Why did the Buddha utter this praise?

In the future, monks dwelling in monasteries will find food and drink easily obtained, yet they will give rise to a conceited mind, saying that the rice is coarse, or that it is overcooked, or that it is too hard, or that the grains are broken, or that it is sour and salty. Such remarks are merely ways of seeking out fine grain, meat, and other delicacies.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"You virtuous ones should serve as the causal conditions for wholesome dharmas for the bhikṣus of future generations; by means of your practice, may the bhikṣus of the future, whether they obtain food and drink that is excellent or inferior, give rise to neither attachment nor aversion."
"In the past, when the Dharma King was still in the world, even the great arhats ate horse fodder; how much more so should we not harbor feelings of disdain or contempt for this food and drink?
[Thus ends] the Mahāmaudgalyāyana Chapter. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana...
"Great" (Mahā) means that among the śrāvakas, his supernatural powers and wisdom are the greatest; therefore, he is called "Great.
"Maudgalyāyana" is his clan name.
"Addressed the Buddha" means he spoke toward the World-Honored One.
He asked, "Why did you speak thus to the World-Honored One?
He replied:

“Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana attained the perfection of a śrāvaka seven days after going forth; furthermore, the Tathāgata praised Maudgalyāyana as the foremost in supernatural powers (ṛddhi). Because Maudgalyāyana possessed such power, he thought: ‘The kingdom of Piḷañña is suffering from a great famine;
it is difficult for the community of bhikṣus to obtain almsfood, and they are extremely exhausted. I shall now turn the earth over and take its essence to provide for the Saṃgha.’”
He further reflected to himself:
"If I were to overturn the earth without informing the World-Honored One, it would mean my supernatural power is equal to that of the Tathāgata, which would contradict my own dharma."
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When the earth was first formed, there was 'earth-fat' (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), which was like fresh butter and had a taste like honey."
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I wish to overturn the earth and take the fertile soil from beneath it to provide for the assembly of monks.
"To overturn" means to take from below and return to above.
"Why is this? It is for the sake of the Sangha.
The Buddha did not wish to grant permission, so he had Maudgalyāyana let out a lion’s roar; then the Buddha questioned Maudgalyāyana:
"All cities, towns, and villages depend upon this earth; yet this earth cannot be suspended in empty space. How, then, will you construct it?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "World-Honored One!..."

I shall now, with one hand, transform it into earth; I will receive all sentient beings of the cities, towns, and villages so that they are no different from the earth itself, and with my other hand, I will deliver those sentient beings who rely upon the earth.
The Buddha replied:
"Stop, Maudgalyāyana!"
Question: "Why did the World-Honored One not permit Maudgalyāyana to turn the earth upside down? Answer:

"Out of compassion for sentient beings who dwell in perversion, I may say 'this is so' or 'this is not so. Yet, in the cities, towns, and villages where I reside, people are mutually alarmed and astonished, saying: 'This is not our city, town, field, garden, pond, or forest.'"
The Dharma Master said:
"Only those with supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) can perform such deeds; it is not for those who lack them.
It is not only a time of scarcity now, but there will also be scarcity in the future; when such times of scarcity occur, who will be able to act like Maudgalyāyana?"
In the future, there will be few śrāvaka disciples possessing supernormal powers. If they enter a village to beg for alms, people, upon seeing them, will say:

"When the World-Honored One was in the world, his śrāvaka disciples were fully endowed with the observance of the precepts; thus they attained supernormal powers and, during times of famine, turned over the great earth to take up the 'earth-flavor' (pṛthivī-rasa) to provide for the assembly of monks."
"Now the assembly of monks does not fully observe the precepts; had they been complete, it would have been no different from before.
Furthermore, there has not been even the slightest gift.
Because others hold such inverted views, they treat the noble ones with contempt; due to this contempt, they fall into hell after death.
"Therefore, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana, 'Do not take pleasure in overturning the earth.
Maudgalyāyana entreated the Buddha to overturn the earth, but he did not succeed; he then made another request."
"Excellent!
The World-Honored One said,
"Cease for now."
The Dharma Master said:
"From the phrase 'Excellent! onwards, as previously explained, you should understand it yourself.
The Dharma Master said:
“There is a slight difference. What is it?
Maudgalyāyana further wished to pull the land of Uttarakuru back and join it to Jambudvīpa.”
Question: "What is the ocean like? Answer:
“The ocean is like a cow’s footprint; one may cross it in a single step. Let the various bhikṣus eat as they do in their respective villages.
Chapter One: Śāriputra. At that time, when Upāli desired to establish the root of the Vinaya Piṭaka, Śāriputra arose from his place of seclusion and had this thought.
Question: "What is meant by 'tranquility'? Answer:
“Silent and without sound, it is also called the stillness of one-pointed mind.
“How does the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time?
“Answering from the perspective of Vipaśyin Buddha, the meaning of the others shall be understood naturally.”
Question: "Why did Śāriputra not simply use his own supernormal powers to observe and know [the situation], instead coming to inform the Buddha? Answer:

"No, Śāriputra. If one were to observe with supernormal power (ṛddhi), one might know whether the Buddhas abide for a long time or not; however, if one attempts to discern the causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) of the Buddhas, one cannot fully comprehend them."
The Venerable Mahāpadma said:
"I am able.
For what reason?"

Since the sixteen kinds of knowledge of the Arhats are not difficult to understand based on such principles, [the interlocutor] came to address the Buddha and inquire in order to demonstrate that the World-Honored One is supreme by relying upon the Tathāgata.
The Buddha replied to Śāriputra: "As for the rest, you shall naturally understand the sequence of the Vinaya rules.
What is meant by 'causal conditions' (nidāna)?
This meaning is easy to understand."

The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Regarding the Buddha Vipaśyin, he was the first; yet all Buddhas are not indolent. Whether for one person, two or three people, or increasing further until for all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, they preach the Dharma according to whether there are differences in their dispositions. For this assembly, which is small, they should speak briefly; for that assembly, which is large, they should speak extensively. Yet they do not preach with partiality or hierarchy, but preach the Dharma equally and in a single way to all."
For example, the lion king rises once every seven days to seek food; when he seizes a sentient being, regardless of its size, he first roars and then captures it.

Why is this? If the lion were to seize a sentient being without first letting out a great roar, because of his lack of gravity, the creature might escape. Therefore, he roars in all cases to cause the beings to be terrified and submissive before capturing them.
The Buddha is likewise; toward all sentient beings, regardless of whether they are great or small, he always speaks with earnest diligence.
If he were to speak only briefly, sentient beings might not cultivate the practice with a diligent mind.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata holds the Dharma in the highest esteem.

Now, when our World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, it is like the water of the great ocean, which has but a single flavor; the Buddhas of the past were likewise so. However, the minds of sentient beings are easily taught; by now preaching the meaning of a single verse to lead them into the Four Noble Truths, the Buddhas of the past did not extensively expound the Dharma or compose verses for their cultivation.
The Dharma Master said:
"Since the preceding sentence has already explained this, it is not repeated here.
This refers to not formulating precepts for the sake of the śrāvakas."
Question: "Why did the Buddhas of the past not establish precepts for their śrāvaka disciples? Answer:

"Because the śrāvaka disciples do not commit transgressions, they do not establish a majestic Prātimokṣa, nor do they recite the precepts every half-month; this continues until the sixth year, during which time the instruction on the Prātimokṣa is suspended for six years."
This teaching was spoken by the Tathāgata himself; he did not have the śrāvakas speak it.

At that time, in Jambudvīpa, at the Kṣemaka Deer Park in Rājagṛha, the capital of Bandhumatī, which was the dwelling place of Vipaśyin Buddha, the entire community of bhikṣus assembled. There, the Buddha performed the *poṣadha*, as did the assembly of monks—whether three persons, two persons, or a single person performing the *poṣadha*.

In the past, there were eighty-four thousand monasteries in Jambudvīpa; in some monasteries there were one hundred thousand or two hundred thousand bhikṣus, yet they were not noisy, all dwelling in tranquility.

At that time, the minds of the devas and humans desired to hear the Buddha preach the precepts; they constantly calculated the years, and when it reached the sixth year, they immediately assembled the great multitude and went to the Buddha’s dwelling to await his preaching of the precepts.
At that time, those bhikṣus who possessed supernatural powers arrived; those without such powers were informed by the devas:
"It is time to depart.
They immediately took up their robes and bowls. Empowered by the supernatural strength of the devas, the bhikṣus reached the Poṣadha hall and went before [the Buddha] to prostrate at his feet.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, knowing that the assembly had gathered, immediately spoke the instruction on the Prātimokṣa:
“Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s highest excellence.
One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the home life Is not called a śramaṇa.”
Commit no evil in any way; Fulfill all wholesome dharmas;
Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Do not harm others, do not speak ill of them, And do not destroy the affairs of others.
Acting according to what is taught in the precepts, knowing moderation in eating and drinking,
being content with all things, and always delighting in secluded places—
this is called the teaching of the Buddhas.
"By such skillful means, all past Buddhas have taught the Prātimokṣa using this verse. This concerns the length of the Buddhas' lifespans; therefore, they spoke thus regarding short lifespans."

From beneath the Bodhi tree, the various Buddhas have established the precepts for their śrāvaka disciples; these are the Vinaya of majestic power (vīrya-prātimokṣa), not spoken by the Tathāgata himself, but spoken by the śrāvaka disciples. Therefore, we Śākyamuni Buddhas, for twenty years from beneath the Bodhi tree, have all taught the instructional prātimokṣa.
Furthermore, on one occasion at the Pāvā Sīmā Monastery, in the hall of Mrgāramātṛ, after the bhikṣus had taken their seats, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer perform the poṣadha, nor shall I recite the Prātimokṣa; you yourselves shall recite it."
"Why is this? The Tathāgata does not recite the Prātimokṣa in an impure assembly.
From that time until now, the śrāvaka disciples have recited the Prātimokṣa of majestic power.
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya that the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The Buddhas of the past did not proclaim the Pratimokṣa of majestic power; they proclaimed the Pratimokṣa of instruction."

“Vipaśyin, the third Buddha, did not preach the Prātimokṣa. After those three Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, their śrāvaka disciples also entered parinirvāṇa. The final śrāvaka disciples were of various surnames and various names; some were of the Gautama clan, some of the Maudgalyāyana clan; some were named Buddhadeva, some were named Dharmagupta. They came from various lineages:
some were of the Brahmin caste, some of the householder caste, and some of the Kṣatriya caste.”

Furthermore, they do not come from a single family—whether from wealthy families, impoverished families, or low-born families—but rather they go forth from such various and diverse backgrounds, from different clans and lineages, to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Because those who enter the True Dharma possess diverse names and surnames, each acts according to their own individual inclinations and does not inherit the Buddha-dharma as a unified whole; for this reason, the Buddha-dharma does not long remain in the world. It is because of these factors that [the Dharma endures only briefly].
Question: "Why do the bhikṣus not cultivate diligence with vigor, such that the True Dharma so quickly declines and perishes? Answer:

"If even the venerable elders of former times were not yet virtuous, how much more so are we, who each fail to protect the treasury of the Dharma, thereby causing the Buddha’s True Dharma to perish so swiftly?"
Those things not strung together with thread will scatter when blown by the wind; "strung" refers to being bound together.
For example, if various kinds of flowers are not strung together with thread, they will scatter when blown by the wind; the Buddha-dharma is also like this.
"Because he does not establish formal precepts, he first observes with his mind and then instructs the śrāvakas.
He asked: "What is the meaning of this?"
He replied:

"The Buddhas of the past first observed the minds of the śrāvakas and then gave them instruction; because the śrāvakas were easily able to realize the principle, the Buddhas did not provide them with extensive explanations."
Regarding the "Forest of Fear": if anyone enters this forest, fear immediately arises.
In the same way, you who practice reflection have three types of reflection;
with renunciation as the first, you should diligently apply your minds to these reflections.
"You should not entertain such thoughts. There are three unwholesome states of mind, of which the desire for [sensual] objects is the first; you must be careful not to think them.
In this way, you should keep this in mind and constantly maintain it in your hearts by contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self."
Do not act in this way; you should not harbor such thoughts: do not contemplate impermanence as permanent, and do not contemplate impurity as pure; you must not entertain such reflections.
"These are the things you should abandon: all unwholesome states you should abandon.
These are the things you should arouse and abide in: wholesome states you should arouse, and those already attained, you should cause to increase."

"Regarding 'liberation of the mind through the non-arising of afflictions': the mind is liberated because it does not grasp at afflictions; it is also said that one is extinguished by means of the extinction of non-arising, rather than through the extinction of what has already arisen."

Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla: from the moment they attain a mind free from the arising of afflictions, all such individuals are Arhats; it is like a lotus flower that blooms as soon as the first rays of the sun appear.

Śāriputra, as for those who previously entered the Forest of Terrors (Bhīṣaṇavana), if a person had not yet abandoned desire when entering this forest, their hair would all stand on end because of the forest’s formidable appearance.
"Śāriputra, this is what constitutes 'causes and conditions'.
The Dharma Master said:
"The meaning of these sequential phrases is easy; you shall understand it for yourself."

Regarding those who do not abide for long: the lifespan of Vipaśyin Buddha was eighty thousand years, and it was the same for his assembly of śrāvakas; from the time the Buddha was in the world until the last of his śrāvakas, the Buddha-dharma remained in the world for one hundred thousand and sixty thousand years.
The lifespan of Śikhin Buddha was seventy thousand years, and the lifespan of his śrāvaka disciples was likewise.
The lifespan of Viśvabhū Buddha was sixty thousand years, and the lifespan of his śrāvakas was also thus.

The lifespans of these two Buddhas will reach their final end, and the Dharma of the Śrāvakas will remain in the world for one hundred thousand, forty-two million years; when counted in this sequence, it is therefore clear that the Buddha-Dharma will not abide for long.

Thereupon, Śāriputra, having heard that the Dharma of the three Buddhas would not remain for long, and desiring further to ask the Buddha about his long abiding in the world, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"By what causes and conditions does the Buddha-dharma abide for a long time?

"The lifespans of the Buddhas are as follows: the lifespan of Krakucchanda Buddha was forty thousand years; the lifespan of Kanakamuni Buddha was thirty thousand years; the lifespan of Kāśyapa Buddha was twenty thousand years; and the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha is one hundred years. The lifespans of his śrāvaka disciples are likewise. For this reason, the Buddha-dharma abides for a long time."

"World-Honored One, I should now take half of Kāśyapa’s lifespan—ten thousand years—and appear in the world at that time; yet, upon observing the faculties of sentient beings, there would be none who have reached maturity.
I should appear after five thousand years, and subsequently after five hundred years, yet again there would be no sentient beings whose faculties are matured.

Only when the lifespan has reached one hundred years would there be sentient beings capable of being saved. For this reason, the Buddha appears in the world during a short lifespan, and his śrāvaka disciples are likewise."

Regarding the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma as previously stated: for the first three Buddhas, the Buddha-dharma perished along with their lifespans; therefore, it is said that their dharma did not endure long. As for the latter three Buddhas, although the Buddhas passed into parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma still remains in the world; therefore, it is said that their dharma endures long.
Thereupon, having heard what the Buddha had said, Śāriputra, desiring that the Buddha-dharma might endure for a long time, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will establish the precepts for the śrāvaka disciples."
As stated in the Vinaya-mūla, Śāriputra arose from samādhi; the sequence of the subsequent phrases for the others shall be understood accordingly.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “Stop!”
"Wait! The time has not yet come.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will establish the precepts for the sake of all disciples.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Stop! Stop!
This Dharma is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it can be known only by Buddha after Buddha, for the defilements have not yet arisen."
Question: "What is meant by 'defilement'? Answer:
"Regarding 'the locus of defilement': that which transgresses the Dharma of the Tathāgata in this life and future lives is called 'defilement.
This has not yet been established as a precept for the śrāvakas. He asked:
"Why does he not establish precepts for the śrāvakas?
He replied:
"If the Tathāgata were to establish precepts before anyone had yet produced outflows (āsrava), sentient beings would conceive thoughts of slander, saying:"

"How is it, Gautama Śramaṇa? Like your śrāvaka disciples, they are all of noble lineage or former royalty; having renounced their wealth, palaces, wives, children, and kinsmen, they do not spare even their own lives. They are all contented and have no further desires for the world."
"How is it, Gautama, that you instead bind them with the *prātimokṣa*?
Gautama, you have not yet mastered the discernment of worldly people.
Thus he spoke as follows:
"If I were to establish precepts, people of the world would not give rise to a heart of reverence.

It is like a physician who is not skilled at treating disease: seeing a person who has just begun to develop an abscess—though the nature of the abscess exists but it has not yet fully formed—he immediately lances it. Once lanced, blood flows profusely and the patient suffers great pain; although he applies medicine and the wound heals, [the initial act was premature]."
The physician said to him, "I have treated your illness; you must give me my fee.
The patient replied:

“This foolish physician—if he were treating my illness, he might do so; yet I was originally without illness, and he has forcibly torn my flesh, causing blood to flow and inflicting great agony, while then demanding payment from me—is this not madness?”

The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: if they first establish a precept and then give rise to slander, saying, "I am personally without fault, yet you have forcibly established this precept for me."
"Therefore, the Tathāgata did not establish the precepts beforehand,
[only] if outflows were to arise.
It was asked:
"What is meant by 'the arising of outflows'?
He replied:
"If an outflow has already arisen within the Saṅgha, at that time the Tathāgata shall establish precepts for his disciples and point out the Prātimokṣa."
For example, it is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness so that it may be cured; he receives great rewards and is praised, saying:
"This excellent King of Physicians has skillfully treated my ailment."
The Tathāgata is likewise; he establishes precepts according to the offenses committed, and [the monks] joyfully accept and uphold them without complaint.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states:
"Stop!..."
"Stop, Śāriputra!
Only when an impure dharma arises will the World-Honored One then establish a precept."
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases shall be understood of themselves.
Within the Buddha-dharma, who was the first to leave the household life?"
The son of Paṅguda was named Upasena. Because of Upasena, a precept was established:

if one has not yet reached ten years of seniority (*vassa*) and yet confers the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a disciple—such as when Upasena had two years of seniority and his disciple had one year—the Buddha subsequently established this rule and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if anyone who has not reached ten years of seniority confers the full ordination upon a disciple, they commit the offense of *dukkaṭa* (transgression)."

After the Buddha had finished establishing the precepts, there was again a bhikṣu who, although having ten years of seniority or more than ten years of seniority, was foolish and lacked wisdom, yet conferred the full ordination upon his disciples.
The Buddha further established a precept and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a person who lacks wisdom bestows full ordination upon another, they commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*."

The Buddha permitted that those who possess wisdom—whether they have ten years of seniority or more than ten years—and are well-able to provide instruction, may be allowed to confer the full ordination upon their disciples.

"As for 'not yet many': when the number of monks among the Sangha was not yet large, and the dwellings were not yet extensive, there might have been those who committed offenses against the rules of leakage had the Sangha been numerous; it was only at such a time that the Tathāgata subsequently established the precepts."
If a bhikṣu stays overnight with one who has not received full ordination for more than two or three nights, that bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu year after year takes on a disciple, that bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a disciple year after year, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a pāyattika offense.
This has already been stated; you should understand it for yourself.
Regarding "great gain and offerings": if the Saṃgha receives great offerings, tainted (sāsrava) dharmas arise; at such a time, the Tathāgata shall establish a precept.
If a bhikṣu accepts a naked ascetic, whether male or female, and gives them food, drink, or other items with his own hands, that bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.

Regarding those who have not heard much: if one has not heard much within the Sangha, yet among the community of bhikṣus there are those who have heard much, then the dharma of outflows arises. If one has mastered the recitation of either one Āgama or five Āgamas, yet with an improper mind explains the meaning in a perverted way—saying what is not the Vinaya is the Vinaya, and what is not the Dharma is the Dharma—for this reason the Buddha established the precept:
if a bhikṣu speaks these words, "I already know the Dharma taught by the Buddha."
"One who speaks these words incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
This is no different from the case of a *śrāmaṇera*.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, based on the existence of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), establishes precepts for my disciples."
"What is meant by 'outflows' (āsrava)?
He replied, "They are bandits."
"What is meant by 'bandits'? He replied,
"Those who violate the precepts within the Buddha-dharma are bandits."
"What is meant by 'bandits'? He replied:
"Those who are not śramaṇas yet claim for themselves:"
"I am a śramaṇa," yet he plunders the property of the four classes of followers. For this reason,
it is said in the Vinaya that as long as there has been no arising of outflows (āsrava-dharma) and no plundering of others, there is likewise said to be no one who has violated the precepts.
"Being without fault" means being without afflictions and being without calamity.
"Not transgressing the precepts and not being defiled by dark dharmas"—dark dharmas refers to the breaking of the precepts, and it also refers to the non-disruption of the Sangha.
"Extremely pure" means extremely luminous.
"Abiding on the ground of reality" means abiding on the ground of reality consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall explain the sequence.
During the previous three months of the summer retreat in the kingdom of Vairaṇyā, five hundred bhikṣus attained the stage of Srotāpanna as their minimum realization."
Question: "What is meant by the path of the srotāpanna? Answer:
“Srotāpanna means ‘one who flows. He asked:
“In what sense does one flow?”
He replied:
"The Way—if a person enters this stream of the Way, it is called the path of the srotāpanna (stream-enterer).
As stated in the sutra, the Buddha asked Śāriputra:"
"What is meant by 'srotāpanna'?
Śāriputra replied,
"This refers to one who has been well-guided by the World-Honored One through the Eightfold Path."
What are the eight? First, right view;
second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'stream-enterer' (srotāpanna)?
He replied:

"If a person, by means of the eight factors, comes to the good path, they are called a *srotāpanna*. Having such a name and such a clan, the fruit is named after the path; therefore, they are called a *srotāpanna*."
You should know for yourself:
that which is of a nature not to fall away is not said to be non-existent.
A stream-enterer does not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Why is this? Because they have severed the afflictions through the Path.
As for "dedicating [the merit] toward Bodhi," it means that by dedicating [it] toward the three preceding Paths, one will certainly reach [Bodhi].
"Why is this? It is for the sake of the Way.
After the Greatly Wise Śāriputra had thus answered the Tathāgata, the three-month summer retreat at Vairaṇyā concluded with the great *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda. "Addresses" means speaks;
it also means awakens.
This Dharma has existed for a long time within the Buddha-dharma; the Buddhas of the past have also addressed it:
"Once you have finished accepting separate invitations from others, you may depart.
The śrāvaka disciples may go as they please, whether they have received such invitations or not.
The Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, wishes to travel throughout all the kingdoms.

Regarding the Buddha’s travels through various lands: there are three spheres of the Buddha’s activity—first, the great sphere; second, the middling sphere; and third, the small sphere. Within these three spheres, he travels according to his will.
Question: "What is meant by 'the great sphere'? Answer:
"Nine hundred yojanas.
"What is meant by the intermediate range?
He replied:
"Six hundred yojanas.
"What is a small realm? He replied:
"One hundred *yojanas*.

When the Buddha wishes to travel through a vast realm, having completed the Great Retreat (*varṣā*), on the first day of the ninth month he departs surrounded by the community of monks. He proceeds in succession to villages to teach and preach the Dharma, accepting various offerings of food and drink; those who are ready for deliverance he delivers, and those not yet delivered he causes to obtain merit and benefit."

On the day of the ninth month, while traveling during the three months of the summer retreat, many bhikṣus had not yet completed their practice of the dharma of samādhi; therefore, the Tathāgata did not perform the great *pravāraṇā*, but waited until the minor *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the ninth month was concluded before departing.
When traveling through the middle realm, he wandered for eight months.

Regarding the minor realms, he would first remain observing until the faculties of sentient beings were matured, and then depart once they had matured; by the first day of the eleventh month, he departed, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus.

On the day of his journey in the seventh month, throughout these three realms, he caused sentient beings everywhere to leave behind their afflictions and attain the fruits of the four paths, for the sake of their transformation and instruction.
It is like a flower-gatherer who wanders throughout the mountains; seeing various flowers in full bloom, he plucks them and carries them away.
The Tathāgata is also like this.

Furthermore, there is a teaching of the Buddha: at the time of early dawn, he enters the bliss of meditative concentration; arising from that samādhi, he surveys the worlds of the ten directions with great compassion, and for those who are ready to be delivered, the Tathāgata immediately goes to deliver them.
Furthermore, there are various Buddha-dharmas: when there are those who have newly arrived from other lands, the Tathāgata immediately greets them with inquiries after their well-being.
Now, wishing to initiate the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma and to establish the prohibitions and precepts, this is the unsurpassed path of the Buddhas.
He asked: "What is meant by the Dharma of the Śrāvakas?
When the Buddha was in the world, he assembled the community on two occasions; what are these two?"

The first time was when he first entered the summer retreat with the intent to attain meditative concentration; the second time was at the conclusion of the summer retreat when he actually attained something.
Because this is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"We should go together."
Having departed, he took leave of the various brahmins.
Taking his leave, he said to the brahmins:
"The summer retreat has concluded; I now wish to travel through other countries."
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his kāṣāya robe, adjusted his garments, and departed at dawn.

Ānanda attended him as he went to the city gate; having arrived, he entered, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the alleys, streets, and houses throughout the city, making them all appear like masses of gold, with the five colors—black, yellow, and the rest—shining like flashes of lightning, as they proceeded toward the house of the brahmin Vairaṇyā.
Standing at the gate, a man suddenly beheld the Buddha’s radiance; he went inside and informed the brāhmaṇa, saying, "The śramaṇa Gautama is now outside the gate."

Upon hearing the sound of the Buddha’s arrival, the brahmin was suddenly awakened; he immediately rose, took a woolen rug and a cotton mat, spread them over his seat, and went out in person to welcome him, saying to the World-Honored One:
"Please enter by this path."
Thereupon, the Buddha entered and sat down.
At that time, the brahmin Vairaṇyā wished to sit near the World-Honored One, but finding no opportunity to do so, he stood with palms joined beside his seat.
The Dharma Master said:
"The subsequent phrase shall be understood in due course.
The Brahmin addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which should have been given has not yet been given.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is the Brahmin who wishes to fulfill his previous vow to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

The Brahmin said, "I previously invited the Tathāgata to spend the three-month summer retreat with me, promising to provide daily offerings of rice, gruel, sweet fruits, and water for the World-Honored One; yet, through my foolish forgetfulness, not even a single iota has been provided."
It was not that I refused to give, nor that I had not yet prepared what to offer.
Because I, as a layperson, am burdened with many affairs, and being oppressed and deluded by anger and ignorance, my mind forgot; for this reason, I did not give.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why did the brahmin speak these words?
Unaware that he was deluded by Māra, he reproached himself for his conduct as a layman and consequently forgot the World-Honored One."
Thereupon the brahmin thought to himself:
"I invited the Buddha for a three-month period of offerings, yet I have not yet prepared anything at all.
I shall now combine the provisions for the three months with a single day's gift; I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept this for tomorrow."
The Brahmin prepared the offerings for the Tathāgata the very next day. Observing that the Brahmin’s heart was filled with supreme joy, the Buddha, out of compassion, reflected:
"If I do not accept this invitation, this Brahmin will give rise to an evil mind and say:
'The Śramaṇa Gautama accepted my invitation for three months but did not receive any offerings; now, out of resentment, he refuses my invitation.'"
Furthermore, there may be those who say:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is not omniscient; he cannot even endure [this] for a moment.
Or they may speak in such a way as to disparage the Tathāgata, thereby incurring the retribution of a great sin.
"Therefore, I should now accept this invitation.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Five;
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Regions during the Xiao Qi Dynasty:
"By remaining silent, he has accepted the invitation. The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa: "Do not let your mind be preoccupied with your household affairs."

When the Buddha had finished speaking, he further observed them and taught the Dharma according to their capacities. He explained matters of this life and future lives, making them all manifest and known; and regarding the virtues they had already accepted, maintained, and diligently cultivated, the Tathāgata then rained down the rain of Dharma.
Having rained down the rain of Dharma, the Buddha rose from his seat and returned to his original place.
At that time, the brahmin gathered his sons, grandsons, and descendants, saying: "Ho!

You all, I previously invited the Buddha for a three-month retreat, yet I was unable to provide offerings for even a single day. I shall now extend the limit of my three-month provisions and provide them all together tomorrow."

Having finished speaking, she immediately prepared food and drink, attending to them day and night. When dawn arrived, she swept and sprinkled the interior of the house until it was pure and clean; she then provided ointments, incense, flower garlands, and necklaces, hung silk streamers, banners, and canopies, and spread out mats and seats, all of which were exquisite and beautiful, constituting various kinds of offerings.
Having completed all the preparations, he came to where the Buddha was and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The food and drink are ready; the time has now arrived."
At that time, the Tathāgata departed, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha went to the house of a brāhmaṇa; having arrived, he sat together with the bhikṣus.
"At that time, the brahmin provided offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; among the bhikṣus, the Buddha was the senior elder (*sthavira*).
The food was most exquisite, of unsurpassed flavor."
"With one's own hand" means giving food with one's own hand until they are full.
"Full" means satisfied, and it also means contented.
"Withdraw" means to stop.
There are three kinds of stopping.
What are the three? First, by means of the hand; second, by means of the eye; and third, by means of the mouth.
The section on the desire for food concludes; this is also easy to understand.

The Brahmin offered three robes to the Buddha; these three *kāṣāya* robes were worth three thousand pieces of gold. He further offered each of the five hundred monks a pair of white cotton cloths (*pāṭa*), which together were worth five hundred thousand pieces of gold.

Although the brahmin had already made such offerings, his mind was still not satisfied; he further gave one *kṣauma* (絳欽婆羅) cloth and one *pāṭuṇa-paṭa* (鉢兜那波咤)—which in the Chinese language means silk.

The Buddha and the bhikṣus cut up their *kambala* woolen cloths, each making meditation belts and loops for alms-bowl bags; they also tore apart their *pāṭa* and *pāṭaka* garments to make two kinds of items: waist-bands and water-strainers.
Furthermore, there are one hundred medicinal ointments, each vessel filled with them being worth one thousand gold coins, to be provided for the monks to anoint their bodies.
The Dharma Master said, “The offerings made to śramaṇas are restricted by the Dharma to four kinds; they do not accord with those of worldly people, and now these are fully provided.”
"What is taught in the Vinaya Piṭaka concerns the three robes and does not extend to these four kinds; I have now expounded them for this reason.

Thereupon, having made this offering, the brahmin together with his retinue prostrated themselves before the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, then withdrew to sit to one side. At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "This brahmin and his retinue invited me to the summer retreat.

During these three months, they were harassed by Māra and did not hear the essentials of the Dharma. Since they have not heard the Dharma for these three months, I shall now, in the space of a single day, extensively expound and explain the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, so that this retinue may each be fully satisfied."

When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma to the brahmin, he rose and departed through the gate, intending to travel to another country. Thereupon, the brahmin and his retinue each prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, weeping as they said:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and come once again at some time, so that we may meet you and have no cause for regret."

At that time, the World-Honored One stayed in the forest hermitage for three days to enter the realm of the Buddha, observing that the bhikṣus had been eating horse barley for ninety days, their bodies so emaciated that they were unable to travel far.

Traveling directly on the straight road, he arrived at the kingdom of Sūli; departing from Sūli, he proceeded toward the place where the Pāyāga was located. Having arrived, he immediately crossed the great river; having crossed it, he headed toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Upon arrival, he departed from there and reached the city of Vaiśālī, where the World-Honored One then resided in the Mahākuṭa Monastery.
The Dharma Master said:
"The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* is titled 'Well-Equipped.
This concludes the account of the causal conditions concerning Vairaṇyā."
The Kalandaka Chapter:

"This *Vibhāṣā* is complete in both meaning and phrasing; it does not intermingle with other doctrines but distinguishes the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). Within the Vinaya, that which is taught regarding the causes, conditions, and fundamental origins is extremely difficult to understand; yet this *Vibhāṣā* is skillfully able to distinguish all of the Vinaya Piṭaka without obstruction, and for this reason it is called 'complete' (*paripūrṇa*)."
“The World-Honored King, out of compassion for sentient beings,
now proclaims the Vinaya-piṭaka to bring them to discipline;
he also leads them with all wholesome practices to eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.”
"At that time, the city of Vaiśālī [is described] in such a sequence that it is easily understood; however, if there be anything profound and difficult to comprehend, I shall explain it for you."
“Kalandaka” is the name for a mountain mouse.

At that time, the King of Vaiśālī, accompanied by his courtesans, entered the mountains for recreation. The king, becoming weary, fell asleep beneath a tree, while the courtesans scattered in all directions to play about him.

At that time, there was a large venomous snake within a cave beneath the tree. Smelling the scent of the king’s wine, it emerged, intending to bite him. A mouse on the tree descended from above, screeching to awaken the king; the snake immediately retreated and retracted itself.
After the king woke up and fell back asleep, the snake emerged once more, intending to bite him, but the mouse again screeched and descended to awaken the king.

Having risen, the king saw a large venomous snake within a cave beneath the tree; he was immediately struck with terror. Looking in all directions for his attendants, he did not see them. The king thought to himself:
"I have now returned to life through the kindness of the mouse."
The king then reflected on how he might repay the mouse’s kindness.

At that time, there was a village near the mountain, and the king immediately summoned the villagers, decreeing: "From this day forward, my entire allotment of provisions shall be diverted to support the mouse. Because of this mouse, the village was thereafter named the Kalandaka Village.

As for Kalandaka-putra: at that time, there was an elder in the village who possessed four billion gold coins; the King granted him the rank of elder, and because of the village's name, he was called the Elder Kalandaka.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Is the Elder alone named Kalandaka, or are others as well?
He replied:
"All are named Kalandaka, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla. Sūdena was the son of the elder Kalandaka and possessed many *jñātis*.
A *jñāti* is one with whom one shares both suffering and joy."
At that time, there was a cause and condition for him to go to Vaiśālī; as for the cause and condition, it was that he was seeking a debtor.
Furthermore, a Dharma teacher said:
"On the ninth day of the ninth month, the people of the country gather in great numbers for recreation; for this reason, Sūdena went to watch."
“At that time, on the fifteenth day of the ninth month before [the rains retreat], the World-Honored One arrived at Vaiśālī and was seen.
Question: “What is meant by ‘was seen’?”
He replied:

"After Śuddhodana had finished his morning meal, he saw many people baring their right shoulders and carrying various kinds of flowers and incense as they departed from the city gate toward the Buddha’s dwelling, intending to make offerings and listen to the Dharma.
Having seen them, Śuddhodana asked: 'O good people, where are you going?'"
He replied,
"I am now going to the Buddha’s dwelling to make offerings and listen to the Dharma. Sudinna said:
"Excellent! I shall also follow you.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, preaching the Dharma for them with a Brahma-voice. When Sūdena arrived, he saw the Buddha preaching the Dharma to the great assembly; therefore, in the Vinaya-mūla, this is called "Seeing."
The Dharma Master said:
"This was due to the causes of merit from Sūdena’s past lives that caused him to attain awakening.
Sūdena thought to himself:"
"How may one obtain the conditions to enter and listen to the Dharma?
For what reason?
Because the fourfold assembly surrounds [the teacher], listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind; it is impossible to move them, and thus entry is difficult to achieve."
At that time, Sūdena, the son of Kalandaka, gradually approached the edge of the assembly.
Someone asked him,
"Why do you not enter the assembly?"
He replied, "Because I arrived later, I sat near the edge of the assembly.
As stated in the *Vinaya-mūla*, after Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, had gone to the assembly and sat in one place, Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, had this thought:
He asked: "Did you have this thought while seated,
or did you have this thought after hearing the Dharma?"
He replied:
"Having heard the Buddha praise the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, I formed this thought. He asked:
"What should one be mindful of? He replied:
"One should form this thought:"

“The Buddha has explained the Dharma to me in detail, and I have understood it; as I reflect upon it again and again, the principles within virtue, concentration, and wisdom are of a single flavor. He then thought:

“To practice the holy life of virtue, concentration, and wisdom while living at home is extremely difficult to accomplish in even a single day. It is not fitting for me to remain at home, like one who is merely grinding and polishing.”
Question: "What is meant by 'polishing'? Answer:
"Just as it is extremely difficult for a person to polish a gem until it is perfectly bright and pure, so too is it very difficult for one living at home to practice like a polisher.
How may I now shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and practice the holy life, thereby leaving the home of conditioned existence and entering the home of the unconditioned?"
Question: "What is meant by the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Answer:
"The house of the conditioned consists of various activities such as plowing fields, planting crops, and trading goods;
the house of the unconditioned is free from all such activities, being tranquil and desireless—this is called leaving the house of the conditioned and entering the house of the unconditioned."

Regarding the phrase "not long after the assembly had risen, he went to where the Buddha was": while the assembly of Sūdena had not yet risen, he went to where the Buddha was, but did not seek to leave the household life. Why was this?
If someone seeks to leave the household life, while his brothers and kinsmen are seated there listening to the Dharma, he should create obstacles and say:
"Your parents have you as their only son; if you seek to leave the household life, who will attend to and support them?"
Having spoken these words, he would certainly seize him and take him back, thereby making my renunciation difficult.
Sudinna retreated with the crowd, but after walking only a few paces, he skillfully turned back and went to where the Buddha was to seek ordination.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that not long after the Saṃgha had been established, Sudinna went to where the Buddha was and said:
"I only pray, World-Honored One, that since Rāhula left the household life following you, those whose parents do not permit their departure may not be ordained by the Buddha."
"For this reason, the Buddha asked Sūpanna:
'Have your parents given you permission to leave the household life?
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of these phrases is easy to understand and should be known by oneself.

Regarding 'having completed what was to be done': Sudinna delighted in the life of renunciation; his mind was not attached to places of amusement; and regarding his creditors, whether he received payment from them or not, he returned in haste—the sequence of these points is easy to understand."
"Amatā" in the language of Han means "mother," and "dada" means "father. "You" is easily understood. As for "only one son," it means you are his only son and have no brothers.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why do my parents speak these words?
It is because they are mindful."

To "dwell in joy" means that from childhood until adulthood one does not undergo any hardship; from the time of birth, being nurtured in the arms of a wet nurse until reaching maturity, one is constantly provided with food and drink of a hundred flavors, and when traveling in carriages or on horseback, one's feet do not even touch the ground—this is called dwelling in joy.
The father said to Sūdena:

"You do not even know what small suffering is; you who do not know suffering have never experienced even a tenth part of a single suffering that would cause me to die rather than be separated from you."
The parents said:
"In this world, even if you were to die, we would not abandon you; how much less is it possible for us to part from you while you are still alive?
As for the phrase "lying upon the ground right there," it means lying upon the bare earth without any woolen rugs or mats.
"One who makes offerings.
He asked: "What constitutes making offerings?"
He replied:

"With male and female musicians, lutes, harps, flutes, pipes, *konghou*, and *pipa*—with all such various sounds—he entertains his acquaintances. Through these acquaintances, he employs skillful means to console and persuade him so that his mind may turn back from [the path], and he may feast upon the five desires."
Question: "What is meant by 'nutriment'? Answer:
"Regarding 'eating,' it means that one's own body and wife mutually enjoy themselves together in the five sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, regarding 'performing meritorious deeds,' it means making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and performing meritorious deeds by receiving various kinds of alms and cultivating the path of goodness."

As he remained silent, his parents exhorted him in various ways to bring his mind to rest; yet when his parents had thus entreated him repeatedly up to three times, his resolve remained unshaken. His parents then called upon Sudinna’s friends and said: "This friend of yours now lies upon the ground;
though we have requested him three times, he is never willing to rise. You must act on our behalf to stop him from leaving the household life."
Thereupon, his friends and acquaintances went to Sudinna and said to him three times: "Friend!
Your parents have you as their only son; if you must leave the household life, who will provide for them when they are old?"
If you, a nobleman, go forth from home, there is no doubt that you will become so sorrowful and emaciated that you will die; what benefit would this bring you?
You, who were once wealthy and honored, must now carry an earthen bowl to beg for food—whether coarse or poor, whether obtained or not—and eat but one meal a day while sleeping alone;
if you practice the holy life in this manner, it is an exceedingly difficult path.
"Through such various skillful means, he never once wavered in his resolve.
His friends and acquaintances deliberated and said:
'We should now permit him to leave the household life.'"
He immediately went to the place where Sudinna’s parents were and exhorted them to allow him to leave the household life.
Having granted their permission, the Vinaya text therefore states: "Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, went to the place where his parents were."
Viśākha said to Sudinna, "Your parents have already granted you permission to leave the household life.

Sudinna immediately rose from the ground, leaping for joy. Sudinna had not eaten for seven days, and his body was emaciated; his parents bathed him with fragrant water, anointed his body with oil, washed and combed his hair, and prepared various kinds of food and delicacies. Within three or four days, his physical strength was restored.
Thereupon, Sudinna prostrated before his parents; shedding tears as he took his leave, he went to where the Buddha was and said, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me ordination."
He asked, "Was this ordained by the Tathāgata, or was it ordained by the Saṃgha?
He replied:
"Monks, let him be ordained.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms standing beside the Blessed One. The Buddha said to that alms-seeking bhikṣu, "You may ordain Sudinna, grant him the going forth, and bestow upon him full ordination."
The bhikṣu replied: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
He immediately took Sudinna, ordained him as a śramaṇa, gave him the name Venerable Yū, and conferred upon him full ordination (upasampadā).
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: at that time, Sudinna obtained the going-forth from the Buddha; having received full ordination, he undertook the dhūta practices.
*Dhūta* means, in the Han language, "shaking off the dust and grime of afflictions"; *pratigraha* means "practice.
*Āraṇya* means abandoning village dwellings to reside in forest hermitages and practice alms-gathering.
As for the practice of begging for food, one does not accept long-term offerings and abandons the fourteen types of food.
As for wearing rag-robes, one does not accept robes from donors.
As for begging in sequence, one does not skip over houses.
As for the village of Vaṃśa, it was the village of King Vaṃśa, whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable.
"Wealth" refers to those things used from morning until night;
"treasures" refers to those constantly kept hidden so as not to be seen by others.
"Immeasurable" means exceeding all number.
"Abundant food and drink" means that every day there is always an overflowing supply of food and drink.
"Attending to the dwellings" means arranging the beds and mats, rolling up the rugs, and covering them with cloths.
"Regarding the sixty large silver platters, each plate can serve ten people; together they provide food and drink for six hundred monks. 'To take' means to receive the meal.
He asked: "What is meant by 'to take'?"
He replied:
"I take the four great elements.
As for returning them to others, I give them to the Sangha with a mind free from attachment."

When he went out to beg for alms, a maidservant in his household took the leftover rice from the previous night—which was unfit for consumption—and went outside to discard it; having remained overnight, perhaps for one or two nights, the rice had become sour and foul-smelling.
He asked, "Is this non-glutinous rice,
or is it millet? He replied:
"It is millet porridge.
Sister, one who has left the household life must not be addressed as a 'slave'; therefore, I called you 'Sister' when I threw it into my bowl. He asked:
“Is it permissible for one who has left the household life to speak these words?
He replied, “It is permissible.”
Why is this? Because the host has discarded it as something trivial; regarding such discarded items, one may say:
"He will give them to me; place them inside my bowl."
The Dharma Master said:
"There was a bhikṣu who, while begging for food, saw someone carrying leftover rice from the previous night whom they intended to throw away. The bhikṣu said:
'If you must discard it, place it into my bowl.'"
"Such a bhikṣu is praised by the Buddha.
He asked: "Is it permissible to receive only one kind of food?"
"May other items also be obtained?
He replied, "All discarded items may be taken; do not harbor any doubt."
"Hands and feet": regarding the hands, when begging for food, one extends the bowl to receive the alms, leaving the hands exposed down to the wrists.
Regarding the feet, it refers to the area four finger-widths above the ankles.
"Voice": it refers to the distance at which one can hear the voice when Sūdena calls out.
Regarding "recollection and recognition," it refers to recognizing the three characteristics [of her].

Twelve years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, Sūdanī went forth as a renunciant. Sūdanī stayed in another country for eight years; after practicing the Way for those eight years, she returned to the village of Kalandaka. Twenty years had passed since the Buddha’s enlightenment, and Sūdanī had been away from her family for eight years; therefore, the maidservant did not recognize her.
"He entered and informed the mistress of the house.
[The other] asked:
"Why did he not ask [me] directly instead of entering to inform the mistress?"

He replied, “Because I was afraid and hesitant, the maidservant did not dare to ask immediately; therefore, she entered in haste to inform me. If this is indeed the case, then look closely at those eating by the wall.”

At that time, in every household within the village, small huts were built along the walls to store water and drinks, intended for the rest of those seeking alms, so that they might have whatever they required at their disposal.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that one should go outside the gate and eat by the side of the wall.
Regarding the person in question:
the father asked Sūdena.
"What person is eating this leftover stale rice by the wall?
An ordained renunciant should not eat such stale food in this manner.
The father then spoke to Sudinna:

"When you were at home, you would criticize the various dishes and meals, saying they were coarse, unpalatable, or that their temperature was improperly adjusted; yet now, as you eat these leftover stale grains, you do so like nectar, without a single word of complaint."
The Dharma Master said:

"Sudinna’s father ought to have spoken these words; however, because his heart was overcome by intense anguish, he was unable to express himself in such a manner. This is the interpretation handed down through the succession of masters."
"Taking hands and returning home together.
He asked, "Why take the hand of a layperson (avadātavasana) and return home?"
He replied, "Sudinna is a man of supreme filial piety; since his father has taken his hand, he will not disobey his father's command, and they shall return home together to accept the invitation."
He remained silent.
A question was asked:
"Sudinna has received the supreme method of alms-seeking; why did he accept his father's invitation?"
He replied:
"Sudinna should think thus: 'I have been away from home for a long time;
if I do not accept the invitation of a donor, the donor will likely give rise to an evil thought. Out of compassion, he should accept one invitation."
"Let the recipient know:
'This is a heap of gold and silver. He asked:
"Is it in bars or in fragments?
He replied,
"As for money and people, they are neither long nor short."
Regarding the later instruction on providing curtains: one should suspect that curtains were installed all around the perimeter of a secluded place.
Regarding the instruction to put on the robes and bowl in the morning: one should invite [the donor] to do so. He asked:
"Why do you not wait for the donor to come to you, instead of going there yourself?
He replied, "I have already informed him; this is not mentioned in the Vinaya."
"Mother" means that which has the function of giving birth to another.
"Maternal property" refers to that which comes from the maternal family following the mother.

Regarding the morning and evening ablutions, the value of the remaining [items] is as follows: first, the property of your mother is not yet released; my own property is not yet released; and the property of your grandparents is also not yet released.
"Those who have not yet left the world" refers to those whose wealth and possessions are immeasurable.
"You may return to secular life" means that his father said to Sudinna:

"You may cast aside your monastic robes, return to secular life, wear fine clothes, and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses. You did not leave the world out of fear of royal officials, nor did you leave the world because you were in debt; therefore, you cannot return to secular life."
Sudinna said to the donor:
"I am exceedingly joyful in the holy life; my mind has no attachment to returning to secular life. I pray that you, O donor, will not be suspicious."
Sudinna said to the donor, "I have something to report;
please do not be angry or reproach me.
His father replied:
"Excellent, excellent!"—
when the father heard Sūdena speak these words, he praised him with "excellent" because his heart was filled with joy.
He took hempen cloth and made a large sack, placed gold and silver inside it, and tied the mouth of the sack securely.
"Ten or more carriages were loaded [with the jewels] and abandoned in the deep waters of the great river.
As for the cause of this, it was the speech of Sūdena.
What is the use of these treasures?"
Because of this treasure, various afflictions can arise; water, fire, thieves, and robbers all originate from it. As for "the hair standing on end":
there may be a king who, seeing that the treasures are many, comes to demand them; or there may be thieves who come to plunder them; or they may be consumed by fire or swept away by water.
Having reflected deeply upon this, his entire body trembled and his hair stood on end.

As for "guarding day and night": before the sun sets, he immediately issues orders to his subordinates, deploying men to maintain watch and patrol, securing the gates and doors so that they are extremely firm and tight, ensuring that no robbers or thieves may enter nor any enemies lie in wait; therefore, it is called "guarding."

Regarding the calling of the new bride: because Sudinna’s father had employed various skillful means to induce Sudinna to return to secular life without any success, he called his new bride and said, "Only you, who previously shared such mutual affection, can cause his heart to turn back."
"Why is this? For all wealth and treasures cannot cause one to turn back; only a woman can do so.
As for the celestial jade maidens who are as beautiful as they are—this is the question of the new bride to Sūpanna."

The reason the bride saw those kṣatriyas and those of noble lineage renounce all wealth, treasures, palaces, wives, children, and retinues was that she thought all these lineages were practicing the holy life solely for the sake of seeking celestial maidens.
"Not being a celestial maiden" means she does not seek to be a celestial maiden.
When the bride heard that Sudinna had replied by addressing her as "sister," she thought to herself:
"Previously, we were husband and wife sharing a bed; now he calls me 'sister,' which carries the same meaning as being born of the same parents."
Thus, he was overcome with great anguish and fell to the ground in a swoon.
"Do not touch or disturb me" means: do not touch my heart with wealth, treasures, or the desire for women.
"One who can continue the lineage may remain"—the parents said this to Sudinna.

"May you always practice the holy life and enter nirvana in the midst of the sky; may you leave behind one son to continue the lineage, so that our wealth and treasures do not perish ownerless, for upon our deaths, they will surely enter the treasury of King Licchavi."
"I only request that you continue the lineage.
Sudinna replied, "This matter is very easy; I am able to do it."
Question: "Why did Sūdena speak these words? Answer:
"Sūdena conceived this thought in his mind:"
"If I do not give seeds to the sower, he will never leave me alone, but will harass me day and night;
if I give him seeds so that his mind may be appeased, he will no longer trouble me, and because of this, I shall be able to dwell securely in the gateway of the Path and practice the holy life."
As for "Moon-Blossom" (*candravati*), it refers to the water-blossoms produced by the moon;

this is a name for blood, which is the natural state of women. When a woman desires to conceive, a mass of blood forms at the site of the embryo; after seven days, it ruptures of its own accord and this blood flows out. If the blood flows out without ceasing, the male seed does not remain but flows out along with it. If the blood is completely discharged, the male seed returns to its place, and only then is the embryo formed.
It is like a farmer who has plowed and prepared his field well, yet when he sows grain there with too much water, the grain floats upon the surface and flows out in all directions. Why is this?
Just as when the element of water is present, grains do not adhere to the mud and thus do not form roots or stalks, so it is with women:
if the blood has been exhausted and the male seed remains, then conception occurs.
"Grasping the wife's arm" means taking her by force into a secluded place to engage in sexual acts together.

At that time, for twenty years after the Buddha left the Bodhi tree, he had not yet formulated the precepts for his disciples. Because the disciples were newly engaged in their studies, the Buddha had not yet established the prohibitions; thus, Sudinna did not recognize the nature of the offense and considered it non-existent. Had Sudinna known the nature of the offense, he would have risked his very life—how could he have dared to transgress?
"Regarding the three acts of impurity: there were three instances of grasping his wife together to commit impurity; because of committing these acts of impurity, she then became pregnant.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Does it exist or not?"
He replied: "There is.
What is meant by 'there is'?"

First, physical contact; second, taking hold of her clothing; third, the emission of semen; fourth, stroking with the hand below the navel; fifth, seeing; sixth, hearing sounds; seventh, smelling odors—it is by these seven things that a woman conceives.
He asked: "What is meant by 'smooth and delicate touch'? [The Buddha replied:

"When a woman experiences the flow of the menses and takes pleasure in a man, if the man touches each of her body parts with his own body, she immediately gives rise to craving and attachment and becomes pregnant; this is conception through physical contact."
Question: "What is meant by 'taking up the robe'? Answer:

“Just as in the case of the bhikṣu Udāyin, who went forth together with his wife; after they had been separated for a long time, Udāyin went to the place of a bhikṣuṇī. Their mutual lustful desires did not cease, and they incited one another until semen was emitted, which soiled Udāyin’s robe. He gave the robe to the bhikṣuṇī; having received it, she licked it and then placed it within her female organ, whereupon she immediately became pregnant.”
"If a woman, when water-lilies are in bloom, touches a man's garment, this is called 'taking the garment.
He asked: "What is meant by 'emitting semen'?"

He replied: "It was like the mother of the recluse Mṛgāra. Long ago, a doe was wandering and came in due course to the dwelling of a recluse. As the recluse was urinating, semen and vital energy were discharged together. At that time, the doe was in her season and water had appeared; she smelled and tasted the urine, and becoming possessed by desire, she wished to drink it. Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth to the recluse Mṛgāra. This is what is called 'inferior semen.'"

Regarding "rubbing below the navel": for example, when the parents of Śyāma Bodhisattva were about to become blind, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived this in advance; he descended to their location and said:
"You should unite in sexual union, and a son shall be born."
Once the husband and wife had both left the household life to pursue the Way, they replied, "We have already become renunciants;
according to the Dharma, we may not do such a thing.
Śakra then spoke again:
"If you do not engage in the union of yin and yang, you may simply rub below your navel with your hand.
Following these words, she immediately conceived and gave birth to Śyāma; this is called "rubbing below the navel with the hand."
"Mindabhaya and Caṇḍapajjota—these two were also born in this same way.
He asked: "What is meant by 'seeing'?"
He replied:

"There is a woman who, though her menses have matured, has not united with a man; her desire is extremely intense, and she sets her heart solely upon seeing men. She is like a court lady in a royal palace. Thus she becomes pregnant; this is called 'seeing'."
Question: "What is meant by 'sound'? Answer:

"For example, there are white egrets that are all female and have no males; when spring arrives and the warm breath of life begins to stir, they cry out, and the females, with single-minded attention upon hearing the sound, immediately conceive.
Chickens are also sometimes like this; merely by hearing the male's call, they likewise conceive. This is called 'conception through sound.'"
Question: "What is meant by 'fragrance'? Answer:
"Just as a cow in the state of Qin conceives a calf merely by smelling the scent of a bull, this is called 'conception through fragrance.

Sudinna was not like this; he practiced the impure dharma in its true sense. When the male and female sexual desires and forms unite, one takes rebirth. Only when these three factors are all combined is a child born; such was the case with Sudinna."
At that time, the Earth Deity saw Sudinna practicing the unwholesome dharma and immediately cried out in alarm, for there is no one who does not know when various evil deeds are committed.

When a person first commits such an act, the deity who protects their body sees it; subsequently, the devas and humans who possess the knowledge of others' minds perceive it. Since such a person is seen by both celestial and terrestrial deities, the Earth Deity cries out in great alarm.
As for the successive transmission that reached as far as the Brahma Heaven, setting aside those in the Formless Realm, all others heard and knew it.

At that time, the son gradually grew up and went forth into homelessness together with his mother; the son, named Anupama, went forth at the age of eight along with his mother, Anupamā. The mother relied upon the community of bhikṣuṇīs, while Anupama relied upon the community of bhikṣus, and each obtained a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that they went forth together and successively attained the fruit of Arhatship.
As for those who gave rise to a mind of remorse, because they had previously committed impure acts, they constantly gave rise to a mind of remorse day and night.

Regarding "I do not obtain this benefit which others obtain": within the Buddha-dharma, they cultivate the holy life and attain the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*); I do not obtain this benefit. This is called "I do not obtain this benefit which others obtain."
Regarding my obtaining an evil gain: while other people who have left the household life obtain a good gain, I have not obtained a good gain but have instead obtained an evil gain.
Those who practice the holy life possess the treasury of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, yet I have not obtained this treasury.
As for being emaciated, it is because one regrets what one has done and food and drink do not pass through; therefore, the flesh and blood are withered and diminished.
As for the transformation of the body's appearance, it is like the leaves of a tree that have withered and turned yellow, on the verge of falling.
"The veins and arteries all appear" means that because there is no flesh or blood, the veins and arteries are fully visible.
"The heart is also obstructed" means that the apertures of the heart are entirely closed.
"Bowing the head in shame" means that one feels shame upon observing one's own unwholesome conduct in contrast to pure practice.
At that time, the bhikṣus were each playing outside their cells when they saw Sūdena, emaciated and gaunt, and asked him:
"Previously your countenance was full and radiant, your body was beautiful and well-proportioned, and your hands and feet were even, firm, and robust; why are you now so thin and weak?"
The bhikṣus said to Sūdena, "What cause for anxiety or resentment do you have regarding the holy life? Do you find no joy in leaving the household life?
Sūdena replied:

"Venerable sirs, it is not that I do not delight in the holy life; I have applied myself with diligence to the cultivation of the pure Dharma, yet this is because I have already committed unwholesome deeds."
"Those who have already committed evil have already acquired evil dharmas, which they constantly see before their eyes.
The bhikṣus said to Sūdena,
"What you have done is sufficient to cause doubt."
Question: "What is meant by 'doubt'? Answer:
"Because he engaged in impure conduct within the pure Dharma, doubt arose and he was unable to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Thereupon, the bhikṣus employed a skillful means to explain Sūdena’s intention and spoke thus:
'It is not so, Elder!'"

Regarding the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma through various skillful means to bring about detachment from desire: it is because the Buddha, for the sake of all sentient beings within the three realms, teaches the nature of the five desires so that they may all become detached from them and not remain joined with them; though the expressions differ, the meaning is the same.
The teaching that brings about the exhaustion of craving leads one to nirvāṇa and prevents dwelling within the three realms; therefore, it does not cause craving to arise.
The Buddha has thus spoken of desire in this way, so as to enable its analytical discernment and its non-commonality [with other teachings].
