"That you have now united with her—this is what the Buddha calls unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*). Yet you have engaged in unchaste conduct with a former wife.
This meaning is easy to understand.

When the Buddha teaches the Dharma in various ways to cause one to leave behind delusion, it is because the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings to eliminate delusion and sever craving (*tṛṣṇā*). It is because all sentient beings thirst for the five desires that the Buddha teaches the Dharma so that sentient beings may sever and eliminate this craving.
Regarding "cutting off the seeds": the Buddha taught the Dharma so that the seeds of the three realms may be severed and craving exhausted, leading to nirvāṇa.
"Craving" refers to the desire for the three realms; it is because of this that sentient beings cannot escape, being bound and fettered by craving and desire.
"Exhaustion" means the cessation through the extinction of craving, whereby one attains nirvāṇa.

Within the three realms, there are four modes of birth, five destinies, and seven consciousnesses, which dwell in the nine abodes of sentient beings. Moving from here to there and returning from there back here, they are like the holes of an embroidered garment that are mutually pierced and entangled. When craving is not yet resolved, one is bound; when it is exhausted, one ceases. That which is the exhaustion of craving is *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, regarding *nirvāṇa*: *ni* means "not," and *vāṇa* means "weaving"; thus, it signifies the meaning of "non-weaving.

When the Buddha speaks of eliminating desire, he intends for all desires—the desires for the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and the desires of the afflictions (*kleśa*)—to be entirely eliminated.
Regarding "knowing desire": one should know each and every one of all desires and then subdue them; this is called "knowing.
Regarding "thirst for desire": it is the extreme seeking of desire among all desires.
"Thoughts of desire" refers to that which is thought together with desire.
"Thoughts of frustration regarding desire" refers to the frustration that arises when one thinks of the five objects of desire that have not yet been obtained.

All these statements pertain to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*); the preceding sentence speaks of worldly phenomena (*laukikadharma*), while the subsequent sentence speaks of supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*).
As for the Elder, he causes those who lack faith to believe; however, for the sake of performing unwholesome deeds, he does not cause those who have not yet gained faith to believe.
The Elder who possesses faith may further turn his mind back;

one whose mind has turned back develops regret regarding the Dharma. However, if a person possesses faith through the Path—like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be moved or shaken by winds from the four directions—this faith is likewise.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, there are cases where such a person exists and cases where no such person exists.

At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the World-Honored One. Regarding the evil deed committed by Sūdena, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha so that he might know of it; they did not do so out of a desire for the Buddha to praise them alone, nor to cause the Buddha to despise or expel Sūdena from the pure Dharma, nor because of a wish to provoke strife over this evil deed, but solely in accordance with the truth.
The bhikṣus each thought to themselves:
"Defiled dharmas have already arisen.
They addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Now that this defiled practice has arisen, I pray that you will establish a precept for the sake of my śrāvaka disciples.
For this reason, he assembled the community of bhikṣus; because Sūdena’s conduct was an evil transgression of the noble Dharma, he therefore convened the assembly of bhikṣus.
As for the Buddha’s disparagement of Sūdena: if a person commits evil deeds, they should be disparaged, and the Tathāgata disparages them;
if there is one who can maintain the precepts with diligence, they should be praised, and the Tathāgata praises them.
The Buddha does not conceal such practitioners of good and evil.

One such as Sūpanna should be held in contempt; therefore, what is stated in the Vinaya-mūla—that he should be held in contempt—is that the Tathāgata, out of a heart of compassion, holds him in contempt. The Buddha said:
"You foolish man, you are empty and possess nothing."
The deluded person fails to do what should be done and does what should not be done; acting without compliance is impure, and because it is impure, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa.
The Buddha asked:
"By what causes and conditions did you do such a thing?
The Buddha said:
"I have spoken of the departure from desire, each point as previously explained.

Having seen that Sudinna had already committed an unwholesome act, the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, addressed him as a "foolish man. It was like a compassionate father and mother who, seeing their child commit an evil deed, also rebuke and scold that child, saying:
"Foolish man, why have you done such a thing?"
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "O foolish man, you would be better off inserting your male organ into the mouth of a venomous snake than inserting it into a woman's organ.
For if a person touches the mouth of a venomous snake, their flesh will immediately rot and they die; yet this death is better.

If a person inserts his male organ into a woman's organ, he will die and enter hell with no prospect of escape. It would likewise be better to insert one's male organ into the mouth of a viper; upon entry, it would rot, and though one would thus end one's life, one would not fall into hell."
If one must cycle through the hells because of the female organ within, it would be better to place the male organ in a great mass of fire than to possess the female organ. Why is this?

Foolish person, if one were to place a mass of fire [upon oneself], one might die or not die; if one dies, the body experiences a brief suffering in this very life, but for this cause and condition, one does not fall into hell to undergo great agony.
"Unwholesome dharmas" refers to the dharmas of evil persons.
"The dharmas of those in the mountains and wilds" refers to the dharmas among those in the mountains and wilds.
"Great offenses" refers to great afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the method of "rubbing water" (*matsui*): after performing an unlawful act, one subsequently uses water; hence it is called "rubbing water. As for being in a secluded place, there are only two people, and they may engage in impure conduct; all evil dharmas are preceded by this.
Question: "Why did the Buddha speak these words? Answer:
"Because Sūdena brought defilement into the pure Dharma, he is called 'Sūdena, who was the first to commit a defilement within the pure Dharma.
When the Tathāgata used various skillful means, he disparaged him in various ways."
Regarding this person who is difficult to sustain: because they cannot protect themselves within the dharma of concealment, they are called "difficult to sustain.

Regarding the one who lacks contentment: because they dwell in a state of concealment, they are called "lacking contentment"; even if they were to obtain treasures as vast as Mount Sumeru, they would still not be satisfied, and thus they are called "lacking contentment."

Regarding the statement that they gather their bodies in one place: it means they assemble together in a single location to praise one another, or perhaps to praise [the Buddha] regarding the afflictions.

As for the "lazy," there are eight things they fully accomplish; the Tathāgata, through skillful means, praises those who have few desires, know contentment, and are easy to support and easy to nourish.

Regarding those with "few desires": they lack a mind of stinginess or greed; if they receive a single offering, they accept whatever is obtained. If they maintain being easy to support, they can restrain the six sense-faculties so as not to follow the six sense-objects; this is called being "easy to support."

One who is "easy to satisfy" is one who knows moderation and is content with the four types of offerings; this is called being easy to satisfy. Whether the food be coarse or fine, accepting whatever is obtained for the sake of having few desires is precisely what constitutes contentment.
"Purity" refers to having few desires and being content; this is called purity.
Because one is pure, one is not defiled by dust and grime, which is "shaking off. Because one shakes off dust and grime, it is called "uprightness."
Furthermore, it is said that when the three karmas are all pure and the three unwholesome karmas have been abandoned, one cannot be reviled by others; this is called "being upright" (*prāsādika*).
As for "not accumulating," it means that the afflictions concealed within the body are made to emerge and dispersed; this is called "not accumulating."
Because they do not accumulate [defilements], they are courageous and diligent.
The Buddha established the precepts for the bhikṣus so that those who are virtuous may faithfully accept and follow them according to their capacity. Why is this?

Those who have few desires and are content are able to receive and uphold [the precepts]; therefore, the Buddha taught the *Śīlaskandha* (Fundamental Precepts) for them. Just as five-colored flowers are strung together in succession, or like seven-jeweled beads threaded in order, he taught them for this life and future lives to inspire a sense of awe and dread.

If a person who delights in learning abides in the stage of training and attains arhatship, or attains the state of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or srotāpanna, or even in the absence of such causes and conditions, they will be reborn in heaven.
"If the Buddha teaches the Long Āgama or the Short Āgama, those who are virtuous will be able to believe and accept them.
The precepts are the stage of training (śaikṣabhūmi).
What is meant by the 'stage of training'?"
He replied:
"The dharmas of dhyāna-samādhi.
What is meant by the stage of training (śaikṣabhūmi)?"
It is because of ten factors.
For the sake of these ten factors, the precepts were established so as to bring peace and security to the Saṃgha.

"Peace and security" means not being subject to ruin or peril. If a person can receive the prohibitions and precepts taught by the Tathāgata, they will attain supreme great peace and happiness in future lives; this is called peace and security.
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who accept my words, I shall establish precepts for them;
if there are those who do not accept my words, I will not speak of precepts, but will only explain the fundamental causes and conditions, nor will I force them into submission."

Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, it is by means of these ten matters that the Saṃgha is made to dwell in peace and happiness: "This action incurs no offense; this action incurs an offense; at this time one should act; at this time one should not act. This is for the sake of delighting in training, so that you may not harbor doubts.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, it concerns a conscientious bhikṣu; it does not say that the rule is established for an unconscientious bhikṣu.
By means of this Dharma, it causes the conscientious to attain peace and happiness.
Why is this? A bhikṣu who lacks a sense of shame and remorse is not permitted to enter the assembly for the communal recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) or the invitation to admonition (pravāraṇā).
A bhikṣu who possesses a sense of shame and remorse attains peace and happiness.
Why is this? Because they have attained the hearing of dhyāna-samādhi.
A monk who lacks a sense of shame and remorse cannot attain it, because he causes disturbance and provocation.

Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that a conscientious bhikṣu attains peace and happiness because he severs the afflictions and outflows of the present life. Regarding these afflictions and outflows of the present life: if one does not restrain the five senses, one commits impure acts with the current body, whereby others may seize, strike, or kill him, or he himself may feel remorse for his transgression.
By severing such various forms of suffering and affliction, he enables himself to attain liberation.
The Buddha established rules to restrain monks who lack a sense of shame and remorse; those who lack shame and remorse are breakers of the precepts.
Furthermore, he said:
"Because such a person has committed unwholesome deeds yet feels no shame, the Buddha has established these prohibitions for them."
"If, after the Tathāgata has established a rule, one commits an unwholesome act and instead questions others:
'What have you seen me do?
What have you heard? "
"What sin have I committed?
Thus he harasses and disturbs the Sangha.
If the precepts are established, the Sangha shall, according to the Vinaya rules, reprove the bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, so that he cannot move or persist.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: "The shameless bhikṣu is prohibited; those who possess a sense of shame and remorse shall dwell in peace and happiness.
If there is a bhikṣu with a sense of shame and remorse who delights in training in the Dharma and the precepts, he should consider: 'This should be done; this should not be done.'"

Regarding the severance of future outflows (*āsrava*): because one does not sever the five sensory desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), one practices unwholesome dharmas; consequently, in a future life, one falls into hell and undergoes all manner of various bitter sufferings. This is not merely a single instance of suffering, but one revolves therein for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The Tathāgata has taught this precept to sever these causes and conditions, so that those who have not yet developed faith may come to believe. This is why the Tathāgata established the precepts: if a virtuous bhikṣu conforms to the Vinaya and is fully endowed with dignified deportment, those who have not yet developed faith will see him and immediately give rise to faith, saying:
"This is a true seed of the Śākya śramaṇas; he is diligent and energetic, capable of performing what is difficult to do, and his deeds are most weighty."
Having seen such actions performed, they will give rise to faith.
If non-Buddhists see the Vinaya Piṭaka and say:
"The Buddha’s bhikṣus also have the Vedas; they are no different from ours."
Thus, they give rise to a heart of reverence.
For this reason, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "It causes those who do not yet have faith to believe, and causes those who already have faith to increase [in their faith].
If one leaves the household life with a faithful mind and acts in accordance with what is taught in the prohibitions and precepts, people will see their conduct and regard them with great respect."
Furthermore, it says:

"How is it that by practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) with only one meal per day for as long as one lives, and by guarding and upholding the prohibitive precepts, one's faith increases upon seeing this?"
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, that which has already been believed is made to increase.
Regarding "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time," there are three kinds of True Dharma.
What are these three?

"First, the long endurance of the study of the True Dharma; second, the long endurance of the faithful acceptance of the True Dharma; third, the long endurance of the True Dharma through the attainment of the Path.
He asked: "What is meant by 'the long endurance of the study of the True Dharma'?"
He replied:
"The study of the Tripiṭaka shall endure for all time.
That which was spoken by the Buddha is called the True Dharma."

Within the Tripitaka, the twelve dhūtas, the fourteen codes of conduct, the eighty-two rules of great decorum, and the meditative concentrations and samādhis—these are called the faithful acceptance and long-term preservation of the True Dharma.
The four fruits of the śramaṇa’s path and nirvāṇa are what is called "attaining the Path" and the long endurance of the True Dharma.
Because the Tathāgata has established the precepts, he causes the bhikṣus to comply with them;
if they comply, they will fully attain the noble benefits. Therefore, training is the primary factor for the long endurance of the True Dharma.

For those who hold the Vinaya in high esteem, because there are established precepts, these four types of Vinaya—*pārivāsika-vinaya*, *pratikṣepaṇa-vinaya*, *saṃtata-vinaya*, and *prajñapti-vinaya*—are held in the highest regard.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, one should hold the Vinaya-piṭaka in high esteem.
The Dharma Master said:
“By means of all phrases—whether initial, middle, or final—you yourself should understand that regarding the offenses and merits within the precepts, a bhikṣu ought to train himself.”
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should recite the precepts.
It is asked:
"What do you mean by this?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"I have already established the precepts; you should proclaim them, uphold them, train in them, and teach them to others, speaking thus:"
"If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse, he incurs a pārājika offense and may not live in community.
Having thus firmly established this rule that severs the root, the first pārājika was formulated; now, following the formulation regarding the monkey, its fundamental basis is explained.
"In this way, the Buddha established the precepts for his śrāvaka disciples; therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, he established these precepts for the bhikṣus.
The First Chapter on the Initial Establishment of Precepts is concluded.
The Dharma Master said:
"If the meaning of a phrase is difficult to understand, I shall now explain it.
At that time there was a bhikṣu; this phrase is easy to understand."

Regarding those who entice monkeys with food: at that time, there were many bhikṣus in the great forest practicing the mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Because of their loving-kindness and compassion, many animals felt no fear; deer, antelopes, monkeys, peacocks, kingfishers, geese, pheasants, and various other birds and beasts would wander and play before the meditation halls.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, seeing a female monkey among a troop of monkeys whose form was plump, robust, and lovely, enticed her with food and drink and committed the act of impurity with her; thus, this bhikṣu practiced the act of impurity.
Regarding "wandering about to inspect the dwellings": various bhikṣus came from other countries to pay their respects to the World-Honored One and consequently arrived there.
At that time, these bhikṣus obtained *agantuka-bhikṣu-bhakta* (Sanskrit for "guest-monks' meal") early in the morning; having finished eating, they thought to themselves:
"We should go and inspect the dwellings of the various bhikṣus."
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: "He went to inspect the lodgings and arrived at the place where the bhikṣus were.

This monkey had previously engaged in unchaste conduct with one bhikṣu. When the monkey saw the bhikṣus approaching, he thought to himself that they were all no different from the bhikṣu he had previously known. He immediately went to where the bhikṣus were and, with lustful intent, behaved in a provocative manner just as he had with the bhikṣu with whom he had previously committed sexual misconduct. Having arrived, he directed his organ toward the bhikṣus, displaying his lewd gestures; he raised his tail and presented it to them, waiting for their response.
Fearing that the bhikṣus might all harbor lustful intentions,
and because he had not seen them for a long time, he assumed the sexual posture himself and displayed it to the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus realized that the monkey intended to engage in sexual acts, they said:
"We may remain in a secluded place and wait for the mendicant who seeks alms to return, so that we may observe his conduct.
This is certainly the Elder; "certainly" means it is truly not false, just as a bandit who has fully seized a storehouse does not dare to conceal it.
Is it truly not the case that the Elder does not act in this way?
The female organ of a woman and the female organ of an animal are no different; the precepts established by the Buddha were all for the sake of this matter.
Regarding human women, whether one sees them, seizes them, or touches them—performing such impure acts—with female animals is likewise; all such actions are entirely unwholesome dharmas.
"Venerable one, by performing such an act through this means—even with an animal—you have committed a *pārājika* offense; you should not live in communion.
If one performs an act of impurity even with a female animal, it is likewise said that a *pārājika* offense is established."
The Dharma Master said:

"The precepts are established so that they may be made firm. There are two aspects to the precepts: first, natural offenses of the world; second, offenses incurred by violating the words of the Sages."

If the mind reveres unwholesome dharmas, this constitutes a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) in the world; as for other offenses, they are those established by the Tathāgata as precepts. These are regulated in accordance with worldly laws to sever the fetters and make them firm; however, this excludes cases occurring in dreams, for one does not commit an offense within a dream.

Regarding the prohibitions established for secondary offenses (*anuvyañjana*), there is no offense of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); as for eating in turns and eating apart from the community, these secondary offenses are established without being offenses of intrinsic nature, and thus one does not violate such worldly laws.
"In this manner, the Tathāgata has established the precepts for the bhikṣus one by one.
The "Chapter on the Monkey" concludes.

"Now other matters will arise; all of them originate with Vatsagotra. For example, when Devadatta obtained the faction of Vatsagotra and split the Saṃgha, this was an occurrence involving Vatsagotra."

Furthermore, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there arose practices that were contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teachings; all of these originated with the Vajjiputtas.

As stated in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, once the Buddha had completed the formulation of the precepts, the Vajjiputtas ate and slept at will and subsequently gave rise to lustful intentions. Without relinquishing their vows, they engaged in sexual conduct, and thereafter their community fell into ruin.

As for "ruination," it refers to when members of the retinue are scattered in all directions and punished by the king, or die and are separated from one another; this is called the ruination of the retinue.
Alternatively, it refers to being oppressed by the suffering of illness.
The sick person’s body is emaciated and impaired; because of this emaciation and impairment, great suffering arises.
"Venerable Ānanda!
We do not slander the Tathāgata, nor do we speak of the Tathāgata’s faults, nor do we revile the Dharma, nor do we disparage the Saṅgha."
"We have brought ruin upon ourselves; we possess neither merit nor majesty.
Now, those who would practice the True Dharma should cultivate the thirty-eight methods of contemplation.
For us to contemplate the Dharma of Bodhi in successive stages—this is the path of the Arhat."
Regarding the cultivation and accumulation of wisdom, it causes [wisdom] to increase.
As for our dwelling, we abandon the dwellings of laypeople and reside in pure places where there is no further activity.
Ānanda replied, "Excellent!
At that time, Ānanda did not know the other's mind; he merely heard the utterance of the great vow.
If one were to obtain such a thing, it would be exceedingly great good; therefore, Ānanda replied, "Excellent!"—
this [objection] that there is no such possibility is thereby refuted.

If one were to attain the fruit of arhatship, it would be said that such a case exists; however, since there is no such fruit [in this context], no such case exists. Therefore, the Buddha replied to Ānanda:
"There is no such case."

The Tathāgata has already observed that for Vatsa and the others there is no causal basis; if the Buddha were to confer full ordination upon Vatsa and the others, they would have already committed a pārājika offense and should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha].

Therefore, what is stated in the Vinaya-mūla is not possible: if one reaches the point where the full ordination (upasampadā) is not to be granted, or if the Saṃgha grants the full ordination [to such a person], it is not the pure Dharma; they do not become a śramaṇa and remain in the status of a śrāmaṇera.

If one dwells on the stage of a śrāmaṇera, it is obtained through the practice of honoring the True Dharma; out of compassion for such individuals, the Buddha both withholds and bestows full ordination (upasampadā).
Why is this? It is so that the precepts may not be violated; by maintaining reverence and respect for the pure Dharma, one will have the cause to attain the Way before long.

Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: whether one has been granted full ordination (*upasampadā*) or not, once these three factors are complete, the Tathāgata, wishing to establish the precepts, addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should recite the precepts in this manner;
otherwise, that bhikṣu shall not dwell together with you.
The Dharma Master said:
"This root of the Vinaya is already complete; I shall now explain it in detail.
'If' (yadi) is a general term and does not refer to any single individual.
The Dharma Master said:

"Regarding the sections on the precepts (*śīla-skandha*), the core of the precepts (*śīla-mūla*), and the points of inquiry (*paripṛcchā*), those who wish to know them should understand that there are four *vinayas* to be known.
Venerable ones who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) should extract [the essential passages] and cause others to know them."
"At that time, when the assembly had gathered.
He asked: "What are the four?"
"First is the root; second is that which follows the root; third is the words of the Dharma master; fourth is one's own intention.
He asked: "What is meant by 'the root'?"
“The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is called the root.
What is meant by ‘conforming to the root’?
The four great elements are called conforming to the root.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have taught what is impure but have not yet prescribed a rule against it; however, this [state] follows into the impure and does not enter into the pure—this is called 'impurity'."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have spoken of impurity without prescribing a rule against it; yet this conforms to purity, and thus it is called pure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have declared that purity is permitted; however, this [perception] follows after impurity and does not enter into purity, and thus it is impure for you.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have declared that purity is permitted; however, this follows after purity and is pure for you. These are called the four great bases (mahābhūta-sthānāni)."
Question: "What is meant by 'the words of the Dharma Master'? Answer:

"When the assembly of five hundred arhats was gathered, the Buddha first spoke the fundamental text, and the five hundred arhats extensively analyzed and propagated it; this is called the speech of the Dharma Master."
Question: "What is meant by 'one's own intention'? Answer:

"Setting aside the original text, setting aside the commentary, and setting aside the words of the Dharma-master, to infer by means of one's own intellect, to infer through skillful means, and to explain extensively according to the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya—what is referred to as 'the words of the Dharma-master' in this context is called 'one's own intention.'"
He asked again: "What is the meaning of this?

[The other replied: "Do not rashly adopt and practice it. One should first examine the root, then examine the meaning of the phrases, analyzing each part individually and weighing them together. Afterward, examine the words of the Dharma Master; if they accord with the text and phrases, then adopt them. If, upon examination, they do not accord, do not adopt them. This is called 'one's own intention'."

Regarding that which arises from one's own mind: if the Dharma teacher’s words are firm and strong, and the Dharma teacher’s words should be examined, one should accept them provided they accord with the original text and phrases;
if the phrases do not accord, do not accept them.
If one follows the words of the Dharma Master and adheres firmly to the original text, then when examining whether the text and its meaning correspond, one should accept it;
if they do not correspond, one should not accept it.

"From the *Suibon* (Commentary on the Root) onwards, all are firm and solid, incapable of being shaken; they are no different from the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha, nor from the Buddha’s presence in this world.
The Dharma Master said:
"If, upon examining the *Suibon*, one cannot achieve full understanding by oneself, one should examine the *Sūtra*. One should adopt whichever version has the root text and commentary in agreement."

The Dharma Master said: "There were two bhikṣus who questioned one another; one bhikṣu declared it pure, while the second bhikṣu declared it impure. They further examined the root and what follows the root. If, regarding both the root and what follows the root, the one who declared it pure was correct, that was well; if he was incorrect, do not accept his view."

If one bhikṣu has examined the original text and found it to be pure, and his textual and doctrinal evidence is extensive, while a second bhikṣu’s textual and doctrinal evidence is meager, one should follow the words of the first bhikṣu.
The Dharma Master said:

"If two bhikṣus are equal in both the letter and the meaning, one should repeatedly contemplate and weigh the fundamental meaning to determine what is acceptable and what is unacceptable; these are the people who study the four kinds of Vinaya."
"If one is to be a Vinaya-master, he must first accomplish three qualities.
He asked: "What are these three?"
He replied:
"First, one must thoroughly master the phrases through recitation from the original texts, and practice the eloquence of meaning while not forgetting the written characters;
this is the first dharma. Second, one must firmly uphold the original Vinaya without allowing it to become corrupted."
"Third, one should receive and uphold [the teachings] from a teacher in successive order, so as not to let them be forgotten.
He asked: "What is meant by 'the root'?"
He replied:
"The entire Piṭaka of Vinaya is called the 'Root.

One who has mastered it through recitation can, without needing to deliberate, answer whatever questions are asked, even if those questions are not posed according to the sequential order of the verses."

Regarding the practice of discerning the meaning of the textual phrases: one who is well able to distinguish the meaning of the phrases in the Vinaya-mūla, and who understands both the primary meaning and its commentaries, is so described.
As for "firmly maintaining without admixture": possessing a sense of shame and remorse is what is called "firm maintenance."

If there are those who lack shame and remorse, even if they possess extensive learning, understand the meaning, and are revered and supported with offerings, yet do not rely upon the Dharma and Vinaya, they are thorns within this Dharma. Why is this?
They can also cause a schism in the Saṃgha and bring distress to the Saṃgha.

Those who possess a sense of shame and remorse constantly maintain such shame and remorse regarding the precepts; they would rather lose their lives than break the True Dharma for the sake of offerings.
It is because of those who possess shame and remorse that the Vinaya exists.

"Unmixed" means that within the words and phrases there is no confusion; if someone asks a question, one answers in proper sequence. If one were to answer by inverting the meaning of the Vinaya root texts and their commentaries, it would be like a person walking through a thicket of thorns—it would be difficult to pass through.

If someone should question one according to this principle, one answers with those very words; if there is one capable of debate who raises challenges, one answers according to each question without any omission or lapse, just as when requesting lion fat with a golden bowl, it must not be spilled—therefore, it is called "unmixed."

Regarding the successive reception and retention [of the teachings] from a teacher without forgetting them: Upāli received them from the Tathāgata; Dvāviṃśati received them from Upāli; Sūdena received them from Dvāviṃśati; Śigava received them from Sūdena; Maudgalyāyanaputra Tiṣya received them from Śigava; furthermore, Caṇḍavajji received them. In this manner, they were transmitted from teacher to teacher down to the present day. One who knows it thus is said to possess firm and steadfast retention.
If one cannot know the names of all the teachers in their proper sequence, one must at least know one or two names.
If one can fully possess these three dharmas, such a person is called a Vinaya Master (vinayadhara).
"If one is a *vinayadhara*, when the assembly of monks gathers to adjudicate various matters of dispute, the *vinayadhara* should first examine six points before responding with composure.
He asked: "What are these six?"

He replied: “First, observing the location; second, observing the origin; third, observing the words and phrases; fourth, observing the three sections; fifth, observing intermediate offenses; and sixth, observing non-offenses.”
Question: "What is meant by 'the objects of observation'? Answer:
"One should come covering one's body with grass or tree leaves; if one enters the monastery naked without covering the body, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Having thus examined the characteristics of the offense, one takes the Vinaya text as authority to settle the dispute; this is called 'examining the basis' (*sthāna-paryeṣaṇā*)."
Regarding "contemplating the root," a questioner asks:
"What is meant by 'contemplating the root'?
The answer is:

"If one intentionally utters a falsehood, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding these five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), one may examine the nature of each offense within the five categories; by taking the original basis as the testimony, one settles the dispute—this is called 'examining the basis' (*mūlādṛṣṭi*)."
“What is meant by ‘examining the words and phrases’?

If one whose body has not yet perished commits an offense, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; thus, regarding the characteristics of the offenses of the seven categories (*sapta-varga*), one should examine the nature of each offense individually. By taking the original rule as the authority, one settles the dispute; this is called ‘each examining the words and phrases.’”

“What are the three? There are three sections regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and there are three sections regarding the *pāyattika*. By examining these three sections, one takes the original [rule] as the authority and thereby settles the dispute.”
"What is meant by 'observing the intermediate offense'?
He replied:

"To lift a firebrand constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Thus, within this root of the precepts (*śīla-mūla*), one observes the intermediate offense and takes the root as the authority to settle the dispute; this is called observing the intermediate offense."
“What is meant by ‘being without fault’?

It means not experiencing pleasure [in wrongdoing], having no intent to steal, no intent to kill, no intent to speak falsely, and no intent to cause division; nor does one intentionally act out of ignorance. Thus, by observing each of these factors as being without fault, taking the original state as the witness, one extinguishes the basis for dispute.”
If a bhikṣu knows the four dharmas of the Vinaya, is proficient in the three dharmas, and has contemplated the six matters such that he has already accomplished the dharma of cessation,
and if the bhikṣu’s dharma of cessation does not revolve together with [defilements], he is no different from when the Buddha was in the world.
If a bhikṣu violates a disciplinary rule and goes to a vinaya master because he has doubts, he asks: "What is this matter? The vinaya master first examines it well;
if there is an offense, he says there is an offense;

if there is no offense, he should say there is no offense; if it is something that can be confessed, he tells him to confess; if it is something for which an *ābhāṣaṇā* (rehabilitation) should be granted, he says so.
If you have not given [the robe], you must say you have not given it. Even if you perceive the characteristics of a *pārājika* offense, do not say, "You have committed a *pārājika*. Why?

Because the characteristics of the first *pārājika*—sexual misconduct and false speech—are easily manifest, whereas the characteristics of the two precepts concerning killing and stealing are difficult to discern. One understands them through their subtlety; therefore, do not speak to those who are doubtful:
"You have committed a *pārājika* offense.
If there is a teacher present, one should reply:
"You may now go and consult your teacher."
He was then sent away and went to the place of the Vinaya-master, asking him:
"What is this offense?

If the Vinaya-master perceived that the characteristics of the offense were such that it could be remedied, and after the bhikṣu received the Vinaya-master's word that it could be remedied, he returned and reported to the Vinaya-master that it could indeed be remedied. The Vinaya-master said, "Excellent," and acted according to his instructions.
If there is no teacher present, one should instruct a fellow student to ask; if that fellow student replies that it may be cured, one returns to inform the Vinaya master, who then says, "Excellent."

If there is no fellow student to instruct the disciple in the interrogation, and the disciple further replies that it may be cured, he returns to report this to the Vinaya Master. The Vinaya Master says, "Excellent," and acts according to those words.
“If a disciple perceives signs of an offense, do not say:
‘You have committed a pārājika offense. Why is this?
The Dharma Master said:
"It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is also difficult to leave the household life; and it is exceedingly difficult to receive full ordination.

Having spoken thus, the Vinaya Master immediately swept and sprinkled the quarters clean, and had the monk who was harboring doubts sit there all day long. Once he had sat, the Master gave him thirty methods of meditation (*dhyāna*) and instructed him to observe them himself.

If his precepts were free from defilement, as he contemplated, the methods of dhyāna would manifest; his deportment would be thoroughly integrated with his mind, and he would enter meditative absorption while seated.
Even if a day passed, he would not be aware of it. When evening came, the Vinaya Master went to his location and asked, "Elder! [Why have you been sitting here so long?]"
"What is the nature of the mind? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"My mind is focused solely on meditative concentration.
The Vinaya Master spoke again: "Elder!..."
It is extremely difficult to be one who has left the household life; regarding the Dharma of the śramaṇa, you must be careful not to be indolent, but should instead practice and study it all.
If one breaks the precepts, the mind will become unsettled upon entering dhyāna, like sitting upon thorns.
"Why is this? Because they are being burned by the fire of remorse, just as if they were sitting upon a hot stone; unable to find stability, they rise and depart.
If a vinaya master goes to that place and says:
"Venerable sir!
What is the state of your mind? Is it concentrated or not? He replied:
"It is indeterminate," said the Vinaya Master.

"When a person commits a sinful act in this world, it cannot be concealed; at the very moment it is first committed, the protective deities of one's body should perceive it beforehand, and furthermore, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have some knowledge of the human mind."
"Elder! You may seek a suitable place for your dwelling as you see fit.
This concludes the Chapter on the Fourfold Vinaya and the Three Dharmas of the Vinaya Masters.
*Samyak-dṛṣṭi-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Six.
*Samyak-dṛṣṭi-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
The Dharma Master said: "I shall now explain the textual passages within the Vinaya. As stated in the original Vinaya, names are not singular;

they are established according to the individual. Through the cultivation of a human body, one acquires a name and surname, as well as precepts, monastic affiliation, conduct, age, and year. These should each be understood individually, which I shall now analyze and explain."
Regarding the human body, whoever obtains such a person—whether tall or short, red, black, or white, fat or thin—is one who practices.
To practice means either to cultivate meditative concentration, to attend to the affairs of the Saṅgha, or to engage in study; this is called "practice."
"Birth" refers to being born into either a Kṣatriya family, a Brāhmaṇa family, a Vaiśya family, or a Śūdra family; therefore, it is called "birth."
As for "name," it may be called *buddha-lekha-ta*, or *dharma-lekha-ta*, or *saṃgha-lekha-ta*; these are what constitute a name.
Regarding "clan" (*gotra*): it may be the clan of Kātyāyana, or the clan of Vāsiṣṭha, or the clan of Kauśika; these are called clans.
Regarding "precept" (*śīla*): it is so named because one observes the prohibitions and precepts according to what one maintains.
"Temple" (sì) refers to the monastery buildings where one dwells; thus it is called a temple.
"Practitioner" (xíngzhě) refers to one who acts according to their karma; thus they are called practitioners.
"Age" (niánjì) refers to being five, ten, twenty, or thirty years old; thus it is called age.
This is called the textual passage of the Vinaya:
"If there is a bhikṣu who practices, that bhikṣu attains [the fruit].
A 'bhikṣu' is a mendicant; whether he obtains [alms] or does not obtain them, he is still called a mendicant, for these are all the practices of virtuous persons."

The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas all practice alms-gathering; whether poor or wealthy, they leave their homes to study the Way, abandoning calves, cattle, fields, businesses, and worldly affairs to subsist by begging. Regardless of whether resources are abundant or scarce, they rely upon the four seas as their home; these are called Bhikṣus.

Regarding those who wear cut-and-sewn robes (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*): even if the value of a robe is worth ten million, once a bhikṣu has obtained it, he cuts and sews it for wear. He destroys its high value by piercing and patching it with needle and thread, ruining its fineness and softness until it becomes coarse and worn. Even if the robe was originally bright white, once its original color is ruined by tree bark, it becomes an old garment;
one who wears such is called a bhikṣu. Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, one who is able to wear cut-and-sewn robes is named a bhikṣu.

A śrāmaṇera is also called a bhikṣu; for instance, when a donor invites bhikṣus, even though a śrāmaṇera has not yet received full ordination, he is nonetheless included in the number of bhikṣus—this is what is meant by a "bhikṣu by name."
"Elder, I am also called a bhikṣu; this is a bhikṣu by designation.
The Dharma Master asked, "In what sense is one a bhikṣu by designation?"
For example, when the Elder Ānanda was walking at night, he saw a monk who had violated the precepts and asked:
"Ho! Who is this? The monk who had violated the precepts should have replied:
“I am a bhikṣu. This is a mere designation, lacking any solid substance.

As for the “Welcome, Bhikṣu,” when a layperson comes before the Buddha desiring to seek renunciation, if the Tathāgata perceives that their faculties and conditions are complete and they are fit for deliverance, he immediately calls out, “Welcome, Bhikṣu! and their hair and beard fall away of their own accord, and they become a bhikṣu.
As for "calling," the Tathāgata extended his right hand from within his saṃghāṭī robe; his hand was the color of gold, and with a Brahma-voice he called out:
"Welcome! You may practice the holy life to bring an end to the source of suffering."

Before the Buddha had finished speaking, he immediately became a bhikṣu and attained full ordination. His three robes and earthen bowl were suspended over his left shoulder; the bowl was the color of a blue *utpala* flower, and the saffron robe was as bright as a red lotus. Needles, thread, an axe, and a water-strainer were all fully provided; these eight items are the common requisites of those who have left the household life, and they appeared spontaneously, complete with perfect dignified deportment.

The World-Honored One himself acted as his preceptor and also as his ordination master; he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Dharma Master asked:
"From the time the Tathāgata first attained the Way until his parinirvāṇa, how many were there of those who became bhikṣus by the call 'Welcome' (Ehi-bhikṣu)?"
He replied,
“There are one thousand three hundred and forty-one such bhikṣus. He asked:

"What are their names? "They are the five, beginning with Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya; next, Yaśas, the son of a householder; his fifty-four kinsmen; thirty from the Vatsagotra; one thousand from the Śāṭhila clan; these two great śrāvakas with their two hundred and fifty followers; and Aṅgulimāla, one person. Therefore, the Vinaya praises these one thousand three hundred and forty-one people."
"One thousand three hundred and forty-one people, possessed of great faith,
all came to the Buddha.
Out of compassion, the Tathāgata raised his golden hand and called out with a Brahma-voice."
"At that very moment they attained liberation; their robes and bowls descended of their own accord, and all were addressed with 'Welcome' (svāgata).

All those of great wisdom were named 'Welcome Bhikṣus. It was not only these bhikṣus who were 'Welcome,' but there were further 'Welcome Bhikṣus': the brāhmaṇa Śaila together with three hundred people, Mahākapphiṇa together with one thousand people, and from the kingdom of Kapilavastu, ten thousand people, as well as sixteen thousand people, who together with the brāhmaṇa Vāseṭṭha went forth from the household life—all of them were 'Welcome Bhikṣus.'"

This is taught within the Sūtras; its name is not mentioned in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Regarding one who obtains the full precepts through the Three Refuges: by reciting the Three Refuges three times in this manner, one immediately attains the full precepts.

As stated in the Vinaya, there are various ways by which the full precepts (upasampadā) may be obtained: through the "Come, Bhikṣu" formula; through the three refuges; through receiving instruction; through answering questions; through receiving the heavy dharmas; through being sent by another; through the eight-word formula; and through the formal motion and proclamation (jñapti-karman).
The Dharma Master said:
"Welcome! Having received the three refuges, you have already attained full ordination. He asked:
"What is meant by receiving instruction?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should train yourself in this way, saying:..."
"I shall give rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward those seated above, in the middle, and below.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should now listen so that all wholesome dharmas enter your very bones and are placed within your heart; I shall now collect my mind and listen to the Dharma with ears pricked."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Kāśyapa, you should train in this way: you must practice mindfulness of the body without abandoning it;
this is how you, Kāśyapa, should train. Venerable Kāśyapa attained full ordination through this very instruction.
Kāśyapa, those who possess the full precepts all obtain them through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Regarding those who obtain the full precepts by answering questions, it was under the Buddha Śubhakara that they were permitted to receive the full ordination.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation at the Puppārāma Monastery. He questioned the novice Śubhakāsa, asking either about the name "swelling" or the name "color," inquiring whether these two phenomena were identical or distinct. Because of these ten impurities, he questioned Śubhakāsa, who answered each question accordingly.
The Buddha then praised him, saying: "Excellent!
He asked again:
"How old are you? Subhaga replied,
"I am seven years old."
The World-Honored One said to Subhaga:
"Since you, together with those of all-encompassing wisdom, are well able to answer questions with a correct mind, I shall permit you to receive full ordination."
This is called receiving full ordination by answering questions.
Regarding receiving full ordination by undertaking the eight weighty rules: Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī received full ordination upon undertaking these eight weighty rules.
Regarding "receiving full ordination by dispatching a messenger," this refers to the case of the courtesan Upāliṅgikā.

Regarding "attaining full ordination through eight utterances," this means that one receives the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, and the Bhikṣu-saṃgha performs another *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; this is called attaining full ordination through eight utterances.
"One who obtains the full precepts through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*—this is the method by which monks of the present age commonly obtain the full precepts using eight utterances.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall take the original source as my testimony."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I permit you to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) after completing the three refuges.
Thus did the Buddha permit the bhikṣus to receive the full ordination.
The virtuous have no evil; those ordinary people of the present world who cultivate goodness up to the level of an Arhat are all called "virtuous persons.
What is meant by "goodness"?
It refers to virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; when one is endowed with these five factors, one is called a virtuous person.
As for "the real," the precepts are the most real; this is what is called "the real.
It is like a white cotton cloth that is dyed with blue; once it has taken on the color, it is then called a "blue cloth."
The true bhikṣu is likewise: because of his precepts, he is called a true bhikṣu; furthermore, the arhat who has abandoned the afflictions and exhausted the internal outflows is also called "true."
Those in training (*śaikṣa*) are ordinary persons and the seven types of trainees who train in the three trainings; these are called "bhikṣus in training.

Those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have already transcended the stage of training and abide in the higher fruits; from this point on, they have no further training remaining, and their outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted; these are called "those beyond training."
Regarding the assembly of monks: the minimum number for an assembly is five; as for more, it depends on how many gather.

Those who should take their *chanda* (consent) must present their consent. Once the Saṃgha has become harmonious and there is no one to raise an objection, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of harmony is then performed.
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* consists of one motion and three formal acts (*karmavācanā*). Regarding those for whom the *karman* should be performed, it is carried out according to the Dharma.
"Not being wicked" means that for a person who is free from obstacles, the *jñapti-karman* is valid.

Regarding "the mind being virtuous and indestructible by the multitude": because there is no meanness, it is called "not evil. As for "virtuous," practicing the Dharma is virtuous, and practicing the Tathāgata’s teaching is also virtuous.
"To have 'feet' means to attain the superior marks;
it is also said to mean 'to arrive. He asked:
"What are called the superior marks?"
He replied:
"The marks of a bhikṣu are called the 'superior marks. One attains these superior marks through the white-four-karmavācanā; this is called the full ordination by white-four-karmavācanā."
I shall now explain among these the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations); the others shall be explained extensively later.

Regarding the *āpatti-laghu* (minor offenses)—which in the language of Han means "small small groups"—there are the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. Following this sequence from the *khandhaka* through to the *parivāra*, if we reach a specific point in the *Karman-mūla*, I shall explain it extensively. If I were to explain them here [in the midst of the *Prātimokṣa*], they would become confused within the initial section on the *pārājika* offenses. Therefore, explaining them at their respective points in the sequence makes them easy for people to understand.
In this context, the Saṃgha has already assembled; the bhikṣu undergoes the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

If this bhikṣu commits an impure act, he incurs a pārājika offense. All other bhikṣus are likewise bhikṣus by name. If a bhikṣu, together with the other bhikṣus, enters into the discipline (śīla-dharma) for as long as life lasts, he should train in the precepts. There are three trainings: higher morality, higher mind, and higher wisdom; these are called the three trainings.
Question: "What is meant by 'supreme precept'? Answer:
"'Supreme' means peerless; 'precept' means training. Thus, it is also called peerless training."
"Superior mind" refers to the fruit-mind.
"Superior wisdom" refers to performing actions in order to know the fruit. He asked:
"What is meant by 'training'?
What is meant by 'higher training'?
And what is meant by 'the mind'?"
What is meant by the superior mind?
What is meant by wisdom?
What is meant by superior wisdom?
He replied:
"The five precepts and the ten precepts are training; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, these precepts always exist within the world."

When a Buddha appears in the world, he instructs others through his disciples; when he has not yet appeared in the world, pratyekabuddhas, śramaṇas of the path of karma, brahmins, universal monarchs (cakravartin), and the great bodhisattvas instruct others through their own wisdom, teaching other śramaṇas and brahmins.

If one is able to train in these merits, upon death they will be reborn in heaven or among humans, experiencing various joys; this is called "training. The *Prātimokṣa* is called the peerless training.

Just as the sun is the king among all lights, and Mount Sumeru is the greatest among all mountains, so too is the training in the *Prātimokṣa* supreme among all trainings in the world. This Dharma exists because a Tathāgata has appeared in the world; were it not for the appearance of a Buddha, no sentient being would be able to establish this Dharma. Regarding those who commit various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, the Buddha has established the peerless training to restrain them.
It is further said:
"If one enters this [state] and likewise enters the fruits of the path, this is called 'superior training' (adhiśikṣā).

As for the mind, there are eight virtuous minds within the six realms of desire; these are the eight mental absorptions (samādhi) of the mundane world, and they are called 'superior mind' (adhicitta)."

Transcending all worldly minds, it is only when a Buddha appears in the world that this mind exists; this is called the "supreme mind" (*uttamacitta*), and it is the mind of the fruit of the Path (*mārgaphalacitta*).
If one possesses this mind, there will be no conduct that is impure.
Regarding the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmaprajñā*): there are causes and there are effects; karma is the cause and retribution is the effect.

To know this through wisdom is what is called "wisdom. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this Dharma exists. When a Buddha appears, his *śrāvakas* instruct others. When he does not appear, practitioners of the path of karma—such as śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), and great bodhisattvas—also instruct others. For example, Ajakara performed great acts of giving for ten thousand years; likewise, the brāhmaṇa Virama, Sphītara, and other men of great wisdom, having perfected the merit of great giving, were reborn in the heavens to enjoy all manner of bliss.
The three characteristics of the turning wheel are suffering, emptiness, and non-self; these are called supreme wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Regarding these two factors—supreme training and supreme mind—wisdom is the most excellent; thus it is called supreme wisdom.
Regarding "supreme wisdom" (*uttara-paññā*): only when a Buddha appears in the world does this Dharma exist; the wisdom of the fruits of the path is also called supreme wisdom.

Therefore, when a bhikṣu enters into the three trainings (*tisraḥ śikṣāḥ*) and commits an impure act, he incurs a *pārājika* offense. Within these three trainings, the training in the *prātimokṣa*—if one enters into it—is termed "for as long as life lasts."
He further said:

"The bhikṣus are not of a single kind; they come from various countries and dwell in different regions, having different surnames and different names. Yet, by residing together in the same dwelling place and studying under the same discipline, they are also called 'living together'."
To remain unoffending in the training of the *prātimokṣa* is called "for as long as life lasts.

Regarding "the weakening of the precepts without emerging": it refers to not relinquishing the precepts while the signs of their weakening are not declared to others; or, if the weakening of the precepts is declared to others but the precepts are not relinquished, the precepts likewise do not emerge.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why do you not say 'abandoning the precepts,' but instead say 'the precepts have become weak'? [He replied:

"As stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one incurs an offense after staying together for no more than two or three nights; since such language is easy to understand, the Buddha spoke thus: 'This weakness of the precepts is also like this.'"
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, it is sufficient that one speaks well and preaches the Dharma without abandoning the meaning of the precepts; why then must one speak of being "weak"?

For example, if a great king has no attendants, wears neither a celestial crown nor necklaces, and is not adorned, people will not find him pleasing upon seeing him. Thus, first stating that one's precepts are weak and subsequently stating that one does not leave [the community]—when these two phrases are joined, it is called "excellent."

There are those whose precepts have weakened but they do not renounce them, and those whose precepts have not weakened but they do renounce them; being weary in heart regarding the training and failing to uphold it is called "weakening of the precepts. As for "sorrowful anxiety," it refers to feeling aversion toward and lack of joy in the Buddha-dharma.
Or one might say:
"I shall go today; I shall go tomorrow; I shall go by this path; I shall go by that path.
To thus heave long sighs and have a mind that is distracted and not concentrated is called sorrowful anxiety.
One who wishes to abandon the dharma of a śramaṇa wishes to abandon the marks of a bhikṣu.

Being weary and loathing them, they regard the marks of a bhikṣu as the ultimate disgrace; seeing the marks of a bhikṣu is like seeing excrement and filth, and they take pleasure in the marks of a layperson.
The Dharma Master said:

"In the sequential Vinaya, this is easy to understand. 'I now abandon the Buddha—excellent! I shall abandon the Buddha'—such words cause others to understand. How can one's precepts be weakened in this way without having actually abandoned them?"
The Dharma Master said: "There are further instances of weakness in the precepts:

'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha; I renounce the training, I renounce the Vinaya, I renounce the Prātimokṣa; I renounce my Upādhyāya, I renounce my Ācārya; I renounce my fellow students, I renounce my disciples, I renounce the disciples of my Ācāryas; I renounce those who share my Upādhyāya and fellow students, and I renounce those who share my Ācārya, Upādhyāya, and fellow students'—these fourteen phrases are all the beginnings of weakness in the precepts."

"I now act as a layman (*avadātavasana*), act as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), act as a steward (*paricāraka*), act as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), act as a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), or act as a lay follower of a non-Buddhist"—these eight phrases are all causes for the weakening of the precepts (*śīla-kaśāya*). From these twenty phrases, there are in total one hundred and ten phrases, which are termed "weakening of the precepts."
From this point onward, I recall seventeen phrases beginning with "mother. Regarding "field" (*kṣetra*), the rice field is the primary example.
Regarding "place" (*sthāna*), that from which sweet fruits, vegetables, or leaves emerge is called a place.
Regarding "crafts," it refers to those who can make earthenware vessels or serve as laborers;

such are the first [category]. Regarding "those still attached to the household": "I have parents whom I must now support"—this constitutes the first of nine phrases. Based on this dependence, "I have a mother whom I should support; my mother looked after and raised me"—such are the first of sixteen phrases.

From this point on, for one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), eating but a single meal and sleeping but a single night are extremely difficult practices. There are eight initial phrases beginning with "I am unable," "I cannot endure," and "I do not delight in"; likewise, there are fifty such phrases, then one hundred and ten, and again one hundred and sixty.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential explanation of the weakness of the precepts has already been given; you should know it for yourself.
Next, regarding the phrase 'renouncing the precepts,' what is meant by 'a bhikṣu'?"
The Dharma Master said: "The sequence of these phrases is easy to understand.

'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha; I renounce the Vinaya, I renounce the Prātimokṣa, I renounce my fellow students; I renounce the disciples of my Upādhyāya and Ācārya; I renounce the disciples of my co-Upādhyāya and co-Ācārya; I renounce my fellow students'—these fourteen phrases are equivalent to the expression of renunciation, spoken for the sake of making people understand."

This is one who wishes to depart from the Dharma and wishes to depart from the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, yet speaks so as to cause others to understand; if this person wishes to say, "I renounce the Buddha," and upon opening his mouth says:
"I renounce the Buddha."
"This is not the correct language of India;

it is spoken using whatever words are available. 'My Buddha is abandoned, my Dharma is abandoned,' and so on in succession down to 'my fellow students. As stated in the Vinaya-mūla, one is thus fulfilled in noble benefit."
"I intended to enter the first dhyāna, but as I was about to set out, I mistakenly said:
'I am entering the second dhyāna.
If one speaks such words, this person intends to abandon the marks of a bhikṣu; it is for this reason that they speak thus."

If one recognizes these words, it constitutes the forfeiture of the precepts; there is no difference between such a person falling [from their status] like Śakra or Brahmā, or like Māra, nor is there any difference from this person falling from the Dharma of the Tathāgata and returning to the state of a layperson.

If one says, "I have already abandoned the Buddha," "I wish to abandon the Buddha," or "I ought to abandon the Buddha"—whether spoken in the past, present, or future; or if one sends a messenger, writes a letter, or makes a hand-gesture to convey this to another person—this does not constitute the abandonment of the precepts.
If one speaks empty, deceptive, or false words, or uses hand gestures to convey such intent, one incurs a grave offense; however, this is not the case here.

If a person intends to renounce [the precepts], they must renounce them before another person; having first formed the intention and spoken the words, only then is the renunciation of the precepts accomplished.

If one speaks these words directed toward a single person, and that person understands them, the abandonment of the precepts is accomplished; however, if that person does not understand them, yet someone else present nearby does understand them, the abandonment of the precepts is likewise not accomplished.
If one speaks to two people, and one understands while the other does not, it constitutes the relinquishment of the precepts; if both understand, it constitutes the relinquishment of the precepts.
If one speaks to hundreds or thousands of people, those who understand constitute the relinquishment of the precepts.
If a bhikṣu, being tormented by lustful desire, wishes to speak of it to his fellow students but feels hesitant and fearful, he might instead go to a secluded place and speak in a loud voice:
"I now renounce the Buddha."

"Should there be anyone who understands—should even a person from a remote region understand—that this bhikṣu intends to relinquish the precepts and falls away from the Dharma of the Tathāgata, then the relinquishing of the precepts is accomplished."
If one understands the words of this bhikṣu neither before nor after [he has spoken], it is no different from ordinary worldly speech.

If, after these words have been spoken by the bhikṣu, one does not understand them immediately but only after reflecting for a long time, and then desires to relinquish the precepts, the relinquishment of the precepts is not accomplished.

If one speaks as if in empty space or offers worship with harsh words—speaking falsely due to anger of body and speech—such speech is no different from that found here [in this world]. If one understands it by applying the mind, one attains [realization] immediately;
if there is doubt and it is only after a long time that one understands, one incurs no offense.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In this way, one whose precepts have become weak constitutes a renunciation of the precepts. However, if one says, 'A layperson has accepted me; I wish to become a layperson,' or 'I am now a layperson,' or 'I have already become a layperson,' and speaks thus, it does not constitute a renunciation of the precepts.

If one says, 'Today I have caused a layperson to accept me,' and speaks while knowing this and keeping it in mind—whether using the language of Central India or a non-Indian language—if another person understands these words, then one immediately renounces the precepts."

The Dharma Master said: "In this sequence, the lay follower (upāsaka) is the first. From these seven phrases, eight phrases, fourteen phrases, and twenty-two phrases, what need have I for them? They are of no benefit to me; I have already explained these four phrases, and you should understand them yourself. Though the words and phrases are many, their underlying principle returns to one."
The Dharma Master said:
"I cannot explain it all; you yourself must know the Vinaya-mūla in its proper sequence.
The Dharma Master said:
Upāli said: "The Buddha has one hundred names;
the names of the Dharma are likewise, and the same applies to all other phrases.
I shall now explain them in brief."

"I now abandon the Buddha and lose my precepts; I abandon the Samyaksaṃbuddha, I abandon the Immeasurable Mind, I abandon the Incomparable Mind, I abandon the Wisdom of Bodhi, I abandon Non-delusion, and I abandon the Penetration of All Things. In this way, according to each title, one completely abandons the precepts.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "renouncing the Dharma," this is not a mere designation; it constitutes the renunciation of the precepts.

One renounces skillful discernment, renounces the retribution of the present body, renounces non-differentiation, renounces the view of coming, renounces the ability to deliver and transcend, and renounces wisdom and true knowledge.

Furthermore, he says: "I renounce the unconditioned dharma; I renounce the departure from desire, renounce cessation, renounce the dharma of ambrosia (*amṛta*); I renounce the *Dīrghāgama*, renounce the *Saṃyuktāgama*, renounce the *Brahmajāla*, renounce the *Āgama of the Original Texts*, renounce the *Saṃgītiparyāya*, renounce the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, renounce the *Jātaka*, renounce the *Abhidharma*, renounce the dharmas of merit, renounce that which is neither merit nor non-merit; I renounce the station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), renounce the well-established, renounce the stage of supernormal powers (*abhijñābhūmi*), renounce the comprehensive grasp, renounce valor, renounce awakening (*bodhi*), renounce the path (*mārga*), renounce the fruit (*phala*), renounce nirvāṇa; I renounce the eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*)—by such declarations as these, one completely effects the renunciation of the precepts."

"I renounce the Saṃgha"—this statement is not a mere name; it means renouncing the good for the sake of the Saṃgha, renouncing the Right for the sake of following [the Saṃgha], renouncing that which accords with principle, renouncing the assembled Saṃgha, renouncing the Saṃgha of the four pairs, renouncing the Saṃgha of the eight ranks, renouncing the Worthy Ones (Arhats), renouncing the palms-joined veneration, and renouncing the Unsurpassed Field of Merit. To say "I renounce the one named Saṃgha" also constitutes the forfeiture of the precepts.

"I now renounce the precepts"—if one speaks these words, it constitutes the renunciation of the precepts; it is the renunciation of the bhikṣu precepts, the renunciation of the bhikṣuṇī precepts, the renunciation of the higher training, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. By means of this name, the renunciation is accomplished.

If one renounces the *vinaya* of monks and the *vinaya* of nuns; renounces the first *pārājika*, the second, third, and fourth *pārājikas*; renounces the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; renounces the *sthūlātyaya*; renounces the *pāyattika*; renounces the *pratideśanīya*; renounces the *duṣkṛta*; renounces the *tuhubahu* (in the Han language, "subtle offenses")—by such names of precepts, the renunciation of the precepts is likewise accomplished.
If one says, "I renounce the *prātimokṣa*," this is not a formal designation and yet constitutes the relinquishment of the precepts.
If one says, "I renounce the *prātimokṣa* of a bhikṣu" or "I renounce the *prātimokṣa* of a bhikṣuṇī," these are formal designations and likewise constitute the relinquishment of the precepts.
I renounce training and thereby complete the renunciation of the precepts.

I renounce the training of a bhikṣu and the training of a bhikṣuṇī; from the first and second [sections] up to the training of the Prātimokṣa; I renounce the training of the Samyaksaṃbuddha and the training of the Immeasurable Mind; I renounce the training of Wisdom and the training of Renunciation—thus, in this sequence, I shall now renounce them all.

"The preceptor who ordained me and conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*)—in such-and-such a place I received ordination, and in such-and-such a place I received the full ordination—I renounce this person. By speaking thus, one renounces the preceptor; by renouncing the name of the preceptor, the preceptorship is relinquished, and the precepts are also relinquished.
If one says, "I now renounce my ācārya," the precepts are lost even though this word is not the formal title;

for if one has been ordained by a person, taught by a person, or relied upon a certain place to inquire and study, and says, "I shall renounce this person," speaking thus using the title of "ācārya," one thereby loses the precepts.
"I renounce my disciple"—this statement is not a mere title; by it, the precepts are immediately relinquished.

If a person was ordained by me, and I conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon them, such that they had already gone forth under me and received the full ordination, and I now say, "I renounce this person," by thus renouncing the disciple through the use of their name, the relinquishing of the precepts is thereby accomplished.
If I now abandon my preceptor or my disciples, I have immediately abandoned the precepts.
If there is someone who ordained me, or someone who instructs or consults with me, if I abandon that person by means of their name, I have thereby abandoned the precepts.
If I now renounce my fellow student, I immediately accomplish the renunciation of the precepts.

If there is a person whom my teacher ordained and conferred full ordination upon, and through whom I received full ordination from my teacher—if I renounce that person by using the title "fellow student," I thereby accomplish the renunciation [of the precepts].
If I now abandon my fellow student and preceptor (*ācārya*), my precepts are thereby abandoned.

If someone has been ordained by my preceptor and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and if that person consults me regarding my preceptor, or if my preceptor instructs them so that they may understand, and I then abandon such a person—thus, by means of the names of one's preceptor and fellow students, the abandonment of the precepts is accomplished.
If I now renounce all my fellow students, I immediately lose my precepts.

If there is a person who shares with me the same intention for study and the same wisdom for study, and I renounce that person—thus, by means of the names of all my fellow students, I have effectively lost my precepts.
"I have now become a layperson (avadātavasana), and thus my precepts are abandoned.

I have returned to my former state; I am now a merchant, and I now plow fields, raise cattle, and indulge in the five desires. By taking on the name and status of a layperson in this way, my precepts are abandoned."
"I now become a lay follower (upāsaka), and thus my abandonment of the precepts is accomplished.
By saying "I now become a lay follower" a second time and a third time;

or by saying "I uphold the five precepts" or "I uphold the ten precepts"; or by saying "I now become a lay follower"—in this way, through the designation of the title "lay follower," the precepts are abandoned.
"I am now acting as a *kappiya-kāraka* (purifier); my precepts are thereby forfeited.
I am employed by the Saṃgha; I am now distributing congee, rice, fruits, and wood-fruits. In this way, by using the title of 'purifier,' one's abandonment of the precepts is established."
"If I become a *śrāmaṇera*, I immediately forfeit the precepts.
If I become a young *śrāmaṇera* or a small *śrāmaṇera*, by the very designation of the name 'śrāmaṇera,' I immediately forfeit the precepts."
"If I now become a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), I immediately forfeit the precepts.
By becoming a Nirgrantha, an Ājīvaka, a Dombuva, a Pārivrajaka, or a Parivrājaka—by adopting such names of non-Buddhists, one immediately forfeits the precepts."
If one becomes an upāsaka of an external path (tīrthika), one immediately forfeits the precepts.

If one becomes an upāsaka of the Nirgranthas, an upāsaka of the Ājīvikas, an upāsaka of the Kāpilas, an upāsaka of the Ta-pa-su, an upāsaka of the Pāribhāṣikas, or an upāsaka of the Pāṇḍurajas—by adopting such names of external paths, one immediately forfeits the precepts.
"I am no śramaṇa; thus my precepts are forfeited. I have committed acts that violate the precepts and are evil dharmas;

I have performed foul and impure deeds that conceal the pure conduct. Being no śramaṇa, I claim to be a śramaṇa; being no one of pure conduct (brahmacarya), I claim to be one of pure conduct. With such foulness festering within, by using the name of 'śramaṇa' when I am not, my precepts are thereby forfeited."
“I am not of the lineage of Śākyamuni; thus, my precepts are forfeited.

I am not a son of the Samyaksaṃbuddha, nor a son of Immeasurable Intention, nor a son of Incomparable Intention, nor a son of Bodhi-wisdom, nor a son of Valor, nor a son of Freedom from Delusion, nor a son of Unobstructed Penetration, nor a son of the Most Victorious. In this way, by the title of being of the lineage of Śākyamuni, my precepts are forfeited.”

"By this cause, by this manifestation, by this expedient means, and by the name of the Buddha—having spoken thus, all these are causes for the relinquishment of the precepts, with the Buddha being placed at the beginning."
"Furthermore, there is no such thing as abandoning the precepts through other words.
The Dharma Master said:

"I have already demonstrated these characteristics of abandoning the precepts. Do not harbor doubts regarding those who do not abandon them; I shall now explain in detail the abandonment of the precepts, beginning with the person, whether the abandonment of the precepts is accomplished because of a person or not accomplished because of a person."
The Dharma Master said:
"As stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'In what way does one not relinquish the precepts?'"
Regarding the first phrase, "one who is deranged": this refers to those deranged by yakṣas or those deranged by *caṇḍālas*, while others follow their own perverted minds.

If such a person renounces the precepts, it does not constitute a valid renunciation. If one renounces the precepts before a deranged person—even if the intention to renounce is very firm—the deranged person does not understand the precepts, and thus the renunciation is not accomplished. One whose mind has been lost is no different from one deranged by a yakṣa.
The Dharma Master said:
"If a yakṣa becomes insane or a person with jaundice becomes insane, there is no offense; this shall be explained later.
Likewise, if one loses one's mind and abandons the precepts, it does not constitute a formal renunciation."

Regarding those oppressed by suffering: if one who has already been struck by the blade of suffering renounces the precepts due to mental distress, the renunciation of the precepts is not accomplished;
or if one speaks toward a person experiencing suffering, because that person is distressed by pain and does not understand these words, the renunciation of the precepts is not accomplished.

Regarding those who take refuge in celestial deities, beginning with the Earth Deity and extending up to the deity Aṭavika: if one renounces the precepts by taking refuge in these various deities, the renunciation of the precepts is not accomplished.

Regarding those who turn toward animals—such as mahoragas, garuḍas, kinnaras, elephants, monkeys, and other such creatures—if one renounces the precepts before these beings, the renunciation of the precepts is not accomplished.
