"Before I am killed, I pray that you come quickly to dismember me;
if you come only after I have been killed, it will be of no benefit to me.
Having first been installed as king, he spoke these words:
“If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas may take grass, wood, and water as they please, this was the king’s own command; does Your Majesty not remember?

At the time when the king first ascended the throne, he beat the drum and proclaimed: ‘If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas take grass, wood, and water as they please,’ it is for this reason that I have taken the royal timber.”
The King replied:
"My previous statement was intended for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and modesty, not for shameless individuals such as yourself.
Such words were meant to allow one to take unowned property from an araṇya hermitage, not to speak of property that has an owner."
Regarding "attaining liberation because of the hair": this refers to how those who have left the household life and don the *kāṣāya* robe are like the hair. Why is this?

It is, for example, like a wise person in the world who wishes to eat much mutton but has no means to obtain it; he employs a stratagem to purchase a fine, large-haired sheep, ties it outside his gate, and marks its head so that it may be slaughtered.
When the people saw this, they valued it all the more for its wool and paid double the price; thus, the sheep was saved.
The bhikṣu Dhanika was likewise: because he possessed the kāṣāya robe, he was able to escape punishment.
The people rebuked the bhikṣu Dhanika in the presence of the king.
As for their rebuke, they said:
"You are not a śramaṇa."
He glared at him with malevolent eyes and recounted his deeds, praising them so as to make others know that this was not the dharma of a śramaṇa and not the way of a son of the Śākya clan.
"To practice the holy life (brahmacarya) is the supreme conduct," and so forth, in four lines.
There was an old minister who, knowing the ancient laws of the king, had left the household life to pursue the Way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One questioned the bhikṣu who was formerly that minister.
The Dharma Master asked:
“The Buddha is omniscient; regarding the precepts established by the Buddhas of the past and future, the World-Honored One fully knows the gravity or lightness of their offenses.
For what reason, then, does he now question the bhikṣu who was formerly a minister?”

"The reason the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu who was formerly a minister is that, had he not discussed the matter with that former minister, he would have incurred a pārājika offense for a single coin, thereby becoming an object of reproach and suspicion by the people of the world."

“The merit of a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts is immeasurable, like space and like the great earth; it cannot be measured. Why then has the Buddha, on account of a single coin, established such a grave offense?”

“The Buddha, through his wisdom, has weighed the matter so that the prohibitions may endure for a long time and that people may have faith and accept them; therefore, it is appropriate to deliberate with the former ministers. [The opponent asks:

“Regarding the rules for laypeople (*avadātavasana*), if one steals even a single portion, or kills, or binds, or expels another, why does the Buddha not likewise abolish the rules for those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*)?”

“An ordained person must not take even a blade of grass or a leaf. For this reason, the Buddha employed wisdom to deliberate and established the prohibitive precepts so as to avoid giving rise to reproach or suspicion; therefore, the Buddha, together with the bhikṣus who were former ministers, formulated the prohibitive precepts based upon worldly conventions.”
The onlookers saw an old minister-monk not far from the Buddha and asked him:
"According to the law of King Bimbisāra, at what value of stolen goods is one bound, exiled, and executed?"
"Magadha" is the name of the country; "Siniyu" means that it is fully equipped with people, elephants, chariots, and horses, and thus it is named Siniyu;
"Bimbisāra" is the name of the king.
"One who is expelled shall be transferred and placed in another country.
The Dharma Master said:
"The subsequent phrase is easy to understand."
Regarding "one part of five māṣakas": at that time in Rājagṛha, twenty māṣakas constituted one kārṣāpaṇa; the kārṣāpaṇa was divided into four parts, and one such part consisted of five māṣakas.
"You yourselves should know this:

this *kāliṃsapa* is indeed the ancient *kāliṃsapa*, not King Rudrāyaṇa who was the first *kāliṃsapa* in the present age. The Buddhas of the past also established the *pārājika* offense by means of a single portion; the Buddhas of the future shall likewise establish the *pārājika* offense by means of a single portion. For all Buddhas, the *pārājika* offenses are established without variation; the four *pārājikas* neither increase nor decrease."
For this reason, the Buddha rebuked the bhikṣu Dhanika because of one portion [of the cloth] and established the second *pārājika*.

As explained in the Vinaya-mūla, beginning with the taking of what is not given—defined as theft—and because it cuts off the very root, the second *pārājika* was concluded; subsequently, the rules concerning washing were further established.
The fundamental rule has already been explained. Thus, the Buddha has finished enacting the precepts for the bhikṣus.
This second supplementary rule is also no different from the previous enactment; you yourselves should understand this.
If I were to repeat the phrases now, it would become tedious; I shall explain them when the questioner arrives.
"As for 'the place of washing': because one washes white cotton cloth and dries it in this location, it is called the place of washing."

Regarding the washerman: it was a washerman washing white cotton cloth. At the hour of *pradoṣa*, the washerman was binding up the white cotton cloth, intending to return to the city; he was suddenly seen in a state of hurried agitation and confusion.
At that time, because of the commotion, the group of six bhikṣus took a bundle with the intent to steal.
Regarding "a village": whether it be a village or a forest hermitage (āraṇya), these have already been explained in the Vinaya; I shall now further analyze and explain them.
A "village" (*grāma*) refers to a single family or a single house, such as the village of Morā; even a single house is called a village, which you should understand for yourself.
A place where there are "no people" (*amanuṣya*) is a dwelling of yakṣas, or a place where people have temporarily fled due to some circumstance and subsequently returned to live there again.
Regarding those with fences: they begin with brickwork and may extend down to being made of grass and wood.
As for those inhabited by *gavaya* cattle, wherever the cattle dwell—whether in a single house or two or three houses—that is also called a village (*grāma*).
Those who dwell as merchants include those who travel by foot carrying their wares and those who travel by carriage;
these are also called "villages. Cities, towns, and hamlets are likewise called "villages."
Regarding the "village boundary" (*grāma-sīman*): this is intended to clarify the "wilderness boundary" (*araṇya-sīman*). As for "standing at the threshold":

if a village, such as the country of Aṇurādhā, has two thresholds, everything outside the inner threshold is considered a wilderness area. If there is no threshold, the place where a threshold would normally be is also termed a "threshold. This is the *araṇya* rule according to the Abhidharma.
A person of average strength is neither robust nor feeble.
As for the one who hurls the stone, he hurls it with all his might; he goes as far as the stone falls, but does not take account of the momentum of the stone’s roll.
If there is no fence around the village, one should throw a stone from where the water falling from the eaves of the house lands.

Furthermore, the Dharma Master explains that it is the place reached by throwing a dung-scoop or a pestle used for pounding grain while an old woman stands inside the doorway; this is the place reached by throwing the stone.

Furthermore, according to the Master’s interpretation: if a house has no fence, one should construct railings at both ends of the house; the area within the reach of a stone thrown from the center of those railings is defined as the "house boundary" (*grha-sīman*).
Question: "If the original village was extensive but has now become narrow and small, to what extent should it be considered the boundary? Answer:
"The boundary of a village (*grāma-sīman*) extends from the place where rainwater falls from a house occupied by people to the distance reached by a stone thrown by an average person.
As for the boundary of a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka-sīman*), the area extending five hundred *dhanus* beyond the threshold of the gate is called the lower grade of an *āraṇya*."
The Dharma Master said:
"I have already explained this meaning in detail.

Regarding the boundaries of houses and the boundaries of villages, these five types were taught for the purpose of eliminating wicked bhikṣus. If one takes even a single portion of property belonging to an owner from within these five locations with the intent to steal, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense."

Taking what is not given means that regarding another's property, whether it be clothing or food, when the other has not bestowed it by means of body or speech, one takes a portion for oneself—either taking it from their hand or taking it from its place.
"Not relinquished" means that the owner has not relinquished their mental claim;
even if it is on vacant ground, it is still termed "not relinquished. To take such an object is called theft; theft is among the various transgressions.
The Dharma Master said:

"In the Dharma, I do not grasp at the literal words, but take only their meaning. As for what is called 'stealing,' it refers to taking away, carrying off, lifting up, stepping beyond [the threshold], moving from its original place, and making a prior agreement."
Question: "What is meant by 'seizing'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu seizes another's grove or garden and disputes over it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If this causes the owner of the garden to fall into doubt, the monk incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the owner of the garden reaches a state of certain conviction regarding the loss [of ownership], the monk incurs a *pārājika* offense. He asked:
"What is meant by 'carrying'?
If a bhikṣu carries a person's belongings upon his head and touches them with a thieving mind, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"If one shakes it with the hand, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one places it down upon the shoulder, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. He asked:
"What is meant by 'storing'?
He replied:
"If a bhikṣu receives an object entrusted to him by another and stores it away in a cache, and its owner returns to the bhikṣu to reclaim it, and the bhikṣu replies:"
If one says, "I do not accept your deposit," having spoken these words, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes the owner of the object to fall into doubt, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
The owner says,
"I do not have this object," and the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Question: "What is meant by 'cutting off the steps'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu intends to steal an object, and while another person is carrying it away, he takes the first step, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense; with the second step, he incurs a pārājika offense."
Question: "What is meant by 'departing from its original place'? Answer:
"If a person places an object on the ground and this bhikṣu touches it with a thieving mind, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If he moves it, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
"If it is moved from its original place, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*.
He asked: "What is meant by 'essential'?"
He replied:
"If a bhikṣu makes a vow to himself, saying:
'When I reach such-and-such a place, I shall take this object with me.'"
If one goes to a certain place to take an object, with one foot inside the boundary and one foot outside the boundary, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If both feet have gone outside the boundary, it is a *pārājika*.

If one passes goods through a customs checkpoint without paying the tax: if one foot has passed beyond the checkpoint while the other remains within the taxable area, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both feet have completely passed outside the taxable area, it is a *pārājika*.
The Dharma Master said:

"This concerns the discussion of miscellaneous items. If one were to discuss them by way of individual objects—starting with such things as a slave who has a master or a domestic animal—if they are seized, taken away, lifted up, have their stride cut short, moved from their original location, or pass through a restricted area, these constitute one type of object. You should understand that if these six phrases are explained in detail, they form twenty-five propositions (five sets of five)."
Thus the second *pārājika* has been explained; it is most excellently explained.

Why? Because it is difficult to understand. As stated at the beginning of the *Vinaya-mūla*, one incurs a *pārājika* offense after stealing by means of five factors. Taking "the object having an owner" as the first, these constitute the five kinds.
The Dharma Master said:
"Having thus explained the branches and leaves, you should take up one matter; it has five aspects and also six aspects. [The interlocutor asked:
"If that is so, does this not fail to constitute five times five?"
He replied: "It is not so. Why is that?"
Regarding the five types of persons involved when taking an object while situated in a single phrase, you should know them yourself.

The former Dharma masters have said that the characteristics of this second *pārājika* offense are difficult to understand; therefore, it is necessary to provide a detailed and analytical explanation. For this reason, I shall now set forth these twenty-five phrases; you should examine them well.
Question: "What are these five?

First, the five kinds of various objects; second, the five kinds of single objects; third, the five involving one's own hand; fourth, the five involving initial preparatory means; fifth, the five involving theft."

Question: "Regarding the various sets of five and the single set of five—these two categories of phenomena can likewise be seized, taken away, lifted up, or moved from their original place; this has already been explained previously, which you should know for yourself.
When the essential locations are added to these, they are called the six."
The place of throwing and the place where it lands are equal in this dharma; therefore, regarding the third phrase, one may obtain five kinds of various objects from among the five.
The five kinds of single objects have already been explained.
"What are the five [cases of] taking with one's own hand?
He replied:
"There are five kinds of taking with one's own hand:
"First, taking with one's own hand; second, instructing another; third, throwing; fourth, being able to take; fifth, the intention to relinquish.
He asked: "What is meant by 'taking with one's own hand'?"
"To take another's property with one's own hand constitutes 'taking with one's own hand.
As for 'instructing,' if a bhikṣu instructs another, saying, 'Take such-and-such an object,' this is called 'instructing.'"
Regarding "throwing": if one is staying within the customs boundary and throws [an object] outside, if it is a heavy object, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
For this reason, it is equivalent to being together with a restricted place (*maryādā*).
Regarding "the one who takes": if a person instructs another, saying, "If you are able to take such-and-such an object, take it;

if you cannot obtain it, then stop," and that person follows the instruction and goes, and if they steal the object, the instructor incurs a *pārājika* offense by having sent them away. If the person who went there takes it at the appropriate time, this is called "the one who takes."
“Regarding the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*): it is the placing of the mind upon an object with a sense of relinquishment; this mind is called the mind of equanimity.

“What are the five initial applications (*pūrvaprayoga*)? They are: first, the initial application; second, the subsequent application; third, the application of binding; fourth, the essential performance; and fifth, the recognition.”
Because it involves instructing others, this is the primary expedient; you yourselves should understand this.
Because it results from departing from one's original location, it is called the secondary expedient.
As for the remaining three, they are as explained in the Vinaya-mūla.
“What are the five kinds of theft?
First, taking by theft; second, taking by concealment; third, taking by compulsion; fourth, taking by concealment; and fifth, taking by casting lots. These are called the five.”
There was a bhikṣu who, while distributing *kāṣāya* robes for the community of monks, used a thieving intent to exchange another's tally and take the robe.
I shall explain this matter of exchanging tallies myself; these are called the five kinds of theft.
Thus, these five sets of five make twenty-five in total, as you yourselves should know.

Among these five sets of five, when a dispute arises, a wise and learned *vinaya-dhara* must not adjudicate the matter hastily; rather, he should first examine five points before passing judgment, as the verse from the past says:
"If one recounts matters of the past, The appropriate times for doing so are five."
"Having observed these five points, wisdom should understand them.
As for "points": if I desire to take this object and have already spoken [of it], I incur an offense.

One should examine whether this object has an owner or is ownerless. One should examine if it has an owner: [in that case] one should relinquish the intention but not the object, so that the owner may properly see it. If one steals it while the intention has not yet been relinquished, one should calculate it as a Vinaya offense; if the intention has already been relinquished, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. Even if the object is later returned to the owner, this is the application of the Dharma.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now set forth the fundamental account.
In the past, during the time of King Bimbisāra, offerings were made to the Great Stūpa."
There was a bhikṣu coming from the south, who had a seven-cubit yellow robe draped over his shoulder.

As this bhikṣu entered the monastery to pay his respects, the king and a great multitude also entered the monastery. The king drove the people away, and as the crowd pressed together to one side, they became a chaotic clamor, jostling and pushing one another. Consequently, the bhikṣu lost his robe and departed without seeing it.
The bhikṣu thought to himself: "The great multitude is so disordered and confused; my robe is lost and cannot be recovered."
Having formed the intention of relinquishment, a bhikṣu later arrives and, seeing this robe, takes it with the intent to steal. Having taken it, he then feels remorse, thinking:
"I am no longer a śramaṇa; I have lost my precepts. I shall now return to lay life."
"I went to the place where the Vinaya-master was, and only after questioning him did I come to know.
At that time, the Vinaya-master was named Cūḷasumana; he was well-versed in the characteristics of the Vinaya and was the foremost among all Vinaya-masters."
The offending bhikṣu went to the place of the vinaya-master and prostrated with his head at his feet, reporting the matter in detail:
"How do I now stand regarding whether I have committed an offense or not?
Having understood this, after the formal legal procedure of the assembly, the bhikṣu took the robe. Knowing that this bhikṣu’s offense was redeemable, the vinaya-master said to the offending bhikṣu:
"Can you bring the owner of this object?
If you can find the owner, I shall provide for you.
The guilty bhikṣu replied:
"How can I possibly obtain it now?
The Vinaya Master said, "Just go;
call out and inquire at every place."
The guilty bhikṣu entered the five great monasteries to search for them but could not find them; he returned once more to question the vinaya masters, who replied:
"From which direction have many bhikṣus come here?"
He replied, "Many have come from the south.

[The Buddha said,] "You previously took a robe to measure its length and width, and you have already finished measuring its color. You should go again and enter each monastery in succession to inquire."
The guilty bhikṣu, having received the instruction, departed according to the command; he encountered the owner of the object and brought him to the presence of the vinaya master.
The vinaya master then questioned the owner of the object, the bhikṣu: "Elder!..."
"Is this your robe? He replied, "It is."
“Venerable sir!
Where was it lost?
The bhikṣu answered according to the facts.
The legal master asked,
"Have you relinquished your mind [of attachment]? He replied:
"Having already formed the intention to relinquish it," he then asked the bhikṣu who had committed the offense:
"From where did you take it?"
He replied, "I took it at such-and-such a time and in such-and-such a place.
The Vinaya Master said:
"If you took it without the intention to steal, there is no offense.
Since you took it with a malicious mind, you have committed a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); you must first perform repentance, and only then will you be free from the offense."
He said to the bhikṣu Wuzhu:
"With a mind of renunciation, give this robe to this bhikṣu.
He replied, "Very well."
Upon hearing the words of the Vinaya Master, the guilty bhikṣu felt as much joy in body and mind as one who has tasted the flavor of ambrosia.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is what is called 'contemplating the locus'."

Regarding "time," it refers to the time of acquisition; this robe may be light at one time and heavy at another. If it is taken when light, one incurs the offense according to its value at that light time; if it is taken when heavy, one should incur the offense according to its value at that heavy time.
The Dharma Master said:
"These words are difficult to understand; I shall now take a person as my witness.

Once, in the midst of the ocean, there was a bhikṣu who obtained a coconut shell that was perfectly formed and complete. Having obtained it, he carved upon it until it was no different from a conch-shell bowl, such that it captivated the hearts of men."
This bhikṣu always used coconut water for drinking and kept a coconut-shell bowl in the middle of the sea.

When the monks from the monastery went to Mount Cetiya, a certain bhikṣu went to the middle of the sea, entered the monastery upon arrival, and while staying there saw the coconut-shell bowl. With a mind of theft, he took it and returned to Mount Cetiya; having arrived, he used the bowl to eat his gruel.
The bhikṣu who was the master of the coconut bowl saw him and asked:
"Ho, Elder! Where did you obtain this coconut bowl?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I obtained it from within the ocean.
The bhikṣu Vastu-svāmin then said:
"This is not your property; it was permitted by me, yet you stole it.
He immediately seized him and brought him before the Sangha to adjudicate the matter in full, but no one was able to judge it.

They then proceeded to the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra) and struck the drum there. Once the assembly had gathered near the stupa, the legal experts (vinayadharas) were still deliberating on this matter without reaching a conclusion.
At that time, there was among the assembly a bhikṣu who was a master of Abhidharma named Gautama; he was extremely skilled in expedient means. The Venerable Gautama spoke as follows:
"In what place did this bhikṣu obtain the coconut shell plate?"
He replied,
"I took it from the middle of the ocean.
[The other asked,] "What was its value?"
He replied, "In that land, they eat these coconuts and discard the remaining shells as broken waste, or even burn them for firewood; they have no value at all.
He then questioned the monk who was the owner of the goods:
"Master, what is the value of this coconut you hold in your hand?
He replied, "A person has already eaten the flesh and drunk the juice of this coconut and discarded the husk; a bhikṣu picked it up, peeled and prepared it to make a vessel. It is worth one māṣaka."
The Venerable Gautama said:
"If it is so, then as long as it does not amount to five māṣakas, one does not commit a grave offense.
At that time, those in the assembly who heard these words exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent! You have skillfully adjudicated this matter.

At that time, King Bātya, wishing to enter the monastery to pay his respects, heard the bhikṣus exclaiming "Excellent! as he was departing through the city gate. Having heard this, the king asked his attendant ministers, "What sound is this?"

The minister then answered in due order, and upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted. The king immediately beat the drum to proclaim an edict: "From this day forward, whenever any monastics have doubts regarding a matter, they shall all come to Gautama for judgment; this Venerable One’s adjudication of affairs does not contravene the Vinaya."
The Dharma Master said:
"In this way, as one observes, value is established according to circumstances; there are things that are newly precious and later become cheap. He asked:
"What is meant by 'initially noble and later base'?
He replied:

"It is like a new iron bowl that is whole, clean, and without holes; it is initially noble, but once it becomes cracked and broken, it is base. Therefore, its value is assessed according to the time."
"As for items used for one's own purposes, such as knives or axes, they are valuable at first but become cheap later.
The Dharma Master said:
"If a bhikṣu steals another person’s axe, he should ask the owner of the axe:"
"How much did you pay for the axe?
"Virtuous One! I bought it for one *māṣa*."
He asked again,
"Have you already used the axe since you bought it?
The owner of the axe replied:
"I have only begun to break twigs for tooth-sticks this day," or he might say,
"I broke firewood to burn my bowl."
Once it has been used, it becomes an old object.
This is like an ointment pestle, or like a door bolt; even if rice husks have been burned over it once or twice, or if it has been rubbed with tile shards, it is still called "old."
Furthermore, it is like a bathing robe: whether it has been entered into the water only once, or folded over the shoulder, or used to wrap the head, or used to wrap sand, it is still called "old."
Clarified butter that has been transferred to another vessel, or into which insects or ants have fallen, is also termed "spoiled.
Likewise, rock honey that was initially firm but later became soft, to the point where it can be indented by fingernails, is also termed "spoiled."
If a bhikṣu steals another’s property, he should question the owner regarding it; you should know that if it has not been used, its value is high, whereas if it has been used, its value is low.
These are the five points which a vinaya master must carefully examine before adjudicating a case, and he shall punish according to the gravity of the offense.
The Chapter on Seizure concludes.
In the eighth fascicle of the *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, regarding the discussion of individual items: first, there are slaves who have an owner, or domestic animals, and so forth.

Whether it is taken away, carried off, lifted up, the stride is interrupted, moved from its original place, or passed beyond the boundary, these constitute one type of object. When these six phrases are explained in detail, they form five sets of five, totaling twenty-five phrases; you should understand this.
Thus has the second *pārājika* been explained; it is most excellently explained. Why is this?
Because it is difficult to understand.
As stated at the beginning of the Vinaya-mūla-sūtra, one incurs the offense of pārājika only after stealing by means of five methods.
Taking "possessing an owner" as the first, these constitute the five types.
The Dharma Master said:
"Having thus explained the branches and leaves, you should take up one matter; it has five aspects and also six aspects. [The interlocutor asked:
"If that is so, does this not fail to constitute five sets of five?"
He replied: "It is not so. Why is this?"
If one dwells upon a single phrase, there are five ways of apprehending persons and things, which you should know for yourself.

The former Dharma masters have said that the characteristics of this second *pārājika* offense are difficult to understand; therefore, it is necessary to provide a detailed and analytical explanation.
"Therefore, I now speak these twenty-five phrases; you should examine them well.
He asked: "What are the five?"

"First, the five cases involving various objects; second, the five cases involving a single object; third, the five cases involving one's own hand; fourth, the five cases involving the initial preparatory effort; fifth, the five cases involving theft."
Question: "Regarding the various sets of five and the single set of five—can these two types of objects also be seized, taken away, lifted up, or moved from their original place? Answer:
"This has already been explained at the beginning; you should know it for yourself."
These essential points complete it;
thus, they are called the six.

Since the essential points (*yāthāsthāna*) and the casting points (*nikṣepasthāna*) are identical in this dharma, the third category among the five also obtains the fivefold variety of objects; the fivefold variety of a single type of object has already been explained.
"What are the five types of taking with one's own hand?

He replied: "There are five kinds of taking with one's own hand: first, taking with one's own hand; second, commanding; third, throwing; fourth, being able to take; and fifth, the intention to relinquish."
Question: "What is meant by 'taking with one's own hand'? Answer:
"To personally steal another's property with one's own hand—this is called 'with one's own hand.'"
"Instruction" means if a bhikṣu instructs another person, saying, "Take such-and-such an object," this is called instruction.
"Throwing" means if one who is staying within a customs barrier throws a heavy object out to the exterior, one incurs a pārājika offense.
Because of these words, it is equivalent to being together with the essential points.
As for "one who takes," it means instructing a person: "If you are able to take such-and-such an object, then take it; if you cannot obtain it, then desist."

This person then departs according to the instruction; if they steal this object, the instructor incurs the offense of *pārājika* by sending them away, while the one who goes and takes it at that time is called the "one who actually takes."
"Regarding the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*): it is the placing of the mind in a state of relinquishment toward objects; this mind is called the mind of equanimity.
"What are the five initial applications (*pūrvakaraṇīya*)?
First, the initial application; second, the subsequent application; third, the application of connection; fourth, the essential task; and fifth, the recognition."
Teaching others is the first preparatory means; you yourselves should understand this.
Because it involves departing from one's original location, it is called the "conforming preparatory means.
The remaining three are as explained in the Vinaya-mūla.
"What is meant by 'throwing with all one's strength'?
It means throwing [the stone] until it reaches the place where it falls, rather than taking advantage of its momentum as it rolls.
If there is no fence around a village, one should throw the stone from where one stands at the edge of the house or the water."
Furthermore, according to the Master’s interpretation, it is the area reached by a waste basket or a pestle when thrown by an old woman standing inside the doorway;

or, according to another interpretation by the Master, if the house has no fence, it is the area reached by a stone thrown from the center of a railing made at both ends of the house—this is called the "house boundary" (*grha-sīmā*).
Question: "If the original village was vast but has now become small, at what point should the boundary be established? Answer:
"In a village where people dwell, the village boundary extends as far as a stone thrown by an average person would reach from the point where it leaks down from the roof.
As for the forest hermitage boundary (*āraṇyaka-sīman*), that which is five hundred bow-lengths outside the door threshold is called the 'inferior' forest hermitage."
The Dharma Master said:
"I have already finished explaining this meaning through detailed analysis.

Regarding the boundaries of a house and the boundaries of a village, these five types were taught in order to eliminate wicked bhikṣus. If one takes even a single portion of property belonging to an owner from within these five locations with the intent to steal, it constitutes a pārājika offense."

Regarding taking what is not given: if another’s property, whether clothing or food, is taken by oneself without being given by the other person through body or speech—whether taken from their hand or from their place—and it is not relinquished, meaning the owner’s mind does not relinquish it; even if it is on empty ground, it is likewise called "not relinquished. To take such an object is called stealing (*steya*); one who steals is a *tshur-po* (thief).
The Dharma Master said:

"Within the Dharma, I do not grasp at the literal words, but take only their meaning. As for what is called 'stealing,' it refers to seizing, taking away, lifting, moving a step, removing from its original place, and making a mutual agreement."
Question: "What is meant by 'taking away'? Answer:

"If a bhikṣu takes away another's grove or garden and they dispute over it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he causes the owner to fall into doubt, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If the owner reaches a state of certain conviction that he has lost [the property], the bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense."
He asked: "What is meant by 'carrying'? " [The Buddha replied:

"If a bhikṣu carries another's property upon his head with the intent to steal, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for touching it; if he moves it with his hand, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); if he places it down upon his shoulder, he incurs the offense of *pārājika* (defeat)."
Question: "What is meant by 'raising'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu receives an entrusted object from someone and sets it aside in storage, and its owner returns to the bhikṣu to retrieve it, the bhikṣu replies:
'I did not receive your entrustment.'"
Having spoken these words, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; if one causes the owner to doubt, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. The owner says:
"I did not obtain this object."
"A bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
He asked: "What is meant by 'walking without interruption'?"
He replied:

"If a bhikṣu intends to steal an object, and while another person is carrying that object away, he takes the first step, he incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya; with the second step, he incurs the offense of pārājika."
Question: "What is meant by 'departing from its original place'? Answer:

"If a person has placed an object on the ground, and this bhikṣu touches it with a thieving mind, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he moves it, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if he removes it from its original place, he incurs a *pārājika* offense."
Question: "What is meant by 'the essential'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu makes a vow to himself, saying:
'When I reach such-and-such a place or such-and-such a place,
I shall take this object with me,' and upon reaching that place he takes the object while one foot is inside the boundary and one foot is outside the boundary, it is a sthūlātyaya."
If both feet are outside the boundary, it is a *pārājika*.
If one passes goods through a customs checkpoint without paying the tax, or if one has passed the checkpoint with one foot still inside the tax zone, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
"If both feet are entirely outside the boundary of the tax area, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is the instruction for one who discusses miscellaneous items: first, the throwing; second, the ability to take; third, the intention of relinquishment."
Question: "What is meant by 'taking with one's own hand'? Answer:
"To personally steal another's property with one's own hand—this is called 'with one's own hand.'"
"Instruction" means if a bhikṣu instructs another, saying, "Take such-and-such an object," this is called instruction.
"Throwing" means if one, while staying within a customs barrier, throws a heavy object out to the exterior, one incurs a pārājika offense.
Because of these words, it is equivalent to being present at a crucial point.
As for "one who takes," it means instructing a person: "If you are able to take such-and-such an object, then take it; if you cannot obtain it, then desist."
This person then departs according to the instruction; if they steal this object, the instructor who sent them away commits a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding "not relinquishing": if the owner does not relinquish it in their mind, even if it is in an open space, it is still termed "not relinquished. To take this object is called "stealing," and the stealer is a *cūḍa*.
The Dharma Master said:

"In the Dharma, I do not grasp at the literal words but take only their meaning. As for what is called 'stealing,' it means to seize, carry off, lift, step beyond [the threshold], remove from its original place, or make a mutual agreement."
Question: "What is meant by 'seizing'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu seizes another's grove or garden and they dispute over it, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
If this causes the owner of the garden to fall into doubt, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if the owner of the garden reaches a state of certain conviction that he has lost [the property], the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense. He asked:
"What is meant by 'carrying'?

If a bhikṣu carries another's property upon his head with the intent to steal and touches it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he moves it with his hand, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if he lowers it and places it upon his shoulder, he incurs a *pārājika* offense."
Question: "What is meant by 'lifting up'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu receives an entrusted object from someone and sets it aside for storage, and its owner returns to the bhikṣu to reclaim it, the bhikṣu replies:
'I did not receive your entrustment.'"
Having spoken these words, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; if one causes the owner of the object to fall into doubt, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. The owner of the object says:
"I did not receive this object."
"A bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
He asked: "What is meant by 'cutting off the stride'?"
He replied:

"If a bhikṣu intends to steal an object, and as the person carries the object away, at the first step taken he incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya; at the second step, he incurs the offense of pārājika."
Question: "What is meant by 'departing from its original place'? Answer:

"If a person places an object on the ground and this bhikṣu touches it with the intent to steal, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; if he moves it, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*; if he removes it from its original place, he incurs the offense of *pārājika*."
Question: "What is meant by 'the essential'? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu makes a private vow, saying:

'When I reach such-and-such a place, I shall take this object with me,' and upon reaching that place he takes the object while one foot is within the boundary and one foot is outside the boundary, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both feet have gone outside the boundary, it is a *pārājika*. If he carries an object through a customs checkpoint without paying the tax, and while passing the checkpoint one foot is inside the tax area, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both feet have gone outside the tax area, it is a *pārājika*."
The Dharma Master said:
"This is a discussion on miscellaneous items."
*The Vinaya-vibhāṣā of the Samantapāsādikā*, Fascicle Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Qi Dynasty.
"Regarding 'passing through a restricted place,' one clings to various phrases and follows their forms and characteristics; concerning the precept against stealing—"
The intermediate sequential analysis:
"Form according to its location" means according to its respective place.
"Name" refers to following its designation; whether it be a single part, a direct single part, or exceeding a single part—such is what constitutes "name."
Why is this? A single *kṛtsna* coin is divided into four parts; these are manifest impure objects, while the value of one part is a manifest pure object.
"Exceeding one portion" means either exceeding one portion of pure items or exceeding one portion of impure items; this constitutes the second *pārājika* offense of "sufficiency."
Regarding the "lord of the land," there are those who rule over the four continents like a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin);
or those who rule over a single continent like King Aśoka, or like a lion king;
or those who rule over a single region like King Bimbisāra or King Prasenajit.
Those who rule over one side [of a region] are kings of a single territory.
Those in the middle who govern one or two villages are also called kings.

As for those who administer the law, they are those who understand the royal code and, according to the gravity of the offense—whether it be execution, amputation of the nose, or amputation of the hands and feet—may punish even high ministers, crown princes, or kings of border territories; these are what are called kings.
"Killing" means to sever life, or to flog with a whip or staff.
"Banishment" means to expel to another country.
"Thieves" refers to those who steal people's property, whether in small or large amounts; all such persons are called thieves.
"Such is the first offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The subsequent sequential phrases are easy to understand."
Beginning with "seizing," there are six phrases; this explanation is concluded.
Whether it be a portion, or exactly a portion, or more than a portion, one manifests what has been taken.
Question: "If one commits an offense by taking even a single portion, why is it necessary to say that the value of a portion must exceed [one kārṣāpaṇa]? Answer:
"In order to prevent evil bhikṣus in future ages, this extensive commentary is composed.
Regarding 'objects on or in the ground': 'objects in the ground' refers to those buried within the earth; this is the explanation found in the Vinaya-mūla."
The Dharma Master said:
"These phrases are difficult to understand; I now wish to explain them in detail.
'Earth-treasury' (bhūmi-kośa) refers to digging into the ground and covering it over with soil, or with stones, grass, and wood; such is the primary meaning, and this is called an earth-treasury."
If a bhikṣu says,
"I wish to steal buried treasures from the earth," then at the time of departing,
he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for all such preparatory means.
Question: "What is the skillful means? Answer:
When he was about to depart, he put on his robes and traveled some distance until he reached the middle of the road, where he had this thought:
"This object is massive; I cannot carry it alone. I shall now seek a companion."
Such coming and going constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
If he goes to his companion’s place and says:
“There is a treasure trove at such-and-such a place; I shall now take it together with you, Venerable Sir,” [he incurs a *duṣkṛta*].
If he answers "very well" and immediately rises, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
He says:
"In such-and-such a place there is a large jar of precious treasures; let us now steal it together with you, Elder."
"If you obtain [something], let us together cultivate meritorious deeds; for this reason, I and the Elder shall have no lack.
If one acts thus, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) in every case.

Having obtained a companion, he then seeks a sharp hoe. If he has one of his own, he goes to fetch it and uses it; if he does not have a hoe, he goes either to another bhikṣu or to the home of a layperson to borrow one.
The owner asks: "What will you use the hoe for?"
If he replies,
"It was used for a minor purpose," he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one intentionally speaks falsehoods, one must use a hoe to return to the monastery to dig the ground; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, according to the interpretation of another school, this is not so;
in all such cases, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Why is this? Because it is a skillful means for stealing.
The Dharma Master said:
"Therefore, it is well explained that one incurs a *pāyattika* for lying.
If an axe has no handle and one cuts down a dead tree in order to obtain a handle, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if one cuts down a living tree, one incurs the offense of a *pāyattika*."
Furthermore, according to another school's interpretation, cutting down a living tree constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Why is this? Because it serves as a preliminary step toward theft.

If one wishes to borrow a hoe but fears others will know, and thus intends to make one's own hoe to dig the earth—seeking iron, damaging the ground, and killing grass—all constitute a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.
Another interpretation is that all [of these] constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Why? Because they are the preliminary means (*upāya*) for theft.
If there is no basket, one may enter the forest to cut bamboo and rattan to make a basket; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, as previously described.

If one forms the intention that it is for making [a gift], and departs with the thought of using this object to make offerings to the Triple Gem, to provide for a vegetarian feast or a lecture assembly, there is no offense at the time of departure. However, if one acts with a thieving mind, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of departure.
If one wishes to reach a place of storage and further cuts down grass and trees to make a path, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if one cuts down dead wood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This applies even to those [beings] that grow within them.
Question: "What is meant by 'arising therein'? Answer:
"If items have been stored for a long time and plants and trees grow upon them, this is called 'growing in the midst.
If one cuts down these plants and trees, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
“There are eight kinds of *duṣkṛta* offenses.
He asked: “What are these eight?”

"First, the *duṣkṛta* of expedient means; second, the *duṣkṛta* of mutual interaction; third, the *duṣkṛta* of heavy objects; fourth, the *duṣkṛta* of non-money; fifth, the *duṣkṛta* of the Vinaya; sixth, the *duṣkṛta* of knowing; seventh, the *duṣkṛta* of formal motion (*jñapti*); eighth, the *duṣkṛta* of hearing."
Question: "What is meant by 'an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) through expedient means'? Answer:

"Just as a thief seeks companions, knives, axes, or spades according to his means—this is called *upāya-duṣkṛta* (offense through expedient means). If it occurs where a *pāyattika* offense applies, one incurs the *pāyattika* offense; if it occurs where a *duṣkṛta* offense applies, one incurs the *duṣkṛta* offense."

Regarding the *duṣkṛta* of common property: if grass or wood grows upon a treasure storehouse and one cuts it down with a knife or an axe, this is called the *duṣkṛta* of common property; herein, what would be a *pāyattika* or a *duṣkṛta* becomes entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
Why is this? Because it is a deceptive act of theft.

Regarding "things that should not be taken": these include the ten kinds of jewels, the seven kinds of grain, and various weapons. If one takes them, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; these are called "things that should not be taken," and for taking them, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "non-money": this refers to all sweet fruits, such as plantains, coconuts, and so forth; if one takes them, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is called the *duṣkṛta* of non-money.

Regarding the Vinaya: if a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food and dust enters his bowl, yet he accepts food and drink without receiving it again, the one who accepts it commits a duṣkṛta offense; this is called a Vinaya duṣkṛta.
"Knowing a *duṣkṛta* offense" means that after hearing someone announce it, one knows [the offense] but does not confess it; thus one incurs a *duṣkṛta*, which is called "knowing a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "a motion" (*jñapti*): if among the ten types of motions, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* by means of a single motion, this is called "a *duṣkṛta* arising from a motion."
Regarding "hearing": the Buddha said to the bhikṣus, "If one hears [of] that which has not yet been manifested or extinguished, one incurs a duṣkṛta; this is called a 'duṣkṛta of hearing'.
This refers to the duṣkṛta incurred through mutual communication upon hearing.
Why is this? As stated in the Vinaya-mūla: if grass or wood grows upon a treasure trove and one cuts it down, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, while in the act of cutting the grass or wood, one gives rise to a mind of regret and immediately returns to one's original state of mind, although one incurs a *duṣkṛta* due to the act of cutting, one who is able to repent is released from it. However, if one lacks a sense of shame and remorse, and exerts all one's strength to dig up the earth to seek the location of the treasure trove, one likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding "piling on one side": if one piles up dead soil on one side, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

Once the previous *duṣkṛta* has ceased, if one rubs the jewel with the hand but it does not move, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for each instance; the previous *duṣkṛta* for piling the soil ceases, and by shaking it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
The Dharma Master said:
"Regarding *duṣkṛta* and *sthūlātyaya*, what is the meaning of these offenses? *Duṣkṛta*:
‘*Duṣ’* means evil, and ‘*kṛta’* means to do; thus it means an evil deed. It is unwholesome within the conduct of a bhikṣu, and is therefore also called *duṣkṛta*."
A verse from the Vinaya-mūla:
"Listen well to the meaning of the offense of *duṣkṛta*:
it is called a 'transgression,' and it is also termed a 'stumble.'"
"Just as when people in the world commit evil, whether it be concealed or manifest before others, this is called a *duṣkṛta*;
you yourselves should know this. As for a *sthūlātyaya*:

*sthūla* means 'great,' and *atyaya* means 'obstructing the path to goodness and subsequently falling into the evil realms. One confesses this before a single person; among all offenses, this is the greatest."
As in a verse from the Vinaya-mūla:
"Listen attentively to the meaning of what is called a *sthūlātyaya* offense:
one repents before a single person, and the one who accepts the confession is likewise one."
"To repent before a single person constitutes the gravest offense.
If, after having completed the act of agitation, one subsequently gives rise to a mind of remorse, it becomes a *sthūlātyaya*; by confessing, one may be liberated from it."
Question: "Among the ten white *duṣkṛta* offenses, how does one incur a *duṣkṛta*? Answer:
If one does not relinquish [the object] after the announcement (*jñapti*) prior to the formal act (*karman*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one does not relinquish it after the first *jñapti-karman*, or if one does not relinquish it after the initial *karman*, or if one does not relinquish it throughout the course of the *karman*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding "taking it away from its original place": if this bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, moves it to another location even by the distance of a single hair, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If he lifts one side of a jar but has not yet moved it entirely away from its original place, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If one erects three pillars around the jar and suspends it with ropes, and then digs the earth on all four sides as well as the ground beneath, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each action.
If one pulls out one or two pillars, it is likewise a *sthūlātyaya*. If all three pillars are removed and the jar falls to the ground, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one ties a jar with a rope to a tree and then digs up the earth to carry the jar out, there is no offense as long as it remains attached to the rope; however, if the rope is untied and separated from the tree, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one does not untie the rope but cuts the tree down, one likewise incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one plants a tree upon a jar to serve as a marker, and its roots grow and entwine the jar, a bhikṣu who digs up the earth to sever those roots commits a pāyattika and a duṣkṛta offense, as previously explained.
If the roots of the tree are severed and the jar rises with the tree, there is no offense.
If one digs the jar out from the root of the tree and it becomes separated from the tree by even as much as a hair's breadth, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the tree falls and the jar emerges from the dust, moving away from its original location, there is no offense.
Once it has moved from that place, it is a *pārājika*.
If there is a stone atop the jar, and one removes the stone to open the jar, there is no grave offense (*pārājika*), but one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
Regarding the "internal vessel": if the jar is so large that it cannot be moved, and one brings the vessel to take the treasure and obtains even a single portion, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If there are pearl crowns or golden chains within the jar and they are pulled out but have not yet left the jar, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; however, if one cuts off a portion, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one takes a full jar of jewels and grasps them with the hand, such that they have not yet left the place where the hand was, and a single portion of them is ejected between the fingers and falls back into the jar, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if they leave the jar, it is a *pārājika*.
There is a Dharma master who explains: "Once one has taken the treasure from the jar, even if one has not yet emerged from the mouth of the jar, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
The Dharma master said:

"Within the Vinaya, one should follow the most stringent interpretation; if drinking once constitutes a *pārājika*, then obtaining even a single coin’s worth [of liquor] in one drink constitutes a *pārājika*."

Furthermore, there is another interpretation regarding the distinctions between the cases: if there is a large jar so heavy that it cannot be lifted, and one drinks from it by bringing the mouth to its interior, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense as long as the mouth has not left the jar; if the mouth leaves it, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one drinks using a bamboo tube, once it has entered past one part of the neck, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one holds the tube in the mouth to sip, and having filled both the mouth and the tube, lifts them up and blocks one end of the tube with the hand such that they can be separated from the jar, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one throws a garment into a vat and absorbs the clarified butter (sarpis) within it, the offense of *pārājika* is incurred once the garment leaves the hand.

Furthermore, the Dharma Master explains that this is not so: if, after throwing the garment [into the vat], one feels regret but has not yet lifted it out, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; however, if one does not feel regret, one incurs a *pārājika* upon lifting it and removing it from the vat.
If, after having thrown it, the owner realizes it and demands its value, if the monk returns the value he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; if he does not return it, he incurs a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu has an empty jar of his own and an outsider comes and places ghee or oil inside it, and the bhikṣu, out of anger, seizes it and throws it elsewhere, he commits no offense;
however, if he does not act out of anger but seizes and throws it elsewhere with a mind of theft, he incurs a *pārājika*.
If one does not move it elsewhere, but instead drills through the jar or vessel so that even a single portion of ghee or oil leaks out, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one drills a ghee jar and at the time of drilling the ghee is solidified and does not come out, but later, being exposed to the sun's heat, it naturally melts and a portion emerges, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If the hole is large and the ghee or oil emerges like glue, flowing out continuously for more than one part (aṃśa), and having seen this, one gives rise to a mind of regret and takes it back again into the jar, one incurs a sthūlātyaya; if it breaks off at one part outside, it is a pārājika.
If one moves a jar to a place where it might fall over onto wood or stone, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If the owner places an empty jar on a level, stable spot and has not yet given ghee or oil, intending to give it later, and the bhikṣu, knowing this, props the jar with large pieces of wood or stone with the intent to break it; if the owner sees the bhikṣu acting for this purpose and, upon its breaking, demands the full value, whether he returns it or not, the bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu, without the intention to cause a schism, places various corpses or excrement and urine inside a jar, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for the initial act of placing them in the jar; if he has placed them there, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and once they have been placed there, if the owner sees it, rebukes him, and demands the value of the jar, if he does not return it, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one does not have the intention to steal, but out of a mind of hatred breaks it, burns it with fire, douses it with water, or employs various other means to prevent the owner from making a living, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) and should return the value to the owner; if one does not return it, one incurs a *pārājika* (defeat).

If one fills a jar with sand, soil, or stones and pours water into it until it overflows outside, the jar can no longer be used; one must return the value to the owner, and if one does not return it, one incurs the same offense as previously described.
The Dharma Master said:
"The discussion of objects placed underground has now been concluded in detail; the discussion of objects placed above ground shall now be addressed.

Regarding 'objects placed above ground,' this refers to placing them on the ground, or upon a palace, or atop a mountain peak, and so forth. If they are placed in such locations without being concealed, this is called 'placing objects above ground. They may be gathered together or scattered about, and may be contained within vessels."
The Dharma Master said:
"This meaning has already been explained in detail; now it shall be stated in summary.
You should know for yourself by grasping it with your own hand."
Ghee, honey, and curd are no different from flowing water; you should know this for yourself.

Regarding the weight of objects—whether it be a golden chain, a string of pearls, or a long piece of white cotton cloth—if they are moved from their original location by even as much as a hair’s breadth, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This concludes the section on the categories of things belonging to the earth.
Regarding things belonging to space, the peacock is the primary example. Within the peacock, there are six constituent parts; what are these six?
First, the mouth; second, the tail; third, the two wings; fourth, the feet; fifth, the back; sixth, the crest.
If a bhikṣu thinks, "I wish to steal a peacock from mid-air," and as the peacock is about to fly, the bhikṣu stands directly in front of it;

seeing the bhikṣu, the peacock is unable to fly and remains with its wings outspread. The bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, and if he raises his hand and touches it, he also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one shakes a peacock, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; if one seizes and pulls it by the tail so that it is separated from its head, one incurs a *pārājika*.
If one pulls the left wing sideways past the right wing, one incurs a *pārājika*; the same applies to pulling them up or down.

If a peacock descends from the air and alights upon each part of a bhikṣu’s body, and if it is on his right hand, should the bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, move it back to his left hand so that it leaves its original place, he incurs a pārājika offense;
if it flies away of its own accord, he does not commit an offense.
If one carries it away with a thieving mind, at the first step taken, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; when the second step is completed, one incurs a *pārājika*.

If a peacock is on the ground and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's peacock—if he lifts each part of the peacock's body one by one but they have not yet left the ground, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; if he lifts all parts of its body and they are entirely off the ground, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a peacock is in a cage, and one steals it with a thieving mind, taking it away by carrying the cage, one incurs an offense proportionate to the value of the bird.

If the peacock is eating in a garden, and one drives it out past the gate with a thieving mind, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if one seizes the peacock with a thieving mind and throws it outside the garden, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a peacock is within a village and one, with the intent to steal, drives it out of the village boundary, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If the peacock is wandering on its own and reaches either a monastery or an open space, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, strikes the peacock with a staff or hurls stones or wood at it, such that the peacock, in alarm, flies toward the forest, onto a roof, or returns to its original place, no offense has been committed.
If one drives it away with the intent to steal, and it leaves the ground by even the width of a single hair, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
In all such cases, whether the birds are guilty or not, they are no different from the peacock.
"Regarding 'clothing': if clothing is blown upward into the air by a whirlwind, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, seizes each individual piece of clothing, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
If one grasps the robe and moves it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it leaves its original place, it is a *pārājika*.

This robe is no different from a peacock feather; if a robe falls from the sky to the ground and a bhikṣu takes hold of it with his hand, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*, but if it leaves its original place, he commits a grave offense.

Regarding "dropped objects": when people adorn their bodies with precious jewels and those jewels fall without their knowledge, a bhikṣu sees this object from afar as it descends through the air; if he seizes the jewel with the intent to steal and it leaves the ground by even the width of a hair, he commits a pārājika offense.
"If a *kāṣāya* falls, it is no different from what was previously explained.
Having finished the detailed explanation of objects in mid-air:
"If various items are placed upon a bed—some of which may be grasped and some of which may not—the matter is no different from what was explained regarding objects on the ground."
If one takes a bed away by folding it up and moving it from its original location, you should know for yourself that this constitutes an offense.

If a *kāṣāya* robe is hanging on a rack, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes the robe from the rack and moves it from its original location, he incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). It is an offense even if he does not grasp both ends while moving it from its original location; it is also an offense if he shakes it until it reaches both ends. If he folds the rack together and carries it away, he incurs a grave offense.
If a *kāṣāya* robe is tied to a clothes rack and swings against both ends, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; if one unties the knot and takes it away, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu ties the four corners of a *kāṣāya* robe together to serve as a ceiling covering, and with the intent to steal, unties one corner up to three corners, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* in each case; if he unties all four corners, it is a *pārājika*.

If a *kāṣāya* robe is placed on a rack such that one end is on the rack and one end touches the ground—if one end leaves the rack but has not yet left the ground, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one end leaves the ground but has not yet left the rack, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*; if it leaves both the rack and the ground, it is a *pārājika*.

"If a bhikṣu hangs a robe-bag or various miscellaneous items on a hook, and that bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, lifts the bag but has not yet moved it off the hook, he commits a sthūlātyaya; once it is outside the hook, he incurs a pārājika offense."

If a bhikṣu places a robe-bag upon a stake and, with the intent to steal, takes it so that it is separated from the stake but not yet separated from the wall, it is a sthūlātyaya; if it is separated from the wall but not yet separated from the stake, it is also a sthūlātyaya; if it is separated from both the stake and the wall, it is a pārājika.

Furthermore, if one places a robe-bag or various miscellaneous items upon a peg, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, attempts to lift them but they fall onto his shoulder—if he then regrets it and returns them to the peg, it is a sthūlātyaya; if he again gives rise to the intent to steal and carries them away, it is a pārājika.
"If one lifts an object from a stake and is unable to support its weight, it falls to the ground; this is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one takes it up from the ground and carries it away, it is a *pārājika*.
He asked: "What constitutes a 'stake'?"
He replied:
"A one-cubit-long peg driven into a wall, a curved peg, an ivory peg—all such pegs are likewise [prohibited]."
If clothing is on a tree and a bhikṣu takes it with a thieving mind, the gravity of the offense is as explained extensively regarding items on a stake.

If clothing is on a fruit tree and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, shakes the tree to take the clothing, there are three cases: if the clothing has not yet fallen and the bhikṣu sees the fruit and gives rise to a thieving mind, and then shakes the fruit so that it falls, it is a *pārājika* offense of the first degree; if neither the clothing nor the fruit falls, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Having finished hanging up the items:
"As for those kept in water, they are placed within the water; taking fear of authorities as the primary concern.
Regarding items stored in water that do not perish therein, copper vessels are the primary example."
Regarding "places with water," ponds are the primary example.

If an object is placed in stagnant water that does not flow, the object remains stationary; if a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, searches for an object in the water at a shallow depth, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for every step he takes upon departing. If he employs a means [to retrieve it] from a deep place, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense accordingly.
Regarding those who enter the water, the immersion of the head is the initial stage.
If, before reaching the location of the object, one sees a venomous snake, a large fish, a crocodile, or various other predatory beasts, and flees in fear upon seeing them, there is no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"Taking hold of an object is the primary factor; it is no different from what was explained previously, as you yourself should know.
Regarding 'locations,' there are six locations for taking hold of an object: the four sides, plus above and below; these constitute the six locations."
Regarding those in a pond, the lotus flower is the primary example.

If a bhikṣu takes a flower with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to its value; even if the filaments of the lotus root have not yet been severed when he plucks the flower, it is still a pārājika offense.
If one takes lotus roots with the intent to steal by digging up the earth, the gravity of the offense is as previously explained.

If various miscellaneous items are placed upon water, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, makes a plan to pull the objects toward a certain place or another, intending to take them there, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) as long as they have not been pulled out of their place; however, if he lifts them and moves them even a hair’s breadth above the water, it is a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion).
If a bundle of flowers is submerged in water and one, with a thieving mind, unties the bundle, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; once separated from the bundle, it is a *pārājika*.
The six bases and their spheres are as previously explained.

If one plucks a flower with the intent to steal, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) if the root has not been completely severed; it is a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion) if the root is completely severed.

If a pond is dry and waterless, if one digs around the flower and severs its roots, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; once it is moved from its original place, the offense is determined according to the value of the object.

If there are fish in a pond and the fish have an owner, and that pond constitutes their dwelling place, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes them by hook, or by net, or by placing them in a fish-trap: if the fish have not yet entered [the trap], it is a duṣkṛta; if they have entered, it is a sthūlātyaya; if he lifts the fish out of the water, it is a pārājika.

If a fish leaps out of the net onto the shore, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one takes it from the shore and moves it to another location, one incurs an offense according to the value of the fish. The same applies to turtles and tortoises.

If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, wishes to take fish from a large pond but cannot catch them, he digs a small pond and leads the fish into it. If the fish enter the small pond, it is a duṣkṛta offense. If he takes the fish from the small pond but cannot catch them and they return to the large pond, it is a sthūlātyaya offense. If the fish have not yet reached the small pond, it is also a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one takes [fish] from a stream or a small pond by removing them from their place, one incurs an offense according to the value of the fish.

If the water in a pond has dried up almost entirely and the fish have gathered together in one spot, and another person gives medicine causing the fish to die, a bhikṣu who does not know this may take them as *pāmsukūla* (refuse) without offense;
however, if he knows they have an owner and takes them with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to the value of the fish.
If the owner of the fish demands payment, it must be returned; failure to do so constitutes an offense.
If the owner has taken the fish and no longer possesses the intention to guard it, yet a bhikṣu takes it with a thieving mind, it is a sthūlātyaya.
The Dharma Master said:
"The gravity of this offense is as previously explained; you should know it for yourself.
This concludes the section on Water.
"Regarding 'boats': generally, anything used for crossing a river, even a rope, is called a boat if it can carry objects.

Whether there are people or no people on board, or whatever miscellaneous items are present, it is as previously explained. If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, intends to steal a boat by capsizing it, he thinks to himself:
'I wish to take this boat, but I have no companion; I shall now seek a companion and go.'"
"Grasping and shaking [the organ] is as previously described.

Regarding 'untying the cord': if one unties the cord, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) while the cord has not yet left its place; once the cord leaves its place, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or a *pārājika* (offense involving defeat)."
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain this in detail.
If a boat is moored in swift water and the rope is cut, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense as long as the boat has not left its place; once the boat has left its place, it is a *pārājika* offense."
If [the boat] is not in flowing water, one commits a *pārājika* offense when first leaving its place and subsequently severing the rope; if the rope is severed, it is a *pārājika*.
If the boat is on land, one commits a *pārājika* offense upon leaving its place.

If one uses two pieces of wood to support a boat, taking away one piece with a thieving mind constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; taking away both pieces so that the boat touches the ground constitutes a *pārājika*.

If the boat is on land, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, uses a long rope and a windlass to pull it to another location, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; once it has left its original place and the rope is released, it is a *pārājika*.

If a boat is floating on the water unmoored, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, boards it intending to go east but is blown west by the wind, he commits a sthūlātyaya; if he gives rise to the intent to steal and takes [the boat] wherever it goes, he commits a pārājika offense.
If the mind of regret is blown by the wind and [the goods] return to their original place, the owner must demand their return; if they are not returned to the owner, it is a *pārājika*.
The "Chapter on Boats" is concluded.
"Regarding 'vehicles,' the chariot is the primary example.
As previously explained, the chariot may contain various items, both animate and inanimate.

If a chariot contains grain and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes some using a vessel or bowl, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense as long as the vessel has not left its place; once the vessel has left its place, it is a *pārājika* offense."

If the carriage is too heavy to pull and one seeks an ox to pull it: at the initial search for the ox, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; upon obtaining the ox and pulling the carriage, when the ox lifts one leg, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; when the ox lifts all four legs, there is a *pārājika* offense.
If one intends to go south, yet the ox moves toward the east or west, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it returns to the original path, it is a *pārājika*.
If a cart is suspended on a wall, taking it with the intent to steal constitutes an offense;
there is no offense if it is like taking a suspended bowl-bag, as they are not different.
The Chapter on Mounting is finished.
Regarding "one who carries objects," it means carrying them upon one's head.
The Dharma Master said:
"I wish to explain this meaning.
'Head' refers to the area from behind the throat up to the hairline; this is called the head.
Whatever miscellaneous objects are placed upon it are all termed 'worn on the head.'"
From the throat and hairline downward, it is called the shoulder.

If [the object] is below the armpit and above the abdomen, this is termed *dhāraṇa-avahāra* (carrying and holding), which is a *duṣkṛta* offense; the rest is as previously explained regarding the receiving of entrusted items or carrying objects on the head.
"The same applies to the areas of the other shoulders and the abdomen; the meaning of these sequential phrases is easy to understand.
[The section on] "Items Worn" is concluded.

"Gardens" refers to flower gardens, fruit orchards, or places where various fragrant herbs grow. If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, digs them up to take them, he incurs an offense according to the value of the items.

If one steals the bark from a tree in a grove with the intent to take it, the offense is determined according to its value; the same applies to flowers and fruits. If there is a dispute over a grove or forest:

if a bhikṣu forcibly disputes and seizes another's grove or forest, at the initial moment of wishing to dispute it, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if he causes the owner to fall into doubt, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the owner forms the intention to relinquish [the property], the bhikṣu commits a *pārājika*.
If the owner of the garden has not yet formed the intention to relinquish it, and a bhikṣu takes the garden, forming the conviction that he has definitely obtained it, he commits a pārājika offense.
If it is said that the official won the dispute over the garden by means of bribery, and the owner of the garden forms the conviction that he has lost it, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If, during a formal judgment within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha knowingly renders a decision contrary to principle, the presiding judge incurs a pārājika offense.
If the Saṃgha deliberates and renders a decision in accordance with principle, yet the disputants do not comply, they incur a sthūlātyaya offense.
The Chapter on Gardens concludes.
Regarding "in the monastery": if various miscellaneous items are placed within the monastery, there are four ways of handling such items, as previously explained.

If a dwelling is offered to the Sangha of the four directions, whether large or small, and a bhikṣu should desire to dispute its possession, such a dispute is invalid; because it has no single owner, he does not incur a grave offense.

If a donor gives [a dwelling] to a group or even to a single individual, and one takes this room with a thieving mind, such that the owner feels it has been lost and the thief forms the conviction that he has definitely obtained it, whether an offense is committed or not is as previously explained.
The brief explanation of the Chapter on Monasteries is concluded.
Regarding "the field," there are two kinds of fields. What are these two?
"The first is the field of *pudgala*, and the second is the field of *araṇya*.
He asked:
"What is meant by the field of *pudgala*?"
“There are seven kinds of grain, with non-glutinous rice as the first.
“What is meant by an *āpa-araṇya* field?

“Starting with beans and extending to sugarcane—if a bhikṣu takes grain from such a field with a thieving mind, once the amount reaches one portion (*māṣaka*), he commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).”

If the grain has not yet been harvested, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, seeks out sickles, seeks out carrying-poles, or seeks out baskets—employing various such expedients—he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he seizes it with his hand, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If he cuts and harvests it while it remains connected to other living stalks and has not yet left its original place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If it becomes detached and separated, the offense is determined according to the value of the goods.

If one takes rice with the intent to steal it for the purpose of making rice, the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one reaps the rice, threshes it, or husks it, for each such act, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If the rice is completed and placed within a vessel, moving it off the ground constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
