If a bhikṣu disputes a field with another as previously described, or if a bhikṣu steals another’s field—even if it is only as large as a single hair—with a resolute intent to steal, he incurs a pārājika offense.
Why is this? Because the ground is deep and there is no one to purchase it.
If a bhikṣu comes and asks the Saṃgha to take possession of this land, and the monks give their assent, they all incur a grave offense.
If there are two markers, if a bhikṣu moves one marker he incurs a sthūlātyaya; if he moves both markers, it is a pārājika.
If the ground has three markers, if he moves one marker it is a duṣkṛta; if he moves two markers it is a sthūlātyaya; if he moves all three markers, he incurs a pārājika.

If a plot of ground has many markers, lifting one marker constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; likewise, lifting up to two markers also constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. For the remaining two markers, lifting one constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, and lifting two constitutes a *pārājika*.

If one takes another's land with the intent to steal by marking it with a cord, when the first cord is placed at one end, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; when the cord is placed at both ends, it is a *pārājika*.
If one writes names upon the ground, writing them at one end constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, while writing them at both ends constitutes a *pārājika*.
If, with a thieving mind, one proclaims:
"This field is mine," and the owner of the field hears this and conceives a state of doubt;

"If I fear losing my field," [thinking thus], that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense; if the owner of the field forms the certain thought that he has lost it, [the bhikṣu] incurs a pārājika offense.
The Chapter on Fields is concluded.

Regarding "land," this refers to residential land and garden land—whether with trees or without trees, with fences or without fences—as described in the Chapter on Flower Gardens and likewise as described in the Chapter on Fields.
The brief explanation of the Chapter on Grounds is finished.
Regarding "villages," they have already been explained in detail within the Vinaya.
As for "araṇya" (wilderness), it refers to land that has an owner.
The Dharma Master asked:
"There are also those without an owner; how do you distinguish between those with an owner and those without?
He replied:
"If grasses and trees are in a grove and one may not take them straightway, these are called 'having an owner.
If grasses and trees are in a grove and one may cut them down at will without anyone rebuking or questioning one, these are called 'having no owner.'"
If a bhikṣu takes property belonging to a master in an araṇya, he incurs an offense according to its value.
If he discards unusable items at an araṇya site that belongs to a master, there is no offense for one who takes them.

If there is a forest hermitage belonging to an owner, where wooden pillars and various miscellaneous items have remained uncollected for a long time, and a bhikṣu takes and uses them, and later the owner comes and requests their return, the one who took them incurs no offense.
If a bhikṣu, carrying payment, goes to a forest hermitage that has an owner and says to the forest guardian:
"Allow me to take some timber for now; once I have finished taking it, I shall return the payment to you."
If the forest guardian replies, "If that is so,
take as you wish," and the bhikṣu then sends someone into the forest to take it as desired, there is no offense for those who take it.
If the owner of the grove says to the forest guardian,
"If there is a bhikṣu who takes [fruit],
you must not take payment from him," yet the forest guardian demands payment, the bhikṣu should give it.

If the forest guardian is asleep and does not notice, or is away elsewhere, and the bhikṣu enters the grove and takes wood, and the guardian returns later and sees him, he may demand payment; the bhikṣu should give it to him.

If a bhikṣu enters a forest to gather wood and is pursued by bandits or tigers, such that he is terrified and unable to return the value immediately, he must later return the value. If he does not return it, he incurs an offense according to the amount of the goods.

If a bhikṣu enters a forest and, without asking the forest guardian, takes another's property with a thieving mind, if he crosses the boundary, he incurs an offense according to the value of the object.
The Chapter on Aranyas is concluded.

Regarding water: when it is kept in vessels, and during a time of water shortage, if each household has placed water in large jars, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, drills into a vessel—even if he only drills slightly or makes a tiny hole—he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he drills but does not penetrate through, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Once he has penetrated through and obtained the water, the offense is determined according to the value of the water.
If the vessel is small, the bhikṣu takes by tilting the vessel; the offense is determined according to the value of the goods.
If the mouth of the vessel is large, and he takes by inserting a small vessel inside it, it is as previously explained regarding the theft of oil.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, digs into the earth or diverts the water of another's pond, and the water flows out by even one part, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣu, by means of a stratagem and with a thieving mind, digs at the edge of another’s pond until he is almost through and then stops, intending that the pond be broken at this spot—whether by a child breaking it or by an ox treading it—and if water consequently flows out from this spot, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.

If there is a large tree in a pond and a bhikṣu, for the sake of seeking water, cuts down the tree so that it falls into the pond, causing waves to rise and the bank to collapse and form a hole through which the water flows out, he incurs an offense according to the value of the amount [of water lost].

If a bhikṣu has two ponds, one containing water and the other devoid of water, situated on opposite sides of each other, and the pond with water is abundant, the bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, digs a channel from the side of the pond that has water so as to connect it to the other pond, causing the water to overflow and flow into his own waterless pond; if he thereby damages the water of the other pond, he incurs an offense according to the value of the loss.

If a bhikṣu’s field is adjacent to another’s land that lacks a water reservoir, and he, with a contrived intention, digs a pond to connect it to his field so that rainwater flows from the pond into the field, and the owner of the pond comes to demand payment for the water, the bhikṣu should repay him; if he does not repay it, he incurs an offense according to the amount of the value.

If several households share a single pond and divert its water to irrigate their fields, and a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, cuts off another's water to cause it to flow into his own field: if the grain has not yet died, it is a sthūlātyaya; if the grain dies, the offense is determined according to the value of the loss.
The section on water concludes.
Regarding "willow branches," it is as previously explained in the section on the garden.
The Dharma Master said:

"If the Sangha has hired someone to fetch willow twigs and they have not yet been returned to the Sangha, such that the twigs still remain in a certain place and still belong to the employer, if a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, goes ahead and selects and takes them, he incurs an offense according to their value."

If the Saṃgha hires someone to manage and distribute goods, and a bhikṣu, without first informing the Saṃgha, takes them with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to the quantity of the goods.

If the Saṃgha appoints a śrāmaṇera to collect willow twigs for the Saṃgha on the fifteenth day, and the śrāmaṇera selects the best ones to give to his preceptor before the monks have had a chance to receive their share, and the bhikṣu selects and takes some with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to the quantity.
"If tooth-sticks are already in a place where they are commonly used by the Saṃgha, there is no offense for one who takes them.
You should know this method for taking tooth-sticks. He asked:
"How can this be known? He replied:

"If the Sangha takes three *śīrṣa-prasādaka* (teeth-cleansing twigs) daily, you may likewise take three with them; if you enter a meditation hall or attend a lecture, you should take five or six; if they are exhausted, it is also permissible to take more."
Why not take many at once, but instead take five or six?
It is because one would be subject to the criticism and suspicion of others.
The Chapter on Tooth-sticks concludes.

"Regarding trees: if it be a Jambu tree, a mango tree, or a pepper vine, and with a thieving mind one cuts the tree or the vine with a knife—if the tree is cut but the bark remains connected, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it is severed, it is a *pārājika*. If the vine is severed but still remains attached to the tree, it is a *pārājika*."

If, with the intent to steal, one cuts a tree more than halfway and leaves it there, and the tree breaks as a result, one must calculate the value of the damage and repay it; failure to do so constitutes an offense.
If one kills a tree by piercing it with a poisonous bone, it is also the same.
This concludes the Chapter on Trees.

Regarding successive theft: if a person steals an object and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, seizes it away from that person, and the object leaves the person's possession—if that person is strong and wrests the object back from the bhikṣu—the bhikṣu, although he does not retain the object, still incurs the offense of pārājika.
Why is this? Because the thief’s intent has been definitively established and the object has been moved from its original location.

If the owner of the object does not relinquish it and a bhikṣu forcibly drags it away, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense when the object has not yet left his hand; once it leaves the hand, he commits a grave offense (pārājika).

If, with the intent to steal, one removes a person's bracelet or ring from their hand, it is a *pārājika* offense once it has left the hand; if it remains in the hand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The same applies to the foot.

If one steals and strips another's garment: at the initial grasping of the garment, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); when pulling the garment and moving it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);
once it is separated from the body, it is a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion). If the garment is pulled and severed, the offense is determined according to its value.

If, with the intent to steal, one steals a person along with the clothing on their body and carries them away: if one first lifts one foot, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both feet are lifted, it is a *pārājika*.

If, with the intent to steal, one again steals a person and their clothing: if the person runs away, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if the person throws the clothing onto the ground and the bhikṣu seizes it with his hand, it is also a *duṣkṛta*; if he moves the clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it is removed from its original place, it is a *pārājika*.
If, with the intent to steal, one steals a person’s body or clothing, and the person runs away and cannot be caught, the bhikṣu says:
“Take off your clothes, cast them on the ground, and leave your body.
If the person first loosens the clothes with their hand, it is a duṣkṛta; when the clothes are loosened, it is a sthūlātyaya; when the clothes are separated from the body, it is a pārājika.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, steals a person and their clothing; the person runs away and takes off the clothing, placing it on the ground; yet the bhikṣu continues to pursue the person without letting go, and though he does not catch up, he turns back, takes the clothing, and moves it off the ground—this constitutes a pārājika offense.

If a person steals with a thieving mind and, fleeing in terror through the wilderness, casts off their clothes and leaves them behind, and a bhikṣu pursues them without ceasing but returns without catching the person, seeing the clothes lying on the ground, the bhikṣu says:
"This person cast off these clothes; I shall pick them up, and there is no offense."
If the thief does not succeed, it is a duṣkṛta offense. If the person turns their head and speaks from afar to the bhikṣu, saying,
"Do not take my robe," yet the bhikṣu takes the robe and it leaves the ground, it is a pārājika offense.
If a person casts away a robe while running with an attitude of indifference, and a bhikṣu pursues them but fails to catch them and returns, seeing the robe on the ground, he says:
"This robe was obtained by my own effort."
If one picks it up immediately, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, another teacher explains that it is not a *duṣkṛta*. Why is this?
Because the owner of the robe has abandoned it with a mind of relinquishment, the section on theft is concluded.
Regarding "receiving an entrustment": if a person leaves an item with a bhikṣu and the owner comes to seek it, the bhikṣu says:
"I did not accept your deposit.
This false speech would normally constitute a *pāyattika* offense; however, because it is a preliminary step toward theft, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"If this person entrusted me with an object and no one else knows of it, shall I now return it or not?"—if [the monk] acts thus, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the monk gains possession of the object with a settled mind while the owner has lost their claim to it, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu says:

"I shall trouble him; if he insists on disputing [the matter], I will return the robe, but if he does not dispute it, I shall take it," and the owner gives the robe to the bhikṣu with a distracted mind, then whoever takes this robe commits a pārājika offense.

If one receives an entrusted object and the owner comes to request it back, yet returns it only in words while the mind is determined not to give it back, and the owner conceives a state of doubt, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.

If one receives a deposit and, with a thieving mind, moves the object to another place, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If one exchanges the object for food and consumes it all, it is still a *dukkaṭa* when the owner comes and asks about it. If the owner returns to inquire and one does not restore the object, it is a *pārājika* offense. However, if the object was borrowed for temporary use, there is no offense.

"If he sees another's bowl is of superior quality, and [the rule] requires that all bowls be given to the place of the Elder, he takes it with a thieving mind; having taken it, he gives his coarse bowl to the place of the Elder, desiring to exchange it for the other's fine bowl. Using skillful means to entice that bhikṣu so as to cause him to lose sleep through the night, he rises secretly and goes to the place of the Elder, saying:
'I wish to travel far.'"
He takes another's bowl and describes its characteristics, saying:
"My bowl and its bag have such marks and such a shape.
When the Elder gives him the bowl and the bowl leaves its original place, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If the Elder has already finished taking the bowl and intends to hand it over to a thief-monk, and the Elder says,
"Who are you that takes the bowl at an improper time?
and the thief-monk, hearing the Elder's words, flees in terror, he also incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the Elder takes the bowl with a benevolent mind, there is no offense;
however, if the Elder forms the thought, "This bhikṣu has already fled;
I shall take it as a theft," this also constitutes a pārājika offense.

If, in the darkness of night, the Elder mistakenly takes his own bowl and gives it to the thief-monk, the thief-monk incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if the Elder mistakenly takes the thief-monk’s bowl and returns it to the thief-monk, the thief-monk incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, while the Elder is without fault.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, paid homage to an elder and said:
"I am a sick bhikṣu; please bring me my bowl.
The elder said:
"If there is no sick monk in this room, you must be a thief.

Furthermore, if the Elder previously had a dispute with a fellow resident monk, and with a thieving intent takes that disputing monk's bowl and gives it to the thief-monk, both the Elder and the thieving monk incur a *pārājika* offense.

If the Elder, with a mind of theft, takes the bowl of a monk who is disputing [with another], but fails to obtain that disputing monk's bowl and instead obtains the bowl of a thief-monk, and gives it to the thief-monk, the Elder incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If the Elder, with a mind of theft, takes the bowl of a monk with whom he is disputing, but fails to obtain that disputing monk’s bowl, and the Elder instead returns his own bowl to the thief-monk, both the Elder and the thief-monk incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"If an elder monk takes an object and hands it to a junior monk, saying,
'I will take you to such-and-such a place,' and the junior bhikṣu,

harboring a thieving intent, takes the object and follows the elder to the destination, but then silently lets go of it while the elder runs off with the object— the junior incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) at the first step and a *pārājika* (offense involving expulsion) at the second step."
If an elder monk takes a junior bhikṣu by the hand while entering a village for alms, and the junior bhikṣu conceives a thieving intent, thinking:
"I shall take hold of him and follow the elder into the village."
He thinks to himself:
"I shall go to the village.

Before reaching the village, with every step he takes, there is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). When one foot is outside the boundary and one foot is inside the boundary, there is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). When both feet have entered the boundary, it is a *pārājika* (offense involving defeat).
If one sets out from a village with the intent to steal, the offense is likewise incurred.
"If a senior monk instructs a junior bhikṣu:
'Take this robe to that village to wash and dye it.'"
If a young bhikṣu conceives a thieving mind and takes away an object, at every step he turns back, the offense is a duṣkṛta; if he passes the designated place, it is a pārājika.
If one goes to a village and exchanges the robe for food or sells it, no grave offense has been committed.
Upon returning, if the owner of the robe asks, "Where is the robe?
[one must answer truthfully].
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have already exchanged it and consumed the food.
The owner demanded that the value of the robe be returned, adding that if it were not returned, he would commit a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, forcibly causes a senior elder (upādhyāya) to wash his robe, and if the elder hands the robe to the bhikṣu who intends to steal it, once the robe leaves the elder’s hand, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu steals with the thought,
"I will take this object once I have brought it to the village," the offense is likewise incurred.
If an elder monk’s robe was soiled and he, by displaying the robe, intended for someone to wash it, and a junior bhikṣu asked with a thieving mind, the elder said:
"I wish to wash this robe."
The youth asked,
"Where did you wash it?
The Elder replied:
"Let it be washed wherever the Elder goes.

If a junior monk follows him to such a place, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he uses the item, he commits a *sthūlātyaya*; if the senior monk seeks the robe and it is not returned, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
"If an elder monk has entrusted a cotton cloth to a donor, and a junior bhikṣu, with a thieving intent, goes to the elder's donor's house under false pretenses and deceives them by saying:
'The elder instructed me to come and take this cloth.'"
If he entrusts it to the husband, entrusts it to the wife, or entrusts it to the husband through the wife, as soon as the cotton enters the bhikṣu’s hand, for each instance, it is a pārājika offense.
If a donor says to the Elder,
"I wish to invite the Elder for a meal and also offer a piece of white cotton cloth," and a junior bhikṣu becomes aware of this,
he goes to the donor's house and says to the donor:
"The Elder instructed me to come and first request the cotton cloth; we shall receive it on the day the meal is served.

The donor then gave the cotton cloth to him. Later, when the Elder learned of this, he demanded the cotton cloth back from the junior monk; if the junior monk does not return the cotton cloth, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If a donor invites two bhikṣus for the summer retreat and, at its conclusion, offers two pieces of white cotton cloth—one coarse and one fine—but does not give them in their presence; later, the elder bhikṣu sends a junior bhikṣu to the donor’s residence to request the cloths, and the donor hands the cloths to the junior bhikṣu, saying:
"Give the fine one to the elder, and the coarse one to the junior."
The youth took the cotton cloth, placed it in one spot, and when the elder asked,
"Which one did you give me?
the youth replied with a thieving mind:
"If the Elder takes the coarse one, it is that.
If the Elder takes the coarse cotton cloth, the junior bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya; if the junior takes the fine cotton cloth and removes it from its original place, it is a pārājika.

If a young bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, writes characters on a cotton cloth—using small characters to create his own name—and later an elder takes the cloth based on that name, the young bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense, while the one who takes the cloth incurs a pārājika offense.
"If a visiting bhikṣu enters a monastery and sees a resident bhikṣu making a kāṣāya, the visiting bhikṣu thinks to himself:
'Because this resident bhikṣu is so skilled, he ought to look after this bowl for me.'"
He remained silent and departed.
Subsequently, this bowl was lost; the visiting bhikṣu may not be held accountable for the bowl. Why is this?
Because it was not entrusted.

If it had been entrusted, the resident bhikṣu would not have understood the guest bhikṣu’s words; yet the guest bhikṣu would have thought that the resident bhikṣu had already accepted the entrustment. Consequently, if this bowl were subsequently lost, the guest bhikṣu could not be held accountable.
Why is this? Because they do not understand the language.
If the bowl is entrusted to them, the resident bhikṣus reply:
"Excellent! If he later loses the bowl, he should be held liable for its value. Why is this?
This is for the sake of entrustment.

If the monk in charge of the bowl-store enters or exits the bowls of the various monks and forgets to close the door, he shall compensate for the loss of those monks' bowls; however, if someone breaks through the wall to steal them, he shall not be held liable for compensation.
If the bhikṣus say to the bhikṣu in charge of the bowls:
"Venerable one!
Take the bowls out and place them outside at dawn; we shall send someone to guard them."
If the person guarding [the storehouse] falls asleep and loses the bowl, the monk in charge of the bowls need not reimburse it.

If the monk in charge of the bowls has had the bowls entrusted to other monks, yet out of laziness fails to open the storehouse and instead places the bowls in his own private room, and they are lost, he must reimburse them. If the monk in charge of the bowl-storehouse opens the door to the storehouse but, before being able to close it, suddenly falls ill and does not entrust them to someone else in succession, and the bowls are lost, he need not reimburse them.
If a bhikṣu in charge of the storehouse falls asleep after closing it, and a thief comes and calls for him to open the door, and the bhikṣu does not open it, the thief says:
"If I cannot get the door opened, I will kill you."
The bhikṣu still did not open it; the thief then struck the door with an axe, and the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If I do not open it, I will die again and lose my bowl once more."
Thereupon, he opened the door, and the thief took all the bowls and departed; the bhikṣu could not be held accountable.

However, if the bhikṣu in charge of the bowl-store gives the key to a visiting bhikṣu, and that visiting bhikṣu subsequently opens the store and steals the bowls and takes them away, the bhikṣu in charge of the store must compensate for the bowls.
If the Elder says to the monk in charge of the bowl-store:

"I wish to entrust my bowl to you; Store-master and Elder, look after the bowl together," and if the door is opened and not closed resulting in the loss of the bowl, the two shall compensate for it together.
If an elder brings someone into the storehouse, the bhikṣu in charge of the bowl-storehouse says:
"Do not bring people in.
The elder says:
"There is no cause for distress.
If a bowl is lost, the senior monk (upādhyāya) shall compensate for it himself.

If it is known that the monk in charge of the Sangha's storehouse was present when the community held a great assembly and various items were being issued or returned, and yet no one was supervising such that something was lost, the monk in charge of the storehouse shall not compensate for it.
If external offerings enter, the *bhikṣu* in charge of the storehouse may receive two shares.

If a *dhūta* *bhikṣu*, although residing within the monastery, does not dwell in a communal monk’s cell, does not eat the food of the assembly of donors, and has built a cell for himself, the Sangha shall not appoint him as a *karmadāna* or assign him administrative duties.

If a bhikṣu, through recitation, instruction, or preaching the Dharma, is able to obtain offerings and benefit the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha shall not appoint him to administrative duties involving the monastery. However, he shall be provided with a dwelling, robes, and a bowl; among these, the best quality items should be given to him first. Furthermore, regarding food, drink, fruits, and wood, he shall be granted an additional portion.

If a bhikṣu makes use of the Sangha’s lodgings, robes, or alms bowls, and through negligence or carelessness causes these monastic items to be lost or damaged, he must compensate for them all. If appointed to oversee the requisites for the Buddha's offerings, he may not decline; whatever is lost must be fully compensated.

"Regarding 'one who evades official taxes': if one who ought to pay taxes does not pay them, thereby stealing and passing over the official tax—if they are caught for the first time, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if they conceal it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if they do not pay the tax and pass beyond the point where the official tax is collected, it is a *pārājika*."

If one throws an object outside the tax zone with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika* offense; if it falls inside the tax zone, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one throws an object outside the tax zone and it subsequently rolls back into the tax zone, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, the Dharma Master says that this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

If there is a large wooden bridge where one end is within a tax district and the other end is outside a tax district, if one with the intent to steal carries goods across the wood, it is a *sthūlātyaya* before the goods have crossed the wood; once they have crossed the wood, it is a *pārājika*.

If two people are traveling together with goods subject to taxation, and one person goes outside the tax boundary while the other remains inside the tax boundary, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if both go entirely outside the tax boundary, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu leads oxen or horses laden with goods past a customs checkpoint and says to the tax collector,

"Take whatever assessment you deem appropriate as tax," and the tax collector forgets [to collect it] such that the oxen subsequently pass out of the customs boundary, the bhikṣu does not commit an offense.
Why is this? Because he has already informed the tax collector.

If a bhikṣu brings [goods] to a place where taxes are levied, and one person desires to tax them while another says to leave them as they are, the bhikṣu passes through without paying; he does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu arrives at a customs office with goods intending to pay duty, and the tax collector says,
"It is a small amount; you need not pay duty," and the bhikṣu passes the goods through, he is without offense.

If a bhikṣu takes goods to the place where a tax collector is located, and the tax collector is engaged in gambling, and the bhikṣu calls out three times without receiving a response and then departs, leaving the goods behind, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu takes goods to a customs station and suddenly encounters the calamities of water, fire, or bandits, and they all flee in panic toward the four directions without paying the tax, it is not an offense for the bhikṣu to abandon them and depart.

Regarding the tax boundary: it is likewise the area reached by the range of a thrown stone; if a bhikṣu carries goods without reaching the tax boundary, one who passes through it does not commit an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
“I wish to demonstrate that there is no offense for one who steals in this manner.”
"How is it that there is no offense? He replied,
"Because there is no owner, there is no offense."
If a person's son has fallen from the path, and his parents dismiss him by pouring water over his head, or if his parents have died, there is no offense for a bhikṣu who takes such a person.
If one owes a debt to another, there is no offense for a bhikṣu to take [the slave] away.
[Slaves are] those born in the household, or those acquired by purchase, or those acquired by conquest.
What is meant by "born in the household"?
"Born as slaves in the household.
How were they acquired? They were acquired by purchasing them with goods."
How is it acquired through plunder?
It is acquired by plundering through the raising of an army.

As stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If one steals from such a person, one incurs an offense. Initially, from the moment of seizing [the object], it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one lifts it up, holding one foot off the ground, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both feet are off the ground, it is a *pārājika*."

If one drives someone away out of fear, it is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) for the initial preparatory act; if one has raised one foot [to depart], it is a serious offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if both feet have been raised, it is a *pārājika*.
If another person is a slave, and a bhikṣu says to them:
"You suffer here; why do you not run away? [it is likewise an offense].
"If I go to another place, I may find what is pleasing.
Once the slave has heard the bhikṣu’s words, the initial thought to depart constitutes a duṣkṛta; if he lifts one foot, it is a sthūlātyaya; if he lifts both feet, it is a pārājika.
If a slave rebels and many bhikṣus instruct him on the way, urging him to flee quickly, the bhikṣus who follow these instructions incur a grave offense.
If a slave is sent running away and a bhikṣu says to him,
"If you run in this manner, you will escape."
The bhikṣu is without offense.
If the slave departs slowly and calmly, and the bhikṣu says to him:
"If you walk so leisurely, your master will surely catch you."
Upon hearing the bhikṣu’s words, the slave immediately fled quickly, and the bhikṣu committed a grave offense.
If the slave had already fled to another country, the bhikṣu said to him:
"You should go elsewhere; your master is searching for you."
Upon hearing the bhikṣu’s words, the slave immediately fled; the bhikṣu committed a grave offense.
If a bhikṣu says: "It is difficult and arduous here, but that place is extremely pleasant," [and the slave flees, the bhikṣu commits a grave offense].
Upon hearing the bhikṣu’s words, the slave immediately fled; since the bhikṣu did not instruct him to leave, he was without fault.
There was another bhikṣu who spoke thus:
"A certain region is extremely pleasant, and along the way there is abundant food and drink everywhere; who would not wish to go there?"
Upon hearing these words, the slave followed the bhikṣu of his own accord; if the bhikṣu then employed this person as a servant, he incurs no offense.
If they encounter the perils of tigers, wolves, or bandits halfway along the road, and the bhikṣu calls out for him to flee, he likewise incurs no offense.
The section on stealing human beings is concluded.
Regarding "footless creatures," this refers to snakes and vipers.

As for those with owners, people of the world have already employed snakes as a form of entertainment; if someone watches them and gives one coin, or even half a coin, and this person places the snake down to sleep while a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, carries it away, the offense is determined according to the value of the object.
If a snake is inside a box and a bhikṣu, with a thieving intent, feeds it a frog or pulls it out by hand, he incurs an offense according to the value of the object.
The Chapter on Footless Beings is concluded.
Regarding "two-footed beings," those such as ghosts (piśāca) are the first; among them, only ghosts are not to be stolen from.
There are three kinds of birds: first, those with feathered wings; second, those with leathery wings; and third, those with bony wings.
Those with feathered wings have the peacock and the chicken as their primary examples.
Those with leathery wings have the bat as their primary example.
Those with bony wings have the bee as their primary example.
If a bhikṣu steals with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to the value of the object, whether it be small or large, as previously explained without difference.
"Four-footed creatures" refers to all animals, with the elephant being the foremost.
If, with the intent to steal, one who possesses great strength is able to lift an elephant off the ground, it is a *pārājika*.

If the elephant is in a stable—whether tied by the belly, the neck, or all four feet—if the bonds are loosened and it is moved from its original place; or if it is not tied and is driven outside the building; or if it is already outside and driven out through the gate; or if it is in a village and driven beyond the boundary of the village; or if it is in an *āraṇya* (hermitage) and driven away from the place where its four feet were; or if it was sleeping and is driven up: in each case of moving it from its location, it is a *pārājika*.
The same applies to all four-footed animals, such as oxen, horses, donkeys, mules, and camels.
If they are half inside a pen, the pen constitutes the boundary; they are to be released from their bonds and driven out as previously described.
If one lures it away with grass, the offense is incurred as soon as it leaves its place.
If one calls the ox by name and it understands the speech and departs accordingly, the offense is incurred just as before.
If the ox is killed while sleeping on the ground, the owner shall demand compensation; the value must be returned, and if it is not returned, a grave offense (pārājika) is committed.
The Chapter on Quadrupeds is concluded.

Regarding "many-footed sentient beings," such as centipedes, millipedes, and earthworms: if one lifts ninety-nine feet at once, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one lifts the final foot, the offense is determined according to the value [of the theft].
The Chapter on Many-Footed Creatures is finished.

"If, for the sake of a thief, one goes to another's house to observe the location of goods or where the fences and walls have been breached, and returns to inform the thief; and the thief, having heard what the bhikṣu says, goes according to the information to take the items; then, as each item leaves its place, all the bhikṣus are guilty of an offense—even if many bhikṣus sent a single bhikṣu to go."
If one instructs a bhikṣu to inspect the location of an object, and another bhikṣu says,
"There is no need to send him away; I will go to inspect it myself," the bhikṣu who gave the instruction commits an offense, while the one who was instructed is without offense.

A group of many bhikṣus forcibly took a certain bhikṣu with them to steal goods; they then drove this bhikṣu to guard the items while his companions went off to search for more. While guarding the goods, this bhikṣu gave rise to a thieving mind and stole whatever was best among the items to carry away. The offense is determined according to the value of the stolen property.
Regarding "a multitude of bhikṣus": a multitude of bhikṣus make this statement, "Let us go together to such-and-such a village or place and steal together.
All the companions go along with them; when one person enters to take the goods and the goods are moved from their original location, all incur a *pārājika* offense.
"In the midst of this inquiry, four people conspired together; three committed an offense while one escaped it. I now ask you: you should reflect well upon this.
He replied: "There were four bhikṣus:
one was the teacher and three were his disciples. They wished to steal six māṣakas. The teacher said to the disciples:"
"You each steal one māṣaka, and I shall steal three.
The first disciple said,
"The preceptor steals three, I shall steal one, and you two shall each steal one."

The other two persons likewise instructed one another in turn in the same manner; if the teacher himself steals three coins, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense, and if he instructs his three disciples to steal, it is also a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Why is this? Because stealing on one's own is distinct from instructing another to steal; therefore, these two constitute two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
How is it that three people incur a grave offense (*pārājika*)?
Because he instructed another to steal five māṣakas, he incurs a grave offense.
"You should reflect well" means that within the precept against stealing, you should carefully contemplate the distinctions of its underlying principles.
What is skillful reflection?
One type of object is placed in one location; another type is placed in many locations; and multiple types are placed in multiple locations. You should understand this matter well.
What is meant by "placing a single object in one location"?

Suppose a person places five *māṣaka* coins in a shop; many bhikṣus see this and dispatch one bhikṣu to retrieve them. Once they have been moved from their original place, all the many bhikṣus incur a *pārājika* offense.

There was a man who had five shops, with one *māsaka* coin placed in each shop. A large number of bhikṣus sent one bhikṣu to collect [the coins] from these five locations; he committed a *pārājika* offense at the final location.

If various items are placed in one location, or miscellaneous goods are placed in one location—whether they are worth five *māṣakas* or exceed five *māṣakas*—and many bhikṣus dispatch a single bhikṣu to retrieve them, if that bhikṣu lifts the items off the ground, the many bhikṣus incur a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

When various items are placed in many locations, and there are five people each with one shop, if a multitude of bhikṣus dispatch a single bhikṣu to retrieve them and he finally moves them from their original places, the multitude of bhikṣus commit a grave offense.
The Chapter on Teaching is concluded.

Regarding "making an appointment," it means saying, "Let us go together at such-and-such a time—whether before noon, after noon, or at night; whether today or tomorrow; or this year or next year. If one makes such an appointment without ceasing and does not fail to meet the appointed time, the offense or non-offense is as previously explained.

If one does not follow the instruction—taking it in the middle or at the end when instructed to take it at the beginning; taking it during the latter part of the night when instructed to take it during the first watch of the night; taking it during the dark fortnight when instructed to take it during the bright fortnight; or taking it in a later year when instructed to take it in this year—the instructor commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta), while the taker commits a pārājika offense.
If the time and the appointment coincide, both incur the offense.
The Chapter on Making Agreements is finished.
*Sifenlü Shanjianlun Bipo Sha*, Scroll Nine.
*The Vinaya-vibhāṣā of the Well-Seen*, Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Regions during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
"Regarding the five ways of signaling to take [something]: the first is signaling with the eyes; that is, either signaling with the eyes or signaling with the hand."

Manifesting signs—whether by manifesting the feet, or manifesting the head from afar, or manifesting by moving the body—and thus instructing through various such manifestations to steal: whether an offense is committed or not is as previously explained.
If one instructs another to take a certain object and that object is obtained, both are guilty of a grave offense.
If one instructs another to take a certain object but a different object is obtained, the instructor commits a minor offense, while the taker commits a grave offense.

Regarding those who instructed this person: there were many bhikṣus, one being the teacher and three being his disciples. The first disciple was named Buddharakṣita, the second Dharmarakṣita, and the third Saṃgharakṣita. While the teacher was walking, he saw another's property and gave rise to a thieving intent.
He called out to Buddharakṣita, saying: "Instruct Dharmarakṣita and instruct Saṃgharakṣita; go and take that object."
When the teacher instructs the first disciple, the teacher incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When Dhammarakkhita speaks and Saṅgharakkhita receives the words, the teacher incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If he goes to take an object and moves it from its original place, both the teacher and the three disciples commit a grave offense (*pārājika*).
The Dharma Master said:
"It is not only these four people who commit an offense; if hundreds or thousands of people teach one another in succession, the offense is likewise.
Regarding those who teach others, the Teacher taught Bhūṣaṇaka:"
"Go and tell Dharmalokita; instruct Dharmalokita to tell Saṃghalokita: 'Go and fetch the goods.
When Buddhalokita saw that Dharmalokita did not speak, or perhaps did not see him, he went himself and said to Saṃghalokita:
"Go and fetch the goods."

If the object has been moved from its original location, the teacher incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, while Dharmarakṣita incurs no offense; however, in the first and third cases, a grave offense is committed.
Regarding that which has been taken and returned: if the Saṃgharakṣita sees someone guarding it and cannot take it, he should return and inform the teacher.
The teacher says: "Take it as you please; do not leave it there."
The teacher incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he subsequently obtains the object, both the teacher and the disciple commit a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If the teacher instructs the disciple to take an object with certainty of acquisition—just as an object thrown into the air is certain to fall to the ground—the teacher commits a *pārājika* offense once the instruction is completed and the object is obtained.

If a teacher, with a mind of theft, instructs a disciple, and after one year, two years, three years, or even up to six years, the teacher either dies or renounces the path, the teacher does not commit a grave offense; rather, it is the thief who incurs the transgression.

After having given the instruction for up to three years, the disciple has not yet committed the theft. The disciple suffers from deafness, but the teacher does not know he is deaf. The teacher develops a sense of remorse and says to the disciple, "Stop! However, because the disciple is deaf and does not hear these words, he follows the previous instructions and goes to take the object, moving it from its original location; both the teacher and the deaf disciple commit a grave offense.
If the disciple is not deaf and replies,
"Excellent, I shall not take it," neither the teacher nor the disciple commits a grave offense; they incur a *duṣkṛta*.
The Chapter on Teaching the Taking [of Robes] is finished.
Now, the five matters concerning the precept against stealing shall be manifested; therefore, they are what is explained in the Vinaya-mūla.
What are these five matters? What are the five?
First, another's property; second, the perception that it is another's property; third, an object of value; fourth, the intent to steal; fifth, moving it from its original place.

If one or two of these factors are absent, it does not constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). If all [the first] two factors are present, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. As for the six factors: the perception that it is not one's own, the perception that the person is not a close friend, the perception that it is for temporary use, the object being of significant value, the intention to steal, and the removal from its original place.

If it is not owned by another and not guarded by another, and one perceives this object as discarded, as ownerless, as one's own, and as for temporary use, without the intent to steal, there is no offense.
Regarding the perception of self: if one perceives another's property as one's own and takes it from its original location, there is no offense.
However, if the owner demands it back, it must be returned; if it is not returned, one commits a grave offense.
Regarding the notion of a close friend: as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five matters by which one may take the property of a close friend. What are these five?"
First, those who know one; second, those who eat with one; third, those who speak kindly; fourth, those born together; and fifth, those who rejoice upon receiving [one's gifts].
"What is meant by a 'friend' (jñātaka)?
One who rejoices upon seeing you for the first time is called a friend.
As for a 'close companion' (suhṛd), one who shares food with you, being exceedingly intimate and without any stinginess, is called a close companion."
"Kind speech" means saying, "If this is my property, you may take it according to your wish; there is no need to ask further.
This is called kind speech.
Regarding "living," it means that from now until death, we shall share these goods together.
Having taken it, one feels joy, thinking, "I have taken this object; when the owner hears of it, they will surely be pleased.
These are the five matters by which one should know that an item may be taken.
Furthermore, there are three matters regarding taking from those with whom one is intimate and close:

First, one gives rise to the notion of "cognition," and having grasped it, one rejoices; second, one gives rise to the notion of "shared food," and having grasped it, one rejoices; third, one engages in speech, and having grasped it, one rejoices.
If one forms a close bond with another, and having received [a gift] from them, feels joy, this constitutes forming a close bond and receiving.
Whether one is a householder or a renunciant, if one first receives with joy but later, due to some circumstance, develops a mind of regret, although one regrets it, one may not take it back.

Furthermore, if there is a friend who does not wish to give it in his heart, yet neither says he will give nor that he will not, and after the item has been taken, the owner later feels resentment, one must not seize it back by force.
Furthermore, there are acquaintances who say:
"If you have anything you need, take it and use it; if I have anything I need, I shall come to you for it.
Later, due to some matter, they become resentful and seize what was given.
Regarding borrowing: after using it, one should return it to the owner; using it in this manner is called "borrowing.
If the owner says, "There is no need to return it," [it is still considered borrowed].
Furthermore, one should practice giving; if they do not give, one should return the object.
This applies equally to communal property and property belonging to the Saṃgha.

Regarding "property of hungry ghosts," the Four Heavenly Kings are included therein as the foremost. If a bhikṣu takes the property of various spirits and ghosts, there is no offense. If Śakra Devānām Indra establishes a shop to sell goods, and a bhikṣu perceives through his divine eye that it is Śakra and takes an item, even if Śakra is stingy and does not return it, there is no offense.
Therefore, there is no offense, for this is an act performed to transform sentient beings.
It is like when people of the world tie an object to a tree; if no one guards it, those who take it are without offense.
Regarding the property of animals: starting with the dragon kings and garuḍas, if they manifest in human form, they are no different from what Śakra has described.
If it be a lion or a tiger that kills deer or cattle for food, a bhikṣu must not seize them.
Why is this? Because tigers and wolves, with minds of anger, might fearlessly kill the bhikṣu.

If he has finished eating, the bhikṣu should drive them away and then take [the food]; if he can have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) roast it for him to eat, there is no offense.
Regarding "rags from a dust heap": these are discarded items; having formed this thought, there is no offense in taking them.
If the owner of such items comes to seek them back, the bhikṣu should return them; if he does not return them, he commits a grave offense.
Regarding those who are insane, the Vinaya-mūla explains at length: initially, before the precepts were established, there was no offense; thus, one who is insane does not commit an offense.
As for the latter case, beginning with the group of six bhikṣus, all subsequent instances constitute offenses.
The Dharma Master said:
"The precept against stealing is ultimately initiated from the mind; you should know that those who commit worldly sinful and unwholesome deeds will experience the three types of sensation."

As for "initiating," it arises from bodily and mental actions; this refers to taking [the object] oneself. As for "instructing another to take," it arises from mental and verbal actions. When one both takes [the object] oneself and instructs another, it arises from bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
The "agent" is one who acts with the body.
"Worldly offenses" are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
"Unwholesome" refers to that which is performed with an evil mind.
"As for feeling, there are three feelings:
suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
The Dharma Master said:
"All preceding *pārājika* offenses have already been explained.
Regarding those established according to specific cases, the group of six bhikṣus were the first.
Those that are easy to understand have already been explained in the Vinaya-mūla."
Regarding those passages that are difficult to understand, I shall explain them in detail.

The minds of ordinary people constantly dwell upon desire and have never abandoned it; if a noble one were to abandon the actions of body and speech while still committing an offense through the mind, there would be no way to achieve liberation. Therefore, the Noble One established the precepts, which must depend upon both body and mind.
Therefore, that which is said in the Vinaya-mūla to be "without offense" refers to when one gives rise to the thought but does not move body or speech; this is called being without offense.
If one gives rise to a mind of theft, one should immediately reproach oneself and restore one's wholesome state of mind.
"Touching and shaking [it] so that it leaves its original place—this is easy to understand.
"Who has stolen it?
He replied:
"I have stolen it.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
"What do you think?
The bhikṣu replied, "I spoke those words impulsively;
in truth, I had no intention to steal."
"If it is so, there is no offense.
Regarding 'a hungry ghost enters': this hungry ghost sees that the corpse has fine clothing, and giving rise to a mind of greed, immediately enters into the corpse.
Regarding 'not accepting the speech': this bhikṣu hears the words of the hungry ghost:"
“Monk, do not take my fine robe.
When the monk heard these words, he did not accept the request.
As for “rising,” it means that when this hungry ghost saw the monk taking the robe away, he rose up and pursued him.

Regarding "one who closes the door": there was a monastery near a *śītavana* (cemetery). A certain bhikṣu was of a robust nature and did not fear ghosts or spirits; therefore, he entered his room, closed the door behind him, and fell to the ground. When this hungry ghost saw that the bhikṣu had closed the door, it said:
"I shall not obtain this robe."
Having cast away the corpse, he departed.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "That which has fallen to the ground but is not yet decomposed" refers to a recently deceased corpse.
It is not permitted to take clothing from a corpse that is not yet decomposed; if one takes it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it is decomposed, taking it incurs no guilt.
He asked, "In what way do they rot and decay?
He replied:
"Starting with vultures, if one takes [flesh] from a wound on a foot or claw, a mouth sore, or even a minor scratch as small as the point of a needle, there is no offense.
However, if the skin has not been broken, taking it is likewise not permitted."
If this corpse has sores or burns when it was alive, one may take [cloth] from each individual sore.
If this corpse is bloated, putrefied, and foul-smelling, one may take [cloth].
If this corpse is intact, yet a bhikṣu intentionally takes cloth from it, he should speak to the person guarding the śmaśāna:
"Fetch it for me.
If there is no one to guard the śmaśāna, he says to another person:
"Please fetch it for me."
If there is no one at all present, a bhikṣu may pierce the corpse with a knife to create an opening so that it can be taken; if the corpse is in such a state, the bhikṣu may take it.

Regarding the "exchanging of counting-sticks" (sūci): when the Saṃgha casts sticks to divide up the robes, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, exchanges his own stick for another’s superior stick, whether he commits an offense or not is as previously explained.
If one steals without the owner seeing it, whether by night or by day, this is a petty thief;

if, however, with a deceitful mind, one treats useless items as if they were of high quality, or exchanges counterfeit goods for another's property, thereby deceiving the person face-to-face, this is a great thief.

If a person has personal power—whether being a king or someone else—and if they rely on their own strength or on the use of force to compel others to surrender property, using heavy scales or oversized measuring cups as previously described in various ways, all such acts constitute the offense of theft.
There are two kinds of vows: first, the vow regarding objects (*vastu-pratijñā*); second, the vow regarding places (*sthāna-pratijñā*).
What is the vow regarding objects?
Suppose a bhikṣu intends to steal a robe and enters a room; if he obtains this robe, he vows that he shall take no other items. This is called the vow regarding objects.
What is the case of a vow?
If a bhikṣu takes another's property and departs with it, making a vow to himself:
"I shall take it when I reach such-and-such a place."
"This is called the place of the vow.
The counting sticks have been exchanged.
The Dharma Master said:
"The explanation of the phrasing follows; I need not elaborate further.

If a monastery is empty and deserted with no one present, and a bhikṣu comes and goes and sees fruit on a tree, he should strike the ghaṇṭā. If there is no ghaṇṭā, he should at least clap his hands three times. Only after doing so may he take and eat the fruit without fault. If he eats it otherwise, he commits the offense of theft."

If there is a monastery outside a village and it is threatened by the dangers of bandits or wild beasts, and a bhikṣu flees into the village, and subsequently a visiting bhikṣu enters the monastery and sees food, drink, or fruit, and eats them with the intent to steal, he incurs an offense according to the value of the items; the sequence of these points is easy to understand.

Regarding the case of taking a tethered pig: if a bhikṣu, at an araṇya hermitage, releases another person’s wild boar caught in a snare with the intent to steal, he incurs a grave offense (pārājika) according to the value of the animal. If he releases it out of a mind of compassion, there is no offense; however, he should return its value.
If a bhikṣu possesses a compassionate heart, he should first attach a rope to the object with a weight attached to it as a counterbalance, and only then release it;
there is no offense. If this pig, seeing the bhikṣu coming, suddenly bolts away and breaks the rope, there is no offense.
If the pig has not yet reached the rope, there is no offense for a bhikṣu to drive it away from a distance.

If another dog bites a wild boar, and the bhikṣu, with a mind of loving-kindness, drives off the dog and releases the pig, there is no offense; however, if the owner demands payment for the damage, he should return it, and if he does not, he commits an offense.

The wild boar had been caught in a snare for three or four days without food; its body was so emaciated that it could not move. A bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, gave it food and drink. After eating, the animal’s strength returned. The bhikṣu let out a loud cry; hearing it, the boar was terrified and broke free from the snare, charging away. The bhikṣu commits a grave offense (*pārājika*); however, if he acted out of a mind of compassion, he does not commit an offense, though he should return the value of the animal to its owner.

A bhikṣu saw a wild boar caught in a snare; with a thieving mind, he cut the rope, leaving a small portion unsevered. The bhikṣu let out a loud cry, and hearing it, the boar was terrified and broke through the snare, fleeing away, as previously described.

If a bhikṣu sees a pig caught in a snare and conceives a thieving intent—either by placing knives or swords near the rope, or by lighting a fire beside the rope with the desire to make the pig pull at the rope and gore itself on the blade, or by burning the pig so that it breaks free and flees—the offense or lack thereof is as previously explained.

If a person intentionally digs the earth to make a pit, intending to capture various beasts such as pigs, deer, elk, or gazelles, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, destroys the pit and its various trapping devices; if the animal passes through and is not caught, the bhikṣu commits a grave offense (pārājika). If the sentient being does not pass through, there is no offense.
If a person sets snares near a monastery to capture various living beings, and a bhikṣu says to that person,
"Do not set snares near the monastery to catch pigs and deer," if the person does not comply,
the bhikṣu may speak to the landowner; if the landowner then orders them to desist, there is no offense.
If a person cultivates a field and it is being eaten by deer, they set out snares to protect it; having caught a deer, they eat its meat.
If, after the protection is complete, the owner abandons the intent [to keep it], and later the deer breaks free or is released, there is no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand.
If someone sets a fish trap to catch fish and then, with a thieving mind, releases it, one incurs an offense according to the value of the fish caught."
If one first pierces holes in a fish trap and agitates the water to startle the fish out, one commits an offense; if they do not come out, there is no offense, as previously stated.
Furthermore, if one steals the fish trap with the intent to steal, taking it away from the water, one commits an offense according to the value of the property.
Furthermore, if one feeds fish with food from outside a fish-trap and the fish, seeing the food, leap out, yet the owner demands payment for them, the monk must return the value.

If the fish-trap is empty and the monk, with a thieving intent, opens or breaks it, and fish subsequently enter or leave through it, the owner may demand payment for their value, and the monk must return it.
If a bhikṣu takes a fish trap and throws it to another place, whether he commits an offense or not is as previously explained.
Stealing a jambu fruit or a vessel of ghee is as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes ghee that does not yet amount to one part, and subsequently gives rise to a remorseful mind, thinking:

"In the future, I shall not do this again," yet on the following day he again steals with a thieving mind, taking less than one part, and again feels remorse and vows not to do it again; if he continues in this manner, stealing until the entire vessel is exhausted, he does not commit a grave offense (pārājika), but incurs *duṣkṛta* and *sthūlātyaya*.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who stole ghee in this manner: taking it by the spoonful day after day, yet without relinquishing his intent, he committed a grave offense as soon as he had taken a full portion.
Regarding those who conspire to steal, there are two kinds of leftover food in the dining hall; the *jambū* fruit is as previously described.

Regarding the distribution of mangoes: when the resident bhikṣus saw the visiting bhikṣus arrive but did not distribute the fruit, the visiting bhikṣus said to the attendants (kappiyakāraka), "Will we receive a share or not?"

Having spoken these words, the visiting bhikṣu struck his own gong to take the fruit; he then divided it and gave it to the resident bhikṣu, so that both the visitor and the resident were able to eat together.
Therefore, as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if there is food or drink that ought to be shared, there is no offense in sharing it."
If one claims to be an original resident monk of one's own monastery, and there are fruits when a guest monk arrives, one should share the food with him without fault.
If, however, the guest monk has departed and only then does the resident monk divide and eat the food, this is called *jūra*.

Therefore, when visiting bhikṣus arrive, the resident bhikṣus should strike the chime and eat fruit together with them. If the resident bhikṣus do not strike the chime, it is no offense for the visiting bhikṣus to strike the chime before eating.

If there is an orchard belonging to the Saṃgha containing fruit trees intended for the fourfold use, resident bhikṣus shall not arbitrarily strike the chime to eat from them, nor shall they take the fruit away.
If there is a grove belonging to the Saṃgha that resident bhikṣus refuse to guard, it will be seized by thieves.

If the Saṃgha collectively establishes a regulation prohibiting the consumption of food [there], this regulation will not be established; however, if they can guard it, this regulation will be established.
"If a donor gives fruit trees to the Sangha, whether intended for robes or for medicinal requisites, the monks must not consume them as food.
If a donor offers fruit trees as a gift for the four requisites, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, diverts them for personal consumption, he incurs an offense according to the value of the items."

If a donor constructs a dwelling for the Sangha and diverts the food intended for it, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense and must return its value; if the gift was intended for a kāṣāya robe, one must instead make a kāṣāya robe from it.

In times of famine, if the Saṃgha performs a formal motion (jñapti-karman) because food and drink are difficult to obtain, and the Saṃgha’s three robes are already sufficient, they may temporarily divert them for consumption so that the Saṃgha may attain peace and happiness; if the Saṃgha is in harmony, there is no offense in consuming them.

If a donor offers the three robes for the Sangha, and the community of monks lacks dwellings, it is permissible for the harmonious assembly to perform a formal motion (jñapti-karman) to divert the offering and use it to construct dwellings; in doing so, there is no offense.

If a donor offers heavy goods for the purpose of building a dwelling, it should be used to build a dwelling; however, if there is a time of famine and food and drink are difficult for the Sangha to obtain, or if there is illness, or if the country is in a state of ruin and disorder, a bhikṣu may leave the monastery.

If there are fruit trees in monasteries of other regions that have no one to take charge of them, and if they are in such a state, these heavy goods may be used for food, for the sake of protecting the residence.

Furthermore, if there are many rooms in a monastery that are falling into ruin with no one to repair them, one should set aside those that are good; the remaining coarse and dilapidated ones may be sold to provide food, for the sake of protecting the residence.

If there is a donor who offers the four requisites as alms, these may not be diverted for other uses; however, if one hires people with this money to guard the grove so that they may reside within it, only then may the funds be utilized.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling through this garden, sees coconut or tāla fruits, the guardian may take them for himself and give them to the Saṃgha to eat. Why is this?
Because they have already been commanded to guard it,
and because one gives fruit to the guardians from the portion allotted to the Saṃgha, one should take food according to the fixed limit and must not exceed it.

If a guardian sells fruits or melons for the sake of the Sangha and obtains pure clothing or requisites to give to the Sangha, it is even better if he gives them to the person who guards and watches over the fruit-eating.

If a donor offers a garden for the purpose of providing flowers, incense, and lamps as offerings to the stūpas and images, or for the repair of monastic quarters, one may take a small fee to hire people to guard the garden. If there is no fee for the produce, one may use property belonging to the Buddha to hire people; if the Buddha has no property, one may use property belonging to the Saṃgha to hire them to remain and guard the garden.
If the guardian sells fruits and melons within the garden as previously described,
regarding ripe *āmra* fruits, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One may accept the gifts of the person guarding the garden."
The Dharma Master said:
"If one guards it, it is wholesome; if one does not guard it, it is unwholesome.
The Venerable Śumāna said:
"If the garden keeper receives fruit daily as an offering for the Saṃgha, there is a fixed limit; it is good to give according to that limit, but it is not good to exceed the limit.
The Venerable Padma said:
"If one hires a garden keeper without a formal contract, he may also give fruit to the Saṃgha as he pleases, and the monks may eat as much as they receive."
He further said:

"If a youth from the village tends the garden for the Saṃgha, and if the youth gives him fruit, the Saṃgha may eat it; however, if the youth takes it for himself, he must not eat the fruit of the Saṃgha or the fruit of the Buddha."

Suppose someone first pays a small deposit to purchase a garden of fruit and immediately takes charge of guarding it. If they give the fruit to the Saṃgha, the monks may eat it. If the Saṃgha employs someone to guard the garden in exchange for fruit, that gardener may give the portion of fruit belonging to himself to the Saṃgha to eat; however, he may not give what does not belong to his own portion.

Furthermore, if among the many fruit trees belonging to the Saṃgha, one tree is designated by pointing it out to hire a gardener, then the fruit from that specific tree may be given to the bhikṣus; they must not take fruit from the rest of the Saṃgha's trees.
"Regarding those who provide timber: borrowing it is without fault.

As for the timber belonging to the Saṃgha intended for the construction of a *poṣadha* hall or a dining hall, one may borrow it only after first informing the Saṃgha. If the Saṃgha’s timber is exposed, uncovered, rotting, or dampened by rain and left in the open, one may use it to build a dwelling. If the Saṃgha later demands payment or the return of the timber, one must restore it according to its original value and quantity."
Furthermore, if there is no direct owner or one who possesses the materials, one should say:
"The property of the Sangha may be taken and used according to the needs of the Sangha.
If a room or pavilion is being built and lacks windows or doors, and the Sangha's timber is borrowed to complete it, this must be returned once prepared; the same applies to any remaining materials.

Regarding water: when water is scarce and the Sangha takes it for themselves, even if they must travel half a yojana, one yojana, or two yojanas to obtain it—such being a time when water is precious—if one takes it with a thieving mind, the offense is determined according to its value.
If one takes one or two vessels to pour over the Bodhi tree for its washing, or to make dye, it is permissible.

However, if the Sangha has established a regulation prohibiting people from taking them, or if one takes them with a thieving mind, one may not take them; if one instead throws them into the water with earth, one incurs an offense according to their value.

If resident bhikṣus have established a very strict regulation that forbids others from washing, boiling, or dyeing [the robes], and other people, taking advantage of the resident bhikṣus' absence, use them with a mind of theft, there is no offense for visiting bhikṣus who see that the resident bhikṣus have already used them and subsequently follow their use.

The Saṃgha has three ponds; the Saṃgha has established a regulation that they are not to be used indiscriminately: the first is for drinking, the second is for bathing, and the third is for miscellaneous use. If this is the case, when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they must comply with each of the regulations set by the resident bhikṣus and may not use them in a confused manner. If no such regulation has been established, they may use them as they see fit.
"If one is in a place where soil is scarce and the Saṃgha is transporting soil, if one takes even a single portion with a mind of theft, one commits a grave offense.
One may only take the soil after informing the Saṃgha; once the work of repairing and protecting the dwellings of the Buddha and the Saṃgha is finished,"

If there is someone who requires it, one must first inform the community of monks before using it; however, if one uses it by borrowing it without prior notice, it is also permissible. The same applies to lime.
Regarding thatched grass: if a person burns the grass or thatch without removing it from its original location, the burner commits a *duṣkṛta* offense and must repay the original value.

If a field of thatch is protected by the Saṃgha, it may be used for covering monastic dwellings; if there is no one to protect it among the Saṃgha, other bhikṣus who wish to protect it may do so, and because they use the thatch field, it remains the property of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, if this bhikṣu departs and the field is burned, the Saṃgha shall not hold him accountable. He asked:

“If this bhikṣu requests a share from the Saṃgha, a share should be given to him. If a share has already been given and he is dispatched to guard it, and this bhikṣu then seeks an increased price, the Saṃgha should give him double the value.”
If the Sangha does not use it, others may use it as they please.
Why? Because it is not being used [by the Sangha].
If the Sangha gives grass or roots and stumps, and the Sangha wishes to use them, they should tell the guardian:
"There is no need for you to look after them anymore; the Sangha will look after them themselves."
"Regarding 'beds,' this is the first [category], which consists of seven items that are easy to understand.
As for stone pillars and wooden pillars—each individual pillar—if a bhikṣu takes one with a thieving mind, he incurs an offense according to its value."

The meditation hall is the first [case]: if the community of monks has no one to guard it and the walls collapse, and someone with the intent to steal takes various materials such as pillars, they shall be charged with an offense according to the value of the items taken.

Why is this? Regarding the property of the Saṃgha, there may at times be a Saṃgha present, and there may at times be no Saṃgha present. If bandits arise in the deep wilderness, the members of the Saṃgha abandon the monastery and flee, as previously described.
If one borrows [an item], there is no offense.
If this bhikṣu subsequently moves away or dies, it should be returned to the Saṃgha.
Minor matters regarding the monastery are easy to understand.

If a bhikṣu borrows beds, mats, or woolen rugs from the Saṃgha, he should give them to visiting senior monks (upādhyāya) upon their arrival. If these items are lost or damaged and not reimbursed, or if he departs for another location without returning them to the Saṃgha, or if he uses them for himself and does not give them to the senior monks, he must compensate for whatever was lost.
If this bhikṣu has borrowed beds, mats, or woolen rugs from another monastery and wishes to depart, and another bhikṣu happens to borrow them for his own use, he should speak as follows:
"I now wish to return these beds and mats to that monastery."
The bhikṣu said, "Just leave it;
I shall deliver it back myself.
If the item is lost, the substitute borrower must make restitution.
Regarding those in the kingdom of Campā, there were three kinds of new gruels: sesame, bean, and rice gruels; these were sometimes served with ghee, milk, curd, granulated sugar, or honey.
"Regarding 'in the city of Rājagṛha,' *mīradhūla* means 'delicious soup' according to the Arhat.
The Dharma Master said,
"The sequence [of the terms] is easy to understand."
Āyuṣmān Āśvaka is easy to understand.

When he was seized by bandits and carried away from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, this bhikṣu used his supernormal powers to observe the householder’s family; seeing that the householder’s son had been taken away by the bandits, the bhikṣu went to retrieve him through his supernormal powers, and thus committed no offense.
What is the power of supernormal faculties?
By means of his supernormal power, a bhikṣu causes a young child to see his own house and enter it; the thief does not see the child or the conjured house, and the child is thus delivered.
The Dharma Master said:
"These two matters are easy to understand.
The second *pārājika* of the Vinaya, having been explained in detail, is named the *Sudarsana*."
“The third [section] on the three purities was well-differentiated by the Buddhas and is called the *pārājika*; we shall now explain it in detail—
listen with virtuous minds!”
"At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Great Forest at Vaiśālī, within the High Hall of the Lecture Hall.
'Vaiśālī' is the name of a country; it was given its name because of a woman's physical marks, and the population of this city was vast, being thrice expanded."
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain at length the fundamental causes and conditions of Vaiśālī.

Long ago, the queen of the King of Vārāṇasī became pregnant. Knowing she was with child, the lady informed the king, who immediately provided her with all necessary provisions and care to ensure her comfort. When the full term had passed, she entered the birth chamber."

If there were a person of merit who was born at dawn, this lady was also born at dawn with a piece of flesh, red as a hibiscus flower. Furthermore, when other ladies gave birth to sons whose complexions were like gold, this lady saw the sons of those other ladies were handsome and exquisite, and she felt shame, thinking to herself:
"If the King sees that the sons of these other ladies are handsome, while my son is merely a piece of flesh without hands or feet, he will surely feel loathing and contempt upon seeing him."

Having had this thought, he immediately took [the child] from within the storage vessel, fashioned a gold leaf, and inscribed upon it with vermilion: "Born of the Queen of the King of Vārāṇasī. He covered the mouth of the vessel, sealed it with the royal seal, wrote the inscription on the gold leaf and placed it outside the vessel, and then set it adrift in the river.
It causes people to abandon [the vessel], while all the spirits and deities protect it so that it is not swept away or submerged by wind and waves.

At that time, there was a Daoist practitioner who lived by the riverbank, relying on a cowherd for shelter. One clear morning, this practitioner went to the riverbank to bathe; seeing the vessel from afar, he thought to himself, "I shall pick it up."

Having approached this vessel and taken it, he saw characters inscribed upon a golden leaf and observed that it was sealed with the king’s seal. Upon opening the vessel to look inside, he saw only a single piece of flesh and thought to himself:
"If this were dead flesh, it would have long since rotted and stunk; there must surely be something extraordinary about it."
He immediately took them back to his dwelling; by skillfully tending to one place, after half a month had passed, they became two pieces.

When the Daoist saw such auspicious signs, he placed them in a favorable location. From that time forward, after another half-month, five vesicles grew on each piece. After another half-month, one piece became a male and the other a female; the male was the color of gold and the female was the color of white silver. Having seen these signs, the Daoist felt deep affection and esteem for them, regarding them no differently than his own children.

By the power of his mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), milk spontaneously flowed from the thumbs of both hands; one thumb fed the boys and the other fed the girls. As the milk entered the children's bellies, they became transparent inside and out, like clear water entering a *maṇi* jewel.
The Daoist named his two sons Li-chezi (in the Han language, meaning "thin-skinned" or "of the same skin").

The Daoist raised these two children with extreme hardship; every day he would enter the village to beg for alms while simultaneously seeking various foods for the two boys, returning home only when the sun was setting.
At that time, the cowherd, seeing the ascetic undergoing such hardship for these two children, came forward and said:
"Virtuous One!
As one who has left the household life, you should properly practice the Way; why do you allow these two children to obstruct and cause you to neglect your spiritual work?"
"You may take it and give it to me; we shall provide for its sustenance.
The Daoist said, "Excellent!"

Thereupon, the cowherds each returned to their respective places; on the following day, together with their companions, they leveled the roads, erected banners and streamers, scattered flowers of various colors, and beat drums to come and welcome the two sons.
Arriving at the Daoist’s dwelling, he said to the Daoist:
"Now these two children are about to depart.
The Daoist replied:
"Excellent," the Daoist replied, and further entrusted them with these words:
