Regarding "counting" (saṃkhyā): it refers to reciting mantras according to the text, counting ten, twenty, and so on up to a hundred; this is called counting.

Regarding "supernatural power" (ṛddhi): it refers to employing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as when nāga kings, garuḍas, yakṣas, devas, humans, or nāga kings kill sentient beings by merely looking at them with their eyes, biting them, or spitting poison upon them, whereby they die instantly.

As for the *garuḍas*, they are able to peck and kill those within a circumference of thirty fathoms—be they nāgas, yakṣas, devas, or human kings—employing various skillful means to cause sentient beings to die.
To provide weapons means to give various implements, even including knives; by giving such items, one causes them to take their own lives while declaring:
"What use have you for this life?"
"It would be better to die.
He then took various instruments of death—iron hammers, stones, wood, ropes, poisons, and so forth—and approaching his body, he praised him, saying:

"Since you have performed all manner of meritorious deeds while in this world, upon death you will surely be reborn in heaven, where you shall enjoy yourself among the celestial beings and jade maidens in the Nandana Grove."
"Why was he born into this world to undergo such suffering and illness?
Some instruct him to throw himself from a cliff—a cliff being a mountain split into two sections with a deep valley between—or they instruct him to enter hell.
The Dharma Master said:
"If one instructs another to commit suicide in this manner, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; if one kills the body of a human being, or any other sentient being, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
Why did the World-Honored One extensively establish this precept?
It was for the sake of evil bhikṣus in future ages; the subsequent phrases are easy to understand in their sequence.
If, by means of poison, a weapon, or various instruments of death, one does not die immediately but later dies because of these causes, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
I now manifest the four similes of the ram.
What are these four similes of the ram?
There was a certain bhikṣu who saw a ram sleeping in one place and formed this recollection:
"I shall kill this ewe tonight," he thought,
and moved his sleep elsewhere.
At the place where the ewe lay, either its father, its mother, or an Arhat came to take its place and slept there, covering its body with a cloth.

This bhikṣu went there; because it was dark at night, he could not distinguish the person and thought it was a sheep. He took a knife and struck it down, killing either his father, or his mother, or an arhat, thereby committing a pārājika offense and a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
Why is this? From the initial intention to kill a sheep, up until the moment the blade is brought down, one gives rise to the thought:
"I do not intend for this to be a sheep, nor do I intend for this to be a human; I am simply severing this life."
For this reason, one incurs the offense of *pārājika* and the crime of parricide.
A certain bhikṣu came to take the sheep’s place and fell asleep; the killer said, "This is it."
He kills it immediately and incurs a *pārājika* offense, but does not incur a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
A yakṣa or spirit comes to take the place of the sheep, and the killer says: "This is it."
If one kills [them] immediately, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*, but does not incur the offense of a *pācittiya*.
If it is a sheep, one incurs the offense of *pācittiya*.
If one intends in one's mind to kill one's father, mother, or an *arhat*, and proceeds to do so, one incurs the offenses of *pārājika* and *ānantarya* respectively.

Knowing his father was within the army, he aimed at the army and shot; if he killed his father, he incurs a *pārājika* offense and the crime of parricide; if it was not his father, he incurs the *pārājika* offense [of killing a human].

"If one instructs another to kill a tall person but kills a short person, or instructs another to kill a person in crimson robes but kills a person in white robes, the instructor is exempt from the grave offense, while the killer incurs a *pārājika*."
If one instructs another to kill as soon as the opportunity arises, one incurs the offense simultaneously with the death.
If one instructs another to kill today, but the instructed person kills tomorrow; or if one instructs another to kill tomorrow, but the instructed person kills this very day;
[in all such cases, the offense is incurred at the moment of death].
In the teachings, if one kills before or after being instructed to do so, the killer incurs a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor is exempt from the grave offense.
However, if one instructs another to kill at a specific time, and the killing occurs accordingly, both incur the grave offense.
The instruction was:
"If anyone comes to this place, you must kill them.

Before the intended person arrived, the instructor went there in their stead. The executor did not distinguish between them and killed the instructor; the killer incurs a *pārājika* offense, while the deceased incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of the initial instruction.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu, and the one being instructed thinks to himself,
"I shall first kill my companion," and upon striking the blow,
he kills the person he intended, both the killer and the instructor incur a grave offense.
If one instructs another in turn to kill, whether an offense is committed or not is as previously stated; whether it is at the proper time or not is also as previously stated.

"If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣu to kill a bhikṣu, and at the time of instruction he has not yet attained the Way, but by the time of the actual killing this bhikṣu has already attained arhatship, both the instructor and the killer incur a pārājika offense and the crime of逆罪 (ānantarya)."
To call what is not tranquil "tranquil" means that one does not see with untranquil eyes, yet claims it is tranquil.
When making offerings, if a hostile bhikṣu comes together with the other bhikṣus and sits before them, one may be obscured by darkness and fail to notice his arrival, saying:
"This person named so-and-so—why did the thieves not kill him?"
"Why does the venomous snake not bite him?
Why do people not administer poison to him?
It is my wish that this man die in the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
Such speech as this is called "claiming tranquility when there is no tranquility.

As for "claiming lack of tranquility when there is tranquility": suppose a bhikṣu comes to a place of offerings and sits down; the bhikṣu who was previously under the spell knows that this bhikṣu has arrived. After the arriving bhikṣu has departed, [the first bhikṣu] unconsciously says he is still there, using the aforementioned spell. This is called "claiming lack of tranquility when there is tranquility. If one uses the aforementioned spells to cause death as described before and after, it constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) in all cases.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now expound upon the praise of death.

As for praising it through physical action, according to one's understanding, one might provide a blade or a staff, or administer poison, or provide a rope, or cause one to throw oneself from a mountain cliff. Through such deaths, once dead, one will certainly obtain wealth; or else one will obtain a human body with immeasurable riches, or attain rebirth in heaven. This is instructing by means of the body."
Whether shaking the hands, shaking the feet, or winking the eyes, one who utters words means opening the mouth to produce sounds and praising according to one's will, instructing the other to die.

When this person recognizes that they are being praised, they incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If, following that praise, the victim dies, [the instigator] incurs the offense of *sthalātyaya* (thullaccaya); if the victim dies from the pain [induced], [the instigator] incurs the offense of *pārājika*. If the victim dies, it is the offense of *pārājika*.
If this person does not understand the praise, but another person understands it and says,
"When I die, I shall certainly be reborn in heaven," and that person then seeks death,
the one who offered the praise is without fault.
If one praises [death] for two people, one incurs the *pārājika* offense upon the death of either one.
If one praises death with no specific person in mind, and someone dies as a result, one incurs the *pārājika* offense.

If one sends a messenger to praise [the target] so as to cause such-and-such a person to die: for the initial speech, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; upon arriving and finishing the speech, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* offense of causing suffering; if the person dies, one incurs the *pārājika* offense.

If a messenger, having heard praise of how death leads to rebirth in heaven, does not speak of it to that person but instead speaks of it to their own relatives and associates, then if someone dies as a result, the messenger commits a *pārājika* offense, while the one who gave the instruction commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the messenger, upon hearing these words, commits suicide out of a desire to be reborn in heaven, the instructor incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

If one composes a letter and dispatches a messenger to carry it, and the messenger dies without knowing the meaning of the written words, the sender incurs the offense of *pārājika*, while the messenger is without fault.

If one writes a letter that does not specify the victim, yet gives it to anyone who happens to receive it with the intent to cause death—should the father be found and the father die, one incurs a *pārājika* offense and the crime of parricide (*ānantarya*).

If one has the intent to kill and personally fabricates a scripture containing various praises of death, and someone reads this scripture, seeing that it praises death as leading to rebirth in heaven, and follows the words of the scripture by dying in various ways, [the author] incurs a *pārājika* offense. If the parents die, one incurs a *pārājika* offense and the crime of parricide. If, later, one feels remorse and burns the scripture, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for the initial fabrication of the scripture.

If a multitude of bhikṣus together recite the *Sūtra on Praising Death*, and while they are reading the sūtra someone dies, all those bhikṣus incur a *pārājika* offense; if, as a result, their own parents die, they incur both a *pārājika* offense and the crime of parricide (*ānantarya*).
If one composes the *Sūtra on Praising Death*, and someone steals it and reads it, and because of this a person dies, the monk who composed it incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the sūtra is damaged by water, lost, or discarded, and someone picks it up and relies upon the sūtra to seek death, the monk who composed the sūtra incurs a *pārājika* offense.
The Dharma Master said: "I shall now explain the initial matters regarding the taking of life.

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, digs the earth and makes a pit so that a certain person might fall into it and die: at the first act of digging up the earth, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; if the person falls into the pit and suffers, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*; if the person dies, he incurs the offense of *pārājika*. If another person falls into it and dies, the bhikṣu is without offense."

If one digs a pit for the purpose of killing all people, and a person falls into it and dies, the perpetrator incurs a *pārājika* offense; if his parents fall into it and die, he incurs both a *pārājika* offense and the crime of parricide (*ānantarya*).

If the pit is deep and someone carrying provisions falls into it but does not die immediately, yet after consuming all the food will certainly die with no prospect of escape, the perpetrator has already incurred the *pārājika* offense at the moment the person first fell into the pit.
If one digs a pit intending to kill a person, and that person dies by falling into it accidentally because no one came, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* at the time of first digging the pit.

Furthermore, if another person falls into the pit, breaks their limbs, but does not die immediately, and later dies as a result of having exited the pit, the one who dug the pit incurs the offense of *pārājika*; however, if they die due to other causes and conditions, there is no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"Regarding the instruction of others to dig a pit, whether an offense is committed or not is as previously explained.

If one digs a pit to capture a spirit or ghost, at the moment the pit is first dug and when the spirit falls into it and suffers, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If the spirit dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. However, if a human or an animal falls into it and dies, there is no offense."
If, later, one feels regret and fills the pit oneself, or if it is destroyed by other circumstances, there is no offense.
Regarding the commission or non-commission of an offense when employing various means of killing to cause someone's death, it is as previously explained.
If one does not act intentionally, or if one digs a pit for some other purpose and someone falls into it, there is no offense.
Or, if one preaches the contemplations on suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and impurity, and a person hears this and takes their own life, there is no offense.
The detailed exposition of the Vinaya-mūla is concluded.
Now, the causes and conditions of the precept against killing are explained.

One incurs an offense through body and mind; one incurs an offense through speech and mind; or one incurs an offense through body, speech, and mind. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); it consists of physical and vocal actions that cause harm and mental suffering.
Regarding compassion: there was once a bhikṣu who was extremely ill and distressed. Seeing that this bhikṣu was gravely ill, the other bhikṣus, out of a heart of compassion, cried out:
"Venerable one!..."
"The Elder is fully endowed with the precepts; because he feared death, he has undergone this present suffering. If the Elder were to die now, why would he not surely be reborn in heaven?
Having heard these words, the sick bhikṣu thought to himself:
"All the bhikṣus praise me for being fully endowed with the precepts, saying that upon death I will surely be reborn in heaven."
If one does not eat and thus dies, the one who praised death incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Therefore, a wise bhikṣu visiting a sick bhikṣu must carefully refrain from praising death; he should instead say: "Venerable sir, you are fully endowed with the precepts.

Do not be attached to your dwelling, your belongings, or your acquaintances and friends. Instead, maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels and mindfulness of the impurity of the body. Within the three realms, be careful not to be indolent, regardless of the length of your life."
"If a sick bhikṣu dies because of this speech, there is no offense in dying thus because of the teaching of the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus wish to sit, they should first press down on the seat with their hands before sitting."
The Dharma Master said:
"Which seat is pressed down before sitting upon it?
Which seat is not pressed down before sitting upon it?"
He replied:
"If only a mat is provided, there is no need to press it down. If there is a woolen rug, a felt mat, or a blanket, one must press it down first before sitting.
If a bhikṣu arrives first and the donor subsequently spreads out a woolen rug, a felt mat, or a blanket, he need not press it down and may sit."
If a donor says,
"Dharma Master, you may sit here," one may then sit without needing to press down [the seat].
If there are already bhikṣus present, a later-arriving bhikṣu need not strike [the seat] again; he may sit immediately.

Regarding the phrase "pestle and mortar": within the section on the pestle and mortar, if one acts unintentionally and lacks the intent to kill, it is as with the meaning of the "mortar and pestle" section, which can be understood and does not require further explanation.
Regarding the case of the elderly monk who had left the household life, there are three points. First, the son said to his father, "Do not let the Sangha wait," so that they might arrive quickly.
Because he pushed his father down to the ground, causing him to die immediately, he is therefore without offense.
Regarding the second case: why would one take pleasure in the death of one's father?
Before the assembly of monks, the monks ask:
"Whose son are you?"
"This is the son of a mahallaka.
Upon hearing these words, the mahallaka’s son felt shame; he then intentionally struck his father until he died, and for this reason, he incurred a grave offense.
The third phrase refers to one who incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
Following this, there are three further phrases which are easily understood and need not be explained.

Regarding the three phrases concerning alms-food: this *bhikṣu* seeking alms values the Dharma above all else; therefore, he gives the food first to his fellow students. Since he harbors no intent to kill, he is without fault.
From the senior monk down to the junior monk, all shall die; the remaining phrases are easy to understand. Regarding the second phrase:

if one obtains food from outside heterodox paths while begging for alms, one must not accept food that is excessively refined. If it has already been accepted, do not give it to others nor eat it yourself; it should be hidden away and discarded, nor should it be given to animals.
One who attempts such a test incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Why is this?
Because it was done with the intent to test; however, if one knows for certain that death will result, one incurs a grave offense (*guru-apatti*).
From here, three phrases are transmitted, which are easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "lust agitating the mind": this bhikṣu thinks day and night of desiring to restrain his mind, yet he cannot restrain his desire; he then reflects to himself:
"I am fully endowed with the precepts; why should I abandon the precepts and return to lay life?"
"I would rather choose death.

For this reason, he climbed to the summit of Vulture Peak and threw himself from the cliff to seek death; however, beneath the cliff there was a man cutting wood, and when the bhikṣu fell, he crushed and killed that man. Since there was no intent to kill, he was without fault.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not take your own life; even one who kills themselves, or even one who refuses to eat, incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
However, if a bhikṣu is critically ill, and seeing that the community of monks and the attending bhikṣus are exhausted from their diligent care, he thinks to himself:"
"Because of me, they have undergone such hardship.
Observing that his own life would not last long, he did not eat nor take medicine; this was excellent.

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who says: "I am suffering from extreme illness, my life span is also coming to an end, and the fruit of the path is as if in the palm of my hand; if one sees such a situation and dies by fasting, there is no fault."
"If a bhikṣu enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) seeking to attain the Path, it is also virtuous if he does not enter a village to beg for food and consequently receives none.

Regarding 'the matter of stones': a bhikṣu must not pile up stones—not only stones, but even grass, wood, or earth. However, it is permissible to pile stones when constructing a stūpa or monastery, or to throw them to break [something]. It is also permissible to repair a dwelling. Furthermore, after the midday meal, it is permissible to toss rice into the air to feed the birds. If a fierce beast approaches to harass him, it is permissible to throw stones or earth to startle it away, provided one does not grasp hold of it."
Regarding the section on "steaming" (*vaṃsaka*), the meaning can be understood through its sequential order.

As for "committing adultery and destroying the fetus": this refers to a woman whose husband has gone on a long journey who secretly consorts with another man and conceives a child; when the fetus has grown large, she requests medicine from a bhikṣu to cause the fetus to miscarry. The section on "the wife" (*bhāryā*) is likewise easy to understand.
According to the text, the woman said to the bhikṣu,
"How can one cause an abortion?
and the bhikṣu replied:
"If you press [her], the child will fall out of its own accord.
If a bhikṣu instructs her to press [her] and the woman uses hot steam to apply pressure, the bhikṣu is without offense;
if the bhikṣu instructs her to press herself so as to kill [the fetus], and the woman calls another person to press her to death, the bhikṣu is without offense.

If one merely instructs her to press [the fetus] and she dies, or if she dies by pressing herself as instructed, there is no offense. However, if another person presses her and she dies, the bhikṣu incurs a grave offense (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
Regarding the phrase "one who has no children": since there is not a single woman who does not conceive, why is she called "one who has no children"?
When it is time for conception, all women conceive; however, if a sentient being with sinful karma enters the womb, they perish in the mere twinkling of an eye, and thus there are no children.

Alternatively, if a woman’s four elements are in disharmony and she dies from a wind-disorder, or if there are worms in the womb that are born and devour the fetus until it perishes, for these reasons it is called "childless."

This bhikṣu did not understand [the situation] and prepared medicine to enable the child to survive; however, by giving the medicine, the child died. The bhikṣu incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Therefore, bhikṣus in the future must not act as physicians; if one acts as a physician, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one prepares medicine for ordained monks, nuns, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs, there is no offense. If fellow practitioners have their own medicine, one may prepare it for them;

if they lack medicine, one may provide what one has oneself. If one lacks it oneself, one may go to the home of a donor who has been formally invited to request medicine, but one must not go to other households.
Furthermore, there are five types of persons with whom one may receive medicine.
What are these five? First, one's father;
second, one's mother; third, a person who attends to and nourishes one's parents; fourth, one's own attendant (śuddhaka-puruṣa); and fifth, a pātra-puruṣa.
He asked: "What is meant by a *pāṇḍubhūta-puruṣa* (a person who has become pale)? [The Buddha replied:

"A son of good family who desires to leave the household life but has not yet obtained robes and alms-bowl, and wishes to reside within a monastery; or one whose parents possess great wealth and have their own excellent medicines so that a physician is no longer required; or one whose parents still occupy the royal throne such that, even if they fall ill, [the physician] cannot but prepare medicine for them."
If one's parents are poor and lowly, when they are ill, one may occasionally take them into the monastery to visit.
When bathing the mother, one must be careful not to touch her body; as for food and drink, one may give these with the hands.

One who eats the food of his father is no different from a *śrāmaṇera*. Whether washing hands and feet or applying oil to the body, the father may give these with his own hands, and by making such offerings, he may cause [the monk] to recover.

As for a *karmadāna* (lay attendant), if he has been hired to enter the forest to cut firewood, if he falls ill before reaching home, a *bhikṣu* may give him medicine; however, if he has already reached home, the *bhikṣu* must not give him medicine.

If there is a virtuous son who relies upon and serves a bhikṣu, and if that bhikṣu falls ill, he may provide him with medicine. Furthermore, there are ten types of persons from whom medicine may be provided:

first, a brother; second, a younger brother; third, a sister; fourth, a younger sister; fifth, an uncle or aunt; sixth, a paternal uncle or aunt; seventh, a maternal uncle; eighth, a paternal uncle; ninth, a maternal uncle; tenth, a paternal uncle. For these individuals, it is appropriate to provide medicine from their own stock; if they have none, it is permissible to borrow it. It is well if it is returned later; if it is not returned, one should not demand it back. In this manner, extending even to the seventh generation, one may beg for medicine or compound medicine from them without violating the precept against defiling other families.

If the wife of one's younger brother or the husband of one's elder sister falls ill, one may provide medicine to the sister or the younger brother, instructing them to give it themselves to their respective spouses.
If there is neither a younger brother nor an elder sister, how can the medicine be given?
One may give [the medicine] to one's maternal nephews and disciples, while you yourself may give it to your own parents.
If the preceptor’s parents reside in the monastery and fall ill, the disciple may also prepare medicine for them and treat their illnesses.
If the preceptor has no parents but possesses medicine himself, it is well.
If he has no disciples but his parents possess medicine, it is well.
If he has no disciples and his parents possess medicine, he may take it for himself.
The Elder Upagupta’s treatment of his disciples was likewise.

If other persons were ill—whether they were robbers or soldiers wounded in battle—and came to seek refuge in the monastery, the bhikṣus should, if they have relatives, ask those relatives for medicine and give it; if they have no relatives, they may also ask a virtuous upāsaka for it and give it.

If there is a donor who supports the community of monks no differently than they would their own parents, and that donor falls ill, the monks must not compound medicine for them nor provide them with medicine;
furthermore, if the donor simply asks, "Venerable sir, what is the remedy for such-and-such an illness? [the monks should respond accordingly].
"How are the medicines compounded? He replied,
"These medicines will effect a cure."
If he speaks thus, it is well.
If the donor further asks the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"My mother is ill; I pray that the Venerable One will prescribe a remedy for her.
The bhikṣu was not permitted to prescribe medicine, so he employed a skillful means and asked a nearby venerable one:
"A certain bhikṣu is ill; what medicine should be used to treat him?"
He replied, "Elder, take this medicine; this medicine will cure you.
After the donor heard the words of the two bhikṣus, he returned home to prepare medicinal decoctions for his parents. If a bhikṣu speaks in such a manner, there is no offense.

"At that time, the Venerable Mahāpadma was visited by Queen Vasava, who had fallen ill. The queen sent a woman from her inner quarters to inquire after him; however, the Venerable Padma remained silent and did not answer, instead conversing with a monk standing nearby."

Having heard the words of the two bhikṣus, this woman returned and prepared medicine for the lady, which she took and was immediately cured. Once the lady’s illness had been healed, she provided three robes and three hundred *kārsāpaṇa* coins, as well as a full *pūrvakroḍa* of medicinal decoctions. She sent these goods as a gift, placing them before the Venerable One and inquiring after his welfare, saying:
"The lady now offers these medicines to the Venerable One for the purpose of providing incense and flowers."
Padma thought to himself:
"This incense is the physician's share; I shall take it with purity and offer it as an act of worship.
The Dharma Master said:
"Thus, a person of wisdom is able to benefit sentient beings; they incur no fault for themselves and thus perform what is wholesome.
If a layperson says:
'Venerable One!'"
"Please perform a spell for [Name].
A bhikṣu must not do so. If he says:
"Venerable One!
Please recite the mantra.
"I shall recite it," [he replied].
One should form this thought:
"This layperson does not understand the Buddha-dharma; if I do not perform the incantation for them, they will give rise to evil thoughts. Therefore, I recite the incantation."
"Having taken water and sprinkled it upon the rope, he gives it; if one makes the rope oneself and gives it with water, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

If a king or a great donor (*mahādānapati*) of a village is ill, they may send someone to the monastery to invite a bhikṣu to recite spells for them. The bhikṣu may recite the *Aṭanāṭa* for them, or go to the place of illness to preach the Dharma; he may go for the purpose of bestowing the precepts."
If a donor says,
"Now such-and-such a king or such-and-such a donor has passed away and is being buried; we request the bhikṣus to accompany the funeral procession," one must not go.
If a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"I shall go to view that burial and contemplate impermanence; by means of this, I may perhaps attain the fruits of the Path," there is no offense in going in such a manner.

Regarding those who beg for alms-food: whether it is appropriate to give or not, one may give to one's parents, but must not give to others even as much as a single *kārsāpaṇa*. One may give to those who provide offerings to one's parents, to *kappiyakārakas* (attendants), and to *pāṇḍubharaṭṭas*; to such persons as these, one must give. Furthermore, if thieves or robbers come to beg, one may give to them.
He asked: "With whom may one exchange greetings?
With whom may one not inquire?"
"If someone comes to the monastery, whether they be noble or base, or even a bandit, everyone is entitled to receive a greeting.

If there is someone who calls for what they require, one may give it if it is one's own property; if it is the property of the Sangha, one must first inform the Sangha, and if they agree, one may give it. If a powerful and wicked person comes to beg, the guardian of the goods may, for the sake of protecting the residence, give as he sees fit. After giving, the Sangha may not reproach or question the guardian, saying:
'This was your own charge, yet you have given it away to a wicked person.'"
"Why is this? It is for the sake of protecting the dwelling place.
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now state the evidence for this.
At that time, in the land of Siṃhala, there was a place named Aṇurādhapura, where there was a bandit named Apaya."

There were five hundred bandits who, surrounded by their attendants, halted at one location and constructed a fortified encampment; from four *yojanas* on every side of this encampment, they went forth to plunder.
Regarding the alternating phrases, they are easy to understand.
As for the offense incurred, you yourself should know it from the *Kṣudrakavastu*. Regarding "lifting up or suppressing":

there were seventeen monks in the group of seventeen who saw one monk from the group of six. One monk from the group of seventeen took his bowl, and six [of them] lifted him up, causing him to fall to the ground. They passed him around as if he were no different from an object, each sitting upon him. Thereupon, the elder monk of the group of six died. Once the offense had been adjudicated, it was explained in the Vinaya.

"Regarding the 'phrase for subduing spirits': it refers to killing yakṣas and ghosts. These yakṣas are able to seize people; when a bhikṣu recites a mantra to cause them to release their victim, they refuse to do so.
The bhikṣu says to them: 'If you do not release him, I am able to kill you.'"

The yakṣa still did not desist. Thereupon, the bhikṣu, using either rice flour or clay, molded the shape of a yakṣa demon and recited mantras to sever its hands and feet; the hands and feet were immediately severed. He then severed its neck, and the neck was likewise severed, whereupon it died. For this reason, he incurred the offense of sthūlātyaya.
Not only does killing a yakṣa constitute a sthūlātyaya offense, but killing Śakra, the Lord of Devas, also constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.

Regarding the phrase "evil yakṣa": suppose there is a monastery where an evil yakṣa dwells; if a bhikṣu, unaware that an evil yakṣa is in the room, instructs another bhikṣu to enter the room so that he may dwell there in peace and comfort, he incurs no offense.
If one has the intent to kill and causes another to enter death, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*); if they do not die, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

This applies not only to evil yakṣas, but also to venomous snakes, tigers, wolves, and the like—all are included within "evil yakṣas. Whether an offense is committed or not is as previously explained.

"Regarding 'perilous phrases,' there are many bandits in dangerous places. If the instructor does not know [of the danger], he is without offense; if he knows and yet proceeds, he commits a grave offense (pārājika) if he dies, and if he does not die, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense."

Regarding "the one who kills is the same [as the one who is killed]": as for this first case, there was a bhikṣu who was an enemy of another bhikṣu. This bhikṣu, wishing to kill his enemy bhikṣu, thought to himself:
"If I kill him during the day, people will immediately find out; I shall wait for night and kill him then."

Having first observed the dwelling place and returned after learning its location, he went at night to the house of the hostile bhikṣu accompanied by many companions; the bhikṣu groped about in the darkness, mistook him for his enemy, and killed him immediately—thus did the enemy commit a grave offense.

There was a bhikṣu who, being suspicious of this person, killed that other person; while staying at the dwelling place of that enemy bhikṣu, he was sleeping with many companions, and in the darkness he groped about, saying, "This is my enemy," and mistakenly killed that other person instead.
There is a bhikṣu who says, "He is that person," yet kills this one; or says, "That person killed him," yet captures that very person. For those who kill in such a manner, all incur a grave offense.
Regarding the phrase "non-human being": at first he said, "Make this ghost come out," and gave a staff to the sick bhikṣu, who struck it and the ghost died;
therefore, there is no offense. He asked:
"If one wishes to make a ghost come out, how can it be made to come out?"
He replied:
"Using palm leaves or binding the hands and feet of the patient with thread, one gives them a staff; having finished reciting the *Raudra* incantation, one says:
'Do not harass those who uphold the precepts; you may go and serve as a preacher of the Dharma.'"
The Dharma Master said:
"This sentence is easy to understand.
The Dharma Master said:
"Regarding the phrase 'cutting wood,' there is a slight difference in meaning: if this tree falls and crushes the bhikṣu, he does not commit an offense.
However, if the bhikṣu has a knife, axe, chisel, or hatchet in his hand, he would rather die than use such tools to cut wood or dig earth in order to save his life."

Why is this? If one digs the earth or cuts wood, one incurs the offense of *pāyattika*; because of incurring this *pāyattika* offense, it is said that one has transgressed the teaching of the Noble Ones. Therefore, a person of wisdom would rather die while observing the precepts than live while violating them.
If there are others who dig up the earth or cut down trees to rescue him, that would be well.
If there is a skillful means by which he can be obtained,
what is that skillful means?
If there is dead wood, it is well for other bhikṣus to lift it up.

If a bhikṣu falls into a pit or a cave, other bhikṣus may lower a rope to pull him up; however, one must be careful not to chop the wood oneself. If necessary, one may speak to laypeople or śrāmaṇeras to have them chop it for you.

Regarding the phrase "setting fire," there is a distinct meaning: if someone sets a burning fire that approaches a monastery, a bhikṣu may, for the sake of protecting his dwelling, clear away grass or dig up the earth to sever the fire's path; he commits no offense.
Regarding the phrase "releasing fire," there is another meaning:

if one thinks to oneself, "I shall now burn all sentient beings," then for every sentient being who dies therein, one incurs an offense—whether it be a *ānantarya* (heinous crime), a *pārājika* (defeat), a *sthūlātyaya*, or a *pāyattika*. If one says:
"If I am now burning grass," one incurs a *pāyattika*;
if one instructs another to burn it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. The sole exception is that one may burn [grass] for the protection of the dwelling. Why is this?
"Because it was permitted by the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase 'buttermilk': you should know for yourself that there is raw buttermilk, cold buttermilk, and warm buttermilk.
"What is called *sūvīra* juice?"

He replied: "First take *āmala*, *harītakī*, and *vibhītaka*. Regarding 'grains,' this refers to the seven grains; begin by taking non-glutinous rice (*śāli*). Then take *āmalakī* seeds, all kinds of tree fruits, all kinds of bamboo shoots, fish and meat, honey, granulated sugar, rock salt, and the three types of garlic. Combine all such items into one mass, place them either inside a large jar or a small vessel, seal the opening with clay, and leave it for three or four years until they have matured. When mature, their color will be like the color of honey; use this to treat illnesses."

Starting with diseases such as wind-induced sores and leprosy, if one takes this medicine, all food and drink must be rich and nourishing; among all medicines, none surpasses this one, which is the most supreme.
When a bhikṣu takes this medicine, he may take it even after midday; if he is not ill, he may take it by mixing it with water.
The third section on the pārājika offenses is concluded.
“The World-Honored One knows the Four Truths; he has skillfully expounded the fourth grave offense.
Now I shall analyze and explain it: it is called *pārājika*.”

"At that time, as for the Buddha dwelling in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, this matter has already been explained previously and need not be recounted again; however, what has not yet been spoken, I shall now explain."

Regarding those who act as servants for laypeople—whether tilling fields or cultivating gardens for them—we should perform all such tasks; yet there are also things that should not be done. This has already been explained in the Vinaya concerning the instruction of laypeople.
A messenger acts as an envoy for laypeople.

That which is called the "Noble Beneficial Dharma" among humans is termed the "Unsurpassed Dharma," also termed the "Dharma that Transcends Humans," also termed the "Brahma Dharma," and also termed the "Dharma of Entry into Nirvana. This dharma is the dharma of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats.
"This bhikṣu has attained the first dhyāna; such was the beginning.
After the bhikṣus had deliberated among themselves, they then spoke to the laypeople:

"There is a bhikṣu named Buddhalekhita who has attained the first dhyāna-concentration; Dharmalekhita has attained the second dhyāna-concentration; Saṃghalekhita has attained the third dhyāna-concentration."
Thus they spoke to the laypeople, proceeding in sequence up to the fourth dhyāna, the state of an arhat, the exhaustion of outflows, and the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Whether the laypeople asked or did not ask, the bhikṣus praised one another in this manner.
The laypeople who provide offerings find their complexions radiant and harmonious, and their physical strength abundant. Why is this?

Because once these bhikṣus have received the offerings, they indulge in delicious food and drink as they please and do not practice dhyāna; for this reason, their complexions are radiant and harmonious.
“Regarding ‘those by the Vālukārā River’: because these bhikṣus observed the rains retreat by the banks of the Vālukārā River, they are called the ‘bhikṣus of the Vālukārā River.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
‘Are you dwelling together in harmony and peace?’”
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Are all your four limbs and nine orifices at ease?
Are you not weary? [They replied: "We do not feel weary."
After the World-Honored One had consoled them, he rebuked the bhikṣus of the Bālukā River:
"For you to engage in such conduct is to be great thieves."
The Buddha, wishing to eliminate such causes, declared that future bhikṣus must not engage in such conduct; therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In this world, there are five kinds of great thieves."
"What are the five?

First, gathering in great numbers—whether one hundred, two hundred, or even up to five hundred leaders—they plunder cities and villages, breaking through and climbing over walls; these are the great thieves of the world, and this is the first."

It is the same for a bhikṣu: having committed a *duṣkṛta* offense or a *pāyattika*, and so on through successive stages until he commits a *pārājika* offense, yet he still receives offerings from others, is treated with respect, is praised, and is saluted with palms joined—this is the beginning [of such behavior].
In this world, there are such evil bhikṣus who abandon their teachers and fellow students to seek after gain and offerings.
Having obtained gain and offerings, they indulge in food and drink at will; their bodies become stout and their physical strength abundant.
They engage in mutual jesting, sometimes speaking of the delicious flavors of food and drink, or of sexual desire, or of...
They dwell on thoughts of wealthy and prosperous lands and villages, or speak of gardens, groves, and delicious foods;
indulging in various recollections and talk that is coarse and vulgar, they let their minds run wild and fail to restrain themselves,
thereby becoming broken in precept as they accept from faithful donors the offerings of clothing, food and drink, medicine, and bedding.
Possessing robes, lodgings, beds, and seats, though not truly a son of the Śākya lineage, they claim to be a son of the Śākya lineage;
though not practicing the holy life, they claim to practice the holy life. To receive these various offerings is called the first great thief.
The *Samantapāsādikā Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Eleven [and] Fascicle Twelve.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
“There are virtuous bhikṣus who either know the Sūtra-piṭaka, or understand the Abhidharma-piṭaka, or understand the Vinaya-piṭaka;

who do not long for food and drink but seek only what is necessary to sustain life; who maintain pure precepts; who preach the Dharma for others with perfect deportment, bringing them joy; who travel from village to village and from country to country, being honored by people and causing the Buddha-Dharma to flourish—such bhikṣus glorify and propagate the Buddha-Dharma.”

There was a wicked bhikṣu who, having heard and received the Dharma from a virtuous bhikṣu, expounded it for others with gentle speech and a clear, resonant voice. People delighted in hearing him and praised him in unison:
"The Venerable One has eloquently expounded the sublime Dharma; from whom did he receive this?"
He replied, "I know this myself; I have not learned it from another.

Claiming such things, he is one who, while the Tathāgata has accumulated [merit] for four *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and a hundred thousand kalpas, fulfilling all the *pāramitās* and undergoing such diligent suffering to attain this wondrous Dharma, seeks gain and offerings by stealing this Dharma. This is called the second great thief.

"Furthermore, there is another great thief: a bhikṣu who is diligent and fully endowed with the precepts, who has attained the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or even arhat; or a bhikṣu who is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) but pure in his observance of the precepts. To slander such a one by charging him with a pārājika offense, out of malice and envy for the other's conduct, while claiming for oneself that one is a pure person—thus slandering the noble ones and stealing the holy Dharma—is called the third great thief."
"Regarding 'valuable items,' they are no different from those in the precept on stealing; even taking as little as five māṣakas constitutes a valuable item.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

'There are five kinds of valuable items that should not be given to an individual, nor may the Saṃgha give them, nor may a group (gaṇa) give them, nor may a single person give them. If one gives them, one incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya.'"
What are the five?
First, gardens; second, land; third, iron objects; fourth, wooden objects; and fifth, earthen objects. These various heavy items must not be given away recklessly to others.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There are five kinds of things that must not be divided; the monastery belonging to a single member of the Saṃgha is the first among them. If one should divide such property, one incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya."
The Dharma Master said:
"As for 'that which cannot be divided,' this shall be explained in detail in the Kṣudrakavastu; here it is explained briefly.

Regarding 'taking by means of this': one uses this heavy object to win over the mind of a layperson (*avadātavasana*). Hoping that the layperson will not give it away to others, one steals it to present as a gift to the layperson, flattery used to capture their favor—this is the fourth great thief."

To present such heavy objects as gifts to laypeople is termed "defiling a household"; because one has defiled a household, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) and should be expelled from the community.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who takes property belonging to the Saṃgha as if it were his own without distinction; if he uses it or gives it away, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense. If he takes it with a thieving mind, the offense is determined according to the amount taken; this is called the fifth great thief.

There is no thief greater than this thief: regarding the noble qualities (*ariyadhamma*), these dharmas are extremely subtle and minute; whereas gold, silver, and precious jewels may be stolen, these dharmas cannot be stolen. Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: regarding the noble qualities, one falsely claims they exist when there are no noble qualities within one's own body, saying, "The noble qualities already reside within my person."
Question: "This has not moved from its original place; why is it called a thief? Answer:
"They cannot be called thieves.
Why? Because they obtain great gain and offerings through the cause of empty, deceptive, and false speech, taking them by means of skillful methods."
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One who steals the food or drink of another is also called a great thief.
For what reason?
Because there is no reality, they falsely claim there is reality, saying:
"I am an Arhat. While the noble dharmas reside in others, they falsely steal them and claim them for themselves.

For example, suppose a hunter wishes to kill a herd of deer. If he were to go there in human form, the deer would see him and surely flee. By means of skillful means, he wraps his body in grass and wood; though his body is not actually grass and wood, he manifests the appearance of being grass and wood. Those deer who see him take him for grass and wood, approach him, and he then kills and captures them.

A bhikṣu is also like this: though not an arhat, he falsely represents himself as an arhat and manifests the marks of an arhat. Faithful donors, believing him to be genuine, provide him with offerings of fine foods and delicacies. This is just like a hunter who assumes a disguise to lure deer; such a bhikṣu assumes a false guise to lure the food and drink of donors. Therefore, a verse in the Vinaya-mūla praises:
“With the outer robe wrapped around his neck, Yet internally practicing impure dharmas, Because he has practiced evil dharmas, Upon death, he falls straight into hell.”
"A glowing iron ball, blazing with heat—better to swallow it and die than for one who has broken the precepts to swallow the offerings of the faithful.

As for those who wear the outer *kāṣāya* around their necks, they wrap the robe and place it upon their shoulders; this is merely assuming the external appearance of a noble one while being empty and void within.
For example, it is like a painted vessel filled with foul substances; such a thing is merely a hollow pretense, and there is certainly nothing in it worth taking up.
An evil bhikṣu is just like this.
As for the second verse, why did the Tathāgata speak in such a way?
"It would be better to swallow iron fire-balls than to swallow the food offered as an act of almsgiving by a donor.

Why is this? Because although swallowing iron fire-balls may cause one's liver and intestines to rot and lead to death, it does not cause one to fall into hell on account of that; for this reason, he spoke thus.
Having rebuked the Bhikṣus of Pāṭaligāma, he addressed the Bhikṣus, saying at the time of the recitation of the precepts:
"If a Bhikṣu speaks empty, deceptive, and false words, this constitutes the first [offense]."
After the Buddha had finalized the fourth *pārājika* rule, he further established the subsequent rules (*anupaññatti*), excluding those who acted out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Thus, having spoken these subsequent rules for the bhikṣus, among those subsequent rules, one who has not seen what they claim to have seen does not perceive the notion of an Arhat through the eye of wisdom, yet claims to have seen it; likewise, they claim to have reached what they have not reached, and claim to have attained what they have not attained.
Those who have not attained the state of realization have not yet attained the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Those who claim to have realized the ultimate reality do so by seeing that reality through the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*).
Those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) speak as follows:
"I have attained the noble and beneficial Dharma.
Within this, he gives rise to conceit, or what is called over-conceit (*adhimāna*), or even excessive conceit (*abhimāna*), thinking to himself:
"Regarding the state of an Arhat, I have already accomplished it."

What is pride? Because of the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the afflictions remain temporarily suppressed; this is called pride. If, later on, one encounters objects of desire and the afflictions arise, only such a person does not commit an offense.
He asked: "Who gives rise to conceit?
Who does not give rise to conceit?"

“Śrāvakas and arhats do not give rise to pride; since they have attained the fruits of the Way and all afflictions have been extinguished, they observe with their eye of wisdom and possess no doubt that they have attained what they claim to have attained.”

“What is doubt? It is when one does not give rise to pride regarding the four fruits of the path—beginning with my attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and non-returning (*anāgāmin*)—nor does one give rise to pride toward those who have broken the precepts.”
Why does it not arise?
Because one has no share in the noble and beneficial dharmas.
It is like a practitioner of dhyāna whose primary concern is sleep; such a person does not arise [from it].

As for those who give rise to conceit: having first maintained the precepts in their entirety and entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and having attained that concentration, they have not yet analyzed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) when they first enter insight (*vipaśyanā*). With the three perceptions fully present and the mind exceedingly courageous, they may attain tranquility (*śamatha*), and for twenty or thirty years they do not arise [from it]. Because of the power of their courageous practice of insight, they think to themselves:
"I have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."

Such is the case with overweening pride; if one can skillfully maintain *śamatha*, then afflictions will not arise for a period of not merely twenty or thirty years, but even up to eighty or a hundred years.
For this reason, having given rise to overweening pride, they say:
"I have attained arhatship.
Therefore, the Tathāgata eliminates overweening pride, for he does not enter into the noble and beneficial Dharma of empty, deceptive, and false speech.
He replied: “To speak of meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and entry into the wisdom-eye of emptiness— with such meditative concentration as the foremost—
these are called all dharmas, which are known as the noble beneficial dharmas.”

An evil bhikṣu regards this Dharma as his own property, or manifests his own person as the Dharma; possessing the view that he has attained noble benefit and fulfillment, he transcends the world and what is beyond the world, perceiving all phenomena with wisdom as if seeing them with physical eyes.
"The wisdom-eye consists of the three knowledges.
He asked: "Are wisdom and the eye one and the same, or are they different?"
He replied:
"They are one; wisdom is the eye, and the eye is wisdom. He asked:
"If that is so, why not simply speak of wisdom?
Why is it necessary to mention the eye, and why is it unnecessary to mention wisdom?
He replied:
"It is not so; because it is like the eye and not different from it, it is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

As for 'explaining the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to men and women,' this indicates the place of teaching; it is not [taught by] devas, Brahmās, or Māras, nor by yakṣas, pretas, or animals."
"When I know thus and see thus," this explains its causal conditions: knowing thus and seeing thus, with meditative concentration as the foundation, I see thus and I know thus.
Whether one investigates or does not investigate, this is intended to make it known that one has already committed an offense; at the very moment it was spoken, one incurred a *pārājika* offense.
Once the offense has been incurred—whether there is subsequent investigation or no investigation—one may then speak of it to others.
Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: "Either with investigation or without investigation.
"What is meant by 'with investigation'? "One asks the Elder:"
"When will one attain dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and the three paths?
Having thus inquired by such skillful means, he may ask the elder:
"Is the attainment of the three perceptions—suffering, emptiness, and non-self—achieved through samādhi?"
Is it attained through samādhi or through vipaśyanā?
Is it by means of form or by means of the formless?
Is it by means of internal form or by means of external form?
"When will it be attained? Will it be attained in the morning, at midday, or in the evening?
He then asked about the location:
"In what place was it obtained?
Was it under a tree, in an araṇya, or in a secluded dwelling?
Having asked this, he asked again:
"If the afflictions have already been extinguished, how many remain to be gone through, and how many remain?
By which path were they extinguished:
by the path of the *srotāpanna* or the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin*?"
"In each and every path, what dharma have you attained?
If there is a bhikṣu who has attained superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma), he will answer each question accordingly;
if he has not attained them, once questioned, he will become confused and unable to answer himself.

If a person attains this, it will be as clear as if it were in the palm of one's hand in the present life; they will answer correctly regarding the day, the time, and the location—whether by day or by night.
If, after answering, one asks again:
"Among the four fruits of the path, which fruit have you attained?
How many afflictions have you destroyed?"
If the respondent adheres to each and every one of these, one asks again:
"What dharma have you attained?
Have you attained the stage of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin?"
If one answers that all [teachings] are adhered to, yet there is even the slightest discrepancy, then one will not be believed. Why is this?
If a wise and intelligent bhikṣu receives even a single phrase or meaning from his teacher, he shall not allow it to become confused or erroneous.
Furthermore, another question was posed:
"What is the initial entry?
If he answered without attachment, then his noble benefit would have been fulfilled, yet you did not grant it and instead drove him out; however, if he answers:

Having entered the Noble Path and abiding long within precept, concentration, and wisdom, he is free from indolence, being diligent and non-regressive; his mind is unstained by the four types of offerings, just like space.

"If a bhikṣu speaks in such a way that his words are consistent and harmonious—just as there is no difference between the waters of a great river and the waters of the Lavanamunā River—then the Buddha has taught the path to nirvāṇa for his śrāvaka disciples, and within each of these teachings there is no error. Therefore, he terrifies them with various challenges; yet if they are not terrified, they are bhikṣus whose craving is exhausted. Like a thunderbolt striking their bodies, they feel no fear. If they were to feel fear, they would not be arhats;

if they do not fear, not even a single hair on their body will stand on end, like a lion king. If such a bhikṣu speaks well of the noble and beneficial Dharma, the king and his ministers who provide offerings shall all be worthy recipients of it."
An "evil bhikṣu" is one who has broken the precepts; a bhikṣu who possesses the precepts is a "virtuous bhikṣu.
To cause others to know me [as such] by falsely manifesting the excellence of a noble one with an evil mind, while lacking any genuine realization, constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "one who has already committed an offense seeks purification for oneself," one thinks to oneself:
"I have already incurred a *pārājika* offense; how can I now become pure?

For this reason, the Tathāgata established the precepts: if a bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense, it constitutes an obstruction for all those dwelling in the bliss of the heavens, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), such that they can no longer attain them.
As stated in a half-verse in the Vinaya-mūla:
“A śramaṇa who does not uphold the precepts will surely enter hell after death.

If, among bhikṣus, one’s observance of the precepts is incomplete and they return to being a layperson (*avadātavasana*), an upāsaka, a śrāmaṇera, or a *pañcaśīladhara* lay follower (*śuklavihārin*), there is no obstacle to their path toward nirvāṇa; therefore, they are pure in their lay appearance.
Therefore, a precept-breaking bhikṣu who desires purity should return to being a śrāmaṇera or a lay follower (upāsaka) of pure faith.
For this reason, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "One who desires to attain purity [should do so]."

To claim to know what one does not know and to claim to see what one has not seen is for me to speak empty, deceptive falsehoods; since speaking empty, deceptive falsehoods is meaningless speech, it relies upon the preceding three *pārājika* offenses. If a person incurs such a transgression, they are said to have committed a *pārājika*.
The Dharma Master said:
“This sentence is easy to understand.
‘I delight in tranquility’ is a brief statement of the dharmas that manifest noble benefit; it is not explained at length so as not to increase one’s transgression.”

Furthermore, there is another point: by means of skillful means, one causes others to understand that those who enter meditative concentration (dhyāna) enter the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; they enter the dhyāna of loving-kindness and compassion (maitrī-karuṇā), the dhyāna of the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), the dhyāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-smṛti), as well as the dhyāna of noble beings (ārya) and the dhyāna of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "Entering meditative concentration first—if one speaks thus, claiming 'I have abandoned the afflictions, abandoned desire, severed [the fetters], and shall not be born again,' one incurs an offense as previously described, namely, a pārājika."
If one says, "I have entered samādhi and attained the Way," and speaks such words so that they are understood, he has already committed a *pārājika* offense.

Or if he says, "I have attained wisdom," or "I have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*)," or "I have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*)," or "I have attained the first power," or "I have attained wholesome action," or "I have attained the eightfold noble path"—in all such cases, he commits a *pārājika* offense.

"My departure from desire begins thus"—this is the path of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). By means of the third path, one departs from ill-will and desire; by means of the fourth path, one departs from delusion. Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If one says, 'I have already departed from desire,' one incurs the offense of *pārājika*."
"If one says, 'Among the six supernormal powers, I have already attained each one individually,' they also incur a *pārājika* offense.
However, if one says, 'I attained the six supernormal powers in a previous life and now wish to attain them again,' such a person does not incur a grave offense."
Some say, "I have attained the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), yet I have committed a grave offense.
Others say, "I have entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), therefore I have not committed a grave offense. Why is this?

The samādhi of cessation is neither the concentration of a noble one nor the concentration of an ordinary person; yet if someone should doubt whether this is an anāgāmin or an arhat, and wishes to let others know that "I am such a one," then when others come to know him, they will immediately understand.
Furthermore, he says: "I have already attained the stage of Srotāpanna since the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; I have not committed a grave offense.
Why is this? The Tathāgata established the precepts for the present age, not for past ages."
Furthermore, it is said that entering samādhi in past lives was also like this.
The Dharma Master said:

“The characteristics of the offense of empty, deceptive, and false speech have already been definitively established; now there are three turns. Taking the first dhyāna as the beginning, up to the point of being free from the five hindrances—this is the first turn.

In the second turn, taking the second dhyāna as the first; in the third turn, taking the third dhyāna as the first: "I thus enter such a concentration, thus emerge from it, and thus act; I have already thus attained unimpeded mastery"—if one makes such statements, one incurs grave offenses in every case.
The Dharma Master said:
"There are three kinds of false speech.
What are these three?"
First, one thinks to oneself:
"I now wish to speak falsely.
Second, one opens the mouth and utters the falsehood. Third, having spoken the falsehood, one thinks to oneself: [that it has been done].
"I have spoken falsely.
This is called the threefold false speech.
Furthermore, there is another form of false speech: at the first thought, one says:
"I am now speaking falsely.
If one utters these words at the very moment of speaking, it does not constitute a false speech, and thus one does not incur a grave offense.

Furthermore, there is another case of false speech: "I wish to practice dhyāna," yet one speaks while practicing dhyāna; "I wish to enter samādhi," yet one enters samādhi—such cases do not constitute a grave offense.

Furthermore, there is false speech: first, the intention to speak falsely arises; then, the words are uttered falsely; finally, having spoken, it remains false speech. When these three characteristics are fully present, this is false speech, and it constitutes true false speech.
The Dharma Master said:
"If it is like this, it does not constitute false speech. Why is that?

The arising and ceasing of each moment of mind occurs within a single kṣaṇa; the preceding mind is not the succeeding mind, and the succeeding mind is not the preceding mind. Therefore, a single mind does not possess the three characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing].
He replied: "It is not so.
For this reason, the Tathāgata established the precepts such that the successive moments of mind are continuous as one without distinction; therefore, it constitutes a grave offense. He asked:
"Which of the three characteristics is the correct one?
He replied, "The initial arousal [of the thought] is the correct one."
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now conclude my explanation as to what constitutes an offense.

To say 'I have now attained' is to commit an offense; if one says 'I have previously attained' or 'I wish to attain,' it does not constitute a grave offense. This concludes the section on the three turnings."

Regarding the intent to speak: if one intends to speak of the first dhyāna but subsequently utters the words "I have entered the second dhyāna," this is an error of speech; the same applies to errors regarding the third and fourth dhyānas, all of which constitute a grave offense.
Why is this? It is because of the basis [of the offense].

For example, if one intends to renounce the Saṃgha but mistakenly renounces the Dharma, or intends to renounce the Dharma but mistakenly says they are renouncing the Buddha, the precepts are likewise lost; however, in the present case, there is a slight difference in that it is merely an empty, deceptive, and false speech.
Question: "What is meant by 'difference'? Answer:
"Although the outward signs of renouncing the precepts may manifest, the precepts are not yet lost; they must be forfeited through the utterance of words.

If one says to another, 'I am a man who has attained the Way,' and the listener does not immediately understand the meaning but only grasps it after a long while, because the offense was not committed at the moment of speaking, there is no transgression of the grave rule; however, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense."

Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who speak of this to others; these people do not understand meditative visualization, nor have they ever attained dhyāna, nor do they comprehend the meaning of dhyāna—they merely speak of meditative concentration according to worldly conventions.
If a bhikṣu speaks [thus], and after hearing it, another says:
"This bhikṣu has already attained meditative concentration;
he has already entered meditative concentration," and if one knows it to be so, one commits a grave offense. This concludes the section on the desire to speak.

Next, regarding the "turning through skillful means": when explaining according to the phrasing of the Vinaya texts, if one speaks to a layperson (avadātavasana) saying that a person who accepts a donor’s food, drink, clothing, housing, and medicine attains arhatship, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense because one has used skillful means without disclosing one's own name. If the donor does not understand the meaning of the words, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Dharma Master said: "Through these various skillful means, I wish to cause people to understand the lightness or gravity of the characteristics of offenses;

you should know this for yourself. I shall now speak of those who are without offense: one is without offense if exempted by *adhimāna* (overweening pride); one is without offense if not intending to speak to others or if speaking erroneously; one does not commit an offense if it is actually obtained, if spoken with intent, or if spoken with consent; the Bhikṣus at the Pāvā River were without offense when the precept had not yet been established; one is without offense if insane or mentally deranged. These causes and conditions originally arise from body, mind, and speech; these are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)."
"Feeling" refers to pleasant feeling.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is what is taught in the Vinaya-mūla; next, we shall follow it with the formal determination."
The Dharma Master said: "I shall now explain those points that follow the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules which are difficult to understand.

Regarding the phrase 'of overweening pride' (*adhimāna*), this has already been explained previously. Next is the second case, the phrase concerning causing others to doubt: 'I now dwell in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*); people will doubt that I have attained Arhatship, or they will doubt that I have attained Sakṛdāgāmin or even Srotāpanna. Because of this doubt, one will receive great gain and offerings. If one first forms such a thought, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. As one proceeds from the monastery toward the forest hermitage, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at every step. Upon arriving at the forest hermitage and performing the preparatory acts, one incurs *duṣkṛta* offenses for each."
Later, whether others suspected him or not, and whether he obtained gains or failed to obtain gains, it was all an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who undertook the dhūta-practices, vowing:

"I ought not to remain in a village; I ought to stay in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage). This is a pure place; if I am pure, I shall attain each of the fruits of the path. Once I have entered this *araṇya*, if I do not attain the fruit of Arhatship, I shall never leave."
Again, he thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata praises dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka-vihāra). If I dwell in such a forest hermitage, my fellow students who see me will also take pleasure in entering forest hermitages."
If one dwells in such a manner, there is no offense. As for the third case:

if I intend to enter a village for alms, put on my robes, take up my bowl, manifest the appearance of a noble one, and so forth until the meal is finished, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense; whether one obtains gain or does not obtain gain, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"I wish to enter the village to beg for food and study the Dharma of the Noble Ones for the sake of this life and future lives. When my fellow students see me holding an alms bowl and begging for food, they will praise me, saying, 'Excellent! This is the true Dharma of the Tathāgata. If we do not practice this Dharma, we would truly feel shame."
If one gives rise to such a thought, there is no fault in begging for food.
As for the fourth case, it refers to saying to a donor:
"If a person resides in the donor's monastery..."
Because he did not state the specific name [of the person], he does not incur the offense of *pārājika*.
As for the phrase "causing another to doubt," this sentence is easy to understand.
Regarding "afflictions" (*kleśa*): if one says to a layperson that their afflictions are exhausted, one incurs the offense of *pārājika* in accordance with those words.
If one says in a secluded and quiet place,
"I have attained arhatship," one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the phrase "if a bhikṣu is supported by a donor," this bhikṣu being an arhat is easy to understand and requires no further elaboration.
As for the phrase "the sick," it means that which others are unable to endure, but I alone can endure such suffering; these words are without fault.
If one says, "This is not something an ordinary person can endure; I alone am able to bear this suffering," and speaks such words, one incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya.
Regarding the term "Brahmin": this Brahmin has faith in the Dharma; therefore, he says, "Welcome, Arhat," and thus addresses each instance of food, drink, and offerings as being for an "Arhat.
It is for the sake of his faith that they are called "Arhats," and while receiving such offerings and provisions, they do not transgress in any single instance.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Regarding such words of praise, you should receive them with a sense of shame and remorse; having received them, you should diligently practice the Path to seek arhatship.”

Regarding the phrase "next, returning to lay life": for those such as ourselves who have already severed ties with worldly dharmas, this is not a statement of arrogance; therefore, there is no offense. Regarding the phrase "obstructing":

although one has obstructed the dharma of the white-robed laity, one also says they have already left it behind; this has already been explained in the *Vinaya-mūla* regarding the perception of an offense.
"Regarding 'one who goes out from the monastery': if a person previously went out from this monastery, this bhikṣu has attained arhatship.
The Dharma Master said:
"This was but a brief explanation; now it shall be explained in detail."
How is it explained in detail?

If one says [the monk] has gone out from the monastery, or from a room, or from the ordination platform, or that he has crossed a river—regarding such various cases, there are already established regulations for the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu goes out first, this bhikṣu is an arhat; if he wishes to let others know that he went out first, he commits a pārājika offense.
However, if there is a valid reason and he has been sent away by his preceptor or the Saṃgha, or if he goes out due to an urgent difficulty involving his parents, he does not commit an offense.
If one leaves for this reason with the intention of manifesting the state of an Arhat, there is no offense.
If one leaves by means of a vehicle or through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), there is no offense.
It is stated in the Vinaya-mūla that if one leaves on foot, there is an offense; however, once a regulation has been established, leaving on that very day does not constitute an offense.

"If an aranyaka bhikṣu establishes a rule such that whoever sits beneath this tree attains arhatship, or whoever practices walking meditation at this place attains arhatship as well, we should honor them with incense and flowers."
If there is an evil bhikṣu who desires to obtain such offerings, whether he sits under a tree or goes to the place for walking meditation, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If a layperson builds a monastery and a bhikṣu enters my monastery, thinking, "This one is an arhat," yet if an evil bhikṣu enters this monastery, he commits a pārājika offense.

If the Sangha establishes a regulation that during the three months of the summer retreat one must not speak, must not sleep, must not go out, and must not accept offerings from donors—if such an unlawful regulation is established, one commits no offense by not complying with it.
"As for the Elder Lekhaṇu, because his physical marks were complete and his body was like that of Brahmā, he was named Lekhaṇu.
He asked: "When did this Lekhaṇu go forth into homelessness?"
He replied,
"I went forth as a *svāgata* (welcome) renunciant together with a thousand brahmins and received full ordination.
He asked again:
"By hearing what Dharma did this Lekhaṇu attain arhatship?
He replied, "By hearing the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, he immediately attained arhatship; from the time Maudgalyāyana left the household life, he attained the Way in seven days."
To manifest a smile with a slight contraction of the lips is the "small smile.
For what reason one smiles is already established in the Vinaya-mūla; there is no need to explain it again.
"That their bones are linked together is the form of hungry ghosts; it is not seen by the physical eye, but can only be discerned by the sacred eye.
He asked:
"Since Maudgalyāyana has seen such beings, why does he not give rise to a heart of compassion, but instead manifests a smile?"
He replied:
"The reason Maudgalyāyana thought to himself was this:
'With the Buddha’s eye of wisdom, I contemplate my own body and see that even such minute beings as these can now be perceived by me.'"
Having thought this, he gave rise to a heart of joy and thus smiled with a faint smile.
He further thought to himself:
"From such suffering as that of the hungry ghosts, I have now been liberated; I have attained a great benefit."
As it is said in the Sūtras, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The retribution of causes and conditions is inconceivable; if one attempts to conceive of it, one will fall into madness."
Therefore, such causes and conditions are inconceivable. As it is said in the Vinaya-mūla-sūtra, Lekhaṇu asked Maudgalyāyana:
"By what cause and condition did you break into a smile?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"If you wish to ask, ask before the Buddha.
As for those whose bones are linked together, their bone-forms are one yojana long and devoid of flesh and sinews.
As for those birds that fly and pursue [them], are they real birds or transformed birds?
These are yakṣas and ghosts, whose mouths have beaks made entirely of iron.
As for the loud cries they emit, these are sounds of wailing and great suffering.
"If anyone were to come and touch these bones, the pain would be like that of a freshly burst abscess; such is the agony.
'Alas! is an exclamation of grief over that suffering.
The Dharma Master said:
"The great phrases following this are easy to understand.
Regarding 'the bhikṣus' censure,' it means that the bhikṣus said:
'Maudgalyāyana speaks empty, deceptive, and false words.'"
"For this reason, he was rebuked.
The Buddha said,
"Maudgalyāyana possesses the wisdom-eye."
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "Maudgalyāyana had already perfected the divine eye and was able to see in this manner.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I have already seen such sentient beings as these. When I attained all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) beneath the Bodhi tree, I saw the dwelling places of sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable worlds, as clearly as one sees an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand."

"As for the ox-killer, he made his living by slaughtering oxen; having slaughtered them, he would scrape off the meat and sell it, leaving the remaining bones connected together and suspended on hooks. Due to this karmic retribution, he remained in hell for a long time, and though he has finally emerged after a long duration, because his residual karma is not yet exhausted, he now receives this form."

Regarding the "meat-piece" phrase: this person, having slaughtered an ox, carves the meat into strips and hangs them on a hook; he discards the remaining bones and makes this his constant livelihood. Due to the retribution of this karma, after death he enters hell. Having experienced the retribution there, when he emerges from hell, he receives a physical form like a strip of meat. He is pursued by various birds, no different from what was described in the previous phrase.

"The second case refers to bird-catchers who, having caught a bird, first sever its head, wings, and feet, and then flay its skin before hanging it on a hook; they constantly take this as their livelihood and, upon death, enter hell, with every detail being exactly as described in the preceding case without any difference."
Regarding the "Skinless Phrase," this person constantly slaughters sheep; it is in every respect no different from the "Bird-Slaying Phrase.
