Regarding the "Razor-Hair Phrase," this refers to a pork butcher who constantly uses a blade to kill pigs and makes this his constant livelihood; upon death he enters hell, as previously described, in every respect no different.

Regarding the phrase "the spear-haired one": this person constantly hunted many deer, killing them by piercing them with a spear. Due to the retribution of this act, he died and entered hell; everything is exactly as described in the preceding passage, without any difference.

Regarding the "Arrow-Hair" (Śarama) class: this person was formerly a ruler of a kingdom who, when people committed various offenses, punished them in manifold ways—piercing, cutting, flogging, or beating them with clubs and whips in a merciless manner. Having such things as these as his primary conduct, he died and entered hell as a result of that retribution, exactly as described previously for each case without exception.

Regarding the "Needle-Hair" karmic phrase: when this person was alive, he served as a soldier and constantly pricked horses with iron needles. Due to this retribution, after death he entered hell; having emerged from hell, he now receives this form, and needles constantly prick his own body.

Regarding the "Needle-Haired" beings: when these people were alive, they engaged in double-tongued speech and harsh words; upon death, they entered hell, and emerging from hell, they receive this form and constantly suffer being pierced by needles.

Regarding those with scrotums as large as water-jars: these were village officials who were unskilled in adjudicating affairs; as a karmic retribution for this, they died and entered hell, and upon emerging from hell, they received bodies with scrotums as large as water-jars.

Why is this? If a person has committed an offense and accepts wealth or goods from others while concealing their guilt, yet reveals that very offense when no such wealth is present, they therefore receive this physical form as retribution.
The Dharma Master said:
"If there is a wise person serving as an official or elder, one must be careful not to pervert justice, lest one receive such retributive fruits of transgression.

Regarding the phrase 'licentiousness,' this person, during their lifetime, delighted in committing lewd acts; though others cherished fine and smooth textures, they would nevertheless engage in secret affairs with them. Upon death, they enter hell, and after emerging from hell, they take the form of a hungry ghost, constantly entering pits of excrement."
The phrase regarding the Brahmin is easy to understand. As for the phrase regarding the "woman without skin":

the woman’s skin was fine and smooth, yet it did not belong to her; it belonged to her husband. Having stolen it and given it to another, she suffered this retribution by dying and entering hell, first experiencing pleasure and subsequently experiencing suffering; thus she now undergoes such a karmic result.
Regarding the phrase "ugly and foul-smelling," it has already been explained in the Vinaya-mūla.
Regarding the phrase "putrid and festering," this woman smeared another woman with fire-charcoal mud; as a result of this karmic retribution, each detail is exactly as previously described.
The phrase "slaying the thief" is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "bhikṣu":

if an evil bhikṣu accepts the offerings of others' faith yet fails to guard his actions of body, speech, and mind, he will, as a result of this retribution, remain in hell for the duration of one Buddha's interval; emerging from hell, he will then take the form of a hungry ghost.
The same applies to evil bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs who fail to guard their actions of body, speech, and mind and thus undergo such punishment.
Regarding the phrase "the river":
the Dharma Master asked,
"From where does this river come?"

"One yojana from the Vimala Mountain, the palace of the Dragon King lies beneath this river; it is one yojana in length and breadth, and its city walls and towers are no different from those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

Due to the causal conditions of the Dragon King’s merit and virtue, pure, cool, fragrant, and beautiful lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels emerge from this water. As the water flows upward through the midst of the three hells, it becomes hot and boiling; this is because the residual heat from the Cauldron Hell (Kumbhīpa) rises up and steams it, causing the water to boil.
Regarding "quarreling," Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"Elders, the donor King Bimbisāra is fighting with the Licchavis.
The donor, Elders, is not prevailing and is retreating."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves, and out of concern for the donor, they said to Maudgalyāyana, "You have spoken empty, deceptive falsehoods.
Regarding the phrase "the herd of elephants": it was by the banks of the river Upavattana; Upavattana is the name of the river.
Regarding "the samādhi of peaceful stillness," a question was asked:
"If body and mind are unmoving, this is the fourth dhyāna; why then did the herd of elephants cry out as they crossed the river?"
He replied:
"There are two kinds of cries: first, when a young elephant wishes to swim across a river but sees the water is deep and fears it, he cries out;
second, when a great elephant obtains water and gives rise to joy, he lets out a loud cry."
Regarding "not yet accomplished": this dhyāna has not been perfected; it is also described as turbid and impure, and for this reason, he hears the sound of elephants.

As for the Venerable Bhikṣu Yaṅhǎo recollecting five hundred kalpas of the past, this is a continuous memory of successive births (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and does not refer to the cognition of *upapāduka* (spontaneous birth).
The Dharma Master said:
"How does he remember his births for five hundred kalpas? [The interlocutor replied:

"This is because, after emerging from the fourth dhyāna of the non-Buddhists, he ended his life and was reborn in the formless realm; when his lifespan there was exhausted, he descended from the formless realm to be born among humans, entered the Buddha-dharma, and attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). For this reason, he remembers five hundred kalpas, but he does not remember the period between those two."
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples who recollect past events, Yaśas the bhikṣu is the foremost."
"Venerable sirs, you have already finished reciting the four *pārājika* rules.
The Dharma Master asked:
"How many *pārājika* offenses are there?"
He replied:
"I shall now speak of all twenty-four *pārājika* offenses in their entirety; you should know them for yourself. He asked:
"What are the twenty-four *pārājika* offenses?
He replied:
"There are four for *bhikṣus*; there are four *pārājikas* that do not apply to *bhikṣuṇīs*; and eleven persons are ineligible [to receive ordination]."
"What are the eleven types of persons who do not attain [the fruit]?
He replied: "First, eunuchs;
second, animals; third, those with dual sexual organs. Because these three lack the conditions for receiving birth [in the noble path], they are termed *pārājika*."

However, these three types of persons do not obstruct the heavenly realms, yet they possess obstacles regarding the four fruits of the path; for this reason, they are termed *pārājika*, and these three persons are not permitted to go forth.

Fourth, one who dwells as a thief; fifth, one who breaks [the community] between insiders and outsiders; sixth, one who kills his mother; seventh, one who kills his father; eighth, one who kills an Arhat; ninth, one who violates a bhikṣuṇī; tenth, one who sheds the blood of a Buddha; eleventh, one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha. Because these eleven persons have committed such acts and because they cannot attain the fruits of the Path, they are called *pārājika*.

Those who live as thieves, those who have abandoned the inner and outer paths, and those who have violated a bhikṣuṇī—these three types of persons do not obstruct the heavenly realms, yet they create obstacles to the four fruits of the path.

Killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—these five grave offenses constitute the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma); they obstruct both the heavenly realms and the fruits of the path entirely.

The Dharma Master said: "There are eight *pārājika* offenses, which together total nineteen; furthermore, there is the case of a bhikṣuṇī who takes pleasure in wearing the clothing of a layperson, which when calculated brings the total to twenty. This bhikṣuṇī also does not break the precepts. Furthermore, there are four cases involving a weak spine or a long organ, such as inserting another's organ, or sitting upon another's organ—these constitute four more, making a total of twenty-four; the final four are subsequent additions."
The Dharma Master said:
"Why is it that taking another's organ is called the dharma of lust?
It is called lust because of the intention of desire."

"One who is not permitted to dwell together with bhikṣus" means that one may not participate in any monastic affairs, including the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), the *pravāraṇā*, or any formal legal act (*karmavācanā*); none of these may be shared with them.
"I now ask the elders: regarding each and every *pārājika*, who is pure?
A second and third time I ask thus: who is pure?"
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases and sentences are easy to understand.
This concludes the four matters in the *Sarvavidvinaya-vibhāṣā*."
"The Chapter on the Parājikas is concluded; next comes the thirteen matters.
Now I shall expound the meaning of these thirteen; you all should know them.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling in the city of Śrāvastī.
"At that time" refers to the time when the precepts were formulated for the śrāvaka disciples; it does not refer to ordinary worldly time.
There are four kinds of "wandering"; what are these four?
First is walking, second is standing, third is sitting, and fourth is lying down; by means of these four modes, it is called "wandering.
It is like when people in the world say that a king goes out on a tour; whether he arrives at a place of recreation, he may walk, stand, sit, or lie down.
The Buddha’s journey to Śrāvastī was likewise so.

“Śrāvastī” is the name of a place where, in ancient times, there lived a religious practitioner (*śramaṇa*). Long ago, a king saw that this land was excellent and requested the practitioner to establish a kingdom there; he named it after the practitioner as Śrāvastī.
Just as with Rājagṛha:
in the past, there were successive universal monarchs (cakravartin) who resided in this city, and because of their names, it was called Rājagṛha, the City of Kings.
Śrāvastī is also like this.
Śrāvastī is also called Bahuputra; why is it called Bahuputra?
Because the precious treasures and various diverse goods of all nations all come to gather in this country, it is therefore named Bahuputra.
“Śrāvastī is most exquisite; those who behold it can never tire.
With the sounds of ten kinds of music, the call for food and drink resounds within.
Abounding in many rare treasures, it is like the palace of Śakra.”
“Kālodayin is the name of this bhikṣu.
As for ‘one whose desire is blazing,’ because he is consumed by the fire of desire, his complexion is parched and his body is emaciated.”
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential phrases are easy to understand and require no extensive explanation; however, should there be any difficult passages, I shall now explain them."
Regarding "sleep with a distracted mind": this refers to falling asleep while the mind is not settled.
If one sleeps during the day, one should first resolve that one shall arise at such-and-such a time, as stated in the Sūtra where the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to sleep after having finished bathing, you should form this thought:"
"I shall rise before my hair has even dried.
Thus one sleeps.

If it is at night, one should also know the time: "When the moon reaches such-and-such a position, I shall rise"; or if there is no moon, "When the stars reach such-and-such a position, I shall rise."
"One should first bring the Buddha to mind; among the ten wholesome courses of action, one should fall asleep while reflecting upon each individual dharma according to one's inclination.
This foolish bhikṣu did not reflect in this manner as he slept, but was instead entangled by sensual desire; therefore, he emitted impurity, except in the case of a dream.
The Dharma Master said:
"The Vinaya-mūla states that 'excepting [the case] within a dream,' yet if one plays with [an organ] and the emission occurs simultaneously with the dream, why is the dream excluded?
He replied:
“The Buddha established the precepts to restrain physical action (*kāyakarman*), not mental action (*manaskarman*); therefore, there is no offense in dreams.
As stated in the *Vinayamūla*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
‘You should recite the precepts in this way: “If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates himself to emit semen, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.’”’”
Regarding "emitting semen": it refers to intentionally emitting it, knowing that semen is being emitted, and taking pleasure in it without a sense of shame or remorse.
As for "semen," there are seven types mentioned in the Vinaya, while the *Vibhāṣā* provides a detailed explanation of ten.
What are the ten?

They are blue, yellow, red, white, the color of tree bark, the color of oil, the color of milk, the color of curd, the color of butter, and the color of semen. Semen leaves its original location; its original location is the waist.
Furthermore, it is said that this is not so; the entire body contains semen, with the sole exception of the hair, nails, and dry skin, which contain no semen.

If the semen leaves its original location—whether it reaches the [sexual organ], does not reach it, or even merely exits to the extent of filling a single fly—one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one performs physical exercise due to a fever, or if a disease spontaneously emerges, there is no offense.

There are four kinds of dreams: first, those caused by the disharmony of the four great elements; second, those resulting from prior perceptions; third, those involving devas and humans; and fourth, those arising from mental conceptualization.
Question: "What is a dream caused by the disharmony of the four great elements? Answer:

“Regarding dreams caused by the disharmony of the four great elements: while asleep, one sees mountains collapsing, or soars through the void, or is pursued by tigers, wolves, lions, or bandits. These are dreams caused by the disharmony of the four great elements; they are empty and not real.”

Regarding dreams preceded by prior perception: whether one sees something white or black, or a man or a woman, during the daytime and subsequently sees it in a dream at night, this is called a dream preceded by prior perception; such a dream is empty and unreal.

Regarding dreams of devas and humans: there are devas who are spiritual friends and devas who are evil associates. If a deva who is a spiritual friend manifests a virtuous dream, it causes people to attain what is wholesome.
A bad friend causes one to conceive evil thoughts and experience evil dreams, and these dreams are real. Regarding those who experience such dream-thoughts:

depending on whether this person possessed merit or committed transgressions in a previous life, one with merit will experience auspicious dreams, while one with transgressions will experience evil dreams. This is like the mother of a Bodhisattva, who, when the Bodhisattva was first about to enter her womb, dreamed that a white elephant descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and entered her right side; this is a dream arising from thought.
"If one dreams of prostrating to the Buddha, reciting sutras, observing the precepts, or performing various meritorious acts such as giving, is this also a conceptualization of a dream?
The Dharma Master said:
"In this dream, one is able to recognize it as a dream; is that not then no longer a conceptualization?"
He replied:

"It is neither sleeping nor waking. If one says that one sees a dream while asleep, it contradicts the Abhidharma; if one says that one sees a dream while awake and perceives sexual matters, it contradicts the Vinaya."
Question: "What contradiction is there? Answer:
"One who dreams of sexual desire cannot escape the offense.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Vinaya that there is no offense except for what occurs within a dream.
"If this is so, then is the dream itself unreal?"
He replied:
"It is not false. Why is that?"
It is like the sleep of a monkey.
As stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the Great King:
"The dreams of people in the world are like the sleep of a monkey; for this reason, there are dreams."
Question: "Is the dream wholesome,
or is it indeterminate?"
He replied:

"There are those that are wholesome, those that are unwholesome, and those that are indeterminate. If one dreams of prostrating to the Buddha, listening to the Dharma, or preaching the Dharma, these are wholesome merits;
if one dreams of killing, stealing, or committing adultery, these are unwholesome."
"If one sees red, white, blue, or yellow colors in a dream, this is an indeterminate dream.
He asked: "If that is so, should one receive karmic retribution?"
He replied:
"They do not receive karmic retribution. Why is this?"
Because the mental karma is weak, it cannot bring about a karmic fruit.
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya that this excludes only those [acts] committed in dreams.
Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: *saṃgha* means the Saṃgha; *āva* means the beginning; and *śeṣa* means remainder.
Question: "In what sense is the Saṃgha primary? Answer:
"This bhikṣu has committed an offense and, desiring purification, has gone to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa*—this is called the first stage.
Once the *parivāsa* has been completed, he is next granted the six-night *mānatva*—this is the middle stage."
"For the remainder, grant the *ābhāhana* (rehabilitation); this is called a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Dharma Master said:

"One should grasp only the essential meaning and need not investigate the literal words. Because this offense can only be dealt with by the Saṃgha, and not by one, two, or three individuals, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
If one incurs the offense of intentional emission of semen, one should understand the preparatory means (*upāya*) and the perception of time.

Regarding what should be understood as the preparatory means: "I shall now emit internal form," "I desire to emit external form," "I shall emit both internal and external forms," or "I move within empty space"—because of such preparatory means, it is called the preparatory means.
There are five occasions for arising: first, arising due to desire;

second, arising due to the urge to defecate; third, arising due to the urge to urinate; fourth, arising due to the movement of wind; and fifth, arising due to the touch of insects. These are called the five kinds.
If, when desire arises, the male organ becomes erect and functional, yet does not become so after this time has passed, the other four [organs] are likewise.
Furthermore, there are also times designated as morning, midday, afternoon, and night.
This is for the purpose of removing illness.
"In this way, there are ten phrases, beginning with 'blue,' because there are likewise ten [categories].

It is stated in the Vinaya-mūla that beginning with 'the aperture of a door,' when internal color and external color touch, it becomes fit for use; moving in mid-air, where there is neither internal nor external color, constitutes an offense because of the movement itself."

Regarding "insects": these insects have hair on their bodies; if they are touched and become itchy, and upon arising they become fit for use—whether for making medicine, for giving as alms, for sacrificial offerings, for testing, for the sake of rebirth in heaven, or for planting—if one acts in such ways, one incurs an offense in every case. If one intentionally emits semen from its original location, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if one intentionally emits semen but does not discharge it, there is no offense; if it flows out spontaneously rather than being intentionally emitted, there is likewise no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The next sentence is easy to understand: if a bhikṣu has committed an offense, he goes to the Vinaya master, and the Vinaya master asks him in sequence:
'I previously instructed you not to conceal your words.'"

As previously instructed, I am like a physician and you are like a patient; yet while you actually have a headache, you falsely claim to have pain in your feet, so that even though the physician prescribes medicine, the illness does not improve.
He then rebuked him, saying:

"The teacher lacks efficacy and does not understand how to prepare medicine; therefore, you must tell me one by one whether the offense is grave so that it may be settled as grave, or light so that it may be settled as light."
"The Vinaya master first contemplates the eleven desires and the eleven expedients.
He asked: "What are the so-called eleven desires?"

He replied: "The first is the pleasure of emerging; the second is the pleasure of right emergence; the third is the pleasure of having emerged; the fourth is the pleasure of desire; the fifth is the pleasure of contact; the sixth is the pleasure of itching; the seventh is the pleasure of seeing; the eighth is the pleasure of sitting; the ninth is the pleasure of speech; the tenth is the pleasure of the household; and the eleventh is the breaking of the forest."

Regarding "delighting in the pleasure of emission": if a bhikṣu, when desire arises, takes pleasure in it, and because of that pleasure in desire emits semen, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense because of the emission of semen.
If one intentionally emits semen but it does not emerge, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu falls asleep while contemplating [the emission], having first employed a means such as clamping with his feet or grasping the organ with his hand, and then dreams of emitting semen while in that state of contemplation, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one wishes to arouse the contemplation of impurity, one should extinguish it by means of that contemplation of impurity; thus, with a pure and stainless mind, one sleeps. If semen is emitted in a dream, there is no offense.
This is called "the pleasure of emission."

Regarding "emission occurring while in a state of pleasure": if a bhikṣu, while sleeping and dreaming, engages in sexual acts and emits semen upon waking without moving his organ, there is no offense; however, if he moves his organ while it is emitting, he incurs an offense.
If, while about to go out, one thinks to oneself:
"I must not soil my robes or mat;
I do not wish to go out," and thus uses the hand to block [the opening] before going outside to wash, there is no offense.
If one experiences pleasure while committing an offense, this is called "pleasure during the act"; having finished and no longer making contact, there is no offense.
If, out of greed for pleasure, one manipulates [the organ] again after it has already emerged, an offense is committed; this is called "pleasure after emergence."
Regarding "sexual desire": if a bhikṣu, out of sexual desire, attempts to seize a woman and semen is emitted, there is no offense.

Why is this? Because it constitutes an act of lust, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); however, if he reaches the physical boundaries [of penetration], he incurs a *pārājika* (defeat). If, after seizing her, he craves her smoothness and softness but does not enter the boundaries of a *pārājika*, and semen is emitted, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) offense; this is called "sexual desire."

Regarding "contact with pleasure," this may be internal contact or external contact. Internal contact refers to, for example, testing with the hand whether something is hard or soft; if semen is emitted due to such contact, there is no offense. However, if there is an intention to emit it out of a desire for pleasure, one incurs an offense. This is called internal contact.

Regarding external contact: if a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, touches a woman’s body—whether by embracing or by stroking her smooth skin—and semen is emitted, he does not commit a pārājika offense; however, because of the act of stroking, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. If there is pleasure in the touch and pleasure in the emission of semen, he incurs both offenses.

Regarding "itching pleasure": if a rash or a scabies mite touches the male organ and causes itching, and semen is emitted by scratching it with the hand, there is no offense; however, if the organ becomes aroused and semen is emitted through the force of movement, one commits an offense.

Regarding "delight through seeing": if a bhikṣu sees the female organ and, while gazing intently at the aroused organ, emits semen, he does not commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, but incurs a duṣkṛta offense; if, having seen it, he moves his organ and emits semen, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. This is called "delight through seeing."

Regarding "sitting for pleasure": if a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a woman and speaks with her, and semen is emitted, there is no offense [for the emission itself], but he incurs another offense due to sitting in a secluded place with her.
If, while sitting, a desire-mind arises and one moves the waist, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; this is called "pleasure of sitting.
As for the "pleasure of speech," it is when one speaks with a woman in a secluded place, saying:
"What is the female organ like?"
"Is it black? Is it white? Is it fat? Is it thin?
If one utters such words and semen is emitted, there is no offense; however, because of the coarse and wicked speech, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one speaks with pleasure and has the intention for emission, thereby committing an offense, this is called "pleasure in speech."

Regarding "delighting in the house": when a bhikṣu returns to the house of a donor, due to lingering thoughts of his mother or sister, he touches or embraces her with his hand; although no offense is committed as the semen is emitted, because of the physical contact, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If the emission of semen occurs because of such touching, he commits an offense. This is called "delighting in the house."

Regarding "breaking the forest" (*chālīna*): it refers to when a man and a woman form a covenant, using incense, flowers, or betel nuts to exchange gifts with one another, saying, "By this, we bind ourselves in kinship."
Why is this? Since fragrant flowers and betel nuts all come from the forest, it is therefore named "Forest-Breaker" (Cchaila).
If a woman were to answer:
"Please accept this, Venerable Sir; it is most fragrant and delicious. I now offer this gift in return so that you, Venerable Sir, may keep me in mind.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu, wishing to arouse energy and emit semen, does not commit an offense.
"If one leaves because of convenience and commits an offense, yet fails to leave for that same reason, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is called the eleventh."

Once the Vinaya master has carefully examined it, whether there is an offense or no offense, and whether it is light or heavy—he shall declare what is light to be light and what is heavy to be heavy. If one acts according to what is prescribed in the original Vinaya texts, it is good.

The first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* has been fully explained.

Whether it be grasping the hand, grasping the hair, or touching what is smooth and delicate, there are twelve varieties of such conceptualization which I shall now manifest.

Regarding a human female: if one perceives her as a human female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if one is doubtful about her being a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one perceives a human female as a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one perceives a human female as a male, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one perceives a human female as an animal, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding a *paṇḍaka*: if one perceives him as a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one is doubtful about him being a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding a male or an animal: if one perceives him as a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one perceives a male as a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one is doubtful about him being a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one perceives a male as a human female or as an animal, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he takes hold of the clothing of all of them together, it is a *sthūlātyaya* for the first woman, a *duṣkṛta* for the second woman, and there is no offense for those from the third woman downward.
If one touches a woman through thick or heavy clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one touches her with the hand through thin or light clothing, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu comes into physical contact with a woman such that their hair touches hair, their body hair touches body hair, or their nails touch nails, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
"Why is this? Because there is no sensation of touch.

"Do not distress this woman; such vulgar commands are utterly improper."
The donor replied:

"We do not wish to debate this matter with the Venerable One. I am a layperson who knows the affairs of a layperson, and you, Venerable One, are a renunciant who knows the Dharma of a renunciant; we are each unrelated to the other's domain."
"If one knows [the affairs of] lay households, this person is no śramaṇa.
Having spoken these words, he ceased.
Udāyin then immediately sent him out.
"Go, go! Do not remain in this place.
"Adorned" refers to all manner of gold, silver, and precious jewels.
"Head-to" (hétuó) means, in the Han language, a person with many desires and passions.

As for "one who is able to make offerings": if a woman, by means of sounds, forms, touches, fragrances, and tastes—indeed, by holding all such exquisite things—offers them to her husband, this is called being able to make offerings.
Regarding gambling together: "If we succeed in obtaining this woman, you shall repay me; if we do not succeed, I shall repay you.
As stated in the Vinaya, a bhikṣu must not engage in gambling for sport.
"Temporary" means for even a single *kṣaṇa*, which in the language of Han is called the duration of a finger-snap; this is termed "temporary.
One may then employ the method of acting as a matchmaker. Why is this?
Because he acts as a matchmaker at the bidding of others, regarding "men and women":
a woman sends provisions to a man.
The bhikṣu transmits the message:
"This woman is thinking of you.
When the man replied with an acknowledgment, the bhikṣu went again to the woman's place and said:
"In such and such a way, this man is thinking of you."
The woman said to the bhikṣu, “I wish to have illicit intercourse with such-and-such a man.
The bhikṣu accepted her words and told them to the man, then returned to report back to the woman; for even a single act of sexual union, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

"A woman has ten types of protection. Regarding protection by her father: the father restrains her and does not permit her to go out or come in, fearing other matters; protection by her mother is likewise. Protected and supervised by both parents, she is not allowed to play in other places, nor is she permitted to travel or enter and exit."

There is protection by brothers, protection by sisters, protection by kinsmen, protection by clan, protection by the Dharma, and protection by punishment. Regarding "protection by the Dharma," this refers to protection by those who share the same Dharma.

Regarding "protection through punishment": if a widowed woman wishes to have illicit relations with another man, she must first inform the authorities; if permission is granted, she may proceed, but if it is denied, she may not act on her own initiative. One who violates this is fined gold and must pay it to the authorities; therefore, it is called "protection through punishment."
"To purchase by means of goods" refers to redeeming [a person] by offering property; this is called "purchasing.
"To live together out of affection" refers to living together out of mutual fondness.
"To live as a hired servant" means to employ someone with goods and entrust all household affairs to them.
Regarding "obtained through clothing": because she was accepted as a wife by being provided with garments to wear, she is a poor woman; this is called "obtained through clothing.
Regarding "obtained through water": because they bathed together and poured water over one another, making a solemn vow to become husband and wife, this is called "obtained through water."
As for "obtaining the ring," she places the ring upon her head and wears it constantly; then, taking the ring and casting it away, she says: "Come and dwell in my house, and always be my wife."
This is called "obtained by ring" (*kaṇṭhaka*).
As for "taken by a maidservant," it refers to taking one's own maidservant back as a wife.
As for "taken by labor," it refers to hiring someone with wages to perform domestic chores and then taking her as one's own wife; this is called "taken by labor."
Regarding "the woman taken as a banner": when a flag is raised and an army is established to invade another country, one captures a woman from that land and takes her as one's own wife.
"If a layperson sends a bhikṣu to another place, saying:
'In such-and-such a region there is a protected girl; seek this girl out and make her my wife.'"
The bhikṣu replied, "Very well," and immediately went to the woman's place. He related these matters to her; the woman was well-disposed, yet she might either agree or disagree.
If a bhikṣu receives such a message and returns it as a report to a man, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a man tells a bhikṣu to convey a message to another bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu instead tells his parents, brothers, or sisters, such a message constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, the Dharma Master said: "It is not so. Why is this?

As stated in the Vinaya-mūla: if one intends to renounce the Buddha but mistakenly says "I renounce the Saṃgha," or intends to renounce the Saṃgha but mistakenly says "I renounce the Buddha," one does not lose the precepts.
"Even if a bhikṣu speaks thus to his parents, brothers, or sisters, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The subsequent phrases are no different from those before; therefore, they are not explained again."
If many women dispatch one bhikṣu to convey a message to many men, and the bhikṣu accepts the message, goes to deliver it, and returns to report it to the women, there are many saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established;
or when acting on the orders of the Saṃgha; or when, by reason of such an order, one goes and says to a woman:
"A certain man desires you as his wife."
"No offense. Why? Because he did not accept the spoken words."
There is no offense for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

There are six matters that constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: first, nodding the head; second, using hand gestures; third, receiving through speech; fourth, shaking the body; fifth, receiving by means of writing; sixth, possessing these five matters—these are called the six matters.
If parents are quarreling and the father sends the mother back to her own home, but the father later feels regret and says to the bhikṣu:
"I am old, and I have no one to attend to me morning and evening; you should speak to your mother and ask her to return and look after me."
If a bhikṣu accepts such a message and speaks to the mother, returning it to report to the father, it is entirely a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This precept does not depend on whether one knows [the truth] or not; if one merely accepts the words, goes to speak them, and returns to report them, it is entirely a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by convention), not a *prakṛti-āpatti* (a natural offense), and it comprises three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Now, following the sequence of the textual phrasing, these are easily understood and need not be explained in detail.
The five *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses] are concluded.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha at the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandaka Feeding Ground;
this concerns the rules for dwellings. 'Ārāmika' is the name of a village. This bhikṣu was born in the village of Ārāmika, and is therefore called Bhikṣu Ārāmika."
"Seeking for oneself" means seeking various materials for oneself, desiring to construct a large dwelling.
"Causing others to build" means instructing others to build or building it oneself; this bhikṣu abandons sitting meditation and reciting sūtras to constantly engage in such inferior activities.
"Without a master" means there is no donor or patron, and one merely begs from place to place.
"For oneself" means for one's own person, not for the community of monks (*saṃgha*).

"A large room" refers to a room that is extremely large and without fixed limits; begging is exceedingly frequent here—whether begging for people or borrowing people, or begging for utensils or borrowing utensils—in these various ways of either begging or borrowing, with the exception of borrowing or begging for meat used for hunting or fish used for fishing (both masters have strictly prohibited these), all other borrowings are pure.

This bhikṣu has constructed a dwelling that is already large; furthermore, fish and meat are difficult to obtain. Fearing that he might, by means of borrowing or hiring others, dispatch them to hunt, [the Buddha] therefore prohibited it.
If one builds a dwelling and thereby acquires fields, there is no offense in borrowing plows, oxen, or other farming implements.

If there are people in the monastery who gather leftover food and, having finished eating, gather together to engage in various forms of play and laughter, there is no offense in employing such people for labor.
If a bhikṣu wishes to build a hall, he goes to a stone quarry and borrows stonemasons to construct it. If he obtains good materials or stone pillars, the bhikṣu asks the donor:
"How shall these pillars be erected?"
"If the donor personally erects a pillar, or if the donor provides another pillar as well, it is likewise acceptable.
If the donor replies, 'There is no one [to do so],' [it is still permissible]."
Or someone might say:
"I have my own business.
The bhikṣu then instructs them to borrow it from another place.
The bhikṣu replied again, "I have no other acquaintances.

If there is no person [to receive the gift] from the donor, it is also well to give the money directly; having received the money, one may take it to a carpenter if timber is needed, to a potter if bricks or tiles are needed, or to a carver if carving is needed. If there is any remaining money, it may be used for what is required for beds, mats, clothing, or dwellings.

If one picks up leftover food for a person who maintains correct conduct, one may give it to them; if there is no food available, one may enter a village to beg for it and give it to them virtuously, but one must not give money in exchange.
"For the sake of a dwelling, he entered a village at an improper time to beg for oil, covering his bowl with his hand.
When he arrived at a donor's house, the donor asked the bhikṣu:
'What do you require?'"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am seeking oil for the construction of the dwelling to provide it to the laborers.
The same applies to rice. If he obtains oil, he shall return it to the person in charge of temple affairs.
If a monk's [robe] is torn, damaged, lost, or destroyed, the monk must repay its full value.
If a donor dedicates a gift specifically for a monk, the monk must not accept it; however, if it is given as an offering to the monastery, he may accept it.

A bhikṣu must not take things himself; he should call a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") and entrust them to him. If he borrows a cart, a dwelling, or various other necessary items, it is no different from the case regarding oxen.
If a bhikṣu is ill and begs for medicine, it is well; however, when laypeople see a bhikṣu coming, they immediately think to themselves,
"This bhikṣu has come again to beg," and each flees to hide away, or, seeing the bhikṣu begging for food, they each close their doors.
"Regarding 'construction according to measure,' what is meant by construction according to measure?

One span of a person of average height is equivalent to one span of the Buddha. The measurement for the interior of the dwelling is twelve Buddha-spans in length and seven Buddha-spans in internal width."

If one reduces the length by one *vitasti* while increasing the width by one *vitasti*, it is likewise not permitted; if one reduces the width while increasing the length, it is also not permitted. How much more so if both the length and the width exceed the prescribed measure? Even before the work is finished, down to the point of applying a single lump of clay, one commits an offense.
If a room is six spans long and four spans wide, one who constructs such a room incurs no offense even if there is no owner, because it does not constitute a "room" [in the technical sense].
Why is this? Because it is not a [proper] dwelling.
"If it is a tile-roofed house, it is an offense if the interior, exterior, upper, and lower parts are all plastered; if it is a thatched house, there is no offense.
The Dharma Master asked:
"At exactly what time does one commit the offense?"
"Is it an offense for the initial construction, for the subsequent construction, or for the completion of the dwelling?
He replied:

"From the initial construction up until the second application of mud, it is all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). At the very end, with the first application of mud, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); when the second application of mud is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting of the Saṃgha)."
Regarding "mud," there are two kinds: first, earthen mud; second, lime plaster.
Regarding "places," these include windows, doorways, pillars, beams, rafters, purlins, and smoke holes; these are places where one does not apply mud.

The bhikṣu should lead the householder to the site where the hut is to be built; the householder should show the bhikṣu the site for building the hut. The householder must first level and smooth the ground so that it is even like the surface of a drum, and then go to the Saṃgha and request them to designate the site for the hut. He should make this request a second and a third time in the same manner.

If the Saṃgha goes to inspect it, that is good; if the Saṃgha cannot go, the Saṃgha shall appoint a wise bhikṣu to go and see whether it is a place free from difficulties and free from obstructions. Once this bhikṣu has gone and inspected it, if it is satisfactory—just as the ground was prepared by the owner of the dwelling—it is well.

"Regarding 'difficult places' (durgama): from tigers, wolves, and lions down to the very smallest ants—if there is an ant's nest within which one cannot dwell, it is unfit for construction; however, if the ants are roaming about seeking food and can be driven away, it is fit for construction."
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata has compassion for sentient beings and for the bhikṣus.

Regarding obstructed places: whether it be a person’s field or garden, a location on a road, a place belonging to an enemy, a place frequented by bandits, a place in a śītavana (cemetery), or a place protected by royal decree—all such obstructed places must not be used for construction.

One should encircle the four sides of the house so as to form twelve rungs for a ladder; between each rung, there should be a space of one fist or one elbow, like the turning of a grass cart. The remaining phrases are already present in the Vinaya text and need not be explained again.

If a bhikṣu builds a large dwelling for himself without a patron and without having it measured according to the prescribed dimensions, then for every act of construction and management involved in building the dwelling, each constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he piles up walls with bricks, for every brick used, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the final two bricks, the first brick is a *sthūlātyaya* offense and the second brick is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Once the house is completed and plastered, the offense is finalized; however, if it is merely smeared or sprinkled with mud, there is no offense.
"If one builds a house and leaves behind surplus bricks and mortar with the intention, 'I shall complete it later,' it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the resolve to build is definitively abandoned, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
If one builds a perimeter wall that does not reach the roof, leaving it open to admit light, there is no offense.

If one is building a house and leaves a patch of mud unformed with the intention to complete it later, and due to some circumstance departs without finishing it, and a visiting bhikṣu arrives and stays there, seeing the incomplete work as already finished—there is no offense for either party.
If it is in a difficult location or an obstructed location, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it or if it exceeds the proper measure, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
If the house is unfinished, or if it is given to the Saṃgha or even to a single person, or if it is broken or thrown away, there is no offense.

If one builds it oneself, completes it oneself, or instructs another to complete it; or if one instructs another to build it and instructs another to complete it—in all such cases, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If two or three people build a house together, there is no offense for a single bhikṣu or a single śrāmaṇera.
Why is this? Because a person does not have a share of a single house.
If it is divided into sections and a person receives a share of one house, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one constructs a cave by stacking bricks, or by stacking stones, earth, or wood, or if it is a thatched hut—even if it exceeds the prescribed measure—there is no offense provided it has not been formally authorized.
If there is a dwelling that is subject to difficulties or obstructions, and the Saṃgha does not designate it as such despite its exceeding the measure, one does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
One who possesses wisdom should understand this meaning:
"If one constructs a hall for reciting the precepts, a heated room, or a dining hall for the sake of others, and does not construct them for one's own residence, there is no offense."
If one dwells together with others for one’s own sake, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There is no offense in the case of the first instance, prior to the promulgation of the rule; the bhikṣu Āravikā is without offense.

It is complete with six factors: first, doing it oneself; second, instructing another to do it; third, not pointing out the location beforehand; fourth, exceeding the prescribed measure; fifth, being in a difficult place; and sixth, being in a place that causes obstruction. This precept comprises three types of action and three types of reception.
The detailed explanation of the dwellings is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Kukkuṭa-gosīta Garden; regarding the precepts concerning these dwellings, "Kukkuṭa" is the name of this garden.
"Gosita’s Park" is the name of a son of a householder.
"Caṇḍana" is the name of a person who made offerings to the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the phrase "let the Venerable One show me the location of a room," there was a donor who said to the bhikṣu Caṇḍana:
"Venerable Sir, please show me a place where I may build a hut for you; I shall build it for you.
As for the tree of a shrine, this is a place where the people of the kingdom and its towns offer daily morning and evening worship, and where spirits and deities dwell.
"Growing a tree" means forming the perception that it is a sentient being.

"Mahāla" refers to a large dwelling built for oneself by one who has an owner; if this dwelling has an owner, is built for oneself, exceeds the prescribed dimensions, and was built by one with an owner for oneself, without the Saṃgha having designated the site, or if there is difficulty or obstruction—this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The remaining phrases are no different from those regarding the previous dwelling.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove; at that time, there was the son of Ṭhappa Māra."

As for the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana), it was surrounded by planted bamboo; the bamboos were eighteen cubits high. At its four corners there were towers, along with fine gatehouses, which from afar appeared dark and billowing like black clouds; thus it was named the Bamboo Grove Monastery, and is also called Kalandaka.
The circumstances regarding Kalandaka have been explained previously and are therefore not repeated here.
*Tapasa* is the name of a bhikṣu, and *Māra-putra* is the name of a king; because this prince left the household life, he was named Tapasamāraputra.

This Venerable One left home at the age of seven; as his hair fell to the ground upon being shorn, he immediately became an Arhat. He attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), was endowed with the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), and there was nothing known by any of the Śrāvakas that he did not thoroughly master. Among all Arhats, he was already the foremost.
As for "entering a quiet place," it is called a "quiet place" because that location is tranquil and free from clamor.
As for "arising from samādhi," he says to himself:
"The wholesome dharmas I have cultivated are now all completed; I shall distribute rooms and various foods and drinks for the community of monks."
The Dharma Master said:
"Virtuous One, why do you speak such words? [He replied:

"This is my final body; that which was to be cultivated has reached its limit, and I shall now attain nirvana. It is like lighting a lamp and placing it in a windy place—it will soon be extinguished, and this body is just the same."

I shall distribute rooms and various foods and drinks for the community of monks. The reason I distribute rooms and various foods and drinks for the community of monks is that I see good sons who are bhikṣus coming from afar to pay their respects to the World-Honored One; since the rooms are cramped and there is no place to stay, I shall, by means of my supernormal power, manifest rooms, beds, mats, woolen rugs, fine woolens, felt, and cushions.

Furthermore, one day he saw several junior bhikṣus who, out of respect for their senior and virtuous elders, yielded their seats and declined invitations to sit at the front; because of this circumstance, they did not receive food and drink at the proper time and consequently became exhausted.

I shall now cause the community of monks to dwell in peace and happiness, so that each may obtain what is appropriate and not suffer on account of food and drink; for this reason, I distribute it so that it is equal for all.
The Dharma Master said:
"Venerable Trapusa, among the three types of action, why do you cultivate only the inferior type?
He replied:
"This is because he was drawn by the power of vows made in a previous life;
therefore, he has this thought. He asked, "When did this Trapusa Māra-putra make this vow?"
He replied:
“In the past, there was a Buddha named Pāṭhikaputta. At that time, this Dharmaruci was born into the family of a lay devotee.

Then, the people of the kingdom and the towns collectively organized a great assembly to invite the Buddha into the country; sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus surrounded him, and the great assembly made offerings for seven days through acts of charity.”

At that time, there was an Arhat bhikṣu who, by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), distributed beds, mats, and various foods among the great assembly. When Trapusa-māra-putra saw this Arhat bhikṣu exercising such supernormal powers, his heart was filled with great joy. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that in my future life, during the time of a future Buddha, I may leave the home life to study the Path and quickly become an Arhat, distributing rooms, beds, mats, and various foods for the community of monks, no different from the supernormal power of this present Arhat."
At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated whether the aspirations of this good man would indeed be fulfilled in a future age.
Having observed the future, the World-Honored One said to Trapusa Māra’s son:

"A hundred thousand kalpas from now, there will be a Buddha named Śākyamuni. At the age of seven, you shall go forth into homelessness; as soon as your hair falls to the ground, you shall become an Arhat named Trapusa Māra’s son. You shall possess the six supernormal powers and surely attain this vow."

"From that time forward, Trapusa and Bhallika practiced giving and observed the precepts, thereby attaining rebirth in the heavens. When their lives in the heavens ended, they were reborn in the human realm. Thus, through successive cycles, until the appearance of Śākyamuni in the world, they descended from the heavens to be born among humans. Having left the household life and attained the Way, they arose from meditative concentration and formed this thought:"
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I now beg two kinds of boons from the World-Honored One: first, that the dwellings be distributed among the various members of the Sangha; second, that those appointed for assemblies be assigned the distribution of food and drink.”
Thereupon the World-Honored One replied: "Excellent!
Since your greed and hatred have been exhausted, you are capable of this task; you should distribute the bedding and seats, as well as the various foods and drinks, for the assembly of monks."
“Why is it that this Trapusa Māra-putra has requested such a boon from the World-Honored One?
He replied:
"In order to prevent future slander:
thereupon, having received the World-Honored One’s command, Daivaputra returned to his dwelling.
The World-Honored One foresaw that because Daivaputra had been appointed to distribute the rooms, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra would inevitably give rise to slander."
In order to stop slander, he said to the bhikṣus:

"You should invite Dharmaruci to assign rooms for the communal distribution of goods for the Saṃgha; once the invitation is completed, you should perform the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint him."
"Those who study together" refers to those engaged in the same Dharma practice, which is also called studying the same Dharma learning.

If bhikṣus study the Sūtras together, they should arrange their seats and stay in one place; if they study the Abhidharma, those studying the Abhidharma should stay together; if they study the Vinaya, those studying the Vinaya should stay together; if they expound the Dharma, those expounding the Dharma should stay together; and if they practice meditation, those practicing meditation should stay together.

Why is this? It is for the sake of avoiding clamor and bustle. Those who engage in indeterminate speech without karmic intent, together with those who speak indeterminate speech, do not cultivate the three types of action; they sleep after eating, and upon waking, bathe and converse together on worldly, indeterminate talk, thereby causing their bodies to become stout and robust.
Question: "Why did Trapusa and Bhallika cause those who were fond of idle talk to dwell together in one place? Answer:
"Because he enables them to abide in the path of peace and because they delight in the path, they attain rebirth in the heavens.
As for entering the fire-light samādhi, this is the fourth dhyāna; having arisen from this meditative concentration, he emits light from the second finger of his right hand."
In a short while, his fame filled the land of Jambudvīpa; monks coming from distant regions, desiring to witness his supernormal powers, arrived and said to Trapusa Māra-putra:
"Venerable sir, please arrange a dwelling place for us and provide seats."
Then, Trapuṣa Māra’s son asked the venerable ones,
“In what places do you take pleasure in dwelling?
Each of the bhikṣus replied:
"I delight in dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain," he said; and again,
"I delight in dwelling on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains."
Again he said:
"I delight in dwelling on the mountain of the heavenly practitioners (ṛṣis).
Again he said:
"I delight in dwelling in Uttarakuru.

Thus, among this great multitude, each *tāpasa-mālava* (son of a hermit) followed a single bhikṣu; for the purpose of providing places of residence, they prepared beds and seats, and for the sake of settling other bhikṣus, they did so entirely through emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), which were no different from their actual bodies.
Having settled the bhikṣus, he returned to dwell at the Bamboo Grove Monastery himself.
As for the bhikṣu Maitrībala, he was the foremost among the group of six bhikṣus.
"Regarding 'poor food,' one does not obtain good food; not only poor food, but even dwellings and bedding are all obtained as poor.
He asked: "For what reason did the bhikṣu Maitrībala always receive poor rooms and poor food?"
"Because he lacked merit in his previous lives, he is also the youngest among the assembly; for this reason, he receives a poor room and poor food.
As for the donor of fine food and drink, this donor constantly prepares various delicacies and meals for the community of monks."
On another day, a generous donor entered the monastery and went to where Trapusa-māra was, asking:
"Venerable Sir,
who will be next to receive the invitation from my disciples tomorrow?"
Dabba replied, "The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra has accepted the invitation.
Upon hearing this, the donor was not pleased; he returned home and said to his maidservant:
"Tomorrow you shall prepare food for the bhikṣu Maitrībala; I am unfamiliar with such matters, so do not serve him as you did before.
She further said to her maidservant:
"If the bhikṣu Maitrībala arrives, simply spread out mats and bedding outside and provide the offerings, but do not allow him to enter."
"Yesterday, the bhikṣu Maitrībala gathered with his companions in one place and discussed together, saying:
'Today we shall obtain excellent food.'"
"Yesterday this donor came to Tapassa's place; it must have been Tapassa who instructed the donor to spread out mats and provide coarse food and drink outside."
"Wind arising where there is no wind" means that a great wind arises in an extremely secluded place.
"Fire within water" means that while water is fundamentally capable of extinguishing fire, now fire emerges from within the water.
The Buddha said to Trapusa:
"Do you recall having done such a thing?
Now the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra has spoken these words."
Dharmadatta replied:
"Only the World-Honored One knows me; the World-Honored One is the All-Knowing One, and I am an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted. Why should I need to speak?"
The Buddha spoke again to Trapusa, saying:
"You must not speak in such a manner. If you have committed such an act, declare that you have it before the assembly; if you have not, answer that you have not."
The Dharma Master asked:
"Why did the World-Honored One not speak directly, saying, 'Tapassu is without fault; this is a false statement by the bhikṣuṇī Cālā'?
He replied:
“Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Blessed One said:
‘I know, bhikṣu, that you have committed a pārājika offense; and the Blessed One also said: ‘I know that you have committed a pārājika offense.’”
If there is a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense, he will certainly slander the World-Honored One.

Why? Because the World-Honored One follows his own likes and dislikes; out of affection for Ṭhapanaka, he did not proclaim that man’s crime, but out of hatred for me, he now proclaims my crime. Therefore, the World-Honored One is certainly not omniscient.
Because of this slander, he fell into hell after death.

Furthermore, for the sake of shameless bhikṣus in the future who will claim they are without fault when they actually have faults, saying, "The Buddha is no longer in the world; who would know of my transgressions?"
Therefore, the Buddha said to Trapusa:
"If you have performed [the action], answer that you have performed it; if you have not performed it, answer that you have not performed it. Trapusa replied:
"I truly did not do it, even in my dreams I have not committed this act.

Regarding the "expulsion" (*nāśana*) of a bhikṣuṇī, there are three types of expulsion: first, expulsion of the person (*kāya-nāśana*); second, expulsion from communal residence (*asahavāsa-nāśana*); and third, expulsion by punishment (*daṇḍa-nāśana*). These are called the three expulsions.
“What is the cessation of the body? He replied:
“The cessation of the agent is the cessation of the body.”
“What is ‘exclusion through non-cohabitation’?
If one commits an offense and does not confess it, nor renounces wrong views, this is called ‘exclusion through non-cohabitation.
What is ‘exclusion by penalty’?”
“Your offenses shall naturally be extinguished simply by your acting; this is the extinction through punishment.
This Bhikṣuṇī Cīrā has attained extinction of her person through one of the three methods of extinction.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Expel the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī.
The Dharma Master said:
"This Bhikṣuṇī Cīmā is pure in body; she was taught by another person to spread such a slander, and the one who taught her should be expelled.
Why, World-Honored One, did you teach that the Bhikṣuṇī Cīmā be expelled?"
“Is he expelled because of his slander, or is he expelled because of his commission of an offense?
If he were expelled because he has committed an offense, then Ṭhapassī the son of Māra would also have an offense;
if he is expelled because of his slander, then Ṭhapassī is without offense.”
It is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If a bhikṣu slanders a bhikṣu with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If a bhikṣu slanders a bhikṣuṇī with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, it is a duṣkṛta."
The case of a bhikṣuṇī slandering a bhikṣu is also like this.
If that were so, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī would incur a duṣkṛta for her slander, and a pāyattika for her lying.
The Dharma Master said:
"To defame a bhikṣu with groundless charges of a pārājika offense constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa; there is no pāyattika offense.
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī committed a duṣkṛta, yet there was likewise no pāyattika offense. The reason for the expulsion of the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī was that she herself admitted her transgression."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and entered his chamber; the bhikṣus immediately instructed the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī to remove her dharma robes, seeking white lay garments for her to wear, and then drove her out.
The bhikṣu Maitrakanyaka, seeing that the bhikṣuṇī Maitrakanyaka had been expelled, said to the Saṃgha:
"Because I was driven by anger, I instructed the bhikṣuṇī to bring false accusations; this is my own fault. Do not expel the bhikṣuṇī Maitrakanyaka."
"Anger" refers to the turning away from a wholesome mind.
"Displeasure" means that because of anger, one loses the mind of joy; this displeasure is also called a defilement of the mind.
Regarding the "groundless *pārājika* offense," this refers to a *pārājika* that lacks reality.
To slander means not to see, not to hear, and not to doubt this matter.
"Not to see" means not seeing it with one's own fleshly eye, nor seeing it with one's own divine eye.
"Not having heard" means not having heard it from another person.
"Not doubting" means not doubting it with one's mind. Regarding "one who has seen and doubted":

there was a bhikṣu who, outside a village, entered some grass and then bent down; a woman also entered the grass. The bhikṣu first emerged from the grass, and the woman subsequently emerged from that same grass; the bhikṣu and the woman were each unaware of the other.
A bystander monk, having seen this, immediately gave rise to doubt and thought to himself:
"Could these two not have an unrighteous intent?
This is called doubt based on what has been seen.

"Doubt based on what was heard" (*śrutakaṅkṣā*) refers to when one hears the sound of a bhikṣu speaking with a woman in the dark; because of this, doubt arises—this is called "doubt based on what was heard.

"Doubt based on doubt" (*vicikitsākaṅkṣā*) refers to when men and women take food and drink into a monastery, and after they have gone away to watch and play, the remaining food and drink lie scattered and impure in their places, and have not yet been swept away.

The next morning at dawn, a visiting bhikṣu came into the monastery; upon seeing this place, he immediately conceived a doubt. Furthermore, when he reached the former bhikṣu and smelled the fragrance on his body, he again doubted, saying:
"It must be that last night this bhikṣu provided food and drink for a woman and engaged in unrighteous sexual misconduct with her."
This is called "doubt regarding doubt.
If the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra neither sees, nor hears, nor suspects [the offense], yet gives rise to slander, this is called "slandering with groundless charges of a pārājika offense."

As for "slandering," it means wishing to cause that bhikṣu to fall away from the pure dharma; if one says, "You have committed a pārājika offense" or "You have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense," or if one instructs another to slander him, every such utterance constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one sends a letter such as this, the messenger who writes it incurs no offense.
There are four kinds of slander:
first, slander regarding precepts; second, slander regarding dignified conduct; third, slander regarding false views; and fourth, slander regarding wrong livelihood.
Question: "What is meant by 'slandering the precepts'? Answer:
"If one slanders [a monk] by means of each of the four *pārājika* rules or the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, this is called 'slander regarding the precepts' (*śīla-vivāda*).
The remaining two *aniyata* rules, the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, and the ninety *śaikṣa* rules are all 'slander regarding deportment' (*īryāpatha-vivāda*)."
Regarding "slandering through wrong view": to say that this body possesses a self or an ego is called slandering through wrong view.
Regarding "slandering through a wicked livelihood": to seek gain and offerings by means of maintaining the precepts is called slandering through a wicked livelihood.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of slander:
first, manifesting the location; second, manifesting the offense; third, not dwelling together; and fourth, not participating in communal Dharma activities.
Regarding "manifesting the location": if one says, "You have committed sexual misconduct with a woman," this is called manifesting the location.
"Manifesting an offense" means that you have committed a grave offense; this is called "manifesting an offense.
"Not living together" means that I do not dwell in the same place with you; this is called "not living together."

Regarding "unshared legal matters" (*asādhāraṇa-karmavastu*): the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and all *karmans* are distinct; these are called unshared legal matters.
If one says, "You have committed a grave offense; you are not a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya," such speech constitutes an offense.
If the one who has been slandered says,
"Why do you not pay homage to me?
he should reply:
"You are not a śramaṇa; you are not of the Śākya lineage.
If one answers in this manner, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one says, "The Dharma Master knows for himself; why rely on my words? such speech does not constitute an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The slanderer and the one who is slandered shall be explained in detail later.
The slanderer goes together with [the victim] before the Saṃgha and addresses the Saṃgha, saying:"
"We pray that the Venerable Ones will joyfully adjudicate this matter for us; we, too, shall joyfully carry it out.
The Saṃgha should then adjudicate this matter.
If one says:
"May the Sangha adjudicate this matter for me without delay; if it is so, I shall accept and uphold it, but if it is not so, I shall not accept it."
If anyone speaks such words, the Saṃgha shall say to the slanderer:
"First, pay homage to the Buddha and let him preach the Dharma for you; afterwards, we shall adjudicate this matter for you."
If they delay until dusk, the offender says to the community of monks, "The sun has already set; I shall now return to my dwelling.
The monks reply, "Very well. Once he has recovered his breath, he returns to the midst of the monks at dawn the following morning to seek a judgment on this matter, and the monks reply:
"Go back for now.
This was said up to three times.
When the three repetitions were thus completed, his mind became softened and subdued; the Saṃgha should then take this matter as the basis for its judgment.
Although he had made his request three times, his mind remained stubborn and his speech coarse;
the assembly of monks said to him, "There are few masters of the Vinaya here, so we cannot adjudicate this matter for you. You should go to another monastery to seek a judgment."
The community of monks asked,
"Have you already requested [ordination] from the Sangha? He replied:
"I have already sought out the Saṃgha, who instructed me to come here.
The monks said, "If that is the case, there is likewise no Vinaya master here; you may seek one at another monastery."
Having searched in this manner in succession without success, their minds softened and subdued, they returned to their original place and addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"We have sought the Saṃgha in various places, but no one has adjudicated. We pray that the Venerable Ones will adjudicate this matter for us; we shall joyfully carry out your instructions."
The assembly of monks should adjudicate according to the Dharma.
The monks shall ask the one who has been slandered:
"Do you have these things?"

The community of monks should perform a formal act of announcement (*jñapti-karman*) to harmoniously settle this matter of contention. If those who lack shame and remorse slander those who possess shame and remorse, the one being slandered possesses wisdom while the slanderer lacks wisdom.
If the assembled monks have dispersed, one should interrogate this matter thoroughly; since this bhikṣu is dull-witted and his responses are erroneous and perverse, the monks should say to him:
"You are ignorant and lack understanding; why do you slander others?"
"You should all return together in harmony and not raise this matter.
If the accuser possesses wisdom and is able to answer before the Sangha regarding the charge based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, the assembly of monks should then question the accused.
If there are those with faults, the Saṃgha should discipline them; if there are no faults, the Saṃgha should reply:
"Each of you should return to your own places.
If one who possesses a sense of shame slanders one who lacks a sense of shame, the slanderer is deluded.
If someone comes to accuse the Sangha, the Sangha should skillfully ask the accuser:
"On what basis do you accuse us?
Do you accuse us on account of the precepts?"
"Is he slandering [me] because of my deportment?
The Dharma Master said:
"Why is it that you teach those who possess shame and remorse, yet do not teach those who lack them? Thus, the Saṃgha follows along with attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion?"
He replied: "It is not so. Why is this?"
It is for the purpose of subduing those who lack a sense of shame and remorse, and so that those who possess such a sense may dwell in peace and happiness;

for if one were to instruct those lacking shame and remorse, their power would increase their unwholesome dharmas, while those possessing shame and remorse would lose their strength and fail to dwell in peace and happiness. Therefore, the Saṃgha does not instruct those who lack shame and remorse.

If both the slanderer and the one being slandered possess a sense of shame and remorse, the Sangha should treat them with gentleness and speak to them for the purpose of teaching and transforming them, saying:
"If you have committed offenses against one another, you should further confess and apologize to each other; you should each return to live together in harmony."

If, regarding a matter of mutual slander, the Saṃgha has reached up to three attempts at reconciliation and harmonization yet they still refuse to desist, the Saṃgha should adjudicate according to the Dharma.
The Dharma Master asked:
"How are the beginning, middle, and end of slandering the Dharma defined?
He replied:
"First, one requests permission; this is the beginning. If the Saṃgha is convened, this is the middle. If the Saṃgha extinguishes [the offense], whether there be guilt or no guilt, this is the end."
Question: "How many faculties (indriya) and how many stages (bhūmi) are there for slandering the Dharma? Answer:
“Slander has two roots, three bases, and five grounds.
“What are the two roots? “Slander regarding dharmas that have a basis and slander regarding dharmas that lack a basis; these are called the two roots.”
“What are the three bases?
‘Seeing, hearing, and doubt’—these are called the three bases.
What are the five grounds?”

"First, it is timely; second, it is truthful and not false; third, it is free from anger and motivated by a heart of compassion; fourth, it is meaningful; fifth, it is not driven by attachment or fear—these are called the five grounds."

Whether questioned or not, if one has slandered another with a groundless *pārājika* offense, and whether the Saṃgha questions him, or two or three persons, or even a single person, if he confesses it himself before the Saṃgha, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"There are four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), and mutual accusation is the first.
What is the meaning of 'dispute'?"
“‘To settle a matter by means of a formal adjudication of an offense—this is called a dispute.
‘Regarding this characteristic of verbal dispute, is it wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?’”
He replied:
"It is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
What is wholesome?"
What is unwholesome?
That which is spoken according to the Dharma is called wholesome;
that which is spoken contrary to the Dharma is called unwholesome.
"That which is not adjudicated according to the Dharma nor according to what is not the Dharma is called 'indeterminate' (avyākṛta).
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining three types of disputes shall be explained later."

If one says: "You are a śrāmaṇera; you are an upāsaka; you are a non-Buddhist; you are a nirgrantha; you are a eunuch; you are a person with dual sexual organs; you are an animal; you have killed your father; you have killed your mother; you have killed an arhat; you have caused a schism in the Saṃgha; you have shed the blood of a Buddha."
"Thus, beginning with this, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Regarding 'doubt' (*vicikitsā*):
it refers to doubt regarding what has been seen or heard; 'suspicion' (*kāṅkṣā*) refers to having two minds, or alternatively, it means forgetting a previous matter, such as a specific time or date."
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are easy to understand.
If a bhikṣu slanders another with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
If one slanders by means of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one slanders by means of the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, out of anger, one slanders someone who is not present, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one slanders another by claiming that their conduct regarding the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) is not manifest, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
This precept arises from body and mind; therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla that bodily, verbal, and mental actions constitute natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
The detailed exposition on the slander of the precepts is concluded.

"At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka-nivāpa. The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra, descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, saw a sheep engaging in sexual intercourse."
The bhikṣu Maitrībala said to his companions:
"Let us take a ram named Ṭhapanaka as the son of Māra, and take a ewe as the bhikṣuṇī Maitrībala."
The bhikṣus replied, "Excellent!
By slandering Dharmatāpasa with this teaching, we shall surely not fail.
Delighted, they went together to where the Saṃgha was and addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"We have seen that Trapusa Māra-putra engaged in sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇī Cīrṇa.
Having heard these words from the bhikṣuṇī Cīrṇa, the community of monks immediately assembled and together adjudicated this matter.
The assembly of monks asked the bhikṣu Cidi:
"In what specific place did you see the Venerable Trapusa engaging in sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇī Cidi?"
They replied:
"We descended from Vulture Peak to enter the village for alms, and on the way we encountered Ṭhapassamāla conversing and joking with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī."
The assembly of monks asked Tapassu (沓婆摩羅子), saying:
"At that time, where were you? Tapassu replied:
“At the Veṇuvana Monastery. “What have you done?
He replied to the assembly of monks:
"I am distributing food and drink for the community of monks.
[The other asked: "Who saw you? He replied:
"Regarding 'the Saṃgha’s knowledge and vision':
when asking, one performs the *jñapti-karman* (motion) to inquire of the Saṃgha:
'At such and such times, did you definitely see Trapuṣa distributing food and drink to the Saṃgha?'"
The assembly of monks replied,
"We truly saw him dividing food for the Sangha.
The assembly of monks then questioned the bhikṣu Maitrībala:
"Your words are inconsistent; they must be a mere expedient and not the truth.
After the community of monks had questioned him thus three times, the bhikṣu Maitrībala replied:
"It is indeed so; this is an expedient."
The assembly of monks rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala, saying:
"How can you give away the remaining portion of the goods to Trapusa? He asked:
"What is meant by 'substitution'? He replied, "'Substitution' refers to this case:
Tapussa is a human being and the sheep is a non-human being; using the sheep in the place of Tapussa is called substitution."
Taking a ewe as an analogy for the bhikṣuṇī Cimidì is also called "an additional portion. Why?
Because the circumstances are analogous.
