Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: whether it be a fragment or something resembling a fragment, the sequential phrases are easily understood and need not be explained in detail; this is called the "remaining portion" (śeṣa).

Regarding those of the same caste: there was a bhikṣu who had likewise gone forth from the kṣatriya caste. Seeing that kṣatriya committing sexual misconduct, he slandered this kṣatriya bhikṣu, saying, "You have committed a pārājika offense."
The community of monks asked him,
"Did you truly see this Kṣatriya committing sexual misconduct?
He replied:
"If it is true that he saw it," [if one says this], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for every such statement.
Regarding the characteristics and names of the dwelling, if one sees that person and slanders another, whether an offense is committed or not is as previously explained.

Regarding those who are without offense: if one has actually seen [the act] committed; if the precept has not yet been established at the outset; if one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain; these do not constitute an offense.
This concludes the detailed explanation of the second section on slander.

At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. Regarding this precept on the schism of the Saṃgha, Devadatta went to where Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta were; having arrived, he spoke to those elders, saying:
"Let us together bring about a schism in the Saṃgha and challenge the majestic power of the Tathāgata."
The causes and conditions regarding the schism of the Saṃgha will be explained later in the section on Khaṇḍaka.
"Excellent, O Venerable One" is a form of request.
"May all bhikṣus dwell in araṇya hermitages for as long as they live"—this is the undertaking of the dhūta practices.
“If a bhikṣu returns to dwell within a village and commits an offense, we pray that the Buddha will establish a precept for the bhikṣus accordingly; the same applies to the other four rules.

We wish to let others know this, so that although the Buddha does not follow our regulations, we ourselves shall practice these dharmas, thereby letting others know that we have few desires and are content, and thus inspire in them a great mind of goodness.”
When the Buddha heard that Devadatta was requesting five points of discipline with the intent to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, he thought to himself:
"For the sake of gain and offerings, this man will surely fall into hell."
The Buddha thought to himself:
"If I were to grant Devadatta these five points, many sons of good family would leave the household life; if they were to accept and uphold these rules, there would be obstacles to the Path."
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "Stop, stop, Devadatta! Do not establish this teaching.
Whether a son of good family dwells in an araṇya or in a village, let each follow what his heart desires without obstructing the Path."
“[The practitioner] practices dhūta by begging for food, discarding rag-robes, staying under a tree for half a month, and abstaining from fish and meat.
The Buddha said:
‘One abstains from eating [meat] except when there are three doubts.’”
What are the three doubts?
First, seeing; second, hearing; third, doubting.
What is seeing?
Seeing that a donor has killed [an animal] for the sake of a bhikṣu.
What is "hearing"?
Hearing that a donor has killed [an animal] for the sake of a bhikṣu.
What is doubt? It is the doubt that [the person] was killed by a bhikṣu.
If one sees with doubt, how does one see with doubt?

A bhikṣu entered a village from an araṇya to beg for food; on the way, he encountered several laypeople entering the mountains to hunt. The next day, there was a great assembly in the village, and the bhikṣus obtained meat at the gathering.
They thought to themselves: "Yesterday we saw these donors going hunting; we suspect this meat must have been obtained through that hunt."
This is called "doubt regarding what has been seen," and one must not eat.
However, if a donor says:
"I originally went hunting for the sake of the king and for myself, not for the sake of the bhikṣus; Venerable Sir, please eat."
"If it is as described above, eating is without fault.
Regarding 'hearing with suspicion': suppose a bhikṣu staying in an araṇya hears that a village has organized a hunting feast.
If a donor invites the bhikṣu to eat, and the bhikṣu eats with a suspicious mind, he incurs an offense."
If a donor says,
"I am hunting for my own sake, not for the sake of the bhikṣus," and if it is so,
there is no fault in eating; this is called "suspicion based on what was heard."
If one does not see, hear, or suspect that a bhikṣu has killed [the animal], eating in such a manner is without fault; however, there are cases where one may eat having seen [the act].
What constitutes eating having seen it?

If one sees someone slaughtering [an animal] and does not act as a bhikṣu [to prevent it], yet later obtains meat to eat, there is no offense; this is called "eating what was obtained after seeing the slaughter" (diṭṭha-vidita), which is without offense.

Regarding "hearing" (suta): if a bhikṣu personally hears the sound of slaughter and does not act as a bhikṣu [to prevent it], and the bhikṣu subsequently obtains this meat, the bhikṣu may eat it without offense; this is called "hearing."

There is no offense in receiving food when one has doubts; as for "having doubts," it means that when a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for alms and sees fresh meat, he hesitates and does not dare to accept it. If a donor says:
"This was not killed for the sake of the bhikṣu."
If one receives food in this way, there is no offense; this is called "receiving food with doubt.
If a donor has killed an animal for the sake of a bhikṣu, yet one neither sees, hears, nor suspects it, there is no offense in receiving and eating the food.
If a donor invites two people for a meal, the junior monk thinks to himself:
"This [food] will be killed for the senior monk and not for me; therefore, it is no fault for me to eat."
The Elder further thought to himself:
"This [food] must have been killed for the junior monk; it was not originally intended for me. Therefore, my eating it is without fault.
If this were the case, both would each suspect it was for the other; thus, whether senior or junior, if they eat while harboring such mutual suspicion, there is no fault.
If a person kills someone for the sake of a bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu does not know it until after he has finished eating, there is no offense in such a case.
However, if a bhikṣu obtains meat, he should inquire before consuming it.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to distinguish between pure and impure food.
Since bear meat resembles pork, and there are other things that likewise resemble it—not only bear and pork—therefore, one should inquire.
"Regarding 'rejoicing and leaping for joy': Devadatta requested five points, but the World-Honored One did not grant them. Devadatta rejoiced and thought to himself:
'I shall now certainly succeed in breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha.'"
Upon hearing these words, Kokālika was deeply distressed in his heart, no different from having swallowed a potent poison.
Devadatta exhorted his companions, saying:
"Why are you so distressed?"

"One who has left the household life to seek the Way ought to be diligent; the śramaṇa Gautama also possesses this rule. Since it does not require the end of one's natural lifespan, I shall now uphold this rule for as long as I live. Why, then, do you grieve?"
"Having heard this, his companions followed him with joy.
The Dharma Master said:

"The foolish Devadatta, unaware and unknowing that he was already heading toward the Avīci Hell, joyfully prostrated before the Buddha and departed. He then returned to Kaukṛtya and the others and said:"
"We shall practice these five dharmas together with you, so that people will know us to be of few desires and content.
To have many desires and no sense of satisfaction means to receive clothing and food without moderation; this is called having many desires and no sense of satisfaction.
Devadatta said to his companions:
"The śramaṇa Gautama constantly thinks to himself, 'How can my śrāvaka disciples obtain clothing and food without it being a hardship for them?'"
"This is a person of excessive desire who knows no contentment.
The Buddha said to Devadatta, "Do not take pleasure in this practice of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; it is a grave offense."

If the Saṃgha is in harmony, like water and milk mixed together, they practice in peace and happiness; if one should cause such a Saṃgha to be split, they will suffer various pains in the Avīci Hell for one kalpa.
If one can cause a split Saṃgha to be reconciled once more, they will rejoice in the heavens for one kalpa, receiving the blessings of Brahmā.

“The monks preached the Dharma to Devadatta using various skillful means. Seeing that Devadatta was destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, the virtuous monks exhorted him through various skillful means, causing him to attain understanding, so that his mind and body became one with the Saṃgha, merging like water and milk.”
"Sameness of mind" means sameness in regard to the Dharma.
"Sameness of body" means that their bodies are together in a single harmonious *poṣadha*.
What is meant by "not being of the same body"?
Although they are in one place together, their minds and conduct follow external dharmas; this is called "form is the same, but mind is different.
To "firmly maintain and not abandon" means to persistently cling to the matter of schism in the Saṃgha without relinquishing it; this is called "firmly maintaining [the position] among the bhikṣus."
Regarding "admonishing that bhikṣu": those bhikṣus who possess a sense of shame and propriety should admonish the [other] bhikṣus, saying, "Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
live in harmony with the Saṃgha. Those bhikṣus should admonish them three times. If they relinquish [the course of action], it is well.

If they do not relinquish it, for failing to relinquish it at the first admonition there is a *dukkaṭa* offense; for failing to relinquish it at the second admonition there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and for failing to relinquish it at the third admonition there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "admonishing from without": when the bhikṣus hear that someone intends to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, they go to that person's location and admonish them, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Do not break the harmony of the Saṃgha."
"If one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha is extremely grave, it would be well if you were to desist.
If he does not desist, they shall take him by the hand and lead him before the Saṃgha, saying:
"Do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha."
Thus he was admonished three times.

When he was further admonished three times with gentle words outside the assembly, and again when he was admonished three times with gentle words upon being brought into the midst of the Saṃgha, yet still did not relinquish [his position], he committed the offense of *duṣkṛta* in each instance.
If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, one should admonish him by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

If he does not relinquish it during the initial motion, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he does not relinquish it during the first proclamation, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense; the second proclamation also results in a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and if he does not relinquish it during the third proclamation, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Question: "Regarding the third *karmavācanā*, does one incur the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end? Answer:
"He who attained [the fruit] last but was the first to commit an offense was Devadatta.
He asked: "If other precepts were not originally committed by anyone else, Devadatta should likewise not have committed them?"
He replied:
"Because he did not relinquish [his position] despite the three-fold admonition by the Saṃgha, he therefore committed an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential phrasing is easily understood and need not be explained in detail.
This precept involves three factors: the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of suffering.
The explanation of the schism of the Saṃgha is concluded."

"At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. Regarding the second precept concerning the breaking of the Saṃgha, those who assist in the schism take pleasure in following [the schismatic] and uphold his doctrine."

"To be apart from the assembly" means to not participate in the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts, or the *pravāraṇā*; to act as an aid in breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha and preventing the Saṃgha from flourishing—this is called being apart from the assembly.
"Venerable sirs, that which we can endure and know—if what they say is such, we shall all endure it and know it.

Venerable sirs, do not assist in the breaking of a harmonious Saṃgha; you should instead assist in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha. When the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and without dispute, it is like water and milk mixed together."
The remaining phrases are easily understood.
The remaining phrases are no different from the previous discussion on schism in the Saṃgha.
The second [section] on schism in the Saṃgha is concluded.

"At that time, the Buddha was staying at Kuśāmbī in the Gosṛta Garden. Regarding the precepts on being difficult to speak with due to a wicked nature, there were those who practiced unwholesome conduct through various physical and verbal actions."
"Elder! Why do you speak such words to me?
These are words of arrogance."
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain its meaning.
This bhikṣu of evil character did not accept the instructions of the other bhikṣus, saying:"
"You should not instruct me; rather, I should instruct you.
Why is this? For the Buddha is the Buddha of my own house."

Why is this? When I accompanied Kanthaka to lead the Buddha into the mountains to study the Way, I did not see a single one of these elders serving as an attendant to the Buddha. Now that the Buddha has attained the Way and turned the Wheel of Dharma, he is the Buddha of my own house, and the Dharma is likewise the Dharma of my own house. Therefore, I ought to instruct these elders; the elders should not, in turn, instruct me.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why did the bhikṣu Channa not say, 'The Saṃgha is my own Saṃgha'?
Because he was quarreling with the assembly of monks, he could not say that the Saṃgha was his own Saṃgha."
"Venerable elders, it is just as when the leaves of trees fall to the ground in autumn and are blown together by the wind into one place;
or as when duckweed floats upon the water and is driven together into one place by the wind."
Just as these elders have entered the Buddha-dharma through various forms of renunciation, so it is with me.
Therefore, these elders should not instruct me; rather, I should instruct them.
Having made himself one with whom he may not converse, when his fellow monks instruct him according to the Prātimokṣa, he refuses their words because of his arrogance.

Those with whom one may converse are so called because they speak together regarding the *prātimokṣa* and emerge together from shared transgressions; it is for this reason that one attains growth within the Buddha-dharma.
The sequential phrases are easy to understand.
The detailed exposition on the precepts for those of evil character is concluded.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Thirteen.
*The Vinaya-vibhāṣā of the Well-Seen*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī; he had defiled the families [of lay supporters]."
There were two bhikṣus, one named Aśvajit and the other named Pūrṇa.
They resided on Mount Kukkuṭapāda—this is the name of a village.

These two bhikṣus constantly managed the monastery buildings within the monastic complex of that village; because of their administrative duties, they conversed and socialized with laypeople without any sense of shame or modesty.
Regarding the bhikṣus who defile their families: these were Aśvakapunarvasu, who were the seniormost among the group of six bhikṣus.
Aśvakapunarvasu were originally farmers who labored together in the fields. The two of them discussed it together, saying:
"We have worked hard at farming; let us go forth together so that food and clothing may be provided for us naturally within the Buddha-dharma."
The companion replied,
"Excellent; so be it," and they deliberated further together:
"We should now go forth under whom?
We shall go forth under Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Having deliberated thus, they went to where Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were and requested to go forth.

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana immediately ordained him and conferred full ordination upon him. After he had finished reciting the Prātimokṣa and completed five years of seniority, he obtained two companions: one named the Bhikṣu Yellow-Red and the other named the Bhikṣu Compassionate Ground.
The four men discussed together, saying:
"In this city of Śrāvastī, there are times of abundance and times of famine. It is not fitting for us to remain gathered in one place; we should instead disperse to other countries."
The three men said to the bhikṣus Huang and Chi:
"Venerable sirs!
Where would you like to dwell?"
The bhikṣu Huangchi replied, “I delight in dwelling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. [The Buddha asked:

“Within the city of this kingdom, there are five hundred and seventy thousand households; outside the city, there are eighty thousand villages belonging to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, and the territory is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”

In your dwelling place within this country, plant many kinds of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, such as the mango tree (*āmra*), the *panasa* tree, and the coconut tree; likewise, plant many such trees, as well as various flowers such as the *campaka*, the *jāti*, and the *mallikā*. With these flowers and fruits, provide for and comfort the householders and their wives. If any among the householders desire to leave the household life, you should ordain them so that the number of your followers may increase.
He asked the bhikṣu Maitrībala again,
"In what place do you delight to dwell?
He replied:
"I delight in dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha.

In the kingdom of Rājagṛha there are eight hundred million households; beyond the towns, there are eighty thousand villages belonging to Rājagṛha. The territory is three hundred yojanas in length and breadth. You shall plant many trees bearing flowers and fruits in this land, and you shall deliver people for them to leave the household life, no different from what was previously described."
Next, he asked the horse trainer,
"Where do you reside?
The horse trainer replied:
"I would like to dwell in the village of Kālaparvata; this village has abundant food and drink, with three harvests a year.
He then asked Pūrṇamāsa, "Where would you like to dwell?"
Pūrṇa replied, "I would delight to dwell together with Aśvajit. [The Buddha said:
"You two should properly maintain the dwelling place, plant many trees bearing flowers and fruit, and thereby provide comfort to the laymen and laywomen."
After these four bhikṣus had thus collectively settled their arrangements, each returned to his own residence to manage his dwelling and ordain others for the homeless life.

Each of the three residences had five hundred disciples; together there were fifteen hundred bhikṣus. The disciples and followers of the Yellow and Red Bhikṣu were all fully endowed with the precepts. Leading his disciples and followers, he traveled from country to country with the Buddha, upholding the precepts established by the Buddha without violation, though he did violate those not yet established.

These three types of people, wherever they dwell, lack a sense of shame and remorse; they commit offenses both when the Buddha has already established a precept and when he has not yet established one.

Such evil bhikṣus do what should not be done and engage in what should not be practiced. Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "As for those who plant flowers—whether planting them themselves or instructing others to plant them, whether a single kind of flower or many kinds of flowers, whether watering them themselves or instructing others to water them, or digging the earth themselves to make ponds or instructing others to dig them to store water, whether for bathing or for sprinkling on flowers—all such acts are unwholesome."
If one constructs a pond for the Sangha, or constructs one for oneself, one must not instruct others by saying "dig"; rather, one commits no offense if one uses pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*).
If one constructs a garden for the Sangha, or constructs a garden for oneself, or plants trees for the sake of providing shade and coolness, in all such cases one must use pure speech.

If one plants various flowers and fruits for the sake of providing relief to laymen and laywomen—whether planting them oneself or instructing others to plant them—it is all *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing). However, if one plants them for the sake of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, there is no offense, provided that one does not dig the ground or damage the seeds. If one plants fruit trees for the sake of the Saṃgha, one may eat the fruit without fault. If there is water free of insects, one may water the plants oneself or instruct others to water them without fault.
Furthermore, the Dharma Master said:
"One may teach others to plant [seeds] by using pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*).
What is pure speech?..."
"You must cause this tree to live and not let it die.

The attendant (kappiya-kāraka) shall tend to it at the proper times and water it. You must not string flowers together to form garlands for laypeople; nor may you scatter loose flowers or tie them into bundles, except when making offerings to the Triple Gem."
Regarding those who must not dance: it is forbidden to move the body, down to the extent of raising one's hands.

There is no offense if, for instance, a layperson (śrāvaka) has a bhikṣu prostrate before the Buddha, recite sutras, or offer prayers; or if they have a bhikṣu strike the chime to assemble the community for various acts of dharma such as giving offerings; being thus employed by a layperson constitutes no offense.
The remaining phrases are found in the Vinaya and are easy to understand.
If a bhikṣu is ill and lacks medicinal decoctions, he may offer flowers, fruits, or other food and drink to others in exchange for medicinal decoctions; this does not constitute an offense.

If one is employed by a layperson (*avadātavasana*), at the very first step of departing, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* for each step; if one receives food or drink, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* for every swallow; even down to acting as a messenger for a layperson, answering questions as they arise constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* in every instance. This does not apply when one is employed by members of the fivefold community of renunciants (*pañca-nikāya*).

If one seeks medicinal decoctions or employs laborers on behalf of a parent who is ill, or on behalf of a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) of the Saṃgha who is ill, there is no offense. The detailed exposition on "defiling another's family" is concluded.
"Once the *pārivāsika* (probation) has been completed, one next undergoes the six-night *mānatva*.
One who practices *mānatva*—in the Han language, this means 'subduing arrogance,' and it is also called 'lowering the mind.'"
"To humble one's mind" means to serve the community of monks and undergo the *ābṛhaṇa* ceremony within a group of twenty monks.
*Ābṛhaṇa* is translated in the Han language as "calling back in," and it is also said to mean "extricating from sin."
"What is meant by 'summoning to enter and extract the offense'?

It refers to performing the communal rites of the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) together with them; because of this shared participation, it is called 'summoning to enter and extract the offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules have been fully explained.
Next come the two *aniyata* rules.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. Then, when there was no one else around, the Questioner asked a female lay follower (*upāsikā*):"
"Are you not troubled by anxiety, fatigue, hunger, or thirst? Does your husband think of you?
Thus he questioned her entirely with the speech of a layperson.
As for "preaching the Dharma upon seeing someone," it means that as soon as one sees a person, one immediately preaches the Dharma for them.

As for those who preach the Dharma, they may preach the five precepts, or the eight precepts, or eating after the time of returning from alms-round, or eating by means of *śalākā* (lots), or eating once every half-month; in such various ways they preach the Dharma for them.
"Many children" means that this upāsikā gave birth to ten sons and ten daughters; thus she was called "One with Many Children.

"Many grandchildren" means that each of her sons and daughters had twenty children of their own, totaling four hundred and twenty descendants. When the people of the country saw that Viśākhā, the mother, had so many sons, daughters, and grandchildren, they all discussed it together, saying:
"How excellent!"
"If there are those who come to take wives or husbands according to custom, this place is fit for the practice of sexual intercourse.

As for 'sitting in a secluded place,' it refers to a bhikṣu sitting with a woman; or a woman lying down while the bhikṣu sits; or the bhikṣu lying down while the woman sits; or both lie down together, or both sit together."
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "The eye-secluded and the ear-secluded.
What is the eye-secluded?
It is in the presence of one who has no eyes.
What is meant by "screening with the ear"?
It means speaking in the presence of a deaf person, or in the presence of a deaf-blind person, or in the presence of a sleeping person, or in the presence of a woman.
A "person of trustworthy speech" refers to a disciple of this upāsikā who is a śrāvaka.
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "One who has attained the fruits [of the path] is called a trustworthy upāsikā.
If a bhikṣu says, "I sat together with an upāsikā," [he is at fault].
"If each individual offense is to be adjudicated according to the testimony of the bhikṣu, it must not be adjudicated according to the testimony of the upāsikā.
Why is this? Because what was seen or heard may not have been thoroughly verified."
The Dharma Master said:
"I now wish to relate this matter.
In the Māra Garden Monastery, there was a bhikṣu named Ājñātakauṇḍinya who one day went to the house of a donor and sat inside."

An upāsikā was standing beside a separate bed leaning against it when an ordinary bhikṣu entered the householder’s home to beg for food. Seeing from afar that the bhikṣu and the upāsikā were facing each other, he said:
"They are sitting together on the same bed and gazing at one another without ceasing."
The monk Āyasmā Piyajātika thought to himself: "This monk will say:
'I sat on the same bed with a woman.'"

Each returned to their respective dwellings. A bhikṣu who wished to raise the charge against him went to the room of the bhikṣu Vītarāga to seek his permission; he knocked on the door, intending to enter.
The bhikṣu who had exhausted all craving anticipated his mind; he immediately used his supernormal power to emerge from the ridgepole of the roof and sat in mid-air.
After [the other] bhikṣu had entered, he searched everywhere but could not find him. Seeing him sitting in mid-air, he said to the bhikṣu who had exhausted all craving, "Venerable sir!..."
"If you possess such supernormal power as this, why did you enter the home of a layperson and sit on the same bed alone with a woman?
The bhikṣu Ajita replied, "Elder!..."
"This is the offense of entering the house of a layperson alone; Venerable Sir, please protect me well.
The Dharma Master said:
"This was seen but not clearly understood; therefore, it constitutes the offense of entering the house of a layperson alone. For this reason, what was seen cannot be trusted."
If a bhikṣu wishes to enter a village and desires to sit in a secluded place with a woman, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense at the moment he puts on his robes and takes up his bowl.
If he sets out and departs, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense with every step.
If one goes to the house of a donor and sits in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika offense.
If, having left, one returns and sits again, there is a pāyattika offense for each instance.
If one sits together with many women, there are as many pāyattika offenses as there are women.
If a bhikṣu is already in a secluded place when a woman enters to pay homage and inquire after his well-being, it is not an offense.
This arises from both body and mind.
The detailed exposition of the first *aniyata-dharma* is concluded.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī. Regarding the phrase 'in an open, uncovered place,' this refers to a location that is not concealed.

'A bhikṣu and a woman' means a place where there is no man present who could engage in coarse or evil speech, with the exception of a man who understands [the nature of such speech]. The remaining phrases are no different from those explained in the initial *aniyata-dharma*."
Regarding those who are without offense: there is no transgression for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
This precept is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) arising from body and mind, and is subsumed under the feelings of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
The detailed exposition of the two *aniyata* [undetermined offenses] is concluded.
Next comes the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offenses involving forfeiture].
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vaiśālī, at the Gautama Temple, where he permitted the bhikṣus to keep the three robes.
What are the three?
First, the antaravāsaka; second, the uttarāsaṅga; and third, the saṃghāṭī.
These are called the three robes.
The Dharma Master said:
"The explanation of the three robes will be discussed in detail in the *Khandhaka* section on the *Cīvara-vastu*.

Regarding the use of other robes when entering a village: one puts on different clothes upon entering a room, and puts on different clothes when entering a village; this continues in such a manner up to nine types of robes."
"The Buddha has already permitted us to keep the three robes; because of these words, each of us kept three sets of the three robes, which resulted in nine robes in total.

As for those we wished to give to the Elder Śāriputra," at that time the Elder Ānanda said, "With the exception of the World-Honored Buddha, among all the other śrāvaka disciples, none can equal Śāriputra."
"Therefore, Ānanda, if you obtain a kāṣāya robe that has been dyed, treated, and purified, offer the best one to Śāriputra;
if you obtain timely food, offer the best to Śāriputra first;
and if you obtain non-timely liquids, seven-day medicines, or lifelong medicines, offer the best among them to Śāriputra as well."
If there are sons of elders who wish to leave the household life and come to seek Ānanda, Ānanda instructs them to go to Śāriputra to request him to serve as their upādhyāya or ācārya.
"One who is the son of an elder ought to provide for his parents.

Therefore, I now provide for the World-Honored One; Ānanda performs all these tasks, while I now abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, Śāriputra, he always honors and respects Ānanda; if he obtains clothing or food, he first offers the finest among them to Ānanda."
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: When [the Buddha] wished to receive Śāriputra, he asked Ānanda, "When will Śāriputra return?
Ānanda replied:
“‘He will return either on the ninth day or on the tenth day.
[The interlocutor] asked:
“Venerable Ānanda, by what means did you know that Śāriputra would return on the ninth or the tenth day?”
He replied:
"The reason I know this is that when Śāriputra wished to travel through various countries, he came to Ānanda’s place and said to him:
'I wish to go to such-and-such a country and such-and-such a country; I shall return at such-and-such a time and on such-and-such a day.'"
"Elder, you should provide excellent offerings to the World-Honored One; be careful not to be indolent.
When the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma for the fourfold assembly and the devas and nāgas, you, Elder, should remember it well, and I shall then explain it to you."
"If the World-Honored One seeks me out, Elder, you should send someone to inform me.

While Śāriputra was in various countries, he would sometimes dispatch a messenger to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health. Having inquired after the World-Honored One’s health, the messenger would go to Ānanda and say to him:
"Śāriputra sends his greetings to the Venerable One, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether you are dwelling in peace and comfort."
Having inquired after Ānanda’s well-being, he said to him,
"I shall return on such-and-such a day.
For this reason, Ānanda knew that Śāriputra would return on the ninth or tenth day.
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "If for ten days one is permitted to keep an extra robe.
The Dharma Master said:
"If Ānanda were to say,
'Śāriputra will return in one month or half a month,' the Tathāgata should likewise establish a precept on this account."
Ānanda said, "I shall return in ten days; for this reason, the Tathāgata permitted the keeping of extra robes within ten days without committing an offense.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the precept in accordance with Ānanda’s words?"
He replied:
"This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition), not a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (an offense by nature); therefore, it was formulated in accordance with Ānanda’s words.

'The robe is finished' means that the robe is obtained according to the circumstances; whether one anticipates the completion of the robe or anticipates the end of the work—cutting, pinning, and sewing—it is therefore called 'made.'"
"Completed" means that all matters have been concluded; this is called "completed.

Regarding "loss of robes": whether they are seized or lost, burned or swept away by water, ruined or the hope for them is cut off, or if the month of Kārttika has passed, or if the *kaṭhina* robe has been removed—through such various causes and conditions, it is also called "completed."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are eight matters by which the kaṭhina robe is relinquished.
What are these eight?"
First, departure; second, completion; third, exhaustion; fourth, loss; fifth, hearing; sixth, severance of expectation; seventh, exiting the boundary; eighth, departing together.
"These are the eight.
The Dharma Master said:
"These eight matters shall be explained separately by Kṣudraka."
"Relinquishing to the Saṃgha" means relinquishing by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*).
"Ten days" refers to the time limit; this robe may be kept for within ten days, but it must not exceed ten days.
Regarding the six kinds of robes, if one asks what each individual robe is, what are the six?
First is *karpāsa* (cotton), second is *kṣauma* (linen), third is *śāṇaka* (hemp), fourth is *kārpāsa* (wool), fifth is *sāṇa* (flax), and sixth is *aurṇika* (woolen).
These are called the six robes.

If each individual robe must be formally dedicated (*śuddhi*) within ten days, and if it exceeds two spans in length and one span in width, it must be formally dedicated; if it is not so dedicated and ten days pass, one commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "I permit the bhikṣus to speak of [a robe as] pure if it is eight fingers in length—these being the fingers of the Sugata—and four fingers in width; this is the minimum requirement for a robe."
"Naiḥsargika" means "to relinquish" in the Han language; this is a rule of the Vinaya, and it is a pāyattika offense that must be confessed.
The Dharma Master asked, "When does it become naiḥsargika?"
When the *aruṇa* (dawn) appears—translated into Chinese as "the appearance of light"—an offense is incurred.
If many robes are tied and bound together in one place and exceed ten days, one incurs one offense.
If the robes are scattered and not tied or bound, one incurs offenses according to the number of robes; once they have been relinquished, one may then perform repentance.
The Dharma Master said:
"How is it relinquished?
As stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:"
"You should renounce it in this manner:
Having adjusted your robes and bared your right shoulder, come before the Saṃgha; first prostrate to the Elder, then kneel with palms joined and speak as follows:

'Venerable Saṃgha, please take note: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe for more than ten days and have thus committed an offense involving forfeiture. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.'"
If there is one robe, he says "one"; if two robes, he says "two"; if three robes, or many, he says "many.
Among the assembly, a bhikṣu who thoroughly understands the Dharma should perform a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) and accept that bhikṣu’s confession, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣu [Name], having intentionally kept an extra robe for more than ten days, has committed an offense involving forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Now that he perceives his transgression, he confesses and repents before the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha grants its consent, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name].
The motion is thus made.
After the *karmavācanā* has been performed, he asks that bhikṣu:
"Do you see your offense?"
He replied, "I see it.
[The Buddha said,] "Do not commit such offenses in the future."
He replied,
"Very well," and then accepted the confession.
If one discards [the offense] before one person, two persons, or three persons, one should say:
"Venerable sirs, please take note: I, the bhikṣu [name], have kept an extra article of property for more than ten days and have thus committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"Now I relinquish this to the Venerable Ones; I now confess my *pāyattika* offense.
One among the three persons should say to the other two:
"Venerable sirs, please bear in mind that I have received the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so; you should remember and keep this in mind."
The one who accepts the confession shall question that bhikṣu, and his response shall be no different from what occurs within the Saṃgha.
One person among the Saṃgha should then announce three times and return the robe to that bhikṣu, saying:
"This *niḥsargika* robe, the Saṃgha now relinquishes to you, Venerable Sir."
Thus he should chant this three times; by doing so, he relinquishes it through formal ritual.
The Sangha, down to even a single person, should properly return the robe to that bhikṣu. If they do not return it, they commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and neither relinquishes the garment nor confesses the offense, for every instance of wearing it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wears it once and does not remove it until it is worn out or destroyed, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika*), yet there is no fault regarding the robe itself, it is called "no fault" provided that within ten days the robe is either formally dedicated (*pāriśuddhi*) or lost.
The monks thought to themselves:

"The Tathāgata has permitted us to keep the three robes; but what shall we do now with these extra items: the rain-cloak, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), the wound-covering cloth, the bedding, the hand-towel, and the *cīvarapaligodha* cloth?"
"Is it for the purpose of declaring purity (*viśuddhi*), or for the purpose of receiving and maintaining [the precepts]?
Having had this thought, he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The three robes (tricīvara) may be kept and worn without the need for formal purification (viśuddhi);
rain-cloths (varṣāśāṭī) may be kept for four months, after which they must be purified;
and the sitting mat (niṣīdana) may be kept and used without the need for purification."
A cloth for covering sores does not require the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification); once the sore has healed, it must be purified.
Bedding and seats (*śayanāsana*) that have been formally accepted do not require purification.
A *cīvara* made of *jūrṇa-parikaṅkara* (worn-out rags) that has been formally accepted does not require purification.
"One need not perform the ritual of 'purifying by declaration' (śuddhika) for the hand-towel when receiving it. He asked:
"How should the three robes be received and maintained?"
He replied:
"Once it has been made, dyed, marked with a seal, and measured to the proper amount, one may then accept and maintain it. [The questioner asked:
"What is the proper measurement?"

"Regarding the measurements of the *saṃghāṭī* and the *uttarāsaṅga*: the largest is slightly smaller than the Sugata-cīvara; the smallest is four cubits in length and one-and-a-quarter cubits in width."

Regarding the measurements of the *antarvāsa*: it is four cubits long and one fist-cubit wide; if its length or width is less than these measurements, it is made into a *cīvarapaligodha*, which in the Han language means a "miscellaneous small garment."
Regarding the one who receives and maintains the three robes: how does one receive and maintain them?

If one has previously received and maintained the *saṃghāṭī* and, having discarded it, receives a new one, one should speak to a venerable (*bhadanta*) bhikṣu with body and speech. If there is no great bhikṣu present, one should hold the *saṃghāṭī* with one's hand and speak for oneself; if one does not hold it with the hand, the declaration is not accomplished. One should state its name.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Regarding the three robes that have been relinquished and accepted as *cīvarapaligodha* robes for wearing, is it not necessary to perform the ritual of 'purification' (*śuddhi*)?
He replied:
"It should be said that they must be purified.
One may keep a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) for personal use, but not two;
as for bedding, one may possess it according to what is obtained, provided it is blue, yellow, or red in color and made of wool with threads."
One may keep one wound-covering cloth, but not more;
two hand-towels may be kept;
as for the *cīvara-pārihārika* (extra robe), one may accept and keep as many as one possesses without committing an offense.
Mats, bedding, cushions, bolsters, and woolen rugs all belong to the category of room-articles and do not require the ritual of "purifying" (śuddhi).
Regarding the three robes (tricīvara), how are they lost?

They are lost if given away to another, if taken by a person or a thief, if lost, if one abandons the path (renounces the precepts), if one returns to the status of a novice (śrāmaṇera), if one dies, if one changes gender, if one renounces them, if they become torn, or if one stays overnight separated from them.
He asked, "How does one bore it? He replied:
“Pierce it as large as a fingernail.
He asked, “What is meant by ‘a fingernail’?”

"The smallest finger-nail: if there is a single horizontal thread remaining within the hole, it is not lost. Regarding the saṃghāṭī and the uttarāsaṅga: if there is a hole within eight finger-widths from the wide edge, it is not lost; if there is a hole within one span (vitasti) along the long edge, it is not lost."

Regarding the *antarvāsa*: if the width exceeds four finger-breadths at the edge, it is lost; if the length exceeds one span (*vitasti*) at the edge, it is lost; if the length or width exceeds [the standard] by as much as a small fingernail, it is lost. Once it is lost, if ten days have passed, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; once it has been mended, it may be formally accepted and worn.
Regarding the *niṣīdana*, the wound-covering cloth, the rain-cloak, the bedding, and the hand-towel:

if one maintains them and they become worn but not lost, even if the robes are about to tear but have not yet developed a hole—whether in one strip or two—one may first patch them with other material and subsequently cut away the old portion; thus, one does not lose the formal maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) of the robe.
"If one has three robes and two of them are double-layered, such that one layer is torn while the other layer is not torn, they are not lost. He asked:
"If the back of the *kāṣāya* is about to tear, and one wishes to turn the center toward the two sides, how can it be turned without being lost?"
He replied:

"First take the two edges and stitch them together so they are joined; then use a knife to cut open the back portion; finally, stitch along the margins, and you will not lose the integrity of its use."

"If the *kāṣāya* becomes significantly reduced in size but the integrity of its possession is not lost, and if the *kāṣāya* is small and supplemented with other materials but the integrity of its possession is not lost.
He asked: "If one washes the *kāṣāya* and its color fades, is the integrity of its possession lost?"
He replied: "It is not lost.

If the smallest permissible measure of cloth is one chi and six cun in length and eight cun in width, this must be formally declared as pure (śuddha) when it is mended with cloth; however, if it is mended with small scraps of material, it need not be declared as pure."
"There are two methods for declaring purity (*śuddhi*): first, face-to-face declaration; second, indirect declaration.
What is face-to-face declaration?
Having tied [the robes] together so they are attached, one goes before a bhikṣu, kneels on the right knee, and speaks as follows:"
"I have this long robe; for the sake of purification, I now give it to you, Venerable Sir. It may be properly kept as a safeguard, but it must not be used.
"In what way may it be used?"
"If a donor says: 'This is my robe;
use it as you please, Venerable Sir,' if one uses it after such a statement has been made, there is no offense. This is called 'purification in the presence' (sammukha-viśuddhi)."
"What is 'successive purification' (*saṃtati-śuddhi*)?
Within the five aggregates [of the monastic community], one obtains a person who acts as a donor; taking an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), one goes to a bhikṣu and says:
'I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, possess this extra robe which has not yet been purified. For the sake of successive purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir.'"
The recipient of the gift says:
"Venerable sir, you have this extra robe which has not yet been purified; for the sake of 'purification through transfer,' you give it to me, and I now accept it."
"Who is the donor?
He replied, "A certain bhikṣu."
Furthermore, he says: "Venerable sir, you have this long robe; for the sake of its purification, you have given it to me, and I have accepted it.
This is the property of the bhikṣu so-and-so; Venerable sir, please keep it as a trust for that bhikṣu so-and-so. When you use it, do as you wish; there is no need to ask the owner."
"This is called 'successive pure giving' (*pāriśuddhi*).
The Dharma Master said:

'If, after receiving the gift, one replies "Excellent," it does not constitute a formal declaration of purity (*pāriśuddhi-vyākaraṇa*); one should seek out another person who knows the Dharma and have them perform the declaration for the former. "
"How is it accomplished? How is it not accomplished?
"If one says, 'I give this to the Venerable One,' or 'I relinquish this to the Venerable One,' this is a true purification and constitutes a valid relinquishment."
“How is it that a gift given for the sake of successive purification constitutes relinquishment?

“If one says, ‘I give this to the Elder for the sake of successive purification,’ or if one says, ‘I relinquish this to the Elder for the sake of successive purification,’ or if one says, ‘I give this to the Elder for him to use as he sees fit for the sake of successive purification,’ then by a single utterance, the relinquishment is accomplished.”
“How is it that the relinquishment is not accomplished?

“If one says, ‘Venerable sir, please accept this robe; may the Venerable’s robe be fulfilled,’ this is called a true indirect pure gift (*parivartaka-śuddha-dāna*), but it does not constitute a true pure relinquishment (*śuddha-tyāga*).”
“What is meant by ‘becoming a recipient’ and ‘not becoming a recipient’?
“If one says, ‘I take,’ or if one says, ‘I receive,’ this is called truly pure becoming a recipient.”
“What is it that does not constitute formal acceptance?
If one says, ‘I shall take it,’ or ‘I desire to take it,’ or ‘I shall make it my property,’ or ‘It shall become my property’—this is a true purification that does not constitute formal acceptance.”
"If one is invited to act as a donor, one must accept; if one does not accept, it is not in accordance with the Vinaya practice.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the words and phrases is easy to understand."
If one has accepted [the gift], one must not fail to return it; if one does not return it, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If, having accepted it, one knows it is not one's own property and intentionally conceals this object through various expedients, one incurs an offense according to its value.

This precept arises from body, mind, and speech. Regarding extra robes that have not been formally accepted or purified through distribution, if they are kept beyond ten days, one incurs an offense. This is not avoided by mere thought; whether one knows that ten days have passed or does not know that ten days have passed, one still incurs the offense. This precept is comprised within the three types of undertaking.
The detailed exposition of the precept regarding extra robes is concluded.
"As for those who travel through various countries wearing the *uttarāsaṅga* and *antarvāsaka*, these *saṃghāṭī* robes have been kept for a long time and have consequently become worn and damaged."
Thereupon, the Elder Ānanda, while inspecting the various rooms, saw the robe being smoothed out.
The Dharma Master asked:
"How did Ānanda see this robe?"
“Ānanda, while on his rounds of inspection, saw this robe? He replied,
“It is for this reason that the Elder Ānanda, when on his rounds through the various rooms, sees anything that is dilapidated or unclean, he immediately repairs it or cleans it up.”
If one sees a bhikṣu who is ill, one should provide for him with timely offerings and care; for this reason, Ānanda inspects the various rooms.

For one who has received the *anāpatti-saha-śayyā* (the formal act of not being separated from [one's robes]), even if he stays overnight apart from his robes, he does not commit the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
He asked, "For how long may one stay overnight apart [from one's robes]?
He replied:
"One may stay overnight apart from one's robe while an illness is still untreated.

If a sick bhikṣu has been granted formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) by the Saṃgha to stay apart from his robe, and having so stayed, travels to another region, he should maintain the constant intention to return; even if he falls ill on the way and cannot return, he does not lose his robe provided he intends to do so."

If one has the firm intention not to return and loses the robe, or if ten days pass and one commits the offense of keeping an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), or if one goes to another region and the illness is cured, and upon returning to the place where the robe was kept the illness flares up again and one wishes to go to yet another region, one may rely on the previous formal act (*karmavācanā*) and need not perform it again.

Regarding "a single boundary for a village": if one belongs to a village where food and drink are shared by a single clan and clothing is kept there, and while staying in a forest hermitage (āraṇya), the sun has not yet risen or set, one does not lose the [privilege of] keeping the robe outside the village boundary.
Regarding the separate boundaries of a village: it refers to a separation of residence; if the robe is in this house while one’s body is staying overnight in that house, one loses the robe.

Regarding "not being separated by an elbow's length": if the robe is within fifteen elbows, one does not lose it; however, if the robe is on the ground and the body is in the air through supernatural power, one loses the robe.

Regarding "separate villages": those with many owners, such as Vaiśālī or the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, are considered separate villages. If one's robe is in a guest house and one's person is outside, if one comes within fifteen cubits (*vitasti*) of the robe, one does not lose possession of the robe.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential phrases are easy to understand.
As for the 'multi-storied pavilion' (kūṭāgāra), it may have five or seven stories; each story constitutes a separate boundary."
What is a single boundary?

If upper and lower stories are both under the authority of one master, and while the robe is kept on this multi-storied building, it does not constitute a loss of the robe—this is called a single boundary.
What is a separate boundary?

In this multi-storied pavilion where many people reside together, if their dwelling places are distinct—such as when the robe is on the upper floor and the bhikṣu is on the lower floor—the bhikṣu must go to the location of the robe; if he does not go to the location of the robe and loses it, this is called a "separate boundary" (sīmā).

Regarding the carriage boundary: if a bhikṣu places his robe on a carriage, the bhikṣu must follow the carriage and may not go far away; as long as the dawn has not yet appeared, he does not lose possession of the robe provided he remains within fifteen cubits of the carriage.
If one goes beyond fifteen cubits from the vehicle and loses the robe, this is called the "vehicle boundary" (*yāna-sīma*).

If one entrusts a robe to a vehicle, and the vehicle overturns or is destroyed, or if the goods on the vehicle are scattered or gathered together, the robe remains at the place where it is gathered; the bhikṣu must go to the side of the robe and may not leave it.

Regarding the "tree boundary" (*vṛkṣasīman*): it is the area covered by the shadow at midday. If the branches and leaves are sparse and their shade does not connect, and the robe is in the sunlight while the bhikṣu is under the tree, he loses his robe.
If a tree branch extends unevenly so that the robe is in the shade of the branch while the bhikṣu is at the base of the tree, the boundary is not lost.

As for the *araṇya* boundary, it is no different from what is described regarding Vīraka and Vīna; "Han" (Chinese) means "great tree," and it is also like an island in the sea where people do not reach.
Regarding the forest boundary (*vana-sīma*): if a robe is within the forest and remains within fourteen cubits (*hasta*) of it, the robe is not lost.
It is the same for a sea island; if it is within fourteen cubits of the shore, the robe is not lost.
In this forest, if there is someone coming or going, there is no boundary of fourteen cubits; the robe should remain with one's person. If it does not, the robe is lost.

When a bhikṣu stays in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and sits in meditation throughout the night, he may suffer from drowsiness as dawn approaches. He takes off his robe and places it on the bank, then enters the pool to bathe. If the first light of day (the *aruṇa*) appears before he has finished bathing, this robe becomes separated from him overnight, and he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If one has neither relinquished nor confessed [the offense], one incurs the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for wearing [the robe improperly].
Furthermore, if one exposes the upper body while on dry land, one again commits the *duṣkṛta* offense. He asked:
"How can one be liberated from this? He replied,
"If there is no bhikṣu present who has not yet received the confession, one may wear [the robe] without fault."
If one sees a bhikṣu and does not abandon or confess [the offense] while following him, for each instance there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu possesses an article subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) and, wishing to take it to another bhikṣu to relinquish and confess it, encounters bandits on the road who seize the garment, he need only confess the *pāyattika* offense.

If one sends a śrāmaṇera or a layperson to carry a robe for a bhikṣu, and [the carrier] avoids the path or falls into a deep sleep, such that by the appearance of the dawn light the robe is lost, it should be relinquished.

If a novice (śrāmaṇera) or a layperson (avadātavasana) enters carrying the robe ahead of them, the boundary of the robe’s non-separation is not lost; yet if a bhikṣu also enters without realizing it and thinks he is outside the boundary, when the dawn appears, the robe is actually still within the boundary—thus, whether it is considered lost or not depends on this.

The same applies to the rule regarding dependence: if a disciple who has not yet completed five years of seniority carries his teacher's robe and follows him on a journey, and while on the road they encounter someone preaching the Dharma, and because of a desire to hear the teaching he remains until the appearance of the dawn, he does not incur the offense of being separated from his teacher.
Why is this? Because the mind has no fixed abiding.

If the preceptor commits the offense of staying apart from one's robes overnight, and this *kaṣāya* robe has already been formally accepted and maintained, then by being separated from it overnight, he incurs the offense.
The remaining phrases are no different from those previously stated.
The detailed exposition of the precept concerning staying overnight separated from one’s robe is concluded.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained an out-of-season robe; this bhikṣu, wishing to make a garment but finding it insufficient, sprinkled it with water, dried it in the sun, and pulled and stretched it in an attempt to lengthen it.
The World-Honored One was inspecting the dwellings; having seen [the monk], he asked:
"Bhikṣu! What are you doing?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"This robe is short; I wish to pull and stretch it to make it longer.
Regarding robes out of season: the final month of summer and the four months of winter constitute the proper season; the remaining seven months are out of season.
Regarding giving at an improper time: one may receive [offerings] according to the order of the *saṃgha*, the order of the *gaṇa*, or receive them individually.
"Saṃgha" refers to the entire community of monks.
"Gaṇa" refers either to a group studying the Vinaya, a group studying the Abhidharma, or a group studying the Sūtras.
If there is a deficiency—provided it is a minor deficiency—one may keep [the robe] for one month.

Regarding "expecting to obtain": this refers to expecting to obtain it from among the Sangha, or from among the assembly, or from relatives and friends, or from acquaintances, or from a place where refuse is discarded, or from one's own property; this is called "expecting to obtain."

If there is an expectation [of obtaining a robe], one may keep it for within one month; if one keeps it beyond that, one commits a *naiḥsargika* offense. If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains the expected robe which is fine while the previous robe was coarse, one should perform the *paryāpanna* (formal declaration) for the previous robe; the newly obtained robe may likewise be kept for another month, as the expectation remains the same.
If one expects to obtain coarse robes, one may further stay for one month; in this manner, proceeding as desired, because they wish to remain together, one must not exceed one month.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential phrases are easy to understand.
If one obtains the robe as expected on the twenty-ninth day, one should accept and maintain it that very day, or perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification)."
If one does not formally take possession of it or perform the ritual of purification (śuddhi), when the dawn appears, it becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).
In this manner, even if one proceeds through successive days until the tenth day and obtains the expected robe, one must on that very day take possession of it and perform the ritual of purification.
If one neither accepts [the robe] nor declares it pure, then upon the appearance of the dawn light on the eleventh day, it becomes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The origin story (*nidāna*) of this precept is no different from that of the first *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The detailed exposition is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Hermitage in Śrāvastī. Then, the Elder Udāyin sent a former wife to wash his old robes.

Regarding the seven generations of one's parents: father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, and so on up to the seventh generation; for the mother’s seven generations, it is likewise.
A father includes paternal uncles, brothers, and even sons and grandsons.
A mother includes maternal uncles, aunts, and even descendants for seven generations—all are one's mother.
If they are daughters down to granddaughters, all are kin and may be permitted to leave the household life.
However, if daughters down to granddaughters are defiled, they may not be permitted to leave the household life;
the same applies to wives and sons who are defiled.
Why is this? Because she is not related [by blood].
A bhikṣuṇī is one who has received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* from within the dual saṃgha; she is thus called a bhikṣuṇī.
"Old robes" refers to those that have already been worn on the body; this is what is meant by "old robes.

Regarding the *niḥsargika* offense for washing: if a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī to wash them, or prepares a hearth to warm the water, or searches for a flint to strike a fire—regardless of each individual act performed, the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Once the washing is finished, it becomes a *niḥsargika* offense.
If, after washing is finished, one wishes to return it to a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣuṇī says it is not yet clean and has it washed again, the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

It is the same for dyeing: if, after dyeing is finished, one has it beaten, for each individual act, the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one who is not a relative makes one who is not a relative wash or dye [the robe], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Regarding "no offense": if a bhikṣuṇī washes [the robe] herself, she does not commit an offense; if she has a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇerī, śrāmaṇera, upāsaka, or upāsikā wash or dye it, she does not commit an offense.

If a bhikṣu has an upāsikā wash or dye a robe, and before it has been washed or dyed, she subsequently leaves the household life and receives full ordination (upasampadā), and only after that does he have her wash or dye it and return it, the bhikṣu incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

If a śrāmaṇerī or a śikṣamāṇā is asked to wash or dye [a robe], and she has not yet washed or dyed it, but later, after she has received full ordination (upasaṃpadā), she does wash or dye it, the bhikṣu incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

If an upāsaka or a śrāmaṇera causes [a robe] to be washed or dyed, and it has not yet been washed or dyed, and later, after he has gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), his faculties transform so that he becomes a bhikṣuṇī and causes it to be washed or dyed, the bhikṣu commits a *naiḥsargika* offense.
If he causes a bhikṣu to wash and dye [the robe], and the same applies if the bhikṣu’s gender changes;

or if he causes a bhikṣuṇī to wash and dye it, and after it has been washed and dyed, the bhikṣu says it is not yet purified and has it washed again, the bhikṣu commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes many unrelated bhikṣuṇīs to wash [the robe], there are multiple *niḥsargika* offenses.

If a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination from the community of bhikṣuṇīs and not from the Venerable One (the bhikṣu-saṃgha), such as the five hundred Śākya women, and one causes this bhikṣuṇī to wash [the robe], it is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
"Regarding 'no offense': if one washes leather sandals, bags for bowls, pillows, belts, or waist-cords—washing such items as these constitutes no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand."
This precept incurs an offense when six factors are complete.

What are these six? First, the body; second, speech; third, both body and speech; fourth, body, mind, and speech; fifth, the actual performance of the act; sixth, the absence of liberation through mere conceptualization. This precept possesses three types of feeling.
The detailed exposition of the precept on washing clothes is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, while the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was residing in Śrāvastī.

Thereupon, in the early morning, Utpalavarna dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having finished his alms-round, he returned to the Andhakavana forest and entered meditative concentration during the day.
He asked, “There is no rule for bhikṣuṇīs to travel alone; why did Utpalavarṇā enter the Andhakavana forest by herself?
He replied:
"Because the Tathāgata had not yet established the precept against traveling alone, the *utpala* flower was able to enter alone.
Once that [precept] was established, it was as if he were practicing the way of a thief.
"In what way does he practice the way of a thief?"
“Those who break through walls and climb over fences to plunder people's property, taking this as their livelihood, are called thieves.
A chief thief is one who commands all such thieves.”
This leader of the bandits had previously been acquainted with the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
As they were traveling along, the leader stole ahead; seeing the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, he feared that the other bandits might violate her, so he said to his companions:
"You all should go by this path."
The bandits then followed their leader and departed.
Regarding "arising from samādhi": when a bhikṣuṇī first enters dhyāna, she makes a vow to herself, saying, "I shall arise at such-and-such a time."
Having arisen from samādhi, the bandits proclaimed these words:
"Whatever a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa requires, we shall give it.
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"This grove has no other people; there is only I alone, so it must surely be given to me.
For this reason, the bhikṣuṇī was permitted to take it.
As for "one who is in the monastery," it refers to Udāyin.
He asked, "Why is Udāyin alone in the monastery?
He replied:
"All the bhikṣus are following the Tathāgata into the village to beg for alms; they have left Udāyin to guard the dwelling place.
If you wish to give it to me, you should give it to me, for this lower robe (antarvāsaka) is of fine quality."
The Dharma Master said:
"Udāyin had but a slight attachment to the *antarvāsaka*; he requested it solely because he wished to see the body of the bhikṣuṇī."
Regarding "having given to one who has already departed": after Udāyin had requested it three times, the bhikṣuṇī immediately took off her robe and gave it to him, then returned to her residence.
Regarding "exchanging": as stated in the Vinaya-mūla, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The five groups [of practitioners] who share the same Dharma may exchange things with one another."
What is meant by "those of the same Dharma"?
Those who share the same teacher and have common precepts and views are called "those of the same Dharma.

At the initial desire to receive [the robe], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; once it has entered one's hand, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This does not constitute an offense except in the case of a relative bhikṣuṇī; it also does not constitute an offense in the case of a non-relative śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇerī, or upāsikā.
There is no offense if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to the fourfold assembly and they joyfully give as an offering;
nor is there an offense if he takes discarded items as *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe material) when they have been thrown away by a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
If one receives full ordination from a single assembly (the Bhikṣu-saṃgha) at the hands of a non-relative bhikṣuṇī, it is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta*.
If one receives full ordination from both assemblies (the Bhikṣu- and Bhikṣuṇī-saṃghas) at the hands of a non-relative bhikṣuṇī, it is an *āpatti* of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one obtains much in exchange for a small amount of goods, there is no offense.
The remaining phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.

This precept comprises six matters; it is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition) involving three types of acceptance, as explained at length previously under the precept regarding the acceptance of robes.

At that time, the Buddha was residing at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Hermitage in Śrāvastī. Among the eighty thousand members of the Śākya clan who had gone forth as monks, Upānanda was the most frivolous; yet he was by nature intelligent and possessed an exceptionally exquisite voice.

Regarding those traveling on a long journey: a great many bhikṣus were traveling from Sāketa to Śrāvastī when they encountered bandits on the road who plundered their robes and belongings. The bandits questioned them, saying:
"You naked ascetics, do you actually possess such a kind heart?"
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa of the Śākya clan; I am not a non-Buddhist.
When the bhikṣus heard that he was a śramaṇa, they went and informed Upāli.
"Venerable One!
You may go and investigate.
Upāli then went to investigate.
"How many years of seniority do you have?
When did you receive the precepts?
Who is your preceptor?"
"How should one receive and maintain the three robes?

Having been asked this, it was known that he was a bhikṣu. "One may beg for robes from a donor who is not a relative; if there is no place to beg, one may enter the monastery with the body covered by grass, but one must not enter the monastery naked."
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain this in sequence.
If a bhikṣu traveling on a road encounters bandits, he should take his robes and bowl and give them to a youth, instructing him to run away and seek refuge."

If bandits plunder the robes year after year, whether it be a senior monk (upādhyāya) or a junior monk (śrāmaṇera), as soon as one person is found, they should pluck grass and tree leaves and give them to the others so that they may cover their bodies and proceed toward the monastery.
If a layperson sees a bhikṣu who has encountered bandits and is naked, and gives him a layperson’s garment or a garment of the five primary colors, he may wear it without fault.
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If a bhikṣu wears a white garment, or a garment of superior color, or a garment with uncut threads, he may wear it without fault."
"Who is this person?
One who possesses wisdom should contemplate this matter.
He replied:
"This is a bhikṣu who has lost his robes after being robbed by bandits.
If there is a bhikṣu who has lost his robes after being robbed by bandits, he may wear the robes of an outsider (tīrthika).

Regarding the robes of an outsider: whether they be robes made of bird feathers or wooden boards, he may wear them without fault; however, he must not change his views or accept the teachings of false views."

If a monk who has lost his robes enters a monastery, one who possesses monastic robes should give him a robe. If it is a robe belonging to a specific room, when the monk enters that room to stay, or even if he does not enter the room to stay, [the owner] may give this robe to him. If there are no robes available, one may tear up bedding or a meditation bolster to give to the monk for him to wear; if it becomes damaged, there is no need to compensate.
If a donor offers robes, they should be returned to the Sangha.

When a monk who has lost his robes enters a monastery, if there are no robes belonging to the Sangha, he may request them from a layperson who is not a relative; the monk who has lost his robes may also request them himself. It is not an offense to request on behalf of another, provided that one does not request gold or silver.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are easily understood and need not be explained in detail.
This precept arises from body and mind and possesses the three types of sensation."
The detailed exposition of the precept regarding begging for robes from those who are not relatives is concluded.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Fourteen.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Regions during the Xiao Qi Dynasty:
"At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery in Śrāvastī. There were many who brought robes;
when the donors heard that the bhikṣus had lost their robes, they each gave them a robe."
Regarding the "invitation of free choice" (*svairakāraṇa*): when a donor says to a bhikṣu,
"If you have anything you require, take it as you please," this is called the invitation of free choice.
Regarding the upper and lower robes: these refer to the *antarvāsa* (inner robe) and the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), while one receives the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe).
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If a bhikṣu loses his three robes, he may receive the upper and lower robes, and seek the remaining one robe from another place;
if he loses two robes, he may receive one robe."
If one loses a single robe, one may not receive [a new one).
If a bhikṣuṇī loses five robes, she may receive two;
if she loses four robes, she may receive one.
If one has lost the three robes, one may not accept [other robes].
However, if they are from a close friend, or from a donor who has invited one at their own discretion, or if they are one's own property, one may accept them as one wishes.

This precept comprises six matters; liberation is not attained through mere thought. This is a formal rule (prajñapti-śikṣāpada); it involves the three types of acceptance through the actions of body and speech.
The detailed explanation of upper and lower robes is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī.

Regarding the value of robes: gold, silver, or coins—if a donor or a donor’s wife wishes to provide the funds to purchase robes for a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu becomes aware of this, he should immediately go and urge them, saying:
"If you are making a robe for me, it must be made fine, long, and wide.

If she instructs [the weaver] to increase the price by even one-sixteenth part, or instructs him to increase the density of the weave by even a single thread, and she obtains such a robe, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a donor wishes to make something large, one should encourage them to make it small; if they wish to purchase it for a high price, one should encourage them to pay a lower price. If one acts in accordance with the donor's wishes in this manner, there is no offense in obtaining the robe.

"If it concerns a relative, or a donor who has invited one at their own discretion, there is no offense in thus encouraging [the gift]; nor is there an offense in encouraging another to increase their offering.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand; there is no need for a detailed explanation."
The second [offense] concerns a householder who is not a relative. The distinction lies in the fact that there are many householders; the remaining phrases are as explained in the preceding precept.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī. He said to the householder:
"You may take this money for robes and purchase clothing to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
When he had spoken thus, the "fifty-cutter" cut [the wood] worth fifty *kārsāpaṇas*.
Regarding the one who waits for the Venerable One, he says: "Venerable One!
I have business today; may the Venerable One wait until this day has passed, and I shall give it to you tomorrow."
"A royal minister" refers to one who consumes the king's stipend; such a person is called a royal minister.
"Sends a messenger" means he dispatches someone to deliver [the message].
"Leads" means he leads [the messenger] to where the bhikṣu is.
"Taking what is pure" means that if one obtains pure items, one should accept them.
Pure items refer to clothing, medicinal decoctions, and medicines; these are called pure items.
"One who guards the monastic quarters" refers to a person employed by the Sangha as a servant.
"I have already informed those who should know; I have told the keeper of the robes:
'If the Venerable One requires a robe, go to him and he shall give you a robe.
When I say, 'The householder has informed me that I require a robe,' it means that according to his understanding, he has made this known."
The second and third times he should likewise request it.
If he succeeds, that is well; if not, then for the first, second, and third times, up to the sixth time, he should remain silent before [the donor].
What is meant by "remaining silent"?
It means not speaking with the mouth, and standing rather than sitting.

If a donor calls for one to sit, one must not sit; if they offer food or drink, one must not accept it, and this applies equally to beverages. If invited to preach the Dharma or recite prayers of blessing, one must not do so in any case.
If a donor asks,
"For what reason have you come here?
one should answer:
"Householder, you should know this for yourself. If he obtains it, that is well. If he does not obtain it, he may seek it through twelve silent requests.

If he makes one verbal request, he breaks two silent requests; if he makes two verbal requests, he breaks four silent requests; if he makes three verbal requests, he breaks six silent requests; and so on, up to six verbal requests, which break twelve silent requests. If he goes further to seek it and obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one goes once and requests once on one day, one may go in this manner for six days.
If one goes once on a day and requests six times, one must not go again to request thereafter, nor may one remain silent.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place from which the price for the robe came and say:
