"I have not been able to use your funds; you yourself should take care of them so that they are not lost."

If the robe is not obtained, one should go in person to inform the owner of the robe; one must not send another to inform them, for if one sends another to inform them, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Dharma Master said:
"There are two kinds of attendants:
first, those who give directions; second, those who do not give directions."
There are two kinds of indications. What are the two?
First, the indication by a bhikṣu; second, the indication by a messenger.
Regarding those who do not point out [the fault], there are again two kinds:
first, when one is not present before oneself; second, when another is not present before oneself.
These are called the four types of administrative officers (vaiyāvṛtyakara).
The Dharma Master asked:
"How did the messenger point it out?
He replied:
"If there is a layperson who has purchased robes for a bhikṣu, and a messenger goes to the bhikṣu's location, having arrived, the messenger says to the bhikṣu:
'Venerable One!'"
"A certain lay devotee has sent me to deliver the price for robes; may the Venerable One accept it.
The bhikṣu replies, "This is an impure object; a bhikṣu may not accept it."
The messenger spoke again:
"Venerable One!
Is there anyone who manages affairs for you?"
The bhikṣu replied, “No.
The messenger sought out an attendant himself; having found one, he brought him to the bhikṣu’s location and said to the bhikṣu:
"This person can serve as the steward for the Venerable One.
He then took the money and handed it directly to the steward. In the presence of the bhikṣu, the messenger said to the steward:
"You may take this money and buy robes to give to the bhikṣu."
If there is an attendant, the bhikṣu says to the messenger:
"The attendant is in such-and-such a village, at such-and-such a place, and his name is so-and-so.
The messenger goes to where the attendant is and says to him:
"You may take this money and purchase clothing for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Having delivered it, he returns to the bhikṣu's location and says:
"Venerable sir, I have already paid the price for the clothing to the official you indicated; if you require clothing, go and fetch it."
Once the messenger has delivered the price for the robe, if he does not come in person to inform the bhikṣu, he shall send someone else to inform him, saying:
"Venerable sir, the price for the robe indicated by you to the steward has already been paid."
"Venerable sir, you need robes; go and take them, and I shall give you robes.
These are called the four types of attendants. Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla:

"If a bhikṣu has an attendant who possesses faith and respects the Dharma, he may entrust the funds directly to that person. If you require robes, you should go and take them; you should take pure items and not accept gold or silver. By means of this expedient cause and condition, one may receive gold and silver; apart from this, there is no other method for receiving gold and silver."
If a messenger says to an official:
"Take this money and buy clothing to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu," once the bhikṣu has handed the price for the clothing to the official, he must inform the bhikṣu;
otherwise, the bhikṣu may not go to the official to request the clothing. If he does obtain the clothing, it constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If there is a householder who takes gold and silver to a bhikṣu and says to him:
"Take this gold and silver and give it to the Saṃgha; I pray that the Venerable One will accept it to construct a monastery, a dining hall, or gardens and fields."
"A bhikṣu must not accept it; if he accepts it, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
He should instruct that it be handed over to a *śuci-puruṣa* (a pure person), after which he may manage and utilize it as appropriate.
If the person sent does not understand, the bhikṣu may instruct the *śuci-puruṣa* to accept it on his behalf, after which he may use it according to the circumstances."

"If a layperson offers gold or silver as a gift to the community of monks, instructing that it be used to prepare food and drink, clothing, medicine, and bedding, [the monks] must not accept it themselves."
If the Sangha accepts gold or silver and subsequently obtains food, drink, clothing, or other requisites for use, they commit the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If the Sangha does not accept it, and the layperson, misunderstanding the matter, takes it back home, a monk who knows the Vinaya sees him on the road and says:
"Give this to the Sangha; why are you taking it back?"
Having heard this, the householder understood and immediately returned it to the attendant.
If the householder gives a gift for use at a specific location, the bhikṣu must not divert it; if he diverts it for other use, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If a dwelling or residence has been constructed for giving, but there is no food and the assembly of monks wishes to disperse, leaving it unguarded, one may purchase food by reducing the value of the dwelling to provide sustenance for those guarding the residence; if one exchanges and uses funds in this manner, there is no offense.

If the dwellings and property belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters are such that there is no food at the residence and the Sangha intends to disperse, one may take from the property of the dwellings to provide for food and drink.
Why is this? It is for the sake of protecting one's dwelling place.
Nevertheless, it must not be used entirely.
If a householder offers fields or ponds as a gift, a bhikṣu must not accept them.
Why may he not accept them?
The bhikṣu says to the householder:
"A bhikṣu may not accept fields or ponds as his property," [the rule states].
A householder said to the bhikṣu, "In these fields and ponds, four kinds of pure things can be produced; I shall use them to make offerings to the Saṃgha."
"If it is as you say, then it may be accepted.
If the householder says:
"I give this pond to the Sangha so that they may bathe, wash their clothes, and for all sentient beings to drink from and use as they please," [then it may be accepted].
"If one gives a pond in this manner, it may be accepted.
If a layperson does not understand the terminology and simply says, 'I give a pond,' the bhikṣu should reply:
'The dharma for those who have left the household life does not permit the acceptance of ponds; however, if you are giving pure water, we shall accept it.'"
The householder replied,
"Excellent, Venerable Sir!
Originally, I was giving water."
If one receives [an offering] with such words, it is acceptable.
However, if a householder does not understand the language and merely says "I give," and subsequently passes away, the bhikṣu may not use that [offering].

If a householder has sons and grandsons, the bhikṣu should instruct those children and grandchildren to practice giving. If the lineage is severed and there are no sons or grandsons, he may say to the elders of the village:
"This householder did not understand the practice of giving; now that his life has passed, the bhikṣus must not make use of his property."
The elder knew this himself.
The elder said to the bhikṣu:
"I, your disciple, offer water as a gift to the Saṃgha."
"If one gives in this manner, a bhikṣu may accept and use it without fault; however, he must not accept gold, silver, or money.
If a layperson offers rice, as well as sweet fruits, clothing, food, or drink, he may accept all of these."

If a layperson personally offers pure food, it may be accepted; however, one must not do so for one's own sake. If one instructs a layperson or an invited guest to prepare food and drink, even if it is obtained, it must not be eaten.
The Dharma Master said:

"In the past, there was a bhikṣu who lived on Mount Cāturmahārājika. Desiring to obtain rice porridge, he went out into the courtyard and saw several lay devotees; he drew the shape of rice porridge upon the plastered ground with water and spoke these words:
'How might such rice porridge be obtained to provide for the Saṃgha tomorrow?'"
The householder immediately untied it and returned home to prepare such food; the next morning, he brought it to offer to the assembly of monks.
The senior monk (upādhyāya) knew that it should not be accepted, and seeing that the senior monk did not accept it, the junior monks (navaka) likewise each refrained from accepting it.
In the past, even when the bhikṣu Contentment manifested such signs, he still failed to obtain food; how much more so now, when one seeks food for the sake of the body!
One cannot accept the gift of a garden, as previously stated without difference.
If a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) or a grove is offered as a gift, it may be accepted.
Should later generations clear the grove to make fields, they may accept rice, sweet fruits, food, and drink; however, if these were not originally given, one must not forcibly demand them.
If a person previously cleared a forest to create a field and then ceased their work, and a later person comes and cultivates it, they should be required to pay the value. Why?
Because they have made the field their own.
If someone wishes to lease a field, they must not accept gold or silver; however, pure items may be accepted.
If the lessee does not know the location and asks a bhikṣu, and if the bhikṣu knows the boundaries, he should indicate the location; if he does not know, he must not point it out falsely.
If someone offers slaves to the Saṃgha, they must not be accepted; however, if it is said that they are offered as "pure persons" (kappiyakāraka) or as "attendants," they may be accepted.
If these pure persons of the Saṃgha prepare food for the Saṃgha in the morning but seek their own livelihood in the afternoon, they may be given food before noon, but not after noon;
as for clothing, nothing at all may be given.

If one serves as an attendant for the Sangha for half a month, they may receive clothing and food; if one performs their own work for half a month, the Sangha may not provide them with clothing or food.

If one does not perform any labor or service for the Sangha at all, but seeks gain for oneself, and later receives a payment, they may accept it for the Sangha; if it is not given, one may not demand it.
"If one offers oxen or sheep, they may not be accepted; however, if one says, 'I offer milk, curd, and the five flavors,' they may be accepted. It is the same for all other livestock.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand."

The origin of the causal conditions for the precepts concerning kings and ministers, the three types of action—of body, speech, and mind—and the three feelings: these constitute offenses by prohibition (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), from which one cannot escape simply because of ignorance.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Ālavī.
Regarding a *kauśeya* bedding: it refers to spreading it out on level ground.
As for "sprinkling with fermented vinegar and mixing," even if it is mixed with a single hair of *kauśeya*, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Kauśeya hair refers to that which is most subtle among the fibers; this bedding is made of felt, not woven cloth.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand."
“At that time, the Buddha was staying at the High Hall (Kūṭāgāra-śālā) in the city of Vaiśālī.
Regarding ‘pure black sheep’s wool,’ it means there is no admixture of other types of wool.
The sequence of the phrases is easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.”
This concludes the section on pure black wool from a ram.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Regarding "placing [white] at the edge": this refers to placing a small amount of white wool at the edge.
This has already been explained in the Vinaya and need not be elaborated upon here.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Regarding 'a sick bhikṣu': if a sick bhikṣu wishes to go elsewhere but finds his bedding too heavy to carry with him, the Saṃgha may perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) for him, whereby he is permitted to obtain new bedding."

"If the illness has not yet been cured, one may act according to one's own will; if the illness has already been cured but recurs, there is no need for another *karmavācanā*, as the previous *karmavācanā* may be used.
The Dharma Master said:
"The sequential phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail."

"At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Hermitage in Śrāvastī. Regarding the rules of conduct for the retreat, he addressed the bhikṣus: 'I wish to enter a place of seclusion for three months.'"
The Dharma Master said:
"For what reason did the World-Honored One enter seclusion for three months?
The World-Honored One surveyed all sentient beings and saw that during these three months none would attain the Way; therefore, he entered seclusion for three months."

"After I have entered [parinirvāṇa], such things will surely occur: once the bhikṣus have heard my words, they will certainly establish an unlawful regulation. Upasena Vaṅganta-putra shall break this regulation and come to my place; having seen him, I shall offer praise."

Because of Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, many bhikṣus who had undertaken the dhūta practices came to see me. After I had completed my three-month retreat in seclusion, I went with the bhikṣus to inspect the various rooms and saw that the sitting mats (niṣīdana) were strewn about in disorder everywhere. On account of these sitting mats, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
After the World-Honored One had formed this thought, he remained in seclusion for three months.

When the Buddha went to where Upasena Vaṅgantaputta was, the Elder Upasena had conferred full ordination upon a disciple less than twenty years of age, thereby incurring a *dukkaṭa* offense. Regarding this, among the *Khaṇḍhakas*, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"You foolish man! You have not yet reached ten years of seniority; how could you recklessly confer full ordination upon one who is less than twenty years old?"
Furthermore, as he did not know how to instruct, he sent another person to do so. Having received the reprimand, Upasena paid homage to the Buddha and departed, thinking to himself:
"I am a son of good family who has left the household life; I have not left it with an evil mind. Why then, for the sake of being a disciple, have I received this reprimand?"
"I shall go and stay ten yojanas away to instruct my disciples so that their deportment is perfectly orderly, no different from my own.
Only after that will he go to inquire after the World-Honored One's well-being; because his disciples' deportment is in accordance with the Dharma, he will receive praise.
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Do you take pleasure in and become attached to the patched robe?
The bhikṣus replied:
"In truth, I do not delight in or cling to it; I wear it only because I follow my teacher.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Upasena! You are well able to instruct your disciples and are fully endowed with dignified deportment.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"The Buddha saw that the *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) were scattered in disorder everywhere.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When those with faith give in charity so that it may be used, do not allow it to be wasted."
"Regarding 'the Buddha having already used various skillful means': the Buddha has already employed countless skillful means to teach the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus.
Therefore, 'an old seat' (niṣīdana) refers to even a single sitting upon it; this is what is meant by 'old'."

Regarding "taking a small amount": take from one of the four sides, whether it be square or circular, and apply it over a new patch; if it cannot be applied as a whole, it is also permissible to tear it into fine pieces and mix them with the new material.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases and sentences are contained within the Vinaya and need not be explained in detail.
The causal origin is as previously described."
The rules concerning the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) are concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery, regarding the rule on carrying wool.
As for "mocking": a layperson encountered a bhikṣu on the road carrying wool and asked him:
"Venerable sir!
Where are you carrying this wool?
Where will you sell it?"
"How much would it fetch if sold?
When the bhikṣu heard the laypeople’s joking and mockery, he went to the monastery and, out of anger, threw it to the ground. The other bhikṣus asked him, "Venerable One!..."
"From where did you bring this wool, that you should throw it on the ground in such anger?
The bhikṣu replied, "Because of this wool, I was mocked by the lay devotees; for this reason, I threw it on the ground in anger."
"Carrying it oneself" means wrapping it in an *uttarāsaṅga* and carrying it oneself.

"Exceeding three *yojanas*" means carrying it oneself for more than three *yojanas* without anyone else assisting; for every single hair's breadth [of the distance], one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Once it has been placed on the ground at a distance of three *yojanas*, if one moves it by flicking it with a staff or rolling it with the foot beyond those three *yojanas*, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika* offense.
If, upon reaching the three *yojanas*, one carries it out beyond the three *yojanas* due to dangers from tigers, wolves, or bandits, it likewise constitutes a *naiḥsargika* offense.
If one is robbed by bandits within three *yojanas*, and after being robbed the bhikṣu returns it, he may carry it again for up to three *yojanas* without committing an offense.

There is no fault if it is a *kambala* or *niṣīdana* that has already been made into a rug; there is no fault within three *yojanas*, and once the three *yojanas* have been reached, if someone else carries it on his behalf beyond the three *yojanas*, there is no fault.
"Regarding those who carry wool: if it reaches as far as covering the ears and exceeds three *yojanas*, one commits an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail."
This precept arises from both body and mind; one cannot escape it by means of ignorance.
The detailed exposition of the wool-precept is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākyaśīrṣa.

Regarding the precept against washing sheep’s wool: it obstructs and causes the abandonment of seated meditation and the recitation of sutras. It was because the bhikṣuṇīs washed, dyed, and carded wool for the group of six bhikṣus that this obstruction and abandonment occurred.
The remaining phrases are easy to understand.
This concludes the precept regarding washing, dyeing, and carding wool.
At that time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Regarding the precept against gold and silver: "Gold" refers to *ka*, lapis lazuli, coral, all manner of precious gems, and items for trade; these constitute the category of gold and silver.

Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: down to even tree-resin coins, whatever is used as currency within a kingdom, one must not grasp them, nor may one instruct others to grasp them; to do so constitutes an offense in every case.
If one takes possession for oneself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one takes possession for the Saṃgha, for a group, or even for a single person, or for the sake of an image, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One who is free from fault does not accept [gold and silver] themselves, nor do they instruct others to accept it.
If a householder offers gold or silver as a gift to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should reply:
"I may not accept it."
The householder spoke again:
"Venerable Sir!
My resolve to give this gift is already fixed; it cannot be taken back."

Having set it down on the ground, he departed. When the bhikṣu saw that the householder had left, he remained behind to watch over it. Then another householder, seeing the bhikṣu staying there, went up to him and asked:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Why do you stay here?
The bhikṣu replied, "A layperson has offered this gold and silver; according to the dharma of a bhikṣu, I am not permitted to accept it."
The householder said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Since you, Venerable sir, may not accept it, I shall give it to your disciple."

The bhikṣu remained silent; the householder accepted it and took it away. Later, the householder exchanged this gold and silver for food, drink, clothing, and pure items, which he gave to the bhikṣu; the bhikṣu was permitted to accept them.

If there is no one capable of understanding the Dharma, one should keep gold and silver within the house with the door closed so that they are not lost. If there is someone who sells robes and bowls, the bhikṣu should summon them in and show them the gold and silver, saying to the seller of robes and bowls:
"I, this poor monk, require these robes and bowls; here is the gold and silver."
"The layperson knows for himself.

If there is no one to sell robes or bowls, but there is someone who sells non-seasonal drinks, seven-day medicines, or lifelong medicines, he should bring them to where the gold and silver are and say:
"There is this gold and silver; the Sangha requires these medicines."
"The layperson knows for himself.
Once the medicine has been obtained, the community of monks may consume it.
However, the monk who was the master of the gold and silver may not consume it; furthermore, no one else—whether laypeople, pure attendants, or even animals—may eat it.
Why is this? Because it is property belonging to the Sangha.
If one does not obtain medicine, and the owner of the gold and silver places it there and departs, there is no further expedient by which one may accept it.
If he saw an upāsaka, he called him over and instructed him to throw it away.
The upāsaka said, "Why should I throw away this gold and silver? I shall pick it up myself."
The bhikṣu replied,
"As you wish.
If the upāsaka understands the Dharma, he may bring an exchange for the robe and bowl and give them to the Saṃgha, which may then accept them.

If there is no upāsaka available to be instructed to throw it away, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. A bhikṣu who knows the five dharmas shall take this gold or silver and, with eyes closed, cast it away; he must not record its location. If he records the location, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are four ways of utilizing what has been received through giving. What are these four?
First, using it as a thief; second, using it as one who owes a debt; third, using it as a kinsman or friend; and fourth, using it as a master.
Question: "In what way is it misappropriated? Answer:
"If a bhikṣu lacks the precepts yet accepts offerings of food and drink according to the monastic order, this is called 'using by theft.
What is 'using by debt'?

If a bhikṣu receives food, drink, or clothing from others, he should first form a mental resolve; if he receives clothing or food without first forming such a resolve, this is called 'using by debt.'"

If there is a bhikṣu who is intelligent, wise, and possessed of faith, when he comes to the time of receiving food, he should bring it to mind at every mouthful. If he is of dull faculties, he should first bring it to mind once before eating. If a bhikṣu of dull faculties uses clothing, he should first bring it to mind in the morning. One of sharp faculties should bring it to mind with every single act. Regarding dwellings, beds, seats, bedding, and all other articles used that are offered through faith, one should first bring them to mind. If one does not first bring them to mind, this is called "using what is borrowed."

If one uses clothing not for the purpose of warding off cold, warding off heat, or warding off shame, or if one accepts food, drink, and medicinal decoctions not for the purpose of alleviating hunger, thirst, or illness, this is also called being in debt.
"If one receives food, drink, or clothing without first forming the mental resolve [to do so], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"What is meant by 'use as a kinsman'?
"When the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) make use of donated goods, it is no different from a son receiving his father's property; this is called 'use as a kinsman.'"
"What is meant by 'primary use'?
"It is the use of donated goods by true persons and arhats.
The Dharma Master said:
"Among the four kinds of enjoyments, theft is the most evil.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of enjoyment.
What are these four?"
"First, the function of having shame and remorse; second, the function of lacking shame and remorse; third, the function of having dharmas; and fourth, the function of lacking dharmas.
"What is the function of having shame and remorse?"

"A person without shame or dread of blame may associate with and receive offerings from one who possesses shame and dread of blame without incurring fault; this is called 'the use of one possessing shame and dread of blame.
What is 'the use of one without shame and dread of blame'?"
"A person possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame who associates with one lacking such shame and dread incurs fault through that association; this is called 'the use of the shameless.
Because a person possessing shame and dread of blame who associates with one lacking it will inevitably follow them in committing evil, they are termed 'one who associates with the shameless.'"

"When a person lacking shame and dread of blame associates with one who possesses shame and dread of blame, they will surely later reform their evil ways and cultivate virtue; such a person is called one who possesses shame and dread of blame.
What is the application of the Dharma?"
“If there is a person possessed of shame and remorse who acquires [wealth] by means of the Dharma, this is called ‘acquisition through the Dharma.
What is ‘acquisition not through the Dharma’?

If a person devoid of shame and remorse acquires [wealth] without using the Dharma, and if they obtain such things, it is no different from obtaining poisonous medicine; this is called ‘acquisition not through the Dharma.’”
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are already contained within the Vinaya and need not be explained at length.

This is an offense by prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada), involving the three types of action—body, speech, and mind—and the three ways of receiving. The detailed explanation of the precept against receiving precious objects is now complete."
"Those who trade in precious precepts are not of a single kind; some have already become vessels [of the Dharma], while others have not yet become vessels.
Regarding 'head items,' these include flower hairpins and all other things used for the head—all such things are considered head items."
Rings, bracelets, tongs, locks, and various other ornaments for the body—these are called "finished articles.

One may exchange finished articles for unfinished ones, unfinished articles for finished ones, a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, or a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Question: "How can one exchange a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture and confession)? Answer:
"To exchange copper coins for gold coins also constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; this is called an *āpatti* of exchanging copper coins for a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
To exchange gold coins for copper coins is called a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; to exchange them is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one exchanges precious gems for iron, and uses that iron to make a bowl, an axe, or any other utensil—one by one—all such items are forbidden to be used; if they are used, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are easy to understand.
The causal origin story is no different from that previously given for the precepts."
The various rules concerning trade have already been explained in the Vinaya; as there are no further divergent meanings, they are not repeated here.
If one keeps an extra bowl for more than ten days, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pātra* (the bowl subject to forfeiture): if one uses it without relinquishing it or confessing the offense, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
There is no offense if the ten-day period has not yet expired, or if the bowl has been purified through *śuddhaka-vyavahāra*, or if it is being held with formal acceptance (*parigraha*).
The Dharma Master asked,
"How many times must a new bowl be fumigated before it is fit to be used?
He replied:

"If an iron bowl has undergone five fumigations, it is fit for use; if an earthen bowl has undergone two fumigations, it is fit for use. If one purchases a bowl from another, one must not accept and keep it until the price has been repaid."
If the owner of the bowl says,
"Just use it, and then return its value," even though the owner speaks these words,
one must not accept and keep it; rather, one should return its value first and only then accept and keep it.

If, after the bowl has been purchased and the price settled, and the owner of the bowl has finished fumigating it and informed the bhikṣu, yet the bhikṣu does not go to take possession of it, he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) once ten days have passed.

If the owner of the bowl has finished fumigating it, and others know that the fumigation is complete, and they pass word of this along the path to a bhikṣu, then even if the bhikṣu hears this, he does not commit an offense even if ten days elapse.

He must wait for the report from the owner; thereafter, if ten days have passed, he may declare his acceptance of the bowl before others. If no one else is present, he may declare his acceptance alone.
If one loses the formal undertaking [of the precepts], it is through: renouncing the path, death, changing one's gender, relinquishing them, or tearing them; these are called losing the undertaking.
If they are torn or pierced even as much as a grain of millet, the undertaking is lost; however, if one mends them with iron filings, the undertaking is regained.
The causal origin is no different from what was stated previously.
The detailed exposition of the precept concerning the extra bowl is concluded.
"The five kinds of medicine in Śrāvastī are: fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar."
Regarding ghee: all pure meats and milk may also be drunk, and ghee may likewise be used as medicine.
He asked: “If flies or ants fall into the seven-day medicine, is it permissible to consume it?”
He replied:
"If it can be strained out and consumed, it may be considered as if one had received curd today.
[The questioner asked: "Is the butter within the curd a seven-day medicine?"

"If one churns the cream until the seventh day and obtains butter, this may be consumed on that seventh day; if it reaches the eighth day, it becomes *niḥsargika* [an offense requiring forfeiture]. The same applies to oil and rock honey."
If one receives curd at an improper time or churns it at an improper time, or if one receives clarified butter at an improper time, one must not consume it; the same applies to oil and rock honey.
If one suffers from a demonic affliction that can only be cured by raw meat or raw blood, their consumption is permitted, provided that human blood is excluded and may not be consumed.

If, having obtained ghee, one says, "It has been placed inside the vessel," and this vessel already contains ghee such that ghee emerges from within the vessel and mixes with the new ghee, one should speak further.
If the ghee is lost by the seventh day, or if it is given to a layperson or a śrāmaṇera, or if the ghee is returned, or if the śrāmaṇera offers it as a gift, one may eat it without fault.
"If one gives alms to a śrāmaṇera before seven days have passed, and on the eighth day there is an urgent need for use, one may go to the śrāmaṇera to beg for food without fault.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are already contained within the Vinaya; there is no need to explain them at length."
This concludes the detailed explanation of the precept regarding medicines for seven days.
This is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by formal rule), not a *prakṛti-āpatti* (a natural offense), arising from body and mind.
Regarding the "rain-bathing robe" permitted by the Buddha in Śrāvastī: in the *Khandhaka*, it was on account of Visākhā Mātā that the acceptance of rain robes was permitted.

When there is one month remaining before the commencement of the summer retreat, one should wash, dye, and sew the rain-bathing robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, having washed, dyed, and cut and sewn the rain-bathing robe, it need not be formally dedicated (*pariṣkāra-uddhāra*), yet it must not be used [until the end of the retreat].

Having completed the period of receiving and using [the rain-bathing robe] on the first day of the fifth month, and since the rainy season lasts four months combined with the fifteenth day at the end of spring, it is used for one hundred and thirty-five days; if the robe for rain-bathing is not obtained during the final month of spring, but is obtained only in summer, then one receives and uses it [from that point].

Regarding "not the time for seeking a rain-bath robe": from the middle of the ninth month until the middle of the fourth month is not the time for seeking a rain-bath robe; if one seeks one during this period, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one has a rain-bath robe but does not use it, bathing naked constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should seek a rain-bath robe; if it is insufficient, one may set it aside provided there is hope of obtaining more to complete the requirement. Once the full amount is obtained, it should be formally accepted and maintained (*parigraha*). If it remains insufficient, it may be set aside until the middle of the ninth month, at which point it need not be declared as pure (*śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*).
If one has received the *kaṭhina* robe, it may be kept until the middle of the first month of spring without the need for formal purification (*śuddhi*).
If the three robes are insufficient, they may be converted into use as a *kāṣāya*; if they are slightly lacking and there is hope of obtaining more, they may be kept for up to one month.

If it is sufficient, one may make a robe; if it is insufficient, one should declare it as *śuddhaka* (pure) or take formal possession (*parigraha*) of it. If one neither declares it as pure nor takes possession of it, by the thirty-first day, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
"One who is blameless" refers to one who, if young, begs from relatives, or if invited at will, begs from a donor; in such cases, there is no offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases and sentences should be explained in detail within the Vinaya; there is no need to repeat them here."
Regarding the "precepts for those who fear [worldly life]," there are two types of dwelling in an araṇya:
first, dwelling in an araṇya for a long duration; second, dwelling in an araṇya for three months.
If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya has his robes worn out and returns to live in a monastic cell within a village for the purpose of mending and protecting them,
he may return to dwell in the araṇya once the mending is complete.
Regarding "bandits during the month of Kārttika": in the month of Kārttika, when there is no rain, bandits arise in the autumn.
Seeing these bandits killing people and plundering goods, a bhikṣu becomes terrified; fearing the loss of his three robes, he deposits each of the three robes, one by one, in a village.
"Fear" refers to either seeing a thief oneself or hearing someone speak of one; this is called fear.

If a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) consists of many rooms that are secure and well-fortified, there is no need to deposit one's robes in a village. Having deposited the robes, one may go to check on them once every six nights; having seen the robes, one returns to the forest hermitage, except when there is a formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-kamma*).
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases have already been explained in the Vinaya and need not be elaborated upon here.

Regarding 'transference of merit' (*parivartana*): when a donor (*dānapati*) provides food for the Buddha and the Saṃgha and intends to offer robes, if a bhikṣu personally redirects that intention, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the moment he first instructs the transference; once the object has entered his possession, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
If one redirects a gift intended for another, even down to an animal—such as intending to give it to this animal but redirecting it to that animal—one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one intends to make an offering to this image but redirects it to that image, in all such cases, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"One who is without fault is one who gives it to the Saṃgha without knowing [the offense].
The Dharma Master said:
"The thirty matters have been explained in detail, exhaustively and without omission."
Next, regarding the ninety matters, you should listen with a single mind.
Within the precept against false speech, the term "Hāta" refers to the name of a venerable one (bhadanta).

Among the eighty thousand who left the household life from the Śākya clan, Hāta was also included; he was by nature fond of debate. When debating principles with non-Buddhists (tīrthika), if he found himself at a logical impasse, he would then contradict his previous words. If the non-Buddhist spoke well, he would turn those words into his own; realizing his own reasoning was fallacious, he would claim they were the words of the non-Buddhist.
If one schedules a debate with non-Buddhists at a specific time, one says to the non-Buddhists:
"We shall debate after midday; come before midday.
One says to the donors:
"Immediately, he ascended the high seat for the debate and addressed the donors, saying:
'Why would the non-Buddhists not come? They must surely fear me; that is why they do not come.'"
Having descended from his high seat, he departed.
Later in the day, the non-Buddhists arrived; not finding the bhikṣu, they rebuked him, saying:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas claims to know the True Dharma; why then has he spoken falsely?"
"False speech" refers to when the mouth and the mind contradict each other; it is also called "empty speech.
There is no offense if one intends to speak of this but mistakenly speaks of that. This concludes the detailed explanation of the precept against false speech.
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Regarding disparaging speech, it is intended to cause the other person shame.
There is no offense except when it is for the purpose of instruction; this concludes the detailed explanation of disparaging speech as a natural offense.

"Regarding double-tongued speech: if one uses double-tongued speech to cause dissension among bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta; for laypeople as well, it is a duṣkṛta. This is a natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya). The detailed explanation of double-tongued speech is concluded."
There are four kinds of those who recite together. What are the four? First, the phrase;
second, following the phrase; third, following the syllable; and fourth, following the flavor.
What constitutes a phrase?
A single line within a verse is called one phrase.
What constitutes a subsequent phrase?
The second phrase is called "conforming to the phrases.
What is meant by "conforming to the syllables"?
To explain in accordance with the written characters is called "conforming to the written characters."
What is "following the flavor" (anvaya)?
When the characters are identical but the meanings differ, this is called following the flavor.
Where there is a combination of characters, meanings, and flavors, this is called a phrase (pada).

If one instructs a person who has not yet received full ordination (upasampadā) to recite "Commit no evil," and the one who has not yet received full ordination recites it in unison with the teacher, it is a pāyattika offense.

If the teacher says "Commit no evil" and the one who has not yet received full ordination skips the preceding words and recites "Practice all that is good" in unison with the teacher, the teacher incurs an offense.
If the teacher says, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and the disciple says, "Impermanent," he also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If the phrasing is identical, he incurs the offense for every syllable.
The words of the Buddha refer to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, Abhidharma Piṭaka, and Sūtra Piṭaka; these are the words of the Buddha.
The words of the Śrāvakas refer to the Aṅguttara-nikāya (Sūtra of Right View), the Aṇumana-sūtra, the Cūla-piṭaka, and the Mahā-piṭaka; these are called the words of the Śrāvakas.
The "language of the brahmins" refers to the single class of all non-Buddhist brahmins; this is called the language of the brahmins.
The "language of devas and humans" refers to what is spoken by Māra, Brahmā, Śakra, and all devas and humans; this is called the language of devas and humans.
"There is no offense for reciting together.
The Dharma Master said:

"If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when Kāśyapa served as the Elder and the Tripiṭaka was compiled by the five hundred arhats, one were to recite this Dharma together with a person who has not yet received full ordination, one incurs a pāyattika offense."
"If the words are composed by a Dharma Master, there is no offense for those who recite them together.
The Dharma Master said:
"The detailed explanation of the recitation of the precepts together is finished."

Regarding "not forming recollections beforehand": when about to sleep, one should first practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of the devas, and mindfulness of impermanence. One should attend to each of these six recollections individually; if one does not practice such recollection, it is called "not recollecting beforehand."

As for those who sleep naked: if one does not first form a mental resolve before sleeping, the mind becomes distracted. Consequently, various sounds issue from the naked body—some like the cries of birds, others like the lowing of oxen or the neighing of horses—and when the upāsakas hear them, they all give rise to derision and reproach, saying:
"How can a renunciant sleep in such a manner!"
Because of this matter, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, you must not sleep in the same room as a person who has not received full ordination."

At that time, having heard the Buddha establish the precepts, Rāhula upheld them and did not transgress. For this reason, Rāhula entered the Buddha’s latrine and spread his *kāṣāya* robe upon the ground to sleep. The reason Rāhula entered the Buddha’s latrine building was because it was clean and many people had offered incense and flowers there; therefore, he went inside to sleep.

Before the light of dawn had appeared, the Tathāgata made a coughing sound while entering the latrine; Rāhula, who was inside, also made a coughing sound. The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Who is there?"
He replied,
"I am Rāhula. Because of Rāhula,
the Buddha thought of all the śrāmaṇeras and permitted them to stay for two nights.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why is it that one may not sleep together in a room? [He replied:
"If it is entirely roofed and entirely enclosed—even if constructed as a hut using cloth curtains—it constitutes an offense."
Regarding "walls": even a wall as high as one and a half cubits is termed a "wall.

If one stays overnight [in such a structure], an offense is committed; this applies even if there are multiple rooms sharing a single door. However, if there are separate doors, no offense is committed.
On the third night, one must leave before the appearance of the dawn; if one does not leave, even staying for the full three nights constitutes no offense.
On the fourth night, one may not remain during the first watch; if one lies on one's side upon the bed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a building has little roof-covering but many enclosures, there is no offense; if it has much roof-covering but few enclosures, there is likewise no offense.

If the four sides of the building each have doors opening inward, yet one uses a single large door for all entry and exit, there is an offense; if there are separate doors for each side, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu sleeps for more than three nights together with an unordained person who is also sleeping, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If the unordained person has already risen from sleep and then sleeps again, the bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense for each instance of such sleeping.
If a person who has not received full ordination stays for more than three nights, and both the unordained person and the bhikṣu sleep, it constitutes a pāyattika offense for both.
If the bhikṣu, having already risen, sleeps again, he incurs as many pāyattika offenses as the number of times he falls asleep.
If houses are connected such that they form a large complex extending even one *yojana*, entering or exiting through the same door constitutes an offense.
If there is a hollow space like a tortoise or eel burrow within a house, where one can only pass through the exterior and the interior is not interconnected, there is no offense.
"If a building is mostly covered and half-fenced, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense; if it is mostly fenced and half-covered, it is also a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail."
The detailed explanation of the precept on sleeping together is finished.
Regarding the precept on sleeping under the same roof with a woman: it refers to constructing a merit hall intended for travelers to stay overnight.
The precept regarding sleeping in the same room as a woman is already established in the Vinaya and need not be explained in detail here.

As for preaching the Dharma, one may preach the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, or speak of heaven and hell; however, provided there is a man capable of understanding—meaning a human male, not a ghost or an animal—if such a man is present, one does not commit an offense even if one speaks more than five or six words.
Regarding "five or six words": if a bhikṣu speaks five or six words [of instruction], there is no offense.

As for "five or six words": if a single verse or a single line is spoken with the sound connected and uninterrupted, it constitutes one pāyattika; if the lines are broken, each line constitutes a pāyattika.
One scriptural verse and five lines of commentary constitute six lines; if these are not exceeded, there is no offense. However, if one exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.

If there are many women, and after finishing the teaching for one woman, one proceeds to teach a second and third woman while the first woman returns to listen, although the number of words exceeds five or six, there is no offense.

Regarding answering questions: if a woman asks about matters within the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and a bhikṣu answers according to her questions—even if he explains the entire Āgama—he does not commit an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.
The origin of the causal conditions is as in the preceding precepts."
Having finished the detailed exposition of the teaching on women, this noble established precept—namely, the fourth *pārājika*—has already been fully explained;

herein it is no different. Because one who has truly attained superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) speaks of them to a person who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
Having finished explaining the superhuman states (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*) to one who has not yet received full ordination, regarding "grave offenses" (*sthūlātyaya*):
the four pārājikas and the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas are called grave offenses.
To speak of these to anyone other than a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī who has not received full ordination constitutes a pāyattika offense.

Regarding "except by formal monastic procedure (*saṃghakamma*)," it means that the procedure is declared at a specific location; if it is declared at a location other than the one where the procedure was prescribed, it is a *pāyattika*.
Except for the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) and the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa], if one speaks of other categories of offenses, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining sequential phrases are already contained within the Vinaya and need not be explained in detail.
This concludes the section on the precepts concerning grave offenses."

Regarding the precept against digging the earth: one must now distinguish between true earth and non-true earth. True earth is that which contains no sand, stones, or rubble, but is pure soil; this is called true earth.
That which is not true ground is that which abounds in sand, stones, potsherds, rubble, and sandy soil; this is called non-true ground.
If the ground is scorched by fire, it is also called non-true ground.
If there is sand or gravel in the earth, how is it to be known? May it be dug?

One should take a small amount of soil and wash it with water to examine it; if four parts are stone and one part is soil, it may be dug. If the soil on top of the stones is four inches thick and dry, it may be taken; however, if it has already rained for four months, it must not be taken. If a bhikṣu digs the raw earth, for every act of digging, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu says to a lay attendant,
"Dig the earth and cut wood for the community of monks," he does not commit an offense.
If one instructs another to dig this or cut that, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one draws on the ground or makes characters thereon, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one holds fire and throws it at the hand or onto the ground, there is no offense.
The remaining textual passages are found in the Vinaya and need not be explained in detail here.
The detailed exposition of the precept concerning digging the earth is concluded.
This is an offense of formal enactment (*prajñapti-āpatti*), arising from both body and mind.
"Not accepting speech" means that the bhikṣu Kāntāra did not accept the words of the spirit; because he was cutting down a tree, he injured the arm of the spirit’s son. The spirit thought to himself:
"One should not arbitrarily kill those who have left the household life. I shall go to inform the Buddha, for when the Buddha hears of this matter, he will establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
He went to where the Buddha was and reported this matter in detail.
Having heard it, the World-Honored One immediately spoke these verses:
"If a person gives rise to a mind of anger, It is like a chariot rushing out of control."
"To restrain a chariot driver is not considered difficult;
but for a person to subdue the mind of anger—this is the most difficult of all.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, this tree deity immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Buddha, knowing that the tree spirit had no dwelling place, observed with his divine eye that the tree was without an owner, and said to the tree spirit:
"You may dwell in reliance upon this tree."
Question: "Where is this tree located? Answer:
“This tree is in the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden.
A tree deity, having taken up residence there, thought to herself:
‘The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, has granted me this palace; from this day forward, I shall make offerings to the World-Honored One.’”

At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma for the devas and humans. If a great deva arrived later, the lesser devas would gradually withdraw their seats until they reached the edge of the ocean.

At that time, the tree deity who had attained the Way withdrew and remained by the tree to listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. During the day, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly; during the first watch of the night, he preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus; during the middle watch of the night, he preached the Dharma for devas and humans; and during the final watch of the night, he preached the Dharma for the nāga kings.
How is this known?

During the middle watch of the night, celestial beings come and strike the upper part of the door panels; during the latter watch of the night, the dragon kings come and strike the lower part of the door panels. Thus, one distinguishes between the celestial beings and the dragons.
"Tree" refers to a growing tree.
"Village" refers to this tree being composed of eight subtle elements (*aṇu*), which is termed a "village.
There are five kinds of trees; *āriṭa* is yellow ginger.
*Uśīra* is fragrant root;
*trāyantika* is *caṅkrama-śīrṣa* (cinnamon);
*rohiṇī* is *chuanlian* (coptis).
"Dhālu" is the name of a foreign grass.
"Śamā" refers to the Bodhi tree.
"Brahmī" refers to the Pippala tree.
These two types of trees are found only in Jiaoguang; they are not seen in other regions.
As for the sumana flower, its fragrance is similar to that of the mālatī.
The *mallikā* flower is found in Guangzhou; its blossoms grow by climbing.
*Sūrapa* is not the name of a plant known here.
*Pukhīna* is the foreign name for a type of grass.
There are two kinds of trees: first, those born in water, and second, those born on land.

The utpala, padma, and kumuda flowers are born in water; if one overturns them while they are in the water, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one overturns them when they have left the water, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one requires flowers or fruit, one may climb the tree branch to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) take them; this does not constitute an offense, provided that the branch is not broken.
If the tree is too high for the *kappiya-kāraka* to reach, the bhikṣu may embrace the *kappiya-kāraka* while the latter takes [the fruit]; this does not constitute an offense.
If a tree falls upon a bhikṣu, one may cut down the tree or dig up the ground to save his life; there is no offense.
This concludes the detailed exposition of the precept concerning injuring plants and trees.
This is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by formal rule), arising from both body and mind.
Regarding the precept against frivolous speech: if one who performs evil deeds does what should not be done, they incur offense through body and speech.
To "conceal" means to be unwilling to let others know [of it].
"Who has committed the offense?
The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain its meaning."

If there are other bhikṣus who ask the Elder whether he has committed an offense, they shall bring him before the Saṃgha to adjudicate this matter together; in the presence of the Saṃgha, he shall answer, saying:
"Who has committed an offense?"
The other bhikṣus said to him,
"Venerable sir, you have committed an offense.
He replied:
"What offense have I committed?
The bhikṣu replied, "Some say it is a pāyattika; others say it is a duṣkṛta."
He asked,
"When did I commit an offense?
and [the other] spoke to him, saying:
"Such-and-such at such-and-such times you committed an offense.
"What did I do to commit an offense?
"You committed an offense by doing such-and-such a thing."
He replied, "What are you saying?
Such an evasion of the question and answer is called *anyavāda* (irrelevant speech).
If a bhikṣu sees Cchanna holding silver coins, the bhikṣu says to him:
"Why are you holding silver coins?
He replies:
"I am holding a tin coin, not a silver coin.
Or, seeing him drinking alcohol, he says:
"Why have you drunk alcohol?
He replied,
"I drank water."
He said to him,
"Why are you sitting alone in a secluded place with a woman?
He replied:
"A wise man"—this is called "speaking otherwise" (*anyavāda*). Sometimes one may remain silent and not answer.
If one knows that [the proposal] is contrary to the Dharma, yet answers the Sangha by speaking otherwise, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one is doubtful as to whether a matter is dharma or adharma, yet answers the Saṃgha with evasive speech, one incurs a pāyattika.
If one knows the truth, yet answers the Saṃgha by saying "I do not know," one incurs a pāyattika.
Fearing that it would lead to strife within the Saṃgha, one remains silent and does not commit the offense.
The remaining phrases and sentences are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.
This is a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya) arising from the actions of body, speech, and mind; the extensive explanation following the questions and answers is hereby concluded.
"If one reviles or slanders a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*; if one reviles or slanders anyone else, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) arising from bodily and vocal karma. The precept concerning reviling is concluded."
Regarding the precept on spreading monastic bedding in the open air: "In winter" refers to the season of frost and snow.
"Having basked one's body" means that during the cold months, one takes the beds and mats of the Sangha and basks one's body in the sun each day.

Regarding "knowing the proper time": if a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) calls for it and one does not raise up the bedding of the Saṃgha, or fails to instruct another to raise it, one commits an offense.
The Dharma Master said:
"In winter there are four months, and in the hot season there are four months. During times when it does not rain, one may spread out the bedding of the Saṃgha; during times of rain, one must not."
Regarding "under a tree": if the foliage is thick and dense such that no birds gather above it, one may spread out bedding for the Sangha without committing an offense.

If a bhikṣu has undertaken the superior dhūta practices, whether he is under a tree or in an open space, he must not even use his *kāṣāya* as a shelter, nor may he take bedding belonging to the Sangha to use outdoors; however, if he can protect it so that it remains dry—even by covering it with his *kāṣāya*—he may use it.

If one observes the dhūta practice regarding bedding, when it is not raining, one should stay in the open air; when it rains, one may stay under a roof or enter a building to receive the bedding of the Saṃgha.

If a donor, seeing a bhikṣu staying in the open, prepares bedding for the community of monks, and the bhikṣu has accepted it, there should be another bhikṣu to whom it is entrusted. If no bhikṣu is available to entrust it to, it should be given to those living nearby. If there are none living nearby, it should be placed in an empty house. If there is no empty house, it should be tied up beneath a thick, dense tree and then one may depart.
If one does not tie it up, or if one departs without first forming the thought: "I shall return from entering the village before long," [one incurs an offense].
"One who departs in such a manner incurs no offense.
If, after entering a village, one is unable to return due to eight kinds of calamitous circumstances, there is no offense in leaving the robes in charge of another.
If it is actually raining, yet one says it is not raining and departs, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing)."
There are four kinds of beds. What are the four?
First, those with *pāmśukūla* legs; second, those with carved hoof-shaped legs; third, those with *kūṭāgāra* (pavilion) legs; and fourth, those with *āyata* (elongated) legs.
Regarding the *pāmśukhāṭaka* bed: the crossbars are inserted into the legs.
Regarding the *vicitrapādaka* bed: the crossbars and the legs are joined together.
Regarding the *kūṭilapādaka* bed: it may have legs shaped like horse hooves, or like sheep hooves, or like those of tigers, wolves, and lions; such are called *kūṭila* legs.
"Āvāsaka-pāda" means that the foot [of the bed] enters the frame.
If a bed is thus spread out in the open air and one leaves it at a distance greater than the range of a stone thrown by an average person, it is a pāyattika offense.

If the senior monk has instructed the junior monk to spread the bedding, and the senior monk places his robes upon the bed, the junior monk may depart; however, if he does not place even a single item there, the junior monk should fold and arrange them. If he does not fold and arrange them, he incurs no offense provided he informs the senior monk before departing.
If the seat has been prepared but not yet sat upon, and another bhikṣu sits there and departs after speaking, there is no offense.

If one prepares a high seat for a Dharma teacher, if the Dharma teacher has not yet arrived, the preparer should guard it; once the Dharma teacher has sat down, the preparer may depart without offense.
If one first lowers a stool or a footstool down to its wooden base, and upon departing neither raises it oneself nor instructs another to raise it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the saṃgha uses a dye-vat, a water-pitcher, or a cord for sprinkling, one should, upon departing, raise them and place them back in their usual location before leaving; if one departs without raising them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is another person’s private property and one does not pick it up, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is one’s own property and one does not pick it up when departing, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if there are circumstances involving the eight calamities (*aṣṭāntarakalpa*), it is not an offense not to pick it up when departing.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.
This precept is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by formal decree), arising from body, mind, and speech."

If one spreads out a monk’s bedding or a *paccattharaṇa* (mat) inside a room—where a *paccattharaṇa* refers to a pillow-sack or a sitting-sack—or if it is a straw mat down to a simple grass mat, and upon departing one neither puts it away oneself nor instructs another to do so:

if there is no enclosure, returning from a distance of one stone-throw constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); returning from beyond two stone-throws constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If there is a fence, one commits an offense as soon as one goes outside the fence.
The detailed explanation of the precept regarding the spreading of monastic bedding within a monastery room is concluded.

"Knowing that another bhikṣu has finished spreading his bedding, to come later and disturb that bhikṣu is a pāyattika; if one does not know it or if one suspects it, it is likewise a pāyattika. There is no offense if it is due to the eight kinds of calamities."
The detailed explanation of the precept against causing distress to others is concluded; this is a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (intrinsic offense).
Regarding "a multi-storied building": from standing leaning against it down to not touching the head [of the structure], there is no offense.
As for "no offense," it means that if it is not a multi-storied building, one does not commit an offense.
The detailed explanation of the multi-storied pavilion precepts is concluded.

"If one applies a double layer of plaster: on both sides of the door and at the top, one may apply a double layer of plaster up to two and a half cubits; if there are walls above and below the door, one may also apply a double layer of plaster there; and on all four sides of the windows, one may also apply a double layer of plaster."
Why is this? It is for the purpose of opening and closing windows and doors.
Regarding "covering," there are two kinds of covering:
The first is covering completely, and the second is covering lengthwise.
If one roof-covering is completed, there is no offense; however, if a tiled roof exceeds three layers, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If it exceeds three layers, for every tile used, one incurs a *pāyattika* for each.
If lime is applied in layers exceeding three strata, for every application of a lump, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If grass is applied in layers exceeding three strata, for every handful of grass used, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one covers what is not well-made or repairs what is damaged, there is no offense.
Regarding "no fault": if one departs after having spoken [of the intention], there is no offense.
If one constructs a hut in an open space exceeding three sections and covers it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); this is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense of formal prohibition).
"Regarding the knowledge that water contains insects, this is known according to the specific circumstances.
Whether one sprinkles it oneself or instructs another to sprinkle it: if one sprinkles it oneself, for every breath one takes, one incurs a *pāyattika*;
if one instructs another to sprinkle it, for every word spoken, one incurs a *pāyattika*."
This is a natural offense arising from body, mind, and speech. The detailed explanation of the precept regarding the use of water containing insects is concluded.

Regarding those who receive great offerings for instructing bhikṣuṇīs: the Venerable Ones received great gains and offerings for the sake of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs; these were neither given by the bhikṣuṇīs themselves, nor were they instructed to be given by them. Among these bhikṣuṇīs, there were daughters of kings, daughters of ministers, or daughters of wealthy householders. When each returned to their own homes, their parents asked:
"Who is the instructor for the bhikṣuṇīs?
They replied,
"The venerable ones instruct us."
Upon hearing this, the parents gave rise to a heart of joy and immediately provided the four requisites—food and drink, clothing, medicine, and bedding—to make offerings to those great virtuous ones.

There was a bhikṣuṇī who returned to her home and spoke of the great virtues of those elders—their observance of the precepts, their diligence, their learning, their patience, and their noble lineage. Upon hearing this, her parents increased their offerings to them.
Due to three causes and conditions, the venerable elders received great gains and offerings.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw that the venerable elders were receiving such great gains and offerings, they spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"We, too, are capable of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs."
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs went to the place of the group of six bhikṣus to request instruction.

After the group of six bhikṣus had explained a small portion of the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, they spoke at length about worldly matters such as the governance of kingdoms, times of famine or abundance, and cities and villages—all of which were words pertaining to the three evil realms.
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If a bhikṣu possesses eight qualities, he is qualified to instruct and admonish bhikṣuṇīs.

What are these eight? First, upholding the precepts; second, guarding the Prātimokṣa; third, being fully endowed with dignified deportment; fourth, feeling fear and dread at the sight of even a minor offense; fifth, firm persistence; sixth, extensive learning; seventh, firmness in that extensive learning; eighth, being able to analyze and expound the Dharma—good in the beginning, middle, and end, pure and singular, complete in the holy life (brahmacarya), possessing right view without deviation, reciting both sections of the Prātimokṣa with clear meaning and characters and fluent pronunciation, being respected and esteemed by bhikṣuṇīs, and being well-able to preach the Dharma in accordance [with their needs]. These are called the eight qualities."

"Regarding 'upholding the precepts' (śīla-dhara): some say it means the precepts are present within the body; others say it means upholding the precepts without transgression—this is called 'upholding the precepts.

Regarding 'protecting and maintaining': it means that the actions of body, speech, and mind do not transgress; or it refers to practicing the unsurpassed Dharma; or it refers to receiving the full ordination of the Prātimokṣa rules—this is called 'protective maintenance.'"
One who is fully endowed with dignified deportment does not maintain themselves through wrong livelihood and does not visit five places:

first, the house of a prostitute; second, the house of a widow; third, a bhikṣuṇī convent; fourth, the home of a young maiden; and fifth, the home of a eunuch. Furthermore, one does not visit the homes of lay female devotees (upāsikās) who have faith; this is called being fully endowed with dignified deportment.
To feel fear upon seeing even a minor transgression means that one regards a minor offense as no different from seeing a large venomous snake; this is called "fear.
To firmly maintain [the precepts] without violating them means that within the practice of upholding the precepts, one does not give rise to a regressive mind; this is called "firm maintenance."
"One who is learned" refers to one who understands one Āgama or, as some say, two Āgamas; this is called being learned.
"Firm" refers to the Āgamas understood by one that remain firm and are not lost; this is called being both learned and firm.
Regarding "good in the beginning, middle,
and end," the Dharma Master said:
"This was explained in the *Vairaṇyabrāhmaṇa-parivarta*."
One whose meaning is clear and distinct explains it for others without confusion or disorder.
One whose voice is fluent possesses eloquent speech and is not stammering.

One who is fluent in recitation recites the two divisions of the *Prātimokṣa* without obstruction; they perform the *poṣadha* every half-month, fully know the six days of fasting, and are able to preach the Dharma for others.

If one recites one Āgama or two Āgamas, one knows them without impediment; one knows the dharmas of the śramaṇa’s meditative concentrations, and even up to the fruit of arhatship, one knows them all without impediment.
"If one has reached twenty years of age, they are able to receive the full ordination for others.
The Dharma Master asked:
"Why does it not say that one must know the Abhidharma?"
He replied:
"If one can know the Abhidharma most excellently, that is best; however, those of inferior faculties who know the Vinaya and the Sūtras may also receive instruction."
[The questioner asked: "Fluent speech is what women delight in hearing; why then do you say that teaching bhikṣuṇīs requires fluent speech?
He replied:
"Women are mostly attached to sound, and only then will they listen to the Dharma."
Regarding "being respected by bhikṣuṇīs": because this bhikṣu possesses virtue and morality, he is held in high esteem by the bhikṣuṇīs and does not defile the three assemblies.
Why, then, is it said that one who defiles the three assemblies is ineligible for instruction?
If it were those who instruct, these nuns would not give rise to a mind of reverence upon seeing them.

One who has reached twenty years of age—if she has reached twenty years—will maintain the Dharma with firm resolve and suffer little decline; whereas one who is young and flighty is easily subject to decline. For this reason, it is prescribed that one must have twenty *varṣas* [of seniority] to be capable of instructing and admonishing bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding the sweeping and sprinkling of the quarters: the purpose of sweeping, sprinkling water, and preparing water is that since the bhikṣus have come from afar, one ought to provide them with bedding, mats, water, and drink; if there are no straw mats or cushions, one should at least provide a layer of grass.

If one preaches the Dharma for a bhikṣuṇī, one must have a companion; it is not permitted to preach within her room. If a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu on the road, she should join her palms if he is at a distance, and pay homage (vaṃdana) if he is near; this applies even in cases of royal danger or when the road is muddy. She should also exchange greetings with him.
During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one may enter the retreat at a distance of half a *yojana* from a bhikṣu monastery, but not beyond half a *yojana*.
If a donor invites a bhikṣuṇī to stay for the summer retreat and there are no bhikṣus upon whom she can rely, and the bhikṣuṇī wishes to depart, the donor says to her:
"Stay, and I, your disciple, shall invite a bhikṣu to come."
If one has not obtained an invitation by the time of the later *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), and there is a monk who can take up residence,
one should depart if the invitation cannot be secured.
If there are dangers to life or dangers to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) on the road, it is not an offense for a monk not to enter the *varṣā*.

If there is a bhikṣu who has completed the formal entry into the rains retreat (varṣā) at the beginning of the season, and that bhikṣu departs for a valid reason—whether due to returning to lay life or illness—and the bhikṣuṇīs do not know of his departure until later, they may not move their residence because the retreat has been formally entered; in this case, they are without offense.

When the *varṣā* retreat has concluded, one must not fail to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with other monks; one should seek them out. Every half-month, one should go among the community of monks and request two things.
What are these two things?
"First, to inquire about the date of the *poṣadha*; second, to request instruction and admonition.
The Dharma Master asked:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata so earnestly entrust the bhikṣuṇīs [to the bhikṣus]?"

Because the bhikṣuṇīs were women of dull faculties, at that time the entire community of bhikṣuṇīs went to the bhikṣus to receive instruction and admonition. People criticized and disparaged the bhikṣuṇīs for this; they reported the matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. Consequently, the Buddha established this regulation.
"From this day forward, many bhikṣuṇīs shall not go to request instruction and admonition; five may be permitted to go.
Because this led to criticism and suspicion, the Buddha said:

'I permit two or three to go. The bhikṣuṇī saṃgha should, by means of a formal act (karmavācanā), appoint two or three to go among the great assembly of monks (bhikṣusaṃgha) to request instruction and admonition.'"
"Even an araṇya bhikṣu should instruct bhikṣuṇīs.
How should he instruct them?
He should make an appointment at a tree or in a guest house. If the bhikṣuṇī fails to go as appointed, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu does not wait at the designated place until the appointed time, he also incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

When the bhikṣuṇīs perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day and the bhikṣu-saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, if the bhikṣuṇīs request that [the bhikṣus] speak [to them], yet [the bhikṣus] do not first speak of the Eight Respectful Rules (*gurudharma*) but instead speak of other matters, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If it is said that after the Eight Respects have been taught, other teachings may be spoken without offense—excluding cases where one does not commit an offense when answering questions, excluding cases where one does not commit an offense when speaking for the sake of others as the nuns permit, and excluding cases where one does not commit an offense when speaking for the sake of śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.
This is an offense by prohibition (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), arising from the mind and speech, and resulting in the three types of sensation."
If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, goes to a bhikṣuṇī monastery to provide instruction, it is a pāyattika.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Fifteen.
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra from the Western Regions during the Xiao Qi Dynasty:
"I shall now explain the fundamental causal conditions of Bandhula. 'Bandhula' means 'born by the roadside' in the Han language."

Why is this? Paṇḍaka’s mother was originally the daughter of a very wealthy elder; that elder had only this one daughter, for whom he constructed a seven-story pavilion and sent a male slave to provide her with all her necessities.
When the slave boy had grown up, this woman began to have illicit relations with him.
She then consulted with the slave boy, saying, "I shall now rebel against you and go to another country.
She asked the slave boy this three times, and the slave boy replied:
"I cannot go.
The girl said to the slave,
"If you do not go, my parents will find out and will surely kill you."
The slave replied, "If I go to another land, I will be poor and have no money or treasures; how shall I make a living?
The woman said to the slave:
"Follow me, and I shall steal precious treasures for us to take away together.
The slave replied,
"If it be so, I shall go with you."
This woman stole precious treasures day after day and gave them to the slave to carry out and hide outside.

Having calculated that they had accumulated a sufficient amount for both of them, she sent the slave out ahead to meet her outside. The woman then put on the clothes of a maidservant, turned the lock from within, and went out; together with the slave, they traveled far away to another country and settled there to live.
Within one or two years she became pregnant.
As she was about to give birth, she thought to herself:
"I am here now; when the time comes for me to give birth, if there is no one to attend to me, I will long for my mother and wish to return home."
Together with her husband-in-law, she deliberated:
"When I give birth, only my mother can attend to me; I wish to go now—will you go as well?"
The slave and his son-in-law replied:
"We cannot go; having fled in rebellion, how could we return?
Our master will surely kill us."
The wife said to her husband, "It is the nature of women that even when angry they cannot kill their own son; for this reason, I wish to leave.
The husband replied:
"If you do not kill me, you must kill me; I cannot leave.
While her husband had gone into the mountains to chop wood and was away, she locked the door and departed. When the husband returned and did not see his wife, he immediately asked the neighbors:
"Have you seen my wife?"
He replied, "Your wife has already gone.
Upon hearing this, the husband immediately pursued her; he caught up with her halfway along the road, by which time she had already given birth to a son. The husband said to his wife:
"You set out because you wished to give birth; now that you have already given birth, why do you need to go?
Upon hearing these words, the woman, out of shame before her parents, immediately returned home with him to manage their household life.
