Not long after that, she became pregnant again. As her time of delivery drew near, she longed for her mother and fled back home; however, having traveled halfway, she gave birth to another son, and her husband pursued them and returned with them halfway along the road.
Because the two sons were born by the side of the road, they were named Paṇḍa.
While the brothers Paṇḍa were playing with their peers, the two boys struck their companions with great force. Their peers scolded them, saying:
"You have no relatives or kinsmen; being all alone here, how dare you strike us?"
Having heard this reprimand, the boy returned home weeping and asked his mother, "Others all have six kinds of kinsmen and relatives; why is it that we alone have none?"
Her mother remained silent and gave no answer; the child wept and refused to eat or drink.
Seeing him thus weeping and refusing food, and out of her compassionate love for her two children, the mother spoke the truth to him:

"I am the daughter of a wealthy elder in a certain country; your father was a slave in that elder’s household sent to serve me. I became intimate with him and could not bear to be parted from him, so I fled with him and gave birth to you here."
Having heard their mother’s words, the two children said to her, "Please send us back to our maternal family; we cannot live here.
Their mother did not permit it, and as the two children wept incessantly, the mother immediately consulted with her husband-in-law:
"This child cries and refuses to stay here; how can we together send him back to his maternal home?
The husband said, "So be it."
They immediately went together to escort her.
Upon arrival, the parents and their son all stood outside the gate. Seeing the family members come out, they said:
"You may return and tell the elder that his daughter, along with her son-in-law, is now standing outside the gate."
Having heard this, the parents replied, "You may let the two boys enter, but you need not see them.

The elder then sent people to welcome the two boys inside; once they had entered, he bathed them with fragrant water, anointed their bodies with perfume, and dressed them in garments and jeweled ornaments.
The elder took the two children in his arms, placed them upon his two knees, and asked:
"How is your mother faring in that distant land?
Is she not suffering from extreme poverty?"
The two children replied, "Our parents are in another land and are impoverished; they sustain themselves by selling firewood.
Upon hearing these words, the mother felt compassion in her heart; she immediately opened the storehouse, filled a sack with gold, and sent someone to deliver it to the daughter, saying:
"Keep your two children and I shall support them myself; take this gold and return to your former dwelling to live well for yourself; there is no need for us to meet again."
When the two sons had grown up, their parents married them off.
When the parents were old and on the verge of death, they entrusted all their household affairs to the two sons, and then the parents passed away.

"At that time, as the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, Mahāpanda went to where the Buddha was to listen to the teaching. Having heard the Dharma, his heart delighted in leaving the household life; he returned home and deliberated with his younger brother:
'I now wish to go forth from the household life; I shall entrust the family affairs to you.'"
Upon hearing his elder brother’s words, the younger brother felt deep distress in his heart and said to him:
"I am now orphaned and destitute, with no one to rely upon; since you now abandon me to go forth into the religious life, how shall I be able to survive?"

Thus his younger brother made this request three times, but his elder brother’s mind remained firm and unshakable; he entrusted the affairs of the household to his brother and immediately went forth into homelessness. Not long after leaving the home life, he attained the state of an Arhat.
After a long time, his younger brother thought to himself:
"My elder brother has abandoned his family estate and given it to me; it is no different from someone's vomit. How could I accept it and give rise to greedy attachment?"
Because he was weary of the world, he went to his elder brother’s place seeking to leave the household life.

His brother immediately ordained him as a monk and taught him a single verse; for four months, he could not master it without forgetting the beginning when reciting the end. Elder Brother Mahāpandita thought to himself:
"This man has no affinity for the Buddha-dharma; I should send him back home."
He then said to Cūḍapanthaka,
"You are dull-witted," and immediately pulled his *kāṣāya* robe and drove him out the door; outside the gate, he wept, unwilling to return home.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing sentient beings with his divine eye, saw that Cūḍapanthaka was ready for the conditions of deliverance. The World-Honored One went to where he was and asked Cūḍapanthaka:
"Why are you weeping here?"
He answered the Buddha, saying:
"Since I am of dull faculties, I have been unable to recite a single verse even after four months; because of my dull faculties, my elder brother Mahāpandita has driven me out of the monastery."
The Buddha said:
"Cease, do not grieve; I shall instruct you.
The Dharma Master said:
“Mahāpandita, do you not see the causes and conditions for his attainment of the Way? Why did you drag him out?
He replied, “Cūḍapanthaka cannot be saved by a śrāvaka; only a Buddha can save him. That is why I dragged him out.”

The World-Honored One comforted his mind and immediately gave a small piece of white cotton cloth to Cūḍapanthaka, saying: "Take this cloth and hold it toward the sun while drying it; you should form this thought:
'Remove the stains! Remove the stains!'"

After the Buddha had finished teaching, he entered the village to accept the invitation of Visākhā-mātā. As the meal was being served, the Buddha observed that Cūḷapanthaka was about to attain the Way, and he immediately spoke this verse:
“The one who enters into stillness rejoices; Seeing the Dharma, they obtain peace and happiness.
In the world, there is no joy greater than non-anger, And none greater than not harming living beings.”
“There is no pleasure in the world like the joy of renouncing sensual desire;
if one subdues the conceit of ‘I am,’ this is the supreme bliss.
When Cūḍapanthaka heard this verse from afar, he immediately attained the fruit of arhatship.
Question: "If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī monastery and recites the Eight Rules of Respect, does he incur three pāyattikas? Answer:
"There are three cases: first, not being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, going to a bhikṣuṇī monastery; third, remaining until sunset. These three constitute pāyattika offenses.
If one goes to a bhikṣuṇī monastery to preach other teachings, one incurs one pāyattika offense and two duṣkṛta offenses."
What are these? First, not being appointed by the Saṃgha; second, going to a bhikṣuṇī monastery. These two constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one remains until sunset, it becomes a *pāyattika*.
Devadatta, Śaṇḍaka, Khaṇḍadravya, Kokālika, and Kāḷudāyin—these names are cited to identify them.
Regarding "eating in a separate group," there are two kinds of eating in a separate group:
first, being invited; second, begging.
How does one come to be eating in a separate group?
There was a lay follower who went to where four bhikṣus were staying and invited them with excellent food, saying, "May the Venerable Ones accept this.
This is called an invitation that constitutes eating in a separate group.

If one accepts an invitation at one time—whether for the following day or a later day—to eat at a single location, it constitutes eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*), and all four individuals incur an offense.

Having accepted the invitation at one time, if they each go to the donor’s house and, because they accepted the meal at one time, return to eat at their respective locations, they incur the same offense as before.
The Dharma Master said:
"For what reason?
Because they receive food all at once."
If one accepts an invitation at one time, yet goes separately, receives [food] separately, and eats separately, there is no offense.

If one is invited separately and goes separately, but then arrives at the donor's house and accepts [the meal] all at once, there is an offense; this is called "receiving an invitation and committing an offense."
What constitutes an offense through begging?
There were four bhikṣus who, whether sitting or standing, saw an upāsaka and said to him:
"Give us four portions of rice."

If one begs from each individual, saying, "Give me rice," it is likewise; whether they go together or separately, if one receives food at the same time, this is called incurring an offense through begging.

Regarding "the sick": when a person's foot is wounded and sand or dirt has entered it, such that they are unable to walk, they are permitted to receive a meal from a separate group; this is called "the sick.

Regarding "when making robes": if one obtains cloth for cutting, or if one has already cut and pieced the cloth to make a robe—even up to the point of attaching hooks and toggles to the garment—this is called "when making robes."
A "journeyer" refers to one who travels as little as half a yojana; the same applies to travel by boat.
When food is so scarce that it is insufficient for the meals of even four people, it is called a time of great famine.

Regarding the śramaṇa who bestows food: whether it be a śramaṇa of the same Dharma or a śramaṇa of a non-Buddhist path, there are seven causes and conditions by which one may partake of a meal from a separate group (bhedabhakta) without committing an offense.

These are: first, those not invited; second, those who have completed the four [requirements] for begging for alms; third, those who have not yet received full ordination; fourth, those who have completed the four [requirements] regarding the alms bowl; fifth, those who are ill. These five sets of four shall now be explained in detail.
What is meant by "not requesting [others] to complete the four"?
Suppose there is a donor who invites four people. One person, having learned of it, does not go to the donor's house. The donor asks:
"Did the Elder come?"
The three bhikṣus replied, "We have not come.

When the donor was about to eat his midday meal, he saw one bhikṣu; he immediately called him in and gave him food. Since all four ate together, they did not commit an offense. This is called "the fourth completing the uninvited."
Why does one not commit an offense?
First, because it was not by invitation.
How are the four requirements for begging for food fulfilled?
If three people accept the invitation while one person begs for alms and does not accept the invitation, they do not incur an offense.
With a śrāmaṇera completing the number four, if three practitioners of the Way and one śrāmaṇera accept the invitation, there is no violation.
Regarding the four permissible cases for the alms bowl: what are the four?
It is not an offense to accept an invitation to eat from three practitioners of the Way using a single bowl.
Regarding the fourth case for the sick: it is not an offense to accept an invitation from three practitioners of the Way and one sick bhikṣu, as these together complete the number of four.
Among the four people, there was one bhikṣu who understood the Vinaya. Fearing that he would commit an offense by eating together with them, he employed a skillful means.
When the donor distributed the food, he covered his bowl and did not accept it. The donor asked, "Why do you not accept?"
He replied, "Give food only to the three men; I wish to offer a prayer of blessing.
After the three bhikṣus had finished eating, he then accepted the food himself, and it was not an offense.
If one is invited for rice and, upon arriving at the house, is given meat, it constitutes an offense; if one is invited for rice and, upon arriving at the house, is given gruel, there is no offense.
"If there is a donor who wishes to feed the Sangha and sends someone to the monastery to invite the monks, saying, 'Please accept our meal.'"
Among the monks was a bhikṣu who understood the Vinaya, and he thought to himself:
"There are many in this Saṃgha who practice the dhūta austerities; it is because the messenger does not understand the Dharma that he makes such a request."
The bhikṣu who understood the Vinaya replied, "You shall know tomorrow.
The messenger came again, but as before, he did not understand the request to invite the Saṃgha; the bhikṣu who knew the Dharma replied:
"Tomorrow you shall know.
Thus it was passed along until half a month had elapsed, yet if [the donor] still did not understand, the monk who knew the Dharma said:
"If a donor invites the Saṃgha in such a manner, they obtain only śrāmaṇeras, not the Great Saṃgha."
The messenger said, "The other venerable ones also accept invitations from other households; why do you now not accept my invitation?
They replied:

"It is not that we do not accept invitations; rather, it is because you do not understand the Dharma. You should simply say, 'I invite the Saṃgha,' and not say, 'I give rice, parched grain, fish, meat, and so forth.
If one simply says, 'I invite the Saṃgha,' a bhikṣu may accept it without committing an offense."
If, despite being instructed in this manner, the messenger still does not understand the message, and [the monk], fearing public censure, says,
"You may simply go," then when the community of monks enters the village the following day to beg for food and goes to the house of the invited donor to receive alms, they do not commit an offense.
The detailed exposition of the precept against eating in a group is concluded.
This is an offense of formal prescription (*prajñapti-āpatti*), arising from both body and mind.

Regarding "eating by turns": if a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation, but the donor has not yet arrived, and the bhikṣu, fearing that it is late and worrying that the donor may not come, enters a village to beg for food.
Having returned from begging for alms, he saw that the invited donors had arrived; the bhikṣu did not eat, so the host asked him, "Venerable sir, why do you not eat?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Because I have accepted the invitation of a donor, I am not permitted to eat.
The donor said to him, "Just eat."
If one speaks in this manner, there is no offense in eating.
If many donors invite one at the same time, eating in this way is not an offense.
This concludes the precept on successive meals.
This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (offense of prohibition), arising from both body and mind.

Regarding the provisions for wives, merchants, or travelers on the road: if one takes one bowlful and departs, one may eat it at will oneself or give it to others. If one takes two bowls, one may eat one bowl oneself and give the other to the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). If one takes three bowls, one may eat one bowl oneself and give two bowls to the community of monks. One must not give them to acquaintances, laypeople, relatives, or donors who have invited one at their own discretion; furthermore, one must not take more than three bowls.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are easy to understand.
This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition), arising from body and mind; one cannot escape it on account of ignorance."
The precept regarding provisions for a woman returning from her husband’s home is concluded.

As for the five kinds of formal meals (*pañca bhojanāni*): rice from *śāli*, rice from *vrīhi*, rice from *kodrava*, red *śāli* rice, and barley meal—these five types of grain may be made into porridge; however, when it first comes out of the cauldron, if lines form characters upon it, one must not eat it. The same applies if rice is mixed with vegetables to make porridge.
If one eats rice with a small amount of grain and a large amount of water, thereby departing from the proper deportment, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food) ritual.
If rice is mixed with meat or fish to make a porridge, even if the pieces of meat appear as small as mustard seeds, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* ritual.
When meat is so soft that it is indistinguishable from water, the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) procedure need not be performed.
When rice is prepared from all kinds of grass roots or tree seeds, the *kṛtapiṇḍa* procedure need not be performed.
Regarding "dry rice": it may be made from millet, or from non-glutinous rice, or from wheat.
As for dry rice, it is dried by exposure to the sun; if it is made from beans or the seeds of trees, the rule for leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*) need not be applied.
Regarding parched grain: there are parched grains of non-glutinous rice, millet, and wheat; once one has finished eating them, one should perform the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-vidhi*).
There are two kinds of parched grain:
first, loose parched grain; second, parched grain formed into balls by mixing sugar and honey so that they adhere together.
Because the rice grains do not break apart, this rice does not require the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food) procedure.
If food is produced from flour, parched grain, or rice, the *kṛtapiṇḍa* procedure is not required.

If one has received the five kinds of formal food, and there is food remaining in the bowl or in the hand while another person is serving food, and one is within arm’s reach [of the donor] yet obstructs the departure from the proper deportment, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* procedure.

If one extends the hand to ward off food from outside, it does not constitute a valid warding-off (*pratikṣepa*). If one is within arm's reach and has finished swallowing the food in the mouth, a warding-off is not valid. If there is rice in the mouth and one extends the hand to ward it off from within, it constitutes a valid warding-off. If it is impure meat or anything otherwise unfit for consumption, a warding-off is not valid.
Why is this? That which is impure is not fit to be eaten.
If one eats impure meat, even if one extends the hand to stop [the act], it does not constitute a valid refusal.
If one refuses [food] to another, it does not constitute a refusal.
Why? Because the perception that the meal has not yet ended has not ceased.
If one is eating, a prohibition against giving to another does not constitute a valid prohibition.

Regarding "within arm's reach": within two and a half cubits from the body, a prohibition constitutes a valid prohibition; beyond two and a half cubits, a prohibition does not constitute a valid prohibition.
If one brings food and places it on the ground, such that it is not within arm's reach for the bhikṣu to receive, then even if one refuses it, the refusal is not valid.
If, however, a person with clean hands holds the food, then refusing it constitutes a valid refusal.
If one gives food to another bhikṣu while intending it for oneself, the refusal is not valid.
There are two kinds of refusal:
first, refusal by body; second, refusal by speech.
What is meant by "refusing with the body"?

It refers to using the hand to ward off, shaking the head, or covering the mouth or bowl with the hand; when one refuses in this manner, saying "I have finished" and will not accept, it constitutes a refusal.
If a soup is made by mixing vegetables with fish or meat, and one says "I accept vegetable soup," the refusal is not valid; however, if one says "I accept meat soup," the refusal is valid.

If one makes a congee by mixing what is permissible with what is impermissible, if one mentions the name of the permissible item, it constitutes a prohibition; if one mentions the name of the impermissible item, it does not constitute a prohibition.
Regarding those who observe the rules of deportment, there is no offense except when using boats or vehicles.
"Regarding 'leftover food of the sick,' it constitutes [an offense] whether the food has been partially eaten or not yet eaten at all.
The detailed explanation of the precept on leftover food is concluded.
This is a proscribed offense arising from body and speech."
All trees and grasses are not fit to be eaten as food; however, their roots, stems, flowers, and fruits may be consumed for as long as one lives.
Among the trees and plants, some have edible bodies that may be eaten at all times, some have edible heartwood that may be eaten at all times, while the remainder serve as medicines for life.
There is a tree whose entire body and form receive medicine.
The detailed explanation of the precept against eating at improper times is concluded.

If one begs for choice foods—milk, curd, fish, or meat—one incurs a *pāyattika*; if one begs for other food, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This does not constitute an offense except when begging on behalf of a sick person.
The precept on begging for fine food is concluded.
"Excepting water and tooth-sticks": if food is offered by a deva or human, or if food is offered by a ghost or spirit, or even by an animal or a flying bird, it all constitutes a valid acceptance.
If food is placed upon the head or carried on the shoulder and given to a bhikṣu, instructing him to take it himself, the acceptance is not valid.
If he lowers his body and the food falls into the bhikṣu’s hands, the acceptance is valid.

If a carrying pole up to twenty *vyāma* in length has food placed at both ends, and a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) carries it together and hands it to a monk, if the monk receives one end, the other end is also considered received.
If, while begging for alms, he encounters wind and rain such that dust falls into his bowl, the bhikṣu should think:
"I shall beg for alms on behalf of the śrāmaṇera.
Having obtained food and returned, he says to the śrāmaṇera:
"I have now gone out for alms, but encountering wind, rain, and falling dust, the food has entered my bowl; thus it cannot be accepted.
For your sake I have begged for this food, and I now bring it to you.
Having received it, the śrāmaṇera said to the bhikṣu:
"This is the food of a śrāmaṇera; I now offer it to you, Venerable Sir.
If one gives in this manner, one may eat the food without offense.
If a bhikṣu holds his bowl in his hand but falls asleep while eating, and someone places food into the bowl without the bhikṣu being aware of it, the act of receiving is not accomplished.
If one falls asleep at the time of receiving food, and someone places the food into one's bowl, the act of receiving is accomplished.
Why is this? Because the intention to receive the food has been formed.
If the dust particles are large, they may be removed and one may eat without offense; if the particles are fine and cannot be removed, one should have someone else pass them over.
If two people are eating together, or while food is being served, if leftover food splashes into a bhikṣu’s bowl, it constitutes a formal acceptance.
If, while eating, sweat flows from the forehead and falls into the bowl, one should receive it again.
If sweat from the arm flows onto the hand, there is no need to receive it.
If food is tossed from the ground and lands on the monk’s hand, it constitutes a valid reception.
If a lay attendant stands atop a tree and ties fruit with a rope to hand it to a bhikṣu, the acceptance is not valid.
If a person has long arms and extends food across a distance of up to ten yojanas to give it to a bhikṣu, the acceptance is valid.

If a bhikṣu is ill, and a śrāmaṇera or a lay attendant (upāsaka) carries him along to see fruit, the bhikṣu asks the attendant for it; once the attendant has taken the fruit and turned his hand toward the bhikṣu’s body to pass it over, the acceptance is accomplished.

If a bhikṣu suffers from heat and walks while holding a branch of a fruit tree to shield himself from the sun, and later sees that there are fruits on the branch, he must not move it; he may instruct a śrāmaṇera to pluck the fruit and hand it to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu may accept it.
If food or drink is being carried on a boat or a cart, and a bhikṣu moves the boat with a pole or pulls the cart so that the food is shifted, he may eat it without fault.

If many bhikṣus are traveling together and there is only one young śrāmaṇera, and each bhikṣu carries his own provisions, when it is time to eat they each divide their portions; once the śrāmaṇera has received his share, he says to the bhikṣus:
"I shall now take my portion and exchange it for yours, Venerable Sirs."

Having obtained it through exchange, he then took it and exchanged it with the second senior elder; having obtained the food from the second senior elder, he then exchanged it with the third senior elder. In this manner, passing it along in succession until it reached many others, eating in such a way is entirely without fault.
If the śrāmaṇera does not understand the Dharma, the bhikṣu may personally take his portion of food and exchange it with the śrāmaṇera;
once the first senior elder has received the exchange, the second senior elder likewise exchanges with the śrāmaṇera, and the second senior elder receives the exchange.
The third elder again requested an exchange; in this manner, many successive exchanges were made, and all obtained food through substitution without offense.

Regarding "staying overnight with what is unwholesome to touch": if a bhikṣu is carrying rice on a journey and a śrāmaṇera is too young to prepare the meal, the bhikṣu may prepare it himself, provided he does not light a fire.
If one instructs a śrāmaṇera to light a fire and, once the food is cooked, distributes it by passing it around as before and exchanging it with the śrāmaṇera, there is no offense.
If one prepares food oneself and the boiling food overflows, the bhikṣu must not blow on it with his breath or stir it with an object; to do so constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one has vomited food that has not yet passed the throat and swallows it back, there is no offense.
If it has passed the throat and entered the mouth before being swallowed back, one commits a *pāyattika*.
If a sprout grows after ginger has been accepted, the validity of the acceptance is not lost.
If a sprout grows after the fire has purified [the ground], the place where the sprout grows should be purified again; it is not the case that one may eat the sprout without fault.
If one first receives salt and the salt turns into water, the original acceptance is not lost.
If there is an urgent cause for illness, one may personally take and consume excrement, urine, ash, or earth.
If there is no ash available, one may break a tree, kindle a fire, and make ash.
"What is illness?
It is to contract a venomous poison, such as being bitten by a snake.
The Dharma Master said:
"The remaining phrases are easy to understand.
This is an offense by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), arising from body and speech.
These two rules concerning sitting in a layperson's home for a meal, along with the two *aniyata* dharmas, have now been explained."

Regarding sitting with a woman in a secluded place: if two people sit together on a bed and converse such that they understand each other, and they extend their hands within reach of one another, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If they do not understand each other's language and one extends the hand inside [the robe] and withdraws it, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son was the nephew of the Buddha; he was born one month after the Buddha and attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
If a donor offers medicine, it should be used for medicinal purposes and not for food.
To request ghee when oil has been given constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
As for the elephant army: there are four men atop each elephant and eight men below; this is called an elephant army.
As for the cavalry, one person is on horseback and two are below; this is called the cavalry.
As for the chariot force, four persons accompany each chariot; this is called the chariot force.
Regarding "infantry": four persons following one another is called infantry.
If food or medicine has been boiled with alcohol such that it possesses the aroma of alcohol, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it lacks the aroma of alcohol, it may be eaten.
If one plays in water that is deep enough to submerge the tops of the feet, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one rocks a boat or splashes about in the water, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding "blue" (*nīla*): it may be verdigris, indigo blue, or madder color.
The "wood-grain color" refers to a clay spot.
One should purify [the robe] with these three types of spots, each as large as a sesame seed; if one does not purify it in this manner, one commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings and drinks it, he commits a pāyattika offense for every breath and every swallow.
If he knows that water contains living beings and pours hot water over it with fire, it is likewise.
The precept regarding water containing insects has been explained.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it, and a second bhikṣu likewise conceals it, and so on until a hundred thousand people conceal it together, they all commit a pāyattika offense."
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), arising from both body and mind.
The section on concealing another’s offenses is concluded.

If one is less than twenty years of age and wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is permitted to count the months of gestation and intercalary months; provided that the count reaches twenty by the time of the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day, one may receive the precepts.
To deliberate with a group of thieves regarding traveling together on the road is an offense of formal prescription (*prajñapti-āpatti*).
To deliberate with a bhikṣuṇī regarding traveling together on the road is an offense of formal prescription.
This has already been explained in the Vinaya.
The heretical view of Ariṣṭa consists of being attached to fine and smooth textures, yet he claims this does not obstruct the path to heaven nor the path to liberation.

The reason Ariṣṭa gives rise to this false view is that he says even *srotāpannas* and *sakṛdāgāmins* who have wives and children do not have their progress on the path hindered; drawing this analogy to himself, he asserts that attachment to fine and smooth textures cannot obstruct the path.

If you say that smoothness and softness can obstruct the Path, then since all woolen rugs and pillows are also smooth and soft, why do you say specifically that the smoothness and softness of women alone can obstruct the Path?
The detailed exposition on the false view and precepts of Ariṣṭa is concluded.
"If one studies the Vinaya, there are five virtues, six virtues, seven virtues, eight virtues, nine virtues, ten virtues, and eleven virtues."
What are the five virtues? First, one personally guards the precepts;
second, one is able to sever the doubts of others; third, one enters the assembly without fear; fourth, one is able to subdue enemies; and fifth, one causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
What is meant by "protecting the precepts for oneself"?
To maintain the precepts with purity, without deficiency or flaw—this is called protecting the precepts.

According to the Vinaya masters, one does not incur an offense through six conditions: first, acting without intent; second, acting out of ignorance; third, acting without doubt; fourth, declaring what is impure to be pure; fifth, declaring what is pure to be impure; and sixth, acting out of confusion.
What is meant by "acting without purpose"?
To act intentionally while knowing [the consequences] is called acting without purpose.

As stated in the Vinaya-mūla: to commit an offense intentionally while knowing it, and to conceal it with full knowledge by going to places where one ought not to go—this is called acting without purpose.
What is "offense through ignorance"?
This person does not know the characteristics of the precepts; they act with the intention to act [without knowing], and this is called committing an offense through ignorance.
What is "offense through doubt"?
If one acts with a mind that gives rise to doubt while performing the act, this is called "incurring guilt through doubt.
What is meant by "calling the impure pure"?
This bear meat is impure, yet one says it is pork and eats it; this is called "calling the impure pure."
To say that tiger meat is deer meat, or to say that food eaten at an improper time is food eaten at a proper time—this is called calling the impure pure.
What is it to call the pure impure?
To eat deer meat while perceiving it to be tiger meat, and so on, up to eating at a proper time while saying it is at an improper time—this is called calling the pure impure.
What is meant by "confusion" (*mūḷha*)?
To stay together with a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights without realizing it is called confusion and constitutes an offense.
There is confusion regarding the lack of awareness of whether it is the proper time or the improper time; likewise, to stay apart from one's robe without being aware of it is also called confusion.
"How does one resolve the doubts of others?

When a bhikṣu has committed an offense and, being uncertain, is unable to reach a decision, if he comes to consult [the teacher], the teacher adjudicates according to the Vinaya; this is called 'resolving the doubts of others.'"
What is fearlessness when entering an assembly?
Because one knows the Vinaya, one is able to act according to the circumstances; this is called fearlessness when entering an assembly.
What is being able to subdue enemies?
Just as when the Licchavis committed ten unrighteous acts, they were able to eliminate them by relying on the Vinaya; this is called being able to subdue enemies.
How does one cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time?

First, one personally conforms to the Dharma; second, one enables others to attain the Dharma. Because they attain the Dharma, they maintain the Vinaya with a rectified mind; because they maintain the Vinaya, they enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and because of meditative concentration, they attain the fruits of the Path. This is called causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
As stated in the Vinaya-mūla-sūtra, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the Vinaya shall be your great teacher.
This is called causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time.

At the very least, if five bhikṣus who understand the Vinaya remain in the world, they can cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time. If the Buddha-dharma should perish in Central India, and if there are five persons in a border region who have received the precepts, once ten persons are complete, they may go to Central India and bestow full ordination upon others; this is called causing the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
In this manner, up to twenty people may be cleared of their offenses; this is called causing the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
Because of the *vinaya*-master, the True Dharma is made to endure; these are called the five virtues of one who upholds the *vinaya*.
"What are the six virtues of one who upholds the Vinaya? First, to guard and lead the Prātimokṣa;

second, to know the Poṣadha ceremony; third, to know the Pravāraṇā ceremony; fourth, to know the method for bestowing full ordination upon others; fifth, to accept others' reliance [upon oneself]; and sixth, to be permitted to maintain śrāmaṇeras."
These are called the six virtues.
What is meant by upholding the Prātimokṣa?

One should know the fourteen-day poṣadha, the fifteen-day poṣadha, the harmonious poṣadha, the saṃgha-poṣadha, the assembly-poṣadha, the single-person poṣadha, the poṣadha for reciting the Prātimokṣa, the pure poṣadha, and the instructed poṣadha; these are called the nine poṣadhas, which are what a vinaya-master must know.
There are nine types of *pravāraṇā*: first, the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day;

second, the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day; third, the *pravāraṇā* of communal harmony; fourth, the *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha; fifth, the *pravāraṇā* of the assembly; sixth, the *pravāraṇā* of a single person; seventh, the *pravāraṇā* by three utterances; eighth, the *pravāraṇā* by two utterances; ninth, the *pravāraṇā* of equal seniority. These are what the Vinaya masters know.
The Sangha has four formal procedures: first, the motion (*jñapti*);

second, the motion-and-one-karmavācanā; third, the motion-and-two-karmavācanā; and fourth, the motion-and-three-karmavācanā. These four procedures are what the Vinaya masters know, not what the Sūtra masters or the Abhidharma masters know.
If one does not understand the Vinaya but only knows the Sūtras and Abhidharma, they may not ordain śrāmaṇeras or receive others' reliance.
There are five virtues and six virtues for a monk; together these constitute the eleven virtues of a Vinaya Master.
Because the Dharma Master Upāli upholds the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma shall remain in the world for five thousand years; for this reason, many bhikṣus come to Upāli to study the Vinaya.
How does one study the Vinaya?
To recite and explain the meaning [of the Vinaya] is called "studying the Vinaya.
Regarding the "miscellaneous minor rules": from the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules down to the *śaikṣa* (training) rules, these are called the miscellaneous minor rules.

If one reviles the precepts in the presence of a *mahābhikṣu*, one incurs a *pāyattika*; if one reviles the precepts in the presence of one who has not received full ordination, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. The remaining phrases are easy to understand and need not be explained in detail.
The section on reviling the precepts is concluded.
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) arising from body and speech.

Regarding "striking": the group of six bhikṣus constantly employed the group of seventeen bhikṣus as servants; because they would not obey their commands, they struck them. If one strikes with a mind of anger, even to the point of death, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one strikes with a mind of anger, even to the point of breaking the head or fracturing the hands or feet, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; if one strikes those who have not received full ordination, down to animals, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one strikes a woman with a lustful mind, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If there is danger from tigers, wolves, lions, or even from those who obstruct one’s holy life (*brahmacarya*), striking with the hand to seek liberation is not an offense.
Regarding "striking with the hand" (*pāṇi-ghāta*): it refers to striking with the hand when the hands do not actually touch the body.
The section on the prohibition against boxing is concluded.

Regarding "listening in a secluded place": if one goes toward a location shielded by a wall or a shaded area, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for every step taken; upon reaching the place where the sound can be heard, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. However, there is no offense if one goes there with the intention of reforming oneself after having previously listened.
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
"If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (*chanda*), later regrets it, there is no [formal] resolution for this offense.
Seventy-sixth: If a bhikṣu rises and leaves in silence while the Saṃgha’s legal proceedings have not yet concluded, there is no [formal] resolution for this offense."

If a bhikṣu first listens with joy and later speaks in such a manner, and the other bhikṣus, following their personal attachments, divert monastic property to him, there is no [formal] release from the offense.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are ten faults in entering a royal palace."
What are the ten?

First, if a king and his consort are sitting together in one place, and the consort sees a bhikṣu and smiles, and the bhikṣu sees the consort and also smiles, the king, having seen this, becomes suspicious and thinks, "This bhikṣu must have had illicit relations with the consort. This is called the first fault.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are further faults in entering the royal palace. Suppose the king has engaged in sexual union with a court lady in the palace and forgets it; later, a son is born, and the king says:
'I have not approached this court lady; how could there be a son?'"
"This must have been done by that bhikṣu.
This is the second fault.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.
"Furthermore, there is another fault: if a treasure is lost within the palace and cannot be found after a search, the king will say, 'There is no one else;
it must have been taken by the bhikṣu.'"
"This is called the third fault.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Furthermore, there is another fault: if private conversation within the royal palace reaches the outside, the king will think to himself:"
"When this bhikṣu spreads [the matter] outside," this is called the fourth fault.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.

"Furthermore, there is another fault: if the king degrades from a great rank to a small one, or promotes from a small rank to a great one, no one will be permitted to enter the royal palace; this must be the work of that bhikṣu instructing the king."
"This is called the fifth fault.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There is another fault in entering the royal palace: if the king dismisses an elder official and dispatches his son as a replacement, people will criticize and find it offensive, saying:"
"When this bhikṣu enters or leaves the royal palace, he will instruct the king in what he should do.
This is called the seventh fault.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.

"Furthermore, there is another fault in a bhikṣu entering the royal palace: if the king dispatches an army at an improper time, people will criticize and disparage him, saying, 'This must have been done by the bhikṣu instructing the king.'"
"This is called the eighth fault.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There is yet another fault regarding entering a royal palace: if the king dispatches an army at an improper time and it retreats midway, people will criticize and disparage him, saying:"
"It was that bhikṣu who instructed the king in what he did.
This is called the ninth fault.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.

"Furthermore, there is another fault in entering the royal palace: if the king trains elephants, horses, or chariots adorned with jewels, people will criticize and find it objectionable, saying, 'This must have been done at the instruction of the bhikṣu.'"
"This is called the tenth fault.
The detailed exposition of the precept regarding entering the royal palace is concluded.
"If one takes up precious objects on behalf of the Buddha or the Sangha, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."

If one finds a lost treasure within a monastic dwelling or a residential area, for the sake of safeguarding it, when departing one should entrust it to someone who knows the Dharma and fears wrongdoing, saying:
"When the owner comes to claim it, you must return it."
If, after a long time, no owner comes to claim it, it may be used for a dwelling or for a pond or well, but it must not be used for one’s own personal needs.
If later on an owner comes to claim it, one should show them the monastery quarters, the pond, or the well, saying:
"This was the property of a donor."
If one abandons the merit of giving, or if one wishes to recover an object previously given that was not offered, the bhikṣu should enter a village and say to a faithful donor:

"On such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, an item was found as a lost article in the monastery. It has been kept in custody for a long time with no one coming to claim it; therefore, we have used it for the monastery’s rooms, ponds, and wells."
"The owner has now come to reclaim it, wishing to receive back its original value. Lay donor, would you be able to redeem it with goods and offer them as a gift to the Sangha?
"If you can redeem it and give it as a gift, that would be excellent."
If there is no one able to redeem it, the bhikṣu should extensively teach and convert others to seek and obtain the price to return it.
This concludes the detailed explanation of the precept regarding the handling of precious objects.
This is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by formal rule), arising from bodily action.
The precept regarding entering a village at an improper time has no commentary.
The precept regarding high beds has no commentary.
The precept regarding sitting mats stuffed with *tūla* cotton has no commentary.
The precept regarding the needle case has no [specific] explanation.
Regarding the *niṣīdana* mat: its length shall be two *vitasti*, and its width one and a half *vitasti*.
As for "adding thread," it means adding one *vitasti*; six feet constitute a "broken head," and one *vitasti* is made into three breaks, which is termed "thread."
The training rule on the Sugata-span *niṣīdana* is concluded.
The training rule on the *vraṇapaṭṭa* (sore-covering cloth) has no commentary.
The training rule on the *varṣāśāṭī* (rain-bathing robe) has no commentary.
The first *pāṭidesanīya* is not understood.

If a husband and wife both attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, even if they were to give away hundreds of thousands of taels of gold, it would all be due to their attainment of the Way; consequently, they would have no stinginess regarding wealth. Because their excessive giving would leave the household impoverished, the Buddha established this precept that one must not accept food [from such a couple].
*Śeṣa* means "training.
*Kāraṇī* means that one should train in making [the garment] such that the legs are large or the thighs are small so that it may be worn below [the waist].

Regarding the discarding of water used for washing the bowl inside a layperson's house: if one scoops up rice grains and gives them to sentient beings, there is no offense in discarding the remaining water; or if one crushes [the rice] and mixes it with the water before discarding it, there is no offense. One must not use pure water for defecation or urination.
There is no offense if it is water not used by people, or seawater;
there is no offense even if it is water suitable for use, provided it is in a remote place where no one uses it.
"Regarding 'staying overnight in a stūpa' and 'storing items within a stūpa,' these two precepts do not exist in the Sanskrit original.
The reason they are absent is that while the Buddha was alive, there were no stūpas; these precepts were established during the Buddha's lifetime.

Therefore, [the following cases] do not apply: entering a stūpa wearing leather sandals, entering a stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hand, or entering a stūpa wearing a *kholapa* (a knee-length robe)."
Entering a Buddhist stūpa; entering a Buddhist stūpa while holding an alms-bowl in one’s hand; eating beneath a Buddhist stūpa; carrying a corpse beneath a stūpa;
burning a corpse beneath a stūpa; burning a corpse facing a stūpa; burning a corpse while circumambulating the four sides of a stūpa;
passing beneath a stūpa carrying the clothes or the bed of a dead person; and defecating or urinating beneath a Buddhist stūpa.

One must not defecate or urinate facing a Buddhist stūpa, nor defecate or urinate while circumambulating a Buddhist stūpa. One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecating or urinating.

One must not chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) beneath a Buddhist stūpa, nor chew a tooth-stick facing a Buddhist stūpa, nor chew a tooth-stick while circumambulating the four sides of a Buddhist stūpa. One must not discharge nasal mucus beneath a Buddhist stūpa.

Regarding spitting: one must not spit toward a stūpa, nor spit while circumambulating the four sides of a stūpa, nor extend one's feet toward a stūpa, nor place a Buddha image in a lower room. These twenty precepts above do not exist in the Sanskrit original;
this is because when the Tathāgata was in the world, there were no stūpas.
At that time, the Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"Why do you preach the Dharma while standing below and with people above you?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a householder named Carpaka.
His wife became pregnant and longed for mangoes; she said to her husband, 'I long for mangoes; please seek them for me.'"
Her husband replied, "This is not the season for mangoes; how could I obtain them?
His wife said to her husband:
"If you do not obtain the mango fruit, I shall surely die.
When the husband heard his wife's words, he thought to himself:
"Only in the king's garden are there out-of-season mango fruits; I shall go there to steal them."
Having formed this thought, that very night he entered the royal garden to steal mangoes.
While he was still gathering the fruit and had not yet succeeded, the break of dawn appeared; unable to leave the garden, he remained hidden upon a tree.
Then the king and the brahmin entered the garden, intending to eat mangoes.
The brahmin sat on the ground while the king was seated upon a high throne; the brahmin then preached the Dharma for the king.
The fruit-thief, while up in the tree, thought to himself:
"I am now a thief of fruit and my crime deserves death; however, because the king permitted the Brahmin to preach the Dharma, I have now been delivered."
I have transgressed the Dharma; the King has also transgressed the Dharma, and the Brahmin has likewise transgressed the Dharma. Why is this?
It was for the sake of a woman that I stole the King’s fruit.
Because the king was still arrogant, he sat on a high seat while his teacher sat below to listen to the Dharma;
because the brahmin craved offerings and gain, he sat on a low seat while preaching the Dharma for the king.
"I have no legal standing with the king or the brahmins; I am now free.
Having thought this, he immediately descended from the tree, went before the king, and spoke these verses:
"Two men do not know the Dharma; Two men do not see the Dharma."
The teacher does not rely on the Dharma, and the listener does not understand the Dharma;
for the sake of eating fine rice and various other delicacies—
for the sake of such food and drink— I declare that this is not the Dharma.
"For the sake of fame and profit, you have destroyed and shattered the laws of your own family.

[The Buddha said: "When I was still an ordinary person, if I saw someone standing above while a Dharma-preacher stood below, I would declare it to be contrary to the Dharma; how much more so now that I am a superior being, yet you, my disciples, stand below me as I preach the Dharma?"
"The one who stole the fruit at that time was my own self.
This concludes the detailed exposition of the training rules for novices (*śaikṣa-dharma*).
The seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*) shall be explained in detail later in the *Kṣudraka-vastu*.
"Next, the Bhikṣuṇī precepts are explained.
Regarding 'touching': from below the collarbone to above the elbows and knees, touching [a male] constitutes a *pārājika* offense."
If a bhikṣuṇī touches a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu experiences pleasure without moving his body, the bhikṣu incurs no offense.
If a bhikṣu comes and touches a bhikṣuṇī and the bhikṣuṇī experiences pleasure without moving her body, she incurs an offense according to the specific circumstances.
The four *pārājika* rules are concluded.
If a bhikṣuṇī says, "Let us go together to the government office," or if a bhikṣuṇī says to a layperson,
"You speak first regarding the principle of the case."
If a layperson is speaking according to the principle, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
Once the layperson has finished speaking, if the bhikṣuṇī further speaks to the official, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a householder further says: "A bhikṣuṇī may be found guilty of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, and even if she is not found guilty, she still commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Or if a householder says regarding a bhikṣuṇī: "The authorities have summoned the bhikṣuṇī; once she has arrived, they say to her: 'Just go back;
the authorities will judge the case themselves.'"
Whether she succeeds in her purpose or not, the bhikṣuṇī does not commit an offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī goes before an official to speak on behalf of someone, and the official asks what kind of person they are, she must not disclose their name. If the official orders a fine to be paid, she commits an offense according to the amount of the value; she must repay it.
If questioned by an official, it is not an offense if one does not state their name.
If the official later investigates on his own and identifies the owner, the official will punish himself [for the error], and [the monk] remains unoffended.
"If someone steals a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, one must not call them a thief; one should simply say, 'This person has taken my robe.'"

If someone is about to plunder a bhikṣuṇī, she may go before the king and beg for protection of her person; however, she must not utter his name. If she mentions his name, she commits an offense as previously described.
When the king heard that the bhikṣuṇī had requested protection for her person, he beat the drum to proclaim an edict:
"If there be anyone who offends against a bhikṣuṇī, they shall be punished according to the law."
"Later, if someone commits an offense against a bhikṣuṇī, the king shall personally adjudicate and punish them according to the law, while the bhikṣuṇī remains innocent.

If someone enters a bhikṣuṇī’s monastery and cuts down trees, one must not seize their axe or hatchet nor strike them to break them; however, if they are struck and broken, the value must be repaid. If it is not repaid, one commits an offense proportionate to the amount of the value."
The remaining phrases and sentences are easy to understand.
The detailed explanation of the precepts for laypeople is concluded.
Regarding the precept for ordaining a female thief, the fifth [section] is not understood.
If one repeatedly goes outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the precepts, there is no lifting of the sixth [offense].
If a bhikṣuṇī crosses a body of water alone in a boat, it is also a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the seventh.
The seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are concluded.
Regarding the thirty matters concerning what is not an offense:
"Garlic" refers exclusively to large garlic; if one eats it, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense. Other small garlics or scallions do not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, it is not an offense to use large garlic as a seasoning or condiment in food.

If washing the area of urination, the two fingers may not exceed one joint; if washing with one finger, it may enter up to two joints but must not exceed them. One must not wash using both fingers; to do so constitutes an offense.

If one begs for grain or wheat, it is a *pāyattika*; begging for beans, gourds, or vegetables does not constitute an offense. Begging for grain or wheat for the purpose of constructing a dwelling does not constitute an offense.
One must never defecate or urinate upon raw vegetables, fruit trees, or standing crops of grain; to do so incurs the guilt of a *pāyattika*.
If one urinates or defecates upon any other fruit trees or grain seeds before they have sprouted, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

To go and watch performances or music—even down to watching monkeys or peacocks playing together—is a *pāyattika* offense; however, if one goes to watch a performance held within a monastery, there is no offense.
If the summer retreat has concluded, one should depart from the monastery for a distance of six *yojanas*; if one does not do so, there is an offense of *pāyattika*.
Regarding the eight *pratideśanīya* rules, there is no further explanation.
The Bhikṣuṇī-śīla is concluded.
The Skandhaka—translated into Chinese as the *Zà jiàndù* (Miscellaneous Khandhas)—states:

At that time, after seven days had passed, the Buddha arose from meditative concentration. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, offered him *harītakī* fruit; having accepted and eaten it, the Tathāgata relieved himself, whereupon Śakra again presented him with a willow twig and pure water for cleansing.

At that time, two merchant brothers came from the village of Ukkala, carrying goods in a cart intending to travel to the Middle Kingdom. Upon reaching the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, the cart stopped of its own accord and refused to proceed further.
Seeing that the carriage would not move forward, the two brothers considered it an ill omen and immediately prepared food and drink to offer as sacrifices to the spirits.
At that moment, the tree deity manifested half of its body and spoke to the merchants, saying:
"Your carriage does not leave because I am holding it back."

"Merchants, you should know that Prince Śuddhodana has left the household life to study the Way; he is now beneath the Bodhi tree and has attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). Having not eaten for seven days, you should offer parched grain and honey to the Tathāgata, so that you may obtain benefit, peace, and happiness throughout the long night."
At that time, the two brothers, having heard the words of the tree deity, immediately offered the flour and honey to the Buddha.
This sequence of phrases has already been explained in the Vinaya: the first to receive the Three Refuges were the two merchants who presented the flour and honey to the Buddha.
After these two brothers had received the refuges and wished to return, they said to the Buddha, "How may the two of us make offerings to the Buddha?
The Buddha stroked his own head with his hand, and his hair fell away immediately as he touched it; he then spoke to the merchants:
"You should honor these hairs as your Great Teacher.
He asked: "Where is the bowl that previously received the milk-rice now?"
"Why has he now again accepted the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings?
He replied:

"When the Buddha previously accepted the bowl of milk gruel and crossed the Nairañjanā River, the bowl sank into the water at that time. The Dragon King of the Sea took it to offer worship; for this reason, he has again accepted the bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, which is as beautiful in color as jade."
If a person seeks to go forth from the household life, and their parents have already granted permission, they are free from illness, and there are no obstacles, they should come before the Saṃgha.
If the assembly is gathered, one should announce it to the Saṃgha; if they are not gathered, one should inform each individual so that they may know.
Having informed the Saṃgha, one should first bathe him; once he has been bathed, the preceptor should regard him as a son and must not harbor thoughts of impurity or contempt. Why is this?
If one attends to them with such a sincere heart, the disciple will then conceive of the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the ācārya as their father.
When it is time for the tonsure, the preceptor should explain five dharmas to him.
What are these five?
First, hair; second, body hair; third, nails; fourth, teeth; and fifth, skin.

The reason these five things are mentioned is that there were those who, having previously contemplated these five things in a former life, now had their hair shaved and fallen to the ground, whereby their past karma was activated and they immediately attained arhatship.
For this reason, one first teaches the five dharmas and only then performs the tonsure.

As in the case of Rāhula, whose hair had not yet fallen out entirely when he became an Arhat; it is like a boil that must be lanced by another person before it can be burst, or like a lotus flower that must wait for the rising sun before it can bloom.
This person seeking to leave the household life is also like this: by means of explaining five dharmas, they immediately attain realization of the Way.

When the hair is being shaved, one should leave five or three strands of hair at the crown of the head; one is then bathed with fragrant water to remove the scent of the layperson's robes. Coming before the Upādhyāya, one kneels on the ground with the right knee touching it.
The Upādhyāya asks: "I am now going to shave the hair from the crown of your head; do you consent?"
He replied, "So be it.
The Upādhyāya then shaved the hair on the crown of his head himself.

Having shaved the hair on the crown of his head, he knelt with his right knee on the ground before the preceptor; the preceptor bestowed the kāṣāya upon him, which he received by placing it upon his head, and having received it, he returned it to the preceptor.
In this manner, he receives it for the second and third times.
Having received it upon his head, the preceptor shall put it on for him; he must not take the *kāṣāya* robe himself and put it on, as it must necessarily be conferred by the preceptor.
Having paid homage in succession to all the bhikṣus, he went to the ācārya, prostrated at his feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms. The ācārya instructed him, saying:
"You should follow my words; I shall teach you how to receive the Three Refuges."
He replied, “So be it.
Having completed the bestowal of the Three Refuges, he next conferred the Ten Precepts.
"What is meant by 'bestowing the three refuges'?
He replied:
"There are two ways of receiving the three refuges:"
"The first is individual reception; the second is collective reception.
"What is individual reception? "Individual reception means:

having taken refuge in the Buddha, having taken refuge in the Buddha, having taken refuge in the Buddha; having taken refuge in the Dharma, having taken refuge in the Dharma, having taken refuge in the Dharma; having taken refuge in the Saṅgha, having taken refuge in the Saṅgha, having taken refuge in the Saṅgha—this is called individual reception."

Regarding the summary reception: one takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Sangha. Having completed taking refuge in the Buddha, having completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and having completed taking refuge in the Sangha—one recites this three times; this is called the summary reception.

One must not first take refuge in the Saṃgha and subsequently take refuge in the Dharma and the Buddha, nor should one speak in a confused manner; however, if the teacher instructs, "Take refuge in the Buddha," and the disciple’s speech is not formal but says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," the taking of refuge is nonetheless accomplished.
If the teacher instructs, "Take refuge in the Buddha," and the disciple says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," the reception of the three refuges is nonetheless accomplished.
However, if both the teacher and the disciple speak incorrectly when saying, "Take refuge in the Buddha," the reception of the three refuges is not accomplished.

If the teacher instructs the disciple to take refuge in the Buddha, and the disciple replies "yes," or fails to speak at all, or speaks without completing the words, in all such cases, the three refuges are not successfully received.
Having completed the reception of the Three Refuges, one next bestows the Ten Precepts.
There are two ways to receive the Ten Precepts:
first, receiving them individually; second, receiving them collectively.
What is meant by "receiving separately"?

It is when one receives [the precept] of not killing, receives [the precept] of not killing, and receives [the precept] of not killing; having completed the receiving of not killing, one proceeds in this same manner for each subsequent item. This is called "receiving separately."
What is the summary precept?
I undertake the first: not to kill;
the second: not to steal.
Third, refrain from sexual misconduct;
fourth, refrain from false speech;
fifth, refrain from drinking intoxicants.
Sixth, not eating past noon;
seventh, not dancing, singing, performing, or playing musical instruments for adornment, nor intentionally going to watch or listen to them, nor even looking at anything from quarrels and disputes;
eighth, not wearing perfumes, flowers, or necklaces, nor anointing the body with fragrances.
Ninth, one must not sit or lie upon high, large beds;
tenth, one must not grasp or hold raw gold or silver.
Regarding "raw gold and silver," this refers to gold, silver, and all precious gems; none of these may be grasped.

If their spoken sounds are different, such that a person from the Cang region and one from the Wu region cannot understand each other, one should explain the meaning to them; even if they do not understand in this way, if the disciple replies that they can uphold [the precepts], it still constitutes the formal reception of the precepts.

If one is of dull faculties, they will not know how to put on their robes, nor how to hold their alms bowl; they will not even know how to eat, and they will be ignorant in all matters of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. Such a person must not be separated from their preceptor and should learn everything by following the preceptor’s example. The preceptor should regard the disciple as his own child.
The procedure for ordaining a śrāmaṇera is concluded.

Regarding the rules for disciples: at dawn, when the first light appears, one should rise early, chew a willow twig, wash one’s hands and face, remove one’s leather sandals, and go to the place where the upādhyāya resides.

Once the teacher has risen, one should present three types of tooth-sticks—large, medium, and small—to the teacher all at once. If the teacher habitually takes the large one every day, one should set aside the medium and small ones and always provide the large one.
If the teacher takes the medium-sized one and places it inside the large-sized one, or if the teacher takes the small-sized one and places it inside the medium-sized one;
or if at times he takes the large, at times the medium, and at times the small—then give all three according to his preference.
One should offer water; there are two kinds of water:
first, cold water, and second, warm water. If the teacher habitually uses cold water, one should set out warm water;
if the teacher habitually uses warm water, one should set out cold water.
If the teacher sometimes uses cold water and sometimes uses warm water, provide both kinds according to his preference.
Once the water has been supplied, if the upādhyāya enters the latrine, you should immediately go to the upādhyāya’s room to sweep it, arrange the bedding, roll up the mats, and fold the garments.

Regarding the one who bestows the *saṃghāṭī*: first, having laid out the inner lining of the *saṃghāṭī*, he hands it over to the *upādhyāya*. When the *upādhyāya* takes it away, [the disciple] follows behind the *upādhyāya* with his robes on and his bowl in hand; he must neither be too close nor too far, walking at a distance of seven feet from the *upādhyāya*.
The teacher should instruct the disciple in the observance of the precepts; if the disciple commits an offense, he should instruct him in its confession.
If the teacher possesses extra robes or an alms bowl, he should give them to the disciple if the latter lacks them; if the disciple falls ill, he should provide for his care.
"If the preceptor has many disciples, one person shall provide for them, while the others may read and recite as they please.
At that time, the brahmin wished to seek ordination, but the bhikṣu did not grant permission; the brahmin then wept and was filled with distress.
At that time, the Buddha saw that the brahmin’s body was emaciated and asked the bhikṣus,
"Why is this brahmin so emaciated?
The bhikṣus replied:
"This brahmin sought to leave the household life, but the bhikṣus did not grant his request; for this reason, he has become emaciated.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "To whom does this brahmin owe a debt of gratitude?"
Śāriputra replied, “This brāhmaṇa lived in Rājagṛha and once gave me food; that is why I recognize him.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should deliver this Brahmin.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what manner should I deliver this Brahmin?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You should confer the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* upon this brāhmaṇa.
At that time, after the Buddha had gathered the bhikṣus and taught them the Dharma, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the conferral of precepts through three utterances is abolished.
Among the assembly, there were bhikṣus possessed of clear wisdom who performed the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations) for the conferral of precepts.
Having received the precepts, they committed many evils and failed to observe the rules of decorum.
A bhikṣu of few desires and contentment rebuked them, saying:
"How is it that you commit various evil deeds and do not observe the rules of decorum?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"Who requested the Venerable One to grant me the precepts?
Who requested the Venerable One to act as my upādhyāya?"
At that time, a bhikṣu of few desires addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are bhikṣus who, without being requested to act as preceptors and without [the candidate] having asked for the precepts, confer the full ordination upon them."

The Buddha, on account of this, established a precept: if one does not request someone to be one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and does not ask for the precepts, one shall not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*); if one bestows it upon such a person, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"I request the Upādhyāya to grant me the precepts. Regarding this in the Vinaya:

at that time, some bhikṣus—whether two or three of them—conferred the full ordination upon others through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Among them were certain bhikṣus of few desires who, being content with little, rebuked [those who acted thus] and went to inform the Buddha. On account of these circumstances, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and declared: "From this day forward, it shall be ordained that ten monks must confer the full ordination upon another person. If fewer than ten persons confer the full ordination, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."

After one or two years, he conferred full ordination upon others; however, not knowing how to provide instruction, his disciples did not maintain the proper decorum. Taking these disciples with him, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha inquired:
"Are your four elements in harmony?
Is almsfood easy for you to obtain?"
He replied to the Buddha, saying,
"The four elements are in harmony, and alms-food is easy to obtain.
Thereupon, the Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"Whose disciples are these bhikṣus?
He replied, "They are my disciples."
He asked, "How old are you?
and she replied:
"Two years. "How many years have your disciples been [ordained]?
He replied:
“One year.
The Buddha then rebuked him, saying:
“You yourself have not yet weaned from milk; how can you deliver others?”

Having rebuked him, he assembled the bhikṣus and declared: "From this day forward, one who has not reached ten years [of seniority] shall not ordain others or confer full precepts; if one does so, they commit an offense.
Even if one has reached ten *varṣas*, if they are foolish and lack wisdom, they shall not receive the full precepts from others."
"Having finished conferring the precepts.
The Dharma Master said:
"Now I shall clarify the rules regarding when one loses and when one does not lose the status of having a *niśraya* (preceptor)."

When a disciple travels together with his preceptor, if he sees his upādhyāya from afar and loses sight of him, he does not lose his status as one who has a preceptor; likewise, if he sees his upādhyāya but perceives him as someone other than an upādhyāya, he does not lose his status as one who has a preceptor.
If the preceptor enters within the boundary or into a house, and the disciple does not know of it, the dependence is lost.

If the preceptor enters within the boundary or into a house, or goes into a village to beg for food, and [the disciple] hears his voice but does not see his form, the dependence is lost in all such cases.
If one hears a voice and forms the perception that it is not one's preceptor, the dependence [upon that teacher] is not lost.

If an outsider first enters the Buddha-dharma, they should be granted the *parivāsa* probation; once they have received the *parivāsa*, if they frequently go to the five improper places, are indolent and unwilling to study the Buddha-dharma, rejoice upon hearing the Buddha-dharma disparaged, or rejoice upon hearing the Saṃgha disparaged, they may not be granted the full precepts.

Even if a non-Buddhist practitioner of the Pārivāsika school has cultivated the four dhyānas and attained the ability to fly through the air, they still may not be granted full ordination; they must wait for a full four months.
If one attains the stage of Srotāpanna within the Buddha-dharma, they may receive full ordination on that very day; it is not necessary to grant them the *parivāsa* probation.

If one is from among the non-Buddhists and, upon hearing the Dharma, attains the stage of Srotāpanna and comes to the Sangha seeking to go forth, they may be granted the going forth and full ordination immediately; it is not necessary to grant them the *parivāsa* probation.

If, when the period of *parivāsa* is nearly completed after four months, one hears disparagement of the Buddha-dharma and feels joy, or hears disparagement of non-Buddhists and feels anger, or takes pleasure in going to the five places where one should not go, one should be granted another four months.
If they are hair-tied non-Buddhists (*jaṭila*) or fire-worshipping non-Buddhists (*agnihotrika*), a period of probation (*parivāsa*) is not required. Why is this?

These two types of non-Buddhists possess the karma of faith in cause and effect; when the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, they studied the perfection of renunciation (*naiṣkramyapāramitā*) within these very paths.
The section on the *pārivāsika* (probationers) among the non-Buddhists is concluded.
Regarding leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), there is numerical leprosy, white leprosy, black leprosy, and scabies; all these are included under leprosy, and such persons may not go forth [into the religious life].
Even those with leprosy or ringworm as small as a fingernail are not permitted to go forth.
Even if it is as small as a fingernail, whether it grows or does not grow when exposed to the open air, in all such cases, one may not go forth.
If a tumor is not visible in a secluded place, one who undergoes growth may not receive ordination, whereas one who does not undergo growth may receive ordination.
If a tumor is in an exposed place, whether it grows or does not grow, one may not receive ordination.

If one does not grow [a tumor] in a private place, one may obtain ordination; if one has a wart or suffers from diarrhea at a young age, one may be granted the tonsure and ordination, for this is not a case of a tumor, and thus one may obtain ordination.
"If one's body has small eruptions like thorns, they all fall under the category of leprosy and may not go forth [into homelessness].
"Regarding 'one who has ordained a man of the king':

At that time, various bhikṣus ordained a military commander and let him go forth. Later, when bandits arose, the king sought out the military commanders, wishing to have them destroy the bandits. He sent men to search for them until they reached the monastery. Seeing that the bhikṣus had already ordained and let him go forth, the messengers returned and informed the king."
"The bhikṣus have already ordained him and sent him forth from home.
Having heard this, the king assembled his ministers to deliberate together, and the king asked the ministers:
"What is the punishment for one who ordains an official of the state?"
The minister replied to the king:

"If the Upādhyāya is to be punished, his head should be severed; the Karmavācanā master should have his tongue cut out; and the other persons present at the ordination platform should have their ribs broken."
At that time, the king had attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Having heard the words of his ministers, he went to the place where the Buddha was and said to him:
"From this day forward, I pray that you do not ordain any of my subjects."
"In future ages, if there are kings who do not believe in the Triple Gem, and if bhikṣus ordain such persons, they shall be punished according to the law.
Whether they be royal officials, ministers, or even those who merely consume the king’s stipend, all such individuals are considered royal subjects.
If the father receives royal stipends while the son does not, the father may not leave the household life, whereas the son may leave it.
If one who receives stipends has not yet completed their term, they may not leave the household life; only after the stipends have been fully received may they leave the household life.
If you are determined to leave the household life, transfer your emoluments to your brothers and sons, and only then may you go forth.
Alternatively, if you inform the King regarding your emoluments and he grants his permission, you may likewise go forth.
"Regarding 'bandits': those who plunder, rob, steal, waylay travelers, or kill people—if their names and identities are known, they may not receive the full ordination and leave the household life.

However, if they are bandits plotting against the state, or if they abandon their evil intentions and desire to leave the household life, they may receive the full ordination and leave the household life, as they act to eliminate the state's troubles; when the king hears of their ordination, he too will be greatly pleased."
If one abandons evil deeds and comes forth to seek refuge with the king, and the king permits them to cross over [to the religious life], they may go forth.
One who is afflicted by the wounds of whips or canes may not be ordained; however, if the wounds have healed, they may be ordained.
If a person who has committed an offense is branded with iron characters, they may not be ordained as a monk; however, if they are cured through medical treatment, they may leave the household life.

Regarding those in debt: whether it be one's own debt, a debt incurred by a grandfather, a father, or a son—if the debt is personally one's own, one may not leave the household life; but if someone else pays off the debt on one's behalf, one may leave the household life.
Regarding slaves, there are four kinds of slaves:
first, those born in the household; second, those purchased; third, those captured from a defeated enemy; and fourth, those who become slaves of their own accord.
One who becomes a slave of their own accord does so by seeking servitude for the sake of food and clothing; this is called becoming a slave of one's own accord.
If a master releases a slave to leave the household life and says to the bhikṣus:
"I release a slave who possesses the aspiration for the Way; if he lacks the aspiration for the Way, he shall return once more to slavery."
"One who speaks in such a manner may not be ordained as a renunciant.
