At that time, there was a household of a lay devotee where an epidemic broke out; first flies, centipedes, and millipedes were killed; next, chickens and pigs; then cattle and sheep; then it reached the female and male servants; and finally, it reached the good people.

When this pestilence breaks out, one must not exit through the door; rather, one should break through the wall to go straight out. One must not look back; if one looks back, one will die immediately. Even if one does not die at once, one will die upon reaching another land.
At that time, the father and his two sons broke through the wall and escaped; they went straight away without looking back, and for this reason they survived.

Once they had reached another land, being poor and unable to support themselves, they went to where a bhikṣu was staying and requested to leave the household life. The bhikṣu immediately ordained them as renunciants.
Having gone forth, he went on alms-round with his two sons.
*Sāriputraparipṛcchā-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 16 [and] Fascicle 17.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Regions during the Xiao Qi Dynasty:
"At that time, the Buddha went from the kingdom of Magadha to the kingdom of Kapilavastu. The Dharma Master said:
"I shall now explain the fundamental causal conditions in their proper sequence."
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"On the day my son first left the household life, he himself proclaimed:
'If I attain Buddhahood, I shall return to this kingdom.'"
The king recalled these words and thought to himself:

"Since my son attained Buddhahood, I have constantly listened with bated breath; I heard that after completing his ascetic practices, he went beneath the Bodhi tree and attained the Way, then proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to turn the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths and deliver the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, by ordaining them."
"Now he resides in the kingdom of Magadha; as I am now old and still living, it is fitting that I see my son.
Having had this thought, he immediately summoned a minister and said to him:
"I have heard people say that my son has already attained Buddhahood and is currently residing in the kingdom of Magadha."
"You may take a thousand men to go and welcome him; once you arrive there, say to my son:
'I am now old in years and wish to see you.
Having received the king's command, the minister immediately took a thousand men to surround him before and behind and departed for the kingdom of Magadha.
Having arrived, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed the minds of the thousand people, immediately preached the Dharma for them; upon hearing the Dharma, the thousand people immediately attained arhatship.

The Buddha called out, "Welcome, bhikṣus," and they immediately attained full ordination. Having attained arhatship, these thousand bhikṣus entered the samādhi of fruition and experienced the bliss of liberation; they remained right there, no longer wishing to return.

After the king had dispatched his messenger, he hoped in vain for the man’s return; yet no news arrived. The king sent another minister, and in this manner, he successively dispatched eight ministers. Each minister led a thousand men to the Buddha’s presence, and they all left the household life to attain the fruit of Arhatship; not a single person returned to report to the king.
The king thought to himself:
"I sent eight ministers away, yet not a single one has returned to report to me.
The king then deliberated within himself:
"Whom else shall I now dispatch?

At that time, there was a minister named Kālodāyin, who had been born on the same day as the Bodhisattva; the King immediately dispatched Kālodāyin to go and welcome the Buddha, with instructions no different from those previously given to the eight ministers.
Kālodāyin had previously made an agreement with the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty permits me to go forth, I shall go to welcome him.
The king replied, "Excellent."
Having received the King’s command, Kālodāyin led those one thousand people to him; the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they immediately attained arhatship.
The Buddha called out, "Welcome, bhikṣus," and they received full ordination.

At that time, Kālodāyin saw the rice and grain forming ears, and the flowers of plants and trees on land and in water blooming in full splendor; as the seasons were harmonious and appropriate, he praised the road with sixty verses.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Kālodāyin,
"For what purpose are you praising the road?
Kālodāyin replied to the Buddha:
"King Śuddhodana has sent me here with something he wishes to report.
The Buddha said,
"I grant you leave to speak."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Father King said:
'I am now old, yet while I still live, I wish to see the Buddha; therefore, I have sent you to welcome the Buddha.'"
"I only pray that, out of compassion for the Great King, you will depart at this time.
The Buddha said to Kālodāyin,
"You may issue a proclamation to tell the bhikṣus:"
“The Buddha wishes to travel; each of you should prepare yourselves and adorn yourselves to follow the Buddha on his journey.

At that time, there were ten thousand bhikṣus from the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, and ten thousand bhikṣus who had come from the kingdom of Kapilavastu to welcome the Buddha. In total, there were twenty thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had attained arhatship. They surrounded the Buddha from front and back as he departed the city from the kingdom of Magadha.
The kingdom of Magadha was sixty yojanas from Śrāvastī; as the World-Honored One traveled by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī after sixty days.

At that time, every morning during the midday meal, the Buddha would regularly partake of the offerings provided by his father, the King. The reason he was able to receive these royal offerings was that Kālodāyin, when the time arrived, would put on his robes, take up his bowl, and fly through the air to Śrāvastī to inform the King, saying:
"The Buddha has already arrived at such-and-such a place."
Then the king prepared a meal for Kālodāyin; having filled a bowl to the brim with rice, he presented it to Kālodāyin, saying:
"Venerable Sir, please offer this bowl of rice to the Buddha."
In this manner, he daily and constantly went to welcome food for the World-Honored One.
After Kālodāyin had eaten the meal provided by his father, the King, he praised the merits of the Tathāgata before the King and the Śākya princes.
When the Śākyas heard this praise of the Buddha’s virtues, their faith increased all the more.
The Śākyas then gathered together and deliberated among themselves:
"The Buddha does not delight in clamor and bustle; we should seek out a quiet place for the Buddha and construct a vihāra there."

At that time, the Śākya son Mīguda had a garden, neither too near nor too far, suitable for establishing a vihāra; then each of the Śākya sons individually contributed their own wealth and property to erect a vihāra for the Buddha.
"When the vihāra was completed, the father-king, leading the Śākya youths, each carrying incense and flowers, went out to welcome him.
When the Buddha arrived, among the father-king and the Śākya youths, those who were senior Buddhas did not prostrate to the Buddha; however, those who were junior Buddhas did prostrate."

At that time, the Buddha saw among the father-king and the Śākya sons those who did not prostrate to him. Knowing the thoughts of the Śākya sons, he immediately ascended into the void and performed the eighteen transformations, no different from the miraculous powers he had displayed when subduing the non-Buddhists.
When King Śuddhodana and the Śākya princes saw such supernatural power of the Buddha, they spontaneously paid homage to him.
After King Śuddhodana had prostrated, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is now my third time paying homage at the Buddha’s feet."
What is the third prostration at the Buddha’s feet?
First, when the Buddha was first born, the sage Asita prophesied:
"If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves home to study the Way, he will certainly attain Buddhahood."
At that time, the earth shook; having witnessed such supernatural power, I immediately paid him homage.

Second, while I was out playing and plowing the fields, the Bodhisattva was beneath a Jambu tree; though the sun had already reached the late afternoon hour, the shadow of the tree remained stationary and did not shift, continuing to cover the Bodhisattva’s body.
Having witnessed such supernatural power, I immediately prostrated to him.
Now, having seen the Buddha’s supernatural power in this way, this is called the third prostration at the feet of the Tathāgata.
When King Śuddhodana prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, all the Śākyas followed suit in paying homage, and not a single person remained standing.
The Buddha descended from the void and sat upon the lion throne; the king and all the Śākyas sat down simultaneously.
When the assembly had settled, the heavens sent down rain of a crimson hue, which soaked the dust.

Those in the assembly who desired to be wet became wet; those who did not desire to be wet remained dry even though the rain fell upon them. Seeing such supernatural power in the rain, the assembly’s joy increased all the more.

At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the assembly. Having heard the Dharma, the king and the Śākya sons attained various stages: some attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, and others attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin. Each rose from their seat, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Neither the King nor any of the Śākyas invited the Buddha for his midday meal.

When the time arrived on the following day, the Buddha and twenty thousand bhikṣus donned their robes, took up their bowls, and proceeded in order, surrounded by attendants, entering the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Having reached the city gate, the Buddha thought to himself:
"How did the Buddhas of the past enter their kinsmen's villages to beg for alms?
I should practice sequential begging as a form of discernment."

He then observed that all past Buddhas had gone on their almsrounds in successive order without making any selections; furthermore, for the sake of future śrāvaka disciples who would rely upon his Dharma, he should likewise go on his almsround in successive order.
At that time, the Śākya women of the city, hearing that the Buddha was entering the city with his retinue to beg for alms, each opened their windows and doors to watch the Buddha as he begged.
Then, Rāhula’s mother, being on the upper floor of her palace, heard that the Buddha had entered the city to beg for alms and thought to herself:

"When I was formerly at home, I wore celestial crowns and necklaces, riding in a palanquin made of the seven treasures, surrounded before and behind by thousands of carriages and tens of thousands of horsemen as I went out and came in; [how can the Buddha now be begging?]"
"Now he has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and carries an alms bowl to beg for food; shall I now go to observe whether he is handsome or not?
Having had this thought, he immediately opened the window to look. From afar he saw the Buddha emitting light of five colors, which illuminated the ground like molten gold.
Having seen this, Yaśodharā immediately went inside and informed the king, saying:
"The King’s son has now entered the city to beg for alms.
Upon hearing this, the king hurriedly went out to the Buddha's location and said:
“Venerable One, your begging for alms puts us to shame. We are able to provide for your assembly;
why must you beg? The Buddha replied, “Such is my way.”
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"In my kṣatriya caste, there are no mendicants; why do you say that my lineage is such as this?
The Buddha replied:
"The Buddhas of the past are my lineage; it is not the present Kṣatriya caste.
The Buddha then spoke these verses for the sake of the Great King:
"Having arisen, do not be indolent; Always practice the wholesome Dharma yourself."
"By practicing the Dharma, one attains peaceful sleep, both in this life and in future lives.
Having heard these words, the king immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke a verse for the great king:
"One who practices the Dharma acts rightly; by not practicing unwholesome dharmas, one who practices the Dharma sleeps in peace, both in this life and in lives to come."
"Having heard the second verse, the king further attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The king was then told the *Tān-mo-po-lo-pen-sheng-jing* (Sūtra on the Jātaka of Dharmapāla); having heard it, the king attained the stage of Anāgāmin."
When the king was approaching the end of his life, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; beneath the White Parasol, he attained the fruit of Arhatship and immediately entered *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, the Great King requested the Tathāgata’s alms bowl and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha. The king himself led the way as they all ascended the palace hall together, whereupon the king provided various kinds of delicacies and foods.
When the Buddha had finished eating, the palace ladies, hearing that the Buddha had concluded his meal, said to Rāhula’s mother:
"We should now go to pay our respects and inquire after the World-Honored One's well-being."
Rāhula’s mother said to the court ladies, “If the Buddha has compassion for me, he will come to see me himself; I cannot go.
Thereupon, each of the court ladies took fragrant flowers and went to pay homage to the Buddha.
After the ladies-in-waiting had departed, Rāhula’s mother thought to herself:
"If the Buddha comes, I shall prostrate myself at his feet.

When the Buddha had finished eating, he gave the bowl to the King. Then, taking two disciples who possessed the power of the divine feet, the Buddha went to where Rāhula’s mother was and instructed his disciples, saying:
"If Rāhula’s mother pays homage and makes offerings, you should comply with her wishes and not create obstacles.
He replied, "Excellent!"
"Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha entered the room of Rāhula’s mother, spread out his seat, and sat down. When Rāhula’s mother saw that the Buddha was seated, she quickly cupped the Buddha’s feet with her hands and bowed her head to them in salutation.
When the King saw Rāhula’s mother pay homage to the Buddha, he said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Rāhula’s mother has conceived a heart of supreme reverence for the Buddha.”
The Buddha replied to the king:
"Rāhula’s mother has held me in high esteem; this is not something that began only now.
The king asked the Buddha:
"When will he develop respect?
the Buddha then recounted for him the *Kinnara-jātaka*, and on that very day, by means of five dharmas, he intended to install Prince Nanda as king.
What are these five things?
First, loosening one's hair; second, tying up one's robes; third, decorating a palace; fourth, taking a wife; and fifth, erecting a parasol.
These are called the five dharmas.
The Buddha then presented his almsbowl to Nanda; though Nanda’s heart was not inclined to go, he followed along with a reluctant air out of respect for the Buddha.

Having followed the Buddha to the monastery, his mind was not inclined toward renunciation; however, the Tathāgata perceived through his past affinities that he was destined to attain arhatship, and therefore compelled him to leave the household life.
"Two days after the Buddha arrived in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he ordained Nanda; seven days later, he ordained Rāhula.
The Dharma Master asked:
"How was it that Rāhula was ordained?"
He replied:

“When the Buddha entered the city to beg for alms, Rāhula’s mother was with him on the upper terrace. From a window, Rāhula’s mother saw the Buddha from afar and said to Rāhula, ‘This is your father.’”
He then gave the necklace to Rāhu to wear and said to him:
"Go to your father's place and beg for precious treasures. When your father was at home, he possessed a vast treasury of jewels; you do not know where it is now, so you may go there to beg for them."
Bāhu said, "I wish to raise the parasol and become a Wheel-Turning King; Bāhu, you may grant me precious jewels.
Having received his mother’s words, Rāhu went to where the Buddha was, entered the Buddha’s shadow, and addressed the Buddha:
"The life of a śramaṇa is supremely cool and blissful.
After the Buddha had finished eating and returned to his original place, Rāhula followed behind the Buddha and begged him for precious treasures.
The Buddha did not answer, and so they gradually pursued him until they reached the monastery.
After the Buddha had spread out his seat and sat down, he said to Rāhula:
"I obtained this precious treasure beneath the Bodhi tree; among all treasures, this wealth is the most supreme and foremost."
"Would you like to obtain it?
Rāhu replied to the World-Honored One,
"I would very much like it, Śramaṇa."
The Buddha then called for Śāriputra.
Once Śāriputra had arrived, the Buddha said to him:
"You may ordain Rāhula and let him go forth."
Śāriputra replied,
“Excellent, World-Honored One.
Śāriputra then ordained Rāhula as a monk.
When King Śuddhodana heard that Rāhula had left the household life, his heart was filled with great anguish. He immediately hurried to the place where the Buddha was and said to him:
"If there are those who leave the household life, they should first inform their parents; if the parents give their consent, they may be ordained and allowed to leave the household life.
If the parents do not consent, I pray that the Buddha will not ordain them."
Therefore, it is stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "If one's parents do not grant permission, one may not go forth as a renunciant.

If, after having been permitted by one's parents to go forth, one returns to lay life and later wishes to go forth again, one must inform one's parents; if the parents do not grant permission, one may not go forth."
If there is someone who seeks to go forth [into homelessness], the bhikṣu asks him:
"Have your parents given you permission to go forth?
He replies:
"I do not permit it.
"If you do not permit it, one cannot go forth," he said to the bhikṣu.
"If you do not ordain me, I shall set fire to the monastery.
In the event of such an emergency, ordaining someone as a renunciant does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, if one ordains someone from another region or another country, it is not necessary to inquire about their parents' permission.
The account of Rāhula’s renunciation of the household life is concluded.
"There are ten evils of a śrāmaṇera that warrant his expulsion. What are these ten?"
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking intoxicants, slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, holding wrong views, and violating a bhikṣuṇī—
these are called the ten unwholesome paths of action.

Only the violation of a bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct results in permanent exclusion from the order, such that one may never again go forth; as for the remaining nine precepts, if one can repent and refrain from committing them again, one may attain the going forth.
If these thirteen types of persons with impediments act as preceptors for others and confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*), they likewise do not bestow the precepts.
This applies whether the teaching preceptor performs the ritual himself or another performs the ritual on his behalf.
There are three kinds of theft regarding those who have left the household life: first, theft of form; second, theft of affiliation; and third, theft of both form and affiliation.
What is meant by theft of form?

To leave the household life on one's own without a teacher, not relying on the seniority of a bhikṣu, not receiving prostrations according to the prescribed order, not participating in the communal rites of the Saṃgha, and not accepting any offerings or sustenance—this is called "stealing the form."
What is "stealing the assembly"?

There is a teacher who has left the household life and received the ten precepts, but has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*). He travels to other regions and claims to have ten years of seniority or twenty years of seniority, successively receiving the prostrations of others, entering the *poṣadha* of the Saṃgha and all *karmavācanā* rituals, and receiving the faithful offerings of others in accordance with his claimed rank. This is called "stealing the assembly."
What is meant by "stealing the form" and also "stealing the communal harmony"?

To leave the household life on one's own without a teacher, to receive seniority according to the sequence of ordination, to participate in all *karmavācanā* rituals, and to receive the offerings and prostrations of others—this is called stealing the form and also stealing the communal harmony.

As for those who have stolen the outward form [of a monk], they do not participate in Dharma rituals, do not receive offerings of faith, and do not receive prostrations; however, if they wish to go forth again and receive full ordination, they may do so.
If one leaves the household life to seek refuge from danger or to escape famine, they do not enter into the affairs of the Dharma;
however, once the danger has passed and the famine has ended, if they wish to leave the household life and receive full ordination, they may do so.

If a bhikṣu who has actually been ordained for one year falsely claims to have been ordained for two years, and based on that second-year status receives offerings, he commits a grave offense (pārājika) when the value of the goods is calculated.

If a bhikṣu removes his robes to bathe in water and says to himself, "The naked body is good," or if he intends to go to the place of the non-Buddhists, he commits a *duṣkṛta* (dukkaṭa) for every step taken; if he regrets it midway and returns to confess, he commits a *duṣkṛta*, but he is permitted to remain [in the order].

If one goes to the place of non-Buddhists and hears their teachings but does not enter into them, and subsequently feels regret and returns to repent, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), and he may remain [in the order].

If, however, upon hearing the teachings of non-Buddhists, his mind becomes fond of them and he accepts their doctrine—even down to the extent of plucking out a single hair—and then, suffering from pain and regret, returns, he should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*) and shall not be allowed to go forth again.
The section on converting non-Buddhists concludes.
"One must not convert dragons. Why is this?
Because dragons cannot attain the fruits of the path through meditative concentration."
A nāga has five matters for which it cannot shed its nāga body.
What are these five?

First, regarding sexual intercourse: if one engages in sexual intercourse with another nāga, one may regain the nāga body; however, if one engages in sexual intercourse with a human, one cannot regain the nāga body.
Second, being born without leaving the dragon body;
third, at the time of shedding the skin;
fourth, while asleep.
Fifth is at the time of death.
These are the five circumstances in which one cannot escape the nāga body.
From the garuḍas up to Śakra Devānām Indra, none may leave the household life, nor may they receive full ordination.
The Chapter on Nāgas concludes.
One may not ordain those who have killed their parents; for the Tathāgata does not permit those who have killed their parents to enter the monastic life.
However, if one has killed the parents of an animal, one may be ordained.
If one kills someone who is actually one’s father while perceiving them as not being one’s father, one is likewise not permitted to leave the household life.
One may not ordain a person who has killed an Arhat; if a layperson (avadātavasana) has attained Arhatship and is killed, that person may not leave the household life.
However, if one kills a person who has attained any of the three lower fruits of the path, it does not constitute an obstacle to leaving the household life.
If one kills an Arhat while perceiving them as an animal, there is no offense;
however, due to the gravity of the karmic obstruction, such a person is unable to deliver others.
"One who violates a bhikṣuṇī" refers to engaging in sexual misconduct with her in any of the three places; all such acts are termed "violating a bhikṣuṇī."
If one touches a bhikṣuṇī, it does not obstruct their renunciation.

However, if one forcibly makes a bhikṣuṇī wear white (lay) clothing and engages in sexual intercourse with her, this is also called "corrupting a bhikṣuṇī," and such a person may not renounce the world.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes pleasure in wearing white clothing, engaging in sexual intercourse does not obstruct her from leaving the household life.
If she has committed the first breach [of the precepts], she may not leave the household life; if she commits the second breach, it does not constitute an obstruction.
If one violates the rules of a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it does not obstruct their going forth.
One who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha may not be ordained or go forth.
What constitutes causing a schism in the Saṃgha?
If one clings to the eighteen matters and does not relinquish them despite three admonitions.
There are three types of those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*):

first, those who can conceive an embryo themselves and can cause another to conceive; second, those who can conceive an embryo themselves but cannot cause another to conceive; third, those who cannot conceive an embryo themselves but can cause another to conceive.
These three kinds of persons are all ineligible for going forth and receiving full ordination; if they have already received full ordination, they should be expelled.
"If there is no preceptor, one may not confer full ordination upon another; if one does confer full ordination, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet that person does obtain the precepts."
If a eunuch acts as an upādhyāya and confers the precepts upon another,
the recipient obtains the precepts, but the master and the saṃgha incur an offense.
If one receives full ordination without robes and bowl, the recipient obtains the precepts, but the master and the saṃgha incur an offense.

If two or three people receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the same time, they each possess an identical seniority (*vassa*). Because their ordination times are equal, they must not pay formal salutations to one another.

When three people receive the full ordination simultaneously under the same preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the same ritual master (*karmakāraka*), they all obtain the same ordination seniority at that same moment; thus, there is no distinction of seniority among them.
"Upādhyāya" is a foreign term; in the Han language, it means "one who knows what is an offense and what is not an offense," and thus he is called an Upādhyāya.

After receiving the precepts, one should measure one's shadow. To measure the shadow: standing upright and still, take the foot that was first planted as the starting point, and then follow the lengthening or shortening of the shadow as one steps.
Having finished the instruction on the shadow-measurements, he teaches the seasons.
As for the seasons, they are either winter, spring, or summer.
Having finished, he teaches the days and months, and the seasonal periods of the days and months.
Next, he instructs on the required number of people in the assembly when receiving the precepts.
After granting the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), he next explains the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*).
Once the ordination is completed, he has the newly ordained person go out first.
The *Prātimokṣa-vastu* (Chapter on Receiving the Precepts) is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, the city of King Śreṇiya, in the kingdom of Magadha.
These three [names] have the same meaning but different designations.
In the language of Han, it is called Rājagṛha; Luoyuecheng (羅閱城) is the foreign pronunciation.
"Luó" (羅) means "king" (rāja), and "yuè" (閱) means "abode" (gṛha); therefore, it is called Luoyuecheng.
"Makkaṭa" is a foreign term. "Makkaṭa" is simply the name of the original country. Regarding the "characteristics of boundaries":
as for the characteristics of mountain boundaries, the large ones are like Mount Sumeru and the small ones are as large as an elephant; these constitute the characteristics of mountains.

Regarding the characteristics of stone boundary markers: the large ones are like oxen, while the small ones weigh thirty *cheng*. If a stone is too smooth, it cannot serve as a boundary marker; one should instead install a separate stone to serve as the boundary marker.
Regarding the characteristics of a forest boundary (*vana-sīmā*): whether it be a grass forest or a bamboo grove, they cannot serve as boundary markers. Why is this so?
Because the substance of grass and bamboo is empty and lacks solidity; therefore, they cannot constitute a boundary.

Regarding the characteristics of a forest: a large forest may extend for as much as one hundred *yojanas*, while even a small forest—down to four trees joined together—is also called a forest. Regarding the characteristics of the boundary of trees:

a withered tree cannot serve as a boundary marker. As for large trees, these are *Jambū* trees; as for those of medium or small size, even one as tall as eight inches and as thin as a needle may serve as a boundary marker.
If there are no self-grown trees, planting trees may also serve as boundary markers.

Regarding road boundaries: paths leading into fields, paths leading toward wells for drawing water, paths leading toward rivers for drawing water, and dead-end roads—all of these may not be used as boundary markers.
Whether it be a main road or a path for carts and pedestrians, even if the road is short—extending only through three or four villages—it may all serve as a boundary marker (*sīmā-nimitta*).
As for ant-hills as boundary markers, whether they are as large as mountains or as small as eight inches in height, they may all serve as boundary markers.
Regarding the boundary mark of a river: if a virtuous king governs and it rains once every five days, this rainwater cannot serve as a boundary mark for the river.
However, if it does not rain for four months and the flow remains constant and uninterrupted with a depth of two feet, it may serve as a boundary mark.

Regarding the characteristics of the water boundary (*āpasīmā*): if it is the water of a natural pond, it may serve as a boundary marker; however, if water flows through into a field, or if water is contained in jars, these all cannot serve as boundary markers.
These are the eight types of boundary marks (*sīmālakṣaṇa*).
There are five kinds of boundary delimitations (*sīmābandha*):
first, square; second, circular; third, drum-shaped; fourth, half-moon shaped; and fifth, triangular.

If a boundary has been established based on a physical mark, the boundary is not lost even if that mark later disappears; even if a person digs the earth down to the water's edge, the characteristics of the boundary are not lost.

If one establishes a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), the expression of consent (*chanda*) is not permitted; however, when establishing a boundary for the *poṣadha*, the expression of consent is permitted.

When establishing a boundary for a dwelling site, it may be as small as to accommodate twenty-one persons; once the boundary site has been established, even if a roofed house is subsequently built over it, the boundary is not lost.
If, after a small boundary (*sīmā*) has been established, a three-story building is erected within it, from the ground level up to the topmost floor, they constitute a single boundary.

If there is a rocky mountain that is broad at the top and narrow at the base, and one establishes a boundary on the summit, it does not obstruct those who are below if there are bhikṣus there. If, after the boundary has been established, water washes away the earth to form a pit with flowing water, and one knows its location and erects pillars to build a pavilion, it is permissible to perform ritual acts (*dharmakarma*) upon it.

If the boundary has already been established, even if water pierces the ground to form a hole, it does not destroy the characteristics of the boundary; thus, a bhikṣu with supernormal powers who dwells in the air inside a cave or beneath the ground may not perform separate ritual acts [within that area].

If there is a large tree on the boundary of the precinct whose branches and leaves extend beyond the boundary, when performing ritual acts, a bhikṣu must not remain in the tree as it would obstruct the performance of the rites; he should be called down.
If a bhikṣu possessing supernormal powers dwells in the open air or in space, he does not obstruct the performance of formal monastic acts (*dharmakarma*).
If the corner of his robe touches the ground and causes an obstruction, he should be called down.

When establishing the boundary for the *poṣadha*, it may extend at most three *yojanas* in width; it must not exceed this. If it exceeds this, the boundary is not established, and one incurs an offense.

"Except for the area outside the village boundary" means within the distance reached by a stone thrown by an average person. If a *bhikṣu* has already established a boundary, it is not a boundary for a *bhikṣuṇī*; however, upon that *bhikṣuṇī* boundary, one may further establish another boundary, and the *bhikṣuṇī* boundary is not thereby lost.
A bhikṣuṇī may also establish a boundary upon the territory of a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu’s boundary shall not be lost.

Regarding the āraṇyaka boundary, its minimum extent is seven *paṭṭhāras* square; one *paṭṭhāra* is twenty-eight cubits. If there are those who do not consent, one may perform ritual acts beyond the twenty-eight cubits.
One may not establish a boundary over any river or stream.

Regarding the natural boundary within water: beyond the point where one has thrown water or sand, if there are monks who are not hindered from taking water, then whether it is a constantly flowing stream or deep or shallow water, all such places may serve as a natural boundary; however, tidal waters cannot be used.
If one performs the *poṣadha* ceremony on a boat, one should lower the mooring stake.
If one lowers a beam, it must not be tied to the bank.
Even if the bank collapses and there are large tree roots in the water, it must not be tied to those tree roots.
If one throws water [to mark the boundary], any tree roots within the water should be cut away; if they are not cut away, the area remains connected to the terrestrial boundary.
If there are large stones, trees, or floating wood in the water, all are included within the water boundary.
"The first case is 'an illegal separate assembly. What is meant by an illegal separate assembly?

Suppose there are four bhikṣus residing in the same dwelling place: one person receives the consent (*chanda*), and three persons recite the Prātimokṣa; or three persons [receive the consent], and two persons recite the Prātimokṣa. This is called illegal, and it is also called a separate assembly; thus, it is called an illegal separate assembly."
Regarding the second case, "an assembly that is not in legal concord": there are four bhikṣus residing in the same dwelling place; these four persons should recite the Prātimokṣa in detail.
Without explaining at length, they perform the ritual for three persons by reciting it face-to-face with each individual; this is called an "unlawful concordant assembly.
What is the third case: a "lawful separate assembly"?

In a single residence, there are four bhikṣus or three; one person receives the consent (*chanda*), and three perform the face-to-face recitation, or there are three persons, one receives the consent, and two perform the face-to-face recitation—this is called a "separate assembly according to the Dharma."

Regarding the fourth phrase: when four bhikṣus dwell in the same location and, being in harmony, recite the Prātimokṣa; or when three bhikṣus, being in harmony, perform the poṣadha by means of the threefold formula—this is called a Dharma-harmonious assembly.
The *poṣadha* on the sixteenth day is the *saṃgha-poṣadha*.

According to the Sanskrit Vinaya, the sixteenth day of the fifth month marks the commencement of the first *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), and the sixteenth day of the sixth month marks the commencement of the second *varṣā*. If one must depart during the *varṣā* due to a valid cause, there is no offense; however, the *varṣā* is not considered formally established [if one leaves], and one must not remain in the open air nor perform the *varṣā* under a parasol.
"As for those who have hair growing from their feet, that hair is a deep blue color, like azure-blue pigment; they obtain such a state as a retribution for their past karma.
He asked: "What karma is it that results in this retribution?"
He replied:

"In a past life, this Śoṇa was the eldest among eighty thousand people; together with the sons of wealthy householders, he built a grass hut for a pratyekabuddha and invited him to spend the three-month summer retreat there."
At that time, Śrona spread a single woolen *kambala* before his grass hut and gave it to a Pratyekabuddha, using it constantly to wipe his feet.
By the fruit of this merit, hair grew on the soles of his feet.
Because these eighty thousand sons of elders together made offerings to the Pratyekabuddhas, they have now become his close friends in this life.
Why did Śrona go to the king's presence accompanied by eighty thousand people?
If the King were to summon Śūṇa alone, we would fear that he might be terrified; therefore, we have commanded eighty thousand sons of elders to go together with him to the King's presence.
"As for the 'five elephant kings,' one father-elephant has six mother-elephants and is called an elephant king; there are five such elephant kings.
Regarding the 'Kāṇābala leather sandals,' these are *mañjaka* leather sandals."
The *mṛgaśṛṅga* leather sandals have their leather carved into the shape of deer antlers.
The *āraḷi* leather sandals have elephant hair attached to the edges of the sandals.
The *udarabaddhaka* leather sandals are made by stitching cotton wool and various other materials onto the leather so that the center bulges upward.
The *candālī* leather sandals are made by weaving grass.
The sandals with braided edges are those with edges braided with peacock feathers.
As for the *bahubandhana* sandals, there is no explanation [for their specific construction].
Regarding those leather sandals resembling peacock feathers, their shape was like that of peacock feathers.
At that time, there was a young girl in Rājagṛha named Bhadrā, who was incomparably beautiful.

At that time, King Bimbisāra appointed her as a courtesan; the king contributed one hundred thousand pieces of gold, and the ministers and elders contributed two hundred thousand pieces of gold, together adorning this courtesan by providing her with a residence, clothing, carriages, gardens, bathing pools, and various kinds of musical entertainment.
Jīvaka is a foreign term; in the Han language, it means "Living Boy.
Why was he named Living Boy?
Once, when Prince Abhaya was traveling by carriage in the early morning to visit the king, he saw a small child on the road and asked a bystander:
"Is this child alive or dead?
A bystander replied, "He is alive. Therefore, he was called the Living Boy (Jīvaka).
The prince asked:
"Why did his mother, after giving birth to him, cast him away on the road?
He replied, "This is the custom of courtesans:
if a daughter is born, she is taught the trade of a courtesan; if a son is born, he is cast away. For this reason, he was abandoned on the road upon his birth."
The prince Vītaśoka took him up, nurtured him, and as he gradually grew up, he established him as his son.
He asked: “Why did the youth Jīvaka not study other arts?”
He replied:
"In the past there was a Buddha named Padma. At that time, there was a physician who constantly made offerings to the Tathāgata Padma.
Having seen this, Jīvaka thought to himself:"
"How might I, in a future life, obtain such a physician to make offerings to the Tathāgata?
Having formed this thought, he immediately made offerings to the Tathāgata for seven days. He went to the Buddha's presence, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha:
"May I, in a future life, become a great physician to make offerings to the Buddha, no different from how this present physician makes offerings to the Buddha."
Having made this vow, he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.

When Jīvaka passed away, he was immediately reborn in the heavens; when his heavenly merit was exhausted, he descended to be born among humans. Thus, through successive cycles until the appearance of Śākyamuni in the world, drawn by the power of his past vows, he did not study other arts, but studied only medical prescriptions.

Question: "As for why Jīva became so skilled in the medical arts: when Jīva was studying under his teacher, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observed this man and saw that once his mastery of medicine was perfected, he would surely come to make offerings to the Buddha."
Therefore, Śakra transformed himself and entered the body of the physician Jīvaka to instruct him; within seven months, Jīvaka mastered the entirety of his teacher’s methods.
After the seven months had passed, having fulfilled the medical arts for a full seven years according to Śakra’s instructions, Jīvaka returned to his own country.
Why did he treat the illness halfway along the road?
The master thought to himself:
"This is a prince who lacks for nothing in wealth and treasures; if he returns to his own country, he will not recognize my kindness."
Having thought this, he immediately gave Jīvaka some old and worn-out clothes, but did not give him any food.
As Jīvaka took his leave of his teacher and departed, he encountered a village along the way; because of hunger and thirst, he asked the villagers, "In whose house is there a sick person?"
The villagers replied,
"A certain elder’s family has a sick member.
He immediately treated them, and he obtained a great quantity of precious treasures.
Jīvaka thought to himself:

"By treating the illness of a single person, I have obtained such precious treasures; if I were to treat the illnesses of many people, I would surely acquire immeasurable treasures. All that I have now obtained is due to the kindness of my teacher."
“There are fifteen locations for receiving offerings: first, the boundary of the *śīma* (precept platform);

second, the boundary of the precinct; third, the boundary of the common *poṣadha*; fourth, the boundary where robes need not be kept [with one]; fifth, the *lava* boundary; sixth, the village boundary; seventh, the hamlet boundary; eighth, the kingdom boundary; ninth, the *apāntaradaśa* boundary; tenth, the water-throwing boundary; eleventh, the regional residence boundary; twelfth, the *yojana* boundary; thirteenth, the *arajya* boundary; fourteenth, the island boundary; and fifteenth, the Cakravāḍa mountain boundary.”
These are the fifteen realms; you should now know them.
Regarding the boundary of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*, it has already been explained previously.

As for the boundary of the precinct (*parisāmantaka-sīmā*), it may be located in the lecture hall or the dining hall; it extends as far back as two stones thrown by a strong man capable of distributing robes. Regardless of the size of the main boundary, there is always a stone-throwing boundary within it, and any bhikṣu who enters it is entitled to a share. This is called the boundary of the precinct.
Regarding the *poṣadha* boundary (*poṣadhakṣetra*): if one enters the *poṣadha* boundary, all [monastics therein] should receive their share;

this is called the *poṣadha* boundary. Regarding the *acīvarāpavāda* boundary (*acīvarāpavādakṣetra*): if one enters within the *acīvarāpavāda* boundary, all [monastics therein] should receive their share; this is called the *acīvarāpavāda* boundary.

Regarding the *lābha* boundary: if a king or a high minister has completed the construction of a dwelling for a bhikṣu over an area of ten *yojanas*, and has erected pillars or established boundary markers, then whatever offerings are made within these markers belong to us; this is called the *lābha* boundary.
Regarding the "boundary of a market town" (*grāma-sīman*): because there is a marketplace, it is called the boundary of a market town.
Regarding the "boundary of a village" (*grāma-sīman*): being without a marketplace, it is named the boundary of a village.
Regarding the "boundary of a kingdom" (*janapada-sīman*): because there are cities and towns, it is named the boundary of a kingdom.
The *āvaṇḍala* boundary refers to the boundary of a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
The water-throwing boundary refers to the boundary of a boat.
The village-residence boundary is defined according to the east and west of a city; this is called the village-residence boundary.
The *raṇa*-boundary refers to the boundary of a kingdom.
The *araja*-boundary refers to the territory governed by a single king; this is called the *araja*-boundary.
The island-boundary refers to a single island within the ocean; this is called the island-boundary.
The "Iron Enclosure Realm" refers to the realm of a single Iron Enclosure Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
If someone says, "I give this field to the Saṃgha of the realm," it belongs to the Saṃgha of that specific field, but it cannot be included within the Poṣadha boundary.
If one says that the boundary for giving is established, it is obtained by means of the stone-throwing boundary.
If one says that the boundary for giving and for the *poṣadha* ceremony is established, it is likewise obtained as the same as the boundary for shared offerings (*lābha*).

If one says that the gift is not lost within the boundary of clothing, it is obtained within both the boundary of the *poṣadha* and the boundary of offerings; however, it is not obtained within the village boundary that exists inside the *poṣadha* boundary.
If someone says, "I give the village boundary," then within that village boundary there are *poṣadha* boundaries; both large and small ones are obtained.
If someone says, "I give the village precinct (*grāma-sīman*)," then within that village there are *poṣadha* boundaries as well as various smaller boundaries; all of these are obtained.
If a person says they are giving away the realm of a country, they obtain the entirety of that country's realm.
If a person says they are giving away the realm of an araṇya (forest hermitage), they obtain the araṇya, but do not obtain other realms.
If a person says, "I give this as an offering to the water-boundary," one may receive it if it is within the water-boundary, but not otherwise.
If a person says, "I give this as an offering to the village-residence boundary," one may receive it both from within the village-residence itself and from within the village-residence boundary.
If someone says they are giving to a *raṇa*, the monks of one district (*janapada*) receive it.
If someone says they are giving to an *ārāma* boundary, the monks of the entire district under the jurisdiction of a single king receive it.

"If someone says they give the island of Siṃhala and the continent of Jambudvīpa as offerings, or that they give to the Saṃgha of both continents, it should be divided equally between them according to the number of monks present. Even if there are five monks on Jambudvīpa and one hundred thousand on Siṃhala, it must still be divided equally."
If someone says they are giving to the Sangha within a boundary, the bhikṣu should ask:
"There are many kinds of boundaries; to which boundary's domain is this gift given?
If the person replies:
"If you do not know," [the donor] says, "I give it to the community of monks within the boundary. It may be received by as many or as few monks as reside within that boundary.
If there are separate residences with shared provisions (*sādhārana-lābha*), it is obtained according to those residences, and the items should be divided among them equally.
Regarding the distribution of alms to the Sangha: if someone says, "I shall give alms to the Sangha," the bell is struck to assemble the community, and those who arrive in time receive them.
If a donor carries a single garment and intends to give it to the Sangha but offers it to a single bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, having accepted it, says, "I ought to accept this," [it is valid].
"This is an improper reception.
What is a proper reception?

Having received [the robes], one should strike the *kṣaṇḍika* to assemble the Saṃgha. Once the Saṃgha has assembled, one should mark out divisions with yellow material so that they are not broken, and show them to the Elder."
"This portion is for the Elder; will you accept it?
The Elder replied, "I do not accept this portion;
I give it as an offering to the Venerable One."

In this manner, a second and a third time, the elders all said, "I do not accept alms from you, Venerable One," and so it was even for the junior monks; yet this bhikṣu was permitted to receive them, which is called receiving properly.

"If there is only one bhikṣu residing at a monastery and a donor brings a robe to offer to that single bhikṣu, this bhikṣu should strike the *khaṇḍika* to assemble the Saṃgha; if other bhikṣus come, they shall share it together. If no other bhikṣus come, he may accept it alone by means of a mental resolve and verbal declaration."
If a donor makes a gift to the Sangha, a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes (pāṃsukūlika) must not accept it.

If a person enters a monastery and makes a gift to the Sangha, the gong is struck to assemble the community; even if visiting bhikṣus from outside come in with their arms linked together for as far as a hundred yojanas, the one who first enters the boundary and the very last one shall both receive a share.
Why is this? Because they are connected and uninterrupted, they are thus entitled to a share.

If a person makes a donation to both divisions of the Saṃgha, it should be divided equally according to the number of people present; even if there are one hundred bhikṣuṇīs and one bhikṣu, they should still divide it equally; likewise, if there are one hundred bhikṣus and one bhikṣuṇī, she too should receive half.
If a person offers to the Sangha an alms-bowl bag, leather sandals, a water-strainer, a needle, a knife, a staff, or a fan, a bhikṣu who accepts discarded rags (pāṃsukūla) may accept them.
If a donor carries an object to give to a single individual and then says, "I give this to the Sangha," one should take a portion according to the order of the Sangha and must not take it separately.
"If a person makes an offering to the Buddha and to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, how is it divided?
It is broken into two portions: one portion is given to the Buddha, and the other portion is shared equally among the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
If someone makes offerings to many bhikṣus, to a single Dharma teacher, and to the Buddha, how should they be divided?
They are to be divided equally among the Buddha, the one bhikṣu, and the many bhikṣus.
If a person offers leftover food to the Buddha and the Sangha, placing the bowl before the Buddha and proceeding in order, who is to receive the Buddha’s portion?
If there is a bhikṣu attending upon the Buddha, he shall receive it; if there is no bhikṣu attending upon the Buddha, a layperson (upāsaka) attending upon the Buddha may also receive it.
If a donor makes an offering to the Saṃgha after the retreat has concluded, those who entered the retreat late do not receive it, nor do those who have broken their retreat.

If a donor says during the winter season that they are giving to the Saṃgha after the retreat has concluded, the monks of both the earlier and later retreats all receive it, with the sole exception of those who have broken their retreat, who do not receive it.
If someone says, "I give this to such-and-such a temple, such-and-such a room," it is obtained according to the donor's words.
If someone says, "I give this to the monks in retreat," then those who have entered the retreat early or late, as well as those who have broken their retreat, all receive it.

If a donor makes an offering to those who are in the latter half of the retreat during the month of Kārttika, the recipients of the latter retreat shall receive it, while those of the former retreat shall not.
If someone makes an offering to the Saṃgha during the retreat at the time of the spring equinox, one should ask:
"Is this an offering for the Saṃgha who have completed the retreat, or for the Saṃgha who will enter the retreat in the future?"
He replied,
"It is for the monks who will enter the rains retreat in the future.
The monks who will enter the rains retreat in the future received it.
The bhikṣu says to the donor:
"In the future, there may be the danger of thieves, and I will not be able to guard it.
The donor then instructs that it be divided; the portion is then distributed according to the share of the donor.
If a donor says,
"Eat my food and I shall give you clothing," one who does not eat it must not accept [the clothing].
My act of giving medicine is likewise.
I point out the donor, and according to where I point, one obtains the robe.
The Khandhaka is concluded.
"In the Bhaiṣajyavastu:
'Kubjottarā’s rice' refers to millet porridge;
'śūpa' refers to green bean soup."
*Kilā* refers to bamboo shoots.
*Nāṇu* refers to a foreign medicine; there is no [Sanskrit] equivalent.
*Khajjaka* refers to all fruits; these are called *khajjaka*.
Harītakī is about the size of a jujube; its taste is sour and bitter, and when consumed, it promotes the ease of excretion.
Vibhītaka is shaped like a peach; its taste is sweet, and when consumed, it can cure *śvāsa* (asthma/cough).
*Āmalaka* refers to the *yūganzi* (emblic myrobalan); it is found in the territory of Guangzhou, and its shape is about the size of a *ruizi* (jujube).
*Citrā* is the name of a foreign medicinal herb.
*Kaṣā* is the name of a foreign medicine.
*Bharibha* is mustard seed.
*Ghuṇṭuka* is a foreign medicine that can treat poisons; it does not exist in the land of Han.
*Tabaja* refers to medicinal incense.
*Kīrajana-kī* refers to red stone (cinnabar).
Eye medicine refers to *tabaja*.
The *dhoṣaja* is born on land; the *jīlaja* is born in water.
As for the *nāga*, it has a long body and no feet.
The flesh of lions, elephants, horses, dragons, and dogs must not be eaten, nor may their hides or hair be used.
Whenever one obtains any kind of meat, one should inquire [as to its source]; if one obtains it without inquiring, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The "shisou-mora" (失守摩羅) is the crocodile; it exists within the territory of Guangzhou.
"Black stone honey" (黑石蜜) is cane sugar that is as hard and solid as stone; hence it is called "stone honey."
*Gani* means honey. *Upadhāpani*:
*pani* means thin cane sugar. "How is a room on the edge [of the monastery] designated as a pure dwelling (*śuddhāvāsa*)?"
When first erecting a pillar, one should first dig a pit and place the pillar near it; the bhikṣus should surround it, supporting the pillar while reciting:
"For the sake of the Saṃgha, this is being made into a pure hall."
When he has spoken thus three times, the speaking is finished and the pillar is erected.
The same applies to the second, third, and fourth pillars; even if one speaks for only a single pillar, the "pure house" (śuddhāvasa) is established.
If it is a completed house, how is it to be purified?
One should summon the owner and say to him:
"This house has not yet been purified; you must perform the purification for the community of monks."
If a donor says,
"I give this pure dwelling to the Sangha; you may use it as you please," it immediately becomes a pure dwelling.
If a house has already been built but there is no owner, how should it be purified?
If there are elders in the village, one should summon them and say: "This house has not yet been purified; we request that you serve as the master of purification."
If the donor does not understand how to explain this, the bhikṣu should instruct him to say:
"This is a pure dwelling, offered to the Saṃgha; please accept and use it as you wish."
"Immediately, one obtains a purified dwelling (kappiya-kuṭi) for use as one pleases; having placed food and drink therein, there is no offense of 'storing overnight' or 'cooking indoors.
As for the Jambū fruit, its shape is like that of a watermelon, purple in color, and sour-sweet."
As for *śālu*, this refers to the root of the *utpala* (blue lotus) and *kumuda* (white water lily) flowers;
having pounded them to extract the juice and clarified it until it is pure, this is called *śālu* juice.
The *pālusa* fruit resembles the *āmra* fruit.
Of all wooden fruits, they may be made into non-time juice (*akālika-pāna*), with the sole exception of the seven types of grain, which are not permitted.
Of all leaves, they may be consumed as non-time food, with the sole exception of the *kanda* (taro/radish), which is not permitted.
All flowers may be consumed at improper times, with the sole exception of the juice of the *mātuluṅga* flower.
Among all fruits, only these six types may not be consumed at improper times: the fruit of the *rāta* tree, the coconut, the *pālaka* seed, the sweet melon, the winter melon, and the sweet gourd.
None of the various beans may be consumed at improper times.
Regarding water vessels, those made of wood, clay, or iron are permitted; no others may be used.
If one possesses seeds on land belonging to the Saṃgha, one should give half to the Saṃgha.
If one possesses land that belongs to the Saṃgha by right of seed-lineage, one should give half to the Saṃgha.
This concludes the Bhaiṣajyavastu (Chapter on Medicines).
*Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Seventeen.
*Samantapāsādikā Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 18, translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghabhadra of the Foreign Lands during the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
“The Khandhaka on the Kaṭhina Robe. Question: “How many people are permitted to receive the kaṭhina robe?”

"Down to a group of five persons, those who have entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) rains retreat may receive the *kāṭhina* robe; those who have broken the rains retreat or those who have entered the *paścādvārṣika* (later) rains retreat may not, nor may they do so if they reside in a different location."

If a residence has fewer than five monks, one may invite monks from another monastery to complete the quorum for the acceptance [of the *kaṭhina* robe]; once the quorum is met, visiting monks are not permitted to receive it.

If there are four monks in a residence and one *śrāmaṇera* whose *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) is about to end, one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon that *śrāmaṇera* so as to complete the number of five required to accept the *kaṭhina* robe; the newly ordained person likewise completes the requirement for the acceptance. The same applies when one monk confers the ordination upon four *śrāmaṇeras*.

If there are five or more bhikṣus residing in a monastery who do not understand how to accept the kaṭhina robe, they may invite a bhikṣu learned in the Dharma from another location to perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for accepting the kaṭhina. This ritual may be performed; however, those [residing monks] who do not themselves accept it shall not receive a share of the robe.
The Dharma Master asked,
"Who is permitted to bestow the kaṭhina robe upon the Saṃgha?
He replied:
"The robes of the seven classes of followers and the robes of devas may be accepted and made into *kaṭhina* robes.
If someone who does not understand how to make a *kaṭhina* robe comes to ask, the bhikṣu should instruct them."
Whether it be a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsaka*, one may accept each individual robe as a *kaṭhina* robe.
When the dawn light appears on the sixteenth day, one should take the *kaṭhina* cloth, cut it, and bring it to the community of monks. The bhikṣus should speak to the owner of the cloth, saying:
"We require needles, thread, and dye, as well as the number of bhikṣus who will make the robes."
Having heard this, the donor should provide food and drink as an offering to the monk who makes the robe.
Regarding the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha, one should know the ritual procedure for accepting the robe.

If the robe has already been cut, one should first wash it; then, together with many bhikṣus, one should cut, pin, and sew it, dyeing it on that very day and performing the *pratyavekṣaṇā* (inspection) before accepting it.
If many people offer *kaṭhina* robes, one robe should be accepted; the remainder should be divided and accepted through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). [The question arises:
To whom shall the Sangha entrust the holding of the *kaṭhina* robe?
One should give [a robe] to one whose robe is ruined.
If there are many monks with ruined robes, it should be given to the eldest among those with ruined robes.
If there is no elder, it should be given to the one with the greatest number of *kappas*.
"One must not [give it] to those who are stingy or greedy. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The *karmavācanā* procedure for the *kaṭhina* robe should be maintained in this manner.

As explained in the Vinaya: if the robe has not yet been completed, one should invite all the bhikṣus to complete it together; one must not create obstacles by speaking of the Dharma or the Path, except in the case of those who are ill.
The Dharma Master said:
"Why are you so earnest regarding the kaṭhina robe?
It is because it is praised by all the Buddhas."
In the past, there was a Buddha named Aśoka-padma (No Lotus), who had a śrāvaka disciple named Sujāta.
While he was making a kaṭhina robe that remained unfinished, the Buddha Aśoka-padma, surrounded by sixteen thousand bhikṣus, together made a kaṭhina robe.
Once it has been completed, the monk who holds the robe shall relinquish his own *saṃghāṭī* that he has been wearing, saying:
"I now hold this *kaṭhina* robe.

Having said this three times, and having so spoken, he shall immediately place it upon his body, bare his right shoulder, go before the senior monk (*sthavira*), and with palms joined toward the Saṃgha, say:
"Venerable Sirs!
I maintain the *saṃghāṭī* robe as a *kaṭhina* robe through the Dharma; may the Saṃgha rejoice in this.
Thereupon, the Elder rises from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Saṃgha, and spoke thus:
"Elder! Since you uphold the kaṭhina robe through the Dharma, I rejoice.
This was said down to the lowest-ranking monk in the same manner.

It is not that the Saṃgha receives and maintains the kaṭhina robe, nor is it that the assembly receives and maintains the kaṭhina robe; rather, one person holds the kaṭhina robe, while the Saṃgha and the assembly express their approval, whereupon the holding of the kaṭhina robe is established.
If a person takes his three robes and offers them to the community of monks to be used as a *kaṭhina* robe, saying:
"Whoever maintains this *kaṭhina* robe shall have all three robes belong to him."

"According to the donor's words, [the robes] shall all be given to the person who accepted them; the rest of the Saṃgha may not receive them. Once the kaṭhina has been spread, the gifts obtained by the Saṃgha are encompassed.

Those who have spread the kaṭhina receive a share of light items, while heavy items belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions. If there are multiple residences within the same poṣadha boundary, one must not separately spread the kaṭhina; rather, they should harmonize and assemble in one place to perform the rite of spreading a single kaṭhina."
One must not sew it; rather, one should stitch it back together.
Regarding "possessing all one's robes": this refers to having them before they have been made up and taken outside the boundary.
"Outside the boundary" means another monastery.
The Dharma Master said:
"Having accepted the kaṭhina robe, why did he go outside the boundary?
It was for the sake of dwelling in peace and comfort."

Regarding "forming the intention not to return": once a bhikṣu has gone outside the boundary, if he sees that this dwelling place has fine lodgings or he has acquaintances there, and forms the intention not to return, he first loses his dwelling place and subsequently loses the kaṭhina robe.
The remaining phrases have already been explained in the Vinaya.
"I neither make the robe nor do I return it"—once this thought has been formed, both the dwelling place and the *kaṭhina* robe are lost.
Regarding "losing the robe being made while making it": one first loses the dwelling place, and subsequently loses the *kaṭhina* robe.
Regarding "hearing that it has been lost": one first loses the *kaṭhina* robe, and subsequently loses the dwelling place.
Regarding "one who has severed hope": first, one loses their dwelling place; subsequently, all further hopes for attainment are severed.

As for the phrase "that which is hoped for is obtained without being hoped for," the wording here is inconsistent throughout, presenting many phrases that lack profound meaning; this is explained in detail in the Vinaya.
The Kāṭhina-cīvara-khandhaka is concluded.

"If a person undergoing parivāsa (probation) is invited by someone, or if they grant ordination to another, they may suspend their probationary duties; having finished those matters, they shall return and continue the practice."
When performing the rite of relinquishing, one should speak thus:
"I now relinquish the *parivāsa*.
This is to be said three times.
If one is undergoing the parivāsa or mānatva penances, and while performing the prescribed rites there are no monks at all present, one should simply form this thought:
"When a monk arrives, I shall inform him."
If for six days there are no bhikṣus available to whom one may report, one is likewise released from the offense.

If there are many bhikṣus in the monastery such that it is difficult to approach them for a report, one may relinquish the practice during the day; before the dawn signs appear, one should go beyond the boundary—two throws of a stone’s distance—with four or five bhikṣus, return to receive the practice, and report to the Saṃgha:
“I am practicing *mānatva*.”
‘Several days have passed; several days remain.
If there is a bhikṣu within the boundary, one should go to his place and inform him; if one does not inform him, the night is lost.”

If a bhikṣu has completed the procedure for receiving and undertaking the *cārikā-dharma* (the practice of wandering), and then returns, he should leave one person behind to wait until the appearance of dawn to relinquish the *cārikā-dharma*. Together they may then return to the monastery according to the previous rules; once the six nights have been fulfilled, he is released from the offense.
The method for the expiation of offenses has already been explained in the Vinaya-mūla; therefore, it is not set forth here.
At that time, there was a certain residence in Kauśāmbī where two bhikṣus lived: one was a master of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), and the other was a master of the Sūtras (sūtradhara).
At that time, after the Sūtra Master had entered the latrine and finished using the washing basin, he did not drain the water but left it overturned.
When the Vinaya Master entered the latrine and saw that the water had not been drained from the washing basin, he asked the Sūtra Master:
"Who entered the latrine and failed to drain the water, leaving the basin overturned?"
The Sūtra Master replied, "It is I.
The Vinaya Master said:
"Do you recognize the characteristics of your offense?
The Sūtra Master replied,
"I truly do not recognize the characteristics of my offense."
The Vinaya master said,
"You have committed a duṣkṛta offense.
The Sūtra master said:
"If I have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense, I ought to confess it.
The Vinaya Master asked:
"Was this done intentionally by you, or not?"
The Sūtra Master said,
"It was not done intentionally.
The Vinaya Master said:
"If one does not act intentionally, there is no offense.
When the Sūtra-master heard the Vinaya-master say there was no offense, the Vinaya-master returned to his room and said to his disciples:
"The Sūtra-master does not know what constitutes an offense, nor does he know what is non-offensive."
Having heard his teacher’s words, the disciple said to the disciple of the Sūtra-master:
"Your teacher does not know what constitutes an offense and what does not.
When the disciple had spoken these words, he reported the matter to his own teacher. Upon hearing his disciple’s report, the Sūtra-master said to that disciple:
"This Vinaya master previously said, 'I am without fault,' but now he says, 'I have committed a fault'; the Vinaya master has spoken falsely.
Having heard these words from their teacher, the disciples of the Sūtra master said to the disciples of the Vinaya master:
"Your teacher has committed the offense of false speech."
Having heard these words, the disciple of the Vinaya Master reported them to his teacher; thus, through such successive transmission, a great dispute arose.
Later, the Vinaya Master found an opportunity against the Sūtra Master, assembled the community, and brought forth the Sūtra Master’s offense, performing the formal act of *karma* for censuring him.
Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya-mūla: "One should raise a charge against another only when in harmony.
A question was asked:
"Why did the Buddha rise from his seat and, by means of his supernormal powers, go to Śrāvastī without speaking to the bhikṣus?"
He replied:
"If the Buddha were to adjudicate among the assembly, those who possessed the truth would rejoice, while those who did not possess the truth would say:
'The Buddha has taken the side of that faction.'"

"He slanders the Buddha, saying that the Buddha follows love and hatred; because he slanders the Buddha, upon death he shall enter hell. Therefore, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed, refusing to adjudicate for him."
The Kauśāmbī-khaṇḍaka is finished.
The Campā-khaṇḍaka is not explained.
Disputes concerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇavivāda*) are settled by two *vinayas*: the *pratyakṣavinaya* (the presence of the accused) and the *yadbhūyasikīya-vinaya* (the majority decision).

As for the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on memory), it is for a monk whose craving is exhausted, down to one who has attained the stage of *anāgāmin*; it is not for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
*Prātimokṣa-viniścaya* (or *Bahudharmika-vinaya*) is so named because, in various places, it involves seeking out many monks who know the Dharma to adjudicate matters;
thus it is called *bahudharmika-vinaya*. *Mātṛkā* refers to the two sets of *prātimokṣa*.
If, when distributing the voting tickets (*śalākā*), those distributed according to what is not the Dharma are numerous, they should be collected and it should be announced:
"Tomorrow we shall distribute the voting tickets again.
During this interval, one should seek out companions who act in accordance with the Dharma.
If the Elder grasps an illegal voting tally (*śalākā*), the distributor of tallies should whisper to him, saying:
"The Elder is advanced in years; why do you grasp an illegal tally?"
"One should take up the voting tally in accordance with the Dharma.
This concludes the Seven Methods for Settling Disputes.
[Question: "In the Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka, why did the Buddha not permit women to go forth?"

“Out of reverence for the Dharma, if women were permitted to go forth and receive ordination, the True Dharma would have remained only for five hundred years; however, because the Buddha established the Eight Rules of Respect for the Bhikṣuṇīs, the True Dharma has been restored to last for a thousand years.”
The Dharma Master asked,
"Will the Buddha-dharma be completely extinguished after a thousand years?
He replied:

"They will not all perish; for one thousand years they shall attain the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā); for another thousand years they shall become Arhats who have exhausted their cravings but lack the three types of supernormal knowledge; for another thousand years they shall become Anāgāmins; for another thousand years they shall become Sakṛdāgāmins; for another thousand years they shall become Srotāpannas practicing the Dharma; and they shall further obtain five thousand years [of existence]."

For five thousand years they will attain the Way; for the subsequent five thousand years they will study but not attain the Way; after ten thousand years, the scriptures and written words will be completely extinguished, and there will remain only those who have shaved their heads and wear the dharma-robes of the *kāṣāya*.
The Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka is concluded.
"Valuable items shall not be divided. The fields, gardens, ponds, and wells belonging to the Saṃgha may not be sold for other goods, except in exchange."
The beds, mats, utensils, and implements belonging to the Sangha must not be divided nor sold, except for exchange.

Eye-salve tubes, ear-pickers, needles and thread, small knives, door-hooks and keys, *khakkhara* staffs, small wooden staves, and iron implements may be divided; other tools for making things may not be divided, with the sole exception of axes for cutting *yānuka* twigs.
With the exception of knives and leather sandals, umbrellas and their accessories may be divided.
If someone donates bamboo, grass, or earth, these may not be divided.
If someone donates medicine, it may be divided, but the boxes and baskets may not be divided.
"If a person donates utensils used within a monastery cell, none of them may be divided; this excludes only oil containers. The *Dharmakhandaka* is concluded.

The Venerable Śāriputra asked Upāli concerning the Chapter on Defilements in the Vinaya. The Venerable Śāriputra asked Upāli: [The Venerable Śāriputra asked Upāli: "The Venerable Śāriputra asked Upāli regarding the Chapter on Defilements in the Vinaya. [Śāriputra asked Upāli: "The Venerable Śāriputra asked Upāli:"
"How many offenses are incurred by means of the body?
How many offenses are incurred by means of the mouth?
How many offenses are incurred by concealing [an offense]?"
“How many offenses are there for physical contact?
Upāli replied to Śāriputra in verse:
“Six offenses are incurred by the body, And six more by the karma of speech; Three offenses are incurred by concealment, And five offenses are incurred by physical contact.”
The second question:
"How many offenses occur when the light of dawn appears?
And how many occur during the three proclamations?"
Regarding these eight matters, how many are there in the entire collection?
He replied:
"The appearance of the light, the three offenses, the three proclamations, and the two kinds—regarding these eight matters, there is one in the entire collection."
The third question:
"Regarding the Tathāgata’s analysis of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many characteristics does the Vinaya have?
How many are the grave offenses of the Vinaya?"
Furthermore, how many types of coarse concealment (*sthūlātyaya*) are there? He replied:
“As the Tathāgata has explained in detail, the Vinaya has two characteristics; the gravity of the Vinaya has two aspects, and coarse concealment likewise has two.”
The fourth question:
"How many offenses are there between villages?
And how many more when crossing a river?"
"How many *sthūlātyaya* offenses are there for eating meat?
How many *duṣkṛta* offenses are there for eating meat? He replied:
“There are four [cases] regarding villages, and likewise four regarding crossing rivers.
One case of meat constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; nine cases of meat constitute *duṣkṛta*.”
The fifth question:
"How many offenses are there for speaking at night?
And how many are there during the day?"
"How many offenses does the giver incur?
How many offenses does the recipient incur?
He replied:
“There are two offenses for speaking at night, and likewise two during the day; one incurs three offenses by giving alms, and four offenses by receiving them.”
The sixth question:
"How many offenses are to be confessed before another person?
How many offenses require a formal ritual (karmavācanā)? And how many, once committed, cannot be remedied—these the Tathāgata has distinguished and established?"
He replied:
"Five offenses may be confessed; the sixth requires a formal ritual (karmavācanā). One offense cannot be confessed; this was distinguished and established by the Tathāgata."
The seventh question:
"How many are the heavy rules of the Vinaya?
The Buddha spoke of bodily and verbal karma; how many grains and flavors are there at improper times?"
"How many *jñapti-caturtha-karmas* are there? He replied:
"The Vinaya has two bases; body and speech are likewise so. Regarding untimely food and the single flavor, there is one *jñapti-caturtha-karman*."
The eighth question:
"How many *pārājika* offenses are there?
How many share the same grounds for communal reconciliation?"
Furthermore, how many instances of *nakṣatrarātri* (loss of the night) are there?
And how many finger-breadths are there in the measurement for binding [the robe]? He replied:
"There are two types of *pārājika*, two regarding the assembly on the ground, two regarding the loss of the night, and two regarding the binding of two fingers."
The ninth question:
"How many kinds of striking the body are there?
How many kinds of schisms in the Saṃgha are there?"
“How many are there for committing the first offense?
And how many are there for making the formal announcement (*jñapti*)? He replied:
"There are two ways of striking the body; due to these two, the Saṃgha is split. There are two initial offenses committed; there are also two types of formal announcements (jñapti)."
The tenth question:
"How many offenses are there for killing?
How many kinds are there of harsh speech?"
"How many kinds of verbal abuse are there?
How many kinds of acting as a matchmaker are there? He replied:
"Killing living beings has three offenses; harsh speech has three offenses; abusive language likewise has three; and acting as a matchmaker has three offenses."
The eleventh question:
"How many people receive full ordination?
How many offenses are there in performing it collectively?"
"How many types of banishment by extinction are there?
And how many types of formal pronouncements are there? He replied:

"Three persons may not receive [the precepts]; there are three ways of gathering [the assembly]; there are also three ways of expulsion; and for the formal act of a single utterance, there are also two."
The twelfth question:
"How many offenses are there for the precept against stealing?
And how many are there for the precept against sexual misconduct?"
"How many right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa) are there?
How many are there due to discarding?
He replied:
“The precept against stealing has three offenses; the precept against sexual misconduct has four offenses; right abandonment likewise has three; and there are three due to discarding.”
The thirteenth question:
"In teaching the bhikṣuṇī precepts, how many pāyattika and duṣkṛta offenses are there?
Among them, how many are new, and how many kinds of robes are there?"
The answer is:
